title: Circuit and electronics foundations for power electronics
text:
Course organisation and assessment
Audience: electrical engineering students refreshing earlier circuit courses.
Teaching time: two sessions of 90 minutes.
Purpose: connect circuit laws, waveforms and system models to the design of real power converters.
Use this lesson in two ways. Follow the teaching route for a refresher on circuit foundations. Later, return with a symptom and use chapter 16 to find a worked example.
Most numerical examples are teaching scenarios. Device data and published measurements are identified where used. Voltages and currents follow the passive sign convention unless stated otherwise.
The aim is to learn how an engineer approaches an unfamiliar circuit. Start with what you can observe. Make a prediction, choose a model and check the result. The equation should help you make a decision. Explain the benefit and cost of your choice. When another route is credible, say what would make you choose it.
The following arrangements were announced in the introductory lesson on 16 October 2026. They apply to the course as a whole, separately from the technical recap and its suggested teaching route below.

Project and examination: choose a power-electronics kit from the course list, preferably a different kit for each student. Analyse its operation using the project checklist, calculations and simulation. Bring the project to the examination and explain its strengths, limitations and possible improvements, including what happens when a component value changes. The exercise mirrors an engineering assignment: understand an existing design well enough to evaluate and improve it. Project material was announced as available on the lecturer’s GitHub; use the course-provided repository and checklist.
Mandatory exercises: assigned exercises contribute to the evaluation and must be submitted by the next lesson. Final numerical results will be supplied for comparison; these are not complete worked derivations. Regular work throughout the course is part of the assessment. No numerical weighting between exercises and the project examination was specified in the recording.
Books, AI and other tools: these may be used for the project and exercises. Students must understand the submitted reasoning and be able to explain and defend their calculations, models and design decisions themselves.
Interactive lessons: interrupt when an explanation is unclear, question assumptions and point out errors. The aim is to practise engineering judgement and problem solving, with regular breaks during the teaching afternoon.
Proposed company visit: a visit near the end of the course in January was discussed, potentially to Regatron in Arbon to see power supplies and EMC facilities. The destination and arrangements were tentative, not a confirmed booking.

title: Circuit and electronics foundations for power electronics
section: Engineering approach: estimate, model, then verify
text:
Engineering approach: estimate, model, then verify
Before opening a simulator, sketch the current path. Mark the voltage references and stored energy. Estimate the expected voltage, current or time scale. Check the units.
Choose the simplest model that can answer your question. Compare its result with your estimate. If they disagree, inspect the assumptions before adding more detail. Add a parasitic or nonlinearity when it could change the decision.
A solver can print six digits without knowing the actual capacitance under bias or the winding temperature. More digits do not make uncertain inputs accurate. Use component data, vary uncertain values and compare with measurements where available.
The roughly 30% uncertainty discussed in the lesson was an example, not a general accuracy limit. Ask what the model can establish. A simple model may explain the failure even when it cannot reproduce every switching edge.

title: 1. Networks: what the source actually supplies
text:
1.1 Voltage, current, power and reference directions
Voltage is the potential difference between two nodes. Current is the rate of charge transfer.
Ground is a reference. A circuit-ground symbol defines a reference potential. That reference is not necessarily protective earth. The symbol does not guarantee an ideal conductor or galvanic isolation.
Power depends on the reference directions. Use the passive sign convention: current enters the terminal marked positive. With these references, positive instantaneous power means that the element absorbs energy.
p(t)=v(t)i(t),\qquad W=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}p(t)\,dt.
Here, W is the energy transferred between t_1 and t_2.
Instantaneous power and dissipation are different quantities. The expression p(t)=v(t)i(t) describes power at one instant. Average power describes net energy transfer per unit time. It can represent useful power or dissipation. In periodic operation, this average is also called active or real power.
Root mean square (RMS) current describes the heating effect in an ideal resistor. For constant resistance, average dissipation is P_R=R I_{\mathrm{rms}}^2. At a constant-voltage port, average power uses average current: P=V I_{\mathrm{avg}}. Do not substitute RMS current into that constant-voltage formula.
Chapter 6 first defines reactive and apparent power for sinusoidal waveforms. It then explains why the simple power triangle is incomplete for distorted waveforms.
Kirchhoff’s laws. The current law expresses charge continuity at a node. The voltage law expresses voltage balance around a lumped circuit loop:
\sum_k i_k=0,\qquad \sum_k v_k=0.
Check the model’s limits. The lumped model neglects propagation delays and distributed field effects. Use it when these effects are negligible at the relevant time and length scales.
Fast switching edges may require a transmission-line model, even at a modest repetition frequency.
An approximation needs a question and an acceptable error. Chapter 17 develops this method with loading, RC, capacitor and propagation examples.

title: 1. Networks: what the source actually supplies
section: 1.2 From resistance to impedance
text:
1.2 From resistance to impedance
For an ideal linear resistor:
v(t)=Ri(t),\qquad p_R(t)=Ri^2(t)=\frac{v^2(t)}{R}.
Here, p_R(t) is instantaneous dissipation. Its time average is P_R=R I_{\mathrm{rms}}^2 when the resistance is constant.
For sinusoidal steady state at one frequency, use complex impedance. The phasors V and I below use RMS magnitudes and include phase:
V=ZI,\qquad Z=R+jX,\qquad R=\operatorname{Re}(Z),\qquad X=\operatorname{Im}(Z).
Here, j^2=-1. The real part R is the resistance in a series representation at that frequency. It need not equal the DC resistance.
An ideal inductor has Z_L=j\omega L. An ideal capacitor has Z_C=1/(j\omega C). Their impedances have zero real part. Real components also have loss terms.
Use the real part for average power. With current entering the positive-voltage terminal, complex power is \mathcal{S}=VI^*=P+jQ. Its magnitude is apparent power. Thus:
P=|I|^2\operatorname{Re}(Z)=|V|^2\operatorname{Re}(1/Z).
For Z=R+jX, the voltage form becomes P=|V|^2R/(R^2+X^2). It is generally not |V|^2/R. The current form uses the real part of impedance. The voltage form uses the real part of admittance, Y=1/Z.
Worked check. Let Z=3+j4\ \Omega and I=2\ \mathrm A RMS. Then V=6+j8\ \mathrm V, so |V|=10\ \mathrm V. Average absorbed power is 12 W. Reactive power is 16 var, and apparent power is 20 VA. Dividing 10^2 by 3 would incorrectly predict 33.33 W.
Active power can supply useful work or become heat. For a resistor, it is dissipation. Chapter 6 develops this distinction and the sinusoidal power triangle.
Combine impedances before taking magnitudes. Series impedances add. Parallel admittances add. Their phases affect the resulting voltage and current division.
The phasor relation applies to a linear port model in sinusoidal steady state. Use time-domain equations for startup and switching transients. For distorted periodic waveforms, evaluate the relevant frequency components separately.
Chapter 18 develops voltage and current dividers, loading, sensor bridges, calorimetric readout and the LLC tank model.
Start with the two-divider and buffer exercise. It compares the same unloaded voltage with different source resistances and losses. The solution has its own reading page.

title: 1. Networks: what the source actually supplies
section: 1.3 Thévenin, Norton and superposition
text:
1.3 Thévenin, Norton and superposition
A linear two-terminal network can be represented by a voltage source with series impedance or a current source with parallel impedance:



Thévenin voltage-source and Norton current-source equivalents connected to the same load, with consistent terminal polarity and delivered-current references.


V_{\mathrm{Th}}=V_{\mathrm{oc}},\qquad I_{\mathrm N}=\frac{V_{\mathrm{Th}}}{Z_{\mathrm{Th}}},\qquad Z_{\mathrm N}=Z_{\mathrm{Th}}.
Continue the divider example. The divider in Section 18.1 has a Norton equivalent of 12 mA in parallel with 500 Ω. The 1 kΩ load takes 12 mA × 500/(500 + 1000) = 4 mA. Its voltage is 4 V, as before. The equivalent changes the calculation, not the load result.
For a purely resistive network, the port impedance becomes a resistance, R_{\mathrm{Th}}. Use the following procedure in the circuit model. Setting a source to zero is a model operation.
Find the equivalent circuit.

Label the port terminals a and b.
Define the output voltage as V_a-V_b.
Disconnect the load.
Keep every source active.
Calculate the open-circuit voltage, V_{\mathrm{oc}}.
Set V_{\mathrm{Th}}=V_{\mathrm{oc}}.
Replace each ideal independent voltage source with a short circuit.
Replace each ideal independent current source with an open circuit.
Keep each dependent source and its control relation active.
Apply a test voltage V_t between a and b.
Calculate the test current I_t entering the network at a.
Calculate R_{\mathrm{Th}}=V_t/I_t.
Calculate the Norton current, I_{\mathrm N}=V_{\mathrm{Th}}/R_{\mathrm{Th}}.
Reconnect the load to the equivalent circuit.

The test source replaces the disconnected load. It does not replace any dependent source. Without dependent sources, series and parallel reduction may give the same resistance more quickly.
Use superposition for voltage and current.

Keep one independent source active.
Set the other independent sources to zero.
Keep all dependent sources active.
Calculate the required voltage or current contribution.
Repeat for each independent source.
Add the signed contributions.
Calculate power from the resulting total voltage and current.

Power is quadratic or bilinear. Adding the separate power results generally gives the wrong answer. MIT’s linear-circuit notes explain source suppression and the equivalent circuits.
Worked practice: two independent sources and one dependent source. This is an original teaching circuit. The ideal sources and constant resistances define its model.



A four-resistor network with a 12 V voltage source, a 1 mA current source, and a dependent current source controlled by the internal node voltage Vx. The output port is a–b.


All four resistors are 2 kΩ. The independent sources are V_s=12\ \mathrm V and I_s=1\ \mathrm{mA}. The dependent source supplies gV_x into node a, with g=0.25\ \mathrm{mS}. The voltage V_x uses node b as its reference. Attach a 4 kΩ load between a and b after finding the equivalent.
Before calculating, predict which sources remain in the resistance-test circuit. Decide whether the dependent source could change the port resistance.

Find V_{\mathrm{Th}} with the load disconnected.
Find R_{\mathrm{Th}} with a 1 V test source.
Find the Norton current.
Calculate the voltage, current and power of the 4 kΩ load.
Check the loaded voltage by direct node analysis.
Use superposition to check the loaded voltage.
Explain why the separate source powers do not add to the correct load power.

Worked check. This is a worked practice example, rather than a withheld assigned exercise.
With the load disconnected, Kirchhoff’s current law gives:
\frac{V_x-12}{2000}+\frac{V_x}{2000}+\frac{V_x-V_a}{2000}=0.
\frac{V_a-V_x}{2000}+\frac{V_a}{2000}=0.001+0.00025V_x.
Voltages are in volts and currents are in amperes. These equations give V_x=52/9\ \mathrm V and V_{\mathrm{Th}}=V_a=16/3\ \mathrm V.
For the resistance test, short V_s and open I_s. Keep the diamond source active.



The resistance-test network retains the controlled current source. The independent voltage source becomes a short, the independent current-source branch becomes an open, and a 1 V test source drives the output port.


The internal-node equation gives V_x=V_t/3. The test source supplies:
I_t=\frac{V_t-V_x}{2000}+\frac{V_t}{2000}-0.00025V_x=0.00075V_t.
At V_t=1\ \mathrm V, the test current is 0.75 mA. Thus R_{\mathrm{Th}}=4/3\ \mathrm{k\Omega} and I_{\mathrm N}=4\ \mathrm{mA}.



Check
Result




Open-circuit voltage
5.333 V


Equivalent resistance
1.333 kΩ


Norton short-circuit current
4.000 mA


Voltage across the 4 kΩ load
4.000 V


Load current

Direct node analysis gives the same 4 V load voltage. With superposition, the voltage-source contribution is 3 V. The independent-current-source contribution is 1 V. The dependent source remains active in both calculations.
The correct load power is 4^2/4000=4\ \mathrm{mW}. Adding the separate powers gives only (3^2+1^2)/4000=2.5\ \mathrm{mW}. The missing cross term explains the error.
Incorrectly removing the dependent source gives 1.200 kΩ in the resistance test. That result describes a different network.
Use the equivalent for repeated load calculations. Use direct node analysis to check the first result and preserve the internal source information.
Converter connection: a regulated supply still has an output impedance. In a local model, a load-current perturbation causes a voltage perturbation approximately equal to minus the supply impedance times that current perturbation.
Choose the convenient equivalent. Thévenin makes voltage drop easy to see. Norton makes branch-current division easy to see. Both describe the same linear port. Change representation when it simplifies the question, retaining dependent sources and the same load.

title: 1. Networks: what the source actually supplies
section: 1.4 Units, prefixes and reference levels
text:
1.4 Units, prefixes and reference levels
Keep physical units in calculations: Ω = V/A, F = A·s/V and H = V·s/A. For example, nH × A/ns gives volts directly. Remember m = 10⁻³, µ = 10⁻⁶, n = 10⁻⁹ and p = 10⁻¹². Confusing millimeters with meters changes a geometry estimate by a factor of one thousand.
Dimensional-analysis check. For the plate-capacitance estimate C=\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r A/d, permittivity has units F/m, relative permittivity is dimensionless, area has units m² and separation has units m. Thus (F/m) × m²/m = F. Reversing A/d would fail this check. Also check the physical trend: larger overlap increases capacitance, while greater separation reduces it. Section 3 applies this estimate to PCB conductors.
A decibel is a logarithmic ratio, not an independent physical quantity. An absolute level needs a reference: dBV refers to 1 V, dBµV to 1 µV, and dBm to 1 mW. For the same RMS voltage, the numerical dBµV level is 120 dB above its dBV level.
Converting dBm to voltage also requires the impedance. Section 12 explains amplitude versus power ratios; never add a dBm power level to a voltage without defining the conversion.
crumbs: 3  1. Networks: what the source actually supplies

title: 1. Networks: what the source actually supplies
section: 1.5 Static resistance versus incremental resistance
text:
1.5 Static resistance versus incremental resistance
Which resistance predicts a small change? A diode carrying 1 mA at 0.650 V has a static voltage/current ratio of 650 Ω. In the teaching model of Chapter 19, its local resistance is only 26 Ω. These values answer different questions.
The static ratio describes the operating point, Q=(V_Q,I_Q). Incremental resistance, also called differential resistance, describes the tangent at that point:
R_{\mathrm{static}}=\frac{V_Q}{I_Q},\qquad r_d=\left.\frac{dv}{di}\right|_Q,\qquad \delta v\approx r_d\delta i.
The complete local approximation retains the bias: v\approx V_Q+r_d(i-I_Q). A resistor connected directly across the full voltage generally cannot reproduce both the bias and the slope.
An ideal positive resistor has the same static and incremental resistance. Nonlinear components generally do not. The slope also depends on what stays fixed, including temperature and other terminal voltages.
A MOSFET needs output resistance and a gate-controlled current contribution. A solar panel needs an explicit current direction and fixed illumination. At higher frequencies, stored charge can require a complex small-signal impedance.
An approximately constant-power load gives another useful example. With input current I=P/V, its static ratio is positive, while r_d=-V_Q^2/P is negative. The load still absorbs power.
Chapter 19: operating points and small-signal models develops the diode, MOSFET, solar-panel and controlled-load examples on separate reading pages. It includes tangent plots, TikZ circuits, an exercise and a dedicated solution.
Section 12.5 applies the controlled-load model to input-filter interaction.

The transformer is a two-port element that couples two winding circuits. Its last-column expression is the input impedance with a specified secondary termination, rather than a standalone one-port impedance like R, L or C. Section 2.4 defines its voltage/current references and practical equivalent circuit.
Finite voltage cannot change ideal inductor current instantaneously. Finite current cannot change ideal capacitor voltage instantaneously. Opening an inductive current path therefore creates a voltage until another path conducts, a parasitic capacitance charges, or breakdown occurs. Connecting an ideal voltage source directly to a capacitor at a different voltage requires an impulse of current in the ideal model.
Waveform pairs to sketch. Because v_L=L\,di/dt, a constant voltage across an inductor produces a linear current ramp: 12 V across 10 µH for 2 µs raises the current by \Delta I=V\Delta t/L=2.4 A. A square voltage therefore gives a triangular current, which is the inductor-current ripple of every PWM converter.
Dually, a constant current into a capacitor ramps its voltage: 1 A into 10 µF for 10 µs gives \Delta V=I\Delta t/C=1 V, and a triangular current gives a parabolic voltage, the output-capacitor ripple of a buck. Read the pairs in both directions as well: a triangular inductor current implies a square inductor voltage, and a voltage step forced onto an ideal capacitor implies an impulse of current.
The volt-second and ampere-second products in these sketches are the quantities balanced in section 7.
Real inductors have winding resistance, core loss, saturation, leakage flux and interwinding capacitance. Real capacitors have ESR, ESL, leakage, voltage dependence and finite ripple-current capability. An apparent wire is part of a current loop with resistance and inductance.

c=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}},\qquad \varepsilon=\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r,\qquad \mu=\mu_0\mu_r.
The familiar 4\pi\times10^{-7} H/m is an excellent approximation to \mu_0, rather than an exact SI definition today. See NIST’s CODATA table. Vacuum wave impedance is not automatically the characteristic impedance of a PCB trace.
For a uniform linear medium, use D=\varepsilon E and B=\mu H. For a simple magnetic circuit:
\mathcal R\approx\frac{\ell_m}{\mu A_m},\qquad L\approx\frac{N^2}{\mathcal R},\qquad v=N\frac{d\Phi}{dt}.
These connect geometry and material properties to inductance, transformer volt-seconds and eventual saturation. Relative permeability in a ferromagnetic material is generally not a fixed constant over all operating conditions.
Reluctance: the magnetic circuit’s resistance. \mathcal R is the reluctance, in A/Wb (ampere-turns per weber). It plays the role of resistance in a magnetic circuit: the winding’s ampere-turns Ni drive flux \Phi through it, as voltage drives current through a resistor. Reluctances in series add, like resistors. Core data sheets give the inverse, the inductance factor A_L=1/\mathcal R in nH per turn², so that L=N^2A_L. Inductance grows with the square of the turns: double the turns, four times the inductance.
Predict. A ferrite core has a magnetic path length \ell_e = 50 mm, cross-section A_e = 50 mm² and \mu_r = 2000. We cut a 0.5 mm air gap into the path. Which part sets the inductance: 50 mm of ferrite or 0.5 mm of air?
\mathcal R_{\mathrm{core}}=\frac{\ell_e}{\mu_0\mu_rA_e}\approx3.98\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{A/Wb},\qquad \mathcal R_{\mathrm{gap}}=\frac{g}{\mu_0A_e}\approx7.96\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{A/Wb}.
The gap is 1 % of the path, yet it holds 95 % of the total reluctance. A_L falls from about 2510 nH to 120 nH, so 20 turns give 1.0 mH without the gap and 47.9 µH with it. The calculation ignores fringing, which makes the real gap look slightly larger in area.
Why accept 20 times less inductance? Suppose \mu_r halves with temperature or DC bias. The ungapped inductor loses 50 % of its inductance; the gapped one loses only 4.5 %. The gap also stores most of the energy and raises the current at which the core saturates. Its cost is more turns for the same inductance, hence more copper loss, and fringing flux that heats nearby winding layers. Choose an ungapped core when inductance per turn matters most and the DC current is small, as in a common-mode choke. Choose a gapped core when the inductor carries DC, as in a buck. Powder cores spread the same gap through the material.
Transformer winding voltage follows the same Faraday relation. Section 2.4 develops the ideal two-port element and adds magnetizing inductance, leakage and losses to form a practical model.

title: 2.4 Transformer as a basic two-port element
text:
Ideal model and dot convention
What it does: a transformer transfers electrical power between winding circuits through a common magnetic field. The ideal element changes voltage, current and impedance according to its turns ratio while conserving instantaneous power. Separate primary/secondary windings allow galvanic isolation; the physical insulation construction determines the actual isolation rating. Interwinding capacitance still provides a high-frequency coupling path.
Define n = N₁/N₂. Label both winding voltages from the dotted terminal to the undotted terminal, and both port currents entering their dotted terminals. Then:
n=\frac{N_1}{N_2},\qquad v_1=nv_2,\qquad i_1=-\frac{i_2}{n}.
p_1+p_2=v_1i_1+v_2i_2=0.
The minus sign follows from the two passive port references: when the primary absorbs power, the secondary delivers it. If instead the secondary current arrow points out of its dot toward the load, the delivered-current relation is i₁ = iout/n. Reversing a winding connection reverses the corresponding voltage polarity. Dots identify relative winding polarity, not protective earth or a common electrical node.
The ideal transformer has perfect coupling, no winding resistance, no leakage and no magnetizing-current requirement. It stores no energy by itself. A pair of perfectly coupled inductors with finite inductance still has a magnetizing energy state, so it is a different model.

section: Reflecting a load and a worked example
text:
Reflecting a load and a worked example
With a load connected across winding 2, define the load current as leaving the secondary dotted terminal. The primary sees:
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{V_1}{I_1}=n^2Z_L.
Resistance, reactance and complex impedance all reflect with n² when moved from secondary to primary. Moving an impedance from primary to secondary divides it by n². This scaling also applies to a local incremental impedance; it does not change the sign of a negative incremental resistance.

title: 2.4 Transformer as a basic two-port element
section: From the ideal element to a practical transformer
text:
From the ideal element to a practical transformer
The figure’s approximate model refers the load and winding losses to the primary, so no turns-ratio element remains in that drawing:

Magnetizing inductance Lm: requires current to establish flux, including at no load. It stores magnetic energy. For an idealized sinusoidal winding voltage, its RMS current magnitude is V/(ωLm).
Core-loss resistance Rcore: represents average core loss approximately around the selected waveform, frequency and flux swing. A fixed resistance is not a universal model of hysteresis and eddy-current losses.
Leakage inductance Lσ: represents flux that does not link both windings. It causes load-dependent voltage drops, switching spikes and resonances with capacitance.
Winding resistance: produces copper loss and load-dependent voltage drop. In a primary-referred approximation, Rcu ≈ R₁ + n²R₂; leakage terms can be referred in the same way when the chosen equivalent circuit permits their combination.
Winding and interwinding capacitance: becomes important at high frequency and across an isolation barrier; it is omitted from the simple low-frequency drawing.

For coupled-inductor descriptions, mutual inductance is M = k√(L₁L₂), with coupling coefficient between zero and one for a passive reciprocal pair. The detailed equivalent model and parameter reference side must be stated. Combining all series losses ahead of the magnetizing branch, as in the figure, is an approximation suitable when magnetizing current is small relative to referred load current.
crumbs: 8  2.4 Transformer as a basic two-port element

title: 2.4 Transformer as a basic two-port element
section: Volt-seconds, flux reset and the limit of the ideal model
text:
Volt-seconds, flux reset and the limit of the ideal model
For the induced winding voltage e₁ and effective core area Ae:
e_1=N_1A_e\frac{dB}{dt},\qquad \Delta B=\frac{1}{N_1A_e}\int e_1(t)\,dt.
For a rectangular pulse this becomes:
\Delta B=\frac{E_1t_{\mathrm{on}}}{N_1A_e}.
Example: 48 V across a 20-turn winding with 100 mm² effective core area for 5 µs changes flux density by 0.12 T. An equal negative volt-second interval brings B back to its starting value. This specifies a flux change, not its absolute peak: initial flux, DC bias and the material’s usable operating range still matter.
With significant copper drop, integrate the induced/core voltage rather than treating the terminal voltage as identical to it.
A repeated nonzero net induced volt-second area causes flux to walk from cycle to cycle. Sustained DC voltage applied to a real finite-core winding ramps flux and can drive saturation; the algebraic ideal-transformer ratios alone do not expose that failure. Periodic operation needs flux reset, provided by the topology and drive waveform.
Converter connection: a forward-type stage transfers energy to the secondary during the transfer interval and must also reset magnetizing flux. A flyback deliberately stores energy in magnetizing inductance, often largely in a core gap, and releases it in another interval. Treating the flyback magnetic component as only an ideal turns-ratio element misses its main energy-storage function. MIT’s magnetics notes provide the next reading step.
Which transformer model? Start with the ideal ratio for reflected load and power. It is easy to inspect but misses magnetizing current and parasitic drops. Use the practical model when those effects can change voltage stress, loss or flux margin.
crumbs: 8  2.4 Transformer as a basic two-port element

title: 2.5 Coupled inductors as a basic energy-storage element
text:
Self-inductance, mutual inductance and dots
What changes from two independent inductors: some magnetic flux produced by either winding links the other. A changing current in one winding therefore contributes to the voltage of the other. Coupling can occur through a shared magnetic core or through the surrounding field. A familiar two-winding symbol does not by itself tell us whether an ideal transformer or a finite-inductance energy-storage model is intended.
Use the same passive references as in section 2.4: voltages from dot to undotted terminal, and both currents entering their dots. For a linear reciprocal pair with fixed parameters:
\lambda_1=L_1i_1+Mi_2,\qquad \lambda_2=Mi_1+L_2i_2.
v_1=L_1\frac{di_1}{dt}+M\frac{di_2}{dt},\qquad v_2=M\frac{di_1}{dt}+L_2\frac{di_2}{dt}.
The flux linkages λ have units of weber-turn. Here M is nonnegative and winding polarity is encoded by the dots. Reversing one current reference reverses the corresponding mutual signs; do not change a sign merely because the two coils are drawn on opposite sides of a core. A rising current entering winding 1’s dot induces a positive voltage at winding 2’s dot under these references.
The coupling coefficient is:
M=k\sqrt{L_1L_2},\qquad 0\leq k\leq1.
k = 0 gives independent inductors. k near one gives tight coupling; k below one means imperfect flux linkage. For a passive linear pair, M² ≤ L₁L₂ ensures nonnegative stored magnetic energy. The k = 1 idealization makes the inductance matrix singular, so a model that needs its inverse must treat the associated constraint correctly.
crumbs: 9  2.5 Coupled inductors as a basic energy-storage element

title: 2.5 Coupled inductors as a basic energy-storage element
section: Stored energy and the distinction from an ideal transformer
text:
Stored energy and the distinction from an ideal transformer
W=\frac{1}{2}L_1i_1^2+Mi_1i_2+\frac{1}{2}L_2i_2^2,\qquad \frac{dW}{dt}=v_1i_1+v_2i_2.
The mutual term can add or subtract, depending on the signed currents. For an allowed passive inductance matrix, the total energy remains nonnegative. Unlike the ideal transformer element, the coupled pair stores finite energy. Even perfect coupling does not remove its magnetizing energy state. Real magnetic saturation, hysteresis and bias dependence also mean that a constant-L energy formula is not valid over every operating condition.
With imperfect coupling, the terminal voltage ratio is not generally fixed by a turns ratio. For example, with winding 2 open, i₂ = 0 and v₂/v₁ = M/L₁ for a changing primary current in this ideal lossless pair. Using √(L₁/L₂) as a turns ratio is only appropriate when leakage is negligible and the inductances correspond to the same common flux path.

title: 2.5 Coupled inductors as a basic energy-storage element
section: Open/short measurements and leakage
text:
Open/short measurements and leakage
With winding 2 open, the ideal input inductance is L₁. With winding 2 ideally shorted, v₂ = 0 requires a secondary current slope that opposes the primary contribution. The resulting input inductance is:
L_{1,\mathrm{short}}=L_1-\frac{M^2}{L_2}=L_1(1-k^2).
The example gives 36 µH, not the 45 µH of series opposition: these are different terminations. Open/short measurements give the estimate:
k=\sqrt{1-\frac{L_{1,\mathrm{short}}}{L_{1,\mathrm{open}}}}.
The 36 µH quantity is the short-circuit input inductance for this ideal pair. It is not automatically an individual winding leakage branch in every transformer equivalent circuit. Real measurements also depend on shorting-lead impedance, winding resistance, frequency, core bias and capacitance.
crumbs: 9  2.5 Coupled inductors as a basic energy-storage element

title: 2.5 Coupled inductors as a basic energy-storage element
section: Where it is used
text:
Where it is used

Flyback: magnetizing energy is stored in one interval and delivered through the other winding in another interval. Use an energy-storage magnetic model with flux reset.
SEPIC and Ćuk: coupling can change winding ripple and component requirements; derive the result from the winding voltages and dot references of the actual topology.
Coupled multiphase buck: winding orientation determines whether relevant phase-current components reinforce or cancel magnetic flux. Tight coupling alone does not guarantee lower ripple in every mode.
Common-mode choke: arrange the intended outgoing and return currents to oppose their core flux, while common-mode currents reinforce. For equal windings, the per-winding modal factors are L − M and L + M, respectively, under the chosen current references. A two-wire loop measurement can introduce an additional factor of two; state which current and voltage define the measured inductance.

Thermal current rating, combined winding ampere-turns, saturation, leakage energy and insulation all need consideration in a real component. Analog Devices’ coupled-inductor modelling article provides a SEPIC example; Coilcraft’s coupled-inductor guide discusses the physical component and coupling tradeoffs.
crumbs: 9  2.5 Coupled inductors as a basic energy-storage element

title: 2.6 Real transformer: voltage drop, losses and operating limits
text:
A circuit with separate winding impedances
Why the turns ratio is not enough: it relates the internal induced voltages. Winding drops separate those voltages from the terminals; excitation current also flows when the secondary is open. Start with section 2.4’s ideal element, then include the effects needed at the operating frequency.
For sinusoidal steady state, use RMS phasors and refer all secondary impedances to the primary. Define:
Z_1=R_1+j\omega L_{\sigma1},\qquad Z'_2=n^2(R_2+j\omega L_{\sigma2}),\qquad Z'_L=n^2Z_L.
Y_m=\frac{1}{R_{\mathrm{core}}}+\frac{1}{j\omega L_m}.
The primary winding impedance Z₁ precedes the excitation branch; the referred secondary impedance Z′₂ follows it. This T equivalent circuit retains the difference between primary current I₁ and referred delivered load current I′₂:
I_1=I_0+I'_2,\qquad I_0=E_1Y_m,\qquad I'_2=\frac{E_1}{Z'_2+Z'_L}.
E_1=\frac{V_1}{1+Z_1\left(Y_m+\frac{1}{Z'_2+Z'_L}\right)},\qquad V_2=\frac{E_1-I'_2Z'_2}{n}.
The physical delivered secondary current is I₂,out = nI′₂. In open circuit, I′₂ = 0 but I₁ = I₀ generally remains nonzero. The real part of excitation admittance accounts for core dissipation; its inductive part accounts for reversible magnetic energy storage. The internal induced voltages obey E₁ = nE₂, while loaded terminal voltages generally do not obey V₁ = nV₂.
This is often called the exact equivalent circuit in introductory transformer analysis: exact within the chosen linear lumped model. It still omits saturation, distributed capacitance, and frequency-dependent loss. Section 2.4’s combined-series circuit is a further approximation; retaining separate branches avoids assigning secondary copper loss to the no-load primary current.

title: 2.6 Real transformer: voltage drop, losses and operating limits
section: Flux, saturation and waveform dependence
text:
Flux, saturation and waveform dependence
For induced primary voltage e₁, the general relation remains:
B(t)=B(t_0)+\frac{1}{N_1A_e}\int_{t_0}^{t}e_1(\tau)\,d\tau.
For a sinusoidal flux centred around zero, and for a symmetric bipolar square induced voltage, respectively:
E_{1,\mathrm{rms}}\approx4.44fN_1A_eB_{\mathrm{pk}}\quad\mathrm{(sine)},\qquad E_{1,\mathrm{sq}}=4fN_1A_eB_{\mathrm{pk}}\quad\mathrm{(bipolar\ square)}.
The square-wave voltage is its constant magnitude in each half-period. Both expressions assume centred periodic flux; DC offset or incomplete reset requires tracking absolute B as well. The sine formula’s 4.44 factor must not be applied to arbitrary PWM. At unchanged induced voltage, reducing frequency increases flux swing.
Saturation reduces incremental magnetizing inductance and can cause a steep current rise. Switching near an unfavourable mains phase, together with remanent flux, can also cause inrush even when the final periodic operating point is acceptable.
Higher switching frequency allows fewer turns or a smaller core area for the same voltage and flux swing, but raises other constraints. Core loss depends on material, frequency, temperature and the actual B waveform. Skin and proximity effects make winding AC resistance frequency dependent; for a linear harmonic loss model, winding loss is a sum of Iₖ,rms²Rac(kf).
Section 2.7 develops this conductor-loss calculation. Insulation thickness, winding arrangement and cooling also matter. A constant Rcore and DC winding resistances cannot predict all of these effects. TI’s Power Transformer Design note discusses the loss and thermal tradeoffs.
crumbs: 10  2.6 Real transformer: voltage drop, losses and operating limits

title: 2.6 Real transformer: voltage drop, losses and operating limits
section: Switching edges: leakage energy and capacitive feedthrough
text:
Switching edges: leakage energy and capacitive feedthrough
At a switching transition, leakage inductance resists rapid current change. Its stored energy must transfer to another element or dissipate:
W_\sigma=\frac{1}{2}L_\sigma I^2,\qquad f_{\mathrm{ring}}\approx\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{L_\sigma C_{\mathrm{eq}}}}.
As a separate switching example, 2 µH carrying 3 A stores 9 µJ. If one such event per 100 kHz cycle is fully dissipated in a clamp, its average contribution is 0.90 W. If that energy instead charges an initially uncharged ideal 200 pF capacitor, the energy-only estimate gives 300 V and a natural frequency of 7.96 MHz.
These are model scales: initial capacitor voltage, rail connections, nonlinear device capacitance, damping and the clamp determine the actual switch peak. Do not simply add 300 V to a rail without deriving the circuit.
Interwinding capacitance provides a displacement-current path across galvanic isolation:
i_{\mathrm{CM}}\approx C_{\mathrm{ps}}\frac{dv_{\mathrm{barrier}}}{dt}.
For 20 pF subjected to 10 V/ns, the instantaneous current scale is 0.20 A. This is edge current, not continuous load current. Its return path determines common-mode EMI. Interleaving windings can reduce leakage while increasing interwinding capacitance; electrostatic shields can redirect capacitive current but need a defined connection.
Insulation and dielectric distance affect both capacitance and isolation construction, linking back to section 3.3. These capacitances are omitted from the 50 Hz T model above; add them when analysing fast switching edges.
crumbs: 10  2.6 Real transformer: voltage drop, losses and operating limits

title: 2.6 Real transformer: voltage drop, losses and operating limits
section: How the model parameters are estimated
text:
How the model parameters are estimated

Winding resistance measurement: estimates R₁ and R₂ at the measurement temperature; operating-temperature and AC loss can differ.
Open-circuit test: at the intended sinusoidal frequency and voltage, measure Voc, Ioc and Poc. When series drops and no-load copper loss are small, Rcore ≈ Voc²/Poc, Im ≈ √(Ioc² − (Poc/Voc)²), and Lm ≈ Voc/(ωIm).
Short-circuit test: with one winding shorted, apply a reduced voltage at the test frequency to obtain the selected test current. With excitation current negligible, Zeq ≈ Vsc/Isc, Req ≈ Psc/Isc² and Xeq ≈ √(Zeq² − Req²). These give the combined series parameters referred to the driven side; they do not uniquely split primary and secondary leakage.

The open/short estimates and their assumptions are described in Rose-Hulman’s notes, pages 12–13. A switching-frequency component also needs impedance, capacitance, loss and bias information relevant to its operating waveforms.
Classroom check: why can the loaded real transformer draw more primary current than the ideal example while delivering less power? Its primary current supplies the referred load, core loss and magnetizing excitation; winding losses also consume input active power. Use phasor addition for currents and an active-power balance for watts.
crumbs: 10  2.6 Real transformer: voltage drop, losses and operating limits

title: 2.7 Skin effect: why copper resistance depends on frequency
text:
Skin depth and useful copper numbers
Physical idea: a changing current produces a changing magnetic field inside the conductor. The induced electric field redistributes current toward the surface. At low frequency, current density in a uniform round copper wire is approximately uniform; at high frequency, much of the interior carries little AC current.
The same total RMS current then produces more resistive heating. This is electromagnetic diffusion, rather than an increase in copper’s intrinsic resistivity caused by frequency alone.
For sinusoidal excitation of a good conductor with resistivity ρ and permeability μ:
\delta=\sqrt{\frac{2\rho}{\omega\mu}}=\sqrt{\frac{\rho}{\pi f\mu}},\qquad \omega=2\pi f.
Near a flat conductor surface, with x measured inward and an exp(jωt) phasor convention:
J(x)=J(0)e^{-(1+j)x/\delta},\qquad |J(x)|=|J(0)|e^{-x/\delta}.
At one skin depth, current-density amplitude is 1/e ≈ 37% of its surface value; it is not abruptly zero beyond δ. This exponential profile assumes a locally flat, sufficiently thick conductor. A round wire whose radius is comparable to δ needs the cylindrical solution used below.
For the teaching calculations, take copper at approximately 20 °C with ρ = 1.724 × 10⁻⁸ Ωm and μ ≈ μ₀. Then:
\delta_{\mathrm{Cu}}\approx\frac{66.1}{\sqrt{f/\mathrm{Hz}}}\ \mathrm{mm}.
For this wire, δ equals its radius at about 17.5 kHz; this is a scale, not a sharp onset frequency. Larger busbars can exhibit significant skin effect even at mains frequency. Temperature changes resistivity, resistance and skin depth, so state the temperature when comparing values. TI’s winding-loss note, pages 1–3, introduces skin depth and the redistribution mechanism.

title: 2.7 Skin effect: why copper resistance depends on frequency
section: PWM currents: apply the resistance to each frequency component
text:
PWM currents: apply the resistance to each frequency component
Skin depth is defined for a frequency component. For a periodic nonsinusoidal current, Fourier analysis and a linear conductor model give:
P_{\mathrm{Cu}}=I_{\mathrm{DC}}^2R_{\mathrm{DC}}+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}I_{k,\mathrm{rms}}^2R_{\mathrm{AC}}(kf_0).
For the 1 m wire carrying 10 A DC plus a 2 A RMS, 1 MHz sinusoidal ripple, total RMS current is √(10² + 2²) = 10.198 A. The loss is:
P_{\mathrm{Cu}}=10^2(0.02195)+2^2(0.08880)\approx2.550\ \mathrm W.
Using total RMS current with RDC would give only 2.283 W, about 10.5% below the calculated loss. Applying the 1 MHz resistance to the entire DC current would also be wrong. A real PWM waveform has multiple harmonics; calculate their current amplitudes and losses rather than assigning one skin depth from the switching edge alone.
In a multiwinding component, proximity losses can depend on the amplitudes and phases of currents in the other windings as well.
crumbs: 11  2.7 Skin effect: why copper resistance depends on frequency

title: 2.7 Skin effect: why copper resistance depends on frequency
section: Skin effect, proximity effect and conductor choice
text:
Skin effect, proximity effect and conductor choice
Skin effect describes redistribution by a conductor’s own alternating field. Proximity effect describes additional redistribution caused by nearby current paths and their fields. In a multilayer transformer winding, proximity losses can dominate. Their size depends on layer arrangement, winding currents and air-gap fringing fields. The isolated-wire curve therefore establishes a reference, not a complete winding-loss prediction.








Construction
Useful effect
What still needs checking




Thicker solid round wire
Reduces DC resistance
At high frequency, effective area grows mainly with perimeter; added copper is less useful than in DC


Thin foil or PCB winding
Can keep conductor thickness small relative to δ
Return geometry and neighbouring layers can crowd current onto one face or toward edges


Several ordinary bare/contacting strands
Provides mechanical flexibility
Does not guarantee independent strand currents or the performance of litz wire


Litz wire
Individually insulated strands and transposition can reduce AC loss
Strand diameter, bundle construction, external field, terminations, insulation fill and extra strand length



For an equal-copper-area comparison, 100 strands of 0.10 mm diameter contain the same copper cross-section as one 1.00 mm wire. At 1 MHz, the isolated 0.10 mm strand has RAC/RDC ≈ 1.0068, versus 4.045 for the solid 1 mm wire. With equal strand currents and the same 1 m strand length, the skin-only bundle estimate is 22.10 mΩ.
This illustrates the benefit of subdivision; it is not a full litz-winding prediction. The bundle’s outside diameter is larger because of insulation and packing, and actual transposition increases strand length. Elektrisola’s litz-wire technical information describes strand insulation and construction; Ansys’s litz-wire modelling documentation states the ideal transposition assumptions.
On a PCB, compare the copper thickness with δ, then include the return and layer fields. At 100 kHz, 35 µm copper is much thinner than the 209 µm skin depth; thickness alone does not suggest severe skin effect, but geometry can still cause proximity or edge crowding.
Skin effect concerns penetration into copper; dielectric distance concerns separation between conductors and changes capacitance, external inductance and proximity fields. They are different dimensions of the same physical layout.
Classroom check: would doubling a thick wire’s diameter halve its resistance? For DC it ideally reduces resistance by four; in the strong skin-effect limit, isolated-wire AC resistance is approximately halved because the perimeter doubles. Check which regime applies first.
crumbs: 11  2.7 Skin effect: why copper resistance depends on frequency

title: 2.8 Proximity effect and a high-power square-wave transformer
text:
Specify power transfer and the current waveform first
Physical idea: neighbouring turns impose a magnetic field on a conductor. The induced currents can reinforce transport current on one surface and oppose it elsewhere, creating additional copper loss. A conductor can even carry zero net transport current while supporting local eddy currents and heating. Thus, total ampere-turn cancellation in a transformer does not imply zero field everywhere in its winding window.
Skin effect already makes a thick conductor costly at high frequency. Proximity effect adds sensitivity to where the turns and their return ampere-turns are placed. A single-layer winding avoids the accumulation across many layers, but still experiences fields from adjacent turns and the other winding. The two calculations below deliberately distinguish these mechanisms.
Use a 1:1 transformer with four primary and four secondary turns, driven from a bipolar bridge. At the load terminals, specify the following operating point:
The load voltage and current have matching, symmetric, flat-topped waveforms with finite transitions. An ideal square wave is their zero-transition-time limit. Here the resistive load makes current follow voltage; a square-wave transformer voltage feeding a different circuit need not produce square-wave current.
During a linear transition from −I to +I, mean squared current is I²/3. Two transitions occur each period, so:
I_{\mathrm{rms}}=I_{\mathrm{pk}}\sqrt{1-\frac{4t_r}{3T}}=49.33\ \mathrm A.
P_{\mathrm{out}}=V_{\mathrm{pk}}I_{\mathrm{pk}}\left(1-\frac{4t_r}{3T}\right)=4.867\ \mathrm{kW}.
The zero-transition-time limit is 5.000 kW. Mean signed voltage and current are zero, but their product has positive mean. Positive and negative half-cycles both deliver power.
This calculation specifies the load waveform and estimates winding loss at that operating point. The source must provide additional voltage headroom and active power for winding drops and losses. It is not a transient simulation of a fixed 100 V DC bus and a lossy transformer.
Magnetizing current is neglected in the load-current comparison. With a 500 mm² effective core area, applying the specified waveform to an ideal induced-voltage winding gives a centred flux peak of approximately 0.0613 T. Actual induced voltage, core loss, material limits, commutation and temperature require a complete converter design.

title: 2.8 Proximity effect and a high-power square-wave transformer
section: Step 1: high loss from skin effect, even with one layer
text:
Step 1: high loss from skin effect, even with one layer
First wind each four-turn winding in a single radial layer of solid 2.00 mm diameter round copper wire. Each winding contains 0.80 m of copper; both together contain 1.60 m. The combined DC resistance is 8.780 mΩ. Evaluated with the actual 49.33 A RMS current, the constant-resistance heating estimate is:
P_{R_{\mathrm{DC}}}=I_{\mathrm{rms}}^2(R_{1,\mathrm{DC}}+R_{2,\mathrm{DC}})=21.37\ \mathrm W.
This is a DC-resistance estimate of AC heating, not a proposal to apply DC voltage to the transformer. At 200 kHz, copper skin depth is only 0.148 mm, much smaller than the wire’s 1 mm radius.
Represent each rounded square waveform as a bipolar square convolved with a unit-area box of duration tr. For odd harmonic k, define sinc(x) = sin(πx)/(πx):
I_{k,\mathrm{rms}}=\frac{4I_{\mathrm{pk}}}{\pi\sqrt{2}\,k}\left|\operatorname{sinc}\!\left(\frac{kt_r}{T}\right)\right|,\qquad k=1,3,5,\ldots
Use the cylindrical wire resistance from section 2.7 at each kf₀. The result is:







Current used with this single-layer round-wire geometry
Combined loss in both windings




Actual RMS current, but resistance held at RDC
21.37 W


200 kHz sinusoidal current with the same RMS magnitude
77.93 W


Specified rounded square current, including its harmonics
93.01 W



The rounded square’s skin-only loss is 4.35 times the DC-resistance estimate, and approximately 19.4% above the same-RMS sinusoidal-current case. The comparison with the sinusoid isolates current-waveform loss; it does not assume identical power transfer or flux for the two voltage drives. This first calculation excludes proximity effect and uses the isolated-wire resistance as a reference.
Single-layer construction therefore does not guarantee a low-loss high-frequency winding; the full winding can dissipate more than this skin-only estimate.
crumbs: 12  2.8 Proximity effect and a high-power square-wave transformer

title: 2.8 Proximity effect and a high-power square-wave transformer
section: Step 2: keep the operating point, compare layered winding arrangements
text:
Step 2: keep the operating point, compare layered winding arrangements
Now consider a separate conductor construction: four one-turn radial layers per winding. Each foil turn is 20 mm wide and 0.20 mm thick, giving 4.000 mm² copper area, with the same 0.20 m mean turn length. Compare two orders across the window:

Grouped: P P P P S S S S.
Interleaved: P S P S P S P S.

All four P turns are connected in series, as are all four S turns. Interleaving changes their physical order, not the 4:4 electrical turns ratio. The foil comparison holds conductor dimensions, copper length, load waveform and turn counts fixed. Its copper area differs from the single-layer round-wire reference’s 3.142 mm², so the two geometries are not an arrangement-only comparison.
In a one-dimensional winding-window model of width b, a layer carrying current Iₖ changes tangential field by Kₖ = Iₖ/b. Set the outer load-current field to zero and neglect magnetizing current. At the 50 A reference and b = 20 mm, K = 2500 A/m. The grouped stack’s boundary fields are:
H/K:\quad 0,1,2,3,4,3,2,1,0.
The interleaved stack instead gives:
H/K:\quad 0,1,0,1,0,1,0,1,0.
Each harmonic scales these fields with its own signed winding-current phasor. A foil layer’s mean boundary field Havg = (Hleft + Hright)/2 drives its proximity contribution. Summing Havg² across eight layers gives 42K² grouped and 2K² interleaved: a factor of 21 in the foil model’s proximity term, even though total primary and secondary ampere-turns cancel in both stacks.



Grouped and interleaved winding layers, boundary field profiles and foil versus litz conductor construction.


Why proximity loss remains in the interleaved case: the field alternates between zero and K rather than disappearing. Each turn still has a nonzero mean field. More interfaces can also increase primary-secondary capacitance and consume space for insulation; minimum copper loss is only one design objective. TI’s winding-loss note, especially its transformer and interleaving examples, provides the physical background for these field profiles.
crumbs: 12  2.8 Proximity effect and a high-power square-wave transformer

title: 2.8 Proximity effect and a high-power square-wave transformer
section: Step 3: replace each foil turn with ideal transposed litz
text:
Step 3: replace each foil turn with ideal transposed litz
For a nearly equal copper area, use 800 individually insulated strands of 80 µm diameter per turn. Their total copper area is 4.021 mm². Retain the same electrical turn counts and 0.20 m strand length per turn for the comparison. Assume equal transport-current sharing and ideal transposition within each turn.
Model the macroscopic field as varying linearly across each litz turn, with a locally uniform applied field at each strand position and no bundle shielding.
The script calculates isolated-strand transport/skin loss and the cylindrical eddy-current response to the applied transverse field, then averages over strand positions and sums the strands and current harmonics. Full transposition samples the mean of H², not just the square of mean H. For the specified linear field profile:
\langle |H|^2\rangle_{\mathrm{turn}}=|H_{\mathrm{avg}}|^2+\frac{|\Delta H|^2}{12}.
The litz field-square sums are therefore (128/3)K² grouped and (8/3)K² interleaved, a ratio of 16. The applied-field proximity term remains; the calculation does not merely substitute the fine-strand skin resistance and assume all remaining AC loss vanishes.









Conductor and order

16.71 W

All entries are combined primary-plus-secondary copper losses at the specified load waveform. The foil and litz DC-resistance estimates are 16.78 W and 16.69 W respectively. Core loss, bridge loss and rectifier loss are outside the table, so these numbers are not total converter loss or efficiency.



Rounded square waveform, single-layer skin-only loss comparison, and grouped/interleaved foil and ideal-litz winding losses.


Engineering conclusion for this example: interleaving strongly reduces the applied field, while subdivision into fine insulated strands reduces conductor eddy loss. They address different parts of the problem. Under the specified model, interleaved foil even outperforms grouped ideal litz. Litz selection therefore needs the harmonic spectrum and winding field, not just a strand-diameter check at f₀.
The litz numbers are idealized applied-field estimates, not predictions for a purchased bundle. Real bundle packing and shielding, local strand-to-strand fields, incomplete transposition, terminations, twist length and departures from the assumed linear macroscopic field change the result. A transposed bundle also occupies more space than its copper area and usually uses more strand length than the winding centreline length.
Consult Ansys’s litz modelling assumptions and Elektrisola’s construction information when moving beyond this teaching comparison.

title: 2.8 Proximity effect and a high-power square-wave transformer
section: Optional model detail: reproducible loss rather than a guessed multiplier
text:
Optional model detail: reproducible loss rather than a guessed multiplier
For a foil of thickness t, width b and conductor length ℓ, solve d²H/dx² = q²H with q = (1 + j)/δ and the two specified boundary fields. With RMS harmonic quantities, let ΔH = Hright − Hleft and Havg = (Hleft + Hright)/2. Integration of ρ|J|² over the conductor gives:
P_{\mathrm{layer}}=\rho b\ell\left[\frac{|\Delta H|^2}{2}\operatorname{Re}\!\left\{q\operatorname{coth}\!\left(\frac{qt}{2}\right)\right\}+2|H_{\mathrm{avg}}|^2\operatorname{Re}\!\left\{q\operatorname{tanh}\!\left(\frac{qt}{2}\right)\right\}\right].
The first term is the transport/skin contribution, the second the proximity contribution. Their cross term integrates to zero in this symmetric one-dimensional model. Sum the layers and the odd harmonics. The script independently checks the result by integrating the complex current-density profile and its Joule heating.
For a fine round strand of radius a in a weakly screened, uniform transverse field H, the low-frequency applied-field limit is:
\frac{P_{\mathrm{strand,prox}}}{\ell}\approx\frac{\pi a^4}{4\rho}(\omega\mu |H|)^2.
The numerical litz calculation uses the full cylindrical applied-field response through the skin transition, rather than extrapolating this ω² approximation to every harmonic. Harmonic sums through k = 1999 were checked against k = 3999; the reported total losses change by less than 0.002%. This checks numerical truncation within the model, not agreement with hardware.
The field model assumes broad layers, uniform tangential boundary fields, negligible fringing and fixed room-temperature copper resistivity.
Classroom checks: why does zero total load ampere-turns not imply zero copper eddy loss? Fields can remain between and inside winding layers. Why is a litz bundle still lossy in a large external field? Insulated strands still support internal eddy currents, and imperfect construction can add further losses.
Winding choice. Interleaving can reduce leakage and proximity loss, but changes capacitance and insulation geometry. Compare it with the grouped winding under the same waveform and constraints. Choose from the combined loss, coupling and construction requirements rather than one curve.
crumbs: 12  2.8 Proximity effect and a high-power square-wave transformer

title: 3. Capacitive coupling on a PCB: why edge speed matters
text:
3.1 From prepreg thickness to displacement current
For overlapping conductors separated by a thin dielectric:
C\approx\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r\frac{A}{h}.
Consider a broad 1 mm wide conductor overlapping another conductor for 10 mm, separated by 0.10 mm of dielectric with assumed \varepsilon_r=4. The overlap area is 10 mm², giving approximately 3.54 pF. This is a parallel-plate estimate; fringing and the actual stackup require a field model for accurate design.
For a prescribed digital edge of 3.3 V in 1 ns, with the other conductor held approximately stationary:
i_{\mathrm{coupled}}\approx C_m\frac{\Delta V}{t_r}=3.54\ \mathrm{pF}\frac{3.3\ \mathrm{V}}{1\ \mathrm{ns}}\approx11.7\ \mathrm{mA}.
A few picofarads can therefore inject milliamperes. The edge rise time, rather than only the clock frequency, determines the fast current.
Reference plane versus victim node. If the second conductor is an ideal grounded plane, this is return current into that plane. Its voltage does not change in the ideal model. A real plane or shared return impedance can develop ground bounce. Coupling into a high-impedance signal or power node is a different circuit and can generate a much larger voltage.
A continuous grounded shield plane also changes the coupling geometry; do not assume that a direct mutual capacitance remains unchanged through it.
crumbs: 13  3. Capacitive coupling on a PCB: why edge speed matters

title: 3. Capacitive coupling on a PCB: why edge speed matters
section: 3.2 A defined lumped victim model
text:
3.2 A defined lumped victim model
Use an ideal aggressor voltage v_a, a mutual capacitance C_m into a victim node, and a victim impedance R_v\parallel C_v to its quiet reference:



Mutual capacitance Cm feeding a victim node with Rv and Cv in parallel to the quiet reference.


Kirchhoff’s current law gives:
C_m\frac{d(v_a-v_v)}{dt}=\frac{v_v}{R_v}+C_v\frac{dv_v}{dt}.
Therefore:
\frac{V_v(s)}{V_a(s)}=\frac{sR_vC_m}{1+sR_v(C_m+C_v)}.
\tau_v=R_v(C_m+C_v),\qquad f_v=\frac{1}{2\pi\tau_v}.
The aggressor-voltage to victim-voltage path is high-pass, with high-frequency limit C_m/(C_m+C_v). The injected-current to victim-voltage impedance is low-pass:
Z_v(s)=\frac{R_v}{1+sR_v(C_m+C_v)}.
These two views explain the apparent contradiction: fast voltage edges couple strongly, while the victim capacitance limits the voltage generated by a given high-frequency injected current.
For C_m=3.54 pF, C_v=10 pF and R_v=50 Ω:
\tau_v\approx0.677\ \mathrm{ns},\qquad f_v\approx235\ \mathrm{MHz}.
For an aggressor ramp of duration t_r, starting from zero victim voltage, the voltage at the end of the edge is:
v_{v,\mathrm{pk}}=R_vC_m\frac{\Delta V}{t_r}\left(1-e^{-t_r/\tau_v}\right)\approx0.451\ \mathrm V.
After the edge it decays exponentially with time constant \tau_v. For an ideal instantaneous edge the initial jump approaches the capacitive-divider value, approximately 0.863 V here. The finite 1 ns edge gives the smaller result above because the resistance conducts during the edge.



Victim voltage from a finite digital edge and its high-pass coupling response.


Design interpretation: reduce overlap or mutual capacitance, control edge speed where permitted, provide an intentional return path, reduce victim impedance, and place suitable filtering near the victim. Adding capacitance reduces a fast voltage jump but can lengthen its decay; calculate both amplitude and duration. A long coupled line needs a distributed coupled-line model including mutual inductance.
The lumped example demonstrates the mechanism rather than predicting near-end/far-end crosstalk on an arbitrary PCB.
crumbs: 13  3. Capacitive coupling on a PCB: why edge speed matters

title: 3. Capacitive coupling on a PCB: why edge speed matters
section: 3.3 Dielectric distance: make the separation explicit
text:
3.3 Dielectric distance: make the separation explicit
Here h is the finished dielectric thickness between the two facing copper surfaces, measured perpendicular to the layers. It is not the copper thickness, lateral trace spacing, or the overall board thickness. In a multilayer PCB, use the relevant finished core/prepreg spacing and the material’s applicable permittivity; εr = 4 is the teaching assumption here, rather than a universal PCB value.
For fixed overlap area and permittivity:
C_m\propto\frac{1}{h},\qquad i_{\mathrm{coupled}}\approx\frac{\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r A}{h}\frac{dv_a}{dt}.
Halving the separation doubles the plate-model capacitance and the approximate current into a stationary victim/reference. With the previous 10 mm² overlap, εr = 4, 3.3 V / 1 ns edge, and the same 50 Ω ∥ 10 pF victim:

The current column is a capacitance estimate with a stationary victim. The victim-voltage calculation instead uses the coupled differential equation in section 3.2, allowing the victim to move. Its peak does not simply double when h halves, because capacitance also changes the time constant and the capacitive-divider ratio.
The figure holds the other circuit parameters fixed to isolate this effect. As separation becomes comparable with conductor width, fringing weakens the accuracy of the plate approximation.



Capacitance and finite-edge victim voltage versus dielectric separation, with overlap and victim impedance held fixed.


An intentional reference plane gives a different design tradeoff. Bringing a signal or power conductor closer to its return plane increases its capacitance to that reference and reduces loop inductance. For wide parallel conductors in a uniform medium:
C'\approx\varepsilon\frac{w}{h},\qquad L'\approx\mu\frac{h}{w},\qquad Z_{\mathrm{line}}\approx\frac{h}{w}\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\varepsilon}}.
Thus thinner dielectric to a continuous quiet reference is often helpful for field confinement and low-inductance current return. Thinner dielectric directly between an unshielded aggressor and a sensitive victim increases mutual coupling. Always identify which conductors the distance separates. In the ideal uniform TEM model, L′C′ = µε, so changing h alone changes impedance but not propagation velocity; changing dielectric permittivity changes velocity as well.
Distance through insulation, clearance and creepage are separate concepts. Thickness h is a path through solid dielectric; clearance is an air path and creepage follows an insulating surface. A uniform-field estimate is E ≈ ΔV/h: for example, 400 V across 0.10 mm corresponds to 4 kV/mm.
This is a field calculation, not a voltage-withstand rating. Material, manufacturing quality, edge geometry, voltage waveform and the applicable insulation requirements determine a qualified design. No universal safe mm/kV rule follows from the capacitance formula. See TI’s explanation of distance through insulation.
Spacing choice. More separation reduces the plate-model coupling capacitance. It also changes the board geometry and stackup. If that change is impractical, compare reducing overlap or edge speed. Recalculate the victim response; injected current alone does not settle the choice.

title: 4. Worked design exercise: how close must the CPU’s source be?
text:
Given
This exercise emulates a fast die-side CPU load transient. It does not assert the measured slew rate of a particular processor. The regulator, board, package and die capacitors supply different frequency ranges.
crumbs: 14  4. Worked design exercise: how close must the CPU's source be?

title: 4. Worked design exercise: how close must the CPU’s source be?
text:
Nominal CPU rail: 1.00 V, with ±30 mV allowed deviation.
Initial rail is settled at 1.00 V under a 40 A load.
Load rises from 40 A to 60 A in 20 ns: an incremental 20 A ramp.
First model: no local capacitance, an ideal source, negligible resistance, and a supply/return pair with assumed loop L'=1 µH/m.
Assign the entire 30 mV downward deviation budget to this one mechanism. The full 60 mV tolerance band is not available from an initially nominal rail.
crumbs: 14  4. Worked design exercise: how close must the CPU's source be?

title: 4. Worked design exercise: how close must the CPU’s source be?
section: Step 1: inductance and distance limit
text:
Step 1: inductance and distance limit
\frac{di}{dt}=\frac{20\ \mathrm A}{20\ \mathrm{ns}}=1\ \mathrm{A/ns}.
\Delta V_L=L\frac{di}{dt},\qquad L_{\max}=\frac{30\ \mathrm{mV}}{1\ \mathrm{A/ns}}=30\ \mathrm{pH}.
\ell_{\max}=\frac{L_{\max}}{L'}=30\ \mathrm{\mu m}.
With the same assumptions, a 1 mm connection would produce a 1 V inductive drop. The result exposes the failure of a remote source alone to supply this fast current ramp. The immediate source must include local stored energy, often on the die or in the package.
It is not a board-placement rule requiring the VRM to sit 30 µm from the CPU. Different interconnect geometry changes L', and capacitance changes the circuit.



Inductive droop against connection length for the stated CPU transient.
crumbs: 14  4. Worked design exercise: how close must the CPU's source be?

title: 4. Worked design exercise: how close must the CPU’s source be?
section: Step 2: negligible inductance, maximum Thévenin resistance
text:
Step 2: negligible inductance, maximum Thévenin resistance
Retain the initially regulated 1.00 V operating point and allocate the 30 mV incremental droop to resistance alone:
R_{\mathrm{Th,max}}=\frac{\Delta V}{\Delta I}=\frac{30\ \mathrm{mV}}{20\ \mathrm A}=1.5\ \mathrm{m\Omega}.
This is an incremental source-impedance requirement around the settled operating point. If instead an uncompensated ideal source is fixed at 1.00 V and all absolute DC drop at 60 A must fit within 30 mV, the resistance bound is 0.50 mΩ.
crumbs: 14  4. Worked design exercise: how close must the CPU's source be?

title: 4. Worked design exercise: how close must the CPU’s source be?
section: Step 3: where the capacitors enter
text:
Step 3: where the capacitors enter
The charge deficit determines capacitance:
C\geq\frac{1}{\Delta V_C}\int(i_{\mathrm{load}}-i_{\mathrm{upstream}})\,dt.
If upstream current stays at its initial value during the 20 ns linear ramp, the deficit is triangular. Its charge is 0.20 µC; capacitance alone would need at least 6.67 µF for 30 mV. If a capacitor must subsequently deliver the full extra 20 A for a separate 100 ns interval, that interval alone needs 66.7 µF. Real selection also includes capacitance derating, ESL, ESR, package impedance and resonances.
The mechanisms share the budget; they cannot each consume the full 30 mV simultaneously:
\Delta V_{\mathrm{droop}}\approx L\frac{di}{dt}+R\Delta I+\frac{\Delta Q}{C}.
In frequency-domain design the same idea becomes a target impedance over a specified frequency band:
|Z_{\mathrm{PDN}}(j\omega)|\lesssim\frac{\Delta V}{\Delta I}=1.5\ \mathrm{m\Omega}.
The required band and allocation between board, package and die are part of the specification. See AMD’s target-impedance guidance and Intel’s board-design guidance.
crumbs: 14  4. Worked design exercise: how close must the CPU's source be?

title: 4. Worked design exercise: how close must the CPU’s source be?
section: 4.1 Classroom riddle: why put 10 nF and 100 nF beside a digital IC?
text:
4.1 Classroom riddle: why put 10 nF and 100 nF beside a digital IC?
Start with the question, then choose the disturbance. Is ripple arriving from the supply, or is switching current being drawn by the IC? These are different inputs to the same network. A CPU/GPU supply current can contain sharp pulses and many harmonics; it need not be a literal clock-frequency square wave. The following model isolates the mechanism rather than representing a measured processor.



Digital-IC small-signal supply model with upstream source impedance, a local capacitor including ESR and loop ESL, optional IC impedance and an independent load-current disturbance.


Let Zs be the regulator-plus-interconnect impedance seen from the chosen IC supply port. Let ZC include the local capacitor’s ESR and complete loop inductance. An independent small-signal current sink represents the load-current disturbance; a separate ZIC can represent the IC’s incremental port impedance. First take ZIC sufficiently large to omit it. With the supply-noise voltage set to zero:
\Delta V_{\mathrm{IC}}=-\Delta I_{\mathrm{IC}}Z_{\mathrm{PDN}},\qquad Z_{\mathrm{PDN}}=Z_s\parallel Z_C.
\frac{I_{\mathrm{up}}}{I_{\mathrm{IC}}}=\frac{Z_C}{Z_s+Z_C}.
The ideal capacitor would be 1/(jωC), but a first practical model is:
Z_C=R_{\mathrm{ESR}}+j\omega L_{\mathrm{loop}}+\frac{1}{j\omega C}.
If ZIC is retained, include it in the parallel admittance when calculating the response to the independent current disturbance. Do not use the same load-current response once as an independent source and again inside ZIC. An IC’s DC ratio V/I is not generally its high-frequency impedance: 0.8 V / 100 A = 8 mΩ is a static operating-point ratio, not a measured ZIC(f).
Quiz A — make the source ideal at the IC pins. Set Zs = 0. The load-current-induced voltage ripple is zero in this ideal model, with or without the capacitor. The ideal source supplies the disturbance current; a capacitor across a perfectly fixed voltage cannot further improve that voltage. This does not describe a remote regulator separated from the die by a package, vias and traces.
Quiz B — apply supply-voltage ripple instead. With the independent load-current disturbance set to zero and ZIC omitted:
\frac{V_{\mathrm{IC}}}{V_s}=\frac{Z_C}{Z_s+Z_C}.
For Zs = 0 this ratio is one: a shunt capacitor does not attenuate ripple imposed by an ideal voltage source at its own node. A finite series impedance can create source-to-load filtering. The identical algebra above describes two different measurements: voltage-noise transfer and the fraction of IC disturbance current flowing upstream. State the excitation and measurement before saying “attenuation.”
Quiz C — add the connection and move the capacitor. Use 1 nH/mm, not nΩ/mm, as the specified two-wire-loop estimate from section 2.3. Inductance becomes impedance through jωL; 45 nH has reactance about 283 Ω at 1 GHz. This number is not a universal PCB-trace impedance, especially when the interconnect is electrically long.
Local capacitance can provide fast load current while the upstream path changes current more slowly. Keep the capacitor-to-power-pin-and-return loop inductance small. “Close” includes the return, vias, package and mounting geometry. A capacitor directly underneath the IC can provide a short loop when the stackup and via arrangement support it; placement on the opposite face is not inherently best. TI’s processor-PDN layout guidance, section 3, discusses mounting and spreading inductance.
Numerical comparison, separate from the 100 A exercise below: choose a small-signal source path of 20 mΩ + jω·5 nH, a 100 nF capacitor with 10 mΩ ESR, and total capacitor-loop inductance of either 0.5 nH or 5 nH. A third case parallels the close 100 nF with 10 nF, 20 mΩ ESR and 0.5 nH loop inductance. These are authored lumped examples, not a GPU rail design.



IC-port impedance and upstream disturbance-current fraction for close/far 100 nF capacitors and a parallel 10 nF plus 100 nF pair.


With 0.5 nH, the 100 nF and 10 nF branches have self-resonances at 22.5 MHz and 71.2 MHz. The 100 nF branch’s impedance at 1 GHz is approximately 3.14 Ω, dominated by inductance. A smaller capacitance can move branch resonance upward, but paralleling capacitor values can also create antiresonance peaks.
Select values, packages and mounting from the complete impedance profile, rather than assuming that adding 10 nF always improves 100 nF.
The plots show conducted current division and port impedance. They do not predict radiated-emission attenuation in dB. Radiation also depends on loop area, return discontinuities and common-mode paths. A passive PDN resonance peak is also not, by itself, proof of control-loop instability; section 12.6 shows how an actively regulated load can destabilize an input filter.
Which capacitor helps? Start by shortening the mounted path of the 100 nF capacitor. The 10 nF addition is a separate candidate, not an automatic improvement. Keep both only if their combined impedance improves the required band without unacceptable peaking. Otherwise, the single close capacitor is the simpler choice.
crumbs: 14  4. Worked design exercise: how close must the CPU's source be?

title: 4. Worked design exercise: how close must the CPU’s source be?
section: 4.2 Board-diagonal quiz: will a 1 GHz signal disappear?
text:
4.2 Board-diagonal quiz: will a 1 GHz signal disappear?
Given: a square board with 10 cm² area, components at opposite corners, and an approximately diagonal route. A 3 cm × 3 cm board would instead have 9 cm² area; neither description means a 10 cm × 10 cm board.
a=\sqrt{10}\ \mathrm{cm}=3.162\ \mathrm{cm},\qquad \ell=\sqrt{20}\ \mathrm{cm}=4.472\ \mathrm{cm}.
First distinguish plane capacitance from trace capacitance. If two overlapping planes use the entire 10 cm² area, εr = 4 and h = 1 mm between copper surfaces, their plate-model capacitance is:
C_{\mathrm{planes}}\approx\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r\frac{A}{h}=35.4\ \mathrm{pF}.
At 0.10 mm dielectric separation, the same estimate becomes 354 pF. Total PCB thickness is not necessarily the signal-to-reference spacing. A signal trace does not use the full board area as its plate: its width, reference geometry, dielectric and fringing fields determine its capacitance and inductance. One cannot infer “45 nH and a few hundred pF” for that trace from board area and diagonal alone.
Does the voltage-divider arithmetic work? If we deliberately build an ideal lumped series 45 nH followed by a shunt 300 pF capacitor, unloaded, its calculated gain at 1 GHz is approximately 0.00188, or −54.5 dB. That is the result for the specified lumped LC circuit. It does not establish that distributed PCB traces behave as one inductor followed by the whole board capacitance at their far end.
A counterexample with a defined signal line. Choose a uniform, lossless 50 Ω line with effective relative permittivity 4 and a matched 50 Ω receiver. This is an illustrative line, not a stackup extracted from the incomplete board geometry:
v_p\approx\frac{c}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{eff}}}},\qquad t_d=\frac{\ell}{v_p}=0.298\ \mathrm{ns}.
L_{\mathrm{total}}=Z_0t_d=14.9\ \mathrm{nH},\qquad C_{\mathrm{total}}=\frac{t_d}{Z_0}=5.97\ \mathrm{pF}.
At 1 GHz the electrical length is about 107.4°. The distributed line therefore cannot be replaced by one end-loaded LC cell. With a matched load:
\frac{V_{\mathrm{receiver}}}{V_{\mathrm{entrance}}}=e^{-j\omega t_d}.
Its magnitude is one: the receiver sees a delayed signal. The ratio is measured from the line entrance, so any source-resistance voltage division during launch is outside this ratio. A real PCB adds frequency-dependent conductor/dielectric loss; a mismatched receiver adds reflections. Neither implies that a 4.5 cm path automatically removes a 1 GHz signal.



Matched lossless-line delay of a 1 GHz rounded square wave, and the difference between distributed propagation and collapsing the same total L/C into one loaded cell.


For CPU-to-RAM signals, use driver/receiver models, the reference path, line impedance, delay and termination. Edge rise time and harmonics matter as well as clock rate. Intel/Altera’s signal-integrity white paper covers distributed interconnects, impedance mismatch and loss. Supply decoupling across a power rail and adding capacitance to a data signal are different circuit interventions.

title: 4. Worked design exercise: how close must the CPU’s source be?
section: 4.3 CPU/POL exercise: translate tolerance into an impedance budget
text:
4.3 CPU/POL exercise: translate tolerance into an impedance budget
Use a teaching scenario, not a claimed Intel or NVIDIA device limit: a nominal 1.00 V rail, initially settled at nominal, with 30 mV allowable downward deviation and an additional 100 A load-current demand at the defined IC port. The one-sided voltage budget gives the target-impedance scale:
Z_{\mathrm{target}}=\frac{30\ \mathrm{mV}}{100\ \mathrm A}=0.30\ \mathrm{m\Omega}.
This applies to the total PDN seen at that port over the specified frequency range. It is a screening/design target, not a guarantee of peak transient voltage for every waveform. The DC/DC’s output impedance alone is insufficient when interconnect and local storage matter. In a simple lumped model, Zs = Zreg + Rpath + jωLpath, with local capacitor branches connected at their actual locations.
A die-side current requirement also needs the package and die network; it must not silently be moved to a board-side port.
Resolve the slew-rate unit before calculating distance. Allocate all 30 mV to inductance alone for this comparison, neglect capacitors and resistance, and retain the assumed loop L′ = 1 nH/mm:
