A millisecond versus a microsecond changes the inductance allowance by a factor of 1000. These distances expose the limit of a remote-source-only model; they do not prescribe practical VRM placement or apply unchanged to closely spaced power/return planes.
Step 2 — negligible inductance: if the full 30 mV incremental drop is resistive, total Thévenin resistance must be at most 0.30 mΩ. If instead we divide the budget into 10 mV for resistance, 10 mV for inductance and 10 mV for capacitor charge deficit:

Total incremental resistance allowance is 10 mV / 100 A = 0.10 mΩ. With an assumed path resistance of 0.04 mΩ, only 0.06 mΩ remains for the regulator’s resistive contribution in this simplified model.
At 100 A/µs, the inductance allowance is 10 mV / (100 A/µs) = 0.10 nH, corresponding to 0.10 mm only under the assumed loop-inductance-per-length model.
A 100 A rise over 1 µs, while upstream current remains at its initial value, leaves a triangular 50 µC charge deficit. Limiting the capacitive contribution to 10 mV requires 5 mF effective capacitance. If the upstream current responds during the ramp, integrate the actual smaller deficit; a different waveform or interval gives a different result.

This is why 10 nF and 100 nF local capacitors address a different portion of the transient spectrum from bulk storage and the closed-loop POL regulator. Account for actual DC-bias derating, ESR, ESL and the handover between board, package and die. Do not assign the full voltage allowance independently to every mechanism and then sum them.
Connection to published methodology: the Intel/Altera PDN Tool User Guide, sections on target impedance and decoupling, uses allowable ripple, transient current and a target frequency range. It is FPGA PDN guidance, not a CPU or NVIDIA GPU electrical specification. To make this a device-specific assignment, provide the exact processor and rail documentation, its allowed DC/load-line/AC deviation, transient current waveform and the port where each requirement is defined.
Then replace the teaching values and verify both impedance and time-domain response.
Where to spend the voltage budget. Use local energy storage for the fast load change and a short path to replenish it. The remote source alone cannot meet the fastest stated slew under the assumed inductance per length. If the actual device has a slower transient, recalculate the allocation before adding capacitors. These distance estimates are not layout dimensions for a named processor.

title: 5. Average and RMS: define these before calculating power
text:
5.1 Definitions and the three useful numbers
For a real periodic waveform of period T:
X_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac1T\int_0^T x(t)\,dt,\qquad X_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac1T\int_0^T x^2(t)\,dt}.
Average is signed. RMS is nonnegative and expresses an equivalent resistive-heating effect. The rectified average \langle|x|\rangle is another quantity; it must not be confused with the signed average of a bipolar signal.
Remember √2 for a sine, √D for a rectangular pulse, and √12 for peak-to-peak triangular ripple. They follow from integration, not from a universal conversion between peak and RMS.
Square-wave distinction: a ±A square wave has RMS A. A 0/A square wave at 50% duty has average A/2 and RMS A/√2. Always draw the zero level and state the duty cycle.

title: 5. Average and RMS: define these before calculating power
section: 5.2 DC plus ripple and zero intervals
text:
5.2 DC plus ripple and zero intervals
For a waveform consisting of a DC component plus a zero-mean AC component:
X_{\mathrm{rms}}^2=X_{\mathrm{DC}}^2+X_{\mathrm{AC,rms}}^2.
For a DC inductor current with triangular peak-to-peak ripple:
I_{L,\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{I_L^2+\frac{\Delta I_{L,\mathrm{pp}}^2}{12}}.
For 10 A DC and 4 A peak-to-peak triangular ripple, the total RMS is approximately 10.066 A. The ripple RMS is only 1.155 A. In an ideal buck with an approximately constant load current, the output capacitor carries the ripple component, rather than the 10 A DC component.
If a known waveform segment occupies only a fraction D of the complete period, with zero elsewhere, its full-period average is multiplied by D and its RMS by √D, relative to the segment’s own average and RMS. Mean squares add for orthogonal signals, including DC plus zero-mean ripple, different Fourier harmonics, and two currents that never flow simultaneously.
Existing course reference: the 2025 script, sections 2.3.8–2.3.10 (pages 34–37) and Appendix A, sections 16.1.1–16.1.3 (pages 299–301), contains the corresponding power rules, waveform collection and RMS derivations. These are incorporated here in fresh notation, with sine and square-wave cases made explicit.

title: 6. Active power, reactive power and heating
text:
6.1 Use average current when voltage is constant
P=\langle vi\rangle.
When the port voltage is constant at U:
P=U I_{\mathrm{avg}}.
Example: an ideal 12 V input bus supplies 20 A rectangular pulses at 25% duty. The average current is 5 A, so the average input power is 60 W. Its current RMS is 10 A; multiplying 12 V by 10 A would incorrectly give 120 W. This is an input-energy calculation at a constant-voltage port.
A diode approximated by a constant 0.7 V forward drop, conducting those same pulses, dissipates approximately 3.5 W, using 0.7 V × 5 A. If the forward characteristic is instead modelled as a fixed drop plus resistance, both average and RMS current enter the loss calculation.
In general:
\langle vi\rangle=V_{\mathrm{avg}}I_{\mathrm{avg}}+\langle\widetilde v\,\widetilde i\rangle.
Do not multiply averages when correlated voltage and current ripple make the second term significant.
For periodic waveforms, section 10.5 calculates the same average power from synchronized voltage/current FFTs, retaining phase and distinguishing peak from RMS spectral scaling.
crumbs: 16  6. Active power, reactive power and heating

title: 6. Active power, reactive power and heating
section: 6.2 Use RMS current for ohmic heating
text:
6.2 Use RMS current for ohmic heating
For a constant resistance:
P_R=R\langle i^2\rangle=R I_{\mathrm{rms}}^2.
With a 20 mΩ conductor or on-state MOSFET resistance, the 20 A / 25% pulses cause:
P_R=0.020\times10^2=2.0\ \mathrm W.
A constant 5 A current has the same average but causes only 0.50 W in that resistance. Pulsing increases heating by a factor of four here. A capacitor’s current can have zero mean while its ESR still dissipates power; for 2 A RMS and 50 mΩ ESR the loss is 0.20 W.
At high frequency, resistance and ESR may vary with frequency and temperature, so harmonic loss calculation may be necessary.
crumbs: 16  6. Active power, reactive power and heating

title: 6. Active power, reactive power and heating
section: 6.3 Active power is not synonymous with loss
text:
6.3 Active power is not synonymous with loss
Active power is net average energy transfer. It may become useful mechanical power, charge a battery, or become unwanted heat. Converter losses are the unwanted part of this real-power balance:
P_{\mathrm{in}}=P_{\mathrm{useful}}+P_{\mathrm{loss}},\qquad \eta=\frac{P_{\mathrm{useful}}}{P_{\mathrm{in}}}.
In periodic operation an ideal inductor or capacitor returns the energy it stores over a cycle. Its net average power is zero, despite nonzero instantaneous power and potentially large RMS current.
crumbs: 16  6. Active power, reactive power and heating

title: 6. Active power, reactive power and heating
section: 6.4 Why reactive current still increases losses
text:
6.4 Why reactive current still increases losses
For sinusoidal voltage and current, with lag angle φ:
P=V_{\mathrm{rms}}I_{\mathrm{rms}}\cos\varphi,\qquad Q=V_{\mathrm{rms}}I_{\mathrm{rms}}\sin\varphi.
S=V_{\mathrm{rms}}I_{\mathrm{rms}},\qquad S^2=P^2+Q^2.
Reactive power describes cyclic exchange in the ideal reactive part; it is not itself dissipated there. For fixed active power and voltage, the required current rises as power factor falls:
I_{\mathrm{rms}}=\frac{P}{V_{\mathrm{rms}}\cos\varphi},\qquad P_{\mathrm{line}}=R_{\mathrm{loop}}\frac{P^2}{V_{\mathrm{rms}}^2\cos^2\varphi}.
Example: 2.30 kW at 230 V RMS requires 10 A at unity power factor. At power factor 0.5 it requires 20 A. With 0.20 Ω total line-loop resistance, losses rise from 20 W to 80 W. The load still receives 2.30 kW; the conductors and source carry more current.



Equal active power at power factors 1 and 0.5: higher RMS current and intervals of returned energy.


For distorted waveforms use true power factor:
\mathrm{PF}=\frac{P}{V_{\mathrm{rms}}I_{\mathrm{rms}}}.
With purely sinusoidal voltage, this equals displacement factor cos φ₁ times the fundamental-current RMS divided by total-current RMS. Harmonic current can therefore lower power factor even when the fundamental current is in phase. The simple sinusoidal P/Q/S triangle is not a complete decomposition of arbitrary distorted waveforms.

THD, displacement factor and true power factor
For periodic AC without DC, define total harmonic distortion relative to the fundamental RMS component:
\mathrm{THD}_I=\frac{\sqrt{\sum_{k=2}^{\infty}I_{k,\mathrm{rms}}^2}}{I_{1,\mathrm{rms}}},\qquad \mathrm{THD}_V=\frac{\sqrt{\sum_{k=2}^{\infty}V_{k,\mathrm{rms}}^2}}{V_{1,\mathrm{rms}}}.
Multiply these ratios by 100 for percent. This is the fundamental-referenced convention (THD-F); a total-RMS-referenced instrument setting gives a different number. State the harmonic range and measurement bandwidth. Switching ripple, interharmonics and broadband noise are not automatically included in a line-harmonic THD number. See TI’s PFC/THD discussion.
Displacement power factor uses only the fundamental phase difference: DPF = cos φ₁. For sinusoidal voltage, and current with no DC:
\mathrm{PF}=\frac{\cos\varphi_1}{\sqrt{1+\mathrm{THD}_I^2}}.
For example, DPF = 1 and current THD = 50% give PF = 0.894, not one. With distorted voltage the shortcut above no longer applies, because matching voltage/current harmonics can also transfer active power:
P=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}V_{k,\mathrm{rms}}I_{k,\mathrm{rms}}\cos\varphi_k,\qquad \mathrm{PF}=\frac{P}{V_{\mathrm{rms}}I_{\mathrm{rms}}}.
Section 10.5 obtains these signed harmonic powers from synchronized FFTs. DPF, true PF, voltage THD and current THD answer different questions; report all four when assessing a distorted supply.


Why a high PF can hide distortion: the conductance-controlled PFC
A common PFC strategy commands a switching-cycle-averaged line current proportional to the sensed instantaneous line voltage:
i_{\mathrm{ref}}(t)=Gv_{\mathrm{line}}(t).
Here G is a positive conductance command, approximately constant over a line cycle, set by a slow output-voltage/power loop. With sinusoidal voltage, this produces an in-phase sinusoidal current. With distorted voltage, an ideal tracking loop copies the voltage harmonics into current: Ik = GVk, with matching phase, so THD-I = THD-V within the tracking bandwidth.
It does not need to generate new harmonic orders to cause harmonic current; real control errors and switching add further distortion. Input-voltage disturbances contaminating the current reference are also discussed in TI’s PFC guidance.
For exact proportional tracking:
P=G V_{\mathrm{rms}}^2,\qquad I_{\mathrm{rms}}=G V_{\mathrm{rms}},\qquad \mathrm{PF}=1.
This is why quoting PF alone can feel like “cheating” as a power-quality claim: the number can be perfect while both waveforms contain large harmonics. The PF calculation is correct; it measures normalized voltage–current alignment, not waveform purity or harmonic compliance. Conversely, a controller that extracts the fundamental voltage and commands a clean in-phase sinusoidal current can have THD-I = 0 yet PF below one on distorted voltage.
With no DC, its PF is 1/√(1 + THD-V²).
The design objective therefore matters: proportional conductance gives minimum total RMS current for a specified total active power at a fixed terminal-voltage waveform. A clean fundamental current instead avoids copying supply harmonics. High PF, low THD and minimum frequency-weighted cable loss are related objectives, but are not interchangeable. Specify the actual waveform and harmonic-current requirements when selecting or testing PFC control.


Cable heating: count each harmonic at its own AC resistance
For a linear conductor model at a fixed temperature, with each resistance representing the complete outgoing/return path:
P_{\mathrm{cable}}=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}I_{k,\mathrm{rms}}^2R_{\mathrm{loop,ac}}(kf_1).
There are two effects. Adding harmonic current while holding the fundamental current fixed increases total RMS and heating even if resistance is constant. Skin and proximity effects can additionally increase AC resistance at higher frequencies, so high-order currents can cost more watts per ampere squared.
The increase depends on conductor size, arrangement and frequency; it is not necessarily large for every cable at low harmonic orders. Sections 2.7–2.8 explain the mechanisms. See also Schneider Electric’s harmonic-loss explanation.
Even identical RMS current and THD can produce different heating if their harmonic content occurs at different frequencies. PF alone does not contain the cable’s frequency-dependent resistance. At fixed total power and distorted voltage, do not assume that copying harmonics always increases heating: with frequency-independent resistance, proportional current actually minimizes it. Frequency-dependent resistance can reverse that comparison.


Worked counterexample: PF = 1 with greater cable loss
Use a prescribed 50 Hz voltage at the load port with 230 V RMS fundamental and 23 V RMS fifth harmonic, hence THD-V = 10%. Compare two ideal current-reference strategies delivering the same 2.30 kW at that port. Assume a loop resistance of 0.20 Ω at 50 Hz and 0.60 Ω at 250 Hz.
These deliberately illustrative resistance values demonstrate the weighting; they are not a claim about a particular cable. Hold the terminal waveform fixed and exclude PFC internal losses and switching ripple.

This makes the limitation precise: perfect PF does not guarantee low THD or minimum AC cable loss, but harmonics do not automatically make conductance control the worse choice under every comparison.

For constant DC:

Thus DC can transfer more average power when AC and DC share the same peak limits. But the third comparison gives DC 20 A RMS versus only 14.14 A RMS for AC; DC conductor heating is then twice as high for the same resistance. It is not a comparison at equal thermal utilization.
Wires and fuses: continuous conductor heating is principally an RMS-current issue, with additional AC skin/proximity effects where relevant. Fuse operation depends on thermal history, time-current characteristics, fault conditions and pulse I^2t, rather than a universal peak-current threshold. AC and DC interruption ratings are also different; DC has no natural periodic current zero.
Do not infer a DC rating by multiplying an AC fuse rating by √2. Eaton’s fuse technology guidance distinguishes current and voltage ratings; its high-speed fuse guide discusses AC/DC application limits.
Grid connection: AC made voltage transformation straightforward with transformers and remains widely used for generation and distribution. HVDC can be advantageous for long cables, long-distance transfer and asynchronous interconnections; cable charging current and reactive exchange are major differences. Converter cost and loss, insulation, protection, conductor count and topology also matter.
A two-wire peak-limit example does not establish that every AC system is oversized or compare it fairly with three-phase transmission. See ABB’s discussion of offshore HVDC.
Compare under one constraint. State the held voltage, current, insulation or conductor limit before choosing AC or DC. A benefit under one constraint may disappear under another. Use the same delivered-power requirement and loss accounting for both candidates.
crumbs: 16  6. Active power, reactive power and heating

title: 7. DC steady state, periodic steady state and transients
text:
7.1 The DC impedance interpretation
For sinusoidal steady-state analysis:
Z_L=j\omega L,\qquad Z_C=\frac1{j\omega C}.
As frequency approaches zero, an ideal inductor’s impedance approaches zero and a capacitor’s impedance grows without bound. This gives the familiar settled DC models: inductor short circuit and capacitor open circuit, provided a bounded DC equilibrium actually exists.
The inductor can carry nonzero DC current; the capacitor can retain nonzero DC voltage. A constant voltage across an ideal inductor instead makes its current ramp forever, so that circuit has no bounded DC steady state. Similarly, constant nonzero capacitor current ramps its voltage.
crumbs: 17  7. DC steady state, periodic steady state and transients

title: 7. DC steady state, periodic steady state and transients
section: 7.2 Why periodic switching also has zero average inductor voltage
text:
7.2 Why periodic switching also has zero average inductor voltage
For a periodic state, the state variables return to the same value each period:
i_L(t+T_s)=i_L(t),\qquad v_C(t+T_s)=v_C(t).
Integrating the component equations gives:
\int_t^{t+T_s}v_L\,dt=L\,[i_L(t+T_s)-i_L(t)]=0.
\int_t^{t+T_s}i_C\,dt=C\,[v_C(t+T_s)-v_C(t)]=0.
Therefore \langle v_L\rangle=0 and \langle i_C\rangle=0. The zero-frequency impedance interpretation is consistent with these DC components, but does not eliminate AC ripple at the switching harmonics. The entire inductor voltage is not zero in a switching converter, and the entire capacitor current is not zero.
Equality of stored energy alone is insufficient to prove a periodic signed state: +I and −I have the same inductor energy. Use repetition of current and voltage as the starting condition. In startup or another transient, the cycle-to-cycle differences are generally nonzero.
crumbs: 17  7. DC steady state, periodic steady state and transients

title: 7. DC steady state, periodic steady state and transients
section: 7.3 Application to an ideal buck
text:
7.3 Application to an ideal buck
In continuous conduction, with approximately constant output voltage over one switching period:
D(V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o)+(1-D)(-V_o)=0,\qquad V_o=DV_{\mathrm{in}}.
The output capacitor has zero average current, so average inductor current equals average load current. Periodic balance establishes the operating point. Transfer functions later describe perturbations around it; dynamics do not disappear because the nominal operation is periodic.
crumbs: 17  7. DC steady state, periodic steady state and transients

title: 8. Linearity, time invariance and the scope of a model
text:
8.1 Why a switching simulation can be expensive
A linear input-output operator obeys additivity and scaling:
\mathcal T\{a x_1+b x_2\}=a\mathcal T\{x_1\}+b\mathcal T\{x_2\}.
Time invariance means that delaying the input delays the corresponding output without otherwise changing its shape. It does not mean that the output is constant. Initial conditions must be handled consistently; fixed nonzero stored energy adds a natural response to a zero-state input-output model.
An LTI circuit can be described by an impulse response and, where the transforms exist, a transfer function. Fourier analysis also applies to signals produced by nonlinear systems. Nonlinearity prevents a general description by one input-independent linear transfer function; it does not forbid taking a Fourier transform of the resulting waveform.
A switching power converter is generally not globally LTI. A prescribed switching schedule may yield a linear time-varying circuit, while modulation, feedback and device characteristics introduce additional nonlinearities. For control design we often average over switching and linearize around a nominal operating point:
d=D+\widehat d,\qquad v_o=V_o+\widehat v_o.
G_{vd}(s)=\frac{\widehat V_o(s)}{\widehat d(s)}.
This local averaged LTI model has an operating range and frequency range, usually sufficiently below the switching frequency. Large startup excursions, saturation, mode changes and switching-frequency detail may need another model.
A converter combines several time scales: the switching period, the much shorter transition time, and the longer startup or control response. A 100 kHz switching frequency gives a period of 10 µs. If an edge lasts 100 ns, a maximum time step of 10 ns gives only ten intervals across that edge.
This is a starting resolution choice, not an accuracy guarantee; faster ringing may require a smaller step. Repeat with a smaller maximum step and compare the quantities that matter.
For scale, a fixed 10 ns step over 100 ms requires 10 million steps; over 10 s it requires one billion steps. Adaptive solvers do not necessarily take that many steps, because they can take larger steps between events, but repeated switching transitions and nonlinear device models still create computational work.
DC is the zero-frequency component; it does not require an infinite simulation. The required duration follows from settling time or the transient being investigated.
An edge also introduces spectral content far above the switching repetition frequency. For a 100 ns edge, 1/tr = 10 MHz is a reciprocal-time scale, not a separate oscillation or a hard bandwidth cutoff. Section 16.1 explains the different 0.35/tr bandwidth estimate for specified response shapes. The simulator must resolve the fastest relevant dynamics, not simply sample the 100 kHz repetition frequency.
Choose the model for the question: use an averaged model for slow startup/control behaviour where its assumptions hold, a switching model for ripple and commutation, and a detailed parasitic model for edge ringing or coupling. Simulate only as long as needed for that question, and distinguish the solver’s internal step from the saved waveform sampling used for an FFT.
Simulation choice. Use an averaged model when the question concerns slow dynamics. It saves computation but hides individual switching events. Use a switched model when those events matter. Keep the operating mode consistent and compare a shared prediction before increasing model detail.
crumbs: 18  8. Linearity, time invariance and the scope of a model

title: 9. Laplace: from a differential equation to dynamics
text:
9.1 Why Laplace as well as Fourier? States, convergence and pole location
The one-sided Laplace transform introduces a complex frequency s=\sigma+j\omega:
X(s)=\int_{0^-}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-st}\,dt.
For the one-sided transform, including initial conditions:
\mathcal L\{\dot x\}=sX(s)-x(0^-).
Thus:
V_L(s)=sLI_L(s)-Li_L(0^-),\qquad I_C(s)=sCV_C(s)-Cv_C(0^-).
Initial energy must be included when solving a transient. The usual transfer-function ratio describes the zero-state response, with the other independent inputs held at zero.
The pairs and properties needed in this course fit in one table. u(t) is the unit step and a>0.
Two limit theorems replace a full inverse transform when only the end points matter:
x(0^+)=\lim_{s\to\infty}sX(s),\qquad \lim_{t\to\infty}x(t)=\lim_{s\to0}sX(s),
the second provided that all poles of sX(s) lie in the left half-plane. The final-value theorem is the formal version of section 7’s DC rule: as s\to0, sL\to0 (the inductor becomes a short) and 1/(sC)\to\infty (the capacitor becomes open). It must not be applied to an unstable or undamped response, where the limit does not exist.
Read a transfer function through its poles. A real pole at -a contributes a mode e^{-at} with time constant 1/a; a complex pair -\sigma\pm j\omega_d contributes a damped oscillation e^{-\sigma t}\cos(\omega_dt+\varphi). A right-half-plane system mode can grow. Setting s=j\omega gives the sinusoidal steady-state response when a bounded steady state exists; an algebraically finite value of H(jω) alone does not establish stability.
The averaged converter models of sections 12.2 and 12.6 are analysed through their poles and frequency responses together.
For a series R feeding a shunt C, measured across the capacitor and with no additional load:
RC\frac{dv_o}{dt}+v_o=v_i,\qquad H_{RC}(s)=\frac{1}{1+sRC}.
Its pole is at −1/RC. The natural response decays with time constant τ = RC, while a step from 0 to U produces:
v_o(t)=U\left(1-e^{-t/\tau}\right),\qquad \tau=RC.
Check the step response with the limit theorems: V_o(s)=U/[s(1+sRC)], so sV_o(s)\to U as s\to0 (final value U) and sV_o(s)\to0 as s\to\infty (the output starts at zero).
For a series RL circuit the current time constant is L/R. A stable first-order response settles to about 1.8% of its initial error after 4τ and 0.67% after 5τ. These percentages refer to a single exponential mode.
Fourier and Laplace describe the same dynamics from different viewpoints; Fourier is not restricted to a single sinusoid or incapable of describing transients. A decaying transient can have an ordinary Fourier transform. Fourier series describe periodic responses, while Fourier integrals describe a wider class of signals.
Initial conditions can also be represented through appropriate equivalent sources. The practical advantage of unilateral Laplace is that initial state enters the transformed differential equations explicitly.
For a constant state-space model, with no impulsive state reset at the initial instant:
\dot x=Ax+Bu,\qquad X(s)=(sI-A)^{-1}x(0^-)+(sI-A)^{-1}BU(s).
The first term is the initial-state response; the second is the zero-state forced response. A transfer function alone retains only the latter input/output relation. In piecewise switching analysis, the end state of one interval becomes the initial state of the next. The time-domain form makes the same separation:
x(t)=e^{A(t-t_0)}x(t_0)+\int_{t_0}^{t}e^{A(t-\tau)}Bu(\tau)\,d\tau.
Laplace also introduces the real coordinate σ in s = σ + jω. It supplies exponential weighting and a region of convergence, not just a formal replacement of a derivative by s. For example, exp(at)u(t), with a > 0, has Laplace transform 1/(s − a) for Re(s) > a, but no ordinary Fourier transform.
Substituting jω into that rational expression lies outside its convergence region. It does not turn the growing mode into a bounded sinusoidal steady state. See Swarthmore’s Laplace exponential examples.
Poles describe natural exponential modes; zeros depend on how a selected input excites a selected output and can shape phase or produce inverse response. A right-half-plane zero does not by itself make a system unstable (§16.10). For a finite-dimensional continuous-time state model, eigenvalues strictly in the left half-plane imply asymptotic internal stability.
Ideal LC poles on the imaginary axis give bounded free oscillations, but not asymptotic stability or BIBO stability: resonant forcing can grow the response. Repeated imaginary-axis modes need additional care. Hidden modes can disappear from a particular transfer function, so a cancellation must not be used to assume internal stability.
Pole placement changes A through feedback, rather than changing the transform used to inspect it. It can be derived directly in state space; Laplace and characteristic polynomials provide a compatible description. Frequency-domain feedback methods are also valid. Section 16.28 joins successive LC pulses, shifted state trajectories and a worked ideal pole-placement example. This is optional advanced reading, not additional compulsory material in the 180-minute route.

title: 10. A switched RC: time-domain envelopes and Fourier harmonics
text:
10.1 Define the circuit before calling it a buck without L
An ideal two-position switch alternately connects to V_{\mathrm{in}} and zero. It feeds a series R and shunt C. Assume negligible loading:
The two-position switch is shown beside the continuous-input RC in section 9. The solid switch arm marks the high state; the dashed arm marks the alternative zero-volt state. They represent alternative positions, not simultaneous connections.
This is a useful dissipative PWM-to-voltage filter, resembling a buck whose energy-transfer inductance has been replaced by resistance. The low state is actively connected to zero. A switch that merely opens during the off interval is a different circuit. With a finite resistive load, the DC gain becomes R_L/(R+R_L) and the time constant becomes (R\parallel R_L)C.
Choose V_{\mathrm{in}}=5 V, D = 0.4, switching frequency 100 kHz, R = 10 Ω and C = 10 µF. Then:
T_s=10\ \mathrm{\mu s},\qquad \tau=100\ \mathrm{\mu s},\qquad f_c=\frac{1}{2\pi\tau}\approx1.592\ \mathrm{kHz}.
crumbs: 20  10. A switched RC: time-domain envelopes and Fourier harmonics

title: 10. A switched RC: time-domain envelopes and Fourier harmonics
section: 10.2 Exact piecewise time-domain response
text:
10.2 Exact piecewise time-domain response
During the high interval, starting at v_{\min}:
v_o(t)=V_{\mathrm{in}}+(v_{\min}-V_{\mathrm{in}})e^{-t/\tau}.
During the low interval, measuring local time from the falling edge:
v_o(t)=v_{\max}e^{-t/\tau}.
Both intervals have the same RC time constant in this circuit. There are upper and lower cycle envelopes, rather than two independent time constants. Define:
a=e^{-DT_s/\tau},\qquad b=e^{-(1-D)T_s/\tau}.
At periodic steady state:
v_{\max}=V_{\mathrm{in}}\frac{1-a}{1-ab},\qquad v_{\min}=b\,v_{\max}.
\Delta v_{\mathrm{pp}}=V_{\mathrm{in}}\frac{(1-a)(1-b)}{1-ab}.
The example gives minimum 1.9402 V, maximum 2.0602 V, mean 2.0000 V, and ripple 119.98 mV peak-to-peak.
For cycle-start samples, starting from arbitrary v_0:
v_{\min,n}=v_{\min,\infty}+(v_0-v_{\min,\infty})e^{-nT_s/\tau}.
The maxima follow a corresponding exponential envelope at the end of each high interval. The slow settling comes from the RC pole; the fast repetition is imposed by switching.
crumbs: 20  10. A switched RC: time-domain envelopes and Fourier harmonics

title: 10. A switched RC: time-domain envelopes and Fourier harmonics
section: 10.3 The same response in the frequency domain
text:
10.3 The same response in the frequency domain
Fourier analysis describes frequency content. For suitable signals the continuous transform is:
X(j\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-j\omega t}\,dt.
A periodic waveform is conveniently described by a Fourier series: a DC term plus harmonics at integer multiples of its fundamental frequency. Its transform can be interpreted as a line spectrum. For a stable LTI system, each sinusoidal component is multiplied by the corresponding complex frequency response: its magnitude changes and its phase shifts.
Evaluating a Laplace-domain transfer function on the imaginary axis gives that response where a bounded sinusoidal steady state exists.
For a unipolar rectangular pulse train, each high interval starting at the cycle boundary, the DC component and nth harmonic peak amplitude are:
V_0=DV_{\mathrm{in}},\qquad A_{n,\mathrm{in}}=\frac{2V_{\mathrm{in}}}{n\pi}|\sin(n\pi D)|.
Each harmonic has its own phase. Its output peak amplitude is:
A_{n,\mathrm{out}}=A_{n,\mathrm{in}}\left|H_{RC}(jn\omega_s)\right|,\qquad \omega_s=2\pi f_s.
\left|H_{RC}(jn\omega_s)\right|=\frac1{\sqrt{1+(n\omega_sRC)^2}}.
For the first harmonic, input peak amplitude is 3.027 V, attenuation magnitude is 0.01591, and output peak amplitude is approximately 48.18 mV. DC plus this harmonic predicts 96.35 mV peak-to-peak, which is smaller than the exact 119.98 mV because higher harmonics still shape the waveform. This is a useful exercise in the limits of a first-harmonic approximation.



Switched-RC startup, exact periodic ripple, first-harmonic approximation and harmonic amplitudes.


The complete response consists of a periodic forced solution plus the decaying natural response. In this linear circuit their difference from any other solution with the same input decays as exp(−t/τ). A switching harmonic is a forced frequency, not a second settling pole.
Power-electronics connection: the resistor dissipates energy while charging and discharging the capacitor. At high switching frequency relative to the RC corner, this example dissipates approximately V_{\mathrm{in}}^2D(1-D)/R=0.60 W even without an external load. Adding an energy-storage inductor changes the efficiency tradeoff fundamentally.

title: 10. A switched RC: time-domain envelopes and Fourier harmonics
section: 10.4 FFT: reading a sampled switching waveform
text:
10.4 FFT: reading a sampled switching waveform
An FFT is an efficient algorithm for computing a discrete Fourier transform. It analyses a finite set of samples; it is not a separate physical transform or a transfer function. Distinguish the acquisition sampling frequency from the converter’s switching frequency.
For N uniformly spaced samples taken at acquisition rate fₐ:
T_{\mathrm{record}}=\frac{N}{f_a},\qquad \Delta f=\frac{f_a}{N}=\frac{1}{T_{\mathrm{record}}}.
The record duration sets the spacing between FFT bins. A longer record gives finer bin spacing; increasing the sample rate at fixed duration does not. Zero-padding interpolates the sampled spectrum but does not resolve two tones that the original record cannot separate.
Apply it to the PWM example: acquire at 10 MS/s for 1 ms. There are 10,000 samples, 1 kHz bin spacing and exactly 100 periods of the 100 kHz switching waveform. The first switching harmonic is at bin 100. Compare its properly normalized peak amplitude with the analytical 3.027 V at the input and approximately 48.18 mV at the RC output.
Finite sampling represents the continuous waveform approximately; the analytical coefficients remain the reference.
For the usual unnormalized DFT, a coherent real sinusoid whose positive-frequency bin is k has peak amplitude:
A_{k,\mathrm{peak}}=\frac{2|X[k]|}{N}.
The DC bin uses |X[0]|/N. Do not double the Nyquist bin for an even-length real record. Divide a sinusoidal peak amplitude by √2 to obtain RMS. Do not apply this sine conversion to the total time-domain square-wave peak.
Four practical checks make an FFT meaningful:

Aliasing: components above the acquisition Nyquist frequency can fold into the record. Use an appropriate analogue bandwidth/anti-alias filter; sampling above twice the switching frequency alone does not capture all switching harmonics or edge ringing.
Leakage: a non-integer number of periods spreads a tone across bins. Coherent acquisition or a suitable window helps, with a main-lobe-width tradeoff.
Scaling: a window changes coherent tone gain and noise bandwidth. Apply the relevant normalization, and state whether the result is peak amplitude, RMS, power spectral density or dB relative to a reference.
Operating state: exclude startup if the goal is a periodic steady-state spectrum. The startup envelope otherwise contributes to the low-frequency content.

The NumPy FFT reference specifies its frequency ordering and normalization conventions. These conventions must also be checked when using an oscilloscope or another software package.
Choose the FFT record. A settled, coherent record makes harmonic amplitudes easier to interpret. A startup record retains transient information but mixes it with the forced response. Choose according to the question; changing the window does not change the circuit poles.

title: 10. A switched RC: time-domain envelopes and Fourier harmonics
section: 10.5 FFT as a tool for real-power analysis
text:
10.5 FFT as a tool for real-power analysis
An FFT can show which frequency components transfer average power. Acquire voltage and current at the same port, with synchronized samples, consistent probe polarity and a known channel delay. Use current into the positive-voltage terminal for absorbed power. Relative phase matters: multiplying only the voltage and current spectrum magnitudes loses the information that distinguishes real power from reactive exchange.
For a coherent periodic record, define complex peak phasors for each nonzero harmonic k as twice the corresponding unnormalized FFT bin divided by N. Retain their phases. Write the associated sinusoids as:
v_k(t)=\widehat V_k\cos(k\omega_0t+\theta_{v,k}),\qquad i_k(t)=\widehat I_k\cos(k\omega_0t+\theta_{i,k}).
The harmonic’s complex power and real-power contribution are:
S_k=\frac{1}{2}V_{k,\mathrm{peak}}I_{k,\mathrm{peak}}^*,\qquad P_k=\mathrm{Re}\{S_k\}=\frac{\widehat V_k\widehat I_k}{2}\cos(\theta_{v,k}-\theta_{i,k}).
The star means complex conjugate. With RMS phasors, divide each peak phasor by √2 and omit the factor 1/2 in their product. Average real power is the DC contribution plus the sum over matching nonzero harmonics:
P=V_{\mathrm{DC}}I_{\mathrm{DC}}+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}P_k.
Products between different harmonics average to zero over a common period. A harmonic with a 90° voltage–current phase difference contributes zero real power, even when both spectral amplitudes are large. A negative Pk indicates net returned power at that harmonic under the chosen sign convention. Section 6 explains why reactive current can nevertheless cause resistive heating elsewhere.
What does a spectral peak mean? The voltage/current amplitude spectra in section 10.4 use peak sinusoidal amplitudes, in V and A. Their RMS equivalents are smaller by √2. A plot of Pk instead shows average watts contributed by each harmonic, calculated from RMS phasors or equivalently half the conjugate product of peak phasors. Its line height is neither peak instantaneous power nor “RMS power.” Label the axes explicitly:







Spectral quantity
Line value and units




Voltage/current amplitude spectrum, peak convention
Sinusoidal peak amplitude, V peak / A peak


Voltage/current amplitude spectrum, RMS convention
Sinusoidal RMS amplitude, V RMS / A RMS


Real-power contribution by harmonic
Pk, W; sum the signed contributions including DC


Voltage or current auto power spectrum
Mean-square contribution, V² or A²; not electrical watts without a load relation


Voltage–current cross spectral density
Complex quantity in VA/Hz; integrate its correctly scaled real part to obtain average W



Worked check. Let v(t) = 12 + 2 cos(ωt) V and i(t) = 1 + 3 cos(ωt − 60°) A. The DC contribution is 12 W. The fundamental contributes (2 × 3 / 2) cos(60°) = 1.5 W, giving 13.5 W total. Multiplying the peak magnitudes alone gives 6 VA and misses both the factor 1/2 and the phase.
Multiplying the RMS magnitudes alone gives 3 VA; the phase factor is still needed.
Cross-check against the time record. For the usual unnormalized full, two-sided DFTs Xv and Xi, discrete Parseval gives an exact identity for the sampled record:
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}v[n]i[n]=\frac{1}{N^2}\mathrm{Re}\!\left\{\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}X_v[k]X_i[k]^*\right\}.
This full-spectrum expression needs no extra one-sided factor. If positive and negative bins are combined, double only the interior positive-frequency cross-products; DC and the Nyquist bin (for even N) remain undoubled. The peak-phasor 1/2 rule above applies to resolved sinusoids strictly below Nyquist. Leakage spreads a harmonic across bins, and windowing changes the weighting: do not apply a single-tone amplitude correction blindly to a broadband power estimate.
Check channel timing, bandwidth and spectral scaling, and compare the final spectral sum with mean(v × i).
Finally, FFT(v × i) is a different spectrum: it describes the DC and oscillating components of instantaneous power p(t), with its DC component equal to average power. Time-domain multiplication corresponds to frequency-domain convolution, whereas the conjugate cross-product above decomposes average power by voltage/current frequency. A peak in FFT(p) at twice a sinusoid’s frequency is power pulsation, not an additional average-power contribution.
See MathWorks’ harmonic power measurement and cross-spectrum estimator documentation.

title: 10. A switched RC: time-domain envelopes and Fourier harmonics
section: 10.6 A pulse train needs both a spectral view and an energy budget
text:
10.6 A pulse train needs both a spectral view and an energy budget
A periodic pulse load is not characterised by its repetition frequency alone. For current alternating between Ilow and Ihigh, with period T, pulse duration tp and duty ratio D = tp/T, its mean is Ilow + (Ihigh − Ilow)D. The nonzero peak harmonic amplitudes are:
\widehat I_n=2(I_{\mathrm{high}}-I_{\mathrm{low}})D\left|\frac{\sin(\pi nD)}{\pi nD}\right|,\qquad f_n=\frac{n}{T}.
An ideal infinite periodic train has discrete spectral lines, not a continuous white spectrum. Those lines can occupy a broad frequency range: pulse duration sets a sinc envelope, with its first null at 1/tp, while edge duration controls additional high-frequency roll-off. An ideal rectangular edge has no finite bandwidth; real finite edges suppress the higher harmonics without introducing a universal hard cutoff.
A finite burst broadens the lines through its time window, and slow workload modulation introduces additional low-frequency content. Use §10.4’s coherent sampling/scaling checks before interpreting an FFT.
Filtering and energy buffering answer connected but different questions. Impedance and transfer functions determine ripple, current sharing and propagation of disturbances. If upstream power is deliberately prevented from following the load, an energy store must supply the difference. Define positive cumulative deficit as energy withdrawn from the buffer, with all powers referred to the same port/conversion boundary:
E_{\mathrm{def}}(t)=\int_0^t[P_{\mathrm{load}}(u)-P_{\mathrm{source}}(u)]\,du.
For a lossless repeating cycle with no energy drift, the minimum usable storage swing is max(Edef) − min(Edef). Repetition rate and pulse width matter through both the spectrum and the area under the power deficit. If average supply power is insufficient, cumulative deficit grows cycle after cycle; no finite capacitor fixes that indefinitely.
An LC filter already stores energy. It can also perform buffering if its energy and allowed voltage/current excursions are sufficient. The point is not that one must always add a battery to a filter, but that an EMC attenuation calculation alone does not qualify millisecond-scale energy delivery, hold-up or recharge. Section 16.25 connects a pulse train, capacitor sizing and Infineon’s AI-PSU energy-buffer example.

title: 11.1 R, L and C on logarithmic axes
text:
In sinusoidal steady state, phasors turn differentiation into multiplication by jω. Use \omega=2\pi f and distinguish peak phasors from RMS phasors consistently.
z=a+jb=|z|e^{j\varphi},\qquad |z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2},\qquad \varphi=\operatorname{atan2}(b,a).
Complex multiplication multiplies magnitudes and adds phases; complex division divides magnitudes and subtracts phases. This is the arithmetic behind impedance dividers and transfer functions.

For impedance magnitude, a logarithmic Ω axis avoids ambiguity. A dB impedance plot needs a reference, such as 20 log₁₀(|Z|/1 Ω). A transfer-function gain plot instead uses a dimensionless ratio. Adding impedance magnitudes generally gives the wrong answer: sum complex impedances in series, or complex admittances in parallel.
Reactance-chart exercise from the lesson. At 10 MHz, estimate the magnitudes for an ideal 1 nH inductor and an ideal 100 nF capacitor, first from a reactance chart and then by calculation:
|Z_L|=2\pi fL\approx0.0628\ \Omega=62.8\ \mathrm{m\Omega},\qquad |Z_C|=\frac{1}{2\pi fC}\approx0.159\ \Omega=159\ \mathrm{m\Omega}.
These answers are impedances in milliohms, not currents in milliamperes. Increase frequency by one decade: the ideal inductive reactance becomes ten times larger and the ideal capacitive reactance ten times smaller. Use the chart to build this intuition, then include ESR and ESL for a real capacitor. The divider and current-sharing equations of section 4.1 explain how these impedances affect decoupling; neither reactance alone gives an attenuation value.



Ideal R/L/C impedance slopes and a real capacitor’s transition through self-resonance.


The real-capacitor example uses 100 nF, 20 mΩ ESR and 1 nH ESL. Its self-resonance is approximately 15.92 MHz; below it the impedance is mainly capacitive, near it ESR sets the minimum, and above it ESL dominates. These are illustrative fixed component values, not a particular capacitor’s measured curve.

title: 11.2 Series resonator: an impedance minimum
text:
For a series R–L–C network:



Series and parallel RLC one-port networks, with the stated series and shunt loss models and their resonance values.


Z_s=R_s+j\left(\omega L-\frac1{\omega C}\right),\qquad \omega_0=\frac1{\sqrt{LC}}.
At resonance the reactances cancel, so the input impedance is R_s. Below resonance the network is capacitive; above resonance it is inductive. Individual L and C voltages may be much larger than the input because the reactive voltages cancel at the port.
Q_s=\frac{\omega_0L}{R_s}=\frac1{\omega_0CR_s}.
crumbs: 23  11.2 Series resonator: an impedance minimum

title: 11.3 Parallel resonator: an impedance maximum
text:
For an ideal L and C in parallel with an explicit shunt loss R_p:
The parallel circuit is shown alongside the series network in section 11.2; all three branches connect across the same port terminals a and b.
Y_p=\frac1{R_p}+j\left(\omega C-\frac1{\omega L}\right),\qquad Z_p=\frac1{Y_p}.
At resonance the susceptances cancel and the input impedance is R_p. Below resonance it is inductive; above resonance it is capacitive. Large inductor and capacitor currents can circulate internally despite relatively small input current.
Q_p=\frac{R_p}{\omega_0L}=\omega_0CR_p.
With L = 100 µH and C = 1 µF, resonance is 15.915 kHz. Choose R_s=1 Ω for the series example and R_p=1 kΩ for the parallel example; the respective quality factors are 10 and 100. These are distinct loss models, rather than equivalent descriptions of one physical lossy component.



Series RLC impedance minimum and parallel RLC impedance maximum for the defined component values.


Why this matters: a capacitor with ESL behaves as a series resonator and becomes inductive above self-resonance. Several decoupling branches can create parallel antiresonance peaks. These peaks can violate a PDN target impedance. An EMI filter’s attenuation also depends on source/load impedances and damping, not only its nominal L and C.

title: 11.4 Two-port recall: Z, Y, transmission and scattering matrices
text:
Source and load are part of the voltage-transfer calculation
A two-port network (quadripole) has a voltage and current at each port; it is not a two-terminal dipole. Use RMS phasors, both port currents entering the network and port voltages measured from their stated reference terminals. These signs must be fixed before converting matrices.
In ABCD, A and D are dimensionless, B is in Ω and C in S. The current −I₂ leaves port 2, so it becomes the entering port-1 current of the next cascaded stage. Here T means voltage/current ABCD, not the different chain-scattering matrix that some RF texts also call T.
Matrix multiplication is valid for these cascade variables; multiplying Z matrices is not a cascade rule. See Michael Steer’s two-port definitions and interconnections.
Terminate port 2 in ZL, so I₂ = −V₂/ZL, and drive port 1 from a Thévenin voltage Vs with series Zs. For transmission parameters:
\frac{V_2}{V_s}=\frac{Z_L}{AZ_L+B+Z_s(CZ_L+D)},\qquad Z_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{AZ_L+B}{CZ_L+D}.
For a valid finite Z representation, the same loaded voltage transfer is:
\frac{V_2}{V_s}=\frac{Z_{21}Z_L}{(Z_{11}+Z_s)(Z_{22}+Z_L)-Z_{12}Z_{21}}.
These are circuit voltage ratios with specified source/load, not unconditional properties of an isolated block. When the first stage’s source is deactivated, its output impedance in the ABCD convention is (B + ZsD)/(A + ZsC). Section 16.22 uses this impedance to explain interstage loading.
crumbs: 25  11.4 Two-port recall: Z, Y, transmission and scattering matrices

title: 11.4 Two-port recall: Z, Y, transmission and scattering matrices
section: Scattering: choose the reference impedance and keep phase
text:
Scattering: choose the reference impedance and keep phase
For an equal real positive reference resistance R₀ at both ports and RMS phasors:
a_k=\frac{V_k+R_0I_k}{2\sqrt{R_0}},\qquad b_k=\frac{V_k-R_0I_k}{2\sqrt{R_0}}.
The absorbed port power is |ak|² − |bk|² in watts. S₂₁ is b₂/a₁ with a₂ = 0, meaning a matched termination at port 2. It is not generally V₂/V₁ or V₂/Vs. A 50 Ω reference is a convention, not a statement that the physical two-port input and output impedances are both 50 Ω. Different reference impedances require the corresponding normalization.
For the equal-reference case:
S_{21}=\frac{2}{A+B/R_0+CR_0+D}.
With source and load both R₀, V₂/Vs = S₂₁/2 for these RMS voltage definitions. The factor two reflects the source’s available incident wave; it does not mean an ideal through connection loses half its available power. For matched source/load, |S₂₁|² gives transmitted power divided by available source power. General mismatches need the complete S matrix and terminations. See Steer’s scattering definitions and parameter conversions.
Recall questions: Which currents are held at zero to obtain Z₁₁ and Z₂₁? Why does ABCD use −I₂? Why do Y matrices add in a true parallel connection? What does a₂ = 0 mean physically? Finally, does every ideal two-port admit every parameter representation? Section 16.21 supplies the counterexamples; section 16.22 supplies the filter riddle. Section 16.37 applies the same conversions to a three-port LISN and separates current partition from power partition. This is optional recall/reading, not an addition to the compulsory 180-minute route.
crumbs: 25  11.4 Two-port recall: Z, Y, transmission and scattering matrices

title: 11.5 Miller theorem: a bridge impedance seen through voltage gain
text:
Connect a bridge impedance Zb between port nodes V₁ and V₂. Let Yb = 1/Zb and let Av(s) = V₂/V₁ be the actual loaded small-signal node-voltage ratio. The bridge current entering at node 1 is:
I_{b1}=Y_b(V_1-V_2)=Y_b(1-A_v)V_1.
Hence its input contribution is admittance multiplied by 1 − Av, or equivalently impedance divided by 1 − Av:
Y_{\mathrm{M,in}}=Y_b(1-A_v),\qquad Z_{\mathrm{M,in}}=\frac{Z_b}{1-A_v}.
At node 2, for Av ≠ 0, the corresponding contribution is Yb(1 − 1/Av), or Zb/(1 − 1/Av). These are the two grounded Miller equivalents. The result is not limited to capacitors: an ideal 100 kΩ bridge with Av = −9 contributes 10 kΩ at the input and 90 kΩ at the output.
Connection to a π two-port. Include input/output shunt admittances Yi and Yo around the bridge:
          Zb
V1 o------[]------o V2
   |              |
   Yi             Yo
   |              |
   +-- reference--+

Y = [ Yi + Yb    -Yb   ]
    [   -Yb     Yo + Yb ]
Substituting V₂ = AvV₁ into the first row gives Yin = Yi + Yb(1 − Av). The bridge alone has the singular Y matrix discussed in §16.21, yet its port currents are well defined. The gain relation supplied by the surrounding active circuit lets us evaluate the admittance seen along that operating condition.
For a bridge capacitor Cb and approximately real, frequency-independent gain over the band of interest, the equivalent input capacitance is Cb(1 − Av). Inverting gain −9 gives 10Cb. A follower with Av approaching +1 suppresses the bridge current, the basis of bootstrapping; exact +1 makes this branch’s input admittance zero.
Non-inverting gain above one can produce a negative equivalent capacitance, requiring the active circuit and a stability analysis. With complex, frequency-dependent Av, use the complete admittance expression rather than assuming a constant physical capacitor.
The replacement is conditional on the stated voltage ratio. It is not a universal diagonal two-port matrix valid when V₁ and V₂ are varied independently. If adding the bridge changes gain, solve for the loaded gain consistently; do not substitute an unloaded gain without checking the approximation. See MIT 6.776, lecture 7, Miller effect, slides 8–10. Section 16.23 gives the worked riddle.

title: 11.6 Feedback changes input impedance: distinguish the internal and external ports
text:
An op amp’s differential input resistance is between its + and − inputs. The complete amplifier’s source-facing input impedance is measured at the external signal input relative to its reference. They need not be equal. Model a voltage-feedback op amp as a two-port: port 1 is the differential input (voltage vd, current id entering + and leaving −); port 2 is the output relative to reference, with current io entering the device.
A unilateral voltage-amplifier model is:
[ vd ] = [ Rdiff       0   ] [ id ]
[ vo ]   [ A(s) Rdiff Rout ] [ io ]
It describes vd = Rdiff id and vo = A(s)vd + Rout io, without assuming Rdiff infinite. The following exercise uses Rout = 0, an ideal controlled output voltage source; its Z matrix is valid but singular, linking back to §16.21. The input port’s negative terminal is the − input, not automatically circuit ground.
In a non-inverting connection, the source drives + while negative feedback drives − close to the same voltage. The voltage across Rdiff can therefore be tiny even when the input voltage relative to ground is appreciable. This is a resistive bootstrapping effect, related to §11.5.
A large stable loop gain can make the source-facing input impedance much larger than Rdiff. The infinite value belongs to an ideal limiting model, not to every real circuit or frequency.
In the conventional inverting connection, + is grounded and the source drives − through an external resistor. Feedback holds the summing node near reference, so the source sees approximately that external resistor, rather than an infinite impedance. Negative feedback does not increase every driving-point impedance in every topology. Analog Devices’ op-amp introduction gives the familiar ideal configurations; §16.24 derives their behaviour without an infinite differential-resistance assumption.
crumbs: 27  11.6 Feedback changes input impedance: distinguish the internal and external ports

title: 11.7 Common and differential modes: choose a more useful vector basis
text:
Orthogonal projections onto sum and difference
Two conductor measurements can hide a simple physical pattern. The common-mode direction is (1, 1): both conductors move together. The differential-mode direction is (1, −1): they move oppositely. These directions are orthogonal, so any two-component voltage or current vector has a unique sum of the two patterns. This is a change of coordinates, not an extra physical current or a filter that removes noise.
Define the ports first. Take two conductors at the same cable cross-section. Measure v1 and v2 relative to the same reference, and orient i1 and i2 in the same longitudinal direction. A normal outgoing/return current then has i1 = −i2. Do not copy the entering currents at opposite ends of an ABCD two-port into these equations without checking their arrows.
A conductor pair at one reference plane supplies two coordinates; a complete input/output differential interconnect generally needs four single-ended ports to retain both modes at both ends.
Normalize the basis vectors to unit length. For either voltage or current, the modal coordinates are
\widetilde v_c=\frac{v_1+v_2}{\sqrt{2}},\qquad \widetilde v_d=\frac{v_1-v_2}{\sqrt{2}},\qquad \widetilde i_c=\frac{i_1+i_2}{\sqrt{2}},\qquad \widetilde i_d=\frac{i_1-i_2}{\sqrt{2}}.
In matrix form:
Geometrically the axes lie at ±45° to the original conductor axes. With the displayed signs and CM-first ordering, det Q = −1: strictly this is an orthogonal basis change, including an orientation reversal, rather than a pure rotation matrix. Reversing one modal axis gives a rotation convention without changing the physics. The useful insight is the projection onto the symmetric and antisymmetric directions.
For measured currents (3, −1) A, the normalized coordinates are √2 A and 2√2 A. Reconstruct the physical conductor contributions:
The coordinates tell us how much of each basis vector is present; the two vectors on the right show the corresponding currents in the original conductors.

title: 11.7 Common and differential modes: choose a more useful vector basis
text:
Q = (1/sqrt(2)) [ 1   1 ]
                [ 1  -1 ]

v_modal = Q v_conductor       i_modal = Q i_conductor
Q Q^T = I                    v_conductor = Q^T v_modal


(3, -1) A = (1, 1) A + (2, -2) A
             CM          DM

title: 11.7 Common and differential modes: choose a more useful vector basis
section: Engineering conventions: preserve power as well as signs
text:
Engineering conventions: preserve power as well as signs
Common circuit conventions use average CM voltage and full differential voltage:

v_{CM}=\frac{v_1+v_2}{2},\qquad v_{DM}=v_1-v_2.

Choose their power-conjugate currents as total CM current and differential loop current:

i_{CM}=i_1+i_2,\qquad i_{DM}=\frac{i_1-i_2}{2}.

Then reconstruction and instantaneous power are

v_1=v_{CM}+\frac{v_{DM}}{2},\qquad v_2=v_{CM}-\frac{v_{DM}}{2},\qquad i_1=\frac{i_{CM}}{2}+i_{DM},\qquad i_2=\frac{i_{CM}}{2}-i_{DM}.


v_1i_1+v_2i_2=v_{CM}i_{CM}+v_{DM}i_{DM}.

The same identity holds for complex power with RMS phasors when current is conjugated. The orthonormal convention also preserves power, using its normalized voltages and currents directly. The engineering convention rescales voltage and current differently; it is not the same Q applied unchanged to both.
Some EMC references call half the conductor-current sum the CM current per conductor. State the convention before comparing values or power formulas. Analog Devices’ common-mode explanation uses the average of the conductor voltages for common-mode voltage.
Power recall: with v = (12, 8) V and i = (3, −1) A, vCM = 10 V, vDM = 4 V, iCM = 2 A and iDM = 2 A. Original power is 12 × 3 + 8 × (−1) = 28 W. Modal power is 10 × 2 + 4 × 2 = 20 W + 8 W.
A coordinate transformation has changed neither the circuit nor its power.
crumbs: 28  11.7 Common and differential modes: choose a more useful vector basis

title: 11.7 Common and differential modes: choose a more useful vector basis
section: Symmetry explains when the modes decouple
text:
Symmetry explains when the modes decouple
For a conductor-domain relation v = Zi, using orthonormal coordinates gives

\widetilde Z=QZQ^T.

A reciprocal, exchange-symmetric two-conductor network has the following form:
Z = [ zs  zm ]          Q Z Q^T = [ zs+zm    0   ]
    [ zm  zs ]                    [   0    zs-zm ]
Its symmetric and antisymmetric directions are eigenvectors. CM current creates only CM voltage, and DM current only DM voltage. The basis change always exists, but decoupling requires the circuit symmetry. For example:
Balanced:    Z = [30 10] ohm     normalized modal Z = [40  0] ohm
                 [10 30]                             [ 0 20]

Unbalanced:  Z = [35 10] ohm     normalized modal Z = [40  5] ohm
                 [10 25]                             [ 5 20]
The off-diagonal 5 Ω terms expose mode conversion. In the engineering normalization above, these modal matrices become diag(20, 40) Ω and [[20, 5], [5, 40]] Ω respectively. Modal impedance numbers depend on normalization, while reconstructed conductor voltages and currents agree. For the unbalanced network, a pure differential loop current of 1 A, i = (1, −1) A, gives v = (25, −15) V: vDM = 40 V and vCM = 5 V.
Differential excitation has created a common-mode response.



A conductor-current vector decomposed along common and differential directions, and modal impedance matrices showing balanced decoupling versus imbalance-induced conversion.
crumbs: 28  11.7 Common and differential modes: choose a more useful vector basis

title: 11.7 Common and differential modes: choose a more useful vector basis
section: Why this helps EMC analysis, and where the PCA analogy stops
text:
Why this helps EMC analysis, and where the PCA analogy stops
A current probe enclosing both conductors responds to their signed sum: the differential components cancel and the remaining net current is iCM in the stated convention. A nonzero net conductor current needs a return elsewhere, such as chassis or parasitic capacitance. The basis makes this external return requirement visible; it does not identify that return path by itself or predict radiation from a modal amplitude alone.
Common and differential modes can contain useful signals as well as disturbances.
Section 16.27 is a concrete example. Balanced interwinding capacitances preserve symmetry: secondary CM injection gives primary CM motion with zero primary differential voltage in the stated fixture. Unequal capacitances introduce mode conversion. Keeping only a differential transformer model would hide that excitation and response.
The analogy with principal component analysis (PCA) is useful because both project vectors onto a new orthogonal basis. In CM/DM analysis the basis is fixed by conductor exchange symmetry and physical interpretation. PCA learns directions from the data covariance and orders them by explained variance; see the scikit-learn PCA guide.
If a real two-channel covariance matrix has equal diagonal entries, the sum/difference directions form an eigenbasis. With nonzero cross-covariance these directions are fixed up to signs and ordering; with zero cross-covariance the equal eigenvalues allow any orthonormal basis. Arbitrary data need not have CM/DM as their principal components.
A change of basis retaining both modes loses no information. Discarding one mode is an additional approximation.
Recall questions: What current arrows make normal supply/return current purely differential? Why is vCM an average while iCM here is a sum? Does a diagonal modal matrix follow merely from changing coordinates? Which off-diagonal term describes CM excitation producing DM response? Finally, what symmetry must a two-channel covariance have for its PCA directions to coincide with CM/DM?
scripts/common_differential_basis.py exports figure 74 and common-differential-basis-checks.json. Checks cover inverse reconstruction, instantaneous and complex-power invariance, and agreement between conductor-domain and both modal impedance conventions. This is an algebraic teaching example linking two-port recall to EMC and the transformer fixture.

title: 12. Bode, LC filtering and Class-D amplifiers
text:
The voltage- or current-transfer magnitude in decibels is:
G_{\mathrm{dB}}=20\log_{10}|H(j\omega)|.
A power ratio uses 10 log₁₀ instead. The two agree when the power ratio is the square of the amplitude ratio, as for voltages across equal resistances. In a factorized transfer function, each first-order pole contributes −20 dB/decade above its corner; each first-order zero contributes +20 dB/decade.
For ordinary left-half-plane factors, their phase contributions tend toward −90° and +90°, respectively. Add gain contributions in dB and add the phases; check the transition regions with the exact response.
crumbs: 29  12. Bode, LC filtering and Class-D amplifiers

title: 12.1 One pole: RC
text:
For the unloaded RC low-pass:
H_{RC}(j\omega)=\frac1{1+j\omega RC}.
At the corner, magnitude is 1/√2, or −3.010 dB, and phase is −45°. Well above the corner, the magnitude falls at −20 dB/decade, and phase approaches −90°. A decade means a frequency ratio of ten; an octave means a factor of two.

title: 12.2 Two poles: loaded LC
text:
Take an ideal series L, followed by C in parallel with a resistive load R. Ignore inductor resistance for this model:



Loaded LC low-pass: series inductor, shunt capacitor and parallel resistive load, with the Class-D example values.


H_{LC}(s)=\frac1{LCs^2+(L/R)s+1}.
\omega_0=\frac1{\sqrt{LC}},\qquad Q=R\sqrt{\frac CL},\qquad \zeta=\frac1{2Q}.
Far above its poles, this low-pass falls at −40 dB/decade and its phase approaches −180°. The natural frequency is not automatically a −3 dB corner for every Q. For the Butterworth choice Q = 1/√2, it is the −3 dB corner. Critical damping instead means Q = 0.5; these are different responses.
crumbs: 31  12.2 Two poles: loaded LC

title: 12.3 Why Class-D uses LC filtering
text:
A Class-D output stage creates a switching waveform whose modulation represents the desired audio. A suitable LC network passes the audio band and attenuates switching components. Ideal L and C exchange stored energy; their filtering does not require a large dissipative series resistor. Real losses remain in winding resistance, core loss, capacitor ESR, switches and the load.
Why not a Class-A amplifier? A Class-A stage biases its transistor in the middle of the output characteristic (section 13), so it carries a standing current even in silence. Predict its best efficiency before reading on.
For a single 24 V supply driving an 8 Ω resistive load directly, the bias is half the supply across the load: I_q = 24 V / (2 · 8 Ω) = 1.5 A. The supply always delivers 24 V × 1.5 A = 36 W. The largest undistorted sine gives the load (12\ \mathrm V)^2/(2\cdot8\ \Omega) = 9 W. The theoretical maximum is therefore 25 %, and it falls further with quieter music, because the 36 W stays. Coupling the load through an inductor or transformer lets the collector swing to twice the supply and raises the ceiling to 50 %. Class B, with two transistors each conducting half the cycle, reaches \pi/4 = 78.5 % at full sine output, at the price of crossover distortion; Class AB trades some of that efficiency back for linearity.
Every one of these classes keeps the transistor in the region where voltage and current coexist. Class D leaves it: the transistor only switches, and the LC filter rebuilds the signal. Practical Class-D amplifiers reach about 90 % at moderate power. The cost is the filter, switching-frequency EMI and distortion from dead time. Keep Class A or AB when the power is small and linearity matters more than heat, as in a headphone driver. Choose Class D when battery life or heat sinks set the limit.
Worked single-ended equivalent: for a 4 Ω resistive load, a 40 kHz Butterworth corner requires approximately:
L=\frac{R}{Q\omega_0}=22.51\ \mathrm{\mu H},\qquad C=\frac{Q}{R\omega_0}=0.7034\ \mathrm{\mu F}.
At 20 kHz the LC gain is approximately −0.263 dB. At 400 kHz it is approximately −40.0 dB, a voltage factor near 0.01. A one-pole RC with the same nominal corner gives only about −20.0 dB at 400 kHz. These are individual-frequency gains, not a guarantee that all output ripple or EMI has those attenuations.



Bode magnitude and phase of RC and Butterworth LC low-pass filters, with audio and switching frequencies marked.


The load supplies damping in this simple LC model. Changing speaker impedance changes Q; an open load removes that damping and can produce severe peaking in the idealized model. Actual speakers are frequency-dependent loads. Bridge-tied-load and different PWM modulation schemes require the correct differential/common-mode equivalents; do not copy these single-ended L/C values into a bridge without conversion.
Some Class-D products use filterless arrangements for specific loads and cable lengths. See TI’s LC filter design note.
RC or LC? LC avoids a large dissipative series resistor, but adds resonance and load-dependent damping. RC is simpler when its voltage drop and loss are acceptable. Check attenuation, load range and current stress before choosing either for a power output.
crumbs: 32  12.3 Why Class-D uses LC filtering

title: 12.4 Feedback and stability
text:
Bode stability checks: which curve crosses which reference?
Refresh the ideal op-amp concept: high open-loop gain makes the input error small under stable negative feedback, provided the output is not saturated and the amplifier stays within its operating limits. A regulator compares a divided output voltage with a reference and drives a pass device or switching modulator.
For a conventional negative-feedback loop with forward gain A and feedback factor β:
H_{\mathrm{closed}}=\frac{A}{1+A\beta},\qquad T=A\beta.
The loop gain T, rather than an arbitrary output-filter gain, is used to discuss gain crossover and stability margins. At a unity-gain crossover, phase margin is 180° plus the loop phase under the conventional sign convention. A margin near 45–60° is a common design starting point, not a universal requirement or a complete stability proof. Multiple crossovers, right-half-plane dynamics, sampling and delays can require more careful analysis.
Here write the loop transfer as L(s) = A(s)β(s), to distinguish it from inductance. Negative feedback gives the characteristic condition 1 + L(s) = 0. In Bode plots, unity loop gain is 0 dB, not zero linear gain. At each gain crossover ωgc, |L(jωgc)| = 1. The usual local phase-margin quantity, on the relevant continuous phase branch, is
PM=180^{\circ}+\angle L(j\omega_{gc}).
At a phase crossing ωpc where the loop phase is −180° modulo 360°, the corresponding gain-margin factor and decibel value are
GM=\frac{1}{|L(j\omega_{pc})|},\qquad GM_{dB}=-20\log_{10}|L(j\omega_{pc})|.
For an already stable conventional loop, these indicate gain-only or phase-only perturbations that can bring the frequency response to the critical point. They are not independent universal bounds on arbitrary simultaneous model changes. With multiple crossings, inspect all crossings and establish the nominal stability first. MathWorks’ all-margin reference distinguishes all crossover margins from the nominal closed-loop stability result.
A downward −20 dB/decade crossing is a useful loop-shaping target, not a stability theorem. One dominant minimum-phase pole contributes roughly this slope and about −90° phase in its asymptotic region, motivating the heuristic. But local magnitude slope does not specify total loop phase. Other poles/zeros, right-half-plane zeros and delays can change that phase, and a later resonance can return the magnitude above unity.
Even a delay has unit magnitude while adding phase −ωτ. The rule therefore cannot certify a loop from one short segment of its magnitude plot.

title: 12.4 Feedback and stability
section: Nyquist: count the whole loop around the critical point
text:
Nyquist: count the whole loop around the critical point
For the scalar loop, plot the complex locus of L(jω). The critical point is −1 + j0 because it makes 1 + L vanish. Assume first a proper rational loop with no poles on the imaginary axis and no hidden unstable cancellations. The full Nyquist contour traverses the imaginary axis from −j∞ to +j∞ and closes through the right half-plane.
For a strictly proper loop the large-arc image tends to the origin. Include negative frequencies; for real coefficients they are the conjugate of the positive-frequency trace.
Use this explicit sign convention: N is net clockwise encirclements of −1, P is the number of open-loop RHP poles, and Z is the number of closed-loop RHP characteristic roots, counted with multiplicity. The argument principle gives

N=Z-P,\qquad Z=P+N.

If P = 0, closed-loop stability requires zero net encirclements and no boundary roots. If P > 0, stability instead requires N = −P: the necessary net encirclements are counterclockwise. “Never encircle −1” is therefore a special case, not the general rule. Poles on the imaginary axis, including an integrator at zero, require a suitably indented contour.
A passage through −1 needs boundary analysis; it is not a positive stability margin. See Swarthmore’s Nyquist stability derivation.
For a finite-dimensional minimal closed-loop realization, Z = 0 with no imaginary-axis roots establishes asymptotic stability. Internal modes hidden by unstable cancellation still require the full-state check of §16.33. The Nyquist plot here is unrelated to the Nyquist sampling frequency in FFT discussions.

title: 12.4 Feedback and stability
section: How Bode, Nyquist, Fourier and Laplace relate
text:
How Bode, Nyquist, Fourier and Laplace relate
The parallel is visual rather than an equality of mathematical extensions. Complete Bode magnitude and phase and the Nyquist locus encode the same loop-frequency values:

L(j\omega)=10^{M_{dB}(\omega)/20}\,[\cos\phi(\omega)+j\sin\phi(\omega)].

Use radians for φ inside sine/cosine. Bode separates log-magnitude and phase versus frequency; Nyquist places each value in the complex L plane, making winding around −1 visible. Keeping both Bode curves, frequency labels and the appropriate phase branch does not discard the information in L(jω). Keeping only local magnitude slope does.







Description
What it shows




Fourier/frequency response
Behaviour along imaginary frequency s = jω where the relevant response exists


Laplace
Complex frequency s = σ + jω, natural modes and convergence (§9.1)


Bode
Magnitude and phase of the frequency response on separate frequency axes


Nyquist stability plot
The image of the frequency/contour path in the complex loop-gain plane, combined with the known open-loop RHP pole count



Nyquist does not add the σ coordinate to a Bode plot. Its stability power comes from the argument principle and the open-loop pole count, while Laplace supplies the complex-frequency framework. A finite measured sweep needs adequate bandwidth/resolution and a model of omitted dynamics; changing the display alone does not establish those assumptions. Section 16.34 makes the distinction concrete with verified counterexamples.

title: 12.4 Feedback and stability
section: Digital control: the actuator applies a command after the measurement
text:
Digital control: the actuator applies a command after the measurement
A pure delay multiplies a continuous loop by exp(−sTd). Its magnitude is one on jω, but its phase contribution is −360 fTd degrees. Thus it can erase phase margin without changing the magnitude plot. A held average PWM command also contributes a baseband hold effect, often approximated by half an update period of delay.
The acquisition, computation, register-update schedule and modulator must be distinguished; sampling alone does not have one universal fixed delay.
Finite ADC/PWM resolution introduces another effect that cannot be certified from the unquantized loop’s margins alone. A stable linear model can coexist with a steady quantization cycle if the controller cannot hold an attainable actuator level inside its measured zero-error band. Section 16.36 contrasts static ADC error, PWM-induced cycling and a finer-resolution remedy.
Use the actual discrete plant/controller model when the crossover is a significant fraction of the update rate. A discrete closed loop is asymptotically stable when all its state eigenvalues lie strictly inside the unit circle, not merely in the left half of the z plane.
The mapping z = exp(sTs) connects the continuous and discrete stability regions. Section 16.35 supplies an exact sampled/held counterexample and separates it from the approximate Bode delay budget. Section 16.31 treats a different sampled mechanism: the inner peak-current comparator’s period-to-period instability.
Classroom question: why might adding a capacitor change stability? It changes the plant’s poles and possibly ESR zeros, affecting loop gain and phase. More capacitance is not automatically a better control design.

title: 12.5 Negative incremental resistance and Middlebrook’s input-filter criterion
text:
Start with a regulated load. Suppose a converter holds its output power constant and its efficiency is approximately constant over a small input-voltage change. Its input power P is then approximately constant over frequencies where regulation can maintain that behaviour:
I_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{P}{V_{\mathrm{in}}},\qquad \frac{dI_{\mathrm{in}}}{dV_{\mathrm{in}}}=-\frac{P}{V_{\mathrm{in}}^2}.
The static DC ratio and the incremental resistance have equal magnitudes and opposite signs in this idealization:
R_{\mathrm{static}}=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}}{I_{\mathrm{in}}}=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}^2}{P}>0,\qquad r_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{dV_{\mathrm{in}}}{dI_{\mathrm{in}}}=-\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}^2}{P}<0.
Example: 60 W input power at 12 V means 5 A input current, a positive static ratio of 2.4 Ω, and incremental input resistance −2.4 Ω. A 0.1 V input drop calls for approximately 41.7 mA more current in the linearized model. The load still absorbs positive average power. Negative incremental resistance describes the response of a perturbation, not reversal of the DC power flow.
This is why a regulated converter connected after an LC input filter can remove damping: a small decrease in filter-output voltage makes the load demand more current, which can reinforce the voltage decrease. An ordinary positive resistor reduces its current when its voltage falls. The constant-power approximation is local and bandwidth-limited; startup, dropout, current limiting, changing efficiency and high-frequency device/input-capacitor behaviour require the actual converter impedance.
Define the interface before comparing impedances:



Middlebrook source–converter interface and the directions used to define source output impedance Zs and converter input impedance Zin.


Zs is the small-signal output impedance looking back into the source and filter, with their independent source deactivated and the converter disconnected. Zin is the converter’s small-signal input impedance at the same interface, under its defined closed-loop operating conditions. Assign any boundary/input capacitor to one side consistently; do not count it twice. Use differential-mode port quantities for this example.
For a scalar source/load interface, the interaction factor is:
T_m(s)=\frac{Z_s(s)}{Z_{\mathrm{in}}(s)},\qquad F_{\mathrm{interface}}(s)=\frac{1}{1+T_m(s)}.
The denominator shows the potential instability at Tm = −1. With independently stable subsystems and a stable open interaction loop, a sufficient small-gain condition is:
\left|\frac{Z_s(j\omega)}{Z_{\mathrm{in}}(j\omega)}\right|<1.
Keeping source impedance well below converter input-impedance magnitude gives useful design margin and is commonly called the Middlebrook impedance-separation rule. For a general model the bound must hold across the relevant frequency range, with the remaining dynamics also accounted for. A comparison of DC resistances alone is insufficient: an input-filter resonance can make source impedance peak far above its DC value.
Magnitude-rule failure is not itself proof of instability. When the ratio reaches or exceeds unity, assess its phase and the Nyquist plot relative to −1, accounting for any right-half-plane poles of the open interaction loop. The full frequency-dependent impedances matter. This source/load interaction loop is also distinct from the converter’s internal voltage-control loop.
Classroom screening exercise: at a frequency where the 60 W / 12 V load can be approximated by −2.4 Ω, a source/filter output-impedance peak of 0.24 Ω gives |Tm| = 0.1, or −20 dB. A 4.8 Ω peak gives |Tm| = 2, or +6.02 dB; the conservative magnitude condition fails there, so phase/full-model analysis is needed.
The first value is a check at that frequency, not a certificate for the entire frequency range.
To reduce interaction, lower source impedance, damp the filter resonance, choose a suitable filter corner, and check the converter/input-capacitor combination. A series resistor provides damping but also DC loss. A properly designed series-RC damping branch across the filter output can add damping without the same continuous DC loss, since its capacitor blocks DC. Its values must be designed from the actual filter and load model.
This connects Thévenin → incremental resistance → parallel resonance → Bode/Nyquist → stable input filtering. Middlebrook’s original paper develops the interaction problem and emphasizes frequency-dependent converter behaviour. TI’s input-filter application note provides an application-oriented follow-up.
