title: 12.6 Worked LC input filter: unstable without added damping, stable with an RC branch
text:
A. Specify the circuit and the operating point
This is an optional worked extension to the two-session recap. We calculate the source output impedance, connect it to the converter’s incremental input impedance, and verify stability from the connected system’s poles. The plots use a local continuous-time constant-power model; they do not represent a switching-converter startup simulation or measured hardware.
The converter draws a constant input power of 60 W around a 12 V input operating point. It therefore draws 5 A and has incremental input resistance −2.4 Ω. Assume this approximation is valid around the filter interaction frequencies, roughly 1–2 kHz here. A physical design must use the actual converter input impedance and control dynamics outside that approximation.
The ideal source is 12.25 V, rather than 12 V, so that the 5 A DC drop across r leaves 12 V at the converter input. The 100 µF capacitor belongs to the source/filter side of the interface. Any real converter input capacitor must be included consistently in the chosen model; it is not silently added a second time here.
“Without added damping” retains the 0.05 Ω resistance; the LC circuit is not literally lossless. The input-filter natural frequency and impedance scale are:
f_0=\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}=1.592\ \mathrm{kHz},\qquad \sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}=1\ \Omega.

title: 12.6 Worked LC input filter: unstable without added damping, stable with an RC branch
section: B. Calculate the source impedance without the added branch
text:
B. Calculate the source impedance without the added branch
Deactivate the independent voltage source and look back from the converter port. The series r–L branch is then in parallel with C:
Z_{s,0}(s)=\frac{r+sL}{1+srC+s^2LC}.
At DC its impedance is just 0.05 Ω, apparently much smaller than 2.4 Ω. Near the filter resonance, however, the inductive and capacitive admittances nearly cancel. The source impedance peaks at approximately 20.025 Ω at 1.592 kHz.
For the constant-power incremental model:
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=-R_n=-2.4\ \Omega,\qquad T_m(s)=-\frac{Z_s(s)}{R_n}.
The peak magnitude ratio is approximately 8.34, or +18.43 dB. This fails the sufficient magnitude condition. We still need the phase or the connected-system poles to establish the actual stability verdict.
crumbs: 35  12.6 Worked LC input filter: unstable without added damping, stable with an RC branch

title: 12.6 Worked LC input filter: unstable without added damping, stable with an RC branch
section: C. Verify that this case really is unstable
text:
C. Verify that this case really is unstable
The interaction denominator is 1 − Zs/Rn. Substituting the source impedance gives the characteristic equation:
LCs^2+\left(rC-\frac{L}{R_n}\right)s+\left(1-\frac{r}{R_n}\right)=0.
With the stated values, its normalized form is:
s^2-3666.67s+9.79167\times10^7=0.
The poles are:
s_{1,2}\approx+1833\ \pm j\,9724\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}.
The positive real part means that a small oscillatory perturbation grows. This establishes instability of the connected linearized model, beyond merely failing the magnitude screen. Its growth-envelope time constant is approximately 1/1833 = 0.545 ms.
For this particular second-order model, both non-leading polynomial coefficients must be positive. That gives the useful conditions:
r<R_n,\qquad rC>\frac{L}{R_n}.
The second condition would require r > 0.417 Ω here. Raising the main-path resistance to obtain damping would dissipate more than 10.4 W at 5 A, even at that boundary, and changes the required source voltage. This motivates damping that does not carry the full DC load current.
crumbs: 35  12.6 Worked LC input filter: unstable without added damping, stable with an RC branch

title: 12.6 Worked LC input filter: unstable without added damping, stable with an RC branch
section: D. Add the series-RC damping branch
text:
D. Add the series-RC damping branch
Connect 1 Ω in series with 400 µF from the filter-output node to return. The resistor is not placed directly across the DC bus and is not added in series with the 5 A load path. The branch admittance is:
Y_{\mathrm{damp}}(s)=\frac{sC_{\mathrm{damp}}}{1+sR_{\mathrm{damp}}C_{\mathrm{damp}}}.
The new source impedance is:
Z_{s,d}(s)=\left[\frac{1}{r+sL}+sC+\frac{sC_{\mathrm{damp}}}{1+sR_{\mathrm{damp}}C_{\mathrm{damp}}}\right]^{-1}.
At DC the ideal damping capacitor blocks current. Around the LC resonance the branch supplies a real admittance that damps the impedance peak. With these values its own RC corner is approximately 398 Hz, below the original LC resonance. The source-impedance peak falls to approximately 1.011 Ω at 1.388 kHz.

Source impedance and Middlebrook impedance-ratio plots, before and after a series-RC shunt damping branch.


The upper panel is an impedance chart, not an insertion-loss measurement. Its dashed line is the magnitude of the negative input impedance; a magnitude plot alone cannot show its negative sign. The lower panel plots the corresponding interaction-loop magnitude. Damping reduces and shifts the resonant peak, bringing it below the converter input-impedance magnitude.
The curve is not an assertion that a real converter remains a constant-power load at every plotted frequency.

title: 12.6 Worked LC input filter: unstable without added damping, stable with an RC branch
section: E. Check the damped poles and the transient
text:
E. Check the damped poles and the transient
Let D₀(s) denote the undamped quadratic characteristic expression above. The damped characteristic equation can be formed independently from the impedance denominator:
\left(1+sR_{\mathrm{damp}}C_{\mathrm{damp}}\right)D_0(s)+sC_{\mathrm{damp}}(r+sL)=0.
For the stated values this becomes, after normalization:
s^3+8833.33s^2+9.3750\times10^7s+2.44792\times10^{11}=0.
The damped poles are approximately:
s_{1,2}=-2798\ \pm j\,8234\ \mathrm{s}^{-1},\qquad s_3=-3236\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}.
All have negative real parts. As a separate algebraic check, the cubic has positive coefficients and satisfies a₂a₁ > a₀, the additional Routh-Hurwitz condition for a normalized real cubic. The plotted transient starts with +1 mV on the main filter capacitor, with zero incremental inductor current and zero incremental voltage on the damping capacitor. The source perturbation is zero; the nominal DC source and load remain present.



Poles and initial-condition voltage response of the undamped and RC-damped LC input-filter models.


Over the plotted 2 ms, the case without added damping grows to about 38 mV maximum absolute deviation; the damped case decays. These deviations remain small relative to 12 V. The growing linear response cannot predict what happens after a real converter reaches current limits, dropout or another nonlinear operating condition.
Power and implementation checks: the 0.05 Ω main-path resistance dissipates 1.25 W at 5 A in both cases. The ideal RC branch adds no steady DC load after its capacitor is charged, but its resistor dissipates AC ripple/transient energy. Its capacitor also stores energy, draws startup charging current, and needs appropriate voltage, ripple-current and ESR ratings.
The chosen values demonstrate the mechanism; they are not a general damping recipe or an EMI-compliance result.
The reproducible script scripts/middlebrook_example.py computes both impedance peaks, checks state-matrix poles against the independently derived characteristic polynomials, and plots the small-signal initial-condition responses. Its numerical results are recorded in middlebrook-checks.json. Use the actual measured/modelled converter impedance and parameter tolerances before applying the result to hardware.
Our damping choice. Keep the 1 Ω / 400 µF shunt branch in this model. The undamped connection is unstable; the added branch brings all connected-system poles into the left half-plane without extra steady DC series drop.
More main-path resistance is a simpler alternative, but costs DC power. The shunt costs a capacitor and AC dissipation. For hardware, check the actual converter impedance and component range before carrying over these values.

title: 12.7 Worked choice: RC, LC or ferrite bead on a low-current supply rail?
text:
A. Specify what “better” means
Classroom riddle: a small IC needs a quiet supply. Must the series component be an inductor or a ferrite bead? Start with the allowed rail drop, load-current spectrum and noise frequency. A resistor may give useful attenuation with very small absolute loss when the current is low. The same reasoning that keeps linear regulators useful also keeps RC supply filters useful.
This exercise filters the power rail, not the digital data trace or the gate-driver output. Signal termination, gate resistance and supply decoupling solve different problems. A gate driver operating at 1 MHz can draw sharp supply-current pulses even though its average consumption is modest.
Assume a nominal 3.3 V rail, a 100 mV DC-drop budget for the series component, and source-voltage ripple near 1 MHz. Compare the following authored models with the same 1 µF local capacitor:
The bead equivalent is an illustrative passive model, not a measured curve, a selected 0805 product, or a fit to a manufacturer’s data. The inductor model omits its parallel capacitance; do not extrapolate its plotted response beyond the stated 10 MHz range. All output capacitors include 20 mΩ ESR and 0.5 nH total ESL. The source has 0.05 Ω resistance. PCB coupling and regulator-control dynamics are omitted.
For the ripple calculation the IC has a fixed 1 kΩ positive incremental input impedance. Its DC current is a separate parameter in the current sweep; an active IC’s incremental impedance need not equal its nominal voltage divided by DC current. These are not constant-power converter models. The curves hold component parameters fixed: they do not include bead DC-bias changes or temperature drift.
Write the voltage divider using the actual impedances:
Z_C(s)=R_{\mathrm{ESR}}+sL_{\mathrm{ESL}}+\frac{1}{sC},\qquad Z_p=Z_C\parallel Z_{\mathrm{load}}.
H(s)=\frac{V_{\mathrm{rail}}}{V_{\mathrm{source}}}=\frac{Z_p}{R_s+Z_{\mathrm{series}}+Z_p}.
For the illustrative bead:
Z_{\mathrm{bead}}(s)=R_{\mathrm{DC}}+\left(\frac{1}{sL_b}+\frac{1}{R_{\mathrm{AC}}}+sC_{\mathrm{par}}\right)^{-1}.
Here the 100 Ω model resistor is not a 100 Ω DC resistance: at DC the parallel inductance bypasses it. The bead approaches its low DCR at low frequency; its real impedance grows over a higher-frequency band.

section: B. Predict the response before plotting it
text:
B. Predict the response before plotting it
Neglect source resistance, loading and parasitics for the first estimate:
H_{RC}(s)=\frac{1}{1+sRC},\qquad f_c=\frac{1}{2\pi RC}=15.9\ \mathrm{kHz}.
H_{LC}(s)=\frac{1}{1+s^2LC},\qquad f_0=\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}=159\ \mathrm{kHz}.
The second expression is an undamped ideal approximation, not a sensible hardware design at resonance. RC has a −20 dB/decade region and no intentional LC resonance. LC eventually has a −40 dB/decade region, but a larger slope does not guarantee more attenuation at a particular frequency.
Here the RC corner is a decade below the LC natural frequency. The bead’s low-frequency inductance and 1 µF capacitor give an approximate resonance at 356 kHz.



Supply-ripple transfer for RC, LC and ferrite filters, including shunt RC damping, alongside the illustrative bead’s impedance components.

RC

−36.13 dB

−17.02 dB


Resonant gain without extra damping
None in the plotted band
+15.37 dB at 158 kHz
+8.46 dB at 342 kHz


Peak after adding the shown damping branch
Not added

Thus 10 mV RMS of source-voltage ripple at 1 MHz becomes approximately 0.156 mV, 0.257 mV or 1.41 mV RMS, respectively, without the added damping branch. Positive gain near resonance means magnification relative to the input voltage; a passive resonator can magnify voltage without generating net energy. These numbers are circuit voltage ratios, not standardized 50 Ω insertion-loss measurements.
The dashed curves add 1 Ω in series with 4 µF from the rail to return, in parallel with the original 1 µF capacitor and load. This reduces the peak substantially but does not remove all peaking. Its capacitor blocks DC after charging, while its resistor dissipates AC/transient energy.
The extra capacitance, charging current and board area are part of the cost. As in section 12.6, choose damping for the actual source/load combination rather than copying a universal value.
A bead’s AC loss is often the intended filtering mechanism. It helps when that resistive impedance lies in the noise band; it does not guarantee damping at a much lower resonance. A headline such as “600 Ω at 100 MHz” gives neither the impedance nor the attenuation at 1 MHz. Use the complex impedance versus frequency and DC bias. ADI AN-1368 explains these limitations and practical damping approaches.

section: C. Find the usable current range: headroom before heating
text:
C. Find the usable current range: headroom before heating
For the series component under DC load:
\Delta V=I_{\mathrm{DC}}R,\qquad P_{\mathrm{DC}}=I_{\mathrm{DC}}^2R.

DC voltage drop and component heating versus load current, showing a 100 mV headroom budget and an illustrative 125 mW thermal allowance.


For the requested package comparison, assume each candidate has a usable 0.125 W dissipation allowance on the chosen board. This is a teaching constraint, not a universal 0805 rating. For the resistor:
I_{\mathrm{thermal}}=\sqrt{\frac{0.125\ \mathrm W}{10\ \Omega}}=112\ \mathrm{mA},\qquad I_{\mathrm{headroom}}=\frac{0.100\ \mathrm V}{10\ \Omega}=10\ \mathrm{mA}.
The rail-drop requirement limits the resistor much earlier than heating does. At 10 mA it uses only 1 mW, so the absolute loss is small even though it is 100 times the magnetic component’s DC loss. There is no DC-loss crossover for these fixed resistances.
At 100 mA, being below the assumed thermal limit does not rescue a 1 V rail drop. Include the separate source/wiring drop in the complete rail-tolerance budget.
The plotted sweep extends beyond the feasible rail-drop region to expose the limits; it does not imply that a 3.3 V source can maintain an arbitrary imposed current after the load runs out of voltage headroom.
For a constant resistor carrying ripple as well as DC:
P_R=R\left(I_{\mathrm{DC}}^2+I_{\mathrm{AC,rms}}^2\right).
For a linear bead model, sum each AC harmonic’s heating using its own real impedance:
P_{\mathrm{bead}}=I_{\mathrm{DC}}^2R_{\mathrm{DC}}+\sum_{n\geq1}I_{n,\mathrm{rms}}^2\operatorname{Re}\{Z_{\mathrm{bead}}(j\omega_n)\}.
A total-loss crossover can exist for a specified ripple spectrum and component models. It cannot be inferred from DC current or package size alone. The two plotted loss curves include DC heating only; they do not assign arbitrary core loss to make a resistor appear more efficient. Evaluate each circuit’s actual AC current, since changing the series impedance changes that current too.
An 0805 outline does not determine thermal performance by surface area alone. Ratings depend on construction, pads/copper, ambient temperature and derating. A bead also needs acceptable impedance at DC bias, and an inductor needs saturation and RMS-current checks. A resistor is often a simple, economical component, but exact cost comparisons require actual parts and quantities.

title: 12.7 Worked choice: RC, LC or ferrite bead on a low-current supply rail?
section: D. Does RC always need the smaller capacitor?
text:
D. Does RC always need the smaller capacitor?
Exercise: require 40 dB attenuation at 1 MHz, initially ignoring loading, parasitics and tolerances. Set a voltage-amplitude target a = 0.01. For RC:
C_{RC}\geq\frac{\sqrt{a^{-2}-1}}{2\pi fR}.
At 10 Ω, this gives 1.59 µF. For an ideal LC evaluated above resonance:
C_{LC}\geq\frac{1+a^{-1}}{(2\pi f)^2L}.
At 1 µH this gives 2.56 µF. In this particular comparison, RC reaches the target with the smaller capacitance and avoids an intentional LC resonance. At only 1 mA, the same 100 mV drop allowance permits 100 Ω, reducing the ideal RC requirement to 0.159 µF. At 100 mA it permits only 1 Ω, increasing that requirement to 15.9 µF. This explains why RC becomes attractive at low current.
The result changes with permitted resistance, selected inductance, frequency and damping. A larger inductor can reverse the capacitance comparison. Neither formula includes capacitor DC-bias reduction, ESR/ESL or design margin. The full bead model is frequency dependent and should be evaluated through the divider, rather than assigned a single RC corner. These ideal calculations are starting estimates, not final component selections.

title: 12.7 Worked choice: RC, LC or ferrite bead on a low-current supply rail?
section: E. Transfer the reasoning to a 1 MHz gate-driver supply
text:
E. Transfer the reasoning to a 1 MHz gate-driver supply
For a separate 12 V gate-driver supply example, assume one MOSFET with 10 nC total gate charge per turn-on at the chosen gate voltage, one turn-on per period and 1 MHz operation. Neglect driver quiescent and internal switching currents initially:
I_{\mathrm{avg}}\approx Q_g f_s=10\ \mathrm{mA}.
A 10 Ω supply resistor then causes approximately 100 mV average drop and 1 mW DC heating. A local 1 µF capacitor supplying one 10 nC event alone loses approximately:
\Delta V_C=\frac{Q_g}{C}=10\ \mathrm{mV}.
This is the charge contribution only; add ESR/ESL effects and verify pulse recharge, startup, UVLO margin and the actual gate-charge waveform. The supply resistor carries recharge ripple, so its true RMS loss exceeds the 1 mW DC-only estimate. A 100 nC gate at the same frequency instead needs roughly 100 mA average: the same resistor loses 1 V and 100 mW before other consumption, making the choice much less attractive.
For multiple independently charged gates, add their charge per cycle. Local bypassing remains necessary with RC, LC and bead filtering.
Finish the riddle by reversing the disturbance: if the IC injects a current pulse while source noise is zero, calculate the rail driving-point impedance, not only H. With the same port definitions:
\Delta V_{\mathrm{rail}}=-\Delta I_{\mathrm{IC}}\left[(R_s+Z_{\mathrm{series}})\parallel Z_C\parallel Z_{\mathrm{load}}\right].
A resistor can improve incoming-noise attenuation while worsening low-frequency load-step droop. Choose RC when its headroom and transient performance meet the requirements; choose and damp an LC or bead network when low DC drop or another noise band makes it worthwhile. An LDO adds regulation and has its own headroom, noise and stability requirements, as discussed in chapter 14.
scripts/filter_choice_example.py generates figures 30–31, checks the divider against a nodal solution and checks the ideal attenuation/capacitance calculations. Parameters and results are recorded in filter-choice-checks.json. Figure 32 has an editable Inkscape source in the same style as the earlier circuits. Treat this as optional worked material alongside the two-session core.
For the 40 dB sizing exercise, start with RC. Its ideal 1.59 µF requirement is smaller than the stated LC alternative and avoids intentional LC resonance. The initial nonideal 1 µF RC comparison does not yet meet 40 dB; recheck the resized network.
Keep RC only while DC drop and pulse recovery meet the rail budget. At higher load current, consider LC or a bead to reduce DC drop, accepting their damping and bias checks.

title: 12.8 Real 0805 bead: manufacturer curves, DC bias and a 1 MHz comparison
text:
A. Read what the manufacturer actually provides
Now replace the illustrative bead with a real Würth Elektronik WE-CBA 782853561, size 0805. Its manufacturer datasheet, revision 001.010 dated 2019-09-18, specifies 560 Ω ±25% at 100 MHz, 0.1 Ω maximum DCR at 20 °C, and 1.5 A rated current for a 40 K rise under its stated conditions.
Page 2 supplies typical zero-bias Z/R/reactance curves and magnitude curves at 0.5, 1 and 1.5 A. These are typical characteristics, not guaranteed bias-dependent limits.
Question: with the same 1 µF local capacitor, how does its 1 MHz supply-noise attenuation change as the DC load increases? Keep the source resistance at 0.05 Ω, the incremental load at 1 kΩ, capacitor ESR at 20 mΩ and total ESL at 0.5 nH.
Keeping the incremental load fixed isolates the bead-bias effect; the DC current is an independent operating-point parameter. This is the same small-signal voltage-divider experiment as section 12.7, not a 50 Ω insertion-loss test.
Approximate readings at 1 MHz are 20 Ω at zero bias and 1.3 Ω at 0.5 A. The zero-bias real part is roughly 3 Ω. The loaded curves provide magnitude only. Furthermore, the 1 A and 1.5 A traces fall below the chart’s 1 Ω vertical limit at 1 MHz. Reading a precise endpoint there would invent data.
For those two currents, read the visible 2, 5 and 10 MHz portions instead and make an explicit local RL approximation:
Z_b(j\omega,I)\approx R_b+j\omega L_b(I),\qquad L_b(I)\approx\operatorname{median}\left\{\frac{\sqrt{|Z_b(f,I)|^2-R_b^2}}{2\pi f}\right\}.
Use Rb = 0.1 Ω as a modelling assumption for the loaded nominal estimates. A maximum DC resistance is not a measurement of AC resistance. The resulting inductance estimates are approximately 0.121 µH at 1 A and 0.092 µH at 1.5 A. Extrapolating this local model down to 1 MHz gives approximately 0.77 Ω and 0.59 Ω.
Those two values are inferred estimates, not manufacturer 1 MHz readings. No full-band RLC fit or loaded phase measurement is claimed.
Solid markers on the left show coarse chart readings; open markers and dotted segments below 1 Ω identify the extrapolation. Connecting the frequency samples is a visual guide. On the right, bars vary impedance magnitude by ±15% and allow any phase from 0° to +90° at 1 MHz.
This is an engineering sensitivity study under an inductive, passive-port assumption. It is neither a confidence interval nor a manufacturing-tolerance envelope, and does not bound model-extrapolation error or temperature effects.

title: 12.9 Pulsed digital-IC load: rail ripple, droop and recovery
text:
A. Use the same capacitor and a fair low-current load
The previous experiment injected voltage noise at the source. Now keep that source quiet and let the IC draw current pulses. This tests whether the local supply can deliver charge while maintaining its voltage. A filter that attenuates incoming voltage noise well can still have a large driving-point impedance and ring under load-current excitation.
Compare a 10 Ω series resistor with a model derived from the real 0805 Würth 782853561. Both use an ideal 3.3 V source, 0.05 Ω source resistance and 1 µF local capacitance with 20 mΩ ESR and 0.5 nH total ESL. The IC is an imposed current load; the previous example’s separate 1 kΩ incremental shunt is omitted. No regulator-control dynamics are included.
The pulse adds 8 mA to the idle current. At 9 mA, even the resistor’s eventual DC drop would be only 90 mV, within the chosen 100 mV component-drop budget. This avoids comparing a usable bead with a resistor that has already exhausted its voltage headroom.
The pulse train is intentionally near the approximate bead/capacitor resonance, making the distinction between attenuation and transient response visible. Its 100 kHz repetition rate is separate from the 1 MHz characterization point used below.

section: B. Build a causal bead model before simulating
text:
B. Build a causal bead model before simulating
An impedance magnitude at one frequency cannot be substituted directly into a time-domain differential equation. Use a passive network:
Z_b(s)=R_{\mathrm{DC}}+\frac{sL_bR_{\mathrm{loss}}}{R_{\mathrm{loss}}+sL_b}.
Match the approximate zero-bias 1 MHz chart readings from section 12.8, Z ≈ 3 + j19.77 Ω, using RDC = 0.1 Ω. From the admittance of Z − RDC, obtain Lb ≈ 3.215 µH and Rloss ≈ 137.7 Ω. The resistor is in parallel with the inductance; it is not a 137.7 Ω DC drop. At DC this network reduces to RDC. Its real impedance increases with frequency.
Model boundary: this is a causal, manufacturer-curve-derived teaching approximation, not a manufacturer-validated transient model or a measurement of the real bead. It matches one complex point, does not match the full MHz/GHz curves, and extrapolates below the chart’s 1 MHz lower limit. The same zero-bias parameters are assumed throughout the 1–9 mA pulse excursion; the available bias curves do not resolve that range.
Saturation, temperature, extra PCB parasitics and parameter tolerances are omitted. The precise ringing and settling numbers below depend on these assumptions.
The resistor path has a dominant time constant of approximately:
\tau_{RC}\approx(10+0.05+0.02)\ \Omega\times1\ \mathrm{\mu F}=10.07\ \mathrm{\mu s}.
The bead model and capacitor form an underdamped network. Its calculated dominant poles are approximately −30,028 ± j556,534 s⁻¹, giving 88.6 kHz ringing with a 33.3 µs amplitude-envelope time constant. All model poles have negative real parts. This is passive transient ringing, not the constant-power-load instability in section 12.6.

section: D. Explain the result with charge and impedance
text:
D. Explain the result with charge and impedance
If the capacitor alone supplied one extra-current pulse, its charge loss would be:
\Delta Q=8\ \mathrm{mA}\times2\ \mathrm{\mu s}=16\ \mathrm{nC},\qquad \Delta V_C=\frac{\Delta Q}{C}=16\ \mathrm{mV}.
This is a useful first-pulse scale, not the full waveform: the upstream path supplies some current and the bead also stores energy. The edge scales from the capacitor branch are approximately ESR × ΔI = 0.16 mV and ESL × ΔI/tr = 0.04 mV. The actual source/capacitor current sharing determines their detailed contributions.
For a long periodic train, the mean rail drops follow the mean current: approximately 26.13 mV for RC and 0.39 mV for the bead’s DC path, including the common source resistance. Superimposed ripple depends on the driving-point impedance at the pulse fundamental and its harmonics:
Z_{\mathrm{PDN}}(s)=\left[R_s+Z_{\mathrm{series}}(s)\right]\parallel Z_C(s),\qquad \Delta V(s)=-Z_{\mathrm{PDN}}(s)\,\Delta I_{\mathrm{IC}}(s).
This explains why the incoming-voltage-noise attenuation chart cannot predict the current-pulse result by itself. In this example the 100 kHz load spectrum excites the bead model near resonance; RC instead trades voltage headroom for damping. Increasing capacitance changes both the charge droop and resonance. Adding a designed damping branch, moving the repetition frequency or changing the source impedance can change the comparison.
scripts/pulsed_load_example.py simulates the finite-edge load using exact linear-state propagation between input samples. It verifies the bead’s complex 1 MHz match, stable model poles, circuit KVL and integrated capacitor charge, then halves the time step from 5 ns to 2.5 ns to check peak and ripple convergence.
Parameters and results are retained in pulsed-load-checks.json. Before using the numbers for hardware sign-off, replace the teaching bead model with measured or vendor-supported complex impedance over the transient’s relevant frequency/current range.
For lower cycle ripple and faster recovery, keep RC as the reference. It gives 12.47 mV ripple and 31.51 µs recovery, but loses more DC voltage. The bead-derived model gives less drop below 3.3 V, yet more ringing and slower recovery.
Choose it only if that headroom benefit matters more and its excursion limits pass. No rail-tolerance specification is given, so these results rank candidates without qualifying either supply.

title: 13. Semiconductor and thermal basics
text:
13.1 Thermal resistance and capacitance: use the RC concepts again
Before detailed converter topologies, students should be able to sketch the basic states of a diode and MOSFET, identify current paths, and explain why an inductor needs a commutation path.
For an approximately constant on-resistance:
P_{\mathrm{cond}}\approx I_{\mathrm{rms}}^2R_{\mathrm{DS(on)}},\qquad P_{\mathrm{sw}}\approx f_s(E_{\mathrm{on}}+E_{\mathrm{off}}).
Where does R_{\mathrm{DS(on)}} come from? Not from a resistor inside the package. It is read from the output characteristic: the family of I_D versus V_{DS} curves, one per gate voltage, that a curve tracer measures. An amplifier biases the transistor in the flat, current-source part of these curves. A switch uses only two places on the same graph: the vertical axis when off (I_D=0) and the steep region near the origin when on (V_{DS}\approx0). Avoid the middle, where voltage and current coexist; that is where a linear regulator lives (section 14).
On the steep region, the on-resistance is the ratio at one point:
R_{\mathrm{DS(on)}}=\left.\frac{V_{DS}}{I_D}\right|_{V_{GS},\ I_D,\ T_j}.
It is a small-signal-style parameter, like g_m or \beta: valid only near the gate voltage, current and junction temperature where it was read. The data-sheet graph of R_{\mathrm{DS(on)}} is this ratio evaluated point by point, not an independent measurement. The front-page value is one such point, usually at the most favourable gate voltage and 25 °C.
Worked example (authored curves, not a catalog part). At I_D = 20 A, suppose the curve for V_{GS} = 10 V passes through V_{DS} = 0.20 V and the curve for V_{GS} = 6 V through 0.30 V. The on-resistances are 10 mΩ and 15 mΩ, and the conduction losses I_D^2R_{\mathrm{DS(on)}} are 4.0 W and 6.0 W. With the assumed 1.5× hot-resistance multiplier of section 13.2, they become 6.0 W and 9.0 W.
Drive at 10 V or at 6 V? The lower gate voltage saves gate-drive power and may allow a cheaper driver supply. It costs 2 W at 25 °C in this example, and that heat needs copper or a heat sink. The higher gate voltage is preferable whenever conduction loss dominates. The lower one becomes reasonable at light load, or when the gate-drive supply is fixed by another part. Check the gate’s absolute maximum voltage before driving harder: it is typically about ±20 V for silicon MOSFETs and much lower for many GaN devices.
Switching frequency, magnetic size and loss. For a fixed applied winding voltage and duty ratio, on-time falls as switching frequency rises. The relation \Delta B=Vt_{\mathrm{on}}/(NA_e) in section 2.4 therefore allows a smaller turns–area product for the same flux swing. Similarly, the inductor ripple relation \Delta I=V_Lt_{\mathrm{on}}/L allows a lower inductance for the same ripple.
These relations help explain why higher switching frequency can reduce magnetic size. Actual size also depends on energy storage, winding space, core loss and cooling.
The tradeoff is visible in the switching-loss equation: with unchanged energy per transition, switching loss rises with frequency. Core and AC winding losses also depend on frequency and waveform, while fast edges increase sensitivity to parasitic inductance and capacitive coupling. Choose frequency together with the devices, magnetics, thermal design and EMC requirements; neither low nor high switching frequency guarantees high efficiency.
Si, SiC and GaN: a first orientation. Si means silicon, SiC silicon carbide and GaN gallium nitride. SiC and GaN are wide-bandgap semiconductors whose properties can enable higher-voltage and/or faster-switching power devices than comparable silicon implementations. Lower transition losses can make higher switching frequency and smaller magnetics practical.
The material name alone does not determine efficiency or a safe switching frequency: compare actual device ratings, switching energy, conduction loss, gate-drive requirements, layout and cooling at the intended operating point. This is an introduction to device selection, not a claim that every SiC or GaN design outperforms every silicon design.
See TI’s introduction to wide-bandgap power technologies.
For a specified steady thermal path:
T_j-T_a\approx P_{\mathrm{loss}}R_{\theta JA}.
Thermal resistance depends strongly on the package, board and cooling conditions. Short pulses need transient thermal impedance; a data-sheet θJA from a particular test board is not a universal package constant.
Heat flow can be modelled with the same tools as a first-order electrical circuit:
For one thermal node connected through Rth to a fixed ambient temperature, let ΔT be its temperature rise:
C_{\mathrm{th}}\frac{d\Delta T}{dt}+\frac{\Delta T}{R_{\mathrm{th}}}=P(t),\qquad \tau_{\mathrm{th}}=R_{\mathrm{th}}C_{\mathrm{th}}.
Rth sets the steady rise; Cth sets how much energy is needed to change temperature. For a uniform body, Cth = mass × specific heat capacity. A real semiconductor or resistor has several spatial regions and time scales, so a single whole-package thermal capacitance may miss a hot junction or resistive-film hot spot. This analogy follows TI’s Thermal dynamics teaching resource; the numerical RC models below are authored illustrations.

text:
13.2 TI semiconductor example: the same MOSFET on different copper areas
Predict. A low-resistance MOSFET carries 40 A continuously in a 12 V ORing path. Does its small electrical loss guarantee a cool junction?
Use TI’s CSD17570Q5B, a 30 V ORing/hot-swap MOSFET that TI explicitly does not intend for switching applications. The SLPS471D datasheet, pages 1, 3–4, gives:







Published quantity

Maximum on-resistance
0.69 mΩ at VGS = 10 V, ID = 50 A, 25 °C


Maximum junction-to-case RθJC
0.8 K/W


Maximum junction-to-ambient board cases in figure 1
50 K/W with 1 inch² of 2 oz copper; 125 K/W with minimum pad area

For an authored 40 A, 40 °C ambient scenario, hold resistance at its 25 °C value initially: P = 40² × 0.00069 = 1.104 W. The two board estimates are 95.2 °C and 178.0 °C. The latter exceeds the operating limit; it is a failed screening estimate, not a valid operating point. These boundary-dependent thermal metrics are not interchangeable; see TI SPRA953D.
Change one thing: improve the PCB heat path. Then repeat the loss calculation with temperature-dependent resistance. For sensitivity only, an assumed 1.5× resistance multiplier gives 1.656 W and 122.8 °C / 247.0 °C in the two fixed thermal paths. This multiplier is not a guaranteed TI hot-resistance specification or a converged electrothermal solution.
A real design uses the applicable temperature curve/data, solves loss and temperature consistently and checks margins and current/voltage limits.
Do not replace RθJA by RθJC while keeping ambient as the reference: that discards the case-to-surroundings heat path. A junction-to-case calculation needs the relevant case temperature and boundary conditions. Nor should RθJC be added to RθJA; the latter already represents the junction-to-ambient system under its stated conditions.
PCB copper, vias, airflow and nearby heat sources change the actual result. The ordinary data-sheet θJA value is a comparison/test-condition metric, not a universal property of a package on every board.
Keep the larger-copper path as the candidate for this 40 A example. The minimum-pad case exceeds the junction limit in the stated calculation. A lower-resistance MOSFET is an alternative way to reduce heat, but requires a new electrical and thermal comparison. Neither approach is qualified by the cold on-resistance alone.

title: 13. Semiconductor and thermal basics
section: 13.3 A short power pulse is not a steady-state load
text:
13.3 A short power pulse is not a steady-state load
For a constant power pulse starting at ambient, the one-node model gives:
\Delta T(t_p)=P R_{\mathrm{th}}\left(1-e^{-t_p/\tau_{\mathrm{th}}}\right)=P Z_{\mathrm{th}}(t_p).
Zth is the thermal step-response impedance in K/W. At long times it approaches Rth. At short times compared with the applicable thermal time constant, little heat escapes and ΔT ≈ E/Cth, where E is the deposited energy. For a normalized manufacturer Zth curve, first multiply by its stated reference thermal resistance. Match the curve’s junction/case/ambient reference and boundary conditions to the calculation.
Worked RC example. Assume Rth = 100 K/W, Cth = 0.020 J/K, hence τth = 2 s. A 10 W, 10 ms rectangular pulse deposits 0.1 J and produces 4.99 K rise from cold. Multiplying 10 W by the steady 100 K/W would predict 1000 K and misuse a steady-state equation for this short event.
Repeat the pulse every 1 s. Average power is only 0.1 W, so the eventual mean rise is 10 K, but the periodic temperature moves between 7.73 K and 12.68 K above ambient. The isolated 4.99 K result cannot be reused from a cold baseline on every cycle. For this one-node model:
\Delta T_{\mathrm{max}}=P R_{\mathrm{th}}\frac{1-e^{-t_p/\tau_{\mathrm{th}}}}{1-e^{-T/\tau_{\mathrm{th}}}}.
T is the repetition period, and P is the on-pulse power. For general waveforms, solve the thermal differential equation or convolve power with the thermal impulse response. Adding square-pulse step responses also works for a linear thermal model. A short-pulse junction-temperature check still does not replace semiconductor SOA or resistor electrical pulse limits.



Authored one-node thermal step response, repeated rectangular pulses, precharge power and isolated versus repetitive precharge temperature rise.


scripts/thermal_examples.py generates figure 63 and thermal-checks.json. It independently checks convolution, pulse energy, thermal energy balance and periodic mean temperature. The Rth/Cth values are not fitted to the TI MOSFET or to a catalog resistor. Sections 16.16–16.17 apply pulse-energy reasoning to gate and precharge resistors.
Thermal choice. Use transient thermal response for the 10 ms event; steady thermal resistance gives the wrong temperature estimate. For an isolated pulse, check local pulse capability and stored heat first.
For repeated or sustained operation, improve the heat path or allow more cooling time. The first costs cooling hardware; the second costs throughput. Neither replaces the part’s pulse qualification.

title: 14. Are linear regulators dead? No: choose the architecture
text:
14.1 Principle and specifications
A load needs 3.3 V, but the available rail is 5 V or 12 V. A battery voltage falls as it discharges. A rectified transformer output has ripple. In each case, the load needs a supply that stays within its limits.
A linear regulator may be the simplest solution. First understand how it controls voltage. Then calculate what it dissipates. That calculation tells us when to keep the linear stage and when to consider a switching converter.
A linear regulator uses a semiconductor as a controllable series resistance between source and load. The output voltage is measured, compared with a reference, and the pass device is driven so that the output stays constant: if the output is too low, the series resistance is reduced, and conversely.
The pass transistor operates in its linear region, not as a saturated switch; the German term Längsregler (series regulator) describes the arrangement.
Read the regulator data sheet in groups:
Linear regulator describes the regulation method; the overall regulator is not necessarily a globally linear system. Avoid using one transistor-region label for all BJT and MOSFET pass arrangements.
With input current approximately equal to output current plus ground/quiescent current:
P_{\mathrm{loss}}=(V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o)I_o+V_{\mathrm{in}}I_q.
\eta=\frac{V_oI_o}{V_{\mathrm{in}}(I_o+I_q)}\approx\frac{V_o}{V_{\mathrm{in}}}\quad\mathrm{if}\ I_q\ll I_o.
The efficiency is set by the voltage ratio, not by the load current. This single fact decides most of the architecture choices in section 14.5.

title: 14. Are linear regulators dead? No: choose the architecture
section: 14.2 The simplest regulator: Zener reference and emitter follower
text:
14.2 The simplest regulator: Zener reference and emitter follower
A resistor R_1 from the input feeds a Zener diode, and the Zener voltage drives the base of an NPN emitter follower whose emitter is the output:



Figure 61. Zener-reference emitter follower and integrated series regulator, exported from CircuiTikZ Designer.


V_o\approx V_Z-V_{BE},\qquad V_{BE}\approx0.7\ \mathrm V\ (\mathrm{single\ BJT}),\ \approx1.4\ \mathrm V\ (\mathrm{Darlington}).
The Zener is modelled as a constant voltage V_Z in series with its differential resistance r_Z. An input change then reaches the reference through the divider R_1 / r_Z:
\frac{\Delta V_{\mathrm{ref}}}{\Delta V_{\mathrm{in}}}=\frac{r_Z}{R_1+r_Z}\approx\frac{r_Z}{R_1},\qquad \mathrm{line\ rejection}=20\log_{10}\frac{R_1+r_Z}{r_Z}.
The output resistance of the follower combines the base-side source resistance divided by the current gain with the emitter resistance V_T/I_o, where V_T\approx26 mV is the thermal voltage:
r_{\mathrm{out}}\approx\frac{r_Z\parallel R_1}{\beta+1}+\frac{V_T}{I_o}.
Worked example. Take V_{\mathrm{in}}=12 V, a 6.2 V Zener with r_Z=10 Ω, R_1=470 Ω and \beta=100. The output is about 5.5 V. The line ratio is 10/480 = 0.0208, a line rejection of 33.6 dB: a 1 V input change moves the output by about 21 mV.
At 100 mA the output resistance is approximately 0.36 Ω. The base current of about 1 mA is drawn from the Zener node, so the Zener current falls from 12.3 mA at no load to 11.4 mA at 100 mA and the reference shifts by about −10 mV.
The reference is therefore load dependent; a Darlington divides the base current by a further current gain and also reduces loss in the reference branch.
These two numbers are section 1.3 applied to a regulator: the output is a Thévenin source whose open-circuit voltage follows the input through the line ratio and whose series resistance is r_{\mathrm{out}}. A simple follower is cheap, but its rejection, output resistance and reference drift are limited by r_Z and \beta. Integrated regulators replace the Zener with a precision reference and add gain.
When is the simple follower enough? Keep it when its voltage variation and reference loading meet the requirement. It uses few parts but offers limited accuracy. Choose a feedback regulator when tighter regulation justifies the added circuit and its stability checks.

title: 14. Are linear regulators dead? No: choose the architecture
section: 14.3 Integrated regulators: fixed, adjustable and low dropout
text:
14.3 Integrated regulators: fixed, adjustable and low dropout
An integrated regulator contains a reference, error amplifier and pass device. The amplifier adjusts the pass device to correct output error. Typical protection includes thermal shutdown and current limiting. Check how the actual device protects the pass transistor’s safe operating area (section 13).
Fixed three-terminal regulators (78xx, 79xx). The suffix gives the output voltage: a 7812 delivers 12 V, an LM78L05 100 mA at 5 V. The basic parts supply 1 A; versions from 100 mA to 5 A exist. In the classic NPN-Darlington structure the minimum input-to-output difference is about 0.7 V across the current-sense resistor plus 1.5 V for two base-emitter junctions plus 0.3 V for the drive current source, about 2.5 V.
That dropout is why a 5 V rail cannot feed a 3.3 V load through a classic 78xx: only 1.7 V of headroom is available.
Adjustable three-terminal regulators (LM317 family, LM337 for negative outputs). Input, output and adjust pins, with no ground pin: the internal current leaves through the output and the divider. The output is set by two resistors:
V_o=V_{\mathrm{ref}}\left(1+\frac{R_2}{R_1}\right)+I_{\mathrm{adj}}R_2,\qquad V_{\mathrm{ref}}=1.25\ \mathrm V,\ I_{\mathrm{adj}}\approx50\ \mathrm{\mu A}\ (100\ \mathrm{\mu A\ max}).
Choose R_1 small enough that the I_{\mathrm{adj}}R_2 term is negligible and that the divider alone supplies the regulator’s minimum load of about 10 mA. For 5 V with R_1=240 Ω, R_2=720 Ω; the divider carries 5.2 mA and the adjust current adds 36 mV, giving 5.036 V.
The lecture data for this family: input-to-output difference up to 40 V and output current up to 1.5 A. Four-terminal adjustable parts with a separate reference pin (for example a 5 V reference with V_{\mathrm{ref}}\leq V_o<V_{\mathrm{in}}-3 V) preceded this simpler arrangement.
Low-dropout regulators (LDO). A low-voltage rail may not have 2 to 3 V of spare headroom. A PNP or P-channel MOSFET pass stage can operate with a smaller drop, sometimes below 0.5 V. Check dropout at the required current.



Figure 62. PNP and P-channel MOSFET low-dropout pass stages, exported from CircuiTikZ Designer.


A PNP needs base current, which flows to ground. This raises ground-current loss. A Darlington adds another V_{BE} and increases dropout. A small base-path resistor can limit current and reduce oscillation tendency.
A P-channel MOSFET needs less steady drive power. Controllers with an external MOSFET can use a sense resistor to set current limit. Output voltage may be internally fixed or set by an external divider. Read the specific device’s circuit before choosing values.
Negative outputs. With a floating input, either output terminal of a positive regulator may be grounded, so no special part is needed. For a symmetric supply from one centre-tapped rectifier, a negative regulator (79xx, LM337) is required; internally it mirrors the positive circuit with the transistor polarities exchanged.

title: 14. Are linear regulators dead? No: choose the architecture
section: 14.4 References: Zener and bandgap
text:
14.4 References: Zener and bandgap
Every regulator, linear or switching, ends its feedback path at a reference.
Zener with series resistor. The simplest reference is a Zener fed through a resistor from the input; its Thévenin model is V_Z in series with r_Z and its input rejection is the r_Z/(R_1+r_Z) ratio of section 14.2. Driving the Zener from a constant current (an op-amp and the Zener’s own output) removes the input dependence and reaches about 80 dB of line rejection.
The Zener voltage has a temperature coefficient that is negative below about 6 V, positive above and close to zero near 6 V, which is why 6 V Zeners are preferred for stabilisation.
Bandgap reference and shunt regulator. A base-emitter voltage falls with temperature. The difference between two base-emitter voltages supplies a term proportional to absolute temperature. Adding the two in suitable proportions gives a compensated reference near 1.2 V.
The TL431 combines a reference and amplifier in a three-terminal shunt regulator. Its internal reference is 2.5 V. A divider sets the cathode voltage through the reference pin. Setting R_2=0 avoids divider tolerance.
A series resistor must provide the minimum cathode current stated in the data sheet. Include the reference-pin current, typically a few microamperes, in the divider calculation. The TL431 returns later as a feedback element in isolated flyback converters.

title: 14. Are linear regulators dead? No: choose the architecture
section: 14.5 Three architecture choices, and where linear is better
text:
14.5 Three architecture choices, and where linear is better








Teaching scenario
Calculation neglecting quiescent current
Design interpretation




12 V → 3.3 V at 1 A
8.7 W loss; 27.5% efficiency
A switcher is strongly motivated by dissipation


5 V → 3.3 V
At most 66% efficiency; needs an LDO because 1.7 V headroom is below a classic 2.5 V dropout
Even a stable input does not rescue a linear stage with a large voltage ratio


3.6 V → 3.3 V at 20 mA
6 mW loss; 91.7% efficiency
A linear stage can be attractive if minimum headroom and accuracy are sufficient


12 V → 3.6 V switcher, then 3.3 V LDO
90% × 91.7% = 82.5% overall
Efficient bulk conversion and local low-noise regulation can coexist



For the third case, assume for illustration an LDO with 10 µA quiescent current. At 20 mA its efficiency is approximately 91.6%; at 10 µA output current it falls to approximately 45.8%. Quiescent current can dominate a sleeping load. This is a numerical illustration, not a specification of the device below.
When the linear stage is a good choice. Ignoring ground current, its efficiency is V_o/V_{\mathrm{in}}. Compare that ratio with the switcher’s efficiency at the actual load. Include dropout, ground current and noise before deciding.
Consider a 3.6 V battery supplying a 3.3 V, 20 mA sensor or ADC front end. An LDO loses 6 mW in its pass device. A buck reaching 85% at this load loses about 11.6 mW. The 85% value is a teaching assumption. The buck also introduces switching noise near the measurement circuit.
Here the LDO deserves consideration. With a larger voltage drop or more current, its heating may instead favour a switcher. Calculate both candidates rather than choosing from the product category.
The fourth case, post-regulation, uses both: the switcher does the bulk voltage conversion efficiently and the LDO removes its ripple. With 40 dB of PSRR at the switching frequency, a 50 mV ripple component becomes 0.5 mV. PSRR falls with frequency, so read it at the actual switching frequency, not at 120 Hz.
As a concrete device reference, the LT3045 targets low-noise instrumentation, data converters and switcher post-regulation. Its published figures include 0.8 µV RMS output noise over 10 Hz–100 kHz and high PSRR under specified conditions. These figures are device- and test-condition-specific; an LDO neither removes all input ripple nor guarantees negligible output noise.
Start-up time: how fast must the rail be valid? Efficiency is not the only rail specification. A handheld instrument may power its measurement circuit only when a button is pressed and expect a result within a few hundred microseconds. Then the time from enable to a valid output decides the architecture.
A switching regulator must start its oscillator and reference, then ramp the output under soft-start so the inrush current does not trip its current limit. Soft-start times are commonly fixed or capacitor-set in the millisecond range; read the actual controller data sheet. A linear regulator has no switching loop to settle. Its start-up is mainly the time its current limit needs to charge the output capacitor.
That charge is the hard limit for either architecture. Bringing 100 µF to 3.3 V needs I=C\,\Delta V/\Delta t: 0.33 A over 1 ms, 1.1 A over 300 µs and 6.6 A over 50 µs. A fast start therefore needs a source and regulator that can deliver this current, and a small output capacitance.
Which rail meets a 300 µs requirement? Keep the switcher running in a low-power mode, if its standby current fits the battery budget. Use a linear regulator with a small output capacitor if the voltage drop is small. Accept the switcher’s soft-start only if the requirement can be relaxed. Each choice trades standby current, heat or response time; calculate the one the specification constrains.
Architecture decision. Compare linear and switching candidates at the actual voltage ratio and load. Linear regulation avoids switching ripple but dissipates the voltage drop. A switcher may reduce that heat while adding filtering and control requirements. Let the rail specifications determine the choice.

title: 14. Are linear regulators dead? No: choose the architecture
section: 14.6 Stability, bypassing and remote sensing
text:
14.6 Stability, bypassing and remote sensing
For a sinusoidal input ripple under specified operating conditions:
\mathrm{PSRR}_{\mathrm{dB}}=20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{V_{\mathrm{ripple,in}}}{V_{\mathrm{ripple,out}}}\right).
For example, 40 dB rejection turns a 10 mV ripple component into 0.1 mV through that input-to-output path. Intrinsic regulator noise and other coupling paths remain. PSRR depends on frequency, headroom, load and external components.
A linear regulator is a feedback loop (section 12.4). Long input leads add inductance and can contribute to oscillation. A nearby bypass capacitor may help, but take its value and placement from the device data sheet.
The output capacitor also affects the loop. Some LDOs require an ESR range; others support ceramic capacitors. A generic instruction to add 100 nF on each side cannot establish stability. TI’s regulator-stability guidance explains the role of output-capacitor ESR.
A load some distance from the regulator sees the copper and contact resistance of the connection in series with the regulator’s low output resistance, which can undo the regulation entirely. Remote sensing brings the voltage measurement to the load with separate sense connections S+ and S−; these carry almost no current, so the drop along them is negligible and the drop along the force leads is regulated out.
With adjustable regulators this can be arranged by connecting the external divider at the load. It is the same four-wire idea as the Kelvin current-sense riddle in section 16.2.

title: 14. Are linear regulators dead? No: choose the architecture
section: 14.7 Worked small-power design: 12 V → 5 V at 0.5 A
text:
14.7 Worked small-power design: 12 V → 5 V at 0.5 A
Design the adjustable regulator of section 14.3 for 5 V at 0.5 A from a 12 V input, with 5 mA ground current, and check the thermal path.

Divider: R_1=240 Ω, R_2=720 Ω, output 5.036 V including the adjust current. Headroom 7 V, well above the 2.5 V class dropout, so a standard regulator is sufficient here.
Loss and efficiency: pass loss 7 V × 0.5 A = 3.5 W, quiescent loss 12 V × 5 mA = 0.06 W, total 3.56 W; efficiency 2.5 W / 6.06 W = 41%.
Without a heat sink: at an illustrative R_{\theta JA}=50 K/W for a TO-220 in free air, the junction rises 178 K above a 50 °C ambient, to about 228 °C. Not possible: the thermal shutdown would act first.
Heat-sink requirement: for T_j\leq125 °C at 50 °C ambient the total thermal resistance may not exceed 75 K / 3.56 W = 21.1 K/W. With an illustrative R_{\theta JC}=4 K/W and 1 K/W for the mounting interface, the heat sink must be below about 16 K/W. Take all three thermal values from the actual data sheet and heat-sink catalogue; the numbers here show the method.

A 90% efficient buck delivering the same 2.5 W loses about 0.28 W. This greatly reduces the thermal burden. It leads to the next lecture’s buck design.
Keep the linear regulator among your options when the voltage drop is small, the current is low or noise matters. Check its thermal path before deciding. scripts/linear_regulator_example.py records this chapter’s calculations in linear-regulator-checks.json.
Keep linear or change architecture? The linear design can work only with the calculated thermal path; its 3.56 W loss cannot be ignored. Keep it when simplicity or noise performance justifies that heat.
If efficiency is the priority, take the assumed 90% buck forward for design: its estimated loss is about 0.28 W. That is a reason to investigate it, not a completed noise, transient or component check.

title: 15. Exit questions with short answers
text:
Why does a loaded divider fall below its nominal voltage? The load draws current through the source’s Thévenin resistance.
What is the RMS of a ±10 A square wave? Of 0/10 A at 25% duty? 10 A and 5 A; their signed means are 0 A and 2.5 A.
Can current with zero mean heat a wire? Yes. Heating depends on the mean square.
Does reactive power disappear as heat in an ideal capacitor? No; energy is exchanged. The resulting RMS current can increase real losses elsewhere.
Does zero average inductor voltage imply zero instantaneous voltage? No. Switching intervals can have opposite nonzero voltages.
Why does the CPU example need local energy storage? The remote interconnect cannot change its current fast enough within the voltage budget.
Is the crosstalk voltage transfer low-pass or high-pass in the defined victim model? High-pass. The injected-current-to-voltage impedance is low-pass.
Can a nonlinear system’s output be Fourier analysed? Yes; that does not make the system describable by one linear transfer function.
Does the switching harmonic define a second RC time constant? No. The circuit pole sets settling; switching supplies forced frequencies.
Which resonator produces an impedance peak? The defined parallel RLC; the series RLC produces a dip.
Why use an LC output filter in Class-D? Stronger high-frequency attenuation with energy storage instead of a large dissipative series resistor.
When is an LDO efficient? When the output/input voltage ratio is close to one and its own current is small relative to the load, while adequate dropout headroom remains.
Why can a 60 W load have −2.4 Ω incremental resistance while absorbing power? At 12 V it draws 5 A, and its regulation increases current when voltage falls; the DC voltage/current ratio remains positive.
Does an input-filter impedance crossing prove instability? No. It fails a conservative magnitude check; the interaction-loop phase, poles and Nyquist behaviour determine the general result.
What changes when the same overlap’s dielectric spacing halves? Plate-model capacitance and current into a stationary reference double. The moving victim’s voltage response must include the changed time constant and divider ratio.
What does a 4:1 ideal transformer do to a 6 Ω secondary load? It presents 96 Ω at the primary; voltage scales by 4 and current magnitudes inversely.
Why is an ideal turns-ratio element insufficient for flyback analysis? The magnetizing inductance stores energy and its flux must be tracked and reset.
What changes when one winding of a series-coupled pair is reversed? The mutual contribution changes from +2M to −2M in the series equivalent inductance.
For L₁ = 100 µH, L₂ = 25 µH and k = 0.8, what are M and the short-circuit primary inductance? M = 40 µH and L₁,short = 36 µH.
Why can a real transformer draw current with its secondary open? Core excitation requires magnetizing current and core loss requires active current; both pass through the primary winding.
Why does the 48 V, 4:1 real example deliver 11.704 V rather than 12 V? Primary and secondary winding impedances cause load-dependent drops; its internal induced-voltage ratio still follows the turns ratio.
What happens to copper skin depth when frequency increases by a factor of four? It halves, with resistivity and permeability held fixed.
Should a DC-plus-ripple current use the switching-frequency resistance for all its RMS current? No. Use RDC for the DC component and frequency-dependent AC resistance for each harmonic; include proximity effects where relevant.
Does one radial layer remove all high-frequency copper loss? No. The worked round-wire case already has 93.01 W of skin-only loss; adjacent conductors can add proximity loss.
In the specified four-layer-per-winding comparison, why does interleaving reduce proximity loss? It reduces the sum of squared layer mean fields from 42K² to 2K² while keeping the turns ratio and load waveform unchanged.
Does zero source impedance at the IC attenuate supply-voltage noise? No; that noise-transfer ratio is one, while load-current-induced voltage ripple is zero in the same ideal model.
Does a 4.47 cm PCB route necessarily block a 1 GHz signal? No. The defined matched, lossless line gives unit amplitude and approximately 0.298 ns propagation delay.
What target-impedance scale follows from a 100 A change and 30 mV allowance? 0.30 mΩ at the defined port, over the relevant band; the teaching numbers are not a processor specification.
Why can a 10 Ω RC supply filter be attractive at 10 mA but fail at 100 mA? It drops 100 mV and dissipates 1 mW at 10 mA; at 100 mA it drops 1 V even though its 100 mW loss is below the illustrative 125 mW allowance.
Does a ferrite bead’s AC loss guarantee a nonresonant supply filter? No. Its loss may become significant above the resonance of its low-frequency inductance and the local capacitor; inspect the complete complex impedance and load.
Why can a classic 78xx-type regulator not make 3.3 V from 5 V? Its NPN-Darlington pass structure needs about 2.5 V of headroom and only 1.7 V is available; an LDO with a dropout below 0.5 V can, at a maximum efficiency of 66%.
Which two numbers turn the emitter-follower/Zener regulator into a Thévenin source? The line ratio r_Z/(R_1+r_Z) sets how the open-circuit voltage follows the input, and r_{\mathrm{out}}\approx(r_Z\parallel R_1)/(\beta+1)+V_T/I_o is its series resistance.
When does a linear regulator beat a switching converter on efficiency? When V_o/V_{\mathrm{in}} exceeds the switcher’s efficiency at that load: 3.6 V to 3.3 V gives 91.7% from a linear stage, with no switching ripple to filter.

title: 16.1 Did the circuit ring, or did the probe? — Williams-inspired
text:
Predict. A 1 V pulse source has a 2 ns rising edge. A scope shows overshoot. Is this evidence that the switching circuit is unstable? First add the measurement circuit to the schematic.



Simplified probe acquisition circuit with 50 Ω source resistance, 10 pF probe capacitance and return-lead inductance.


Use a 50 Ω source, 10 pF probe input capacitance, and either 100 nH or 5 nH effective probe-return inductance. The displayed voltage is across the capacitance. The simplified acquisition transfer function is:
H_p(s)=\frac{1}{1+sR_sC_p+s^2L_gC_p},\qquad f_0=\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{L_gC_p}},\qquad \zeta=\frac{R_s}{2}\sqrt{\frac{C_p}{L_g}}.
For 100 nH, f₀ = 159.2 MHz and ζ = 0.25. For 5 nH, they become 711.8 MHz and 1.118. The first model is underdamped; the second is overdamped. The finite 2 ns ramp produces a calculated 1.375 V peak in the first case, approximately 37.5% overshoot, while the short-return model approaches 1 V without overshoot.
The ideal-step overshoot formula would give a different value because the applied edge here has finite rise time.



Finite-edge probe responses and acquisition Bode gains for 100 nH and 5 nH return inductance.


The familiar bandwidth scale 0.35/tr ≈ 175 MHz is a useful single-pole/Gaussian-style estimate, not a hard spectral cutoff. It explains why a fast edge can excite the 159 MHz acquisition resonance even if pulses repeat at only 100 kHz. Shortening the ground connection changes the measurement network, not necessarily the device under test.
Change one thing: compare a long lead with a short ground spring while keeping the source and probe point unchanged. Use a low-voltage, ground-referenced demonstration; floating switching-node measurements require an appropriate differential measurement arrangement. The plot omits scope bandwidth, probe compensation and distributed cable effects and is not a complete commercial-probe model.
Why the basic matters: an observed waveform belongs to the circuit and its measurement connection. Williams, AN47, discusses probe grounding and loading; its probe appendix includes material contributed by Tektronix.
First decision. Change the probe return before changing the circuit. This tests measurement-induced ringing with little disturbance to the board. If the ring persists with a suitable measurement setup, investigate the circuit resonance. A cleaner trace alone does not prove the circuit is stable.

title: 16.2 Why does a precise current shunt give a 50% error? — Pease/Ott-inspired
text:
Predict. A 2 mΩ shunt carries 20 A. The amplifier has negligible offset and input current. It reports a voltage that corresponds to 30 A. Find the missing resistance before changing the amplifier.



Identical force-current paths with shared-path sensing and separate Kelvin sensing, including shared copper resistance and inductance.


The intended signal is 20 A × 2 mΩ = 40 mV. If the sense wires include 1 mΩ of current-carrying copper, the amplifier sees 60 mV. Dividing by the nominal 2 mΩ produces 30 A, a 50% error. The amplifier can accurately measure a voltage that is not the voltage we intended.
V_{\mathrm{sense,bad}}=I(R_{\mathrm{sh}}+R_{\mathrm{shared}})+L_{\mathrm{shared}}\frac{dI}{dt}.
Now ramp the current from 0 to 20 A in 100 ns. A shared 5 nH adds 1 V during the ramp, much larger than the useful millivolt signal. The ideal Kelvin connection excludes the shared-path contributions, giving only the 2 mΩ resistive signal in this model.



DC calibration error and transient sense-voltage spikes with shared resistance and inductance versus ideal Kelvin connections.


Change one thing: move the sense endpoints directly to the shunt’s sense terminals. Does the error disappear? Still check shunt inductance, amplifier common-mode limits and magnetic pickup in the sense loop. A 1 V spike may overload the amplifier.
Why the basic matters: a ground reference and a component terminal are physical locations. Draw the voltage actually measured. Pease’s noise-rejection discussion, collected in Volume 3 and Ott’s mixed-signal grounding discussion motivate this treatment of reference nodes; this particular shunt exercise is authored here.
Kelvin sensing excludes the shared copper drop at the measurement points. Choose it for accurate sensing through fast current changes. The cost is separate sense routing and careful endpoint placement.
Calibration keeps the existing wiring. Scaling the reading by 2/3 corrects this example’s DC error while the resistance ratio stays constant. It can be acceptable for steady or slowly varying current. Verify the error across the required current and temperature range. A fixed gain correction cannot remove the inductive spike or prevent amplifier overload.
Our decision. Use Kelvin sensing here because the measurement must follow the 100 ns current ramp. Calibration alone cannot meet that requirement. For a DC-only measurement on an existing board, calibration remains an option if its verified error meets the specification.

title: 16.3 Why did the “better” ceramic input capacitor cause failure?
text:
Predict. Connect a 24 V source through cable inductance to an initially empty ceramic input capacitor. Its voltage rating is 35 V. Is the rating obviously sufficient because 24 < 35?



Series cable inductance and total resistance feeding an initially discharged input capacitor from a 24 V step.


Let L = 1 µH, C = 10 µF, and initial conditions iL = 0, vC = 0. With no load, the series-RLC equation is:
LC\frac{d^2v_C}{dt^2}+RC\frac{dv_C}{dt}+v_C=24,\qquad R_{\mathrm{crit}}=2\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}=0.6325\ \Omega.
With R = 0.05 Ω, the damping ratio is 0.0791 and the calculated first peak is 42.71 V. In the lossless ideal-step limit, the capacitor reaches 48 V. At 0.6325 Ω, the response is critically damped; at 1 Ω, it is overdamped. The latter two approach 24 V without overshoot in this model.



Input voltage overshoot and cable current for lightly damped, critically damped and overdamped hot-plug models.


Check the energy after settling: the capacitor stores ½CV² = 2.88 mJ. For each nonzero series R, this ideal step also dissipates 2.88 mJ; the ideal source supplies 5.76 mJ net. Changing resistance changes the peak and duration, not this final loss for the specified unloaded initial/final states. The numerical script independently checks source work against resistor heat plus stored energy.
Change one thing: add damping or a suitable damping branch. Simply adding main-path resistance has a DC cost once a load is connected: 0.6325 Ω carrying 1 A loses 0.6325 W and drops 0.6325 V. Real designs may use a deliberately damped capacitor branch instead.
Include source current limits, connector bounce, capacitor bias dependence and load behaviour when predicting hardware. The plotted source is ideal and can absorb reverse current; a real adapter may behave differently.
Why the basic matters: startup is not DC steady state, and lower ESR is not universally better. AN88, Ceramic Input Capacitors Can Cause Overvoltage Transients is by Goran Perica, not Jim Williams. It is included as a directly relevant companion source.
Damping choice. Reject the 0.05 Ω case: its 42.71 V peak exceeds the 35 V capacitor rating. For this unloaded model, use 0.6325 Ω as the critically damped reference. The 1 Ω alternative also avoids overshoot but settles more slowly.
With a load, series resistance costs DC voltage and heat. Then compare a damped shunt branch before keeping the main-path resistor. Its values must be checked in that circuit.

title: 16.4 Why did splitting the ground plane make the system worse? — Ott-inspired
text:
Predict. A designer separates analog and digital ground copper, then routes a clock across the gap. Ask students to draw the forward and return path before deciding whether the partition helps.



Conceptual continuous and split reference-plane layouts, with nearby versus detoured return-current paths.


Use a stipulated effective path model to quantify the consequence: R = 5 mΩ, with L = 5 nH for the nearby return and 50 nH for the detour. These are authored example values, not inductances extracted from the illustrated geometry. For a 1 A / 20 ns rising current edge:
V_{\mathrm{return}}=Ri+L\frac{di}{dt}.
The inductive contribution is 0.25 V or 2.5 V, respectively; after the edge, the inductive contribution vanishes and the resistive drop is 5 mV. The specified linear ramp has abrupt changes of slope, so the plotted path voltage has idealized jumps at its ends. The model stipulates the current waveform; it does not claim a real logic driver can maintain that waveform against any resulting impedance.



Same current edge applied to assumed 5 nH and 50 nH effective return-path models.


Change one thing: provide a continuous nearby return, or route signals through a deliberately designed bridge with their return path. Component placement and current-loop organization remain necessary on an unbroken plane. At low frequencies current distribution is influenced strongly by resistance; at high frequencies inductance and field coupling become important. Avoid treating “current always takes the shortest path” as a universal law.
Why the basic matters: KCL still requires a closed path when the drawing hides it behind ground symbols. The simple lumped model illustrates voltage consequences, not radiated-emission levels. See Ott’s slots-in-ground-planes explanation and PCB layout/stackup chapter description.
Layout decision. Keep a continuous return under the clock in this example. It avoids the detour but still requires sensible placement. If a partition is required, route the crossing with a designed return bridge. The partition alone is not an interference remedy.
crumbs: 46  16.4 Why did splitting the ground plane make the system worse? — Ott-inspired

title: 16.5 How can DC isolation transmit switching current? — Ott-inspired
text:
Predict. An isolated transformer or insulated heatsink has no intentional conductive connection across its barrier. Why does a cable current probe still see switching pulses?



A parasitic capacitor from a switching node to chassis, with an explicit external return to the source reference.


Represent winding-to-winding or switch-to-heatsink coupling by 100 pF. Apply a 48 V waveform at 100 kHz with 10 ns linear rising and falling edges. The capacitance experiences 4.8 V/ns, so each edge produces a 0.48 A peak displacement-current pulse:
i=C\frac{dv}{dt},\qquad Q_{\mathrm{edge}}=C\Delta V=4.8\ \mathrm{nC}.
There are two opposite-polarity pulses per 10 µs cycle. Their signed average is zero. Their rectified mean is 2Qf = 0.96 mA, and their ideal rectangular-pulse RMS is:
I_{\mathrm{rms}}=I_{\mathrm{pk}}\sqrt{\frac{2t_r}{T}}=21.47\ \mathrm{mA}.



Switch-node voltage and opposite displacement-current pulses through the specified 100 pF coupling capacitance.


Change one thing: reduce coupling capacitance, slow the edge, or deliberately manage the current’s return route. Reducing plate spacing can increase capacitance; an insulation barrier’s DC rating does not specify zero high-frequency coupling. A cable carries common-mode current only as part of the complete return network.
The plotted current assumes an ideal return that permits the prescribed voltage across the capacitance; a floating chassis can move in voltage, changing the result.
Why the basic matters: distinguish galvanic conduction, displacement current, peak, signed average and RMS. This is not a prediction of touch-current compliance or radiated EMI. Ott’s common-mode current measurement tip explains measuring net cable current by enclosing the relevant conductors together so differential currents cancel.
Which change first? Reducing the 100 pF coupling lowers both edge charge and current. Slowing the edge lowers peak current but leaves charge per transition unchanged; it can also increase switching loss.
First investigate the coupling geometry while preserving the required insulation. If it cannot change, evaluate slower edges. In either case, trace the return path before predicting what a cable probe will measure.

title: 16.6 Where does leakage energy go when the switch opens? — Basso-inspired
text:
Predict. An ideal-transformer model works, but the real switch exhibits a sharp drain spike. Add the leakage energy and a receiving capacitance before choosing a voltage rating or clamp.



Incremental leakage-inductance commutation cell, with an optional parallel damping resistor or ideal diode clamp.


Use an isolated commutation cell, with Lleak = 1 µH, initial current magnitude 2 A, and an initially empty 100 pF capacitance. These are incremental cell variables, not the complete flyback drain voltage. Initially stored energy is 2 µJ. Without damping or a clamp, conservation gives the first voltage-amplitude scale:
\frac{1}{2}L I_0^2=\frac{1}{2}C V_{\mathrm{pk}}^2,\qquad V_{\mathrm{pk}}=I_0\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}=200\ \mathrm V.
Its natural frequency is 15.92 MHz. A parallel 50 Ω resistor gives critical damping for this particular parallel RLC cell, since Rcrit = ½√(L/C). This is an equivalent damping illustration, not a ready-to-use series-RC snubber value or a resistor continuously connected across a real drain supply.
Alternatively, an ideal 100 V clamp begins conducting at 5.236 ns, when the remaining inductor current is 1.732 A. Holding the cell at 100 V reduces that current to zero in 17.32 ns, so the first clamp interval ends at 22.56 ns. The clamp absorbs 1.5 µJ; 0.5 µJ remains on the 100 pF capacitor.
Their sum is the original 2 µJ. The ideal clamp voltage source represents an energy sink, not a complete TVS/RCD implementation.



First positive leakage-cell voltage excursion for unclamped, resistively damped and ideal-clamped cases, with repetitive energy-power scales.


Dissipating the entire 2 µJ every cycle at 100 kHz means 0.2 W. The plotted first-clamp-event contribution alone is 0.15 W at that repetition rate, but the remaining capacitor energy also needs an eventual destination. A real clamp may absorb additional energy from the rest of the converter.
Add input voltage, reflected output voltage, nonlinear device capacitance and the actual topology before calculating absolute MOSFET VDS or total clamp power.
Change one thing: vary leakage, turn-off current or receiving capacitance; observe the square-law energy dependence on current. This exercise connects the earlier coupled-inductor model to switching commutation. See Basso’s Trade Secrets of the Flyback Converter, particularly its leakage-inductance discussion. The plotted cell is an authored simplification.
Clamp or damping? Use the ideal 100 V clamp to study a bounded first excursion. It absorbs 1.5 µJ, while 0.5 µJ remains on the capacitor. The 50 Ω alternative damps the ring instead of imposing a clamp voltage.
Keep the clamp as this voltage-limiting reference, and account for the remaining energy. A real clamp circuit needs its own voltage and repetitive-power checks. The parallel resistor is not a drop-in drain snubber.
crumbs: 48  16.6 Where does leakage energy go when the switch opens? — Basso-inspired

title: 16.7 Why does a 1 A DC supply heat its transformer and capacitor?
text:
Predict. A low-voltage full-wave rectifier supplies a nominally constant 1 A load through a reservoir capacitor. Is a 1 A RMS secondary current a sufficient heating estimate?



Full-wave bridge rectifier, reservoir capacitor and nominal constant-current load, with the assigned charging-pulse model identified.


For an intentionally simple assigned waveform, let rectifier/secondary current be 10 A for 1 ms, then zero for 9 ms. This gives 1 A average, a 100 Hz charging repetition rate and duty d = 0.1. It is not a solved diode-bridge waveform from a sinusoidal source; actual conduction angle depends on source impedance, voltage, diode drops, load and capacitance.
I_{D,\mathrm{avg}}=I_p d=1\ \mathrm A,\qquad I_{D,\mathrm{rms}}=I_p\sqrt{d}=3.162\ \mathrm A.
The capacitor current is iC = iD − 1 A: +9 A during charging, then −1 A during discharge. Its mean is zero, but:
I_{C,\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{9^2\times0.1+1^2\times0.9}=3\ \mathrm A.
With 0.2 Ω secondary winding resistance, copper loss is 2 W, rather than the 0.2 W associated with 1 A DC. With 0.05 Ω capacitor ESR, its heating is 0.45 W. The plotted secondary/bridge-output current magnitude should not be mistaken for each individual diode’s current: in a symmetric full-wave bridge each diode conducts on alternate charging events.



Assigned rectifier and capacitor currents and the corresponding ideal reservoir-capacitor voltage over one charging cycle.


For C = 4700 µF, the 9 ms discharge removes 9 mC and produces 1.915 V ideal capacitor ripple. The assigned waveform charges it by exactly the same amount. The plotted capacitor voltage starts at 11 V, rises to approximately 12.915 V, then returns to 11 V.
ESR is excluded from that voltage trace; if included, the 10 A capacitor-current change would add an ideal 0.5 V ESR step. Capacitance determines charge ripple; RMS current and ESR determine heating.
Change one thing: reduce conduction duty while retaining 1 A average. Peak and RMS charging currents rise. This original exercise applies the average/RMS and charge-balance fundamentals from chapters 5–7; it is not attributed as a particular Williams, Pease, Ott or Basso worked circuit.
What should we change? First size the winding and capacitor for their RMS currents. The assigned pulses give 2 W of winding loss and 0.45 W of capacitor loss despite a 1 A DC load.
A larger reservoir is an alternative when voltage droop is the problem. It is not yet a cure for heating: changing capacitance changes the real charging waveform, which this assigned-current model does not solve.

title: 16.8 Why does a larger gate resistor reduce coupling but increase heating? — Williams-inspired
text:
Predict. Compare two MOSFET switching speeds at the same 48 V, 5 A and 100 kHz. Slower edges reduce parasitic displacement current, but do they reduce transistor loss?



Gate driver, total gate resistance, switching transistor and parasitic switch-to-chassis capacitance.


Use a simple overlap-loss model: drain current is approximately 5 A during each linear drain-voltage transition. Compare equal turn-on and turn-off transition durations of 20 ns versus 100 ns:
E_{\mathrm{cycle}}\approx\frac{1}{2}VI(t_{\mathrm{on}}+t_{\mathrm{off}}),\qquad P_{\mathrm{overlap}}=f_sE_{\mathrm{cycle}}.









Transition duration at each edge
Cycle overlap energy
Overlap loss at 100 kHz
Current through 100 pF during voltage ramp
