Prescribed drain-voltage fall and instantaneous overlap-power waveforms for fast and slow switching transitions.


For an illustrative Miller charge Qgd = 5 nC, the corresponding approximately constant plateau currents are 0.25 A and 0.05 A, using t ≈ Qgd/Ig. If the driver has 5 V available across the total gate-path resistance during the plateau, the first estimates are 20 Ω and 100 Ω.
This is a local gate-charge estimate; Qgd, plateau voltage and driver impedance depend on operating conditions. Gate threshold voltage alone does not predict transition time.
Change one thing: vary the total gate resistance or separately control turn-on and turn-off currents. Slowing the edge reduces this specified capacitive current by five while increasing the model’s overlap loss by five. It does not guarantee five times less radiated EMI: the full return paths, resonances and spectrum matter.
Conduction loss, output-capacitance energy, reverse recovery, dead time and detailed gate-loop dynamics are excluded, so the overlap numbers are not total MOSFET losses.
Why the basic matters: power is the area under v(t)i(t), while capacitive coupling depends on dv/dt. Williams’s AN70 uses controlled slew rates to reduce switching-related interference; the numerical MOSFET example here is authored separately.
Fast or slow edge? The 20 ns case gives 0.48 W overlap loss and 0.24 A capacitive current. At 100 ns, these become 2.4 W and 0.048 A. We gain less coupling by accepting more transistor heat.
Keep 20 ns if that coupling meets the requirement. Move towards 100 ns only if the coupling reduction is needed and the added heat is acceptable. With no coupling limit specified, these calculations cannot select a final gate resistor.

title: 16.9 Optional advanced extension: the capacitor that remembers — Pease-inspired
text:
Outside the two-session core. Predict. Charge a capacitor, briefly short its terminals and disconnect the short. Why can terminal voltage reappear even though an ideal capacitor would remain at zero?



One dielectric-absorption RC branch in parallel with the main capacitance, with externally selected charge, short and open terminal modes.


Model a 1 µF main capacitor C0 in parallel with a 1 MΩ–10 nF series branch. The branch is a crude representation of slow polarization, not a universal dielectric model. Charge fully to 5 V, then short the external terminals for 1 ms. The main capacitor falls to zero, but the hidden capacitor decays with RDA CDA = 10 ms:
V_{\mathrm{DA}}(0^+)=5\exp\left(-\frac{1\ \mathrm{ms}}{10\ \mathrm{ms}}\right)=4.524\ \mathrm V.
Remove the short. With ideal infinite-impedance measurement, charge redistributes between the capacitors. The recovered terminal voltage tends to:
V_\infty=\frac{C_{\mathrm{DA}}V_{\mathrm{DA}}(0^+)}{C_0+C_{\mathrm{DA}}}=44.79\ \mathrm{mV}.
\tau=R_{\mathrm{DA}}\frac{C_0C_{\mathrm{DA}}}{C_0+C_{\mathrm{DA}}}=9.901\ \mathrm{ms},\qquad v(t)=V_\infty\left(1-e^{-t/\tau}\right).



Voltage recovery after removal of a short, including a finite-resistance meter and dependence on the short duration.


No energy is created: the hidden polarization branch retained charge and energy. A 10 MΩ meter also discharges the network, so its trace differs from the ideal unloaded recovery and eventually returns to zero. Dielectric absorption, steady leakage and ESR are distinct effects, even though more detailed equivalent circuits can contain several dissipative branches.
Change one thing: lengthen the short, change the sample history, or attach a finite-impedance measurement. Discuss errors in sample-and-hold circuits, reset integrators and precision voltage sampling. Real absorption spans multiple time constants; these values are not a specified recovery percentage for any material. See Pease’s What’s All This Soakage Stuff, Anyhow?, collected in Volume 2.
Accuracy or waiting time? Lengthening the short lets hidden charge decay without changing the capacitor, but delays the next measurement. A lower-absorption capacitor is another candidate when the cycle cannot wait. It still needs an error check with the actual charging history.
For this demonstration, change the short duration first. If the resulting recovery still exceeds the measurement budget, reconsider the capacitor. Changing the meter resistance also changes the observed recovery; it does not remove the stored-charge mechanism.

title: 16.10 Optional advanced extension: ask for more boost voltage and initially get less — Basso-inspired
text:
Outside the two-session core. Predict. An ideal continuous-conduction boost converter operates at 12 V input, 24 V output, D = 0.5, L = 100 µH, C = 100 µF and Rload = 24 Ω. Increase duty slightly. Does the output immediately rise?



Ideal boost switching stage showing inductor, diode, controlled switch, output capacitor and resistive load.


The output load draws 1 A and the nominal inductor current is 2 A. Use the averaged state equations:
L\frac{di_L}{dt}=V_{\mathrm{in}}-(1-D)v_o,\qquad C\frac{dv_o}{dt}=(1-D)i_L-\frac{v_o}{R}.
Step duty from 0.500 to 0.505, so ΔD = 0.005. At the instant of the change, inductor current and capacitor voltage cannot jump. Output-delivery current therefore falls by iL ΔD = 10 mA. The initial output slope is:
\left.\frac{d\Delta v_o}{dt}\right|_{0^+}=-\frac{I_L\Delta D}{C}=-100\ \mathrm{V/s}=-0.1\ \mathrm{mV/\mu s}.
Meanwhile the increased on-time builds inductor current. Eventually that larger current can deliver more output power. The local linear model predicts an initial 0.828 mV undershoot at 16.6 µs and a final +0.24 V change. The exact ideal DC equilibrium at D = 0.505 would be 24.2424 V; the small difference from 24.24 V is linearization error, not a simulation inconsistency.
Linearizing the two state equations gives the duty-to-output transfer function:
G_{vd}(s)=\frac{V_o}{1-D}\frac{1-s/\omega_z}{1+sL/[R(1-D)^2]+s^2LC/(1-D)^2},\qquad \omega_z=\frac{R(1-D)^2}{L}.
Thus the zero is at s = +60,000 s⁻¹, or 9.549 kHz in frequency. The numerator 1 − s/ωz produces increasing magnitude but additional phase lag above its corner, unlike a left-half-plane zero. The model’s poles remain stable; an initial inverse response is not itself instability.



Local boost duty-step response, enlarged initial inverse response, and magnitude/phase plots highlighting the right-half-plane zero.


Change one thing: vary load resistance or operating duty and recalculate the zero. Its position depends on the operating point, so a compensation design must check the relevant range. This example has no controller; it does not prescribe a universal crossover frequency or phase margin.
The model is continuous-time, local, averaged and assumes CCM. Switching ripple, DCM transitions, losses and sampling effects are excluded; the plotted 100 kHz Bode endpoint is mathematical, not evidence of physical accuracy up to an unspecified switching frequency.
Why the basic matters: more on-time initially means less output-delivery time. Bode phase follows the physical energy path. Basso’s Understanding the Right-Half-Plane Zero explains the consequence for control design. The Python script independently compares the transfer-function response with the linearized state-space equations.
Control decision. Use the model containing the right-half-plane zero for compensation. The simpler DC conversion ratio predicts the final direction but misses the initial dip. It cannot justify a fast voltage loop.
Choose bandwidth only after checking the zero across the operating range. If the required response cannot tolerate that restriction, reconsider the power-stage or control architecture. Increasing gain alone does not remove the inverse response.
The first ten plots are generated by scripts/practical_examples.py; practical-examples-checks.json records results and checks. Their matching schematics are native SVG objects with editable text in figures/inkscape/45_…svg through 54_…svg. Select these figure numbers in scripts/make_winding_schematics.py; use --export-only after manual edits to preserve the source artwork.

title: 16.11 Optional converter-design extension: extract and tune a series-RC snubber
text:
A. First confirm the ring belongs to the circuit
Design task. A switching-node ringing tail suggests an LC resonance. Estimate the effective parasitics from two frequency measurements, select a series-RC branch, then compare voltage stress and heat. This extends section 16.6: the resistor is now in series with a capacitor, rather than continuously across the node. It is detailed worked material for a later converter lecture, outside the two-session core.
The method follows the frequency-shift approach in Nexperia AN11160, Designing RC Snubbers. All numbers and waveforms below form an authored synthetic measurement/design exercise, not recorded hardware data or a reproduction of Nexperia’s device example.
Use a short, consistent measurement return as in section 16.1. Keep operating voltage, load, probe loading and component placement fixed between tests. Identify the same ringing mode before and after adding a known, low-inductance test capacitor directly across the ringing node and its local return. The test assumes the effective loop inductance stays unchanged and capacitance can be treated as linear around the observed excursion.
Suppose the fitted natural frequencies are f₀ = 50 MHz before the test and f₁ = 25 MHz with Ctest = 1.2 nF added. From the two LC equations:
f_0=\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{L_pC_p}},\qquad f_1=\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{L_p(C_p+C_{\mathrm{test}})}}.
C_p=\frac{C_{\mathrm{test}}}{(f_0/f_1)^2-1}=\frac{1.2\ \mathrm{nF}}{4-1}=400\ \mathrm{pF},\qquad L_p=\frac{1}{(2\pi f_0)^2C_p}=25.33\ \mathrm{nH}.
The inferred Cp includes the effective capacitance present during the test, including the probe. Subtract or otherwise account for known probe loading if the probe will not remain in service. These are effective circuit parameters, not necessarily individual package or device values. Nonlinear Coss, multiple resonances and a changed ringing operating point can invalidate the simple extraction.
Damping refinement: an oscilloscope measures the damped frequency fd, rather than exactly the natural frequency fn. If the envelope is proportional to exp(−αt):
\alpha=\frac{\ln(A_1/A_2)}{t_2-t_1},\qquad f_n=\sqrt{f_d^2+\left(\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\right)^2}.
For this fixture, the synthetic tails have fd ≈ 49.975 MHz and 24.951 MHz, with α ≈ 9.870 × 10⁶ s⁻¹. Correcting gives the 50 and 25 MHz values above. Neglecting the correction is a small approximation here, but can be poor for a strongly damped ring.
The script checks the decay and period from successive positive peaks. Under the assumed series-loss model, the decay also gives Rloop = 2Lpα = 0.5 Ω.

title: 16.11 Optional converter-design extension: extract and tune a series-RC snubber
section: B. Choose the starting capacitor and resistor
text:
B. Choose the starting capacitor and resistor
Use a first capacitor candidate Cs = 3Cp = 1.2 nF. This is a starting trade-off, not a universal optimum. The direct test capacitor is removed or reused as the final capacitor behind a series resistor; do not leave an unintended extra 1.2 nF directly across the node.
The original tank’s characteristic impedance is:
Z_0=\sqrt{\frac{L_p}{C_p}}=7.96\ \Omega.
Choose the nearby standard value Rs = 8.2 Ω and check it with the actual series-RC network. The snubber time constant is RsCs = 9.84 ns, much shorter than the illustrative 5 µs half-period at 100 kHz and 50% duty. At 50 MHz, the capacitor’s reactance magnitude is 2.65 Ω, so the branch presents a substantial real component in the ring band while blocking steady DC current.
Do not label this automatically “critical damping.” The added capacitor creates a third-order network. The best resistance depends on the capacitance ratio, source impedance and commutation waveform. The numerical sweep below checks 2.2, 4.7, 8.2, 15 and 33 Ω for the same 1.2 nF capacitor.

title: 16.11 Optional converter-design extension: extract and tune a series-RC snubber
section: C. Compare the same finite edge in three circuits
text:
C. Compare the same finite edge in three circuits
Use an idealized edge-test fixture: a prescribed 0 → 48 V linear rise in 5 ns, followed by a held input, drives Rloop = 0.5 Ω and Lp = 25.33 nH in series. The output has the 400 pF parasitic capacitance to return. Compare no added branch, a direct 1.2 nF capacitor, and the 8.2 Ω + 1.2 nF series branch. Initially all currents and capacitor voltages are zero.
For the snubbed case, the simulated state equations are:
L_p\frac{di_L}{dt}=v_d-R_{\mathrm{loop}}i_L-v,\qquad C_p\frac{dv}{dt}=i_L-i_s.
i_s=\frac{v-v_s}{R_s},\qquad C_s\frac{dv_s}{dt}=i_s.
Here vd is the imposed drive, v is the observed node voltage, and vs is the voltage across the snubber capacitor. The resistor sees v − vs, not the entire node voltage at all times. The rising edge is held for long enough that both circuits settle before any subsequent falling edge.



Normalized synthetic ringing tails used for extraction and finite-edge voltage responses before and after adding capacitance or the series-RC snubber.

The series RC cuts overshoot amplitude by approximately 60% and shortens settling substantially in this model. The direct capacitor mainly changes the frequency; it does not provide the desired damping. It also increases charging current and energy throughput. The circuit already has 0.5 Ω loss, so “capacitor only” is not literally lossless.
The final 63.73 V peak would still be unsuitable for a hypothetical 60 V absolute-maximum device. The example demonstrates improvement, not an automatic device-rating pass. More capacitance, a different resistance, lower loop inductance, controlled slew rate, a clamp or a different device rating may be required. Recheck tolerances and operating corners after any change.



Snubber-resistance sweep showing a nonmonotonic peak-voltage trade-off, and integrated losses in the existing loop resistance and added snubber resistor.


At fixed Cs, the selected 8.2 Ω gives the lowest peak among the five sampled resistor values. Neither “as little resistance as possible” nor “as much resistance as possible” gives the best result. This is a discrete tuning comparison, not proof of a global optimum.

title: 16.11 Optional converter-design extension: extract and tune a series-RC snubber
section: D. Check losses without double-counting the ringing energy
text:
D. Check losses without double-counting the ringing energy
A useful fast-edge budget for a capacitor charged and discharged through a full bus swing once per switching cycle is:
P_{\mathrm{added}}\approx C_sV_{\mathrm{bus}}^2f_s=1.2\ \mathrm{nF}\times48^2\times100\ \mathrm{kHz}=0.2765\ \mathrm W.
There are two edges per cycle: ½CsV² per edge, not CsV² per edge. This budget assumes complete charge/discharge. Finite edge duration, the actual voltage across Cs and the surrounding converter determine the real loss distribution.
For the explicit linear fixture, integrate each resistor’s instantaneous heating over one rising edge. A falling edge from the fully settled high state has equal heating by linear symmetry. Multiply the one-edge integrals by 2fs:
P_{R_s}=2f_s\int i_s^2(t)R_s\,dt,\qquad P_{R_{\mathrm{loop}}}=2f_s\int i_L^2(t)R_{\mathrm{loop}}\,dt.









Model dissipation at 100 kHz, two settled edges per cycle

Direct 1.2 nF only

The added total loss is 0.2762 W, close to the simple 0.2765 W budget. But the snubber resistor itself loses 0.3131 W: it also takes over some dissipation that previously occurred in the loop. Thus CsV²fs is an added-system-loss estimate, not an exact component-temperature calculation. The no-snubber total is slightly below the ideal abrupt-step CpV²fs budget because the model uses a finite 5 ns drive.
Do not add another leakage-energy term to these already integrated losses: the simulated currents and energy balance already include the tank dynamics. A real converter may have additional recovery/commutation energy absent from this fixture, and it requires a full topology-specific accounting.

title: 16.11 Optional converter-design extension: extract and tune a series-RC snubber
section: E. Average power is not enough for resistor selection
text:
E. Average power is not enough for resistor selection
The simulated snubber resistor sees approximately 4.52 A peak and 167 W peak instantaneous power, despite only 0.313 W cycle-average heating. For a separate ideal forced-discharge estimate, if a fully charged 1.2 nF capacitor is suddenly discharged through 8.2 Ω:
I_{\mathrm{pk}}=\frac{48}{8.2}=5.85\ \mathrm A,\qquad P_{\mathrm{pk}}=\frac{48^2}{8.2}=281\ \mathrm W,\qquad E_{\mathrm{pulse}}=\frac{1}{2}C_s48^2=1.382\ \mathrm{\mu J}.
This discharge estimate is a different limiting waveform, not an extra pulse to add to the simulated energy. Check repetitive pulse energy, pulse duration, peak voltage, average-power derating and mounting conditions in the selected resistor datasheet. A hypothetical 0.125 W part is inadequate for the calculated average loss; even a nominal 0.5 W part is only a candidate until its pulse and thermal limits are checked.
Use a suitable low-inductance capacitor and short snubber loop, and verify its voltage and pulse-current capability. Extra lead/trace inductance can bypass the intended high-frequency damping.
Snubber choice. Retain 8.2 Ω with 1.2 nF as the starting candidate: it gives the lowest peak among the five sampled resistances. Adding the capacitor alone has almost the same total model loss, but does not provide the same tuned damping.
The RC resistor dissipates 0.3131 W and sees a much larger pulse peak. Carry those stresses into component selection. If the voltage target still fails, compare new RC values rather than assuming more capacitance is free.
scripts/rc_snubber_example.py generates figures 55–56 and rc-snubber-checks.json. It checks the frequency extraction, fitted decay, stable poles, peak convergence on halving the time step, and source-work balance against both resistor integrals and final stored energy. Figure 57 has an editable native Inkscape source; select --figures 57 in the schematic generator, with --export-only after manual edits.
Model limits: this is a linear edge fixture with constant parasitic capacitance and an imposed source that can absorb current. It excludes nonlinear Coss, diode/body-diode clamping, reverse recovery, driver impedance, snubber ESL and temperature. The full-cycle loss comparison assumes complete settling and symmetric edges. It is not a complete half-bridge or flyback simulation, and its peaks are illustrative rather than hardware ratings.

title: 16.12 Optional extension: select real snubber components and include the PCB
text:
A. A concrete pair of component candidates
Question: can the 8.2 Ω / 1.2 nF design be built with ordinary surface-mount parts, and will it behave the same when placed several connections away from the device? Retain section 16.11’s 48 V, 5 ns edge, 100 kHz fixture. Separate a datasheet screening calculation from final hardware qualification.
The resistor’s P70 rating is 0.75 W, conditional on the stated mounting/thermal resistance, with ambient derating above 70°C and a 155°C film-temperature limit. Its continuous-pulse and pulse-voltage charts start at 1 µs. Use these rather than its single-pulse curve for repetitive switching. See Vishay document 20043, revision 17 March 2026, pp. 1, 3, 5–6.
The capacitor code identifies 122 = 1200 pF, J = ±5%, 1 = 100 V, G = C0G. The family specifies −55°C to +125°C operation and stable capacitance with applied DC voltage. Its short-duration dielectric-withstand test is not an operating-voltage allowance. See KEMET C1003, 20 February 2025, pp. 1 and 4–5.
These are real ordering codes; the simulations below use their nominal R/C values and initial tolerances. Neither manufacturer supplies the complete nanosecond package/PCB model used here. Saved manufacturer PDFs and SHA-256 hashes are recorded with the numerical results.

title: 16.12 Optional extension: select real snubber components and include the PCB
section: B. Resistor heating, pulse power and the limit of the published chart
text:
B. Resistor heating, pulse power and the limit of the published chart
From section 16.11, with zero added branch inductance:
E_R=1.565\ \mathrm{\mu J/edge},\qquad P_R=2f_sE_R=0.3131\ \mathrm W.
I_{R,\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac{P_R}{R_s}}=0.1954\ \mathrm A,\qquad P_{R,\mathrm{pk}}=167.35\ \mathrm W.
There are 200,000 pulses per second. The mean is small because each pulse is short, not because its instantaneous stress is small. The energy-equivalent rectangle has width
t_{\mathrm{eq}}=\frac{E_R}{P_{R,\mathrm{pk}}}=9.35\ \mathrm{ns}.
This is an energy comparison, not a claim that the waveform is rectangular. A separate fully charged-capacitor discharge estimate gives 281 W peak at nominal bus voltage; it is not added to the integrated fixture energy.
For an assumed 85°C ambient, use the ambient derating curve:
P_{\mathrm{allow}}(85)=0.75\frac{155-85}{155-70}=0.6176\ \mathrm W.
The nominal mean uses 51% of that allowance. At 125°C, the same calculation permits only 0.2647 W, so this candidate fails the nominal mean-power check there. The power rating requires adequate PCB heat removal; package size alone does not establish it. The resistor’s headline voltage limit also does not permit arbitrary continuous voltage across 8.2 Ω: continuous power remains a separate constraint.
Repetitive-pulse screening: reading the 1206-HP curve at its 1 µs left endpoint, choose 400 W as an intentionally conservative screening reference below the plotted curve, not a precisely digitized rating. Both the 167 W simulated peak and the separate 281 W discharge estimate lie below it.
At a +10% bus, the latter becomes approximately 340 W before resistance tolerance. Nominal resistor peak voltage is only 37.0 V, or 48 V in the separate discharge estimate, well below the pulse-voltage curve at 1 µs.
What this establishes: reasonable average-power and coarse peak-stress margins for a candidate. What remains open: the published curve does not qualify 9 ns equivalent pulses. Do not extrapolate its slope into the nanosecond region or label this a manufacturer-guaranteed repetitive-pulse pass. Obtain manufacturer confirmation for the actual waveform and verify heating, resistance drift and failures on hardware.
A 1 µs rectangle at the actual repetition rate would have a different, much larger mean power; it is not the loss calculation used here.



Simulated nanosecond resistor power and manufacturer ambient-power derating, with nominal and tolerance-screened mean dissipation.

text:
C. Capacitor voltage is not the switching-node voltage
The resistor separates the two nodes. With zero added branch inductance, the switching node reaches 63.73 V, while the actual snubber capacitor reaches only 48.01 V. Use the voltage across the capacitor’s own terminals for its rating check. For bipolar or offset waveforms check the largest absolute terminal voltage, including ringing; do not compare only the AC RMS component with a DC rating.
The following sensitivity sweep includes R ±1%, C ±5%, a +10% bus and all five branch-inductance cases below. Each maximum is taken independently; they need not occur in the same corner.

Initial component tolerance is included; temperature drift, aging, edge-speed variation and uncertain extracted tank parameters are not. These are bounded calculations for the stated fixture, not a universal worst case.
The capacitor must additionally carry the computed current. The family datasheet does not give a part-specific repetitive-current or MHz ESR/thermal limit sufficient to complete that qualification. A low-frequency dissipation-factor measurement cannot simply be turned into an ESR valid across the nanosecond pulse spectrum. title: 16.12 Optional extension: select real snubber components and include the PCB
section: E. Translate the model into PCB placement
text:
E. Translate the model into PCB placement



Editable circuit including total snubber-branch inductance and conceptual compact versus remote PCB placement with both outgoing and return paths.


Place the series RC branch across the same two physical terminals whose ringing is being damped. Keep the outgoing connection and return close together and minimize the enclosed loop. A nearby capacitor with a long connection to a distant ground via can still form a poor snubber. In an actual switch-node-to-return design, check the local power return rather than assuming every ground symbol is equipotential at 50 MHz.
Give the resistor copper for heat removal while keeping its high-frequency loop compact. Keep the branch away from sensitive signal loops; coupling is absent from this model. If two layers or parallel paths are used, include their actual return geometry and vias in the inductance extraction. Smaller packages may reduce ESL but can also reduce thermal/pulse capability: geometry and ratings must be considered together.
Measure with a short probe connection or a suitable differential/coaxial fixture, then repeat the ringing extraction and tuning on the actual layout. This linear example has no nonlinear Coss, reverse recovery, diode clamps or mutual coupling. The simulated 71.7 V peak is not a switch-voltage rating approval.
Component decision. Retain the named resistor and capacitor as candidates, not as a completed selection. The available resistor chart does not qualify the nanosecond repetitive pulse. Keep the compact loop and obtain suitable pulse evidence before accepting the pair.
A different part or footprint is an alternative if qualification fails. It may improve pulse capability, but changes layout and branch inductance. Repeat the waveform check after that change.
Reproduce: scripts/snubber_components_layout.py generates figures 58–59 and snubber-components-layout-checks.json, including source hashes, corner results, stable-pole checks, independent energy balance and time-step convergence. Figure 60 is a native three-layer Inkscape SVG; select --figures 60, or --figures 60 --export-only after manual edits. This section remains optional and is outside the 180-minute teaching route.

title: 16.13 The DC link has a huge capacitor: why does the switch still see overvoltage?
text:
Predict. A 48 V switching stage has a large bulk capacitor, but the capacitor is connected through a cable or a long PCB loop. During commutation, 20 A in a stipulated 100 nH stray commutation inductance falls to zero in 100 ns. Can increasing the distant bulk capacitance eliminate the switch-voltage overshoot?
First draw the complete commutation loop, including the bulk/local capacitor, switches or diodes, outgoing path and return. A DC voltage rating alone says nothing about the voltage needed to change current in that loop. With voltage referenced in the direction of the original inductive current:
v_L=L\frac{di}{dt},\qquad |\Delta V|=100\ \mathrm{nH}\frac{20\ \mathrm A}{100\ \mathrm{ns}}=20\ \mathrm V.
In a turn-off circuit where this induced voltage adds to a 48 V blocking voltage, the estimate is 68 V at the switch, before additional ringing or device effects. The sign and stressed component follow from KVL in the actual topology; an arbitrary cable-current change does not always add 20 V to every node.
Here the specified current is the current in the stray inductance being commutated, not automatically the load current or the distant supply current.
Change one feature, predict again.







Change, keeping the other stated quantities fixed
Inductive voltage magnitude




Original: 100 nH, 20 A change in 100 ns
20 V


Reduce effective commutation inductance to 20 nH
4 V


Slow the current transition to 200 ns
10 V


Double the distant bulk capacitance, keeping loop inductance and current slew fixed
20 V



A local low-inductance capacitor can close the fast switching-current loop near the devices, allowing the remote cable current to change more slowly. Its value, ESL, mounting, vias and return path all matter. More microfarads at the far end do not remove the intervening inductance. Slowing a transition can reduce the inductive voltage but may increase switching loss (§16.8).
The initial energy in this stray inductance is:
W_L=\frac{1}{2}LI^2=20\ \mathrm{\mu J}.
It must be transferred to capacitances, returned to another port or dissipated in a clamp/snubber or device. This energy estimate helps size an absorption path; it is not an additional loss to add blindly to a waveform-integrated loss calculation. Sections 16.6 and 16.11 develop the clamp and snubber cases.
Why the basic matters: bulk energy storage and a fast local current path are different design needs. Compare this with §16.3: hot-plug excites the cable-L/input-C network from its initial state, whereas this example concerns an already energised switching circuit. Neither the prescribed-slew estimate nor the lumped LC example predicts distributed cable reflections; electrically long cables need a transmission-line model. Measure with the short-return or differential arrangement discussed in §16.1.
Placement choice. Put the fast capacitor path near the commutating devices. It reduces local loop inductance but consumes placement area. The remote bulk bank remains useful for slower energy demands. Compare the two time scales before paying for more distant capacitance.
crumbs: 55  16.13 The DC link has a huge capacitor: why does the switch still see overvoltage?

title: 16.14 Why does stopping the motor raise the DC-link voltage?
text:
Predict. A motor drive has a 470 µF DC-link capacitor initially at 48 V. During deceleration, 1 J of net electrical energy reaches the capacitor after motor/converter losses. Assume the upstream supply cannot sink current, and no other load or braking branch absorbs energy. Is the bus still approximately 48 V?
Conservation of energy gives:
\frac{1}{2}C(V_f^2-V_0^2)=E_{\mathrm{return}},\qquad V_f=\sqrt{V_0^2+\frac{2E_{\mathrm{return}}}{C}}.
For the stated values, Vf ≈ 81.0 V. A small-looking amount of energy can therefore produce a large voltage increase. Do not use ΔV = E/C: its units are wrong, and capacitor energy depends on voltage squared. For small excursions only, ΔV ≈ E/(CV₀) is a local approximation; it is inaccurate for this large excursion.
How much can the bus accept? To remain at or below a hypothetical 60 V ceiling, the capacitor can absorb only:
E_{\mathrm{headroom}}=\frac{1}{2}C(60^2-48^2)\approx0.305\ \mathrm J.
Storing the full 1 J between 48 V and 60 V would require at least 1.54 mF of effective capacitance in this ideal energy calculation. This is an energy minimum, not a complete component selection: operating margin, capacitance tolerance/bias, ripple current, ESR and control delay remain relevant.
Connect it to mechanics. A rotor/load with inertia Jm has kinetic energy Jmω²/2. Reducing speed releases the difference in kinetic energy; only the fraction actually returned electrically reaches the bus. The energy calculation above deliberately starts with the net returned 1 J so it does not assume lossless motor regeneration.
Change one thing: add capacitance, provide an appropriately controlled braking resistor, or use a source/storage interface capable of absorbing the returned energy. A diode-fed supply or a supply that only sources current does not automatically provide that sink. A resistor/chopper must handle the returned energy, peak power and repetition rate; a finite capacitor cannot absorb continuous regeneration indefinitely. See TI’s discussion of motor-drive overvoltage and bulk capacitance.
Why the basic matters: the supply voltage setting cannot hold the bus down unless there is a path for the returned energy. Ask the same question for an actuator lowering a load, an externally driven motor or a shared DC bus: where can the energy go?
Where should the energy go? The 470 µF bank fails the hypothetical 60 V ceiling: the energy calculation gives about 81 V. For one bounded 1 J event, investigate a bank above the 1.54 mF ideal minimum, with margin.
Repeated braking needs a repeatable energy sink. A braking resistor spends the energy as heat; a regenerative interface can return it, with more conversion and control hardware. Choose that path from repetition and sink capability, not capacitance alone.

title: 16.15 Both capacitors meet their voltage ratings: why does the connector spark?
text:
Predict. Two 1 mF capacitors share a common return. One is charged to 48 V, the other to 0 V. Connect their positive terminals through a resistive path, with no external source attached. Assume constant capacitance and enough resistance for eventual settling. What is the final voltage, and where does the energy go?
Charge conservation fixes the final common voltage:
V_f=\frac{C_1V_1+C_2V_2}{C_1+C_2}=24\ \mathrm V.
Initially the capacitors store 1.152 J in total. At 24 V they store 0.576 J. The other 0.576 J is dissipated during equalisation. More generally, defining the series-equivalent capacitance for the voltage difference:
C_{\mathrm{eq}}=\frac{C_1C_2}{C_1+C_2},\qquad E_{\mathrm{diss}}=\frac{1}{2}C_{\mathrm{eq}}(V_1-V_2)^2.
This is not missing energy: charge conservation determines the endpoint, while resistance dissipates energy on the way. With loop inductance, energy can oscillate between L and C before losses settle it. A perfectly lossless LC connection does not settle to the common final voltage assumed here.
Add a precharge resistor. In the resistance-dominated model, choose 10 Ω between the positive terminals. Since Ceq = 0.5 mF:
i(t)=\frac{48}{10}e^{-t/\tau},\qquad \tau=RC_{\mathrm{eq}}=5\ \mathrm{ms}.
Initial current is 4.8 A, initial resistor power is 230.4 W, and the resistor absorbs 0.576 J over the complete equalisation. After five time constants, 25 ms, the remaining terminal-voltage difference is approximately 0.323 V. Each capacitor approaches 24 V; the initially empty capacitor does not charge to 48 V in this isolated two-capacitor circuit.
Increasing resistance reduces peak current and peak power and lengthens the transient. It does not change the total equalisation energy for these fixed initial/final states. Check resistor pulse-energy and repetitive thermal capability; a low cycle-average wattage alone does not qualify the resistor. Real connection inductance also prevents an instantaneous current jump, so the exponential model applies where that inductance is negligible on the RC time scale.
Change one thing: precharge through a resistor and bypass it only after the terminal-voltage difference is sufficiently small for the actual bypass path. A fixed five-time-constant delay is an illustration, not a universal closing criterion; residual current depends on the remaining voltage difference and the bypass impedance.
Distinguish a stiff source. Charging one empty 1 mF capacitor from an ideal fixed 48 V source through resistance is a different problem. The capacitor ends at 48 V, stores 1.152 J, and the resistance dissipates another 1.152 J. The source supplies 2.304 J. Ask students to explain why the final voltage and dissipated energy differ from the isolated two-capacitor case before calculating a precharge resistor.
Why the basic matters: voltage ratings do not limit equalisation current. The initial voltage difference, complete connection impedance and stored energy determine the connection event. These are calculation exercises; predict the waveforms with a circuit model or a suitably scaled, current-limited demonstration rather than deliberately arcing charged capacitors.
Precharge decision. Keep 10 Ω as the reference precharge path. It limits the initial current to 4.8 A and spreads the 0.576 J event over time. More resistance lowers the peak further, but increases the waiting time.
Bypass only when the measured residual voltage permits the actual connection current. A fixed 25 ms delay leaves about 0.323 V here; it is not proof that every bypass path can close acceptably. Direct connection gives faster equalisation at the cost of uncontrolled peak current.

title: 16.16 Can a gate resistor see 18.8 W while dissipating only 56.4 mW on average?
text:
Predict. A 0–12 V gate driver charges and discharges an ideal 5 nF capacitor at 100 kHz. The external gate resistor is 4.7 Ω, with another 1.3 Ω in the driver/internal gate path. Assume the same total 6 Ω for both edges and enough time for each charge/discharge to complete. Is a resistor’s continuous wattage rating sufficient to choose it?
The electrical time constant is 30 ns, and initial current is 2 A at each edge. External-resistor initial pulse power is 2² × 4.7 = 18.8 W. It decays exponentially with a 15 ns power-decay time constant, since power is proportional to current squared. Each complete charge or discharge dissipates half the capacitor’s CV² across all series resistance. The external resistor’s share is:
E_{\mathrm{ext,edge}}=\frac{R_{\mathrm{ext}}}{R_{\mathrm{total}}}\frac{1}{2}C_g V_g^2=0.282\ \mathrm{\mu J}.
There are two edges per cycle, giving 0.564 µJ per cycle and 56.4 mW average at 100 kHz. At 1 MHz, with the same complete transitions, average loss becomes 0.564 W although individual pulse energy and peak power remain the same. The 56.4 mW value is only the external resistor’s loss; the idealized complete gate path dissipates CgVg²fs = 72 mW at 100 kHz.
Driver and internal gate resistance dissipate the remainder.
Change one thing: increase external resistance. This lowers peak current/power and stretches each pulse, but in this fully settled linear-capacitor model the complete path’s energy per cycle remains CgVg². The external resistor’s fraction changes with its share of total resistance. Meanwhile slower switching can increase MOSFET drain-side overlap loss (§16.8). A lower peak gate current therefore does not automatically mean a more efficient converter.
For a real MOSFET, gate charge and Miller behaviour replace the single fixed Cg model; driver source/sink impedances and turn-on/off resistance may differ. Qg × drive swing × switching frequency is a useful conventional total gate-drive estimate under its stated drive conditions, not a universal external-resistor loss formula. The nonlinear gate waveform determines the actual external resistor integral of i²R.
Thermal lesson: use pulse energy and the relevant local thermal response, not peak power times steady Rth. Conversely, low average watts do not qualify a nanosecond pulse. At such short times the resistive element and hot spots matter; whole-package mass × specific heat can overestimate the available effective Cth.
Check the resistor manufacturer’s pulse curve, peak voltage/current, repetition and mounting conditions. Do not extrapolate a microsecond pulse curve into nanoseconds without supporting data. Vishay’s pulse-capability note explains the separate pulse-energy, voltage and average-power checks; it does not validate the 30 ns teaching case.
Gate-path choice. First seek a resistor qualified for the stated pulse waveform and repetition rate. Its 56.4 mW average does not settle the selection. Keep 4.7 Ω only if that pulse check passes.
Increasing resistance is an alternative when the peak is limiting, but it stretches the pulse and may increase transistor overlap loss. Recheck both components before treating the lower gate-current peak as an improvement.

title: 16.17 The precharge resistor passes average watts: why can it still overheat?
text:
Predict. Reuse §16.15’s isolated two-capacitor equalisation: two 1 mF capacitors, 48 V initial difference and a 10 Ω resistor. The resistor sees 230.4 W initial power, 0.576 J total energy, and a 5 ms electrical RC time constant. It is not a constant 230.4 W pulse lasting 5 ms:
p_R(t)=230.4e^{-2t/(5\ \mathrm{ms})}\ \mathrm W.
The power-decay time constant is 2.5 ms, and integrating power gives the known 0.576 J. Now assume the authored thermal node from §13.3: Rth = 100 K/W, Cth = 0.020 J/K. Its 2 s thermal time constant is much longer than the electrical pulse. The approximately adiabatic estimate is:
\Delta T\approx\frac{E}{C_{\mathrm{th}}}=\frac{0.576}{0.020}=28.8\ \mathrm K.
Solving the thermal equation with the actual exponential power gives a 28.56 K peak at 16.73 ms from cold. The slight reduction comes from heat escaping during the event. A short energy pulse can produce appreciable temperature rise despite a small long-term average power.
Repeat the event once per second. Assume the initial capacitor voltages are restored externally before each event; simply leaving the equalised capacitors connected does not repeat the pulse. Average resistor power is 0.576 W, giving 57.6 K mean temperature rise. But the steady periodic peak is 72.67 K above ambient, about 14.40 ms after each connection, because each event starts from a warm baseline.
At 40 °C ambient, this model predicts approximately 112.7 °C peak, not the 97.6 °C inferred from mean power alone. A hypothetical 60 K temperature-rise budget would pass the average calculation and fail the peak calculation.
Figure 63 compares the isolated and repetitive cases. The peak temperature was computed by convolution with the one-node thermal impulse response; integrating heat flow plus the change in stored thermal energy independently recovers the pulse energy.
Change one thing: compare three different interventions. Increasing thermal mass reduces short-event temperature rise; improving the heat path lowers steady/accumulated temperature; increasing the repetition interval gives more cooling. Changing the electrical precharge resistor changes the pulse shape and duration, but the equalisation energy remains 0.576 J for the stated isolated initial/final conditions. With a sufficiently long electrical pulse, more energy leaves during precharge, reducing its temperature peak.
What this does and does not select. Rth and Cth above are illustrative parameters, not a specific 10 Ω part. A real precharge resistor also needs a pulse-energy rating for the waveform/duration, applicable voltage/current limits, repetitive endurance and mounting-dependent thermal data. Its internal resistive layer can be hotter than the package surface.
Manufacturer transient data or an appropriate multi-node model is preferable to assigning the whole body one thermal capacitance. A stiff 48 V source charging one empty 1 mF capacitor dissipates 1.152 J in the resistance (§16.15), so it is a different thermal load. See Vishay’s pulse-loading guidance.
Cooling or repetition? At one event per second, use the 72.67 K periodic peak for the thermal check, not the 57.6 K mean rise. More thermal mass reduces short-event rise; a better heat path reduces accumulated heating.
If throughput permits, a longer interval is another route. Keep the one-second schedule only after a suitable part and mounting meet the peak-temperature and pulse limits. No part is selected by the illustrative thermal node alone.

title: 16.18 The source is rated 300 W: why can it not deliver 300 W through this cable?
text:
Predict. A supply holds 24 V up to its 300 W output rating. A cable has 0.50 Ω total outgoing-plus-return resistance. At the far end, a regulated converter requests 300 W input power. Can its controller simply increase input current until it gets that power?
Ignoring cable inductance and transients for this steady-state calculation, KVL gives Vload = Vs − RI. Delivered load power is:
P_{\mathrm{load}}=I(V_s-RI)=V_sI-RI^2.
This parabola has a maximum at I = Vs/(2R), with load voltage Vs/2:
P_{\mathrm{load,max}}=\frac{V_s^2}{4R}=288\ \mathrm W.
Even an unlimited stiff 24 V source could not deliver 300 W through this resistance in the stated model. At the 288 W maximum, the cable dissipates another 288 W, and the source must supply 576 W. This is the familiar maximum-power-transfer point, with only 50% efficiency; it is not an attractive design target.
Now apply the source rating. The actual source reaches 300 W at 12.5 A, before the parabola’s 24 A peak. At 12.5 A, cable drop is 6.25 V, cable heating is 78.125 W, and the load receives only 221.875 W at 17.75 V. A supply may enter current limit, foldback or shutdown beyond its rating; it cannot be assumed to hold 24 V indefinitely.
Thus 288 W is the unrestricted cable-model bound, while about 222 W is the bound with this stipulated source limit.
Try a feasible request. At 200 W load power, the high-voltage solution is 18.633 V and 10.734 A. The cable dissipates 57.60 W, so source power is 257.60 W, within the source rating. Solving the quadratic can also produce a low-voltage/high-current root; it must be checked against source limits and converter operating range, not accepted merely because it is mathematically real.
Change one thing: halve cable resistance or raise transmission voltage while respecting device ratings. With half the resistance and the same 24 V / 300 W source limit, the maximum delivered power becomes 260.94 W. With a 48 V / 300 W source and the original 0.50 Ω cable, rated current is 6.25 A and the load can receive 280.47 W.
Explain both improvements through I²R rather than memorising a voltage preference.
Why the basic matters: source watts and delivered watts are different quantities. A constant-power converter asks for more current when its input voltage falls; cable drop then increases further. These static limits complement the negative incremental resistance and dynamic input-filter discussion in §§1.5 and 12.5–12.6. A feasible operating-point root alone does not establish startup success or closed-loop stability.
Cable or bus voltage? Reject the 300 W load request with the stated source and cable. Halving cable resistance raises delivered power only to 260.94 W. Moving to 48 V with the same 300 W source gives 280.47 W. Neither delivers 300 W at the load.
The 200 W request has a feasible static operating point. Keep it only if the converter accepts 18.633 V and starts reliably. If 300 W at the load is mandatory, revise both the source allowance and delivery path.

title: 16.19 The high-side MOSFET switches correctly: why can it not stay on?
text:
Predict. A conventional bootstrap-fed high-side driver works at moderate duty ratio but fails near continuous on-time. The gate draws little DC current, so why does its supply run down?
The bootstrap capacitor supplies gate charge plus driver bias/leakage while the switching node is high. In a simple charge-budget model:
\Delta V_{\mathrm{boot}}=\frac{Q_g+I_{\mathrm{bias}}t_{\mathrm{on}}}{C_{\mathrm{boot}}}.
Use authored values Cboot = 100 nF, Qg = 60 nC, on-state bias 100 µA, and an initial fully charged bootstrap voltage of 11.3 V relative to the moving source/switch node. A 10 µs on-interval removes 61 nC, giving 0.61 V droop. With an assumed 2 V droop allowance, one fully charged capacitor can support at most 1.4 ms in this model.
Gate charge is an event cost; bias current keeps consuming charge for the entire interval. A larger capacitor delays discharge but does not provide an indefinite supply.
Recharge is not instantaneous. Suppose the switch node is clamped low during every off interval, allowing recharge toward 11.3 V through 10 Ω. The recharge time constant is 1 µs. At 100 kHz and 95% duty, the 0.5 µs off-time recovers only 39.35% of the voltage deficit, rather than fully recharging the capacitor.
Let δ be the charge-loss voltage per on-event, and let a = exp(−toff/(Rcharge Cboot)). If d is the voltage deficit at the beginning of an on-event, then dnext = a(d + δ). The periodic end-of-on deficit is δ/(1 − a):

With an assumed 9.3 V minimum usable bootstrap voltage, the 95% case passes this simple supply check, but the 99% case does not. The on-event charge loss barely changes; reduced recharge time causes the failure. An actual driver may enter undervoltage lockout or change operation before reaching the tabulated low-voltage extrapolation. These values and threshold are hypothetical, not specifications for a TI part.
Change one thing: compare longer recharge intervals, different charging impedance/capacitance, or a driver architecture with a charge pump or independent high-side supply. Conventional bootstrap operation needs an available recharge path; some devices explicitly support 100% duty by other means. Read the actual architecture rather than assuming every high-side driver has the same limitation. See TI, Understanding 100% mode in low-power DC/DC converters.
Why the basic matters: use voltage relative to the MOSFET source, not ground, and count both charge removed and charge restored. The example omits off-state bias, voltage-dependent gate charge, diode dynamics and switching-node ringing; those refine the budget rather than replace charge conservation.
Driver choice. Retain bootstrap operation at 95% duty for this model: 9.751 V remains above the assumed 9.3 V threshold. Reject the unchanged circuit at 99%. Its shorter recharge interval causes the failure.
Longer off-time is the simplest remedy if the output requirement permits it. If continuous ON is required, choose a driver supply architecture that supports it, accepting the added supply or charge-pump requirements.

title: 16.20 Can two converters with triangular ripple produce an almost flat total current?
text:
Predict. Two buck phases feed one output capacitor and a constant 10 A load. Each phase carries 5 A average. Use 12 V input, 6 V output, 100 kHz per phase and 10 µH per inductor, with continuous conduction. Does adding a second phase necessarily increase output-capacitor ripple current?
At ideal duty ratio 0.5, each inductor sees +6 V for 5 µs and −6 V for 5 µs. The peak-to-peak ripple is:
\Delta I_{L,\mathrm{pp}}=\frac{(V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o)DT}{L}=3\ \mathrm A.
Each current swings between 3.5 A and 6.5 A. With simultaneous switching, their ripples add to 6 A peak-to-peak. With a 180° phase shift, one matched current rises exactly while the other falls; the sum is 10 A constant in this ideal steady-state case.
KCL gives the capacitor current, not the sum of individual RMS magnitudes:
i_C=i_{L1}+i_{L2}-i_{\mathrm{load}}.
For the perfectly matched interleaved case at this duty ratio, iC is zero. With in-phase switching it is a zero-mean triangle of 6 A peak-to-peak. Integrating it through an ideal 100 µF capacitor gives 75 mV peak-to-peak voltage ripple. This also follows from ΔVpp = ΔIpp/(8fsC) for this triangular capacitor current.
Break the cancellation deliberately. Keep the phase shift at 180° but change the second inductor to 12 µH, maintaining the stipulated 5 A mean phase currents. Its ripple is now 2.5 A peak-to-peak. The sum has 0.5 A peak-to-peak residual ripple, giving 6.25 mV peak-to-peak on the same ideal capacitor in the prescribed-current model.

Timing errors, current-sharing errors, ESR/ESL, load transients and layout leave additional requirements. An output capacitor is still necessary.

title: 16.21 A T-network: when can Z be inverted to obtain Y?
text:
Additional comparison: an ideal transformer has different constraints
Predict. Take a T-shaped circuit, not a transformer: series impedances Za and Zb connect the input and output to a middle node; impedance Zc connects that node to the common return. Derive Z, then decide whether Y = Z⁻¹ always exists.
Its determinant is ZaZb + ZaZc + ZbZc. It is not identically zero: for three positive resistances, both finite Z and Y exist. For example, Za = Zb = Zc = 10 Ω gives Z₁₁ = Z₂₂ = 20 Ω, Z₁₂ = Z₂₁ = 10 Ω and determinant 300 Ω². The topology alone does not prevent the conversion.
Make the inverse fail at a specific frequency. Replace both series arms by ideal 10 µH inductors, and the shunt arm by an ideal 1 µF capacitor. With Za = Zb = sL and Zc = 1/(sC):
\det Z=s^2L^2+\frac{2L}{C},\qquad \omega_r=\sqrt{\frac{2}{LC}},\qquad f_r\approx71.18\ \mathrm{kHz}.
At this frequency, each series impedance is j4.472 Ω and the shunt impedance is −j2.236 Ω. None of the three branch impedances is zero or infinite, yet:
Z is a valid finite representation, but it is singular, so no finite unrestricted Y = Z⁻¹ exists at that ideal frequency. In particular, equal entering currents I₁ = I₂ give V₁ = V₂ = 0. The inverse problem cannot uniquely recover currents from prescribed port voltages. In common mode, the two inductors act in parallel against the shunt capacitor; the ideal resonant mode explains the singularity physically.
Can another representation still work? Yes. At fr, ABCD is finite and invertible:
The equal-real-reference scattering matrix is also finite. Thus det Z = 0 does not mean the physical two-port is undefined or that its transmission matrix must have zero determinant. Add 0.10 Ω series resistance to each inductor: at the same frequency, det Z becomes approximately 0.010 + j0.4472 Ω², restoring a finite Y. The ideal singularity becomes a loss-limited resonant response; small parasitics can matter greatly near it.
Change one thing: compare three resistors, the ideal L–C–L T, and the same T with winding resistance. Ask students to identify the independent variables and check the determinant before calling a matrix inverse. The numerical script verifies all three cases and the finite ABCD/S descriptions.
Predict. Describe an ideal transformer with ratio n = N₁/N₂ = 2, using the signs of §11.4. Can you measure its open-circuit Z parameters by independently imposing I₁ with I₂ = 0?
The transformer imposes V₁ = nV₂ and I₁ = −I₂/n. Open-circuiting port 2 forces I₁ = 0, so an arbitrary nonzero input test current cannot be imposed within this ideal model. Likewise, its two port voltages cannot be independently prescribed for Y measurements. There is no finite unrestricted Z matrix or Y matrix for the ideal transformer. Its transmission and equal-real-reference scattering matrices are nevertheless well defined:
The transmission determinant is 1, not zero. With port 2 matched, reflected and transmitted power fractions are 0.6² = 0.36 and 0.8² = 0.64, summing to one for this lossless network. The winding voltage ratio remains V₂/V₁ = 0.5, while S₂₁ is 0.8; these are different quantities.
Where does the singular inverse appear? For equal real R₀, write the conversions using the identity matrix Id:
For this ideal transformer, both Id − S and Id + S are singular. The required inverses fail. It would be incorrect to invent a finite Z matrix, assign it determinant zero and claim that was the transformer’s missing representation.
Two simpler counterexamples. A two-port consisting only of a nonzero series impedance Zs between its signal terminals, with common return, has a valid singular Y matrix. A nonzero shunt admittance Yp at a through-connected signal node has a valid singular Z matrix:
A singular matrix can therefore be a valid representation in its own variables, while preventing conversion to another representation. The resonant T-network above has a finite singular Z; the ideal transformer has no finite unrestricted Z in the first place. These are different reasons that a requested parameter conversion can fail.
Why the basic matters: a matrix representation is a choice of independent variables, not a universal mandatory description. Keep the network’s constitutive constraints, the existence of a representation and the invertibility of a parameter matrix separate. Practical transformer parasitics can regularize ideal constraints over an applicable frequency range, but do not justify silently converting the ideal transformer with a singular inverse.
Representation choice. Use parameters whose independent variables remain valid for the circuit. Z is convenient for open-circuit relations; ABCD helps with cascades. At a singular conversion, keep a valid representation or solve the circuit constraints directly. Adding fictitious loss merely to invert a matrix changes the problem.

title: 16.22 Two LC filters: why does multiplying their measured gains give the wrong answer?
text:
A. Find the loading factor before calculating every matrix entry
Predict. Two second-order LC low-pass sections each have a −40 dB/decade high-frequency asymptote. If connected directly in cascade, can their individually measured voltage gains simply be multiplied? Does swapping their order matter?
Use a series inductor followed by a shunt capacitor for each stage, common return and no mutual magnetic coupling:
The connection is a cascade, not a parallel connection of two complete two-ports. With the ABCD convention of §11.4, a series impedance and shunt admittance have:
Multiply the transmission matrices to obtain the full cascade, then calculate loaded Vout/Vs with the actual source and final load. This multiplication is valid and includes loading. Multiplying Z matrices, multiplying S matrices directly, or multiplying scalar gains measured with different terminations does not implement the same connection.
Let H₁,oc be stage 1’s open-output gain from Vs, including its actual source impedance. Let H₂ be stage 2’s input-voltage-to-output-voltage gain with the final load attached. Define Zout,1 with stage 1’s source deactivated, and Zin,2 with stage 2’s final load present. Thévenin gives:
\frac{V_{\mathrm{out}}}{V_s}=H_{1,\mathrm{oc}}H_2\frac{Z_{\mathrm{in},2}}{Z_{\mathrm{out},1}+Z_{\mathrm{in},2}}.
If |Zout,1| is much smaller than |Zin,2|, the interface factor approaches one. If the second stage has very low input impedance compared with the first stage’s output impedance, it nearly shorts the first stage’s output and changes the response substantially. The comparison uses complex frequency-dependent impedances; around resonance the sum can also become small and produce peaking.
Low output impedance of the first stage is generally helpful, not the mechanism that shorts the next stage.
An ideal unity-gain unilateral buffer isolates the stages, making the product of these separately defined gains valid. A real buffer has bandwidth, impedance and power limits. No buffer is included in the passive cascade below.
The same interface in Z parameters. Let Za and Zb describe the first and second two-ports, respectively. Eliminating their shared-port voltage and opposite internal port currents gives, where the denominator is nonzero:
This explicitly exposes the first network’s Z₂₂ and the second network’s Z₁₁ in the interface calculation. These are open-circuit Z parameters; they are not automatically the actual terminated Zout and Zin used in the Thévenin expression. If Dint vanishes, use the original port equations or another valid representation rather than performing a singular elimination.

title: 16.22 Two LC filters: why does multiplying their measured gains give the wrong answer?
section: B. The fourth-order asymptote survives, but the poles can move far apart
text:
B. The fourth-order asymptote survives, but the poles can move far apart
For the lossless limiting circuit, take Zs = 0 and an open final load, with all four L/C values nonzero. Then:
\frac{V_{\mathrm{out}}}{V_s}=\frac{1}{1+s^2(L_1C_1+L_2C_2+L_1C_2)+s^4L_1C_1L_2C_2}.
The product of the two isolated open-output gains misses the s²L₁C₂ term. It therefore misses the interstage interaction, despite having the same fourth-order leading term. section: C. The same riddle in scattering language
text:
C. The same riddle in scattering language
With a consistent common real reference impedance at the interface, the forward scattering transmission of a cascade is:
S_{21,\mathrm{total}}=\frac{S_{21,2}S_{21,1}}{1-S_{22,1}S_{11,2}}.
The denominator accounts for repeated interstage reflections. The simple scalar S₂₁ product is valid when the reflection product is zero or negligible, not for every pair of passive filters. ABCD or chain-scattering matrices can be multiplied in their defined conventions; ordinary S matrices cannot simply be multiplied for cascade.
Figure 65 uses 50 Ω reference resistances for its S comparison, so that panel is a different termination question from the voltage-gain panels with ideal source and 1 kΩ load.

section: D. What if the two filters really are connected in parallel?
text:
D. What if the two filters really are connected in parallel?
If both input ports share the same input voltage and both output ports share the same output voltage, with the same reference conductor, then Ytotal = Y₁ + Y₂, where the Y descriptions exist. For two identical series-L/shunt-C sections, the equivalent circuit has L/2 and 2C (and half the identical series winding resistance).
It is still second order, with the same LC product and natural frequency, not a fourth-order cascade. Port conditions and final loading still determine damping and measured gain.
Connection choice. For these directly connected passive filters, use the loaded cascade calculation. Multiplying isolated voltage gains omits the interface current and moves the predicted poles.
A buffer can make separate voltage transfers useful, but adds an active stage with power, bandwidth and load limits. Retain the passive connection here and compare its two orders and damping. Choose a buffer only when the application permits those extra requirements.
Numerical verification: scripts/two_port_examples.py generates figure 65 and two-port-checks.json. It independently checks the loaded ABCD response against two-node KCL, the Thévenin loading factor, the scattering reflection denominator, both high-frequency slopes, the ideal transformer’s unitary S matrix and singular conversions, and true-parallel Y addition. Deep in the stopband, directly evaluating AD − BC subtracts huge nearly equal numbers; determinant verification is restricted to a numerically well-conditioned frequency band.
Models are authored fixed linear lumped circuits, not measured filters or a converter-control simulation.

title: 16.23 How can a 100 pF capacitor look like 1 nF without changing the component?
text:
Predict. An ideal small-signal voltage amplifier imposes V₂ = −9V₁, with zero output impedance and otherwise infinite input resistance. A 100 pF capacitor bridges its input and output. A source drives the input through 10 kΩ, and a separate 20 pF capacitance connects the input to reference. Predict the input loading, source-to-input bandwidth and the effect of changing the sign of gain.
1. Calculate the current before using the theorem. If V₁ changes by +10 mV, V₂ changes by −90 mV, so the bridge voltage changes by 100 mV, ten times the input change. If this occurs as a linear ramp over 1 µs, bridge current entering node 1 is 10 µA.
The same current would flow into a grounded 1 nF capacitor under that input ramp. This is a small-signal charge/current result; the physical capacitor remains 100 pF.
From §11.5, CM,in = 100 pF × [1 − (−9)] = 1 nF. The output equivalent is 111.1 pF, because its factor is 1 − 1/(−9), not ten. Input and output therefore do not generally see the same apparent capacitance.
2. Translate current loading into bandwidth. Including the separate input shunt gives 1.02 nF. With the prescribed constant gain, the original circuit’s input KCL reduces exactly to:
\frac{V_1}{V_s}=\frac{1}{1+sR_s[C_{\mathrm{in}}+C_b(1-A_v)]}.
The time constant is 10.2 µs and source-to-input −3 dB frequency is 15.60 kHz. With the output instead AC-grounded (Av = 0), the input sees 120 pF and the corner is 132.63 kHz. The bridge has not changed; the output motion makes the input driver supply more capacitive current. With fixed Av = −9, the source-to-output transfer has the same pole and nine times the magnitude, with inversion.

The active output source permits non-passive input behaviour; a positive output voltage gain larger than one does not simply multiply the input capacitance into a larger positive number.



Equivalent bridge input capacitance versus signed gain and input bandwidth for inverting, grounded-output and bootstrapped cases.


Connection to power electronics. A transistor’s gate–drain capacitance bridges two moving nodes. During an inverting common-source transition, the driver supplies charge associated with the gate and drain voltage difference. This motivates the Miller-charge discussion in §16.8. For switching design, use the device’s nonlinear capacitances/gate-charge curves and the actual voltage trajectory; this fixed 100 pF linear-amplifier model is not a MOSFET switching-loss or plateau-duration prediction.

Use bootstrapping when following the input is acceptable. If inversion is mandatory and loading is excessive, revise the source or amplifier interface instead of counting a different gain as an equivalent solution.

title: 16.24 Can a 200 Ω differential input look like 2 MΩ to the source?
text:
A. Non-inverting: the − input follows the + input
Predict. Use §11.6’s voltage-amplifier two-port with Rdiff = 200 Ω, DC open-loop gain A₀ = 100,000 and zero output resistance. There are initially no input-to-ground leakage paths, bias currents or capacitances. Compare a non-inverting gain-of-ten connection and a conventional inverting gain-of-minus-nine connection, retaining the finite 200 Ω in both calculations. These are authored model values, not specifications for a real op amp.
Drive + with Vin. Connect Rf = 9 kΩ from output to − and Rg = 1 kΩ from − to reference. The unloaded feedback divider has β = 0.1 and Thévenin resistance Rt = Rf ∥ Rg = 900 Ω. Let Iin flow from + through Rdiff into the feedback node. Then:
v_-=\beta v_o+R_t I_{\mathrm{in}},\qquad v_{\mathrm{in}}-v_-=R_{\mathrm{diff}}I_{\mathrm{in}},\qquad v_o=A R_{\mathrm{diff}}I_{\mathrm{in}}.
Adding the first two voltage relations gives the exact source-facing impedance for this model:
Z_{\mathrm{in,noninv}}=R_{\mathrm{diff}}(1+A\beta)+R_t.
The corresponding closed-loop voltage gain is:
\frac{v_o}{v_{\mathrm{in}}}=\frac{A}{1+R_t/R_{\mathrm{diff}}+A\beta}.
At DC, Zin = 2.0011 MΩ and voltage gain is 9.9945. With 100 mV input, output is about 0.99945 V, but the differential input voltage is only 9.9945 µV. The current through the 200 Ω resistor is therefore only 49.97 nA. The resistor has not changed: feedback makes both its terminals move almost together.
Using Miller’s resistive form, the ratio v−/v+ is approximately 0.9999001, so Rdiff/[1 − (v−/v+)] gives the same 2.0011 MΩ. As A tends to infinity in this specified linear model, the differential voltage and input current tend to zero while the source-facing impedance tends to infinity. It is the open-loop voltage gain that is very large; the feedback-set signal gain remains near ten.
Do not silently neglect divider loading. Since 900 Ω is not small relative to 200 Ω, the usual unloaded-divider shortcut is not exact. The actual loop gain in this model is Aβ/(1 + Rt/Rdiff). The impedance can also be written (Rdiff + Rt) times one plus that loop gain. This retains the same mechanism while accounting for the loading.
Sweep the open-loop gain from 100 to one million: approach both ideal ports. For this additional DC calculation, change the internal output resistance from zero to 100 Ω so that the effect of feedback on the output can be seen. Keep Rdiff = 200 Ω, Rf = 9 kΩ and Rg = 1 kΩ.
There is no external output load; the feedback divider remains connected. Vary only A₀. This is a separate finite-output-resistance model, so its input values differ slightly from the zero-output-resistance calculation above.
Input resistance increases; output resistance decreases. Both are approaching the ideal voltage-amplifier behaviour: no current drawn from the signal source, and little output-voltage change when load current changes. They do not both grow toward infinity. The closed-loop voltage gain approaches ten, rather than growing to one million.
To measure output resistance, set the ideal input voltage source to zero (short it to reference), keep the controlled source and feedback active, inject a small current at the output and calculate ΔVout/ΔItest. Do not deactivate the dependent amplifier source. Here Rg ∥ Rdiff = 166.67 Ω, and the output’s passive return through the divider is M = Rf + (Rg ∥ Rdiff) = 9166.67 Ω.
The loaded feedback fraction is 1/55. Including the 100 Ω internal output resistance gives the DC loop gain L₀ = 0.0179856 A₀, and improvement factor F = 1 + L₀.
The exact resistance scaling for this model is:
R_{\mathrm{in}}=R_{\mathrm{in},0}F,\qquad R_{\mathrm{out}}=\frac{R_{\mathrm{out},0}}{F}.
The baselines keep all resistors connected but set amplifier gain A₀ to zero: Rin,0 = Rdiff + [Rg ∥ (Rf + Rout,int)] = 1100.990 Ω, and Rout,0 = Rout,int ∥ M = 98.921 Ω. These are not simply the bare internal 200 Ω and 100 Ω. Retaining the feedback network in the baselines makes the same improvement factor apply to both ports without neglecting divider loading.
For L₀ ≫ 1, input resistance is approximately proportional to A₀ and output resistance approximately inversely proportional to A₀. The proportionality is not exact at low loop gain: A₀ = 100 gives L₀ only about 1.80, explaining the substantial gain error in the first row.
In the ideal A₀ → infinity limit of this circuit, Rin → infinity and Rout → zero. Real leakage, input capacitance, finite bandwidth, output current limits and interconnection impedance constrain that limit. TI’s Handbook of Operational Amplifier Applications likewise explains the reduction of output impedance by negative feedback.

section: C. Does this make the transistor input resistance irrelevant?
text:
C. Does this make the transistor input resistance irrelevant?
No: it separates feedback action from intrinsic device properties. First, a real current path from the signal input to reference bypasses differential bootstrapping. Adding an illustrative 1 MΩ input-to-ground shunt puts it in parallel with 2.0011 MΩ, reducing external input impedance to 666.8 kΩ. Bias currents, common-mode leakage and input capacitance are not removed just because the differential voltage is small.
Second, loop gain falls with frequency. Let A(s) = 100,000/[1 + s/(2π × 10 Hz)], a one-pole open-loop model with approximately 1 MHz unity-gain frequency. The low 200 Ω resistance loads the feedback divider, producing a non-inverting closed-loop corner of 18.19 kHz. Changing only Rdiff to 10 MΩ moves that corner to about 100.0 kHz.
Their DC gains are both near ten, but their bandwidths differ substantially. At frequencies where A approaches zero, the non-inverting model’s source-facing impedance approaches Rdiff + Rt = 1.1 kΩ, not 2 MΩ.



Source-facing input impedance for non-inverting and inverting feedback, a common-mode shunt limitation, and the bandwidth effect of finite differential input resistance.


Change one thing: reduce open-loop gain, change only Rdiff, or add an input-to-ground shunt. Predict separately the differential voltage, source current and closed-loop bandwidth. Do not assume v+ = v− first and then use that assumption as proof that input current is zero; obtain the small error from the finite-gain equations.
The effect also requires a stable negative-feedback loop operating within its linear input/output range. Analog Devices’ discussion of differential input capacitance explains why real differential and common-mode input loading must be distinguished.
Topology choice. Use the non-inverting connection when positive gain near ten and low source loading are required. Feedback gives about 2 MΩ input impedance in this model. The cost is relying on adequate loop gain over the signal band.
Choose the inverting connection when inversion or summing is required, accepting current through its input resistor. Its gain of −9 is a different signal requirement; high input impedance alone cannot make the two circuits interchangeable.

The additional DC sweep with 100 Ω internal output resistance is checked with separate input-drive and output-current-injection solutions, including the common resistance improvement factor.
The models exclude output saturation/current limits, bias/offset currents and intrinsic input capacitances; they describe a voltage-feedback amplifier, not a current-feedback op amp. This is an optional fourth two-port application after the T-network, LC-cascade and Miller exercises.

title: 16.25 The EMC filter attenuates noise: can it also supply the next GPU-like pulse?
text:
A. The repetition frequency is only one part of the spectrum
Predict. A regulated 48 V bus supplies an authored load of 20 A idle / 100 A high, with 20 ms high every 100 ms. Upstream power is held constant at the ideal average. What spectrum does the load produce, how much energy must come from storage, and where must that storage be connected?
These are bus-level teaching values, not measurements or limits for a specific GPU or its approximately 1 V core rail.
The pulse rate is 10 Hz, duty is 20%, mean current is 36 A and total current RMS is 48.17 A. The first nonzero current harmonic has 29.94 A peak at 10 Hz. Harmonics occur at multiples of 10 Hz under a sinc envelope whose first null is at 50 Hz; the spectrum does not end there.
For example, after the null further lobes and harmonics remain. An optional 100 µs linear-edge smoothing in the spectrum plot adds another sinc roll-off. The energy calculations below retain the stated ideal rectangular load.
An infinite periodic train has a line spectrum; a short burst spreads each line. The high-frequency edge content, the pulse envelope and any slower workload variation can therefore challenge different parts of the power chain. A filter specified for switching-frequency EMC attenuation does not automatically address the energy deficit of a 20 ms workload pulse.

title: 16.25 The EMC filter attenuates noise: can it also supply the next GPU-like pulse?
section: B. Integrate the missing power, not just the total load power
text:
B. Integrate the missing power, not just the total load power
At regulated 48 V, idle power is 960 W, high power 4800 W and ideal average source power 1728 W. During the high interval, the buffer supplies 3072 W:
E_{\mathrm{pulse}}=(4800-1728)\times0.020=61.44\ \mathrm J.
During the other 80 ms, the source has 1728 − 960 = 768 W spare, returning 61.44 J to an ideal lossless buffer. This is a periodic storage swing, not a fresh 61.44 J added to the required capacity for every pulse. Missing recharge, a longer high interval or a burst pattern with a different mean changes that result.
For a separate capacitor bank feeding the regulated bus through an ideal bidirectional converter, allow the bank to swing from 48 V to 40 V while the bus stays at 48 V:
C_{\mathrm{bank}}\geq\frac{2E_{\mathrm{pulse}}}{V_{\mathrm{bank,max}}^2-V_{\mathrm{bank,min}}^2}=0.17455\ \mathrm F.
At an assumed 95% discharge efficiency, the same bus-energy event requires at least 0.18373 F. This is only an energy minimum. The interface must also supply 3.072 kW peak; at 40 V bank voltage and 95% efficiency, the corresponding bank current is about 80.84 A.
A 61.44 J event is only 0.0171 Wh: the apparently small energy number does not imply a tiny battery or converter can provide the required power.

section: C. A directly connected bus capacitor is a different voltage constraint
text:
C. A directly connected bus capacitor is a different voltage constraint
If a capacitor is directly across the bus, its voltage is the bus voltage. With source current fixed at 36 A and the same prescribed current load, capacitor discharge current is 64 A during the 20 ms pulse. Allowing droop from 48 V to 46 V requires:
C\geq\frac{\Delta I\,t_p}{\Delta V}=\frac{64\times0.020}{2}=0.64\ \mathrm F.
A 100 µF capacitor reaches that 2 V droop in only 3.125 µs under this current deficit. It can be useful for fast local decoupling while being far too small for the full pulse. The direct-capacitor case delivers 60.16 J over the allowed droop, rather than 61.44 J, because its bus voltage falls and the specified currents no longer correspond to constant 48 V powers.
Keep the charge model and regulated-bus power model distinct. A constant-power load would require a different drooping-bus current calculation.
ESR adds an immediate current-dependent voltage drop; ESL and the connection loop affect the edge; capacitance governs subsequent charge droop. Check ripple current, thermal loss, tolerances, bias/aging, converter current limits and control interaction as well as stored energy. A rack-level CBU cannot replace low-inductance decoupling at the GPU pins.

section: D. Recharge losses can make a seemingly balanced pulse train unsustainable
text:
D. Recharge losses can make a seemingly balanced pulse train unsustainable
The 36 A average-source result assumed a lossless buffer. With 95% charge efficiency and 95% discharge efficiency, the high interval withdraws 61.44/0.95 = 64.67 J from storage, while the low interval restores only 0.95 × 61.44 = 58.37 J. The store loses 6.31 J per period despite the source matching the ideal average load power.
For the same pulse shape, a constant source of about 1792.97 W, or 37.35 A at 48 V, balances both conversion losses and periodic state of charge in this simplified model. Recalculate the waveform and capacitance with that source level. Energy capacity, charge/discharge power and average replenishment are three separate constraints.

section: F. Where EMC filters, local capacitors, CBU and BBU fit
text:
F. Where EMC filters, local capacitors, CBU and BBU fit
Infineon’s Power Pulsating Buffer article, pp.4–7, describes a capacitor backup unit (CBU) with a bidirectional converter that discharges for peak loads and recharges during lower demand. It also discusses integrating a power pulsation buffer (PPB) into the PSU instead of separate capacitor shelves. A battery backup unit (BBU) addresses backup needs; whether it also handles repeated workload pulses depends on its interface and operating limits.







Function
Main design question




EMC filter and controlled return paths
Which disturbance transfer/current path must be attenuated over which band?


Local package/board capacitors and POL conversion
Can the fast load edge be served within rail droop and loop-inductance limits?


Capacitor bank with CBU/PPB interface
Can peak power and cumulative energy swing be supplied and recharged repeatedly?


Battery-backed storage / BBU
Can the required backup duration, discharge power, SOC and cycling be supported?



There is no universal requirement that every GPU system use both a CBU and a BBU, nor one universal “large enough capacitor.” Identify the port, workload, allowed upstream slew, voltage window, losses and required backup interval. Use spectral impedance/current-sharing analysis for the fast response and the cumulative energy integral for the slower buffer requirement.
A suitably sized passive filter may provide the needed energy; an active buffer can permit a larger storage-voltage swing while maintaining the bus voltage.
Change one thing: keep pulse peak and average fixed but increase pulse duration and period by ten. Ideal storage swing becomes 614.4 J, while mean power stays 1728 W. Move the same energy requirement to a different allowed voltage window and recalculate capacitance. Finally, shorten only the edge: the high-frequency spectrum changes substantially while the ideal rectangular pulse-energy budget remains the reference.
Students should explain which design decision each change affects.
Storage choice. The EMC filter alone cannot cover this pulse. First allocate the calculated energy deficit to storage and include recharge losses. A bus capacitor is the simpler candidate if its capacitance and allowed voltage swing are practical.
Use an interfaced buffer when another storage-voltage window justifies the conversion hardware. Reject the ideal-average source setting for the 95%/95% case: storage loses energy each cycle. Recalculate source power before choosing either buffer.
