The waveform and converter interfaces are imposed teaching models, not a measured GPU, complete switching simulation or qualified CBU/BBU design. This is optional material linking the earlier FFT, PDN, thermal and energy examples.

title: 16.26 A large input capacitor: why does the battery still supply the switching ripple?
text:
Riddle: a buck draws a pulsed input current. A large capacitor is fitted directly across its input, but the battery current still looks almost like the switching pulses. Does increasing capacitance by ten solve the problem?
The topology matters. Here the resistance is in series with the capacitor, representing its ESR. It is not a resistor inserted in the main battery feed. The battery’s relevant impedance is its output impedance plus connections, evaluated at the frequency of interest. This is the same current-sharing problem as §4.1, viewed from the buck input.
Battery voltage -- Zsource --+-- buck input (pulsed current sink)
                            |
                           ESR
                            |
                           ESL
                            |
                            C
                            |
Return ---------------------+-- buck return
For each AC harmonic, suppress the ideal battery voltage source and let positive battery and capacitor currents flow toward the buck. Then

Z_C=R_{ESR}+j\omega L_{ESL}+\frac{1}{j\omega C},\qquad \frac{I_{bat}}{I_{buck}}=\frac{Z_C}{Z_s+Z_C},\qquad \frac{I_C}{I_{buck}}=\frac{Z_s}{Z_s+Z_C}.

The capacitor collects most of the ripple only when its branch impedance is sufficiently smaller than the source branch impedance. A large capacitance alone does not guarantee this. title: 16.27 The secondary is shorted: why can a common-mode injector still disturb the primary?
text:
Riddle: join the two secondary terminals and drive that joined node with a voltage injector relative to chassis. The secondary’s terminal-to-terminal voltage is zero. Should every voltage on the primary also be zero?
Specify the measurement before answering. Shorting the secondary removes its differential voltage, but does not clamp its common-mode voltage to chassis. Interwinding capacitance provides an AC displacement-current path across the isolation barrier. It is not a galvanic short circuit or evidence of failed insulation. A finite capacitance becomes a low impedance only relative to the other impedances and at sufficiently high frequency.
TI’s transformer common-mode measurement discussion describes a function-generator/oscilloscope test of this coupling; TI’s isolated-bias transformer discussion explains the interwinding-capacitance current path.
Define a reproducible fixture. Tie secondary terminals s1 and s2 together at node s and impose Vin between s and chassis. Terminate primary terminals p1 and p2 with one resistor R each to chassis. These resistors are external fixture impedances, not resistances through the isolation barrier.
Put C1 from s to p1 and C2 from s to p2. The primary winding, with the secondary shorted, presents differential impedance Zw between p1 and p2:
 s --------||--------- p1 -------- R -------- chassis
 |         C1          |
 |                     Zw  (primary short-circuit impedance)
 |         C2          |
 +---------||--------- p2 -------- R -------- chassis
 |
 Vin
 |
 chassis (injector return)
Both primary resistors return to the same chassis/injector reference. This closes the displacement-current loop. Grounding, floating or probing a different node changes the circuit and the answer. The injector is an imposed ideal source in this exercise; its actual source impedance would be another part of the fixture.
The magnetic path has not been silently discarded. For coupled windings with series resistances and a shorted secondary, the magnetic driving-point impedance is

Z_w(s)=r_1+sL_1-\frac{s^2M^2}{r_2+sL_2}.

With negligible secondary resistance this reduces to primary resistance plus the short-circuit leakage inductance. For the worked example use the reduced approximation Zw = rw + sLsc. An ideal perfectly coupled, lossless transformer with its secondary shorted instead has Zw = 0 and clamps the primary differential voltage to zero. It still does not constrain the primary’s absolute common-mode potential.
Derive the transfer functions. Define g = 1/R and Yw = 1/Zw. KCL gives

(g+sC_1+Y_w)V_1-Y_wV_2=sC_1V_{in},\qquad -Y_wV_1+(g+sC_2+Y_w)V_2=sC_2V_{in}.

Define the determinant and the two measurement ratios:

D(s)=(g+sC_1)(g+sC_2)+Y_w[2g+s(C_1+C_2)].


H_{CM}(s)=\frac{(V_1+V_2)/2}{V_{in}}=\frac{s[g(C_1+C_2)+2sC_1C_2+2Y_w(C_1+C_2)]}{2D(s)}.


H_{DM}(s)=\frac{V_1-V_2}{V_{in}}=\frac{sg(C_1-C_2)}{D(s)}.

In the balanced case C1 = C2 = C, these become

H_{CM}(s)=\frac{sRC}{1+sRC},\qquad H_{DM}(s)=0.

Both primary terminals move together, so no current flows through Zw. At high frequency the primary common-mode voltage can approach the injected voltage even though magnetic transfer of the imposed secondary differential voltage is zero. With unequal coupling capacitances, finite Zw allows different primary-node voltages: common-mode excitation is converted into differential disturbance. Unequal terminations can also break symmetry, but are held equal here to isolate the capacitance effect.
Worked frequency and time-domain comparison. Use R = 1 kΩ per primary terminal and Zw = 2 Ω + s × 10 µH. Compare 100/100 pF with 150/50 pF, keeping total interwinding capacitance at 200 pF. These are authored lumped-model values. In the time-domain test, drive a 100 V pulse with a 100 ns linear rise, a 1 µs flat top and a 100 ns fall; start from zero stored energy.

The 6.12 V pulse result includes the broadband edges and the network dynamics; it is not obtained by multiplying the pulse height by the 1 MHz gain.

Time-domain equations: let iw flow through Zw from p1 to p2. The simulated equations are

C_1(\dot V_1-\dot V_{in})+gV_1+i_w=0,\qquad C_2(\dot V_2-\dot V_{in})+gV_2-i_w=0.

It also checks the closed-form transfers against a nodal solve at 41 frequencies, KCL and the balanced high-pass/zero-differential limits.

Change one thing: balance C1 and C2 without changing their sum. The differential response disappears in this fixture while common-mode feedthrough remains. Next reduce both capacitances, or reduce Zw toward an ideal short: predict separately the two voltages and the injected current. Finally, change R or add probe capacitance to chassis.
This illustrates why a transformer is a four-terminal object whose common-mode coupling is not captured by a differential-only two-port model.
The reduced circuit excludes distributed winding capacitance, core loss, self-resonance, nonlinear effects and real injector/probe models; the plotted frequency sweep is the mathematical model’s response, not a qualified transformer bandwidth. Electrostatic shielding changes the capacitance and return network and must be modelled with its actual connection. This exercise extends §§2.6 and 16.5; it does not predict insulation compliance or hardware stress ratings.
What should change? For differential pickup in this fixture, first balance the coupling capacitances. This removes the differential response without reducing their sum. It does not remove common-mode motion.
If common-mode current is the limiting disturbance, reducing total coupling addresses the relevant quantity. A shield is another possible route, but its connection changes the return network. Choose from the measured mode before changing the transformer geometry.

title: 16.28 Identical pulses, different LC trajectories: did the phase or the poles change?
text:
Define an LC with two independent ports
Two linked riddles: why do identical voltage pulses produce different LC waveforms during startup, and how can feedback turn the same energy-storage elements from lightly damped to rapidly settling—or unstable? Use initial-state analysis for the first question and pole location for the second. Changing an initial condition does not move the poles of a fixed linear model.
An imposed voltage u drives a series R–L branch into a capacitor node v. A prescribed load current iℓ leaves that node; inductor current i enters it:
The current load is an ideal bidirectional port in this teaching model, not a resistor or a rectifier. Its current can be imposed independently of v. The equations are
C\dot v=i-i_\ell,\qquad L\dot i=u-v-Ri.
The state is (v, i). For R = 0, zero drive and zero load current, the familiar natural trajectory conserves Cv²/2 + Li²/2. With constant u = U and iℓ = Iℓ, instead define deviations from the equilibrium (U, Iℓ). Then
\omega_0=\frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}},\qquad Z_0=\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}},\qquad (v-U)^2+[Z_0(i-I_\ell)]^2=\text{constant}.
In the normalized plane (v, Z0i), the orbit is a circle centered at (U, Z0Iℓ). It is an ellipse if unscaled amperes and volts are used as axes. Nonzero sources shift the center; they do not invalidate the natural LC frequency. With two imposed bridge voltages across a resonant branch, the net branch drive can be their signed difference; actual converter conduction intervals and load laws must be derived for the chosen topology.
The exact lossless solution during a constant-source interval of duration τ is
v(\tau)=U+[v(0)-U]\cos(\omega_0\tau)+Z_0[i(0)-I_\ell]\sin(\omega_0\tau).
i(\tau)=I_\ell+[i(0)-I_\ell]\cos(\omega_0\tau)-\frac{v(0)-U}{Z_0}\sin(\omega_0\tau).
Both initial capacitor voltage and initial inductor current determine the resulting sine/cosine mixture. Reading this mixture as merely an input/output phase lag can hide the accumulated state. A sinusoid about a fixed center can of course be written with an amplitude and phase; that parametrization does not make the changing startup state a new steady-state transfer phase.
The shifted quadratic invariant is not a claim that the physical stored energy stays constant with active sources. For R = 0 the actual energy obeys dE/dt = ui − viℓ; the two imposed ports can exchange energy with the tank.

section: Laplace retains the initial-energy terms
text:
Laplace retains the initial-energy terms
For the same circuit with R included, unilateral transformation gives

(LCs^2+RCs+1)V(s)=U(s)-(Ls+R)I_\ell(s)+(LCs+RC)v(0^-)+Li(0^-).

The usual zero-state voltage transfer is H(s) = 1/(LCs² + RCs + 1), with the other independent input set to zero. It does not contain the last two terms. Each new interval can use a local time origin with its inherited initial state. Equivalently, solve the whole input history at once by superposition; repeatedly resetting the physical state is not required by either transform.

Now use R = 0.1 Ω and work with small deviations around a constant operating equilibrium. Assume both state deviations can be measured and an ideal voltage actuator applies

\delta u=-k_v\delta v-k_i\delta i.

With a fixed load-current perturbation of zero, the closed-loop characteristic polynomial becomes

s^2+\frac{R+k_i}{L}s+\frac{1+k_v}{LC}.

Matching it to s² + 2ζωns + ωn² gives

k_v=LC\omega_n^2-1,\qquad k_i=2\zeta\omega_nL-R.

kv is in V/V; ki is in V/A, or Ω. This two-state/single-voltage-input model is controllable, so these two coefficients can be assigned with full-state feedback. For ζ = 0.7 and ωn = 2π × 60 kHz, kv = 0.4212 and ki = 5.1779 Ω.

Real actuators have voltage/current limits, delay, sampling and unmeasured states; moving poles arbitrarily far left is not a physically free operation. section: What does an imaginary-axis plot fail to settle by itself?
text:
What does an imaginary-axis plot fail to settle by itself?
For a particularly clear counterexample, compare the rational expressions 1/(LCs² + 0.5Cs + 1) and 1/(LCs² − 0.5Cs + 1). Their algebraic magnitudes on jω are identical, although one has damped poles and the other growing poles. Their phases differ. The unstable causal system’s growing impulse response has no ordinary Fourier transform, so its rational jω evaluation must not be presented as a stable measured steady-state frequency response.
This does not prove that Fourier contains no stability information. Full complex frequency data, causality and an appropriate model support stability analysis; an FFT of a growing finite record also shows features of that record. It does show why magnitude alone, or a formal substitution s = jω without convergence and natural-mode analysis, is insufficient. Laplace and state space make the exponential real part and the initial state explicit.
Change one thing: first change only the state at the second pulse and keep A fixed; its poles remain unchanged. Next change only ki; the damping and poles change. Finally compare Fourier spectra before and after startup exclusion in a damped version. Ask which differences arise from initial state, forcing, damping or the acquisition window.
Timing or damping? To explain the different startup traces, keep the poles fixed and carry each pulse’s final state into the next interval. Changing feedback would answer a different question.
For a faster settling requirement, use the pole-placement model and include the sensing and control cost. Pulse timing can change the orbit, but cannot by itself move the poles of this fixed linear LC model.

Authored example: hold the negative rail and chassis at the same reference and put 1 nF from A to chassis and 1 nF from B to chassis. Impose simultaneous linear 0 → 48 V transitions on A and B in 100 ns. Then hold both high and later return both to zero with the same fall time.
Ignore dead time, leg mismatch and device nonlinearity in this first model. Because the two voltages are identical at every instant, the differential voltage stays zero, including during the edges. Yet the total current into chassis is

i_{ch}=C_A\dot v_A+C_B\dot v_B=(C_A+C_B)\dot v_{CM}=0.96\ \mathrm{A}

during the rising edge. The two capacitor currents add; they do not cancel like an outgoing/return differential load current. The rising-edge charge is 96 nC. The falling edge returns the same signed charge with opposite polarity: zero net charge per complete pulse does not mean zero peak or RMS current.



Synchronous H-bridge zero-state transitions with zero differential output voltage, changing common-mode voltage and opposite chassis-current pulses.


The high-state energy in the two capacitors is 2 × C × Vdc²/2 = 2.304 µJ. A differential-only load calculation misses this storage and its charging current. This is not automatically the energy dissipated in a particular transistor; that requires the charging/discharging paths.
Change one thing: use only one zero state in a modulation interval, or change the order of zero and active states while preserving the required differential average. Predict the new CM steps before calculating displacement current. An actual modulation scheme must also satisfy load-current, switching-loss and dead-time requirements.
If chassis floats, its potential and the complete return capacitances must be solved instead of imposing the same 0.96 A result. This exercise predicts current in the stated fixture, not radiated EMI or a universal ranking of PWM schemes.
Zero-state choice. Keep both common-mode and differential voltages in the model. The two zero states give the same load voltage but different chassis excitation. A differential-only model is sufficient only when that coupling is outside the question.
For modulation, compare sequences with the same required differential output. Fewer common-mode transitions may help this fixture, but the sequence must also carry load current and meet switching-loss limits. No universal PWM winner follows from this current calculation.

Q(V)=\int_0^V C(v)\,dv,\qquad E(V)=\int_0^V vC(v)\,dv.

The energy integrand is voltage-weighted. A local small-signal capacitance C(V) is generally neither Q(V)/V nor 2E(V)/V². If energy is recovered into an inductive network, or partly dissipated elsewhere, the switch loss differs. Nor is comparing LI²/2 with one Eoss value a complete ZVS design: all relevant capacitances, circuit constraints, current direction and available commutation time must be checked.

title: 16.31 The current peak is controlled: why do alternate cycles diverge?
text:
Optional advanced riddle: a fixed-frequency buck operates in continuous conduction with ideal peak-current control. A small valley-current error reverses sign every period and grows, although the output voltage is held constant in the model. How can a controller that checks every peak fail to stabilize the current waveform?
Let m1 > 0 be the current’s rising slope during on-time and m2 > 0 the magnitude of its falling slope during off-time. Add a positive compensation ramp ma to the sensed current before comparing it with a fixed threshold. Express all slopes in equivalent inductor-current units.
For the local calculation, assume fixed Vin, fixed Vout, a fixed period T, no comparator delay, and a switching crossing strictly inside the period.
If the initial valley current rises by δin, the comparator crossing moves by δton = −δin/(m1 + ma). The next valley changes by the original error plus the effect of this changed on/off duration:

\delta i_{n+1}=\delta i_n+(m_1+m_2)\delta t_{on}=\frac{m_a-m_2}{m_1+m_a}\delta i_n=\lambda\delta i_n.

This is a sampled pole λ. Its stability criterion is |λ| < 1, rather than a negative real part in the continuous s plane. A negative λ alternates the error sign. Without compensation, λ = −m2/m1. In the ideal CCM buck, volt-second balance gives m2/m1 = D/(1 − D), so D > 0.5 makes |λ| > 1.
At exactly 0.5 the ideal multiplier is −1: the perturbation does not decay.

Solving the exact ideal comparator crossing and both current ramps reproduces this recurrence over the demonstrated intervals.



Alternating sampled valley-current errors for stable and unstable peak-current cases, and the period-to-period multiplier versus duty with and without slope compensation.


For nonnegative ma, the local stability condition is

m_a>\frac{m_2-m_1}{2}.

At D = 0.75 the boundary is 0.3 A/µs; equality is marginal, not a design margin. This is the small-perturbation mechanism behind subharmonic, period-doubling behaviour. TI’s subharmonic-oscillation discussion gives the practical context. Do not generalize the 50% statement to all current-control methods or converters.
The growing local map cannot be extrapolated indefinitely: duty clipping, DCM, output dynamics and other nonlinearities change it. The plot stops before the ideal crossing leaves the period and does not claim a simulated final period-two limit cycle. Change one thing: increase ma until λ = 0; in this ideal local map the valley error is removed in one period.
Then investigate a larger ramp: stronger compensation is not synonymous with faster convergence for every ramp value. This connects §16.28’s continuous poles to the extra dynamics introduced by switching and sampling.
Ramp choice. Keep the 0.6 A/µs ramp as the stable reference at 75% duty. It changes the multiplier from −3 to −1/3 while retaining the nominal operating point. No compensation is acceptable in the demonstrated 25% case, but fails at 75%.
A ramp giving zero multiplier corrects the ideal local error in one period. Use it as a comparison, not a hardware optimum. More ramp can slow convergence; check the required duty range and implementation limits before choosing it.

title: 16.32 Only 50 ns of imbalance: why does the transformer flux keep walking?
text:
Riddle: a bridge applies almost equal positive and negative voltages to a transformer. Each cycle looks nearly symmetric. Can the small difference matter after fifty cycles?
Faraday’s law applies to the induced core voltage, not blindly to the bridge-terminal voltage when winding resistance and leakage drops are significant:

\Delta B=\frac{1}{NA_e}\int v_{core}(t)\,dt.

Start with an ideal imposed core voltage of ±48 V at 100 kHz, N = 8 turns and Ae = 100 mm². Positive duration is 5.025 µs, negative duration 4.975 µs: their difference is only 50 ns. The net increment per period is

\Delta B_{cycle}=\frac{48(5.025-4.975)\times10^{-6}}{8\times100\times10^{-6}}=0.003\ \mathrm{T}.

The ripple repeats around an increasingly shifted state. With initial B = −0.15 T, the first positive peak is +0.1515 T. The nth positive peak is 0.1515 + (n − 1) × 0.003 T. An assumed 0.30 T screening threshold is crossed during the 51st positive interval, about 0.5 ms after startup.
The threshold is an authored teaching value, not a material saturation rating; the calculation predicts its crossing and does not model the nonlinear current after it.
This separates three ideas: flux excursion within a cycle, initial/remanent flux, and accumulated cycle-to-cycle bias. In a linear magnetic model Lm ∝ N², but the actual B excursion still follows volt-seconds divided by NAe. A nearly symmetric oscilloscope trace can conceal a small integral error. TI’s full-bridge design report, §3.2.1 discusses flux walking and volt-second asymmetry in bridge/push-pull structures.
Now distinguish terminal from core voltage. Add an authored winding resistance of 0.2 Ω and a linear 50 µH magnetizing inductance, driven by the same bridge-terminal waveform. For this no-load reduced model,

L_m\dot i_m=v_{bridge}-R_pi_m,\qquad B=\frac{L_mi_m}{NA_e}.

The terminal waveform has a 0.24 V average. In the eventual periodic linear state, its average is balanced by Rp times the 1.2 A average magnetizing current, leaving zero average induced core voltage. The computed positive peak B tends to 0.2250 T, below the assumed 0.30 T threshold in this particular model.
The bias has not vanished; it has become bounded. A different resistance, excitation or nonlinear core could give a different outcome.



Small per-cycle transformer flux walk and the difference between an ideal imposed core voltage and a resistive winding model that approaches a biased periodic state.


Therefore a bridge-terminal volt-second imbalance does not prove inevitable unlimited flux growth in every physical transformer. Check whether balancing drops or control establish an acceptable periodic state before the material’s nonlinear region. A series blocking capacitor can change the bias dynamics, but it creates another state and must be analysed with the rest of the circuit.
Change one thing: reverse the timing imbalance, change the initial B, or halve N while preserving the imposed core-voltage waveform. Predict direction, margin and rate separately. This extends the earlier low-frequency transformer note: winding resistance affects both measurement and operating dynamics.
Flux-margin decision. First correct the cycle-to-cycle induced-voltage imbalance. More turns reduce flux change per volt-second, but do not cancel a nonzero volt-second sum in the imposed-voltage model.
A blocking capacitor is an alternative circuit change; it adds a state whose dynamics must be checked. Keep the winding and bias solution only after an acceptable periodic state is demonstrated. A symmetric-looking trace alone does not establish flux margin.

title: 16.33 The unstable pole cancels on paper: is the system internally stable?
text:
Optional advanced riddle: put an unstable plant P(s) = 1/(s − a), a > 0, in cascade with a compensator C(s) = b(s − a)/(s + b), b > 0. The reduced reference-to-output transfer is

P(s)C(s)=\frac{b}{s+b}.

It looks like an ordinary stable low-pass. But cancelling a numerator/denominator factor in this zero-initial-state channel does not remove a physical state. Use this deliberately simple cascade counterexample before attempting a full feedback controller; the cascade is not a stabilizing feedback design.
One realization, with reference r and output y = x, is

\dot z=-bz+br,\qquad w=br-(a+b)z,\qquad \dot x=ax+w.

Its internal eigenvalues are −b and +a. Define e = x − z. Then

\dot e=ae,\qquad e(t)=e(0)e^{at},\qquad y(t)=z(t)+e(0)e^{at}.

With exactly e(0) = 0 and the exact model, the reference does not excite the unstable mode, so y = z and the stable reduced transfer predicts that particular experiment correctly. With a nonzero initial mismatch, a disturbance in the plant, or model error, the growing mode is exposed.
In this realization it is uncontrollable from the nominal reference channel but observable at the output; reduction of the transfer function concealed its existence.
Authored example: choose a = 1000 s⁻¹ and b = 2000 s⁻¹, with a unit reference step. From zero state the nominal output is 1 − exp(−2000t). Compare that with a 1 mV initial x − z mismatch, and separately a plant pole 1% higher, at +1010 s⁻¹, while leaving the compensator zero at +1000 s⁻¹.



Experiment
Output after 6 ms




Exact model, zero initial state
0.999994 V


Exact model, 1 mV initial mismatch
1.403423 V


Plant pole +1%, zero initial state
3.808260 V






Unreduced poles and the coincident compensator zero, followed by nominal, initial-state-sensitive and model-mismatch step responses.


The full state realization, its resolvent and direct time integration agree. The lesson is stronger than finite numerical precision: even exact cancellation does not establish internal stability. Uncertainty merely makes the problem harder to conceal. The author-hosted Hoagg and Bernstein discussion of nonminimum-phase systems discusses the hidden instability associated with unstable pole–zero cancellation.
Change one thing: keep the same initial error but move the uncancelled internal pole into the left half-plane; the mismatch then decays. For an actual control design, use feedback to stabilize the physical unstable mode and assess all relevant disturbance channels. Stable-pole cancellation has its own robustness limitations, but the unstable case already fails the internal-stability requirement.
This completes §9.1’s distinction between a transfer function and the full state dynamics. Saturation, finite precision and sensor noise are excluded from the model; they are not needed to produce the counterexample.
Control decision. Reject the unstable-mode cancellation as a stabilizing solution. Design feedback to stabilize the physical mode, then inspect internal states and disturbance paths. Reducing a transfer function is useful algebra; it cannot replace that check. These two descriptions are not equally valid evidence of stability.
Reproducibility for §§16.29–16.33: scripts/five_further_examples.py exports figures 77–81 and five-further-examples-checks.json. It verifies CM charge/energy integrals, nonlinear-capacitance quadrature and charging dynamics, exact comparator-crossing current maps, per-cycle Faraday increments and resistive periodic-state balance, and the cancellation state realization against transfer and transient predictions. All numerical fixtures are authored; none is a measured device, a nonlinear magnetic model or a complete implemented converter/controller.

title: 16.34 The loop crosses 0 dB at −20 dB/decade: must it be stable?
text:
A. A reference loop with one crossover
Riddle: a negative-feedback loop has its first unity-gain crossover near 1 kHz with slope about −20 dB/decade. Its phase there is around −84°, apparently giving a generous positive phase margin. Is this enough to declare stability if a resonance appears later?
No. Test the complete loop, rather than one favourable local crossing. The following are authored continuous-time SISO loops, with all open-loop poles in the left half-plane and no imaginary-axis poles. They are a deliberately isolated control example, not fitted converter hardware. With unity negative feedback, characteristic roots solve 1 + L = 0.
Define
L_A(s)=\frac{10}{(1+s/\omega_p)[1+2\zeta_A s/\omega_r+(s/\omega_r)^2]},\qquad \omega_p=2\pi\times100,\quad \omega_r=2\pi\times100000,\quad \zeta_A=0.01.
The low-frequency pole is at 100 Hz; the second-order resonance is at 100 kHz. Its first and only gain crossover is 995.087 Hz, with slope −19.796 dB/decade, phase −84.273° and local phase margin +95.727°. The resonance peak remains around −6 dB, below unity. The full Nyquist curve has N = 0 with P = 0, and the three closed-loop poles all have negative real parts.
This loop is stable in the stated model.
Its phase reaches −180° at about 100.001 kHz, giving a gain-margin factor of about two, or +6.02 dB. That number is a gain-only margin of this stable nominal loop, not a substitute for checking a modified loop’s new dynamics.

title: 16.34 The loop crosses 0 dB at −20 dB/decade: must it be stable?
section: B. The exact same magnitude curve, but unstable
text:
B. The exact same magnitude curve, but unstable
Multiply the reference loop by a stable-pole, RHP-zero all-pass factor:

L_B(s)=L_A(s)\frac{1-s/\omega_z}{1+s/\omega_z},\qquad \omega_z=2\pi\times500.

Its open-loop pole at −ωz is stable; its zero is at +ωz. For every real frequency,

\left|\frac{1-j\omega/\omega_z}{1+j\omega/\omega_z}\right|=1,\qquad \Delta\phi=-2\arctan(\omega/\omega_z).

Therefore every magnitude value, crossover frequency and local magnitude slope is unchanged from A. Yet the phase at the same crossover is now −210.917°, giving the local quantity −30.917°. The full Nyquist curve makes two net clockwise encirclements of −1. Since P = 0, Z = 2: the closed loop is unstable.
Its unstable pole pair is approximately +1256.9 ± j4486.6 s⁻¹. A magnitude-only view cannot distinguish A from B.
The corresponding −180° crossing is about 591.55 Hz, with gain-margin value −4.44 dB. Calling that a positive robustness margin would be incorrect: this nominal loop is already unstable.

title: 16.34 The loop crosses 0 dB at −20 dB/decade: must it be stable?
section: An optional counterexample with exactly −20 dB/decade
text:
An optional counterexample with exactly −20 dB/decade
To remove the word “approximately,” compare K/s with

L_{exact}(s)=\frac{K}{s}\frac{1-s/a}{1+s/a},\qquad K>0,\quad a>0.

Both have |L(jω)| = K/ω and hence exactly −20 dB/decade everywhere. The unmodified negative-feedback loop has pole −K. The modified characteristic polynomial is

s^2+(a-K)s+Ka.

If a < K, the modified closed loop is unstable despite the exact slope. For normalized K = 1 and a = 0.5, its roots are +0.25 ± j0.66144. This extra example has an open-loop integrator at zero, so its Nyquist contour needs an indentation; it is not included in the three unindented counts above. The all-pass magnitude identity and polynomial roots are checked explicitly.
Change one thing: start from A and reduce only ζ, listing every gain and phase crossing as the resonance rises. Then restore ζ and add only the all-pass factor. Explain why the first experiment changes both magnitude and phase, while the second changes phase alone.
Finally reconstruct each Nyquist sample from its Bode magnitude and phase using §12.4’s equation. This demonstrates that complete Bode and Nyquist views contain the same frequency-response information; the one-crossing heuristic discards the context required by the general stability test.
Which loop can we accept? Keep case A as the stable reference. B has the same magnitude curve but fails through phase; C fails after the resonance creates more crossings. Neither is rescued by the first crossover’s favourable appearance.
Lower bandwidth or added damping are redesign routes with response or implementation costs. After either change, repeat the full Nyquist and pole checks. Do not select a remedy from one local margin.

It records all unity/phase crossings, local slopes and margins, open/closed-loop pole counts and full-contour clockwise winding. Counts are checked at two frequency resolutions and against state-space/polynomial roots. Models exclude sampling, delay and hidden unstable cancellations; their mathematical high-frequency response is not a converter bandwidth claim. This optional extension connects the Bode, Middlebrook, Laplace, sampled-control and internal-stability discussions.

title: 16.35 The firmware calculates the same gain: why does one PWM period make the loop unstable?
text:
Separate the command hold from the update latency
Riddle: a proportional controller stabilizes a first-order plant. The controller is implemented digitally without changing its gain, but a new PWM command takes effect one update later. Why can a plant with just one stable pole now oscillate with growing amplitude?
The controller acts on an old measurement. Reading the formula correctly is not sufficient if the timing differs from the design. TI’s digital-control timing discussion describes how dedicated PWM register-load events can delay a computed update and reduce phase margin. The CPU’s execution time alone is not the full sample-to-actuation latency.
Use a single sampling/update rate fs = 1/Ts, synchronized with the PWM period in this example. The numerical model holds the average actuator command constant during each period; it does not simulate individual switching edges. Distinguish these schedules:
The first schedule is an ideal zero-latency reference, not a claim of instantaneous ADC/CPU hardware. The second has one complete period of additional command latency. Faster code may not shorten it unless the command meets an earlier register-load deadline. Actual carrier type, sampling phase and update policy determine the effective modulator timing; imperix’s delay-identification note distinguishes sensing, sample-to-update and modulation delays.
A normalized continuous baseband representation of a zero-order hold is
H_h(s)=\frac{1-e^{-sT_s}}{sT_s},\qquad H_h(j\omega)=e^{-j\omega T_s/2}\frac{\sin(\omega T_s/2)}{\omega T_s/2}.
Below the first hold zero, the sine ratio is positive and the hold phase is −ωTs/2. Well below the update rate its magnitude is close to one, motivating the half-period delay approximation. One extra period contributes exp(−sTs), giving an approximate hold-plus-update budget of 1.5Ts. This is the budget for the stated schedule; it is not a universal PWM delay.
Additional ADC, filtering and sensor delays would need their own defined contributions. Do not count the same hold twice when using an exact discrete plant.

title: 16.35 The firmware calculates the same gain: why does one PWM period make the loop unstable?
section: A simple plant and an exact discrete model
text:
A simple plant and an exact discrete model
Take the authored normalized plant

P(s)=\frac{1}{1+s\tau},\qquad \tau=100\ \mu\mathrm{s},\qquad u=-Ky.

The variables are normalized deviations around an operating point, so command and output can have either sign. Continuous proportional feedback with K = 3 gives pole −(1 + K)/τ = −40,000 s⁻¹, crossover 4501.58 Hz and phase margin 109.47°. This is the continuous reference; the digital implementation is a different interconnection.
For a command held over each sampling interval, direct integration gives

y[k+1]=ay[k]+bu[k],\qquad a=e^{-T_s/\tau},\qquad b=1-a,\qquad P_d(z)=\frac{b}{z-a}.

This plant already includes evolution during the held-command interval. With the ideal immediate controller, L0(z) = Kb/(z − a), and the closed-loop pole is a − Kb. With the one-period-late command,

y[k+1]=ay[k]-Kb\,y[k-1],\qquad L_1(z)=\frac{Kb}{z(z-a)},\qquad z^2-az+Kb=0.

The extra z⁻¹ has unit magnitude on the unit circle. It preserves the discrete loop’s entire magnitude curve and its crossover, while adding −360 f/fs degrees of phase. It also increases the closed-loop state dimension: the previous sample or pending command is a state.

title: 16.35 The firmware calculates the same gain: why does one PWM period make the loop unstable?
section: Why a phase-budget estimate is useful, but not the final proof
text:
Why a phase-budget estimate is useful, but not the final proof
At the old continuous crossover of 4501.58 Hz, a half-period hold at 20 kHz would cost about 40.51°, and the extra period another 81.03°. Subtracting those from the continuous margin warns of a serious problem. It is not the exact digital margin: the crossover and the sampled frequency response must also be recalculated.
Here crossover is roughly a quarter of the 20 kHz update rate, so a simple low-frequency delay approximation is not quantitatively reliable. The table uses the exact discrete loop, not that subtraction.
The plotted free responses start with y[0] = 0.01 and, for the delayed cases, y[−1] = 0.01. A small perturbation decays in the stable cases and grows in the delayed K = 3 / 20 kHz case. Between samples, the continuous plant is integrated with the applied command held constant, so the simulation checks both the sampled recurrence and the intersample trajectory.



Closed-loop poles relative to the unit circle and continuous intersample free responses; one-period latency destabilizes the high-gain 20 kHz controller, while lower gain or a 40 kHz update restores stability in the model.


Change one thing: keep the hardware rate and lower K to move crossover down; or keep K and shorten the period. Both remedies work in the stated example, with different performance and implementation costs. A higher sampling rate alone is not a remedy if the PWM command is still updated at the old rate; the model must use the actual actuation schedule.
Avoiding an extra missed update can be as valuable as reducing arithmetic time. Predictive control is another possible design approach, but needs a validated model rather than treating the delay as absent.
This is an exact linear analysis of the specified sampled first-order plant with a held average PWM command. It excludes carrier ripple, nonlinear duty limits, sensor filters, quantization and jitter; the ideal no-latency case is a reference bound. The growing linear response is not a prediction that hardware amplitudes grow without saturation.
Continuous-time Nyquist intuition still applies through the correct discrete contour, but the definitive test here is the complete augmented-state pole set inside |z| = 1.
Two valid remedies. With 20 kHz hardware fixed, choose K = 2 as the demonstrated stable remedy. Its lower crossover costs response speed. If the faster response is required, investigate the 40 kHz update with K = 3, accepting tighter timing demands.
Both pass this model’s pole test. A faster ADC alone is not the second remedy: the command must actually reach the PWM at the higher update rate.
scripts/digital_pwm_delay.py exports figures 84–85 and digital-pwm-delay-checks.json. It checks analytical crossover against numerical frequency roots, polynomial poles against augmented-state eigenvalues, each held interval against adaptive ODE integration, and sample trajectories against state propagation. It also verifies that one extra update period changes phase without changing magnitude. This optional exercise extends §§12.4 and 16.34 and complements the distinct peak-current sampled instability of §16.31.

title: 16.36 The linear poles are stable: why does the digital regulator keep cycling?
text:
Define the plant, quantizers and update order
Riddle: the unquantized sampled loop has every pole inside the unit circle. Without changing its gain, sampling schedule or plant, round the ADC measurement and PWM duty command to finite grids. Can the regulator oscillate forever even with noiseless measurements?
Yes. Linear asymptotic stability describes the unquantized equations. Quantizers change those equations into a nonlinear, piecewise system and can prevent the existence of the desired static equilibrium. The phenomenon is deterministic; it is not necessarily measurement noise, linear instability or an unfinished startup transient. Peterchev and Sanders’ original paper discusses ADC/DPWM resolution, zero-error bins, steady limit cycling and controlled dither.
The following numbers and reduced plant are newly authored for this exercise.
Use a normalized first-order average-command voltage model, with Vin = 12 V, τ = 100 µs, fs = 20 kHz and Ts = 50 µs:
\tau\dot v+v=V_{in}d,\qquad v[k+1]=av[k]+bd[k],\qquad a=e^{-T_s/\tau},\quad b=V_{in}(1-a).
This is an authored output-envelope model with a buck-like DC duty conversion, not a complete LC buck or a carrier-switching simulation. At each sample, measure voltage, update the integrator, quantize its duty command and hold that average command through the next interval:
v_q[k]=Q_{ADC}(v[k]),\qquad c[k]=c[k-1]+g(r-v_q[k]),\qquad d[k]=Q_{PWM}(c[k]).
Set r = 5 V and g = 0.015 duty/V/update. Start from v[0] = 4.8 V and c[−1] = 0.4001. There is no additional one-period command delay in this example; that separate effect was studied in §16.35. Quantizers round to the nearest grid point, with exact half-step ties upward.
All reported steady states and cycles avoid ties and active saturation. Integrator arithmetic is not rounded further; for ADC cases, summing integer error codes avoids floating-point accumulation drift.
For the ADC, define an output-referred span of 8 V, including any measurement-divider gain. An ideal 8-bit quantizer then has ΔvADC = 8/256 = 31.25 mV. The 5 V reference is exactly code 160. Its zero-measured-error bin is
4.984375\ \mathrm{V}\ \leq v<5.015625\ \mathrm{V}.
For the coarse PWM, use 64 duty increments, Δd = 1/64. A one-count change corresponds to VinΔd = 187.5 mV in the static output model. These are output-referred comparisons; comparing the two nominal bit counts without full-scale ranges and plant gain would be misleading.

First prove that the unquantized linear controller is stable
Remove both quantizers while retaining sampling and integral action. In error coordinates [v[k] − r, c[k−1] − r/Vin], the closed-loop matrix is
M = [ a - b g    b ]
    [   -g       1 ]

title: 16.36 The linear poles are stable: why does the digital regulator keep cycling?
section: Remedies and the accuracy tradeoff
text:
Remedies and the accuracy tradeoff
Increase PWM resolution to Δd = 1/1024. The output-referred step becomes 11.71875 mV, and code 427 gives 5.00390625 V, strictly inside the ADC zero-error bin. The observed trajectory can now stop. This removes the demonstrated envelope cycle, but leaves a +3.906 mV true offset. Eliminating cycling is not the same requirement as exact regulation.
Having an attainable actuator level inside the zero-error bin is an equilibrium-feasibility check, not a general guarantee that nonlinear limit cycles are absent for every controller gain or initial condition. Conversely, adding ADC bits alone can narrow the zero-error band without adding any available actuator level. Compare the output-referred ADC and PWM steps over the operating range, including the voltage-to-duty gain; do not adopt a universal bit-count difference.
Other design choices include controlled dither or pulse-density sequences to synthesize an average duty between codes, coordinated gain/resolution changes, or a deliberate deadband. Dither trades the location and form of residual ripple rather than making finite resolution disappear; a wider deadband trades regulation accuracy for fewer corrections.
Their behaviour must be evaluated with the actual plant and update schedule. The present five-way comparison explicitly verifies the finer-PWM remedy; it does not claim an implemented dither or deadband controller.
Recall questions: Why can a stable linear model coexist with a periodic nonlinear response? Why does ADC-only error not necessarily cause cycling? Why does a 5 V mean fail to prove that the output has settled? Finally, can a more accurate ADC make the absence of a compatible PWM equilibrium more apparent?
Resolution or tolerated ripple? For a settled output, choose the demonstrated 10-bit PWM case over the 6-bit case. It removes this orbit but leaves the reported static output error inside the ADC bin. More PWM resolution costs implementation capability.
Deadband or dither are alternatives when some error or ripple is acceptable. They are not verified here. A correct 5 V mean does not justify retaining the 6-bit regulator when instantaneous ripple matters.

It verifies the unquantized state model, full-state steady repetition, an analytical period-three orbit, strict quantizer-bin inequalities, integrator closure and held-interval ODE integration. All cases are noiseless authored examples without active saturation, extra command-period delay or coefficient/accumulator overflow. This optional nonlinear extension complements the timing-instability example in §16.35; linear pole and margin checks remain necessary for the baseline but do not describe the quantized system completely.

title: 16.37 A LISN presents 50 Ω to the DUT: does all its disturbance power reach the receiver?
text:
Level 1: build the Y matrix from Kirchhoff’s current law
Predict. A line impedance stabilization network (LISN) sits between the mains supply, the device under test (DUT) and an EMI receiver. The data sheet says it presents 50 Ω to the DUT at radio frequencies. Does the receiver therefore absorb all the disturbance power that the DUT generates? Sketch your answer before reading on.
The LISN has three functional connections. Number them as ports of one network, with every port current entering and a common reference conductor:
The network has three jobs. It passes supply power to the DUT with low impedance at the supply frequency. It keeps supply-side RF disturbance away from the receiver. It couples the DUT’s RF disturbance into the receiver. A fourth property matters as much: it presents a defined, reproducible RF impedance to the DUT, so that measurements in different laboratories agree. A LISN is not an ideal high-pass and low-pass pair.
This exercise uses the same conventions as §11.4 and the same reduction tools as §16.21 and §16.22. Level 1 is an idealized three-element network that students solve by hand. Level 2 adds the shunt elements of a 50 Ω / 50 µH + 5 Ω V-network and is solved numerically.
Take L = 50 µH between the supply and the DUT, C = 100 nF between the DUT and the measurement port, and an external RM = 50 Ω receiver termination. The values are inspired by the 50 µH / 50 Ω networks; the circuit is not a complete LISN.
With YL = 1/(jωL) and YC = jωC, write the entering currents as functions of the port voltages:
Each row is KCL at one port; each off-diagonal entry is minus the admittance that joins two ports. Every row sums to zero, so Y·[1, 1, 1]ᵀ = 0 and det Y = 0. The matrix is singular because no element connects a port to the reference: raising all three voltages together drives no current. A finite Z = Y⁻¹ does not exist for the isolated three-port. That is a valid singular representation, not an error, as in §16.21.

section: Reduce the three-port to a two-port by terminating port 3
text:
Reduce the three-port to a two-port by terminating port 3
Connect RM at port 3, so I₃ = −V₃/RM. Eliminate V₃ from the third row and substitute into the others:

Y^{\mathrm{red}}_{ij}=Y_{ij}-\frac{Y_{i3}Y_{3j}}{Y_{33}+1/R_M},\qquad i,j\in\{1,2\}.

This Kron reduction gives a two-port between the supply and the DUT, whose entries now depend on the removed termination. For this circuit it reproduces the direct result: a series L between ports 1 and 2 with the branch ZM = RM + 1/(jωC) shunting port 2. At 150 kHz, ωL = 47.12 Ω and 1/(ωC) = 10.61 Ω, so ZM = 50 − j10.61 Ω and:
Z = inv(Yred) = [ 50 + j36.51    50 - j10.61 ]  ohm
                [ 50 - j10.61    50 - j10.61 ]

ABCD = [ 0.809 + j0.902     j47.12 ohm ]       det = 1
       [ 0.01914 + j0.00406 S     1    ]

|S| at 50 ohm references = [ 0.582  0.581 ]
                           [ 0.581  0.227 ]
Z exists once a termination makes the reduced Y invertible. ABCD follows the series-impedance/shunt-admittance product of §16.22. S follows the equal-reference conversion of §11.4; with the 50 Ω receiver inside the network, SᴴS is no longer the identity, because RM dissipates.

title: 16.37 A LISN presents 50 Ω to the DUT: does all its disturbance power reach the receiver?
section: Current partition versus power partition
text:
Current partition versus power partition
For the RF analysis, short the supply at port 1, drive port 2 with an ideal disturbance current source IN and keep the 50 Ω receiver. The current divides between the supply path ZS = jωL and the receiver path ZM:

\frac{I_M}{I_N}=\frac{Z_S}{Z_S+Z_M}=\frac{j\omega L}{j\omega L+R_M+\frac{1}{j\omega C}},\qquad \frac{I_S}{I_N}=\frac{Z_M}{Z_S+Z_M}.

The same ratio follows from the reduced two-port with V₁ = 0: IN = Y₂₂ V₂ and IM = V₂/ZM. At 150 kHz:



Quantity, 150 kHz
Value




|IM/IN|
0.761, or −2.37 dB


|IS/IN|
0.826


Sum of the two magnitudes
1.59


Active power in the receiver, per A² of IN
28.97 W


Active power in the ideal supply path
0



The magnitudes add to more than one because the two currents are not in phase; only the phasors add to IN. The receiver branch and the inductor resonate in series at 1/(2π√(LC)) = 71.18 kHz, where |IM/IN| = ω₀L/RM = 0.447. Above that frequency the ratio rises towards one; it never exceeds one, because RM adds a positive term to the denominator.
Now the answer to the opening question. In this ideal model the supply path carries 83 % of the disturbance current and dissipates nothing, because an ideal inductor has no real part. Every watt of active disturbance power reaches the receiver, although most of the current does not:

P_k=|I_k|^2\operatorname{Re}\{Z_k\}.

Add 5 Ω of real part to the supply path and the two partitions separate numerically. At 150 kHz the receiver then carries 0.718 of the current, the supply path carries 0.774, and the receiver absorbs 89.6 % of the active power. Current partition and power partition are different questions about the same network.

section: Level 2: a 50 µH V-network with its shunt elements
text:
Level 2: a 50 µH V-network with its shunt elements
Replace the three-element model by the nominal elements of a 50 Ω / 50 µH + 5 Ω V-network: L₁ = 50 µH between supply and DUT; C₁ = 8 µF in series with R₁ = 5 Ω from the supply node to the reference; C₂ = 0.25 µF from the DUT node to the receiver terminal; R₂ = 1 kΩ from the receiver terminal to the reference; the 50 Ω receiver remains external. The shunt elements make the three-port Y invertible, so Z and the full 3 × 3 S matrix exist without any termination. The nominal impedance that the standard assigns to the DUT port is (R₁ + jωL₁) ∥ 50 Ω, with a ±20 % magnitude tolerance.

Nominal |Z| is 32.7 Ω at 150 kHz and 50.0 Ω at 30 MHz. The 8 µF + 5 Ω branch is what makes the DUT-side impedance nearly independent of whatever the mains presents above 150 kHz. Below 150 kHz the level-1 model and a shorted mains both leave the tolerance band, which is why low-frequency conducted-emission work needs a different network, such as the 250 µH variants discussed in the references.



Current and power partition in the ideal network, impedance presented to the DUT against the nominal curve, three-port scattering of the 50 µH network, and its voltage division factor.


With 50 Ω references at all three ports, the S matrix of the level-2 network at 150 kHz has |S₃₂| = 0.848 (−1.4 dB, DUT to receiver), |S₃₁| = 0.082 (−21.8 dB, supply to receiver) and |S₂₂| = 0.414. The isolation improves to −37 dB at 1 MHz. The reflection |S₂₂| is not zero at 150 kHz because the nominal impedance there is 32.7 Ω, not 50 Ω; the DUT port is matched only at high frequency, where |S₂₂| falls to 0.025. The voltage division factor V₃/V₂ with the receiver attached is −0.03 dB at 150 kHz and −5.1 dB at 9 kHz: the 0.25 µF coupling capacitor and the 50 Ω ∥ 1 kΩ load form a high-pass divider.
Change one thing: terminate port 3 with 1 kΩ instead of 50 Ω and repeat the reduction; remove the 8 µF branch and watch the shorted-supply curve leave the band; replace the ideal current source by a DUT with 10 Ω source impedance. Ask students to predict which of the four panels moves before running the script.
Recall questions: Why is the ideal three-port Y singular, and which single element would make it invertible? Why does the reduced two-port depend on the termination at the removed port? Why can |IM/IN| + |IS/IN| exceed one? Which representation answers “what impedance does the DUT see”, and which answers “how much of the supply-side disturbance reaches the receiver”? Finally, what does |S₃₂|² mean, and under which terminations does it equal a power ratio?
Representation choice. Build Y from KCL when the circuit is given as elements between nodes. Reduce to Z or ABCD once the terminations are fixed, because those matrices answer impedance and cascade questions directly. Use S when the receiver, cables and the standard all speak in 50 Ω reference waves. The impedance seen by the DUT, the transfer to the receiver and the isolation of the supply are three different properties of the same multiport. A 50 Ω data-sheet value fixes the first and says nothing by itself about the other two. To speak of disturbance power through S parameters, distinguish incident waves, reflected waves and absorbed power at stated reference impedances; |IM/IN| is a current ratio, not a power ratio.

Both levels are authored lumped linear models with the nominal element values of a 50 Ω / 50 µH + 5 Ω network. They are not a complete or certified CISPR 16-1-2 instrument; phase tolerance and the exact frequency ranges must be read from the standard. The DUT is an ideal current source in the split; a real DUT adds its own source impedance.

title: 16.39 Everyone draws the ideal transformer: what exactly is it, and can SPICE model it exactly? — Ben-Yaakov-inspired
text:
Definition: two algebraic constraints and nothing else
Credit: the riddle and its three questions are Sam Ben-Yaakov’s, from his video Ideal transformer riddle (11 September 2020). The answer, the netlist, the checks and the figure below are authored for this recap.
Predict. Sam Ben-Yaakov posed this riddle in a short video and withheld the answer. Every textbook model of a transformer ends in the symbol of an ideal transformer, behind the magnetizing inductance, the leakage inductances and the winding resistances. Answer three questions before reading on. What is the definition of an ideal transformer? What are its network equations? How can a circuit simulator model it exactly, not approximately?
Most first answers describe a physical device: perfect coupling, no resistance, infinite permeability. Those are properties of a limit, not a definition. The definition is shorter, and it contains no magnetism at all.
With the signs of §11.4, both port currents entering and n = N₁/N₂, an ideal transformer is the two-port defined by:
v_1(t)=n\,v_2(t),\qquad n\,i_1(t)=-i_2(t).
Both relations are algebraic and hold at every instant. Three consequences follow without any further assumption:
Compare §2.5: a perfectly coupled pair with k = 1 and L₁ = n² L₂ is a different element. Its inductance matrix has rank one, so it imposes v₁ = n v₂ exactly, but it replaces the current constraint by a state:
i_1=-\frac{i_2}{n}+i_m,\qquad L_1\frac{di_m}{dt}=v_1.
A k = 1 pair is therefore an ideal transformer with a magnetizing inductance L₁ across its primary. The ideal transformer is the limit L₁ → ∞ at fixed L₁/L₂, and the limit is where the energy state disappears.

title: 16.39 Everyone draws the ideal transformer: what exactly is it, and can SPICE model it exactly? — Ben-Yaakov-inspired
text:
No energy. v₁i₁ + v₂i₂ = 0 at every instant, so the element neither stores nor dissipates. Power that enters port 1 leaves port 2 immediately.
No frequency. Nothing in the definition differentiates or integrates. The element transforms a DC voltage exactly as it transforms a 100 kHz sine. A physical transformer cannot, and that is the clearest sign that the ideal transformer is not a magnetic device.
Impedance scaling. A load Z_L at port 2 appears as Z_in = n² Z_L at port 1, for any complex Z_L.

title: 16.39 Everyone draws the ideal transformer: what exactly is it, and can SPICE model it exactly? — Ben-Yaakov-inspired
section: Network equations: which matrices exist
text:
Network equations: which matrices exist
Section 16.21 showed why the ideal transformer has no finite Z and no finite Y. Z needs I₁ and I₂ as independent variables, and n I₁ + I₂ = 0 forbids that. Y needs V₁ and V₂ independent, and V₁ − n V₂ = 0 forbids that. The representations that do exist are the ones whose independent variables the definition allows:
ABCD (with -I2):  [ V1 ]   [ n    0  ] [  V2 ]        det = 1
                  [ I1 ] = [ 0   1/n ] [ -I2 ]

Hybrid H:         [ V1 ]   [ 0    n ] [ I1 ]           V1 = n V2
                  [ I2 ] = [ -n   0 ] [ V2 ]           I2 = -n I1

Inverse hybrid G: [ I1 ]   [  0   -1/n ] [ V1 ]        G = inv(H)
                  [ V2 ] = [ 1/n    0  ] [ I2 ]

S, 50 ohm references, n = 2:  [ 0.6   0.8 ]            real, symmetric, S^T S = Id
                               [ 0.8  -0.6 ]
The hybrid matrix is the one to remember. Its two rows are the two defining equations written with mixed variables: a voltage controlled by a voltage and a current controlled by a current. That is exactly the vocabulary of a circuit simulator.

title: 16.39 Everyone draws the ideal transformer: what exactly is it, and can SPICE model it exactly? — Ben-Yaakov-inspired
section: An exact SPICE model: two controlled sources
text:
An exact SPICE model: two controlled sources
A simulator offers four controlled sources. The H rows name two of them: a voltage-controlled voltage source (E) for V₂ = V₁/n and a current-controlled current source (F) for I₁ = −I₂/n. The F source needs a current to sense, so a 0 V source sits in series with the E source:
* Ideal transformer, n = N1/N2. Primary p-0, secondary s-0.
E1   s   x   p   0   {1/n}      ; V(s,x) = V(p,0) / n
Vs   x   0   0                  ; 0 V sense: I(Vs) is the current entering at s
F1   p   0   Vs  {-1/n}         ; current -I(Vs)/n flows from p into F1
The sign deserves one line. SPICE counts I(Vs) positive from the + node x through the source to the − node. The current that enters the secondary at s flows through E1 into x and then through Vs, so I(Vs) = i₂ with the entering convention. F1 with a positive gain would draw g·I(Vs) out of node p into the source, which is the port current i₁ entering from outside; i₁ = −i₂/n fixes the gain at −1/n. The two sources exchange no energy with the rest of the circuit: E1 delivers exactly the power that F1 absorbs.

The step response says the same thing in time. A 10 V step on the primary gives a 5 V step on the ideal secondary that lasts forever. On the 100 µH pair the 5 V decays with τ = 3.1 µs, because the magnetizing current ramps until the primary source carries it all. Coupling below one works at the other end of the spectrum. With L₁ = 100 µH the open-circuit ratio falls to k/n and the short-circuit primary inductance L₁(1 − k²) rolls the loaded ratio off: 3 dB down at 2.5 MHz for k = 0.99 and at 217 kHz for k = 0.9. A real transformer is an ideal transformer bracketed by these two corners, which is why the engineer’s T-model keeps the symbol in the middle.
Change one thing: set n = 1 and ask what the element still does; replace the 8 Ω load by a capacitor and check that Z_in is n² times that capacitor’s impedance, not a different capacitor; drive the ideal element with a DC source and no load and ask why the simulator is happy while the laboratory transformer would saturate; swap the gain of F1 to +1/n and find which conservation law the netlist now violates.
Recall questions: Which two equations define the element, and which words in the usual description (coupling, permeability, resistance) are absent from them? Why does V₁ = n V₂ survive for a k = 1 pair while n I₁ = −I₂ does not? Which matrix has the defining equations as its rows, and which two SPICE primitives are those rows? Why does a coupled pair with K = 1 and a large inductance approximate but never equal the ideal element? Finally, what would the 0 V source Vs be for if the simulator could sense the current of E1 directly?
Representation choice. Define an element by its constraints, then ask which independent variables those constraints leave free; that choice fixes which matrix exists. For the ideal transformer, ABCD serves cascades, S serves matched measurements, and H serves the simulator. The engineer’s T-model of §2.6 is the ideal element plus the two states that the definition removed. When a result needs the magnetizing current or the leakage corner, use that model; when it needs only the ratio, the two controlled sources are the honest and exact choice.

title: 16.40 The duty cycle is free to choose: where do the switch conduction losses go? — Ben-Yaakov-inspired
text:
The switched inductor: one circuit, three converters
Source and credit: this exercise follows Sam Ben-Yaakov, The effect of PWM converters’ duty cycle on conduction losses, lecture video, 2025. The switched-inductor view, the loss expressions per topology and the DCM ratio check are his; the derivation conventions, component values, tables, figure 92 and the numerical script are authored here.
Predict. A synchronous buck delivers 12 V at 10 A. The input can be 15 V, 24 V or 48 V, so the duty cycle can be 0.8, 0.5 or 0.25. Which input gives the lowest total conduction loss in the two MOSFETs? Then answer the same question for a boost that delivers 12 V at 10 A from 3 V, 6 V or 9 V. Sketch both answers before reading on.
Sometimes the input and output voltages are given and the duty cycle follows from them. Often the designer can choose the input bus, the turns ratio of a coupled inductor, or the operating mode, and the duty cycle becomes a degree of freedom. This exercise asks what that choice does to the conduction loss of the switches. The model is deliberately simple: constant on-resistance R_on for every transistor, constant forward drop V_D for a diode, inductor ripple neglected, continuous conduction unless stated. Switching loss, ripple-dependent RMS and magnetics loss are left out; §13 and §16.8 touch on them.
Buck, boost and buck-boost are the same cell: one inductor whose free terminal is connected alternately to two switches, Q1 for a fraction D of the period and Q2 for the rest. The inductor current I_L is nearly constant. Seen from the inductor, there is always exactly one R_on in series, so the total conduction loss of the pair is:
P_{\mathrm{tot}}=I_L^2 R_{\mathrm{on}},\qquad P_{Q1}=D\,P_{\mathrm{tot}},\qquad P_{Q2}=(1-D)\,P_{\mathrm{tot}}.
The duty cycle only decides how P_tot is shared between the two devices. Whether P_tot itself depends on D is decided by one question: is the output port the inductor, or one of the switches?
The ratio I_out/(1 − D) is the lossless power balance: Q1 conducts I_L for the fraction (1 − D) of the period, and its average must equal I_out. For the buck-boost it is also I_in + I_out.

section: Non-synchronous buck: a diode has a drop, not a resistance
text:
Non-synchronous buck: a diode has a drop, not a resistance
Replace Q2 by a diode. The transistor keeps I_out² R_on D. The diode conducts I_out for (1 − D) at a constant drop, so its loss is I_out V_D (1 − D), linear in current rather than quadratic:

\frac{P_Q}{P_D}=\frac{D}{1-D}\cdot\frac{I_{\mathrm{out}}R_{\mathrm{on}}}{V_D}.

With 10 A, 10 mΩ and 0.5 V the second factor is 0.2: the transistor drop is 0.1 V against the diode’s 0.5 V. At D = 0.5 the diode loses 2.5 W and the transistor 0.5 W. The two are equal only at D = V_D/(V_D + I_out R_on) = 0.83. Below that the diode dominates, which is why low-voltage bucks are synchronous. Reverse-recovery loss is a separate, switching-type term.

section: Flyback in CCM: the turns ratio moves the loss and the stress together
text:
Flyback in CCM: the turns ratio moves the loss and the stress together
A flyback is a buck-boost with a coupled inductor of ratio n = N_p/N_s. Take 48 V to 12 V at 2 A, R_on = 50 mΩ. The gain is V_out/V_in = D/(n (1 − D)), so for fixed voltages choosing D fixes n. The secondary plateau is I_out/(1 − D), the primary plateau is that divided by n, and the primary RMS is the plateau times √D. Substituting n gives a short result:

P_Q=\frac{I_{\mathrm{in}}^2 R_{\mathrm{on}}}{D},\qquad I_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{I_{\mathrm{out}}V_{\mathrm{out}}}{V_{\mathrm{in}}},\qquad V_{DS,\mathrm{off}}=V_{\mathrm{in}}+nV_{\mathrm{out}}=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}}{1-D}.

The primary carries the average input current, 0.5 A here, compressed into a fraction D of the period, so its RMS squared is I_in²/D. A small D means a large n, a tall narrow primary pulse and high loss. A large D means a small n and a low pulse, but the reflected voltage n V_out and the switch stress grow as V_in/(1 − D). The diode loses I_out V_D = 1 W whatever D is.

section: Flyback in DCM: energy per cycle sets the peak, D sets the RMS
text:
Flyback in DCM: energy per cycle sets the peak, D sets the RMS
In DCM every cycle stores L I_pk²/2 in the primary and delivers all of it, so P = L I_pk² f/2 and the peak follows from the power. The primary current is a triangle of width D T, whose RMS squared is I_pk² D/3. Eliminating I_pk:

I_{\mathrm{rms}}^2=\frac{2PD}{3Lf},\qquad P_Q=\frac{2PD}{3Lf}R_{\mathrm{on}},\qquad \frac{PD}{I_{\mathrm{rms}}^2}=\frac{3Lf}{2}.

At a given power and inductance, a larger D now costs more loss, the opposite of the CCM trend: the peak is fixed by P, so a longer on-time only widens the triangle. The last expression is the check the lecture ran in simulation: for fixed L and f the ratio P D/I_rms² must be a constant, independent of D and of V_in. scripts/pwm_duty_conduction_losses.py repeats it on a constructed waveform with L = 50 µH, f = 100 kHz, n = 1, 100 Ω load, D from 0.20 to 0.65 and V_in of 30 V and 15 V. Why is a diode loss linear in current and a MOSFET loss quadratic? In the CCM flyback, which two stresses move in opposite directions when D changes? Why does a larger D increase the loss in DCM but decrease it in CCM? What does the constancy of P D/I_rms² test, and why did the lecture’s simulation give 7 instead of 7.5?
Representation choice. Express every loss in terms of the quantity the load dictates, I_out, and translate to the inductor or primary current through the duty cycle. The buck’s independence from D is the exception, not the rule: the moment the output leaves the inductor port, the total loss acquires a 1/(1 − D)² factor, and the same inductor current drives the switching loss. Treat the duty cycle as a design variable that trades conduction loss against device stress and control limits, and check which converter you are in before quoting a trend.

title: 17. Engineering approximation: how simple can the model be?
text:
17.1 Start with the decision and an error budget
A model can reproduce many details and still answer the wrong question. A simpler model can support a decision if its errors remain acceptable.
This chapter develops the model-limit warning in Section 1.1. It is a separate methods chapter, outside the two-session refresher route. Its examples are authored teaching cases, not measured hardware results.
Suppose a calculation predicts a 0.40 V output drop against a 0.42 V limit. A neglected 0.04 V term changes the decision. Calling that term small does not make the design acceptable.
An approximation is useful when it preserves the conclusion within a stated error budget. Its value depends on the question, operating range and available margin. It is not a property of an equation alone.
Before calculating, answer these questions:
For an estimated value y_a and a reference value y_r, define:
e_{\mathrm{abs}}=|y_a-y_r|,\qquad e_{\mathrm{rel}}=\frac{|y_a-y_r|}{|y_r|}.
Relative error is unsuitable when the reference value is zero. Use an absolute limit there. The reference calculation also has assumptions. Agreement with it does not validate the physical hardware.
The engineering skill is choosing which detail could change the decision. A larger model costs time, parameters and interpretation. Add detail when its expected effect competes with the error budget.

title: 17. Engineering approximation: how simple can the model be?
section: 17.2 Use ratios, dimensions and limiting cases
text:
17.2 Use ratios, dimensions and limiting cases
Compare terms with compatible units. A resistance is not small by itself. Its ratio to another relevant impedance may be small.
Useful ratios include R_{\mathrm{source}}/R_{\mathrm{load}}, t/RC, and propagation delay divided by edge time. Each ratio identifies a particular mechanism. None is a universal accuracy certificate.

Check the dimensions of the proposed result.
Calculate the controlling dimensionless ratio.
Test a limiting case with an obvious physical answer.
Restore the omitted term.
Check whether the decision changes.

For a voltage divider, an open load should recover the open-circuit voltage. A shorted load should give zero terminal voltage. An expression that fails either check needs correction before refinement.
Dimensional agreement is necessary but insufficient. Two incorrect expressions can have the same units. Limiting cases and independent conservation checks provide different evidence.

title: 17. Engineering approximation: how simple can the model be?
section: 17.5 Example: a small capacitor ESR term changes the decision
text:
17.5 Example: a small capacitor ESR term changes the decision
A capacitor alone supplies a constant 2 A current deficit for 20 µs. Its effective capacitance is 100 µF and its series resistance is 20 mΩ. Neglect inductance, controller response and capacitance variation during this interval.
The model predicts the voltage drop from the initial steady value:
\Delta V=\Delta I R_{\mathrm{ESR}}+\frac{\Delta I\Delta t}{C}=0.04+0.40=0.44\ \mathrm V.
Ignoring series resistance predicts 0.40 V. Against a 0.42 V limit, that approximation predicts a pass while the fuller model predicts a failure. The omitted 40 mV exceeds the apparent 20 mV margin.
Now consider an 80 µF minimum capacitance and a 25 mΩ maximum series resistance. The same model predicts 0.55 V. These are stated teaching limits, not a particular capacitor’s datasheet values.
Capacitance alone answers part of the charge-balance question. The ESR term matters when its voltage step competes with the allowed drop. At faster edges, neglected inductance may require another model.

title: 17. Engineering approximation: how simple can the model be?
section: 17.6 Example: switching frequency does not define the fastest time scale
text:
17.6 Example: switching frequency does not define the fastest time scale
A 0.20 m connection has a propagation speed of 2\times10^8\ \mathrm{m/s}. Its one-way delay is 1 ns.
At 100 kHz, the switching period is 10 µs. The delay-to-period ratio is only 0.0001. That ratio alone makes the connection look unimportant.
For a 2 ns edge, the delay-to-edge ratio is 0.5. For a 100 ns edge, it is 0.01. The fast-edge case deserves a distributed-line check despite the same switching frequency.
These ratios screen the time scales. They do not bound reflection error by themselves. Line impedance, termination, edge amplitude and the allowed disturbance also matter.
Use the lumped model when propagation effects stay within the required accuracy. Use a transmission-line model when travel time and reflections affect the observed edge.

section: 17.7 Distinguish approximation error from uncertain inputs
text:
17.7 Distinguish approximation error from uncertain inputs
An exact solution with an unknown capacitance is not an exact prediction of the hardware. Separate three questions:







Question
Useful check




Did we solve the stated model correctly?
Independent equations, integration or conservation checks.


Does omitted physics affect the decision?
Restore the effect and compare against the error budget.


Are the input values credible?
Datasheet conditions, tolerance limits and measurements.



Vary uncertain parameters over justified ranges. Keep worst-case bounds separate from a nominal prediction. Do not assume that several errors cancel without evidence.
A simulation can challenge a hand calculation. It cannot validate an effect that both models omit. Add a measurement that observes the mechanism under the stated conditions.

17.8 Reading and provenance
The examples and numbers above are original. The reading route supplies methods and model cautions, rather than borrowed circuit designs.

Sanjoy Mahajan, The Art of Approximation in Science and Engineering, MIT. Follow its dimensional reasoning, limiting cases and successive refinement.
Mahajan, Street-Fighting Mathematics, MIT Press. The publisher describes tools for educated estimates. This is further reading, not a claim that the complete book was reviewed here.
Agarwal and Lang, Foundations of Analog and Digital Electronic Circuits, MIT reading map. Start with lumped abstraction and linear equivalent circuits.
John Ardizzoni, Analog Devices: datasheets and SPICE macromodels. Check which device behavior a model actually includes.

title: 18. Dividers: from reference voltages to sensors and resonant converters
text:
A divider is a network that shares voltage or current according to its impedances. It can set a reference, measure a sensor or describe a resonant tank.
The engineering question is what connects to the divider. Source impedance, sensor impedance, measurement loading and frequency can all change the result.
Choose a topic below. Each has a separate reading page. The numerical examples use authored teaching values, not selected commercial components.
crumbs: 83  18. Dividers: from reference voltages to sensors and resonant converters

title: 18.1 Start with the loaded impedance divider
text:
An impedance divider driven by Vs, with series Z1, shunt Z2 and the output voltage Vo measured at their junction.


For a sinusoidal source, calculate the complex voltage ratio before taking its magnitude:
H(j\omega)=\frac{V_o}{V_s}=\frac{Z_2}{Z_1+Z_2}.
The same form describes a DC resistive divider when Z_1=R_1 and Z_2=R_2. It assumes the source impedance is included in Z_1 or is negligible.
If the measurement or load impedance is Z_L, replace Z_2 with:
Z_b=Z_2\parallel Z_L=\frac{Z_2Z_L}{Z_2+Z_L},\qquad H_L=\frac{Z_b}{Z_1+Z_b}.
Do not replace these complex impedances with their magnitudes before adding them. Phase cancellation near resonance can change both gain and component stress.

title: 18.3 Measure an unknown impedance with a known resistor
text:
Put a known reference resistor R_{\mathrm{ref}} in series with the unknown impedance Z_x. Measure the source voltage and the voltage across Z_x at the same frequency.
Define the measured complex ratio H=V_x/V_s. Then:
H=\frac{Z_x}{R_{\mathrm{ref}}+Z_x},\qquad Z_x=R_{\mathrm{ref}}\frac{H}{1-H}.
Both amplitude and relative phase matter. A magnitude-only ratio does not generally identify both the real and imaginary parts of Z_x.
Worked example. Let R_{\mathrm{ref}}=1\ \mathrm{k\Omega} and H=0.5-j0.25 at 1 kHz. The recovered impedance is Z_x=600-j800\ \Omega. Its magnitude is 1 kΩ, but its real part is only 600 Ω.
This could represent a 600 Ω resistor in series with about 199 nF at that frequency. It does not identify a unique physical network over all frequencies.
With a 1 V RMS source, the unknown voltage is 0.5-j0.25\ \mathrm V. Series current is 0.5+j0.25\ \mathrm{mA}. The unknown absorbs 187.5 µW in this model.

Include the source output impedance in the known series impedance.
Check the loading of both voltage channels.
Calibrate channel gain and relative phase.
Choose an excitation that keeps the sensor in its intended linear range.
Repeat across the required frequency range.

The inverse calculation becomes sensitive when H approaches one. When H approaches zero, the measured unknown voltage becomes small. Select the reference impedance for useful signal levels and manageable sensitivity.
Analog Devices’ impedance-analyzer guide explains the measured voltage vectors. AP Instruments derives the corresponding complex divider conversion.

I_1=I\frac{Z_2}{Z_1+Z_2},\qquad I_2=I\frac{Z_1}{Z_1+Z_2}.
The opposite branch impedance appears in each numerator. These are complex ratios for AC. Use the actual return paths before deciding which branch carries the measured current.

A shared 5 mΩ connection adds 10 mV at 2 A. If included in the 50 mΩ sense voltage, it causes a 10% current overestimate. Kelvin sensing avoids that shared resistance in the voltage measurement.
At fast edges, shunt inductance can also contribute voltage. A constant-resistance conversion is then incomplete. Section 16.2 develops the shared-path error.
For pulsed current, calculate shunt heating from RMS current. The average current alone does not determine resistive heating.
