title: 18.5 A Wheatstone bridge compares two dividers
text:
Two resistor dividers form a Wheatstone bridge. The differential output is the left midpoint voltage Va minus the right midpoint voltage Vb. R2 is the sensing arm.


Let R_1 and R_2 form the left divider. Let R_3 and R_4 form the right divider. Assume a high-impedance differential measurement:
V_d=V_a-V_b=V_{\mathrm{ex}}\left(\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}-\frac{R_4}{R_3+R_4}\right).
The bridge balances when the two divider ratios match. It compares ratios rather than measuring one resistance in isolation.
For a quarter bridge, take R_1=R_3=R_4=R and R_2=R(1+\delta). Then:
V_d=V_{\mathrm{ex}}\frac{\delta}{2(2+\delta)}\approx V_{\mathrm{ex}}\frac{\delta}{4}.
With 5 V excitation and a 1% resistance increase, the exact signal is 12.438 mV. The linear estimate is 12.500 mV. Its relative error is 0.5%. At a 10% resistance change, that approximation error reaches 5%.
The sensor can respond to strain, pressure or temperature. The complete transducer needs the relation between that physical quantity and its resistance changes.
Ratiometric measurement. If the converter reference follows the bridge excitation, its result can depend on V_d/V_{\mathrm{ex}}. This reduces sensitivity to common excitation changes within the measurement bandwidth. Analog Devices CN0601 shows this arrangement.
Higher excitation increases the output signal. It also increases resistor heating. Ratio measurement does not cancel temperature changes caused by that heating.
Lead resistance, amplifier bias current, common-mode range and resistor tracking still matter. Choose excitation and gain from the signal requirement and the permitted sensor disturbance.
crumbs: 88  18.5 A Wheatstone bridge compares two dividers

title: 18.6 Calorimetry: read temperature, then infer heat or power
text:
A resistive thermometer can occupy a bridge arm and sense a calorimeter’s temperature rise. The bridge provides an electrical readout. A thermal model and calibration connect that readout to heat or power.
Use an authored linear thermometer model R_s=R_0(1+\alpha\Delta T). Let R_0=1\ \mathrm{k\Omega}, \alpha=0.00385\ \mathrm{K^{-1}} and bridge excitation be 1 V. In the quarter bridge above, a 1 K rise gives about 0.9607 mV.
For a separate lumped thermal model, let thermal resistance be 100 K/W and heat capacity be 0.020 J/K. Keep the environment fixed. A constant absorbed power of 10 mW gives a 1 K steady rise. The time constant is 2 s.
The model obeys:
C_\theta\frac{d\Delta T}{dt}+G_\theta\Delta T=P_{\mathrm{abs}},\qquad G_\theta=1/R_\theta.
At 2 s after the power step, the rise is only about 0.632 K. A bridge reading before thermal settling does not equal the steady-state response.
For an energy pulse, heat capacity also matters. The short-pulse estimate E\approx C_\theta\Delta T neglects heat lost during the pulse. Use the dynamic model when that loss affects the required accuracy.
The readout also heats the sensor. At bridge balance, the 1 kΩ sensing arm dissipates 0.25 mW with 1 V excitation. If all that heat enters the modeled thermal body, it adds 0.025 K. Doubling excitation quadruples this heating.
The thermal coupling of the real sensor and its leads determines the actual disturbance. Include that coupling and the baseline heat input in the calibration.
Electrical substitution measures a power difference. Hold the receiver at the same temperature with and without absorbed radiation. Keep the environment and other heat inputs unchanged. In the ideal equivalent-heating model:
P_{\mathrm{abs}}=P_{\mathrm{heater,dark}}-P_{\mathrm{heater,lit}}.
A heater reduction from 12 mW to 2 mW therefore represents 10 mW of absorbed power. Absorptance and differences between electrical and optical heating affect the uncertainty.
NIST’s electrical-substitution review describes the temperature-control, heater and thermometer arrangement. Its cryogenic-radiometer description explains the same power-difference principle. The numbers here are illustrative, not NIST instrument specifications.
crumbs: 89  18.6 Calorimetry: read temperature, then infer heat or power

title: 18.7 The LLC tank as a frequency-dependent divider
text:
The inductor-inductor-capacitor (LLC) converter contains switches, a resonant tank, a transformer and a rectifier. Its complete switching operation is not a linear two-impedance network.
The fundamental harmonic approximation (FHA) retains the tank’s fundamental-frequency response. It represents the rectifier and load by an equivalent primary-referred AC resistance, R_{\mathrm{ac}}.



The LLC fundamental-frequency model has series Cr and Lr followed by parallel Lm and Rac. The output phasor is measured across that parallel branch.


Define:
Z_s=j\omega L_r+\frac{1}{j\omega C_r},\qquad Z_p=(j\omega L_m)\parallel R_{\mathrm{ac}}.
The tank’s fundamental voltage gain is the divider:
H(j\omega)=\frac{V_p}{V_{\mathrm{in},1}}=\frac{Z_p}{Z_s+Z_p}.
The magnetizing inductance affects Z_p, so the load and frequency both affect the ratio. The load conversion depends on the chosen rectifier model. Recovering DC gain also needs bridge waveform factors and transformer turns ratio.
Worked model. Take L_r=20\ \mathrm{\mu H}, C_r=100\ \mathrm{nF} and L_m=100\ \mathrm{\mu H}. The series resonant frequency is about 112.54 kHz.

title: 18.10 Exercise: two dividers and a buffer
text:
Circuit A and circuit B
Two dividers produce the same unloaded voltage. Which remains closer to that voltage under load, and what does that improvement cost?
This is an original public practice exercise. All component values describe teaching models. The numerical answers are on the separate solution page.
The supply is ideal and constant at 12 V. All resistors are ideal and constant. Disconnect the load for the unloaded case. Use the same load resistance for both circuits.

Two loaded voltage dividers supplied by 12 V. Circuit A uses two 1 kilohm resistors. Circuit B uses two 100 ohm resistors. Each load connects across the lower resistor.

title: 18.10 Exercise: two dividers and a buffer
section: Add an op-amp voltage follower
text:
Add an op-amp voltage follower
An operational amplifier (op-amp) can separate the reference input from the load-current path. Negative feedback connects its output to its inverting input.



Divider A drives the noninverting input of an op-amp voltage follower. The output feeds a 100 ohm load and returns to the inverting input. The op-amp supply connects to 12 V and the common return.


The ideal follower draws no input current and holds its output at the reference voltage. Load current comes through the amplifier’s supply connections. It does not pass through the reference divider.
For the calculation, assume that the follower can supply the required current from a 12 V supply. Use a 100 Ω load. Neglect input current, voltage offset and quiescent supply current.

Calculate the divider voltage and load current.
Calculate the divider loss and load power.
Calculate the active stage’s dissipation using a linear output-stage power balance.
Calculate the total supply power, including the divider.
Explain how a 40 mA output-current limit invalidates the ideal result.

A real buffer provides finite isolation. Input bias current still loads the reference. Output current, voltage swing, common-mode range and temperature limit its usable load range. Bandwidth and load capacitance affect settling and stability.
A buffer reduces direct load-current interaction with the reference. It does not provide galvanic isolation or remove shared supply and return impedances. A supply-derived reference still follows supply changes.

title: 18.10 Exercise: two dividers and a buffer
section: Compare an NPN emitter follower
text:
Compare an NPN emitter follower
A single NPN transistor can also provide current gain. Its collector draws most of the load current from the supply. Its base still draws current from the reference divider.



Divider A drives the base of an NPN transistor. Its collector connects to 12 V. Its emitter supplies a 100 ohm load to the common return. Base and emitter voltages have separate labels.


Use a constant current gain \beta=100 and a constant base-emitter drop V_{BE}=0.7\ \mathrm V. Assume forward-active operation. These values are model assumptions, not device specifications.

Express base current in terms of load current.
Include base current in the divider’s Thévenin model.
Calculate the base voltage, emitter voltage and load current for 100 Ω.
Compare the result with the ideal op-amp follower.
Explain why the transistor does not preserve a precise 6 V output.

Actual V_{BE} and current gain change with operating conditions. A bare emitter follower therefore provides approximate buffering, with a voltage shift and residual reference loading.
Analog Devices’ emitter-follower laboratory explains the current gain and voltage shift. Its AN-581 discusses divider bias, input-current errors and supply coupling in op-amp circuits.
Continue to the solution: loading, losses and buffer power after completing the calculations.

section: 3. A voltage reference needs a load specification
text:
3. A voltage reference needs a load specification
The relative reduction from 6 V is:
\varepsilon=\frac{6-V_o}{6}=\frac{R_{\mathrm{Th}}}{R_{\mathrm{Th}}+R_L}.
For at most 1% reduction, R_L\geq99R_{\mathrm{Th}}. Divider A needs at least 49.5 kΩ. Divider B needs at least 4.95 kΩ. These bounds include loading error only.

title: 18.11 Solution: loading, losses and buffer power
section: 4. The ideal op-amp follower separates the current paths
text:
4. The ideal op-amp follower separates the current paths



Divider A drives the noninverting input of an op-amp voltage follower. The output feeds a 100 ohm load and returns to the inverting input. The op-amp supply connects to 12 V and the common return.


The ideal input draws no current, so divider A remains unloaded. The output is 6 V. The 100 Ω load draws 60 mA and absorbs 360 mW.
For the stated linear output-stage model, the active stage draws 60 mA from 12 V. Its dissipation is:
P_{\mathrm{stage}}=(12-6)\,0.060=0.360\ \mathrm W.
The divider still consumes 72 mW. Total supply current is 66 mA, giving 792 mW input power. The balance is 360 mW load power, 360 mW active-stage loss and 72 mW divider loss.
The buffer improves load regulation without the 720 mW standing divider loss of circuit B. It does not eliminate conversion loss. In this idealized model, active-stage load loss falls to zero when the load disconnects. A real amplifier also consumes quiescent power.
The calculated 60 mA exceeds a hypothetical 40 mA output limit. That amplifier cannot maintain the assumed 6 V across 100 Ω. Its actual voltage requires its limiting and thermal models.
Low input current and low output impedance provide practical decoupling within specified operating limits. A buffer does not make the supply-derived reference immune to supply variation. Chapter 14 compares this linear power loss with other supply architectures.

6. Design conclusion
Specify reference accuracy, load range and permitted dissipation together. A low-resistance divider trades standing power for lower source resistance. A buffer separates reference sensing from load-current delivery within its operating limits.

title: 19. Operating points and small-signal models
text:
Why can a diode have a 650 Ω voltage/current ratio and respond to a small perturbation like 26 Ω? Why can a MOSFET need two slopes? Which current direction gives a solar panel’s negative slope?
This chapter develops one method across these examples. Start with the nonlinear relation, find the operating point, calculate derivatives and test a finite perturbation. Each section has a separate reading page.
The numbers describe original teaching models. They are not measured device data or component selections. The exercise and its solution also have separate pages.

title: 19.1 The operating point, the secant and the tangent
text:
Let a two-terminal device obey i=f(v) under fixed external conditions. A bias circuit establishes its operating point, Q=(V_Q,I_Q), with I_Q=f(V_Q).
See the two slopes first. This Python plot uses the diode model from Section 19.2. The dotted line joins the origin to Q. The dashed line is tangent at Q.



Python diode curve with the operating point at 0.650 V and 1 mA, the 650 ohm static line and the 26 ohm tangent. A second panel enlarges the local current response.


Both lines pass through Q. Only the tangent follows the nearby nonlinear curve closely. Its accuracy decreases as the perturbation grows.
Write total voltage and current as bias plus perturbation:
v(t)=V_Q+\delta v(t),\qquad i(t)=I_Q+\delta i(t).
The static ratio is R_{\mathrm{static}}=V_Q/I_Q when I_Q\ne0. On an i-versus-v graph, the line from the origin has slope I_Q/V_Q. That line describes a ratio, not the curve’s local response.
The first-order Taylor expansion gives:
i\approx I_Q+g_d(v-V_Q),\qquad g_d=\left.\frac{di}{dv}\right|_Q.
Subtract the bias to get \delta i\approx g_d\delta v. Where g_d\ne0, the differential resistance is r_d=1/g_d. Thus the graph’s tangent slope is conductance, not resistance, when current is on the vertical axis.
The tangent usually misses the origin. Replacing the complete nonlinear device by r_d alone would give I_Q=V_Q/r_d. That generally destroys the original bias point. The small-signal resistor relates changes after the bias has been removed from the equations.







Question
Quantity




What voltage and current exist before the perturbation?
Operating point V_Q,I_Q.


What is their ratio?
Static resistance V_Q/I_Q.


What current change follows a small voltage change?
Differential conductance g_d.


What voltage change follows a small current change?
Differential resistance r_d.



For v=Ri with constant R, the curve is a straight line through the origin. Both resistances equal R. Nonlinear behavior makes that equality a special case.
Temperature can move the entire curve. The LED driver case adds this second sensitivity and compares voltage, resistor and current drive. It then tests self-heating and thermal stability.
Continue with the Python curves: diode, MOSFET, solar panel or constant-power load.

title: 19.2 Diode: bias determines the local resistance
text:
Consider a forward-biased diode with current entering its positive-voltage terminal. Use the exponential model:
i_D=I_S\left(e^{v_D/a}-1\right),\qquad a=nV_T.
Here, n is the ideality factor and V_T is thermal voltage. Hold temperature fixed. For this teaching example, choose a=26\ \mathrm{mV} and I_S=1\ \mathrm{mA}/(e^{0.650/a}-1).
The operating point is therefore exactly V_Q=0.650\ \mathrm V, I_Q=1\ \mathrm{mA}. Differentiation gives:
g_d=\frac{I_Q+I_S}{a},\qquad r_d=\frac{a}{I_Q+I_S}\approx\frac{a}{I_Q}.
The static ratio is 650 Ω. The incremental resistance is approximately 26 Ω. A 1 mV diode-voltage increase therefore predicts a 38.462 µA current increase.



Diode current curve with its static secant, followed by a local comparison between the nonlinear current change and the tangent at 1 mA.

A 10 mV perturbation looks small beside 0.650 V. It is not small beside the 26 mV exponential scale. Judge smallness against curvature and the required error.
The surrounding circuit sets the perturbation across the diode. A source variation can divide between a series resistor and r_d. It need not appear entirely across the junction.



A voltage source and series resistor bias a diode. The corresponding incremental circuit retains the series resistor and replaces the diode by rd. The source is only the voltage perturbation.


At a 2 mA bias, the same model gives approximately 13 Ω. A 1 kΩ series resistor then receives most of a small source-voltage change. Section 19.7 asks you to calculate that division.
At higher frequencies, junction and diffusion capacitances also matter. A constant resistor describes only the stated low-frequency local model. MIT’s diode recitation develops the conductance and charge-storage terms.

title: 19.3 MOSFET: output resistance and gate control are different derivatives
text:
A metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor (MOSFET) has several terminals. Its drain current depends on more than drain voltage. Begin with a low-frequency model at fixed temperature and fixed body bias:
I_D=F(V_{GS},V_{DS}).
Near the operating point:
\delta i_D\approx g_m\delta v_{GS}+g_{ds}\delta v_{DS},\qquad r_o=1/g_{ds}.
Here, g_m=\left.\partial I_D/\partial V_{GS}\right|_Q holds V_{DS} fixed. The derivative g_{ds}=\left.\partial I_D/\partial V_{DS}\right|_Q holds V_{GS} fixed. These conditions define different measurements.



MOSFET drain-current curves versus drain voltage at fixed gate voltages, and a gate-voltage curve with its tangent at fixed drain voltage.


On the I_D–V_{DS} plane, one fixed-gate curve gives g_{ds} from its local slope. Moving the gate voltage moves between curves. One output resistor cannot describe that gate-controlled current change.
The incremental drain-source model therefore contains r_o in parallel with a controlled current source g_m\delta v_{GS}:



An NMOS has independently biased gate and drain terminals with its source grounded. The local model contains an open gate input and parallel ro and gm times delta vgs drain-to-source branches.


Authored saturation model. Use:
I_D=\frac{K}{2}(V_{GS}-V_{\mathrm{th}})^2(1+\lambda V_{DS}).
Choose K=2\ \mathrm{mA/V^2}, V_{\mathrm{th}}=1\ \mathrm V and \lambda=0.020\ \mathrm{V^{-1}}. At V_{GS,Q}=2\ \mathrm V and V_{DS,Q}=5\ \mathrm V, the model gives:



Quantity
Result

The exact derivatives are g_m=K(V_{GS}-V_{\mathrm{th}})(1+\lambda V_{DS}) and g_{ds}=K(V_{GS}-V_{\mathrm{th}})^2\lambda/2. For this model, r_o=(1+\lambda V_{DS})/(\lambda I_D). The familiar 1/(\lambda I_D) expression drops the channel-modulation factor.
With a +10 mV gate change and +0.2 V drain change, the tangent predicts +26.000 µA. The nonlinear model gives +26.1904 µA. The error relative to the current change is about 0.727%.
The plotted curves include an illustrative triode-region extension. The derivative values above use the stated saturation equation. Keep every perturbed point in its intended operating region.
This square-law model illustrates derivatives. It is not a prediction for a selected power MOSFET or a nanoscale transistor. Short-channel effects, body variation, capacitances and self-heating can require a different model. The local-derivative method still applies where that model is differentiable.
Changing body voltage adds another controlled-current term. High-frequency models also require capacitances. MIT’s MOSFET circuit-model notes develop these extensions.

title: 19.4 Solar panel: fix illumination and label the current direction
text:
A photovoltaic (PV) panel supplies current from incident light. Define terminal voltage as positive at its upper terminal. In this section, I is current delivered out of that positive terminal.
An illustrative single-diode model, with zero series resistance and infinite shunt resistance, gives:
I(V)=I_{\mathrm{ph}}-I_0\left(e^{V/a_{\mathrm{PV}}}-1\right).
Use I_{\mathrm{ph}}=5\ \mathrm A, a_{\mathrm{PV}}=1.5\ \mathrm V and I_0=5/(e^{21/1.5}-1)\ \mathrm A. The parameter a_{\mathrm{PV}} represents the module’s effective exponential voltage scale. The open-circuit voltage is exactly 21 V in this model.
Hold irradiance and temperature fixed. Then:
\frac{dI}{dV}=-\frac{I_0}{a_{\mathrm{PV}}}e^{V/a_{\mathrm{PV}}}<0.
At 18 V, the panel delivers about 4.3233 A. The local delivered-current slope is −0.45112 A/V. Thus \delta I\approx-0.45112\delta V, and the signed ratio \delta V/\delta I is about −2.2167 Ω.
Translate the sign convention before comparing devices. Passive current enters the positive terminal, so i_{\mathrm{in}}=-I. Consequently di_{\mathrm{in}}/dV is positive here. The passive-port incremental resistance is +2.2167 Ω.



An illuminated current source and diode form the simplified photovoltaic model. Its incremental passive-port model is a positive resistor when light and temperature stay fixed. Delivered current and entering current use opposite arrows.


The static load ratio is 18/4.3233\approx4.1635\ \Omega. Neither that ratio nor a generic negative resistor describes every perturbation. Recalculate the slope when the operating point, light or temperature changes.



Photovoltaic delivered current versus voltage with a tangent at 18 V, and delivered power with its maximum-power point.


Maximum power gives a useful derivative test. Delivered power is P=VI(V). At an interior maximum-power point (MPP):
\frac{dP}{dV}=I+V\frac{dI}{dV}=0,\qquad \left.\frac{dV}{dI}\right|_{\mathrm{MPP}}=-\frac{V_{\mathrm{MPP}}}{I_{\mathrm{MPP}}}.
For this model, the MPP is about 17.2143 V, 4.5992 A and 79.1726 W. The delivered-current incremental ratio is −3.7429 Ω there. In the passive convention, its sign reverses.
This condition follows from the nonlinear power curve. It does not make the panel a fixed Thévenin source or prove a complete converter is stable.
If light changes, \delta I_{\mathrm{ph}} adds a source term. Temperature changes the model parameters. Series resistance, shunt leakage and capacitance require additional terms. Sandia’s PV modeling guide describes the fuller single-diode circuit.

title: 19.5 A controlled constant-power load: negative slope while absorbing power
text:
Return to passive references: current enters the positive-voltage terminal. An ideal constant-input-power load obeys I=P/V. With P fixed:
R_{\mathrm{static}}=\frac{V_Q^2}{P},\qquad g_d=-\frac{P}{V_Q^2},\qquad r_d=-\frac{V_Q^2}{P}.
At 60 W and 12 V, current is 5 A. The static ratio is +2.4 Ω, while incremental resistance is −2.4 Ω. A −0.1 V voltage perturbation predicts a +41.667 mA current change. The exact constant-power relation gives +42.017 mA.



Python plot comparing a 60 watt constant-power current curve, its negative-slope tangent at 12 V and a positive 2.4 ohm resistor. A second panel shows tangent error for finite voltage changes.


All three curves pass through 12 V and 5 A. The resistor current increases with voltage. The constant-power current decreases with voltage. Their static ratios match at Q, but their slopes have opposite signs.
The lower plot compares the predicted current change with the exact change. For this ideal constant-power model, the relative change-error is |\delta v|/(12\ \mathrm V). At zero perturbation, the plotted value is its zero limit.
The load still absorbs positive power. Its controller demands more current when the voltage decreases. The negative incremental resistance describes that response.
This is different from the solar-panel sign change above. The constant-power load has a negative slope even with passive current references. Its input power does not reverse.
The approximation requires the controller to maintain input power over the perturbation’s time scale. Current limits, loss variation and control bandwidth change the response. A real converter generally has a frequency-dependent input impedance.
Section 12.5 connects this response to source impedance and input-filter interaction. A slope alone does not establish closed-loop stability.

title: 19.6 Build and check a local model
text:
Define the terminal voltage and current directions.
State the temperature, illumination and other terminal conditions that stay fixed.
Solve the nonlinear bias circuit for its operating point.
Calculate each required derivative at that point.
Draw the circuit for perturbations, including controlled sources and relevant storage elements.
Compare a finite perturbation with the nonlinear model.
Decide whether the error changes the engineering conclusion.

Independent DC sources become zero only in the perturbation circuit. Their bias values still determine the operating point and derivative values. Keep dependent sources active.
Check the change you need to predict. A small error in total current can hide a large error in its incremental change. State whether the error limit concerns bias, gain, current change, distortion or settling.
For a smooth scalar curve, the next Taylor term is approximately f''(V_Q)(\delta v)^2/2. Compare it with the retained linear term over the intended range. Near a zero slope, relative slope-error measures can become misleading.
A differentiable curve can support a useful local model over a limited range. Discontinuities, hysteresis, region changes and internal dynamics can require more states or another representation. Small amplitude alone does not justify ignoring those effects.
Use the tangent model for local gain and impedance when its checked range fits the question. Use the nonlinear model for larger excursions or operating-region changes. A physical measurement can test both models near the actual bias point.
Course connection. The processed October 23 afternoon transcript, turns T009–T013, emphasizes small perturbations around an operating point. The examples here develop that local-model idea with explicit derivatives and error checks. Their numbers are authored additions.
Linear system models support superposition and transfer-function reasoning. Fourier and Laplace transforms also apply to many individual signals produced by nonlinear systems. Transforming a waveform does not make its generating system linear.
scripts/small_signal_examples.py checks derivatives by centered differences and compares finite perturbations with the nonlinear equations. It also solves the diode bias circuit and independently optimizes PV power. The script writes small-signal-checks.json and plots 104, 106, 108, 109 and 110. It exports SVG reading figures and PNG previews.

title: 19.9 An LED warms up: which quantity should the driver regulate?
text:
Manufacturer anchors and model assumptions
A white light-emitting diode (LED) draws 350 mA at 25 °C. Its supply has a fixed 5 V rail. Can the current stay within ±5% as junction temperature rises to 125 °C?
Predict the current change before looking at the plots. Keep the LED junction temperature separate from ambient temperature and driver-component temperatures.
This is an original worked teaching case based on the Cree XLamp XP-E2 white family. The exercise and its solution have separate reading pages. The source data are typical values, not a worst-case model of every manufactured LED.
These anchors refer to the white LED at 85 °C. They are not white-LED measurements at 25 °C. The manufacturer datasheet, revision CLD-DS56 Rev 25B, also supplies its typical I–V curve.
Use the following monotonic voltage model for positive current:
V_F(I,T_j)=2.84+a\ln\left(\frac{I}{0.350}\right)+r_s(I-0.350)+k_T(T_j-85).
Voltages are in volts, current is in amperes and temperatures are in degrees Celsius. Choose the logarithmic scale a=0.030\ \mathrm V as an authored curvature parameter. A least-squares fit of the two higher-current anchors gives r_s=0.379359\ \Omega.
The largest voltage residual at the three anchors is about 3.57 mV. This checks agreement with those anchors only. The temperature-shifted curves and low-current extension remain model estimates.
At 350 mA and 25 °C, the model gives 2.930 V. The static ratio is 8.371 Ω, while differential resistance is:
r_d=\left.\frac{\partial V_F}{\partial I}\right|_{T_j}=\frac{a}{I}+r_s\approx0.4651\ \Omega.
The temperature relation adds another independent contribution:
\delta v_F\approx r_d\delta i+k_T\delta T_j.
At fixed voltage, \delta i\approx-k_T\delta T_j/r_d. At fixed current, \delta v_F\approx k_T\delta T_j. Current regulation changes the response to temperature. It does not make the LED temperature or optical output constant.
The following sections compare the drivers, add self-heating and check a practical current-source concept. Start the exercise before opening its separate solution.

title: 19.11 Self-heating: equilibrium, temperature limits and instability
text:
Find a root before classifying stability
Now let the junction warm itself. Ambient temperature is fixed at 25 °C. The LED and cooling path share one lumped thermal state.
Use a heat fraction f_h=0.75 and C_\theta=0.5\ \mathrm{J/K}. These are teaching assumptions, not XP-E2 transient specifications. The electrical input and heat input differ:
P_{\mathrm{heat}}=f_h V_F I,\qquad R_\theta=5.8+R_{\mathrm{board-air}}.
The remaining fraction represents optical energy leaving the junction in this simplified model. Real optical conversion and thermal coupling can vary with current and temperature. Driver heating is outside this LED thermal node.
The one-state equation is:
C_\theta\frac{dT_j}{dt}=P_{\mathrm{heat}}(T_j)-\frac{T_j-T_a}{R_\theta}=F(T_j).
The package’s 5.8 K/W does not include the complete board-to-ambient cooling path. Compare authored board-to-air resistances of 20 K/W and 140 K/W. The total resistances are 25.8 K/W and 145.8 K/W.
A thermal equilibrium T_* satisfies F(T_*)=0. At that equilibrium, a small temperature perturbation obeys:
\frac{d\delta T}{dt}\approx\lambda_\theta\delta T,\qquad \lambda_\theta=\frac{P'_{\mathrm{heat}}(T_*)-1/R_\theta}{C_\theta}.
A negative pole predicts local decay. A positive pole predicts local growth. A zero pole requires further analysis. The derivative at a point that is not an equilibrium does not establish equilibrium stability.
With the 20 K/W board path, all three cases have stable equilibria inside the design range:
The voltage-driven case is thermally stable here, despite its substantial current drift. Stable does not mean compliant with the current requirement.
With the 140 K/W board path, no admissible equilibrium appears below 125 °C. The simulations stop at that limit after approximately 62.87 s, 154.40 s and 197.44 s, respectively.
The current-regulated case still carries exactly 350 mA when it reaches the temperature limit. Its current control passes while its cooling fails. These results establish a design-limit violation, not a particular physical failure mode.

title: 19.12 A practical linear current-source concept
text:
Check voltage and power before accuracy
A current source needs a reference, current measurement and an output device. Use an op-amp to compare a 0.350 V setpoint with the voltage across a 1 Ω sense resistor.
The regulated current is approximately:
I\approx\frac{\beta V_{\mathrm{ref}}+V_{\mathrm{OS}}}{R_s},\qquad \beta\approx0.14.
Adjust the nominal divider ratio at 25 °C to obtain 350 mA. The adjustment removes initial error at that condition. It does not remove subsequent temperature drift.
At the initial LED voltage of 2.930 V, the sense resistor drops 0.350 V. The MOSFET has 1.720 V across drain and source. The teaching compliance allowance is 0.300 V.
The OPA197 requires at least 4.5 V supply. Its own supply requirement still applies even when the LED load path has enough headroom. Reference and amplifier quiescent losses are additional to this load-path balance.
The transistor is a circuit requirement, not a completed device selection. Its DC safe operating area, available gate drive and cooling require checks. The 0.300 V allowance is an authored model parameter.

text:
A bounded current-error budget
Keep driver-component temperatures independent of LED junction temperature. Each component may range from 25 to 125 °C in this conservative comparison. The calculation enumerates endpoint error signs after the initial adjustment.







Contribution
Selected basis




Reference

The reference specification uses a box method over −55 to 125 °C. Use its complete 180 K span as a bound on peak-to-peak drift. Do not interpret that specification as a guaranteed local derivative at every temperature.
The 256 enumerated corners give approximately 345.10–354.98 mA, or −1.40% to +1.42%. Those declared DC contributions fit inside the ±5% current requirement. They do not establish a complete hardware accuracy guarantee.
Use the complete shunt’s 75 ppm/K specification. Its less-than-20 ppm/K resistive-element value does not include the complete component behavior.
The feedback model is quasi-static on the thermal time scale. It does not prove electronic loop stability with a particular MOSFET gate capacitance. Layout, compensation, reference hysteresis, aging and device thermal qualification remain outside this calculation.

text:
D. Defend a choice
Recommend a driver and cooling condition for the original requirement. Support the recommendation with current error, loss and junction-temperature results.
State one changed requirement that could make the resistor alternative preferable. Explain which measurement would most reduce uncertainty in the thermal model.
The course supplies the numerical model. The private command is python scripts/led_electrothermal.py. The task is to predict, calculate and interpret its results, then defend the decision.

title: 19.14 Solution: current regulation and thermal stability
text:
A. Temperature-sensitive electrical behavior
This page solves the LED driver and cooling exercise. All results use the stated teaching model and its typical manufacturer anchors.
The initial LED voltage is 2.930 V. Its static ratio is 2.930/0.350=8.3714\ \Omega. Its differential resistance is 0.030/0.350+0.379359\approx0.4651\ \Omega.
The ballast is (5-2.930)/0.350=5.9143\ \Omega. The model gives:
The permitted band is 332.5–367.5 mA. At 75 °C, resistor and current drive pass, while voltage drive fails. At 125 °C, only ideal current drive passes.
The resistor provides useful feedback and misses the full-range requirement by a relatively small margin. It is not equivalent to applying a fixed voltage directly to the LED.
For the resistor alternative, set the hot current to its permitted maximum, 367.5 mA. Subtract the hot and cold circuit equations:
R_{b,\min}=\frac{V_F(0.350,25)-V_F(0.3675,125)}{0.3675-0.350}\approx8.1084\ \Omega.
The cold supply must then be 2.930+0.350R_{b,\min}\approx5.7680\ \mathrm V. This solution changes the original rail and increases standing load-path loss. Keep it as an alternative when those changes are acceptable.

title: 19.14 Solution: current regulation and thermal stability
section: C. A genuine unstable equilibrium in the explicit counter-model
text:
C. A genuine unstable equilibrium in the explicit counter-model
Removing fitted series resistance changes the model. With the counter-model’s 9.10125 K/W total thermal resistance, the equilibria are 39.333 and 51.994 °C.
The corresponding poles are −0.06227 and +0.07685 s⁻¹. Small temperature errors decay at the lower root and grow at the upper root. The nonlinear integrations confirm those signs.
At the upper root, current is 1.34972 A. A positive perturbation drives current upward until the declared current limit stops the simulation. A negative perturbation moves toward the lower equilibrium.
The anchored model under the same cooling gives a different heat-balance curve. The exponential-only result is a model-sensitivity demonstration, not an XP-E2 instability claim.

section: D. Practical current-source screen
text:
D. Practical current-source screen



An op-amp drives an NMOS current sink with LED drain load and source sense resistor. Source-voltage feedback regulates the measured current.


For R_s=1\ \Omega, the setpoint is 0.350 V. At the initial operating point:
P_s=I^2R_s=0.1225\ \mathrm W,\qquad P_M=(5-2.930-0.350)I=0.6020\ \mathrm W.
The transistor has 1.720 V drain-source voltage, above the authored 0.300 V allowance. The amplifier’s separate 4.5 V minimum supply requirement is also satisfied by 5 V.
This does not select the transistor. DC safe operating area, gate-drive compatibility, amplifier compensation and both devices’ cooling still need checks.
After initial adjustment, the enumerated DC error corners span approximately 345.10–354.98 mA. This is −1.40% to +1.42%, within the ±5% requirement for the declared error terms.
The reference box-drift allowance uses its full specified temperature span. The shunt uses complete-component TCR. Input-bias and common-mode transfer allowances supplement the offset and drift terms.

title: 19.14 Solution: current regulation and thermal stability
section: E. Conditional recommendation
text:
E. Conditional recommendation
For the original 5 V rail and full imposed junction-temperature range, choose current regulation with a cooling path that meets the separate temperature requirement. The modeled 20 K/W board path meets that thermal requirement at 25 °C ambient.
The component-based DC screen supports the current-regulation concept. It is not a completed hardware qualification. The 140 K/W path fails despite accurate current.
For a narrower temperature range, a relaxed current tolerance or a higher permitted rail, reconsider the resistor solution. It has fewer active components but retains temperature drift and continuous loss.
Measure the actual junction-to-ambient path or a calibrated temperature transient to reduce the thermal uncertainty. Report any assumption about emitted optical power when converting electrical power into junction heat.

title: Lesson 1 — The buck converter: what happens, why, and how to design it
text:
Power Electronic Systems · HTWG · 2026
Teaching source: lecture 1, Anwendungen der Leistungselektronik, WS 2025/2026, Riccardo Tinivella / Kurt Schenk.
Prerequisite: the 2026 circuit-foundations recap. Language: English, following the intro lesson.
A converter design starts with a question, not a component value. What must the circuit do? Which physical limit matters first? We will use the answer to choose each part, then check whether the choice works.
Our example is TI’s PMP31349 reference design. This synchronous GaN buck converts a 30–60 V bus to 12 V at 20 A. An LM5148 peak-current-mode controller drives an LMG2100R044 half-bridge at 350 kHz.
We start from the specification and work towards a complete design. At each step, we compare our estimate with TI’s chosen part and published measurements.
How we work. First, estimate by hand. State the assumptions and predict what the circuit should do. Then simulate the same model and compare the results. Finally, compare with TI’s measurements and explain any gap.
A failed choice is useful evidence. We keep it on the page, marked No!, and explain what must change. Before moving on, explain why we chose this option. Name its main benefit and cost. Then say when a credible alternative would become preferable.
This sequence follows C. Basso, Switch-Mode Power Supplies: SPICE Simulations and Practical Designs, McGraw-Hill, 2008, §5.1. The worked examples are our own. The Example scripts reproduce the calculations. §9 explains the two PLECS models to draw.
Where the buck is used. The German name says what the buck can do: Tiefsetzsteller, the converter that only sets the voltage lower. Its output must stay below its input. The boost of a later lesson is the Hochsetzsteller.
Use a buck when the load needs a lower voltage and galvanic isolation is unnecessary. Applications range from small point-of-load regulators to high-current stages with several phases. Switching frequencies span roughly 20 kHz to 10 MHz. A few hundred kilohertz is common.
Efficiency depends on the complete design and operating point. PMP31349 reaches 95.5 % at 48 V and 20 A (TI, measured, §8).
Reading route. Follow Part I (§1–11) for the complete design. Use Part II (§12) to practise diagnosing a waveform, choosing a model and defending a decision. The appendices hold background and longer derivations. §13 gives the sources and numerical checks.
The recap supplies the circuit foundations. Return to it when a current path, RMS calculation or balance equation is unclear.

title: Learning outcomes and teaching route
text:
By the end, students should be able to:

write a converter specification and say which limits are given and which are their own
derive the conversion ratio from volt-second balance and find the duty-cycle extremes
size L, C_{\mathrm{out}} and C_{\mathrm{in}} from ripple, load-step and RMS limits
check the chosen values against real parts with DC-bias derating, ESR and saturation
calculate mean and RMS stresses with the correct current measure for each loss
explain how dead time and the sign of the valley current shape each GaN switching edge
read a current-mode loop gain and say which input sets its crossover and phase margin
estimate losses and junction temperature from datasheets, and say what a calibration against measurement adds
predict what changes in critical conduction, discontinuous conduction, at another switching frequency or with another LC filter
explain why a fixed-duty CCM buck does not regulate current, and evaluate sensitivity at a stated operating point (Part II).

title: 2. Duty-cycle extremes
text:
2.1 Two switch positions, two ramps
In the synchronous buck the high-side switch connects the switch node to V_{\mathrm{in}} for the time DT_s. The low-side switch then clamps the node to ground for (1-D)T_s. §4 checks that the output voltage barely moves within one period. The inductor then sees two constant voltages, and its current is two straight lines:
\frac{di_L}{dt}=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o}{L}\quad\mathrm{(high\ side\ on)},\qquad \frac{di_L}{dt}=-\frac{V_o}{L}\quad\mathrm{(low\ side\ on)}.
The inductor resists a change of current, not current itself. While the low side conducts, the current still flows toward the load and the inductor releases energy. The output capacitor takes the difference, i_C = i_L - i_o. The output ripple is therefore a consequence of the inductor ripple, and §4 checks it after we choose the capacitor.

The input voltage is constant, so the input power is V_{\mathrm{in}} times the mean input current: P_{\mathrm{in}} = V_{\mathrm{in}}\cdot D\cdot I_o = V_o\cdot I_o = P_o. The ideal buck is a DC transformer with ratio D: it steps the voltage down and the mean current up, and it loses nothing. The losses of §8 come from the components, not from the principle.
What the extremes decide. At 60 V, D_{\min} gives the shortest on-time and the largest inductor ripple (§3). The low side conducts for 80 % of the period, so it has the larger conduction loss (§8).
At 30 V, D_{\max} = 0.400 is closest to 0.5. This gives the largest input-capacitor RMS current within our input range (§5). Different checks have different worst cases.
TI chose, TI measured. TI chose the 30–60 V range and the 12 V output, so the extremes follow directly. On the board, the conduction and dead-time losses push the duty slightly above the ideal D = V_o/V_{\mathrm{in}}.
Our datasheet loss model with TI’s parts needs D = 0.2565 at 48 V and 20 A (ours, loss-estimate-checks.json). §8.2 shows where the extra duty goes. TI measured the switching frequency at 344.9 kHz rather than 350 kHz (TIDT427A fig. 3-2). We keep TI’s range and f_s and continue with the inductor.
What we can choose. The required voltage ratio fixes the ideal duty. We cannot lower duty independently and keep the same output. A different bus voltage is an alternative system choice. It changes ripple, timing and device stress together.

title: 3. The inductor
text:
3.1 The ripple ratio sets L
Integrate either ramp of §2.1 over its own interval and substitute D = V_o/V_{\mathrm{in}}:
\Delta I_L=\frac{(V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o)\,D}{L\,f_s}=\frac{V_o}{L\,f_s}\left(1-\frac{V_o}{V_{\mathrm{in}}}\right).
At fixed V_o the ripple grows with V_{\mathrm{in}}, so the worst case is the maximum input, 60 V. A shortcut warning: V_{\mathrm{in}}\cdot D(1-D) peaks at D = 0.5 only if V_{\mathrm{in}} stays fixed while D changes. Here V_o stays fixed and V_{\mathrm{in}} sweeps, so V_{\mathrm{in}} and D are coupled. Find the worst case from the equation above, not from D(1-D).
We ask for a ripple of r = 0.30 of the full load at 60 V. Solving for L:
L=\frac{V_o\,(1-D_{\min})}{r\,f_s\,I_o}\tag{3.1a}
L=\frac{12\ \mathrm{V}\cdot(1-0.200)}{0.30\cdot350\ \mathrm{kHz}\cdot20\ \mathrm{A}}=4.571\ \mu\mathrm{H}\tag{3.1b}
So our inductor is 4.571 µH (ours). This is an ideal minimum: it carries no allowance for tolerance or for the drop of inductance with current. The ripple ratio is a full-load specification: at a 2 A load the same ripple is three times the load current. Always state the ripple against full load.

title: 3. The inductor
section: 3.2 Peak and RMS current, with the right measure
text:
3.2 Peak and RMS current, with the right measure
We now take TI’s 4.7 µH and evaluate it at the worst case, 60 V:
\Delta I_L=\frac{V_o\,(1-D_{\min})}{L\,f_s}\tag{3.2a}
\Delta I_L=\frac{12\ \mathrm{V}\cdot0.800}{4.7\ \mu\mathrm{H}\cdot350\ \mathrm{kHz}}=5.836\ \mathrm{A}\tag{3.2b}
I_{\mathrm{pk}}=I_o+\frac{\Delta I_L}{2},\qquad I_{L,\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{I_o^2+\frac{\Delta I_L^2}{12}}\tag{3.3a}
I_{\mathrm{pk}}=20+\frac{5.836}{2}=22.92\ \mathrm{A},\qquad I_{L,\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{20^2+\frac{5.836^2}{12}}=20.07\ \mathrm{A}\tag{3.3b}
That is a ripple of 5.836 A and a peak of 22.92 A (ours, TI’s part). Which current measure enters a loss depends on the element, as the recap derives (§6.1, §6.2):

Never use the mean current for a resistive loss. It is the most common error in loss estimates.
Same mean, very different RMS. A narrow pulse carries a much larger RMS value than a DC current with the same mean. Take a 1 A mean current as 10 A pulses for 10 % of the period. Its RMS value is 10\ \mathrm{A}\cdot\sqrt{0.1} = 3.16 A, so a resistor in its path dissipates ten times more than with 1 A DC. A constant-drop element dissipates the same in both cases, because it sees only the mean. For pulsed currents a constant-drop device can therefore have less loss than a resistive one with the same drop at the mean current.
Two rules from the recap (§5.1–5.2) give every current of the stage without new integrals. Compressing a waveform into the fraction D of the period, with zero elsewhere, multiplies its mean by D and its RMS value by \sqrt{D}. title: 3. The inductor
section: 3.3 Checks against the real part
text:
3.3 Checks against the real part

Saturation. Würth specifies a 10 % drop of inductance at 20.9 A (reverse-engineering-checks.json, datasheet). Our 22.92 A peak at 60 V and full load lies past that point, so the strict rule “peak below the saturation current” fails: No! The metal-composite core loses inductance gradually. The cost is therefore a slightly larger ripple than (3.2b), not a collapse. TI’s schematic notes “~24 A Ipk” for this inductor, close to our 22.92 A.
Current limit. TI sets the peak current limit at 35 A (TIDMDL2 note: 60 mV across the 1.714 mΩ shunt). That leaves headroom for the load step, but in an overload the inductor sees 35 A, far past 20.9 A. Always check the inductor at the current limit, not only at full load.
Heating. The BOM lists the part as a 17 A, 3.85 mΩ inductor (TIDMDL6). At 20.07 A RMS it runs above that rating. TI measured 95 °C on the inductor at 20 A with a heat sink fitted (TIDT427A §2.3.2).
Slew rate. A larger L lowers the ripple but also the current slew rate the controller can command, (V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o)/L, which limits the load-step response (§7.3).
Tolerance. Würth specifies the inductance at ±20 %. At −20 %, 3.76 µH, the ripple at 60 V grows to 7.29 A and the peak to 23.65 A (ours). Across parts, DC bias and temperature the spread can reach 20–50 %. Check the design at the low end of the inductance, and use a sensitivity study (T4) for the other parameters.

Hard and soft saturation. The inductance is L = \mu_0\mu_r N^2 A_e/l_e, with N turns, core area A_e and magnetic path length l_e. A ferrite core has \mu_r of about 3000–5000. When it saturates, \mu_r falls towards 1 within a small increase of current. The inductance collapses, the current slope v_L/L rises steeply, and the current runs away within a few cycles until the current limit acts or the part overheats. With a gapped ferrite core, therefore, keep the peak below the saturation current, with margin.
A metal-composite core, like TI’s, has a distributed gap. Its inductance falls gradually, so a peak slightly past the 10 % point costs ripple, not a collapse. Saturation usually occurs in transients, not in steady state: at start-up, in a short circuit or after a fast duty step, when the volt-seconds do not balance yet. T3 simulates this case.
TI chose, TI measured. TI chose a 4.7 µH Würth 74439370047 (WE-XHMI, shielded metal composite). Our ripple ratio of 0.30 at 60 V asks for 4.571 µH. TI’s 4.7 µH is a standard value just above it. The ripple at 60 V, 5.836 A, is therefore slightly below our target.
TI did not measure the inductor current. §9 checks the ripple it causes at the output and the input. From here on the lesson continues with TI’s 4.7 µH.

text:
3.4 What if we allow 10% or 100% current ripple?
Our 30% target is a design choice. To see its consequences, compare two extremes. Here ripple means peak-to-peak inductor current divided by the 20 A full-load current. It is not duty ratio. Keep 60 V input, 12 V output and 350 kHz fixed. Use the ideal CCM equations of §3.1–3.2.

Choose 10% when ripple-current stress matters. Peak current and capacitor RMS current are lower. The cost is ten times more inductance. At the same applied voltage, current changes ten times more slowly. Check the load-step response before accepting that cost.
Choose 100% when less inductance and faster current change justify the ripple. The capacitor carries ten times more RMS ripple current, and the inductor must handle a 30 A peak. This remains CCM at full load: the valley is still 10 A. It is not boundary conduction.
Less inductance does not by itself guarantee a smaller or more efficient part. Compare actual saturation curves, winding and core losses, capacitor losses and transient response. With diode emulation, reduced load can also move the high-ripple design into DCM sooner.
Is low ripple always more efficient? No. It depends on which loss dominates. Low ripple lowers the inductor core and AC losses and the output-capacitor RMS current. It barely changes the switch conduction loss, because I_{L,\mathrm{rms}} stays close to I_o (20.008 A against 20.817 A in the table). It also barely changes the input-capacitor stress. At 60 V that RMS current is 8.00 A at 10 % ripple and 8.41 A at 100 % ripple (ours), because the pulsed input current dominates it. In industry the final choice is usually cost, weighed against efficiency and volume.
Our decision. Keep 30% for the base design and continue with TI’s 4.7 µH. The 100% alternative requires relaxing that ripple target. The 10% alternative reduces ripple, but its larger inductance still needs a transient check. Neither alternative is a qualified replacement part.
Your choice. Suppose capacitor ripple-current capability is the limiting constraint. Which direction would you try first? Now suppose current rise is too slow during a load step. Explain what you would change and which earlier check you must repeat.
scripts/ripple_tradeoff.py writes data/ripple-tradeoff.json. It checks the table against independently integrated current ramps, including mean/RMS current, capacitor charge and ideal power balance.

title: 4. The output capacitor
text:
4.1 Charge balance
The capacitor has the dual property of the inductor. In periodic steady state the charge delivered to a capacitor equals the charge removed, so its mean current is zero (recap §7.2).
\int_0^{T_s}i_C(t)\,dt=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad I_L=I_o.
The output capacitor carries the ripple of the inductor current. It cannot supply a lasting DC deficit without its voltage drifting. Only the loop can correct that.

title: 6. The power stage: GaN half-bridge and dead time
section: 6.2 Which device switches at zero, and at which edge
text:
6.2 Which device switches at zero, and at which edge
Resonant converters were the first answer to switching loss. Today, soft switching does the same where possible: the circuit and its timing bring the voltage or the current to zero at the transition. Zero inductor current, zero device current and zero device voltage are different conditions.
ZCS means negligible current through the device at its switching event. ZVS means negligible voltage across it, usually at turn-on. Name the device and the edge before calling a transition soft.
At 48 V TI’s 4.7 µH ripples by 5.47 A (ours). The sign of the valley current decides the turn-on of the high side:
I_v=I_o-\frac{\Delta I_L}{2}<0\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad I_o<\frac{\Delta I_L}{2}\tag{6.2a}
I_o<\frac{5.47\ \mathrm{A}}{2}=2.74\ \mathrm{A}\quad(48\ \mathrm{V},\ 4.7\ \mu\mathrm{H})\tag{6.2b}








Edge
Valley positive (I_o > 2.74 A at 48 V)
Valley negative (forced PWM, light load)




High side off → low side on
the inductor current swings the node to ground. The low side turns on at zero voltage
the same


Low side off → high side on
the node stays low and the low side conducts in reverse for t_d. The high side turns on hard, charging the output capacitance and overlapping V_{\mathrm{in}} with the valley current
the reversed current lifts the node toward V_{\mathrm{in}} during t_d. The high side turns on at reduced voltage (partial ZVS)



TI’s board runs forced PWM: the low side stays on through the valley even when the current reverses. Below 2.74 A at 48 V the valley goes negative and the high side gains partial ZVS. Above it, every turn-on is hard and pays the output-charge and overlap losses of §8.
The ZVS is only partial, because charge and time must both suffice. Under a constant-current approximation the node must swing through the switch output charge within the dead time:
t_{\mathrm{comm}}\simeq\frac{Q_{\mathrm{oss}}}{|I_v|}\leq t_d\quad\Rightarrow\quad|I_v|\geq\frac{Q_{\mathrm{oss}}}{t_d}\tag{6.3a}
|I_v|\geq\frac{55\ \mathrm{nC}}{20\ \mathrm{ns}}=2.75\ \mathrm{A}\tag{6.3b}
The valley never quite reaches −2.75 A (at no load −2.74 A), and the 55 nC is the total node charge at 50 V. Across the useful load range the node does not finish its swing within 20 ns. Forced PWM therefore buys partial ZVS at light load, not full ZVS.
Our loss model in §8 uses an energy condition without this time limit, so it treats the light-load turn-on as softer than it is. Never call a transition ZVS before checking current direction, charge and time. A published buck example optimizes exactly this negative current: Tang et al., Optimization of Minimum Negative Current BCM Synchronous Buck Converter.
TI chose, TI measured. TI chose the LMG2100R044 and the LM5148 with its adaptive dead time t_{\mathrm{DEAD}}, 20 ns typical (SNVSC01 §7.5). TI does not publish the dead time measured on the board. We keep forced PWM and 20 ns to reproduce TI’s measured design. The negative light-load current helps commutation but costs circulating-current loss. Diode emulation avoids the reversal, but it changes the mode and the response (§10.2). Neither choice guarantees ZVS.

title: 7. Closing the loop
text:
7.1 The LM5148 loop with TI’s parts
The LM5148 runs peak current mode. Each cycle it compares the sensed inductor current with the error-amplifier output and ends the on-time when they meet. The controller senses the current across R7 ∥ R10 = 1.714 mΩ and amplifies it by G_{CS} = 10 (SNVSC01). An internal slope ramp keeps the current loop stable at any duty.
The board uses the fixed 12 V mode, so the feedback gain is V_{\mathrm{REF}}/V_o = 0.8 V/12 V with no external divider. The compensation is type II on EXTCOMP: R23 = 6.8 kΩ in series with C57 = 6.8 nF, and C56 = 220 pF in parallel (TI parts, TIDMDL2). An amplifier of g_m = 1.2 mS (SNVSC01) drives it.
In current mode the inductor behaves as a controlled current source at low frequency. The power stage then shows one pole, formed by the load and the output bank, and the ESR zero of §4.4. It also shows a double pole at f_s/2, which the slope ramp damps.
With our ramp of 84 mV/µs (ours, derived from SNVSC01 Eq. 9), the ramp ratio is m_c = 1.64. That double pole then has Q = 0.436 and is well damped. We use Ridley’s current-mode model with TI’s compensation, untuned (ti-pmp31349/scripts/loop_design.py).
|T(j2\pi f_c)|=1,\qquad \varphi_m=180^\circ+\angle T(j2\pi f_c)\tag{7.1a}
f_c=21.8\ \mathrm{kHz},\qquad \varphi_m=100.8^\circ\qquad(48\ \mathrm{V},\ 20\ \mathrm{A})\tag{7.1b}
At 48 V and 20 A our model crosses at 21.8 kHz with 100.8° of phase margin (ours) and 13.7 dB of gain margin.

title: 7. Closing the loop
section: 7.3 The load step, and the price of a lower crossover
text:
7.3 The load step, and the price of a lower crossover



The averaged model drops 233 mV on the 10 → 20 A step, TI measured −276 mV, both inside our 360 mV limit.


On the 10 → 20 A step at 48 V the averaged model drops 233 mV (ours) and recovers within about 90 µs. TI measured −276 mV (TIDT427A fig. 3-7, scope minimum including switching ripple and noise). Both sit inside our 360 mV. The model is optimistic because it crosses higher than the board.
Our 35 kHz target sized the bank at 126.3 µF with (4.2a). TI crossed at ≈15.3 kHz, and its schematic notes “fcc ~15 kHz” as the design intent. At that crossover the same estimate asks for 290 µF. Our 126.3 µF would drop ≈825 mV and fail the 360 mV limit. TI’s 340 µF gives ≈307 mV by the same estimate.
TI pairs a lower crossover with more capacitance. Our 126.3 µF holds only if the loop really reaches 35 kHz. With the type II network R23, C57, C56, TI measured about 15 kHz crossover at every input voltage. The phase margin was 67–73° and the gain margin 17–19 dB. We keep TI’s compensation with its larger bank. A smaller bank or a higher crossover is a new design target: redesign the compensation and verify the load step again.

section: 8.2 The losses change the duty
text:
8.2 The losses change the duty
Replace each switch and winding by its resistance. Replace the input filter by its resistance r_{\mathrm{in}} and the dead time by its drop. Keep the current in each output-side drop at I_o. Then apply volt-second balance again:
V_o=D\,(V_{\mathrm{in}}-I_{\mathrm{in}}\,r_{\mathrm{in}})-I_o\left[r_L+r_s+D\,R_{HS}+(1-D)\,R_{LS}\right]-2\,t_d\,f_s\,V_{SD}
Here I_{\mathrm{in}}\,r_{\mathrm{in}} is the drop of the mean input current across the input filter, so the switch node sees slightly less than V_{\mathrm{in}}. With TI’s parts at 48 V and 20 A, this equation asks for D = 0.2565 against the ideal 0.250 (ours, datasheet values only, loss-estimate-checks.json). The controller adds duty to cover the drops.
This is a CCM average model. If its valley goes below zero with diode emulation, or it predicts a negative output, its assumptions have failed. Its result is then not a prediction (§10.2).

8.3 The estimate against TI’s measurement



Our datasheet estimate is optimistic everywhere, by 2.65 pp rms, and most at light load where the fixed losses dominate.


TI’s data have 147 rows, three of them at 0 A. Against the 144 measured points with nonzero load, the datasheet estimate errs by 2.65 pp (percentage points) rms (ours vs TI). It is optimistic everywhere, and most at light load, by up to 14.2 pp at 60 V and 0.5 A, where the fixed losses dominate.
Our curves have a kink between 2 A and 2.5 A at 48 V and 60 V, and between 1.5 A and 2 A at 30 V. There the model’s high-side turn-on becomes hard (§6.2).

title: 8. Losses, efficiency and temperature
section: 8.5 Junction temperature
text:
8.5 Junction temperature
T_j=T_a+P_{\mathrm{GaN}}\,R_{\theta JA}\tag{8.2a}
T_j=25\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}+1.58\ \mathrm{W}\cdot29\ \mathrm{K/W}=70.8\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\qquad(48\ \mathrm{V},\ 10\ \mathrm{A})\tag{8.2b}
R_{\theta JA} = 29 K/W is the datasheet value on a JEDEC board (SNOSDF9B Table 5.4). The GaN loss of 1.58 W is our datasheet estimate. TI measured 85 °C at the same operating point, without heat sink (TIDT427A §2.3.1, fig. 2-3). That is the thermal-camera hot spot on the board bottom under the GaN IC. It is a PCB surface temperature, not T_j, and TI gives no ambient temperature.
The reading is therefore a lower bound on T_j. Our junction estimate lies 14 K below a surface that cannot be hotter than the junction. No! Our estimate is optimistic three times over. The JEDEC R_{\theta JA} is not this board, the 25 °C ambient is our assumption, and the datasheet losses are low (§8.3). Always compare like with like: a thermal-camera reading is a surface temperature.
Other TI temperatures. At 10 A without a heat sink, the GaN thermal-pad vias reached 81 °C and the inductor 76 °C. At 20 A with a heat sink, TI measured 95 °C on the inductor, 92 °C on the vias and 76 °C on the heat sink (TIDT427A §2.3).
What would we improve first? At full load, investigate inductor DCR and low-side conduction, two of the largest datasheet loss terms. A lower-resistance candidate may help, but its magnetic, switching and thermal costs must also pass. At light load, get better core-loss evidence first. The fit shows that a loss is missing. It does not show which replacement part reduces it. Let the intended operating range decide which investigation comes first.

title: 9. Proof by simulation
text:
9.1 Python waveform checks against TI’s scope captures
ti-pmp31349/scripts/ripple_checks.py solves the operating point TI captured: 48 V to 12 V at 20 A, at the measured 344.9 kHz. It uses TI’s parts and the losses calibrated on TI’s measurement (§8.4). The model gives D = 0.2565, an on-time of 0.744 µs and \Delta I_L = 5.64 A (ours, calibrated to TI). It then compares the ripple equations of §4 and §5 with TI’s scope captures (ripple-checks.json):
The ideal-capacitor formula misses the output ripple by almost a factor of ten. On a mixed bank the ceramic branch carries most of the ripple current, and the polymer ESR adds the triangular part. The branch impedances, not the total capacitance, therefore set the ripple.
Never size a mixed bank’s ripple with the ideal-capacitor formula alone. At the input the measurement implies ≈8.8 µF effective. Our DC-bias estimate of 10.5 µF is therefore high, and the input ripple misses our 1.0 V target (§5).
The other two proofs are already on the page: the efficiency curve against TI’s measured points (§8.3) and the averaged load step against TI’s capture (§7.3).

title: 10. What if? Four variations of the finished design
text:
10.1 Critical (boundary) conduction
The base design runs in continuous conduction (CCM, heavy mode on the slides): the inductor current stays above zero through the cycle,
I_{L,\min}=I_o-\frac{\Delta I_L}{2}>0,\qquad K=\frac{2\,L\,f_s}{R}>K_{\mathrm{crit}}=1-D,
with R = V_o/I_o the load at the operating point. At the boundary I_o = \Delta I_L/2, which for TI’s 4.7 µH at 48 V is the 2.74 A of §6.2. The duty balances the volt-seconds, while the load sets the mean current. Each variation below changes one thing and states what changes in the numbers, the waveforms and the parts (variation-checks.json).
Hold the current triangle so that it just touches zero each cycle. Its peak is then twice the load, and the frequency or the inductance follows:
I_{\mathrm{pk}}=2\,I_o,\qquad f_s=\frac{V_o\,(1-V_o/V_{\mathrm{in}})}{2\,L\,I_o},\qquad L=\frac{V_o\,(1-V_o/V_{\mathrm{in}})}{2\,f_s\,I_o}\tag{10.1a}
I_{\mathrm{pk}}=40\ \mathrm{A},\qquad f_s=\frac{12\cdot0.750}{2\cdot4.7\ \mu\mathrm{H}\cdot20}=47.87\ \mathrm{kHz},\qquad L=\frac{12\cdot0.750}{2\cdot350\ \mathrm{kHz}\cdot20}=0.643\ \mu\mathrm{H}\tag{10.1b}
Keeping TI’s 4.7 µH means running at 47.87 kHz (ours). The 40 A peak then lies far above the 20.9 A at which that inductor has lost 10 % of its inductance. Keeping 350 kHz needs a different 0.643 µH inductor rated for 40 A.
Either way the RMS current rises to 2/√3 of the load, and the high side now turns off at twice the load current. Critical conduction gives a high-side turn-on at zero inductor current, so the turn-on overlap loss disappears. The output charge is still hard-switched unless the current goes slightly negative (§6.2).
Critical conduction does not make the switching loss zero. Only the turn-on overlap disappears. The turn-off at 2I_o and the output charge remain. Appendix D.9 shows how to read both edge energies from a datasheet.
Critical conduction does not mean a fixed frequency. At fixed V_{\mathrm{in}}, V_o and L, (10.1a) makes f_s inversely proportional to I_o. A controller that stays on the boundary detects zero current and starts the next pulse there. Its frequency therefore moves with load and input: at half the load, twice the frequency.
Once a deliberate negative valley is added for ZVS, recalculate the current area: I_o = I_{\mathrm{pk}}/2 holds only for the zero-valley triangle.
When would we choose the boundary? Keep CCM for the stated board. Boundary operation at 20 A needs a 40 A peak, above its 35 A current limit. It also changes the magnetic and RMS-current requirements.
Boundary control remains a redesign option when reduced turn-on overlap justifies those costs. It needs suitable parts, protection and a controller that accommodates the frequency range. Changing the conduction mode alone is not enough.

title: 10. What if? Four variations of the finished design
section: 10.2 Discontinuous conduction
text:
10.2 Discontinuous conduction
With diode emulation the controller turns the low side off when the current reaches zero, instead of letting it reverse as forced PWM does. Below the boundary the current then rests at zero until the next pulse (DCM, light mode on the slides). The cycle has three intervals: high side on (D), low side on (D_2), and both off.
Which mode at 48 V and 2 A? The CCM candidate would have a valley of 2 A − 2.74 A, below zero. With diode emulation that candidate is invalid, and the converter is in DCM. With TI’s forced PWM it is valid. The negative valley then circulates current that costs conduction loss but gives the partial ZVS of §6.2.
For DCM, with M = V_o/V_{\mathrm{in}} and the current triangle supplying the load:
K=\frac{2\,L\,f_s}{R},\qquad D=M\sqrt{\frac{K}{1-M}},\qquad D_2=D\,\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o}{V_o},\qquad I_{\mathrm{pk}}=\frac{(V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o)\,D}{L\,f_s}\tag{10.2a}
K=\frac{2\cdot4.7\ \mu\mathrm{H}\cdot350\ \mathrm{kHz}}{6\ \Omega}=0.548<0.750,\qquad D=0.250\sqrt{\frac{0.548}{0.750}}=0.2138,\qquad D_2=0.6413,\qquad I_{\mathrm{pk}}=4.678\ \mathrm{A}\tag{10.2b}
Always check D + D_2 < 1: here 0.855, so the zero interval exists and the DCM model applies. The triangle area checks the load: I_{\mathrm{pk}}/2\cdot(D + D_2) = 2.0 A. Substituting K = 1-D recovers M = D, so the two models meet at the boundary.
Why M no longer equals D. The third interval puts zero volts across L, and the length of the low-side interval depends on V_o. The duty falls from the CCM 0.250 to 0.2138. The conversion ratio for a given duty now depends on the load, and the control-to-output transfer function changes.
When DCM is chosen on purpose. Each DCM pulse starts from zero current, so it stores the same energy L\,I_{\mathrm{pk}}^2/2, independent of the previous cycle. The converter then delivers defined packets of charge or energy. Capacitor chargers and pulsed supplies for X-ray tubes and magnetrons use this property. The output then behaves more like a current source: for a given duty, V_o depends on the load. With a pulsating load, such as a processor, V_o moves unless the loop corrects the duty.
TI’s board runs forced PWM and stays in CCM instead. With KM^2 = D^2(1-M) the DCM gain is M = 2/(1+\sqrt{1+4K/D^2}). Appendix E gives the full derivation and a worked DCM case.
At light load. Keep forced PWM to reproduce the TI board, and accept its circulating-current cost. If light-load loss is the priority, investigate diode emulation. Compare its losses and control in DCM before choosing. The CCM calculation cannot decide the DCM case.

Halving or doubling C moves the corner by √2 but not the peak: without ESR and DCR the load alone, 0.6 Ω, damps the filter.


Without ESR and DCR, L and C cancel at f_0 and the peak |Z_{\mathrm{out}}| equals the load, R = 0.6 Ω at full load, for every C. It grows as the load gets lighter and R rises. Then only ESR, DCR and the control loop limit it.
Z_0 is what more capacitance buys: the open-loop deviation for a load step is about \Delta I\cdot Z_0, which the loop then reduces by the factor 1 + T (Part II). The ideal model here ignores ESR, ESL and DCR. With TI’s polymer, the ESR of §4.4 damps the peak further.

title: 11. What to retain
text:
Write the specification first, and label every limit as given (TI) or chosen (ours). A missing limit is a design decision, not a free parameter.
Worst cases sit at the ends of the range. The inductor ripple peaks at the maximum input. The input-capacitor RMS current peaks at the duty nearest 0.5, here the minimum input.
The load step, not the ripple, sizes the output bank. Then check the ESR against |Z_C| at crossover: a failed check moves the crossover or the bank. It does not go away.
Check real parts under real conditions: ceramics under DC bias, the inductor at its peak and at the current limit, the input bank against measured ripple.
The sign of the valley current and the dead time decide each switching edge. Name the device and the edge, and check charge and time, before calling anything ZVS.
A model gap points to an input first. The max-rated polymer ESR explains the loop gap. The impedance-curve core loss explains most of the loss gap.
Estimate from datasheets, then calibrate against measurement. The fit says what we missed, never what we predicted.

title: 12. Training: problem-driven exercises
text:
T1 — Ripple shape: rounded, triangular or rectangular?
Start each exercise by making a prediction. Sketch the current path or waveform before calculating. Then choose a model and solve the problem. Compare the alternatives and explain which one you would use.
Try the problem before reading its solution. For every exercise, state your choice, one benefit and one cost. Compare a credible alternative and name the condition or measurement that would change your choice. Keep the operating point and requirements clear.
Operating points. T4 works on PMP31349 itself, with the calibrated model of §8.4. The others need a mechanism that the finished GaN design hides: a diode buck, a deliberately saturating core, an authored filter or an authored loop. They use the simpler teaching model of Appendix E, a diode buck from 30–48 V to 24 V and 10 A at 100 kHz with 60 µH and 100 µF, or a stated variant of it.
Every Problem states its own operating point; never carry a number from one operating point to another.
E2–E5 examine the same LC network through four questions. How does it filter voltage (E2)? What output impedance does the load see (E3)? Where are its poles (E4)? What changes when feedback is added (E5)?
The filter equations impose an ideal switch-node voltage and place R across C. They require continuous conduction or a synchronous stage that permits current reversal. A diode buck in DCM needs Appendix E’s three-interval model. The feedback examples describe small changes about a positive-current CCM equilibrium. Keep the load resistance R separate from the series resistance r.
The exercises go beyond the live route. Session 3 works one or two of them in class; the rest are assigned as reading.

title: 12. Training: problem-driven exercises
text:
Problem
The scope shows the output ripple of a buck. On one board it is rounded, almost sinusoidal; on a second it is a triangle; on a third it carries a step at every switching edge. If the waveform becomes more angular, which part of the output capacitor is responsible, and how would you prove it? Start with the simplest current waveform and find the contribution of each parasitic on its own.
Operating point. A prescribed capacitor current: the 2 A peak-to-peak, zero-mean triangle of the teaching model at 48 V input and 100 kHz, into C = 100 µF with series resistance r_C (ESR) and series inductance l_C (ESL). The current is imposed; the converter around it is not solved.


Why we do it
The shape of the ripple is the first clue the scope gives about which impedance dominates. Read it right and you know whether to add capacitance, lower the ESR or shorten the current loop. Read it wrong and you buy the wrong part. The same ESR also moves the loop (§4.4, §7.2), so a misread parasitic costs twice.


What matters
Model the output-capacitor branch as an ideal capacitance C with series r_C and l_C. For branch current i_C, with a consistent passive voltage reference:
v_{\mathrm{terminal}}=v_C+r_Ci_C+l_C\frac{di_C}{dt},\qquad \frac{dv_C}{dt}=\frac{i_C}{C}.

The three terms do three different operations on the same current: integrate, multiply, differentiate.
Their extremes need not occur at the same instant. Adding peak-to-peak magnitudes gives a bound, not the ripple.
A measured edge spike can also contain ringing, coupling and probe-loop pickup, so the shape alone does not uniquely identify a component.



Where it appears in practice

PMP31349’s output bank (§4.4). The polymer ESR sets the bank impedance at the loop crossover, while the ceramics carry most of the ripple current near f_s. TI’s scope capture of the output ripple (§9.1) is the measured shape to read.
Point-of-load (POL) regulators for processors and FPGAs. An all-ceramic bank has little ESR, so the ESL of the parts, pads and vias shows up as steps at the edges.
Choosing between polymer, electrolytic and ceramic banks. The shape says which term to buy down first.



Possible solutions
Solution A — superpose the three terms in the time domain. For the ideal CCM buck with approximately constant load current, i_C is a continuous, zero-mean triangle. Its three voltage contributions have different shapes:








Term
Operation on the triangular current
Resulting shape




Ideal capacitance
Integrate current
Continuous, piecewise parabolic; rounded and often approximately sinusoidal in appearance


ESR
Multiply current by r_C
Continuous triangular component


ESL
Multiply current slope by l_C
Piecewise constant component, with steps where the current slope changes



Increasing the ESR alone therefore moves this ordinary buck’s output ripple toward a triangle; it does not generate a square wave. A rectangular contribution points to a different current waveform or to the derivative term. E1 asks which inductor model provides exactly such an additional current component.
Prescribe the 2 A peak-to-peak triangle at 100 kHz into C = 100 µF and vary only the capacitor parameters, so the comparison isolates their voltage contributions:








ESR, with ESL = 0
ESR-only ripple magnitude
Total computed terminal ripple
