10 mΩ
20 mV peak-to-peak
29.0 mV peak-to-peak


100 mΩ
200 mV peak-to-peak
200.0 mV peak-to-peak



Why 25 mV + 20 mV does not equal 45 mV here: the capacitive and ESR extremes occur at different instants. Adding their peak-to-peak magnitudes is a conservative bound; summing their instantaneous waveforms gives the actual result. At high ESR, the triangle dominates.
The current slopes of this symmetric triangle are ±0.4 A/µs. An illustrative 50 nH of effective series inductance adds ±20 mV, a 40 mV peak-to-peak rectangular contribution. This ESL value is an intentionally visible capacitor-plus-connection example, not a selected capacitor’s specification.



The same prescribed capacitor current with separate ESR and ESL sweeps, showing rounded, triangular and rectangular voltage contributions.


Solution B — read the branch impedance against frequency. In a simple model the ESR adds a zero at 1/(2\pi r_C C) to the capacitor branch; the ESL adds a series resonance above it. Whichever term dominates |Z| at f_s and its first harmonics sets the shape: the capacitive slope gives the rounded wave, the flat ESR shelf the triangle, the inductive rise the steps.
This is the view §4.4 uses for TI’s bank, and it shows at once that the same ESR zero also changes the loop phase (§7.2).
Solution C — change one thing, in the model or on the bench. Set the ESL to zero and sweep the ESR. Then restore a fixed ESR and vary only the ESL. On hardware, swap one capacitor type at a time and probe at the capacitor terminals with the shortest ground connection available.
Analog Devices’ Input and Output Noise in Buck Converters Explained separates the capacitive, ESR and high-frequency parasitic contributions this way.


Pros and cons








Solution
Pros
Cons




A. Time-domain superposition
Exact for a prescribed current; shows the instantaneous shape and why peak magnitudes do not add
Needs the current waveform; does not solve how a changed component alters the converter’s own current


B. Impedance against frequency
Fast; ranks the terms at f_s; links ripple and loop through the same ESR zero
Loses the time shape and the phase between the terms; one frequency hides the harmonics


C. Change one thing
Separates cause from effect; works on real hardware
Each run answers one question; the probe adds its own loop, ringing and pickup





Conclusion
Use time-domain superposition first to explain the shape. It separates capacitance, ESR and ESL with little calculation, but assumes a prescribed capacitor current. Use the impedance view when the frequency range matters, and a switching model when that current assumption fails.
For the 100 mΩ case, investigate ESR before buying more capacitance: its triangular contribution dominates. For an edge step, first repeat the measurement with a short probe return. Then change one suspected element. A terminal-current jump is another explanation, examined in E1.
Our next action follows the observed shape. We do not select a replacement capacitor until a change-one-thing check supports the cause.

title: 12. Training: problem-driven exercises
section: T2 — Is a CCM buck a current source?
text:
T2 — Is a CCM buck a current source?

Problem
An LED string or a battery needs a set mean current, not a set voltage. A designer proposes the teaching-model buck at a fixed duty and argues that its inductor already makes the current smooth. Does a fixed-duty CCM buck regulate current? If not, how would you deliver a commanded mean current, and what does each way cost?
Operating point. Teaching model, diode buck: V_{\mathrm{in}} = 48 V, L = 60 µH, f_s = 100 kHz. Fixed duty D = 0.5 into a 2.4 Ω or 4.8 Ω resistor, or into a stiff voltage such as an LED string or a battery. For the peak-controlled routes: a commanded peak of 1 A, with the load voltage between 12 V and 36 V.


Why we do it
Smooth current and regulated current are different requirements. An inductor makes current continuous on a short timescale; a current source must hold its mean delivered current close to a setpoint as the load voltage changes. Mixing up the two is a common design error, and it hides until the load voltage moves.


What matters
The duty sets a voltage. At fixed duty, the ideal CCM steady-state relations are:
V_o=DV_{\mathrm{in}},\qquad I_o=\frac{DV_{\mathrm{in}}}{R}.
At D = 0.5 a 2.4 Ω load takes 10 A and a 4.8 Ω load takes 5 A, and both stay in CCM with 60 µH. The duty sets a voltage, not a current independent of the load.
A stiff load has no preferred current. A battery or an LED string imposes a fairly stiff voltage instead of behaving as a resistor. For the ideal averaged inductor:
L\frac{dI_L}{dt}=DV_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o.
If the imposed output voltage equals DV_{\mathrm{in}} exactly, any initial mean current is an equilibrium of this simplified model: there is no preferred setpoint. A small mismatch makes the current drift instead of restoring it. At 48 V, an absolute duty error of 0.01 gives a 0.48 V average error across L, an initial slew of 8 A/ms with 60 µH, before load dynamics or resistance restore balance.
Compliance. The requested current must lie within the available output-voltage range and the component ratings. An open load cannot absorb a programmed current, so the controller needs a voltage ceiling. These limits define the compliance range.


Where it appears in practice

LED drivers. The forward voltage of a string is stiff and moves with temperature, so the driver regulates current; many use peak or boundary control.
Battery chargers in constant-current, then constant-voltage operation. TI’s CC/CV buck discussion gives an implemented current-feedback example.
PMP31349 itself. The LM5148 runs peak current mode (§7.1) as an inner loop under the voltage loop. Its peak control shapes the power stage; it does not hold the mean current at a setpoint.
Laser-diode, plating and electrolyser supplies, where the process is set by current, not by voltage.



Possible solutions
Solution A — let the passive stage do it: more inductance, or the series resistance. Double L while keeping V_{\mathrm{in}}, D and R fixed in ideal CCM: the ripple halves, and the settled mean current remains DV_{\mathrm{in}}/R. Inductance changes ripple and dynamics, not the ideal fixed-duty DC current; a larger L only slows the drift above. With series resistance and a diode drop, an approximate CCM relation is:
I_o\simeq\frac{DV_{\mathrm{in}}-(1-D)V_f-V_o}{r_L+Dr_Q}.
The resistance does set a current, but poorly. At fixed D, a 0.2 V change of the imposed output voltage moves the current by about 1 A if the effective series resistance is 0.2 Ω. Lower resistance improves efficiency and makes this open-loop current sensitivity larger, and temperature moves the winding resistance, the MOSFET resistance and the diode drop.
The right-hand plot of the DCM example in Appendix E shows these local slopes; negative-current extrapolations need a bidirectional stage and lie outside the diode-buck CCM domain.
Appendix E.8 gives a complete fixed-duty comparison. It changes inductance through CCM, the zero-current boundary and DCM, with independent charge and power checks. Appendix E.9 applies this reasoning to an inverter’s neutral leg and compares alternative control approaches.
Solution B — an average-current loop in CCM. Sense the current, compare it with a reference and adjust the duty so that the mean current error is driven toward zero. A current-regulated CCM buck is entirely practical; a battery charger or LED driver uses this principle within its voltage and duty limits.
The difficulty of Solution A concerns operation with a fixed duty or with voltage regulation only, not a fundamental inability of CCM to act as a controlled current source. Peak control is not automatically average-current regulation. In CCM, approximately I_o = I_{\mathrm{pk}} - \Delta I_L/2.
If the ripple changes with the input or output voltage, a constant peak limit lets the mean current move. Average-current accuracy needs the appropriate sensing and loop objective; a peak-current ceiling by itself is a protection limit. A current-mode controller inside a voltage regulator can use peak current to regulate its power stage while the outer loop still regulates voltage.
Solution C — peak control in boundary mode. In ideal boundary operation with peak-current control, each pulse starts at zero, rises to the commanded peak and returns to zero just as the next pulse begins. The current has no inherited valley to determine, and its area gives:
I_o=\frac{1}{T_s}\frac{I_{\mathrm{pk}}(t_{\mathrm{on}}+t_d)}{2}=\frac{I_{\mathrm{pk}}}{2}.
This assumes approximately constant voltages during a cycle, linear ramps, no extra zero-current interval and no negative-current commutation area. The rising and falling ramps need not last equally long. For a buck with 0 < V_o < V_{\mathrm{in}}:
t_{\mathrm{on}}=\frac{LI_{\mathrm{pk}}}{V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o},\qquad t_d=\frac{LI_{\mathrm{pk}}}{V_o},\qquad f_{\mathrm{BCM}}=\frac{1}{t_{\mathrm{on}}+t_d}.
With V_{\mathrm{in}} = 48 V, L = 60 µH and a commanded 1 A peak: at V_o = 24 V, t_{\mathrm{on}} = t_d = 2.5 µs, the switching frequency is 200 kHz and the mean current 0.5 A. If the imposed output voltage falls to 12 V, t_{\mathrm{on}} becomes 1.667 µs and t_d 5 µs; the frequency falls to 150 kHz, but the mean current stays 0.5 A.
At 36 V the ramp durations exchange and the mean current is again 0.5 A. A controlled 1 A peak delivers a 0.5 A mean, and the load decides the voltage: a 24 Ω resistor settles at 12 V, a 48 Ω resistor at 24 V.
An open circuit, or a load needing V_o \geq V_{\mathrm{in}}, lies outside this compliance range.
The current is not set by inductance alone. With fixed ON time, L and the applied voltage set the peak. With a fixed peak threshold, changing L mainly changes the time to reach that peak, and so the frequency. The control law is part of the current-source behaviour.
This is a useful current-regulation architecture: the controller sets a peak and detects the zero-current boundary, while the load determines the voltage required to accept that current. Sensor error, propagation delay, nonlinear inductance and additional commutation intervals introduce practical current error.
Solution D — pulse charge in DCM. In DCM the same current triangle is followed by a zero-current interval. Its occupied fraction of the period is:
\rho=\frac{t_{\mathrm{on}}+t_d}{T_s}=D+D_2<1.
The delivered charge per cycle and the mean current are:
Q_o=\frac{I_{\mathrm{pk}}}{2}(t_{\mathrm{on}}+t_d),\qquad I_o=f_sQ_o=\frac{I_{\mathrm{pk}}}{2}\rho.
Why the denominator matters: I_{\mathrm{pk}}/2 is the mean during the triangle, not over a full DCM period. At V_o = 24 V and a 1 A peak the triangle lasts 5 µs and delivers 2.5 µC. Repeated every 5 µs it gives boundary operation and 0.5 A; repeated every 10 µs it gives DCM, \rho = 0.5 and I_o = 0.25 A. The repetition rate sets the mean.
Peak control alone is not enough at a fixed DCM frequency. Keep the 1 A peak and 100 kHz repetition rate. At V_o = 12 V or 36 V, the triangle lasts 6.667 µs and gives 0.3333 A mean. At 24 V, the mean is 0.25 A. The DCM mean therefore still depends on V_o:
I_o=\frac{D^2}{2Lf_s}\left(\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}^2}{V_o}-V_{\mathrm{in}}\right).
At D = 0.15 this gives 0.135 A at 19.2 V and 0.060 A at 28.8 V, both in DCM. To hold the current, control the pulse area or the repetition rate, compensate for the conducting fraction, or close an average-current loop; feedforward can estimate the duty while feedback corrects losses and uncertainty.
Every such calculation needs a physically valid \rho < 1. This pulse-charge view explains why DCM and boundary operation can be especially convenient for current delivery: resetting the inductor current removes one inter-cycle initial-current uncertainty. It does not remove output-capacitor state, load compatibility or the need to define a controller.
DCM is not an ideal current source either, and the two-state CCM transfer functions of E2–E5 must not be carried unchanged into DCM or variable-frequency boundary operation.



Identical peak-controlled current triangles at boundary and DCM repetition rates, and their different mean-current dependence on imposed output voltage.




Pros and cons








Solution
Pros
Cons




A. Passive: more L, or the series resistance
No sensor and no controller
Sets no current: L only slows the drift; the resistance gives a poor, temperature-dependent setpoint and costs efficiency


B. Average-current loop, CCM
Accurate mean current at fixed frequency; low ripple, so low RMS current
Needs a current sensor and a compensated loop; a peak ceiling alone is not this loop


C. Peak control, boundary mode
Mean current I_{\mathrm{pk}}/2 independent of V_o in the ideal model; each pulse starts at zero, so commutation is favourable
Variable frequency (200 kHz to 150 kHz here); for a 0.5 A mean, 1 A peak and 0.5774 A RMS instead of about 0.5 A in low-ripple CCM, about one-third more winding I²R loss; sensor error, delay and nonlinear L add current error


D. Pulse charge, DCM
Every pulse starts at zero, which removes the inherited initial current
A fixed peak at fixed frequency does not hold the mean; shorter occupied fractions raise the RMS-to-mean ratio further; the CCM transfer functions of E2–E5 do not carry over



For the ideal triangles of C and D, the inductor RMS current is I_{\mathrm{pk}}\sqrt{\rho/3} against a mean of I_{\mathrm{pk}}\rho/2. Easier pulse-current control and favourable commutation have a conduction-loss cost.


Conclusion
A fixed-duty CCM buck does not set a preferred current. More inductance slows a current change but does not regulate its mean.
For accurate mean current at fixed frequency, choose the average-current loop. It needs sensing and compensation, but keeps ripple and RMS current low. A peak ceiling alone is not an equivalent regulator.
Boundary peak control is a valid alternative when variable frequency and higher RMS current are acceptable. Here it delivers half the peak current in the ideal model. Choose fixed-frequency DCM only with pulse-area or repetition-rate control, or feedback that corrects the mean.
For a charger requiring accurate current, keep the average-current loop as the design route. For a driver prioritising simple boundary operation, investigate the peak-controlled alternative. State the compliance range and current-error budget before selecting hardware.

title: 12. Training: problem-driven exercises
section: T3 — Saturation: is the peak current safe?
text:
T3 — Saturation: is the peak current safe?

Problem
An inductor passes the steady-state ripple and RMS checks, and the voltage loop is stable at every operating point. Can a load step or an input step still drive the inductor into saturation? If so, what would you add to keep the peak current safe, and what does it cost?
Operating point. Teaching model, a buck whose freewheeling path carries positive current only (diode emulation), regulated to 24 V at about 8 A, f_s = 100 kHz, C = 100 µF, winding resistance 50 mΩ. Disturbances: a load step from 3 Ω to 2 Ω at V_{\mathrm{in}} = 48 V, and an input step from 30 V to 48 V at R = 3 Ω.
Authored magnetic curve: 60 µH up to 14 A, falling linearly to 6 µH at 18 A, and 6 µH above that, with no hysteresis, thermal dependence or core loss. A real Isat rating normally describes a specified percentage inductance drop, rather than an abrupt universal failure current; use the manufacturer’s bias and temperature information.
The sampled voltage controller sees only the output voltage:
e_n=24-v_o(nT_s),\qquad d_n=\mathrm{clip}(x_n+K_pe_n,\ 0.02,\ 0.95),
x_{n+1}=x_n+K_iT_se_n,
with K_p = 0.03 duty/V and K_i = 100 duty/(V·s), one duty update per period, and the integrator frozen when it would push the duty further beyond a bound. This simple anti-windup acts at those bounds; it does not track the separate current-limit override. Its local linear sampled model has all poles inside the unit circle at the three nominal conditions, so local voltage-loop instability is not required to produce a current excursion.
This is an intentionally weakly damped teaching loop, not an optimised regulator or a model of a particular IC.


Why we do it
Voltage regulation commands energy delivery in response to the output error. By itself it imposes no instantaneous ceiling on the current in the inductor or the switch. The steady-state checks are the easy ones; the transient peak decides whether the part survives. This is a limitation of an unprotected voltage-only control path, not a rule that every voltage-mode regulator lacks protection.
A voltage-mode controller may include a separate fast current comparator, overload timer and shutdown logic; the PWM regulation architecture and its fault protections must be assessed separately.


What matters
Flux linkage accumulates over cycles. Do not impose the steady-state conversion ratio on every cycle:
\lambda_{n+1}-\lambda_n=\int_{nT_s}^{(n+1)T_s}v_L(t)\,dt,\qquad v_L=v_x-v_o-r_si_L.
For linear L this flux-linkage change is L times the current change. In periodic steady state the integral is zero. During a transient it can be positive for several consecutive periods, moving the current and the flux to a higher operating point. That is how the converter meets a new load; a nonzero cycle integral is not automatically a fault.

CCM does not require the current to return to zero, only to its previous-cycle value once periodic operation is re-established. The concern is whether the transient peak exceeds the magnetic and semiconductor limits before the controller restores balance. Saturation can also exist in an undesirable periodic waveform: zero net volt-seconds alone does not prove that the core stayed out of saturation within the cycle.
Load step: inductor current cannot jump, so the capacitor supplies the deficit and V_o falls. The controller lengthens the ON time to restore V_o and recharge C; the inductor must supply both the new load and the recharge current, so its transient peak can exceed the final load current plus half the ripple.
Input step: if V_{\mathrm{in}} rises before the duty falls, each existing ON pulse applies more voltage to L. As a frozen-state estimate, at 8 A and 24 V from 30 V with 50 mΩ, D ≈ 0.81333; raising the input to 48 V adds about 14.64 V to the cycle-average inductor voltage. At 100 kHz that is 146.4 µV·s per cycle, an initial 2.44 A rise per cycle with 60 µH, until V_o, current and duty respond.

Saturation steepens the ramp. For a nonlinear but memoryless magnetic characteristic, define the differential inductance:
L_{\mathrm{diff}}(i)=\frac{d\lambda}{di},\qquad \frac{di}{dt}=\frac{v_L}{L_{\mathrm{diff}}(i)}.
As the core approaches saturation, L_{\mathrm{diff}} falls, and the same 24 V across L rises at 0.4 A/µs with 60 µH but 4 A/µs with 6 µH. A controller still requesting ON time can therefore underestimate the peak severely if its design assumes constant L.
Do not use v = d[L(i)i]/dt with a datasheet differential-inductance curve as though L(i)i were the flux linkage: integrate the curve to obtain \lambda(i), and use \lambda as the magnetic state.



Authored differential-inductance and flux-linkage curves, showing the saturation knee and a peak-trip setting below it.




Where it appears in practice

PMP31349 (§3.3). TI sets the peak current limit at 35 A, while the Würth inductor has lost 10 % of its inductance at 20.9 A. In an overload the inductor runs far past that point: always check the inductor at the current limit, not only at full load.
Start-up into a large capacitive load, where the inrush current, not the load, sets the peak.
48 V battery buses and other supplies with line transients, where an input step is part of the specification.
Voltage-mode controllers with a separate fast current comparator: TI discusses such controllers in its voltage-mode/current-mode comparison.



Possible solutions
Each solution is compared with the same voltage controller and the same disturbances. Peaks and energy checks use a 2 ms simulation with the disturbance at 0.2 ms (scripts/saturation_transient_example.py):









Disturbance, starting at 24 V and approximately 8 A
Linear 60 µH, no current trip
Saturable L, no current trip
Saturable L, 13 A trip plus 200 ns delay




Load resistance 3 Ω → 2 Ω at V_{\mathrm{in}} = 48 V
16.30 A peak
18.49 A peak
13.083 A peak


Input 30 V → 48 V with R = 3 Ω
21.58 A peak
48.73 A peak
13.076 A peak



For the load step the final load current is about 12 A, below the 14 A knee, yet the unprotected transient crosses the knee into the 6 µH region. The input step is worse: the nonlinear curve more than doubles the peak that a constant-60-µH calculation predicts.
Solution A — a bigger core. Keep the controller and choose an inductor that stays linear past the largest transient peak: the linear column says above 21.58 A in this example, plus margin for tolerance and temperature. No new circuit is needed, and the loop sees the inductance it was designed for.
Solution B — a separate fast peak-current comparator. Keep the existing inductor and voltage loop. Add a comparator with a 13 A trip, below the saturation knee. Allow an illustrative 200 ns propagation delay. After a trip, hold the switch off for the rest of the period.
If current remains at or above the threshold at the next cycle start, skip that ON pulse. The simulated peaks are 13.083 A and 13.076 A. They exceed 13 A because current keeps rising during the comparator and gate-drive delay:
I_{\mathrm{pk}}\simeq I_{\mathrm{trip}}+\frac{v_{L,\mathrm{on}}}{L_{\mathrm{diff}}}\,t_{\mathrm{delay}}.
With about 24 V, 60 µH and 200 ns the extra rise is about 80 mA, consistent with the protected traces. If the comparator acted only after L_{\mathrm{diff}} had fallen to 6 µH, the same voltage and delay would add about 0.8 A. With zero delay the trip caps the current at 13 A, which makes the delay overshoot directly measurable.



Switched load-step and input-step responses using the same sampled voltage PI, comparing linear inductance, unprotected saturation and a separate peak-current trip.


The figure shows the first 550 µs after each event, a transient window, not a claim that every trace has settled. The output-voltage and delivered-duty panels show the price of limiting current: in the input step even the protected model reaches about 30.02 V at its output. Limiting the current below the knee does not by itself prevent an output overvoltage.
Solution C — shape the disturbance instead of clipping it. Input-voltage feedforward cuts the duty disturbance of a line step. Appropriate voltage compensation, soft start, anti-windup and enough transient energy storage reduce unnecessary excursions. Sustained overload may need longer OFF intervals, foldback, hiccup or shutdown. None of these sets a hard instantaneous ceiling.
Solution D — peak-current-mode control. Make the current comparator the PWM itself: every ON pulse ends when the sensed current reaches the command, and a clamp on the command is a cycle-by-cycle limit. This is how the LM5148 runs PMP31349 (§7.1). The sensing, blanking and timing constraints of B remain.


Pros and cons








Solution
Pros
Cons




A. Bigger core
No added circuit; the loop keeps its designed inductance
Size, weight and cost; sized for the largest transient, not the operating point; still no protection against a fault or a short


B. Separate peak comparator
Hard ceiling within one pulse, below the knee; works with any voltage loop
Overshoot from delay, sensing error, threshold tolerance and blanking; does not stop output overvoltage (30.02 V here) or establish safe average power or fault behaviour in sustained overload, especially when little output voltage is available to ramp current down


C. Feedforward, soft start, anti-windup, foldback
Smaller excursions and gentler start-up; foldback or hiccup bounds fault power
No instantaneous ceiling; depends on modelling the disturbance correctly


D. Peak-current-mode control
The limit is built into every cycle; the current loop also simplifies the voltage loop (§7.1)
Needs slope compensation and clean current sensing; the same delay overshoot as B; a peak limit is not an average-current limit (T2)





Conclusion
Keep the separate fast peak comparator for this transient problem. A stable voltage loop does not enforce the magnetic limit. The 13 A trip keeps the demonstrated peaks below the 14 A knee, while the delay explains why they exceed 13 A.
A larger core is an alternative when the required normal transient needs more current. It costs magnetic hardware and still needs an overload check. Better damping can reduce excursions, but does not impose a hard ceiling.
Retain the trip and improve the transient response if necessary. If it interrupts a required load step, reconsider the core and threshold together. Include sensing error, delay, tolerance and temperature before treating that threshold as a hardware setting.
The model predicts electrical stress, not component failure. A slower average-current limit can miss a peak inside one pulse.
Change one thing: replace the saturable element by constant 60 µH, then restore it and add only the peak trip. Finally set comparator delay to zero. Each comparison isolates one cause.
Coilcraft explains the link between saturation and increased current slope. Analog Devices’ AN-149 discusses voltage and current control and transient limiting.

title: 12. Training: problem-driven exercises
section: T4 — Which parameter is worth improving? Sensitivity of PMP31349
text:
T4 — Which parameter is worth improving? Sensitivity of PMP31349

Problem
A colleague has budget to improve one thing on PMP31349, to raise its efficiency and tighten its open-loop output: a lower-DCR inductor, a lower-resistance GaN stage, a faster switching edge, a larger inductance or a higher switching frequency. Which parameter matters most, and does the ranking still hold at light load? Rank the parameters at two operating points and say what your ranking depends on.
Operating point. PMP31349 at V_{\mathrm{in}} = 48 V and V_o = 12 V, f_s = 350 kHz (TI), at I_o = 20 A and at 5 A. The model is the calibrated loss model of §8.4: our datasheet parameters plus the terms fitted to TI’s measurement (ti-pmp31349/scripts/sensitivity.py, sensitivity-checks.json).
Each parameter is raised by 10 % on its own. Every number in T4 comes from that file; the base efficiencies are ours, calibrated to TI, and the sensitivities are results of our calibrated model, not measurements.


Why we do it
A sweep shows how a model changes across a range; a local sensitivity is the slope at one specific point. A ranking without its operating point ranks nothing: the part that wins at full load can lose at light load. And the money for a better part is spent once, while the converter runs at every point of its range.


What matters

State what is fixed before differentiating. Two views answer different questions. Open loop: V_{\mathrm{in}}, the duty D and the load current are held, and V_o moves. Regulated: the loop holds V_o = 12 V, the duty moves, and the cost shows as efficiency.
Know which terms are fitted. The overlap time, the core-loss factor, the output-charge factor and the resistance rise with load are fitted to TI’s measurement (§8.4). Their sensitivities say what the fit contains.

A local sensitivity is a tangent. The prediction for several small changes is
\Delta V_o\simeq\sum_p\frac{\partial V_o}{\partial p}\Delta p,
not a guarantee for a large change. Recompute the operating point when a change is large or crosses a mode boundary, such as the high side’s change to hard turn-on (§8.3) or the CCM boundary (§10).
Absolute or normalised. An absolute sensitivity has units, such as V/Ω. A normalised sensitivity compares fractional changes:
S_p^{V_o}=\frac{p}{V_o}\frac{\partial V_o}{\partial p},\qquad \frac{\Delta V_o}{V_o}\simeq S_p^{V_o}\frac{\Delta p}{p}.
Raising every parameter by 10 % is a normalised comparison. A specified change, such as “10 mΩ less”, needs the absolute slope. Normalisation misleads near a zero nominal value.


Where it appears in practice

Choosing between two inductors or two GaN stages for a 48 V to 12 V intermediate-bus or battery-bus converter such as PMP31349.
Cost-down reviews: which specification can be relaxed without losing efficiency where the product actually runs.
Tolerance and worst-case analysis: the open-loop output shift and the duty headroom over production spread and temperature.
Light-load efficiency claims in a datasheet, where the ranking differs from full load.



Possible solutions
Solution A — analytic derivatives of the averaged equation, open loop. Start from the loss-corrected volt-second balance of §8.2:
V_o=D\,(V_{\mathrm{in}}-I_{\mathrm{in}}\,r_{\mathrm{in}})-I_o\left[r_L+r_{sh}+D\,R_{HS}+(1-D)\,R_{LS}\right]-2\,t_d\,f_s\,V_{SD}
Here r_{sh} is the current shunt (r_s in §8.2; in T3 and E1 r_s is a winding resistance). Hold V_{\mathrm{in}}, I_{\mathrm{in}}, D and I_o and differentiate:
\frac{\partial V_o}{\partial r_L}=\frac{\partial V_o}{\partial r_{sh}}=-I_o,\qquad \frac{\partial V_o}{\partial R_{HS}}=-D\,I_o,\qquad \frac{\partial V_o}{\partial R_{LS}}=-(1-D)\,I_o,\qquad \frac{\partial V_o}{\partial r_{\mathrm{in}}}=-D\,I_{\mathrm{in}},\qquad \frac{\partial V_o}{\partial f_s}=-2\,t_d\,V_{SD}.
Why: the winding and the shunt carry the current for the whole cycle, the high side only during D, the low side during 1-D, and the dead-time drop grows with every switching edge. At D = 0.2565 (20 A) the low side conducts for almost three quarters of the period.
Both sides are the same LMG2100R044 resistance in the model, so the ratio of their effects is D/(1-D): +10 % gives −3.16 mV on the high side and −9.16 mV on the low side. This is the synchronous form of the diode-buck rule that a diode drop is especially visible at low duty (Appendix D): the low side has taken the diode’s place.
The winding gives −10.0 mV at 20 A and −2.50 mV at 5 A, a ratio of four, as \partial V_o/\partial r_L = -I_o predicts. The dead-time drop hardly depends on the load: +10 % f_s costs −2.10 mV at 20 A and −2.08 mV at 5 A.
Solution B — perturb the full loss model, one parameter at a time, regulated. Hold V_o = 12 V. Increase one parameter by 10 % and solve the operating point again. Retain ripple, partial high-side ZVS, fitted overlap and fitted core loss.
The calibrated base point at 20 A is 95.62 %, with D = 0.2565. At 5 A it is 95.66 %, with D = 0.2519. The table gives the efficiency change in percentage points. It also gives the fixed-duty output-voltage change at 20 A for comparison with Solution A.

Efficiency change for a +10 % change of each parameter at 48 V, at 20 A and at 5 A, on the calibrated model.


At 20 A, conduction and fitted overlap dominate. A 10 % parameter change affects efficiency by about 0.07–0.08 pp. At 5 A, the fitted core term dominates. Increasing L by 10 % gains 0.327 pp because ripple falls. The fitted core loss scales with \Delta I_L^{2.2}.
The frequency result needs caution. Increasing f_s by 10 % gives +0.177 pp at light load in this model. The sign of the hardware improvement is not established.
At fixed L, increasing f_s reduces flux swing: \Delta B \propto 1/f_s. Steinmetz gives P \propto f^{\alpha}\cdot\Delta B^{\beta} \propto f^{\alpha-\beta}. Our fitted term omits the f^{\alpha} factor. It therefore credits a saving near f^{-2.2}, rather than f^{-(\beta-\alpha)}. The actual core-loss saving may be much smaller. It may erase the predicted +0.177 pp net gain.
Decision. Use the ranking to choose what to investigate. Check the magnetic-loss model before changing frequency. §10.3 shows the same limitation. A sensitivity calculation describes the model we supplied.
The regulated view also says what the loop must supply. With equal high- and low-side resistance the duty of §8.2 is D \approx [V_o + I_o(r_L + r_{sh} + R_{LS}) + 2t_d f_s V_{SD}]/V_{\mathrm{in}}, so \partial D/\partial r_L \approx I_o/V_{\mathrm{in}}. The loop absorbs the open-loop shift of Solution A by adding duty, while efficiency and temperature still deteriorate.
Regulation hides the output-voltage sensitivity, not the loss; near the maximum duty a small added drop can leave the controller without headroom.
Solution C — a global sweep over the operating range. Recompute every point of the map, for example TI’s 147-row efficiency grid of §8.3, instead of a tangent at two points. A sweep catches the mode boundaries that a slope cannot see: the high side’s change to hard turn-on, the kink of §8.3, and the DCM edge of §10.2.
A continuous-looking surface beyond a mode boundary can be mathematically smooth and physically wrong. The ntbees2 Pareto study over f_s and L (ti-pmp31349/figures/04_pareto_fs_L.svg) is such a sweep; it predates the parameter alignment and is cited as a side study only.


Pros and cons








Solution
Pros
Cons




A. Analytic derivatives, open loop
Shows why each term matters (D, 1-D, I_o, f_s); checks B by hand
Only the terms in the averaged equation; misses ripple, ZVS and core loss; open loop only


B. One-at-a-time perturbation, regulated
Every loss term, the regulated converter, a ranking in efficiency
Local and one parameter at a time; ranks what the model contains, fitted terms included; a 10 % step is not a specified part change


C. Global sweep
Catches mode boundaries and nonlinear trends over the whole range
Costly; harder to read as a ranking; still only as good as the model





Conclusion
At 20 A, investigate conduction resistance and switching overlap first. At 5 A, obtain better magnetic-loss evidence before changing a part: the ranking is dominated by a fitted core term.
Use the simple derivative to explain a mechanism. Use the regulated perturbation model to rank its local efficiency effect. A wider sweep is preferable when the change approaches a conduction-mode boundary, but needs more computation and careful interpretation.
For the proposed light-load frequency change, keep the hardware unchanged until the core model is improved. Its predicted benefit is not established by the fitted ripple term. At full load, compare actual resistance and switching candidates using the relevant losses.
Report the operating point, held quantities, regulated or fixed duty, and model limits. Keep percentage changes separate from percentage points. Check selected points with current area, volt-second balance or power balance.

title: 12. Training: problem-driven exercises
section: E1 — Inductor loss: a step in the terminal current
text:
E1 — Inductor loss: a step in the terminal current

Problem
Can an inductor have a step in its terminal current? The output ripple shows a step at each switching edge. Capacitor ESL is negligible. Compare at least two inductor models.
In the drawn model, r_s is in series with the parallel combination of L and R_p. At switch turn-off, calculate the terminal-current jump, output-voltage jump and mean R_p loss. Use these four cases:

No parallel branch, with r_C = 50 mΩ.
R_p = 240 Ω, with r_C = 50 mΩ.
R_p = 24 Ω, with r_C = 50 mΩ.
R_p = 24 Ω, with r_C = 0.

Which loss mechanisms can this R_p represent? Where does the model stop being useful?
Operating point. Use the teaching-model diode buck. Set V_{\mathrm{in}} = 48 V, L = 60 µH and C = 100 µF. The load is R = 2.4 Ω and winding resistance r_s = 50 mΩ. Set f_s = 100 kHz and fixed duty to 0.5104167. This gives a 24 V mean output and 10 A mean load.
The output capacitor has ESR r_C and no ESL. Let i_L denote current in the ideal inductance and v_L its voltage. The terminal current delivered to the output is i_t.



Explicit series winding resistance and parallel loss resistor around the ideal inductance, connected to a capacitor with ESR and a resistive load.




Why we do it
T1 showed that a rectangular ripple contribution needs a current jump or a derivative term. Yet an ideal inductor’s current is continuous. Resolve the apparent contradiction by separating branch current from terminal current.
Then ask a second question: does this equivalent circuit describe the part, or did we choose it merely to reproduce the waveform?


What matters

Keep the ideal inductor current i_L apart from the terminal current i_t; continuity constrains i_L and the capacitor voltage, nothing else.
Ask which current the output capacitor actually receives: the current in the ideal inductance, or the current at the component’s terminals?
An element added to make a waveform also changes the impedance at every other frequency; those linked predictions must agree with the part.
Every lumped model has a bandwidth, and an ideal switch edge shows its limits.

Choose a model for the observed step. What independent impedance measurement could make you reject it?


Where it appears in practice

PMP31349 (§8.4). Our core-loss factor comes from exactly such a parallel resistance, read at the impedance peak of the Würth inductor, and it is low by about an order of magnitude at 350 kHz.
Inductor simulation models from manufacturers, which put resistors across the inductance to represent AC loss over a frequency band.
Diagnosing ripple steps and spikes on a scope, where an inductor, a capacitor or the probe can each be the cause.



Solution
Released after the deadline in the Enrolled companion.

title: 12. Training: problem-driven exercises
section: E2 — Design the LC filter frequency first
text:
E2 — Design the LC filter frequency first

Problem
Can you start the design from the filter, rather than choosing L from a current-ripple percentage? Treat the buck as a PWM source driving an LC filter loaded by R. Choose L and C for a natural frequency of 2 kHz with Butterworth damping, \zeta = 1/\sqrt{2}, at the nominal load.
Then find the attenuation at f_s, the switching ripple at the output (from the fundamental alone and with the harmonics), the inductor ripple, and the damping if the load resistance rises to 12 Ω. Compare your design with the ripple-first design of the teaching model, 60 µH and 100 µF.
Operating point. Teaching model: V_{\mathrm{in}} = 48 V, D = 0.5, f_s = 100 kHz, R = 2.4 Ω (24 V, 10 A), with an ideal imposed switch-node voltage and continuous conduction.


Why we do it
The output ripple is what remains of the switching spectrum after the filter. The usual ripple equations are a compact time-domain route to the same result; the frequency view also exposes the passband gain, the resonant peak and how both change with the load. A duty ratio varying slowly relative to the switching frequency changes the low-frequency component of the switch-node voltage; the filter passes that component and attenuates the carrier and its harmonics.
A Class-D amplifier is designed this way, and the buck shares its filter. A full audio amplifier also needs suitable signal bandwidth, bridge arrangement and treatment of output DC; this exercise reconstructs a DC output.


What matters
For an ideal voltage source driving series L into C in parallel with R, the filter transfer and its standard second-order parameters are:
H(s)=\frac{v_o(s)}{v_x(s)}=\frac{1}{LCs^2+(L/R)s+1},
\omega_0=\frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}},\qquad Z_0=\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}},\qquad \zeta=\frac{Z_0}{2R},\qquad Q=\frac{R}{Z_0}.

Specifying f_0 alone fixes only the product LC; the damping fixes the pair.
For a general damping ratio, the natural frequency, the resonant-peak frequency and the −3 dB frequency are different quantities.
The rectangular switch-node voltage has a DC component and a fundamental of peak amplitude 2V_{\mathrm{in}}/\pi at 50 % duty, plus odd harmonics with their phases.

Recommend a design route for this application. Name the requirement that favours it and a changed requirement that would favour the other route.


Where it appears in practice

Class-D audio amplifiers, whose reconstruction filter must pass the signal band and stop the carrier. TI’s LC Filter Design discusses load-dependent damping and filter selection for Class-D stages.
Second-stage output filters on switching supplies: Analog Devices’ Designing Second Stage Output Filters for Switching Power Supplies.
PMP31349’s LC variation (§10.4), where the same resonance and characteristic impedance decide the output impedance.



Solution
Released after the deadline in the Enrolled companion.

title: 12. Training: problem-driven exercises
section: E3 — How stiff is the output? The output impedance of the LC
text:
E3 — How stiff is the output? The output impedance of the LC

Problem
What does the load see when it asks for more current? Derive the source impedance seen from the output terminals with the duty fixed, first without and then with the load resistor. A load step of 5 A may move the output by no more than 50 mV.
Compare three ideal filters with the same natural frequency: 60 µH / 100 µF at 2.4 Ω, 15 µH / 400 µF at 2.4 Ω, and 60 µH / 100 µF at 12 Ω. Give f_0, Z_0, \zeta and the loaded impedance at 100 Hz and at \omega_0, and the inductor ripple at 48 V input.
Propose ways to meet the target.
Operating point. Use the teaching model at 24 V output. Compare R = 2.4 Ω (10 A) with 12 Ω (2 A). Set V_{\mathrm{in}} = 48 V and f_s = 100 kHz. Keep duty fixed and assume ideal components, with series resistance r = 0. Both cases are in continuous conduction.


Why we do it
A regulator is judged by how little its output moves when the load changes. Before any loop, the passive LC sets that behaviour, and the impedance view shows where it is weak. It also answers a question the ripple view cannot: whether two filters with the same corner frequency behave the same for the load.


What matters
Look back into the output with duty fixed. Suppress the independent input-voltage perturbation. Where does the input end of L sit for AC? Draw the impedance seen from the output port, including L, C and series resistance r.

Say which port and which elements define the measurement. Z_s excludes the load resistor; Z_{\mathrm{out}} includes it. A current leaving the output pulls the voltage down: \hat{v}_o = -Z_{\mathrm{out}}\cdot\hat{\imath}_\ell.
A stiffness requirement has a frequency range. For a sinusoidal current of amplitude \Delta I, require |Z_{\mathrm{out}}(j\omega)| \leq \Delta V_{\mathrm{allow}}/\Delta I over the disturbance band. A current step is broadband; checking one frequency does not bound its peak droop.
For voltage-source behaviour under loading, the related interface condition is |Z_s| much smaller than |Z_{\mathrm{load}}| in the required band. Higher-current loads normally have lower operating V/I and demand lower source impedance for the same percentage voltage accuracy.
For electronic loads the incremental impedance can differ from V/I; a constant-power load even has a negative incremental resistance. Here the loads are ordinary resistors.

Choose how to meet the stiffness target. Compare the current stress, damping and hardware cost of your proposal with one alternative.


Where it appears in practice

Point-of-load regulators for processors, specified by a target impedance over a frequency band.
Cascaded converters, where a downstream regulator is a constant-power load with negative incremental resistance.
PMP31349’s LC variation (§10.4): Z_0 is what more capacitance buys, and the loop must then cut the rest down.



Solution
Released after the deadline in the Enrolled companion.

title: 12. Training: problem-driven exercises
section: E4 — Place the poles of the buck
text:
E4 — Place the poles of the buck

Problem
If the buck is a PWM voltage source driving a second-order network, which dynamics can you choose, and with what? Find the open-loop poles. Then assume both state deviations are measured, apply full-state feedback \hat{u} = -k_v\cdot\hat{v}_o - k_i\cdot\hat{\imath}_L with \hat{u} = V_{\mathrm{in}}\cdot\hat{d}, and find k_i and k_v for a natural frequency of 3 kHz and a damping ratio of 0.7.
Compare the free responses from a +100 mV capacitor-voltage error with zero current deviation, find the largest duty perturbation, and decide whether proportional voltage feedback alone could do the same.
Operating point. Use L = 60 µH, C = 100 µF and R = 2.4 Ω. The input is V_{\mathrm{in}} = 48 V. Analyse small deviations about V_o = 24 V, I_o = 10 A and D = 0.5. Use the ideal averaged CCM model.


Why we do it
Choosing L and C already places the poles, at one load. Feedback moves them. Seeing how many independent coefficients each kind of feedback can set explains why a current loop, or a dynamic compensator, appears in nearly every buck controller.


What matters
The deviation state equations are:
L\dot{\hat i}_L=\hat u-\hat v_o,\qquad C\dot{\hat v}_o=\hat i_L-\frac{\hat v_o}{R}.

The open-loop characteristic polynomial is s^2 + s/(RC) + 1/(LC); match the closed-loop polynomial to s^2 + 2\zeta_t\omega_n s + \omega_n^2.
The gains act on deviations about one equilibrium; reference tracking and rejection of a permanent load change need feedforward or integral action.
Delay, sensing noise, duty saturation and switching limit how far the poles can move.

Choose a feedback arrangement for the requested poles. Explain its sensing cost and when a simpler arrangement would be sufficient.


Where it appears in practice

Current-mode control, which feeds back the inductor current, the second state, as on PMP31349’s LM5148 (§7.1).
Digital state-feedback controllers for converters and inverters.
Active damping of LC filters in grid-connected inverters. The recap’s example Identical pulses, different LC trajectories shows the same network from the time side.



Solution
Released after the deadline in the Enrolled companion.

title: 12. Training: problem-driven exercises
section: E5 — Feedback lowers the output impedance through 1 + T
text:
E5 — Feedback lowers the output impedance through 1 + T

Problem
How does feedback lower output impedance? Where does it stop helping? Derive the closed-loop output impedance using the open-loop impedance and T = C_c\cdot G_{vd}. Assume unity voltage sensing.
For the compensator below, choose K for a 5 kHz crossover. Find the phase margin and check the closed-loop poles. At 100 Hz, 1 kHz, 5 kHz and 10 kHz, tabulate |T| and |1 + T|. Include both open- and closed-loop output impedances.
Finally, add a +0.5 A current sink while keeping the 2.4 Ω resistor connected. Find the peak voltage dip with and without feedback.
Operating point. Teaching model: 48 V input, 24 V output, 10 A nominal load, L = 60 µH, C = 100 µF, R = 2.4 Ω, series resistance r = 50 mΩ, equilibrium duty 0.51042. Continuous-time averaged model, without delay, PWM sampling, ESR or ESL. Illustrative type III compensator, an authored teaching loop rather than the network of a particular IC:
C_c(s)=\frac{K}{s}\frac{(1+s/\omega_z)^2}{(1+s/\omega_p)^2},
with two zeros at 1 kHz and two poles at 50 kHz. The plant is:
G_{vd}(s)=\frac{48}{LCs^2+(L/R+rC)s+1+r/R}.


Why we do it
Part I (§10.4) leaves the output impedance at Z_0 and says that the loop must cut it down by 1 + T. This exercise shows by how much, at which frequencies, and where feedback makes things worse instead of better.


What matters

T is dimensionless and is not G_{vd} alone. With a sensor ratio and a separate modulator gain, include both in T.
Divide by the complex quantity 1 + T before taking its magnitude; near crossover “divide by the loop-gain magnitude” is inaccurate.
A crossover and a phase margin complement the closed-loop poles; check both.
A node outside the sensed feedback point needs its own port analysis.

Recommend how to divide the disturbance requirement between passive filtering and feedback. State the cost of each and the frequency range in which you rely on it.


Where it appears in practice

PMP31349 (§7): TI’s type II network on a current-mode stage, and the 10 → 20 A load step that the loop must hold inside the limit.
Point-of-load regulators designed to a target impedance, where the loop sets the low-frequency part and the capacitors the rest.
Voltage amplifiers: the recap’s negative-feedback example uses the same mechanism.



Solution
Released after the deadline in the Enrolled companion.

title: Appendix A — What power electronics does
text:
A.1 Definition
Background to §1. No design step depends on this appendix; it places the buck among the converters of power electronics.
Power electronics comprises the technologies for the static conversion of electrical energy using semiconductors as switches. “Static” means that no rotating machine performs the conversion. The semiconductor is operated as a switch, not as an adjustable resistance; this is the property that the rest of the lesson builds on.
Power electronics converts electrical energy using semiconductor switches, storage elements and control. The purpose is to deliver the voltage, current, frequency or power flow required by a load with acceptable losses and size.

title: Appendix A — What power electronics does
section: A.3 Classification by application
text:
A.3 Classification by application
The second classification asks where the converter is used:

Power supplies for electronic equipment. At the smallest powers this is voltage stabilisation. Unregulated rectifiers serve undemanding loads. Supplies with a regulated output voltage sit in almost every mains-powered device: consumer electronics, office and household equipment.
Variable-speed drives. Actuators, automation and robots; electric and hybrid vehicles, where power electronics makes high efficiency possible, among other things by returning braking energy to the battery; locomotives. Pumps and fans are increasingly speed-controlled. Drive powers range from a few watts to about 100 MW.
Renewable generation. Variable-speed wind turbines need their variable frequency and voltage adapted to the public grid. Photovoltaic plants invert the generated DC voltage into single- or three-phase AC.
Energy transmission. Connecting grids that are not synchronised, for example a railway supply with its own frequency, or two interconnected grids such as the central and northern European ones. High-voltage DC (HVDC) transmission, for example through submarine cables.

Beyond these, power electronics appears in household appliances, telecommunications, information technology, industry, transport and the energy sector.
A regenerative drive also needs a path for energy to return from the mechanical system. A converter is therefore more than a voltage ratio: isolation, current direction and allowed power-flow direction matter.

title: Appendix A — What power electronics does
section: A.4 Voltage classes: what “low voltage” means
text:
A.4 Voltage classes: what “low voltage” means
Ask an engineer what low voltage means and you may hear 60 V. Ask the European Low Voltage Directive (2014/35/EU) and the answer is 50–1000 V AC and 75–1500 V DC. “Low” there means below the medium-voltage grid, not safe to touch. The two answers belong to different questions.
The touch-safety question has its own limits. In the product-safety standard for IT and audio/video equipment, IEC 62368-1, energy class ES1 is the class an ordinary person may touch. Its voltage limits are 60 V DC and 30 V rms (42.4 V peak) AC; a circuit may alternatively qualify by limiting the touch current to 2 mA DC or 0.5 mA rms. The older IEC 60950-1 called the same idea SELV (safety extra-low voltage). Road vehicles draw the line in the same place: ISO 6469-3 applies its shock-protection requirements to voltage class B, above 60 V DC or 30 V AC.
These limits are conventions. Body impedance hand to hand is of the order of 2 kΩ at these voltages, so 60 V can still drive tens of milliamperes. The standards set the limit from current-effect data and duration, with margin; it is not one current multiplied by one resistance. Treat the number as a defined boundary and read the standard that applies to the product.
Why PMP31349 stops at 60 V. A 48 V bus stays below the 60 V DC boundary across its whole operating range, including charging. Below it, touch protection is not required. In a vehicle, that removes the insulation monitoring, orange cabling and interlocks of the high-voltage system. This is the reason for 48 V automotive and telecom systems. A 60 V maximum input (§1) is therefore not arbitrary. Moving the bus above 60 V would cut current and copper for the same power. It would also move the whole system into the protected class, a cost that often outweighs the copper saved at 48 V power levels.
Above the Low Voltage Directive’s range, medium voltage begins; grid practice uses classes up to about 35 kV, with high voltage above. The exact boundaries differ between standards and countries, so quote the one that governs the product.

title: Appendix B — Why switch?
text:
B.1 Switched-mode converters: advantages and costs
A switched-mode converter, also called a switching regulator or switched-mode power supply, operates its power semiconductors in only two states. A semiconductor is either off, so it carries no current, or fully on (saturated), so it has practically no voltage across it. Voltage and current therefore do not appear across the device at the same time, which gives far lower losses than a linear regulator.
The last disadvantage is not on the original slide; it follows from the switching itself and returns in §4, §5 and §9, and in T1 (§12).
Worked comparison with a linear regulator. A linear pass element simultaneously supports a substantial voltage and conducts the load current. For a 48 V → 24 V, 10 A supply (the teaching model of Appendix E):
P_o=24\cdot10=240\ \mathrm{W},\qquad P_{\mathrm{linear}}=(48-24)10=240\ \mathrm{W}.
Its idealized efficiency is only 50%. An ideal switch, by contrast, has zero voltage when conducting and zero current when blocking, so its instantaneous dissipation is zero in either state. Real switches have conduction resistance and finite transitions, so real switching converters still lose power. The inductor and capacitor allow the load to receive approximately continuous power while the semiconductor switches.
Why this matters: higher switching frequency allows smaller energy-storage components for a given ripple, but increases many switching-related losses. Frequency is a tradeoff, not a free way to shrink the converter.

title: Appendix B — Why switch?
section: B.2 Remarks: where the buck converter is used
text:
B.2 Remarks: where the buck converter is used
The opening of the lesson compresses the remarks slide (l01-s36, deck slide 38); here they are in full.

Efficiency. Buck converters can reach efficiencies above 99 % when the voltage ratio is moderate, conduction resistances are low and switching is soft. The figure belongs to a particular design, not to the topology: the deliberately lossy parasitics of Appendix D.9 give about 92 % from conduction loss alone, and PMP31349 reaches 95.5 % at 48 V and 20 A (TI, measured; §8).
Switching frequency depends on the application. It is normally at least 20 kHz, to stay above the audible range. The upper end is around 10 MHz, for applications where small size and very fast dynamic response matter. Most applications run at roughly 100 kHz to 500 kHz. These are indicative ranges, not design limits; B.1 explains the tradeoff behind them, and §10.3 prices it for PMP31349’s 350 kHz.
Power range. The buck is used over a very wide power range, from integrated point-of-load regulators to high-current stages with paralleled phases.
Limits. The buck is suitable only if the output voltage is lower than the input voltage and no galvanic isolation is required. Other cases need the boost, buck-boost or an isolated topology of the following lessons.

title: Appendix C — From one switching event to PWM
text:
C.1 Closing the switch starts a transient
Start with an ideal changeover switch S, inductor L, output capacitor C and load resistor R. Initially the capacitor is discharged. Connecting V_{\mathrm{in}} to the inductor starts a transient.
The German slides call the input U_e and the output U_a. Other slide symbols map as follows: R_{DSON} to r_Q (with R_{HS} and R_{LS} in Part I), R_L to r_L, U_D to V_f, and the DCM fractions D_1, D_2 to D, D_2. The slides also call CCM heavy mode and DCM light mode. After settling, the ideal inductor acts as a short and the capacitor as an open circuit:
V_o(\infty)=V_{\mathrm{in}},\qquad I_L(\infty)=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}}{R}.
How the circuit gets there depends on the damping; a lightly loaded LC rings around the final value. During a short interval at the beginning, however, two simple statements hold: the output voltage changes only a little, and the inductor current rises approximately linearly, because almost the full input voltage appears across L:
v_L=V_{\mathrm{in}}-v_o\approx V_{\mathrm{in}},\qquad \frac{di_L}{dt}\approx\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}}{L}.
This holds when the interval is much shorter than the oscillation period and the time constants of the transient. For the teaching model of Appendix E, L = 60 µH and C = 100 µF give a natural period of
2\pi\sqrt{LC}=2\pi\sqrt{60\ \mu\mathrm{H}\cdot100\ \mu\mathrm{F}}\approx487\ \mu\mathrm{s},
about 50 times the 10 µs switching period. This separation of time scales is the premise of the whole lesson: within one switching interval, voltages are almost constant and currents are almost straight lines. Part I starts from it in §2.1.

title: Appendix C — From one switching event to PWM
section: C.2 The buck as a Class-D amplifier
text:
C.2 The buck as a Class-D amplifier
A buck stage is a switched voltage source followed by a low-pass network. Hold the duty ratio approximately constant and it delivers DC. Vary duty ratio slowly relative to switching frequency and the filtered output can follow a signal, which is the basic connection to Class-D amplification. A half-bridge or bridge and appropriate modulation are needed for bipolar output waveforms; the single-ended buck shown here produces a positive output.
Seen from the switch node, L and C with the load R form the loaded second-order low-pass of the recap (§12.2), and the recap’s Class-D example (§12.3) designs exactly this filter for an audio band. For the teaching model the corner frequency 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC}) is about 2.05 kHz, far below the 100 kHz switching frequency; for PMP31349 it is 3.98 kHz against 350 kHz (§10.4).
Exercise E2 (§12) designs a buck from this filter view.

title: Appendix D — The diode buck
text:
D.1 Realisation with a MOSFET and a diode
The classical buck freewheels through a diode. PMP31349 replaces that diode with the low-side GaN switch (§6.1), but the diode buck remains the clearest place to see a constant-voltage loss, the drop at low duty and the third interval of DCM. The teaching model of Appendix E is a diode buck, and this appendix uses its numbers.
The changeover switch is built from a controlled switch and a diode. Low and medium powers use a MOSFET; larger powers use an IGBT. Bipolar transistors are no longer used for this purpose, because of their drive power. When the MOSFET is on, the diode blocks.
When the MOSFET turns off, the inductor current commutates into the diode, which turns on. Each state has its own equivalent circuit, the two switch positions of §2.1.
Let x be the switch node. Inductor current flows from x toward the output; inductor voltage is measured from x to the output. The diode has its anode at the common return and cathode at x. It supplies a path for positive inductor current when Q turns off. Its symbol is labelled Dᶠ to distinguish the device from duty ratio D.
The third interval occurs in DCM (Appendix E.4). The switch node is no longer clamped to zero by a conducting diode. In the ideal small-ripple model it sits at V_o; real switch-node capacitances can ring. Replacing the diode by a second MOSFET gives the synchronous buck of Part I (§6) and of Appendix E.7.

D.3 Which current measure gives the power?

section: D.5 Pulsed current: the buck input and the boost output
text:
D.5 Pulsed current: the buck input and the boost output
Case 2: pulsed charging through a diode or switch. The capacitor receives charge in pulses while the load draws nearly constant current I. Between pulses, the capacitor supplies that current alone. Call this interval t_x. The removed charge is a rectangle:
\Delta V=\frac{I\,t_x}{C}.
The output capacitor of a boost converter works this way. In the buck, it is the input capacitor that sees pulsed current. If the source supplies only the mean input current D\cdot I_o, the input capacitor must supply the difference (1-D)\cdot I_o during the ON time DT_s:
\Delta V_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{(1-D)I_o\,DT_s}{C_{\mathrm{in}}}=\frac{D(1-D)I_o}{f_sC_{\mathrm{in}}}.
Case 1, the triangular current of the output capacitor, is §4.2; §5 applies case 2 to PMP31349’s input bank.

title: Appendix D — The diode buck
section: D.7 A useful nonideal CCM model
text:
D.7 A useful nonideal CCM model
Use inductor winding resistance r_L, MOSFET ON resistance r_Q and a constant diode forward drop V_f. With small current ripple, replace current in their voltage drops by I_o:
v_{L,\mathrm{on}}\simeq V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o-I_o(r_L+r_Q),
v_{L,\mathrm{off}}\simeq -V_o-V_f-I_or_L.
Volt-second balance gives:
V_o=DV_{\mathrm{in}}-(1-D)V_f-I_o(r_L+Dr_Q).
For a resistive load, substitute I_o = V_o/R:
V_o=\frac{DV_{\mathrm{in}}-(1-D)V_f}{1+(r_L+Dr_Q)/R}.
This is the model swept in buck_loss_parametric.ipynb. It is a CCM average model. Negative predicted output voltage or a computed current valley below zero tells us that its operating assumptions have failed; those regions must not be presented as valid diode-buck predictions. §8.2 gives its synchronous form for PMP31349.



Notebook-style sweeps of winding resistance, MOSFET ON resistance and diode forward drop at 30 V input and 1 Ω load. Only points consistent with the approximate CCM model are drawn.



Check the formula: units, then limit cases
Before you trust a derived formula, test it in two steps.

Units. Both terms of the numerator are voltages, and (r_L + D\,r_Q)/R is a ratio of resistances. The result is a voltage.
Limit cases. Set the parameters to values where you know the answer:

No losses, r_L = r_Q = 0 and V_f = 0: the formula gives V_o = D\,V_{\mathrm{in}}, the ideal buck.
D = 1: the diode never conducts, so V_f drops out and V_o = V_{\mathrm{in}}/[1 + (r_L + r_Q)/R]. With the D.8 values (30 V, 0.1 Ω each, R = 2.4 Ω) the output is 27.69 V. With r_L = R and r_Q = 0 the output is half the input: a plain voltage divider.
D = 0: the switch never conducts, so r_Q drops out and V_o = -V_f/(1 + r_L/R), that is −0.96 V with the D.8 values. A diode buck cannot make a negative output. The CCM model is therefore invalid at this limit, as stated above.


What the limits teach. Near D = 1 the diode hardly matters, and the switch carries the current: spend the money on the switch. Near D = 0 the switch hardly matters: spend it on the diode. The winding resistance r_L carries the current in both intervals, so D never weights it. A good inductor pays at every duty.

title: Appendix D — The diode buck
section: D.8 Worked example: required duty changes
text:
D.8 Worked example: required duty changes
Choose illustrative r_L = r_Q = 0.1 Ω and V_f = 1 V. At V_o = 24 V and I_o = 10 A:
D=\frac{V_o+V_f+I_or_L}{V_{\mathrm{in}}+V_f-I_or_Q}.
At 30 V the required duty is 26/30 = 0.86667; at 48 V it is 26/48 = 0.54167. The ideal values were 0.8 and 0.5. The controller must increase duty to overcome the losses.
With only V_f = 1 V and zero resistances, the corresponding duties are 25/31 = 0.80645 and 25/49 = 0.51020. Diode conduction loss at 10 A is then about 1.94 W and 4.90 W respectively. Why worse at high input? Lower required duty means a larger fraction of the period is spent freewheeling through the diode.
crumbs: 128  Appendix D — The diode buck

title: Appendix D — The diode buck
section: D.9 Estimate dissipation with the correct current measure
text:
D.9 Estimate dissipation with the correct current measure
The approximate CCM conduction losses are:
P_L=r_LJ,\qquad P_Q=r_QDJ,\qquad P_D=V_f(1-D)I_o.
For the full illustrative parasitic case at 48 V → 24 V, 10 A, D = 0.54167, the OFF-slope estimate gives ripple about 1.986 A. The winding dissipates about 10.03 W, Q about 5.43 W, and the diode about 4.58 W. Conduction-only efficiency is approximately 92.29%.
These illustrative resistances are deliberately large enough to make their effects visible. This is not a prediction for a chosen converter. The mean-drop voltage model neglects small waveform corrections; including ripple in the RMS losses adds a small correction to its DC power balance.
Other losses include MOSFET voltage/current overlap during transitions, gate drive, device capacitance, diode reverse recovery, inductor core loss and frequency-dependent winding/connection loss. A first switching-overlap estimate is:
P_{\mathrm{sw}}\simeq\frac{1}{2}V_{\mathrm{in}}I_o(t_r+t_f)f_s.
At 48 V, 10 A, 40 ns combined transition time and 100 kHz this gives 0.96 W. It excludes capacitance and reverse recovery and assumes the stated overlap shape. It is a screening estimate, not a complete loss model.

Switching loss from datasheet energies
Device datasheets give the switching energies E_{\mathrm{on}} and E_{\mathrm{off}} against current, at a test voltage and temperature. Read each energy at the current of its own edge. In a buck, the switch turns on at the valley I_o - \Delta I_L/2 and turns off at the peak I_o + \Delta I_L/2. Scale both energies to the operating voltage, to first order in proportion to V_{\mathrm{in}}/V_{\mathrm{test}}. The switching loss is a power:
P_{\mathrm{sw}}=f_s\,[E_{\mathrm{on}}(I_{\mathrm{valley}})+E_{\mathrm{off}}(I_{\mathrm{pk}})]
An energy times a frequency gives watts. A 600 V IGBT that loses 5 mJ per cycle at its operating current dissipates 5 mJ · 100 kHz = 500 W at 100 kHz. This is why large IGBTs switch at a few kilohertz to some tens of kilohertz.
Which edge costs more depends on the device. In a hard-switched MOSFET the turn-on often dominates, because the switch also discharges its own output capacitance. In an IGBT the tail current can make the turn-off the larger loss (Appendix F). Read both curves, and do not assume a fixed ratio.
A figure of merit. Within one device technology, a lower on-resistance needs a larger die, and a larger die has more gate charge. The product Q_g\,R_{DS(\mathrm{on})} is therefore nearly constant within a technology, and it compares technologies. A lower product allows a higher frequency for the same loss, and a higher frequency allows smaller magnetics and capacitors.
Why soft switching can help: reducing switch voltage or current during the transition reduces overlap loss. It requires suitable circuit and timing conditions; simply operating at the CCM/DCM boundary does not prove that those conditions are satisfied.

Stored charge, subsequent reverse voltage and ringing; recovery stress is often reduced


High-side Q is commanded ON after the zero-current boundary
Initial load-related inductor current is zero
Q may still support a large V_{DS}; capacitive discharge can cause turn-on loss


High-side Q is turned OFF at the positive current peak
Boundary/DCM alone does not make its current zero
Current/voltage overlap, capacitance charging and device-specific turn-off loss


A synchronous/resonant dead-time transition moves x toward V_{\mathrm{in}}
Correctly directed current can discharge high-side output capacitance
Enough commutating charge/energy and appropriate gate timing are required for high-side ZVS turn-on



ZCS describes negligible current through the relevant device at its switching event. ZVS describes negligible voltage across it at the relevant event, often gate turn-on for a MOSFET. A high-side buck MOSFET can start with zero load current while its output capacitance still holds substantial voltage. Thus a favorable load-current condition does not eliminate all turn-on energy.
To obtain high-side ZVS in a synchronous buck, the switch node must rise close to V_{\mathrm{in}} before that device is turned on. A suitably controlled negative inductor-current interval can provide that node transition during dead time. Resonant extensions can also exploit the L/C_{\mathrm{oss}} trajectory. The required polarity, energy and timing depend on V_{\mathrm{in}}, V_o, parasitic capacitances and the actual conduction paths.
A strict positive-triangle boundary waveform touching zero does not by itself establish this transition. §6.2 checks this transition for PMP31349’s GaN half-bridge.
Once a deliberate negative valley or a finite resonant interval is added, recalculate the current area. The simple I_o = I_{\mathrm{pk}}/2 expression applies to the ideal zero-valley triangle, not automatically to triangular-current-mode variants with negative current. This distinction matters when combining average-current accuracy with soft-switching control. A published buck example explicitly optimizes the required negative current: Tang et al., Optimization of Minimum Negative Current BCM Synchronous Buck Converter.

title: Appendix D — The diode buck
section: D.11 Sensitivity means “at this operating point”
text:
D.11 Sensitivity means “at this operating point”
T4 (§12) applies this method to PMP31349 with its calibrated loss model. Here it runs on the diode buck of D.7, where every derivative has a closed form.

Start by stating what is fixed
A sweep shows how a model changes across a range; a local sensitivity is the slope at one specific point. Before differentiating, state the operating point, the mode, and what is held fixed. For the following open-loop CCM calculation, hold V_{\mathrm{in}}, duty D and resistive load R fixed when varying a parasitic parameter. The output is allowed to change.
Define:
N=DV_{\mathrm{in}}-(1-D)V_f,\qquad A=1+\frac{r_L+Dr_Q}{R},\qquad V_o=\frac{N}{A}.
The local prediction for several small changes is:
\Delta V_o\simeq\sum_p\frac{\partial V_o}{\partial p}\Delta p.
This is a tangent approximation, not a guarantee for a large parameter change. Recompute the operating point and mode when a change is large or approaches the critical boundary.


Derivatives explain the sweep shapes
\frac{\partial V_o}{\partial V_{\mathrm{in}}}=\frac{D}{A},\qquad \frac{\partial V_o}{\partial V_f}=-\frac{1-D}{A}.
\frac{\partial V_o}{\partial r_L}=-\frac{V_o}{RA},\qquad \frac{\partial V_o}{\partial r_Q}=-\frac{DV_o}{RA}.
\frac{\partial V_o}{\partial D}=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}+V_f-V_or_Q/R}{A}.
Why: winding resistance acts throughout the conducting cycle. High-side ON resistance acts only during D. Diode drop acts during 1-D. Lower load resistance increases current and makes resistive drops more important. Notice also that the duty derivative includes the change of conduction resistance with duty; differentiating only the numerator would miss it.
For r_Q compared to r_L, the ratio of the absolute slopes is exactly D in this model. But this compares equal changes measured in ohms. Component selection usually compares achievable changes, losses, cost and temperature, not just raw derivative values.


Worked comparison at two operating points
Hold V_{\mathrm{in}} = 30 V, R = 2.4 Ω, r_L = r_Q = 0.1 Ω and V_f = 1 V. Both operating points below are in CCM with L = 60 µH and f_s = 100 kHz. Their output voltages differ because duty differs; this is a deliberate open-loop comparison.

At D = 0.2, reducing diode drop by 0.1 V raises output by about 76.2 mV, whereas reducing r_Q by 10 mΩ raises it by only 3.93 mV. At D = 0.8, the same changes give about 18.6 mV and 68.7 mV respectively. The relative value of those two changes reverses with operating point.
This does not mean the diode is always the largest loss at low duty. The comparison includes the size of each proposed parameter change, and other losses may dominate. The lesson is to calculate the effect where the converter will actually operate.



Local diode sensitivity over duty and load, plus output changes predicted for separate 1% parameter increases at two operating points.





Winding-resistance sensitivity at several loads and DCM mean-current dependence on imposed output voltage.


The sensitivity map leaves points outside approximate CCM blank. A continuous-looking algebraic surface beyond a mode boundary can be mathematically smooth and physically wrong.


Absolute and normalized sensitivity answer different questions
An absolute sensitivity has units, such as V/Ω. A normalized sensitivity compares fractional changes:
S_p^{V_o}=\frac{p}{V_o}\frac{\partial V_o}{\partial p},\qquad \frac{\Delta V_o}{V_o}\simeq S_p^{V_o}\frac{\Delta p}{p}.
For the parasitics:
S_{r_L}^{V_o}=-\frac{r_L}{RA},\qquad S_{r_Q}^{V_o}=-\frac{Dr_Q}{RA},\qquad S_{V_f}^{V_o}=-\frac{(1-D)V_f}{N}.
Use absolute sensitivity to assess a specified change such as “10 mΩ less resistance.” Use normalized sensitivity to compare percentage uncertainties. Normalization becomes misleading near zero output or zero nominal parameter; use absolute changes there.


A regulated converter has a different sensitivity
If a voltage loop holds V_o fixed, output voltage is no longer the freely moving result of the open-loop calculation. Duty must move to compensate. At fixed target V_o and R, so I_o is also fixed:
D=\frac{V_o+V_f+I_or_L}{B},\qquad B=V_{\mathrm{in}}+V_f-I_or_Q.
\frac{\partial D}{\partial r_L}=\frac{I_o}{B},\qquad \frac{\partial D}{\partial r_Q}=\frac{DI_o}{B},\qquad \frac{\partial D}{\partial V_f}=\frac{1-D}{B}.
At the 48 V, 24 V, 10 A parasitic operating point, B = 48 V. An added 10 mΩ winding resistance requires approximately 0.002083 more duty, or 0.2083 percentage points. This keeps output near its target if the loop has enough gain and duty headroom, but adds approximately 1 W winding loss at 10 A. Regulation can hide output-voltage sensitivity while efficiency and temperature still deteriorate.
Why the operating point matters twice: it sets the derivative, and it sets whether the controller has enough range to compensate. Near maximum duty, a small added drop can make the requested voltage unattainable.


Bridge to small-signal dynamics
Static sensitivity describes the settled change. It does not say how fast or stably the converter gets there. For an ideal averaged CCM stage with resistive load:
L\frac{di_L}{dt}=d v_{\mathrm{in}}-v_o,\qquad C\frac{dv_o}{dt}=i_L-\frac{v_o}{R}.
Write each quantity as its operating value plus a small perturbation. Linearizing the product d\cdot v_{\mathrm{in}} gives:
L\frac{d\hat{i}_L}{dt}=V_{\mathrm{in}}\hat{d}+D\hat{v}_{\mathrm{in}}-\hat{v}_o.
The duty perturbation is multiplied by the operating input voltage; the input-voltage disturbance is multiplied by the operating duty. The neglected product of the two perturbations is second order. With fixed input and zero initial perturbations:
\frac{\hat{v}_o(s)}{\hat{d}(s)}=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}}{LCs^2+(L/R)s+1}.
Even this ideal model has operating-point-dependent gain and load-dependent damping. Adding losses, current regulation or crossing into DCM changes the model further. This is why a notebook sweep and a Bode plot need stated conditions, not only a topology name.

section: D.12 Why is a diode drop especially visible at low duty?
text:
D.12 Why is a diode drop especially visible at low duty?
Answer: the diode conducts during 1-D, so \partial V_o/\partial V_f = -(1-D)/A (D.11). The same added forward voltage acts for more of each period at low duty. Its loss still depends on current, so voltage sensitivity alone is not a complete thermal ranking. In PMP31349 the low-side GaN switch takes the diode’s place, and T4 finds the same pattern in its resistance.

title: Appendix E — The 24 V teaching model in DCM
text:
E.1 The teaching model’s design numbers
The teaching model comes from the U1 notebooks: 30–48 V input, 24 V output, 10 A nominal output, 100 kHz switching, with L = 60 µH and C = 100 µF. Numerical scenarios are teaching models, not selected hardware. We start with ideal components, a resistive load and small output-voltage ripple; Appendix D adds the losses. All current ripple values below are peak-to-peak unless labelled RMS.
The model is a diode buck. T1–T3 and E1–E5 (§12) use it, or a stated variant of it, because it shows mechanisms that the finished GaN design hides. The worked numbers of Appendices B–D come from it. Never carry its numbers to PMP31349, or the reverse.
These are the numbers that Part I replaced with PMP31349’s.
First numerical example. For regulated 24 V output, the ideal CCM duty ratio is 0.8 at 30 V input and 0.5 at 48 V input. At 100 kHz the period is 10 µs, so the ON times are 8 µs and 5 µs respectively.
Check: use L = 60 µH at 48 V input. The current rises at 0.4 A/µs for 5 µs, then falls at −0.4 A/µs for 5 µs. The net current change is zero and peak-to-peak ripple is 2 A.
The inductor. The notebook specification asks for ripple no greater than 20% of the nominal 10 A, so the limit is 2 A. This is a nominal-current specification: at a 1 A load, a 2 A peak-to-peak ripple would be 200%, even though the component has not changed.
L_{\min}=\frac{24(1-0.5)}{100000\cdot2}=60\ \mu\mathrm{H}.
At 30 V input, the same inductor gives 0.8 A ripple. At 48 V input and 10 A mean current, its current ranges from 9 A to 11 A.
The capacitors. A 50 mV ripple requirement and 2 A ripple give an ideal minimum of 50 µF. Choosing an illustrative effective capacitance of 100 µF reduces the capacitive contribution to 25 mV.
At 48 V input (D = 0.5), 10 A and 100 kHz, an illustrative effective input capacitance of 20 µF gives a capacitive ripple of 1.25 V, before ESR. This is much larger than the 25 mV at the output with five times as much capacitance: the pulsed current is not smoothed by an inductor. The corresponding RMS current stress follows below.
With 10 mΩ ESR this is 20 mV. Adding the two magnitudes gives a conservative 45 mV estimate; the maxima need not occur at the same time. ESL and switching spikes require a higher-frequency model. Use effective capacitance at operating bias and temperature, not only the printed nominal capacitance.
Why ripple sizing is not enough: a sudden 5 A increase in load lasting 20 µs before the inductor supplies it would remove 100 µC. A 100 µF capacitor would drop by 1 V, plus an immediate ESR contribution. Actual droop depends on current slew, control response and the time integral of the current deficit.
Mean and RMS currents. At 48 V input, use D = 0.5, I_o = 10 A and \Delta I_L = 2 A. The inductor RMS current is 10.0167 A. The switch RMS current is 7.0828 A. Average input current is 5 A, and output-capacitor RMS current is 0.5774 A. Ideal input and output power are both 240 W.
Why the input capacitor matters: the stage draws pulsed input current even though its output-inductor current is continuous. A local input capacitor supplies much of that AC component. Neglecting inductor ripple and assuming a source that supplies only the average, its RMS current is approximately I_o\sqrt{D(1-D)}, or 5 A at D = 0.5. Input and output capacitor stress are very different.

E.2 Continuous conduction mode



Two periods each of CCM, critical and DCM inductor current at 48 V input and regulated 24 V output.


For the diode buck considered here, CCM means the inductor current stays positive throughout the cycle:
I_{L,\min}=I_o-\frac{\Delta I_L}{2}>0.
The inductor retains a nonzero current from one period to the next. Duty ratio balances volt-seconds, while the load determines the mean current. This distinction explains the current-source behavior of T2.
