title: Appendix E — The 24 V teaching model in DCM
section: E.3 Critical conduction mode: just touching zero
text:
E.3 Critical conduction mode: just touching zero
At the boundary:
I_{o,\mathrm{crit}}=\frac{\Delta I_L}{2},\qquad R_{\mathrm{crit}}=\frac{2Lf_s}{1-D}.
At 48 V input with L = 60 µH, the boundary is 1 A or 24 Ω. At 30 V it is 0.4 A or 60 Ω. To guarantee strictly positive current across the entire input range at regulated 24 V, load resistance must be below 24 Ω. Equality is the critical boundary.
Using the dimensionless parameter:
K=\frac{2Lf_s}{R},\qquad K_{\mathrm{crit}}=1-D,
CCM has K > 1-D, the boundary has equality, and DCM has K < 1-D. Here R = V_o/I_o is the resistive-load value at the operating point.
CrCM terminology: a converter can happen to sit at this boundary at one fixed frequency. A controller operating intentionally in critical conduction mode normally detects zero current and starts the next pulse there, so switching frequency varies with load and voltage. For an ideal triangular waveform at the boundary:
I_{\mathrm{pk}}=2I_o,\qquad f_s=\frac{V_o(1-V_o/V_{\mathrm{in}})}{2LI_o}.
At 48 V → 24 V with L = 60 µH, maintaining the boundary at 0.5 A would require 200 kHz; at 1 A it requires 100 kHz. A fixed 100 kHz converter at 0.5 A instead operates in DCM. Critical operation can avoid diode turn-off at positive current, but has higher peak/RMS current than low-ripple CCM at the same mean and does not automatically guarantee zero-voltage switching of Q. §10.1 applies the same relations to PMP31349.

title: Appendix E — The 24 V teaching model in DCM
section: E.4 Discontinuous conduction mode: a third interval appears
text:
E.4 Discontinuous conduction mode: a third interval appears
Reduce load current further and the diode blocks the negative current that the two-interval solution would predict. The actual waveform reaches zero and remains there until the next ON pulse. Its cycle now has ON, diode conduction, and zero-current intervals.
Let D be the ON fraction and D_2 the diode-conduction fraction. Under the same ideal small-output-ripple assumption:
I_{\mathrm{pk}}=\frac{(V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o)D}{Lf_s},\qquad D_2=D\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o}{V_o}.
The mean current is the area of the triangle divided by the full period:
I_o=\frac{I_{\mathrm{pk}}}{2}(D+D_2)=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}(V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o)D^2}{2Lf_sV_o}.
Why M no longer equals D: the OFF interval is not clamped to ground for its full duration. The third interval contributes zero inductor voltage, and the duration of diode conduction depends on the output voltage. Current area must also equal the load current.
For a resistive load, let M = V_o/V_{\mathrm{in}} and K = 2Lf_s/R. Then:
KM^2=D^2(1-M),\qquad M=\frac{2}{1+\sqrt{1+4K/D^2}}.
For a specified output voltage and load, solve instead for duty:
D=M\sqrt{\frac{K}{1-M}}.
Always check D + D_2 < 1. If the computed conducting fractions occupy the full period or more, use the boundary or CCM model. Substituting K = 1-D in the DCM gain expression recovers M = D, so the models meet at the boundary. §10.2 applies this model to PMP31349 with diode emulation.

section: E.7 A synchronous buck needs a different mode check
text:
E.7 A synchronous buck needs a different mode check
Replacing the diode with a controlled low-side MOSFET reduces its conduction drop. If the controller keeps that MOSFET on, current can become negative at light load: the converter can remain in forced continuous operation. Diode-emulation control turns the low-side switch off near zero current and permits DCM. The diode-buck mode diagrams above assume negative current is blocked. PMP31349 runs forced PWM; §10.2 shows what diode emulation would change.

title: Appendix E — The 24 V teaching model in DCM
section: E.8 Worked example: does the inductor set the output current?
text:
E.8 Worked example: does the inductor set the output current?
A designer reduces inductance to make a buck converter smaller. Will the output current change, or will only its ripple change?
Predict first. Compare 300 µH with 150 µH. Then predict what happens at 10 µH. Explain which model you would use and what could invalidate it.
This is an authored variant of the teaching model, with a different duty, load and inductance. Its output is free to settle. The 24 V target of E.1 does not apply.







Quantity
Fixed value or assumption




Input voltage
V_{\mathrm{in}} = 48 V


Switching frequency
f_s = 100 kHz, so T_s = 10 µs


Duty ratio
D = 0.70, so t_{\mathrm{on}} = 7 µs


Resistive load
R = 8 Ω


Output capacitor
C = 100 µF, with negligible voltage ripple in the calculations


Power stage
Ideal switch, ideal diode and linear inductor


Operating condition
Periodic steady state, fixed duty, no feedback and no losses



The same DCM analysis applies to a synchronous buck with diode emulation. A forced-PWM synchronous stage can conduct negative current instead (E.7).

Start with the averaged CCM model
For the next two equations, lower-case current and voltage denote averaged states. The duty ratio is d:
L\frac{di_L}{dt}=dV_{\mathrm{in}}-v_o.
C\frac{dv_o}{dt}=i_L-\frac{v_o}{R}.
These are averaged equations. The instantaneous switching waveforms still have ripple. At the steady operating point, the averaged derivatives are zero:
V_o=DV_{\mathrm{in}},\qquad I_L=I_o=\frac{V_o}{R}.
Thus, while CCM remains valid:
V_o=0.70\cdot48=33.6\ \mathrm{V},\qquad I_o=\frac{33.6}{8}=4.20\ \mathrm{A}.
Inductance does not appear in this equilibrium. It sets current slopes, ripple and transient response. Its value also determines whether the assumed conduction mode is possible.
Why CCM retains current memory. The two averaged states are inductor current and capacitor voltage, written as x=(i_L,v_o). For the instantaneous inductor current between successive cycle boundaries:
i_L(t_{k+1})=i_L(t_k)+\frac{1}{L}\int_{t_k}^{t_{k+1}}v_L(t)\,dt.
In CCM, the next cycle inherits a nonzero initial current. In periodic steady state, the integral is zero and the boundary current repeats. Volt-second balance fixes the voltage relation. It does not independently select the current offset. The capacitor balance and load relation complete the equilibrium calculation.


Check the 300 µH current waveform
During the 7 µs ON interval, the inductor voltage is 48 − 33.6 = 14.4 V. During diode conduction, it is −33.6 V. Therefore:
\left.\frac{di_L}{dt}\right|_{\mathrm{on}}=\frac{14.4}{300\ \mu\mathrm{H}}=0.048\ \mathrm{A/\mu s}.
\left.\frac{di_L}{dt}\right|_{\mathrm{off}}=\frac{-33.6}{300\ \mu\mathrm{H}}=-0.112\ \mathrm{A/\mu s}.
The current rises by 0.048 × 7 = 0.336 A. It falls by 0.112 × 3 = 0.336 A. The cycle returns to its initial current:
\Delta I_L=0.336\ \mathrm{A},\qquad I_{L,\min}=4.032\ \mathrm{A},\qquad I_{L,\max}=4.368\ \mathrm{A}.
The valley is positive, so the CCM assumption passes. Here and below, current ripple means peak-to-peak ripple.
The RMS current includes the ripple:
I_{L,\mathrm{RMS}}=\sqrt{I_o^2+\frac{\Delta I_L^2}{12}}=4.20112\ \mathrm{A}.
For the ideal CCM triangle, the mean current during the ON interval equals the full-cycle mean. The input and output powers agree:
I_{\mathrm{in}}=DI_o=2.94\ \mathrm{A}.
P_{\mathrm{in}}=48\cdot2.94=141.12\ \mathrm{W},\qquad P_o=33.6\cdot4.20=141.12\ \mathrm{W}.
With 100 µF, the approximate capacitive output ripple is only 4.2 mV, from \Delta V_o\simeq\Delta I_L/(8f_sC). This supports the small-output-ripple assumption for this case.


Halve the inductance, then find the boundary
At 150 µH, both current slopes double. Ripple becomes 0.672 A, and the current ranges from 3.864 A to 4.536 A. The valley remains positive. Output voltage stays at 33.6 V and mean output current stays at 4.20 A.
Further reduction eventually makes the CCM valley reach zero. Use the boundary condition \Delta I_L=2I_o:
L_{\mathrm{crit}}=\frac{R(1-D)}{2f_s}=\frac{8\cdot0.30}{2\cdot100000}=12\ \mu\mathrm{H}.
At 12 µH, the current rises from zero to 8.4 A and returns to zero exactly at the next switching boundary. Its mean remains 4.20 A. There is no finite zero-current interval.
At 10 µH, the CCM candidate gives 10.08 A ripple and a −0.84 A valley. The diode blocks this negative current. Reject that candidate and use the three-interval DCM model.


Solve the 10 µH DCM operating point
In DCM, the current starts at zero, rises to a peak, then falls continuously to zero. It remains zero until the next ON pulse. The current has no instantaneous jump or reset.
Let D_2T_s be the diode-conduction interval. With negligible output-voltage ripple:
I_{\mathrm{pk}}=\frac{(V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o)D}{Lf_s},\qquad D_2=D\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o}{V_o}.
The triangular current area, divided by the full period, supplies the mean load current:
I_o=\frac{I_{\mathrm{pk}}}{2}(D+D_2)=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}(V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o)D^2}{2Lf_sV_o}.
The output voltage is unknown because there is no voltage-control loop. Combine this equation with I_o=V_o/R. Define:
K=\frac{2Lf_s}{R}=0.25,\qquad M=\frac{V_o}{V_{\mathrm{in}}}.
Then:
KM^2=D^2(1-M),\qquad M=\frac{2}{1+\sqrt{1+4K/D^2}}=0.728918.
The operating point becomes:
V_o=34.9881\ \mathrm{V},\qquad I_o=4.37351\ \mathrm{A},\qquad I_{\mathrm{pk}}=9.10836\ \mathrm{A}.
Check the interval lengths. The diode fraction is 0.260328. The occupied fraction is D+D_2 = 0.960328, which is below one. Diode conduction lasts 2.60328 µs, followed by 0.39672 µs at zero current. This confirms DCM.
Check delivered charge and power. The current triangle delivers 43.7351 µC per cycle. Multiplying by 100 kHz gives 4.37351 A. The input supplies current only during the ON interval:
I_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{DI_{\mathrm{pk}}}{2}=3.18793\ \mathrm{A}.
P_{\mathrm{in}}=153.0205\ \mathrm{W},\qquad P_o=\frac{V_o^2}{R}=153.0205\ \mathrm{W}.
The output rises because the fixed-duty DCM equilibrium depends on inductance and load. It does not establish a regulated current setpoint.

The 10 µH waveform gives approximately 0.118 V capacitive output ripple with 100 µF, about 0.34% of its mean voltage. Integrate i_L-I_o between its zero crossings to get the charge excursion. The CCM ripple formula does not apply to this DCM waveform. These numbers remain small-ripple estimates, not an exact switched-LC solution.


Explain the energy without confusing storage and power
An ideal linear inductor stores energy whenever its current is nonzero:
E_L=\frac{1}{2}Li_L^2,\qquad \frac{dE_L}{dt}=v_Li_L.
Integrate instantaneous power over one complete period in periodic steady state:
\Delta E_L=E_L(T_s)-E_L(0)=\int_0^{T_s}v_L(t)i_L(t)\,dt=0.
The capacitor obeys the same energy balance:
E_C=\frac{1}{2}Cv_C^2,\qquad \Delta E_C=\int_0^{T_s}v_C(t)i_C(t)\,dt=0.
These integrals use instantaneous waveforms. They allow energy exchange within the period while requiring the stored energy to return to its initial value.
For 300 µH, stored energy rises from 2.43855 mJ to 2.86191 mJ during ON. It returns to 2.43855 mJ during OFF. Net inductor-energy change over the complete period is zero. The source still supplies 141.12 W to the load.
At 10 µH, stored energy rises from zero to 0.41481 mJ and returns to zero. The source also supplies the output directly during ON. Therefore, \frac{1}{2}LI_{\mathrm{pk}}^2f_s is not the total buck output power. Here it gives 41.48 W, while the full power balance gives 153.02 W.
The capacitor also returns to its initial energy in periodic steady state. Zero net stored-energy change does not mean zero energy transfer to the load.


Connect filtering, dynamics and current control
For an ideal inductor, Z_L(j\omega)=j\omega L. Its DC impedance is zero, while its reactance increases with frequency. This explains its filtering role. It does not make the complete switched converter a linear time-invariant circuit.
Z_L(0)=0,\qquad |Z_L(j\omega_s)|=\omega_sL=2\pi f_sL.
At 100 kHz, the 300 µH inductor has 188.5 Ω reactance. Each switching harmonic sees its own frequency-dependent reactance. Ripple also depends on the applied voltage harmonics and the complete LC network.
For an inverter filter, also check the fundamental-frequency voltage drop. Its inductor reactance need not be negligible relative to the load impedance.
For advanced work, linearize the averaged CCM model about a positive-current equilibrium. Keep input voltage fixed and assume zero initial perturbations:
Ls\hat i_L(s)=V_{\mathrm{in}}\hat d(s)-\hat v_o(s).
\left(Cs+\frac{1}{R}\right)\hat v_o(s)=\hat i_L(s).
Substitute the second equation into the first:
\left(LCs^2+\frac{L}{R}s+1\right)\hat v_o(s)=V_{\mathrm{in}}\hat d(s).
This gives the duty-to-output-voltage transfer function:
G_{vd}(s)=\frac{\hat v_o(s)}{\hat d(s)}=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}}{LCs^2+(L/R)s+1}.
For this fixed resistor, \hat i_o=\hat v_o/R. Therefore:
G_{id}(s)=\frac{\hat i_o(s)}{\hat d(s)}=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}/R}{LCs^2+(L/R)s+1}.
Use \hat i_L=(Cs+1/R)\hat v_o to get the inductor-current transfer function:
G_{i_Ld}(s)=\frac{\hat i_L(s)}{\hat d(s)}=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}(Cs+1/R)}{LCs^2+(L/R)s+1}.
Load current and inductor current differ during transients because the capacitor carries their difference. These transfer functions support current-loop design in CCM. They do not apply unchanged to DCM.
In the low-frequency DCM model, each pulse starts from a known zero current. The cycle-average inductor current follows algebraically from duty, input voltage and output voltage. The remaining output-capacitor equation gives an approximately first-order voltage model. This reduction assumes operation well below switching frequency and continued DCM.
With d and v_o changing slowly compared with a switching period, that equation is:
C\frac{dv_o}{dt}=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}(V_{\mathrm{in}}-v_o)d^2}{2Lf_sv_o}-\frac{v_o}{R}.
Only the capacitor voltage remains an independent dynamic state in this reduced model. The physical inductor current still changes continuously within each pulse. Its zero-current interval removes the inherited initial-current uncertainty before the next pulse.
Choose from the requirement. For low ripple at the stated 4.20 A operating point, retain enough inductance for positive valley current. Smaller inductance may reduce component size, but increases peak and RMS current. This calculation alone does not select a real magnetic component.
For a commanded mean current, use feedback that measures the required current and adjusts duty within the available voltage range. Across an 8 Ω resistor, 4.20 A requires 33.6 V. If resistance doubles, the same current needs 67.2 V, beyond this 48 V buck’s capability. T2 compares average-current feedback with peak-controlled boundary operation.
Verification. scripts/current_memory_example.py writes data/current-memory-example.json and figure 19. It independently integrates the current ramps and checks mean/RMS current, capacitor charge, energy and power balance. A separate numerical root solves the DCM operating point from integrated charge. It uses the same stated small-output-ripple model.

title: Appendix E — The 24 V teaching model in DCM
section: E.9 Worked example: the fourth leg and a resonant neutral point
text:
E.9 Worked example: the fourth leg and a resonant neutral point
A three-phase four-wire inverter supplies an unbalanced load. Its neutral current disturbs the midpoint of two split DC-link capacitors. An added half-bridge connects to that midpoint through an inductor. This independently controlled neutral leg must carry the neutral current and keep the capacitor voltages balanced.
Engineering question. Does an observed oscillation require DCM, or can a different controller stabilize the continuous-current stage and suppress neutral-point ripple?
Predict first. Choose between current feedback, a resonant controller and DCM. State one benefit, one cost and the measurement that would change your choice. Then test whether damping the resonance necessarily reduces ripple at every frequency.
This example extends the buck reasoning to a bidirectional neutral module with split capacitors. A four-leg inverter without this split-bus connection needs its own model. The values below are authored teaching assumptions. They do not describe PMP31349 or reproduce any cited prototype.







Quantity
Teaching value or assumption




Total DC bus
V_{\mathrm{dc}} = 800 V, held stiff


Split capacitors
C_1=C_2 = 1 mF, with zero ESR in the model


Neutral inductor
L = 0.5 mH, linear


Physical branch resistance
r = 0.05 Ω


Switching frequency
f_s = 20 kHz


Disturbance
One 10 A peak sinusoidal neutral current at a time


Test frequencies
50 Hz, 150 Hz, 350 Hz and 450 Hz


Screening target
Neutral-point displacement below 2 V peak at each test frequency


Initial model
Averaged bidirectional stage, without delay, saturation or switching ripple



The frequency tests apply separate sinusoids. A simultaneous harmonic spectrum requires superposition with its actual amplitudes and phases, followed by current-rating checks.

Derive the neutral-module plant
Let v_n be the midpoint displacement from the center of the bus. The upper capacitor voltage is V_{\mathrm{dc}}/2-v_n. The lower capacitor voltage is V_{\mathrm{dc}}/2+v_n. Their voltage difference is therefore -2v_n. Keep this factor of two when comparing a voltage-imbalance specification with a midpoint-displacement specification.
Let i_L enter the midpoint from the neutral leg, and let i_n leave toward the load. The midpoint sees the sum of the two capacitances because both DC rails are stiff:
C_\Sigma=C_1+C_2=2\ \mathrm{mF}.
This is the capacitance for midpoint motion. The series capacitance across the complete DC bus is a different quantity.
Define u as the average half-bridge voltage relative to the bus center. With upper-switch duty d:
u=V_{\mathrm{dc}}\left(d-\frac{1}{2}\right).
The averaged state equations are:
L\frac{di_L}{dt}=u-v_n-ri_L,\qquad C_\Sigma\frac{dv_n}{dt}=i_L-i_n.
Substitute i_L=C_\Sigma\,dv_n/dt+i_n into the inductor equation:
LC_\Sigma\frac{d^2v_n}{dt^2}+rC_\Sigma\frac{dv_n}{dt}+v_n=u-L\frac{di_n}{dt}-ri_n.
For zero initial perturbations, define the denominator:
D_0(s)=LC_\Sigma s^2+rC_\Sigma s+1.
The command and disturbance transfer functions follow:
\frac{V_n(s)}{U(s)}=\frac{1}{D_0(s)},\qquad \frac{V_n(s)}{I_n(s)}=-\frac{Ls+r}{D_0(s)}.
The same resonance appears in the control path and the neutral-current disturbance path. Stable command tracking alone does not establish adequate disturbance rejection.
For this model:
\omega_0=\frac{1}{\sqrt{LC_\Sigma}},\qquad Q=\frac{1}{r}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C_\Sigma}}.
The teaching values give f_0 = 159.15 Hz and Q = 10. At the natural frequency, command gain is 20 dB above DC gain. The phase falls toward −180° above resonance. A 150 Hz neutral-current component is therefore close to a weakly damped mode.
Do not transfer the buck damping formula unchanged. A resistively loaded ideal buck has Q=R\sqrt{C/L}. This neutral module has Q=\sqrt{L/C_\Sigma}/r. Here, doubling both capacitors lowers f_0 to 112.54 Hz and Q to 7.071. Larger capacitance moves the resonance, but does not automatically increase its peak.
Second-order dynamics also do not prove loss of controllability. With duty as the input, the determinant of the two-state controllability matrix is:
\det[B\ \ AB]=\frac{V_{\mathrm{dc}}^2}{L^2C_\Sigma}>0.
Here A is the state matrix and B is the duty-input vector of the averaged equations. Duty limits, current ratings and sampling delay can still limit achievable performance.


Approach A: compensate the voltage loop directly
Use midpoint error to command voltage, u=-C_v(s)v_n. Then:
\frac{V_n(s)}{I_n(s)}=-\frac{Ls+r}{D_0(s)+C_v(s)}.
A proportional-integral controller has C_v(s)=K_p+K_I/s. Multiplication by s gives the closed-loop characteristic polynomial:
LC_\Sigma s^3+rC_\Sigma s^2+(1+K_p)s+K_I.
For positive gains, the cubic stability condition includes:
K_I<\frac{r(1+K_p)}{L}.
At K_p = 1, the ideal-model bound is K_I<200\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}. Increasing integral gain without sufficient damping can destabilize the loop. A compensator with phase lead can provide another route. Evaluate gain and phase margins with the actual delay and tolerances.
This approach needs only voltage feedback, but a sharp resonance makes a simple PI controller restrictive. A stable low-bandwidth loop can still leave excessive harmonic ripple.


Approach B: add physical damping
A series resistor increases r and reduces Q. It gives damping without relying on sensor bandwidth or software timing. It also dissipates I_{L,\mathrm{RMS}}^2r_{\mathrm{add}} and requires thermal design. An added 0.95 Ω would dissipate 95 W at an assumed 10 A RMS branch current.
This loss example assumes the stated RMS current. It is not a loss prediction for the three frequency-response cases below. A separate RC damping branch is another option, but changes the plant and requires its own design.


Approach C: use inductor-current feedback for active damping
Add a feedback term with gain k_i, measured in volts per ampere:
u=u_c-k_i i_L.
The inductor equation now contains effective resistance r_d=r+k_i. Define:
D_d(s)=LC_\Sigma s^2+(r+k_i)C_\Sigma s+1.
Then:
\frac{V_n(s)}{U_c(s)}=\frac{1}{D_d(s)},\qquad \frac{V_n(s)}{I_n(s)}=-\frac{Ls+r+k_i}{D_d(s)}.
With k_i = 0.95 Ω, effective resistance becomes 1 Ω and Q falls to 0.5. This is critical damping in the simplified command plant. The PI stability bound at K_p = 1 rises to K_I<4000\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}, before delay and other limits.
However, current feedback also changes the disturbance numerator. It opposes the inductor current needed to carry the neutral disturbance. Damping the resonance can therefore increase neutral-point ripple at another frequency. Active damping avoids the added physical resistor, but requires sensing, control headroom and a bus that accepts returned energy.


Approach D: use cascaded current and voltage loops
An inner current loop makes i_L follow i_{\mathrm{ref}}. An outer voltage controller supplies the balancing correction. If the inner loop is much faster than the outer dynamics, use:
i_{\mathrm{ref}}=i_n-C_v(s)v_n.
With ideal current tracking:
C_\Sigma\frac{dv_n}{dt}=-C_v(s)v_n.
For an outer PI controller, the characteristic polynomial becomes C_\Sigma s^2+K_{pv}s+K_{Iv}. The inner loop has removed the LC pair from this reduced outer-loop model. Its gains have current-command units, unlike Approach A’s voltage-command gains.
Real tracking is finite. If G_i(s)=I_L(s)/I_{\mathrm{ref}}(s), the same neutral-current feedforward gives:
\frac{V_n(s)}{I_n(s)}=\frac{G_i(s)-1}{C_\Sigma s+G_i(s)C_v(s)}.
This equation exposes the residual from current-loop lag. Sensor filtering, PWM delay, current saturation and feedforward delay must enter the final model.


Approach E: shape a feedback path with a notch filter
A generic notch building block is:
N(s)=\frac{s^2+2\zeta_z\omega_n s+\omega_n^2}{s^2+2\zeta_p\omega_n s+\omega_n^2},\qquad 0<\zeta_z<\zeta_p.
At \omega_n, its magnitude is \zeta_z/\zeta_p. It reduces the selected path’s gain over a frequency band. In a current-feedback architecture, frequency shaping can alter the trade-off between damping and harmonic ripple.
Filter location matters. A notch in a damping path can also remove needed damping. Component tolerances can move the LC resonance away from the selected notch. Check the complete loop instead of assuming exact pole cancellation.
This generic filter illustrates the design mechanism. Its location and coefficients do not reproduce the published NF-ICFS controller cited below.


Approach F: add proportional-resonant control
A finite-bandwidth proportional-resonant controller can increase correction near a selected neutral-current harmonic:
C_{\mathrm{PR}}(s)=K_p+\frac{2K_r\omega_b s}{s^2+2\omega_b s+\omega_h^2}.
Here \omega_h selects the harmonic and \omega_b sets the resonance bandwidth. Several branches can address several harmonics. A 150 Hz branch is a candidate for this example’s dominant disturbance.
Use a stable inner plant and verify the complete loop. More harmonic gain consumes phase margin and current headroom. Frequency drift and digital delay limit how narrow or strong the resonant branches can be.


Approach G: feed the neutral current forward
For Approach C, add the illustrative feedforward term u_{\mathrm{ff}}=k_i i_n:
u=u_c-k_i i_L+k_i i_n=u_c-k_i(i_L-i_n).
The feedback now acts on the current entering the split capacitors. The denominator remains damped, while the extra disturbance-numerator term cancels:
\frac{V_n(s)}{I_n(s)}=-\frac{Ls+r}{D_d(s)}.
This feedforward removes the virtual-resistance contribution to the disturbance numerator. Physical inductance and resistance still leave an error. An exact model-inverse term would require (Ls+r+k_i)i_n, including a derivative. Noise, parameter error and delay make exact cancellation impractical across arbitrary frequencies.
Neutral-current feedforward can also enter the current reference, as in Approach D. The two implementations need their own scaling and timing checks.


Check the damping and feedforward trade-off numerically
Hold u_c=0 to isolate the three current-path responses. These are screening calculations, without an outer voltage controller. They do not rank fully tuned voltage-control systems. Every column uses the same capacitors, inductor, resistance and disturbance amplitude.









Neutral-current frequency
Natural damping
Current feedback, k_i = 0.95 Ω
Current feedback plus k_i i_n feedforward




50 Hz
1.828 V
9.213 V
1.500 V


150 Hz
32.419 V
5.854 V
2.510 V


350 Hz
2.865 V
2.547 V
1.886 V


450 Hz
2.021 V
1.925 V
1.573 V



All entries are peak midpoint displacement. Capacitor-voltage difference has twice this amplitude. At 150 Hz, current feedback strongly reduces the resonance response. At 50 Hz, the same feedback increases ripple. Feedforward improves both cases, but still misses the 2 V target at 150 Hz.
The 150 Hz case without active damping also predicts 68.41 A peak in the averaged inductor current. This warns that hardware current limits could invalidate the linear response before the predicted oscillation develops.



Command gain and phase with natural and active damping, followed by neutral-current disturbance response for natural damping, current feedback and current feedback with neutral-current feedforward.


Check what averaging hides. At a centered midpoint, forced PWM near 50% duty gives approximately:
\Delta I_{L,\mathrm{pp}}\simeq\frac{V_{\mathrm{dc}}}{4Lf_s}=20\ \mathrm{A}.
This switching ripple is additional to the averaged current. Halving inductance doubles it. A real component selection must check the resulting peak, RMS current and losses. Continuous bidirectional operation can cross zero without having a finite zero-current interval.


Approach H: synthesize a robust controller
An H_\infty design selects a controller against weighted disturbance and control-effort objectives. A generic statement is:
\min_K\left\|T_{w\to z}(K)\right\|_\infty.
Disturbances w can include neutral current, bus perturbations and measurement noise. Weighted outputs z can penalize midpoint displacement and actuator effort. The plant should include relevant uncertainty, delay and sensor dynamics. Actuator saturation still requires a separate nonlinear check.
This method can address competing objectives more systematically than one gain adjustment. It requires a defensible model and weighting choices. No H_\infty controller is synthesized or numerically ranked in this example.


Approach I: change to controlled bidirectional DCM
DCM changes the pulse dynamics rather than only the compensator. For this neutral leg, both current polarities must be supported. A positive pulse rises under the upper switch, falls under the lower switch and reaches zero. A zero-current interval follows before the next pulse. Reverse the switching roles for a negative pulse.
Crossing zero during forced PWM is not DCM. The zero-current interval requires appropriate gating, current detection and semiconductor conduction paths. Parasitic ringing and dead time need a switching model.
For a first pulse calculation, assume v_n\simeq0, neglect r and use bus voltages of ±400 V. Each linear ramp lasts:
t_r=t_f=\frac{2LI_{\mathrm{pk}}}{V_{\mathrm{dc}}}.
For one signed triangular pulse per period:
\rho=f_s(t_r+t_f)=\frac{4Lf_sI_{\mathrm{pk}}}{V_{\mathrm{dc}}}\leq1.
|I_{L,\mathrm{avg}}|=\frac{I_{\mathrm{pk}}\rho}{2}=\frac{2Lf_sI_{\mathrm{pk}}^2}{V_{\mathrm{dc}}}.
The pulse polarity sets the sign of the mean current. For a commanded +5 A mean at 20 kHz:
I_{\mathrm{pk}}=\sqrt{\frac{(5\ \mathrm{A})V_{\mathrm{dc}}}{2Lf_s}}=14.142\ \mathrm{A}.
Each ramp lasts 17.678 µs. The triangle occupies 35.355 µs of the 50 µs period, leaving 14.645 µs at zero current. Its delivered charge is 250 µC. Its RMS current is:
I_{L,\mathrm{RMS}}=I_{\mathrm{pk}}\sqrt{\frac{\rho}{3}}=6.866\ \mathrm{A}.
A −5 A command uses the opposite pulse polarity with the same ideal durations and RMS current. At 10 A mean magnitude, peak current reaches 20 A and \rho=1. That is boundary operation, with 25 µs per ramp and 11.547 A RMS. Strict DCM at this frequency and inductance supports mean magnitudes below 10 A in this idealized pulse model.
The instantaneous neutral-current demand also needs a balancing correction. Commanding its estimated pulse area alone does not guarantee zero capacitor-voltage error. Away from v_n=0, the ramp voltages and charge change. Feedback or voltage-dependent pulse calculation must correct them.
This calculation establishes feasible ideal pulse timing. It does not validate a DCM controller, switching transitions, current ratings or hardware efficiency. The capacitor remains an energy-storage state. Changing conduction mode does not remove the charge needed to correct its voltage.


Change the task: a small leg that only rebalances
The case above assumes that the leg carries the full neutral current. Some designs use the fourth leg only to rebalance the split capacitors. The useful mean current is then small. The inductor is also small, to keep the leg cheap. This changes which effect dominates.
Ask this first for any design. Must the leg carry the full AC neutral current, or only correct the capacitor imbalance? The answer sets the current rating, the inductance and the preferred mode.







Quantity
Teaching value or assumption




Total DC bus
V_{\mathrm{dc}} = 800 V, held stiff


Split capacitors
C_1=C_2 = 12 mF, so C_\Sigma = 24 mF


Neutral inductor
L = 100 µH, linear


Switching frequency
f_s = 20 kHz, so T_s = 50 µs


Useful mean balancing current
2 A


Response target
Correct a 10 V capacitor difference within 2 ms, one tenth of a 50 Hz cycle



The resonance is not the main problem here. The natural frequency is 102.7 Hz. With Q=\sqrt{L/C_\Sigma}/r, a 50 mΩ branch gives Q = 1.29 and a 10 mΩ branch gives Q = 6.45. In this series topology, small inductance and large capacitance lower Q. They do not sharpen the resonance peak. The mode still sits near 100 Hz, so check the neutral-current spectrum there.
Compare the ripple with the useful current. Forced PWM near d = 0.5 gives:
\Delta I_{L,\mathrm{pp}}\simeq\frac{V_{\mathrm{dc}}}{4Lf_s}=100\ \mathrm{A}.
Around a 2 A mean, the current swings from −48 A to 52 A. Its RMS value is:
I_{L,\mathrm{RMS}}=\sqrt{I_L^2+\frac{\Delta I_{L,\mathrm{pp}}^2}{12}}=28.94\ \mathrm{A}.
The leg carries about 29 A RMS to deliver 2 A of useful current. Forced-PWM CCM would need 1 mH, ten times the inductance, to cut the ripple to 10 A peak-to-peak.
Small timing errors move the mean current. At a centered midpoint, the averaged inductor equation is:
L\frac{di_L}{dt}=V_{\mathrm{dc}}\left(d-\frac{1}{2}\right).
A persistent duty error of 0.1 percentage points changes the mean current by 8 A per millisecond. Dead time, PWM resolution and gate-delay errors can reach this size. Current sampling has a similar problem. Each ramp has a slope of 4 A/µs. A 100 ns sampling-phase error reads 0.4 A wrong, which is 20% of the useful current. These errors do not make the loop unstable. They make an accurate small mean current hard to hold.
Command a charge packet instead. Let v_1=V_{\mathrm{dc}}/2-v_n be the upper capacitor voltage and v_2=V_{\mathrm{dc}}/2+v_n the lower one. A positive packet applies v_1 for t_{\mathrm{on}}. It then applies -v_2 until the current reaches zero:
I_{\mathrm{pk}}=\frac{v_1t_{\mathrm{on}}}{L},\qquad t_f=\frac{v_1}{v_2}t_{\mathrm{on}}.
The packet charge is the triangle area:
Q_+=\frac{I_{\mathrm{pk}}}{2}\left(t_{\mathrm{on}}+t_f\right)=\frac{v_1V_{\mathrm{dc}}t_{\mathrm{on}}^2}{2Lv_2}.
For a commanded mean current I^*, the packet charge per period is Q^*=I^*/f_s. Invert the charge equation:
t_{\mathrm{on}}^*=\sqrt{\frac{2LQ^*v_2}{v_1V_{\mathrm{dc}}}}.
A negative packet applies -v_2 first, then v_1. Exchange v_1 and v_2 in both equations for that case. The controller calculates each pulse from the measured capacitor voltages. It does not need a continuous current loop that tracks a small mean inside a large ripple.
At 2 A with balanced capacitors, the packet has a 5 µs ON time and a 20 A peak. It occupies 10 µs of the 50 µs period. Its RMS current is 5.16 A.








Quantity at 2 A mean
Forced-PWM CCM
DCM charge packets




Peak current
52 A
20 A


Valley current
−48 A
0 A


RMS current
28.94 A
5.16 A


Current between periods
Persists and crosses zero twice per period
Stays at zero for 40 µs


Main error source
Duty, dead time and sampling phase
Zero-current detection and pulse timing



Conduction loss in the same resistance scales with the square of RMS current. Here the ratio is 31.4. Each DCM packet also starts at zero current. The device still discharges its output capacitance at turn-on.
Close the outer loop on charge. The capacitor equation sets the outer task:
C_\Sigma\frac{dv_n}{dt}=i_L-i_n.
Command the mean leg current with an estimate \hat i_n of the neutral current:
i_L^*=\hat i_n-\frac{C_\Sigma}{\tau}v_n.
With ideal tracking and an exact estimate, v_n decays with time constant \tau. Limit i_L^* to the leg capability. The packet law then turns each i_L^* into an ON time. A one-period choice, \tau=T_s, would demand a very large current with these capacitors.
The charge limit applies in every mode. A 10 V capacitor difference is a 5 V midpoint displacement. Correcting it moves:
Q=C_\Sigma\,\Delta v_n=24\ \mathrm{mF}\cdot5\ \mathrm{V}=120\ \mathrm{mC}.
In 2 ms this needs a 60 A mean, thirty times the 2 A design current. In the ideal pulse model, DCM at 100 µH and 20 kHz supports at most:
|I_{L,\mathrm{avg}}|_{\max}=\frac{V_{\mathrm{dc}}}{8Lf_s}=50\ \mathrm{A}.
The 60 A demand therefore also leaves DCM. No modulation removes this charge requirement. Reduce the imbalance that the leg must correct, accept a slower response, or size the leg for the current. A balancer that only holds small imbalances can stay small. A leg that must cancel large neutral-current transients needs the full-current design of the first case.
What this case shows. With a small inductor and a small useful current, the CCM difficulty comes mainly from ripple, timing errors and sampling. The LC resonance is not the main cause. DCM charge packets match the current waveform to the charge that must move. This supports DCM for a low-current balancer. It does not make DCM the right choice for a leg that carries the full neutral current.


Compare the choices and the published evidence
The controller equations above are teaching forms. The numerical comparison checks natural damping, proportional current feedback and one feedforward implementation. The pulse calculation checks ideal bidirectional DCM timing. Notch, PR, complete cascaded and robust controllers require further synthesis and validation.









Approach
Benefit
Cost or condition
Evidence in this example




A. Direct voltage compensation
Uses voltage error directly
LC phase transition restricts simple PI gains
Plant and PI stability condition derived


B. Physical damping
Acts without control delay
Dissipation, temperature and changed impedance
Loss relation and conditional resistor example


C. Current feedback
Adds active damping
Can increase disturbance ripple elsewhere
Frequency response and physical ODE checked


D. Cascaded control
Separates current tracking and voltage balance
Needs bandwidth separation and current sensing
Reduced model derived, published experiments cited


E. Notch shaping
Changes a selected feedback band’s gain
Sensitive to placement, drift and lost damping
Generic filter explained, no tuned implementation


F. PR control
Increases correction at selected harmonics
Phase margin, frequency drift and current headroom
Generic controller explained, no tuned implementation


G. Neutral-current feedforward
Anticipates the disturbance
Sensing, scaling and timing errors
Illustrative implementation calculated and checked


H. Robust H_\infty control
Balances weighted competing objectives
Model, uncertainty and synthesis effort
Objective explained, published experiments cited


I. Bidirectional DCM
Removes inherited pulse-current uncertainty
Pulse-current ratings, zero detection and mode boundaries
Signed pulse charge, timing and RMS checked, small-balancer comparison with CCM checked



Zhao et al. (2017) identify the neutral-module resonance and the ripple cost of current feedback. They report notch-assisted, PR-assisted and neutral-current-feedforward control schemes, tested on a 10 kW prototype. These results support the trade-off being taught. They are not measurements of our numerical cases.
Zhong et al. (2006) report robust neutral-point control on a 30 kW inverter. Their abstract gives an 800 V bus and 32 A RMS neutral current. Passalacqua et al. (2022) report a state-space model and experimentally tested cascaded neutral-leg control. These studies show successful control without establishing that our illustrative DCM scheme is necessary or validated.
Conditional recommendation. Begin with a measured plant, a current limit and the neutral-current spectrum. For fixed-frequency continuous operation, investigate cascaded current control with neutral-current feedforward. In this screening example, the 150 Hz residual still exceeds the target. A resonant branch or another compensator is therefore a candidate for the next checked design step.
Choose DCM when its pulse-current limits, zero-current timing and both current polarities meet the requirements. The small balancing leg is the clearest such case: at 2 A, its DCM packets carry 5.16 A RMS against 28.94 A in forced-PWM CCM. For the first case’s ideal pulses, a 10 A mean already reaches the boundary. A larger required current needs different inductance, repetition rate or conduction mode. Compare losses and disturbance rejection before choosing hardware.
Verification. scripts/neutral_leg_example.py writes data/neutral-leg-example.json and figure 20. It checks transfer functions against a state-space solution and an independently written physical KVL/KCL ODE. It also checks periodic energy balance and integrates positive and negative DCM pulse charge and RMS current. For the small balancing leg, it integrates the CCM ripple and the charge packets, and checks the inverse packet law with unequal capacitor voltages. It does not model PWM delay, capacitor ESR, device parasitics or a complete switched inverter.

title: Appendix F — How semiconductor technology changes commutation
text:
F.1 A charge and timing screening example
§6.2 checks charge and time for PMP31349’s 48 V GaN edge. This appendix widens the view to a high-voltage bus and to other device technologies. Every number in it is an authored example, not a selected device.
A charge/timing screening example. Consider a separate illustrative 400 V half-bridge with a constant effective node capacitance of 400 pF. Moving the node through the full bus requires 160 nC. A 2 A commutating current of the correct polarity would require about 80 ns under a constant-current approximation:
Q_{\mathrm{comm}}=\int C_{\mathrm{node}}(v)\,dv,\qquad t_{\mathrm{comm}}\simeq\frac{Q_{\mathrm{comm}}}{|I_{\mathrm{comm}}|}.
This calculation checks charge and time only. It does not prove that the actual circuit can supply the trajectory’s required energy or sustain that current. With zero commutating current, the node does not traverse a capacitive voltage step merely because a zero-current detector has fired.

title: Appendix F — How semiconductor technology changes commutation
section: F.2 Why semiconductor technology changes the preferred commutation
text:
F.2 Why semiconductor technology changes the preferred commutation
Many modern majority-carrier power switches can have relatively low turn-off energy compared with hard turn-on energy. They do not have the channel minority-carrier tail characteristic of an IGBT. That can make a design with low-voltage turn-on and nonzero-current turn-off attractive. It does not make turning off arbitrary current lossless: overlap, gate drive, parasitic inductance, output capacitance, reverse conduction and thermal limits remain.
Compare actual device switching-energy curves at the intended voltage, current, temperature and gate drive. Infineon’s SiC versus IGBT discussion explains this difference in switching-loss mechanisms.
IGBTs add stored minority charge. After the gate is turned off, current can persist while the collector-emitter voltage has already recovered. The resulting tail can contribute substantial turn-off energy. Reducing current through a suitable resonant commutation before high blocking voltage is established can therefore be especially valuable for an IGBT.
ZVS at turn-on alone does not remove a later turn-off tail. Device generations differ greatly, so “ZCS is always better than ZVS for every IGBT” is too broad; compare the complete switching cycle and required commutation time.
Two separate authored loss examples, neither representing a selected device or either 48 V converter of this lesson:

If a 400 V device has a post-transition tail i(t) = 2 A·exp(−t/100 ns), holding approximately 400 V during that tail, its tail energy is 80 µJ. At 100 kHz that mechanism alone contributes 8 W.
A single constant 200 pF device capacitance at 400 V stores 16 µJ. If that stored energy is dissipated at each hard turn-on, it represents 1.6 W at 100 kHz, even with zero preceding load current. A successful resonant transition can redirect or recover this energy, but residual capacitance-related losses still require evaluation.

For a voltage-dependent output capacitance, use the appropriate device energy/charge data or integrate the curve; the small-signal capacitance at one voltage is not sufficient:
E_{\mathrm{oss}}(V)=\int_0^V v C_{\mathrm{oss}}(v)\,dv,\qquad E_{\mathrm{tail}}\simeq V_{\mathrm{bus}}I_{\mathrm{tail},0}\tau.



Separate illustrative models of a capacitive commutation transition, an exponential current tail and loss versus switching frequency.


Why soft switching can support higher frequency: for a repeated event, P_{\mathrm{sw}} \approx f_s\cdot(E_{\mathrm{on}} + E_{\mathrm{off}}). Reducing the dominant event energy allows higher frequency for the same switching-loss budget. Boundary/DCM timing and resonant commutation provide opportunities to do that, while higher peak/RMS current, gate-drive loss, magnetic loss, circulating current and variable-frequency behavior limit the benefit.
Conduction mode, current-control law and commutation strategy should therefore be stated separately when comparing converters.

title: Lesson 2 — The boost converter: what happens, why, and how to design it
text:
Power Electronic Systems · HTWG · 2026
Teaching source: lecture 2, Anwendungen der Leistungselektronik, WS 2025/2026, Riccardo Tinivella / Kurt Schenk, and the boost opening of the lecture of 2026-10-30.
Prerequisite: Lesson 1 (the buck) and the 2026 circuit-foundations recap. Language: English.
A boost converter charges an inductor from the input and then releases that energy into the output capacitor. Every cycle adds a packet of charge, so the output voltage climbs above the input. How far it can climb, and what that climb costs, is the subject of this lesson.
Our example is TI’s PMP21274 reference design. This synchronous boost converts 12–50 V to 54 V at 2.5 A. An LM5122 peak-current-mode controller drives three BSC072N08NS5 silicon MOSFETs at 230 kHz: one high-side synchronous rectifier and two paralleled low-side switches. When the input reaches the output voltage, the controller stops switching and passes the input through.
We start from the specification and work towards a complete design. At each step we compare our estimate with TI’s chosen part and published measurement, as in Lesson 1.
How we work. First, estimate by hand. State the assumptions and predict what the circuit should do. Then simulate the same model and compare the results. Finally, compare with TI’s measurements and explain any gap. A failed choice stays on the page, marked No!, with what must change. Before moving on, name the benefit and the cost of the choice, and say when a credible alternative would become preferable.
This sequence follows C. Basso, Switch-Mode Power Supplies: SPICE Simulations and Practical Designs, McGraw-Hill, 2008, §5.1. The worked examples are our own. The Example scripts reproduce the calculations. §9 explains the PLECS models to draw.
Where the boost is used. The German name is Hochsetzsteller, the converter that only sets the voltage higher. Its output must stay above its input, and it offers no galvanic isolation.
Use a boost when the load needs a higher voltage, and above all when the source wants a continuous input current. A solar panel, a fuel cell or a wind generator is a voltage source with a high internal impedance: load it harder and its voltage drops. Each has one operating point of maximum power. The maximum-power-point tracker (MPPT) that sits in every solar inverter is a boost converter whose input current is modulated until the converter’s input impedance matches the source. A continuous input current also makes the EMC filter easier (lecture of 2026-10-30). Switching frequencies span about 20 kHz to 1 MHz. Most designs run between 70 and 300 kHz.
Not the exact dual of the buck. Read the buck from right to left, exchange the switch and the diode, and you have a boost. The equations look like the buck’s. The stresses do not. The boost works at the input current, which is the output current divided by 1-D. Its output current is pulsed, not continuous. Its switches turn on against the full output voltage. Lesson 1’s buck reaches 95.5 % at 48 V and 20 A. PMP21274 reaches 95.3 % at 12 V and 2.5 A and 97.1 % at 24 V (TI, measured, §8). The lecture put it bluntly: the efficiency a buck reaches is not reachable by a boost at the same ratio.
Reading route. Follow Part I (§1–11) for the complete design. Use Part II (§12) to practise choosing a model and defending a decision. The appendices carry the derivations of the lecture deck: the ideal boost, its characteristic values, the boost with parasitic elements, and critical and discontinuous conduction. §13 gives the sources, the slide map and the numerical checks.

title: Learning outcomes and teaching route
text:
By the end, students should be able to:

explain how a boost converter works and draw its inductor, switch, diode and capacitor currents
derive M(D) = 1/(1-D) from volt-second balance, find the duty extremes, and say why the ratio cannot grow without limit
state the inductor ripple against the input current, and find the input voltage at which it peaks
size L, C_{\mathrm{out}} and C_{\mathrm{in}} for a pulsed output current and a continuous input current, and check real parts under DC bias, saturation and the current limit
calculate mean and RMS stresses of the switch, the rectifier and the output capacitor with the right current measure
explain what the body diode of a silicon MOSFET adds at each switching edge, and what a synchronous rectifier saves
read a boost loop with its right-half-plane zero, and say why the crossover must fall as the input voltage falls
estimate losses and junction temperature from datasheets, and say what a calibration against measurement adds
analyse a boost with parasitic elements, and predict what changes in critical conduction, discontinuous conduction, with a diode rectifier, and in bypass
decide which measurement would change a design choice (Part II).

Never mix the two labels: a curve fitted to TI’s measurement is not our prediction.
Design sequence. Start with the duty range (§2). Then choose the inductor (§3), the output capacitor (§4) and the input capacitor (§5). Check the power stage (§6), the loop (§7), the losses and the temperature (§8). In §9, compare the complete model with TI’s scope captures.
Each step starts with our estimate. We then compare it with TI’s choice and use TI’s actual part in the next step. This keeps the final model comparable with the measured board. All current ripple values are peak to peak unless labelled RMS.
What TI measured. TI published efficiency tables at four inputs and 13 load points (52 rows), thermal images at full load, output-ripple captures, a start-up, a load step at 12 and 24 V and loop gains at four inputs. At 12 V full load the board reaches 95.34 % and loses 6.65 W. Its hottest surface reads 107 °C. TI’s loop crosses at 2.86 kHz at 12 V and at 7.15 kHz at 48 V (all TI, TIDUDX6). The rest of Part I explains these numbers.
Predict before you calculate. Write down three guesses before you read §2–8. At 12 V input, which current does the inductor carry: 2.5 A or about 11 A? At which input voltage is the inductor ripple largest: 12 V, 27 V or 50 V? Which capacitor bank works harder: the input bank or the output bank? Keep the guesses. Each section below checks one of them.

title: 2. Duty-cycle extremes
text:
2.1 Two switch positions, two ramps
While the low side Q2 ∥ Q3 conducts, for DT_s, the switch node sits at ground. The inductor sees the full input, v_L = V_{\mathrm{in}}, and its current rises. While the high side Q1 conducts, for (1-D)T_s, the switch node sits at V_o. The inductor sees v_L = V_{\mathrm{in}} - V_o, which is negative, and its current falls into the output.
Compare the buck. There the inductor voltage during the on-time depended on the output, here it depends on the input. Appendix A.1 draws the two positions of the slides with a diode in place of Q1.
The inductor is in series with the input. The input current is therefore the inductor current at every instant: a triangle around its mean, never zero in CCM. The output gets that current only while Q1 conducts. The boost has a continuous input current and a pulsed output current, the exact opposite of the buck. This one swap explains most of §3–5.
Both switches block the output voltage, whatever the input. The 80 V rating of all three MOSFETs therefore follows from the 54 V output, not from the 50 V input (§6.1).

section: 2.2 Volt-second balance sets the duty
text:
2.2 Volt-second balance sets the duty
In periodic steady state the inductor current returns to its starting value. The mean inductor voltage over one period is therefore zero. Appendix A.2 applies this to the two positions of §2.1 and gets M(D) = V_o/V_{\mathrm{in}} = 1/(1-D), equation (A.2a). With V_o regulated, the duty follows the input. The extremes sit at the ends of the input range:
D_{\max}=1-\frac{V_{\mathrm{in,min}}}{V_o},\qquad D_{\mathrm{nom}}=1-\frac{V_{\mathrm{in,nom}}}{V_o},\qquad D_{\min}=1-\frac{V_{\mathrm{in,max}}}{V_o}\tag{2.1a}
D_{\max}=1-\frac{12}{54}=0.778,\qquad D_{\mathrm{nom}}=1-\frac{24}{54}=0.556,\qquad D_{\min}=1-\frac{50}{54}=0.074\tag{2.1b}
At 48 V the duty is 0.111 (ours). The gain is M = 4.5 at 12 V, 2.25 at 24 V, 1.125 at 48 V and 1.08 at 50 V (ours, design-checks.json). Note the direction: the largest duty belongs to the lowest input.

(ours, ideal, design-checks.json and variation-checks.json). The input current falls by a factor of four over the range, while the output stays at 2.5 A. The duty sweeps almost from 0 to 0.8. A controller that must work over this span needs a stable current loop at high duty (§7.1) and a short enough minimum on-time at low duty.
Can the ratio grow without limit? On paper M = 1/(1-D) goes to infinity as D approaches 1. In the lecture of 2026-10-30 I asked the class where it goes, and the answer came at once: infinity. Then I asked: “do you believe in Santa Claus?” Nobody did. The losses grow with the input current, and the input current grows as 1/(1-D). Beyond a certain duty the real gain stops rising and then collapses (Appendix C.2).
For a reasonable boost in CCM, a ratio of about ten is the practical limit. Above ten or twenty it becomes really difficult. When I was young I built a boost with a ratio of 600. It worked only with discontinuous conduction, soft switching, capacitors that did not leak and a very good inductor. So a higher ratio is possible, but every part must earn it.
The remarks slide puts the CCM limit near M = 6 (Appendix D.3). T1 in Part II computes where the slide’s own example peaks, at M = 5.119 (ours, teaching-checks.json), and shows that the limit scales with the load and the series resistance. PMP21274 stays at M = 4.5, inside every one of these limits.
Practical duty limits. The LM5122 needs a minimum low-side on-time, about 158 ns with this slope resistor (ours, from SNVS954H). At 230 kHz that is a duty of 0.036 (ours, variation-checks.json). Our D_{\min} = 0.074 at 50 V is about twice that, so the board still regulates at the top of its range. §10.4 shows what happens above it. At the low end, D_{\max} = 0.778 leaves the high side 22 % of the period. That is short, but far from the limit.

2.3 What each current does, and why the ideal boost is lossless
The input power must equal the output power in the ideal boost, so the mean input current follows from the power balance:
I_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{V_o\,I_o}{V_{\mathrm{in}}}=\frac{I_o}{1-D}\tag{2.2a}
I_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{54\ \mathrm{V}\cdot2.5\ \mathrm{A}}{12\ \mathrm{V}}=11.25\ \mathrm{A}\tag{2.2b}
That is 11.25 A (ours) for a 2.5 A load. TI measured 11.844 A at 12.039 V and 2.522 A (TI, TIDUDX6 Sec. 4.2). The difference pays the losses of §8. At that point TI’s table gives 142.586 W in and 135.937 W out (TI, measured_efficiency.csv).
The boost works at the input current. Every element in series with the inductor, the shunt, the winding and the low-side pair, carries 4.5 times the load current at 12 V. This is where the boost hurts, and §8 counts the cost.

The inductor RMS includes the ripple. With the 4.06 A ripple of §3 included, the low side, high side and output capacitor carry 9.975, 5.332 and 4.710 A RMS (ours, equations (B.7b) to (B.9b)). The small-ripple values are less than 0.7 % lower.
Read the last two rows together. The output capacitor carries 4.68 A RMS for a 2.5 A load: it takes the pulse, +8.75 A while Q1 conducts and −2.50 A while it does not (ours). The input capacitor carries only the 1.17 A of the triangle. In the buck it was the other way round.
The input power is V_{\mathrm{in}}\cdot I_{\mathrm{in}} = V_o\cdot I_o = 135 W (ours). The ideal boost is a DC transformer with ratio 1/(1-D): it steps the voltage up and the mean current down, and it loses nothing. The losses of §8 come from the components, not from the principle (Appendix B.4).
What the extremes decide. At 12 V, D_{\max} gives the largest input current, so the largest conduction loss in the shunt, the winding and the low side (§8). It also gives the longest low-side on-time and the largest output-capacitor charge per period (§4). The inductor ripple, in contrast, peaks in the middle of the range (§3). Different checks have different worst cases.
TI chose, TI measured. TI chose the 12–50 V range and the 54 V output, so the extremes follow directly. On the board, the conduction and dead-time losses push the duty slightly above the ideal value. Our datasheet loss model with TI’s parts needs D = 0.781 at 12 V and 2.5 A, against the ideal 0.778 (ours, loss-estimate-checks.json). TI’s scope shows a period of 4.39 µs, that is 228 kHz (ours, read from figure, TIDUDX6 Sec. 6.1).
What we can choose. The voltage ratio fixes the ideal duty. A different source voltage changes the duty, the input current and every stress together. At a ratio far above ten, the decision is no longer a duty but a topology: two stages, a coupled inductor or a transformer (T1). We keep TI’s range and continue with the inductor.

title: 3. The inductor
section: 3.3 Checks against the real part
text:
3.3 Checks against the real part

Saturation. Coilcraft specifies a 10 % drop of inductance at 18.0 A, 20 % at 21.5 A and 30 % at 23.4 A (TI’s part, Coilcraft Doc 644-1). Our 13.28 A peak at 12 V and full load leaves 4.72 A of margin (ours). It passes.
Hard saturation. The SER2915H is a ferrite E core, not a metal composite like Lesson 1’s Würth part. A gapped ferrite keeps its inductance flat and then loses it within a small increase of current. The current slope v_L/L then rises steeply, and the current can run away within a few cycles. With a ferrite core the rule “peak below Isat” is strict.
Current limit: No! The LM5122 ends the low-side pulse when 75 mV appear across R2. With 4 mΩ that is 75 mV/4 mΩ = 18.75 A (ours, from SNVS954H Sec. 7.3.10). This lies above the 18.0 A at which the core has lost 10 %. In an overload or a start-up into a short, the core saturates before the limit acts. Only the 65.5 mV minimum of the threshold, 16.4 A, lies below Isat (ours). Always check the inductor at the current limit, not only at full load. To fix it, raise R2 so that the limit falls below Isat. The shunt loss of §8.1 then rises in proportion. Or choose a core with a higher Isat.
Heating. Coilcraft rates the part at 20 A RMS for a 20 K rise and 30 A for 40 K (TI’s part). At 11.31 A RMS it runs well inside. The DCR is 1.86 mΩ typical and 2.05 mΩ maximum.
Self-resonance. The 15 MHz self-resonant frequency is far above the 230 kHz switching frequency and its first harmonics (TI’s part).
Tolerance. Check the ripple and the peak at the low end of the inductance tolerance, and with the inductance the core still has at the peak current. With a hard-saturating core the second effect is small below Isat and large above it.
Slew rate. A larger L lowers the ripple but also the current slew rate V_{\mathrm{in}}/L that the controller can command. In a boost the RHP zero (§7) already limits the loop. A slower current makes it worse.

Why the inductor sits on the input side of the shunt. TI places R2 between the input and L1 (TIDRTY1). The shunt therefore sees the inductor current continuously, not only during the on-time. The LM5122 can sense the peak, the valley and the zero crossing (§10.2) with one resistor. The cost is the loss of §8.1: 0.55 W at 12 V (ours), because the shunt carries I_{\mathrm{in}} all the time.
TI chose, TI measured. TI chose a 10 µH Coilcraft SER2915H-103KL, below our 12.0 µH. The ripple at 12 V is therefore 0.36 of the input current, a little above our 0.30. TI did not measure the inductor current. §9 checks the ripple it causes at the output. From here on the lesson continues with TI’s 10 µH, and with the current-limit failure on the page.

In a boost, the inductor ripple is the input ripple. The triangle of §2.3 flows into the input bank. Its RMS value, \Delta I_L/\sqrt{12}, grows ten times from the 10 % to the 100 % design. The output capacitor barely notices. Its current is the pulse of I_{\mathrm{in}}, and the pulse depends on the mean, not on the ripple.
Choose 10 % when input-ripple and peak-current stress matter. The input bank and the EMC filter see a small triangle, and the peak stays near the mean. The cost is three times the inductance of our design, a larger part, and a current that changes three times more slowly.
Choose 100 % when a small inductor justifies the ripple. The inductance falls to 3.607 µH. The peak reaches 16.88 A, and the new part must be rated for it with margin. The input bank must take ten times the ripple current. This remains CCM at full load: the valley is still 5.63 A. At light load it moves into DCM or into negative current much sooner (§10.2).
Is low ripple always more efficient? No. It depends on which loss dominates. Low ripple lowers the core loss and the input-capacitor RMS current. It barely changes the conduction loss, because I_{L,\mathrm{rms}} stays close to I_{\mathrm{in}} (11.255 A against 11.709 A). In a boost, lower ripple also raises the valley. A higher valley raises the turn-on overlap loss at V_o (§8.1). In industry the final choice is usually cost, weighed against efficiency and volume.
Our decision. Keep 30 % at 12 V as the target and continue with TI’s 10 µH, which gives 36 %. The benefit is a moderate peak, 13.28 A, inside a strict ferrite Isat. The cost is a 4.06 A triangle at the input. The 10 % design becomes preferable if the input filter, not the inductor volume, limits the product. A measurement of the conducted emissions on the input would change the choice.
Your choice. Suppose the input EMC filter is the limiting constraint. Which direction would you try first? Now suppose the load step is too slow. Explain what you would change and which earlier check you must repeat.

title: 4. The output capacitor
text:
4.1 Charge balance with a pulsed current
Before calculating, predict. In the buck of Lesson 1 the output ripple was millivolts and the input ripple was volts. Which bank of the boost will show volts?
The capacitor has the dual property of the inductor. In periodic steady state the charge delivered to a capacitor equals the charge removed, so its mean current is zero. In the boost this balance has a sharp shape. While the low side conducts, Q1 is off and the output capacitor alone supplies the load: i_C = -I_o for DT_s. While Q1 conducts, the inductor current refills it: i_C = i_L - I_o for (1-D)T_s.
The capacitor loses a rectangle of charge every period. No inductor smooths this current: the output of a boost sees what the input of a buck sees. Appendix B.3 derives the ripple, \Delta V_o = I_o D/(f_s C), equation (B.3a).

title: 4. The output capacitor
section: 4.2 The ripple-only choice: No!
text:
4.2 The ripple-only choice: No!
Solve (B.3a) for the capacitance at our 540 mV limit. The worst case is the largest duty, 12 V:
C\geq\frac{I_o\,D_{\max}}{f_s\,\Delta V_o}\tag{4.1a}
C\geq\frac{2.5\ \mathrm{A}\cdot0.778}{230\ \mathrm{kHz}\cdot0.54\ \mathrm{V}}=15.7\ \mu\mathrm{F}\tag{4.1b}
Our ripple limit alone asks for 15.7 µF (ours).
Real parts: DC bias. TI places four 4.7 µF 80 V X7R 1210 ceramics, C5–C8, at the Q1 node (TI, TIDRTY2). At 54 V a class-II ceramic keeps only a fraction of its nominal value. We assume 2.0 µF per part at 54 V, read from the shape of Murata’s DC-bias curve (ours, an assumption). The bank gives 8 µF. With (B.3a) that is a ripple of 1.06 V at 12 V (ours), twice our 540 mV limit. No!
Why so much more than a buck? Put the same 8 µF on a buck-like triangle of the same 4.06 A. The ripple would be \Delta I_L/(8 f_s C) = 0.276 V (ours). The pulsed current gives 3.83 times more (ours, design-checks.json). A boost’s output bank must be sized for a pulse, not for a triangle.

title: 4. The output capacitor
section: 4.3 TI’s second stage: L2 and C20
text:
4.3 TI’s second stage: L2 and C20
TI does not add ceramics. TI adds a second filter stage instead: L2 = 1 µH (XAL4020-102, 10 mΩ), then C20 = 47 µF 80 V aluminium at VOUT (TI). The feedback divider and the test point TP7 sit after L2 (TIDRTY1). The pulsed Q1 current flows into node A, the ceramics C5–C8. Node B, VOUT, is fed from node A through L2.
With Z_{C1} = r_{C1} + 1/(sC_1) for C5–C8, Z_{C20} = r_{C20} + 1/(sC_{20}) and Z_{L2} = r_{L2} + sL_2, the two node impedances and the transfer to VOUT are:
Z_B=\frac{1}{1/Z_{C20}+1/R},\qquad H=\frac{Z_B}{Z_{L2}+Z_B},\qquad Z_A=\frac{1}{1/Z_{C1}+1/(Z_{L2}+Z_B)}\tag{4.2a}
|Z_A|=0.091\ \Omega,\qquad |Z_B|=0.678\ \Omega,\qquad |H|=0.427\qquad(230\ \mathrm{kHz},\ r_{C20}=0.7\ \Omega)\tag{4.2b}
(ours, design-checks.json). The L2–C20 corner is at 23.2 kHz (ours), a decade below f_s. With an ideal C20 the stage would divide by about 100: |H| = 0.010 (ours). With the BOM’s 0.7 Ω it divides by only 2.3. At 230 kHz C20 is a resistor, so its ESR, not its capacitance, sets the attenuation.
Harmonic series. The pulsed Q1 current has a Fourier series I_k at k\,f_s. Each harmonic drives Z_A, and H carries it to VOUT. Summing 400 harmonics gives 1.09 V peak to peak at C5–C8 and 0.378 V at VOUT at 12 V (ours, design-checks.json). The output passes our 540 mV limit. TI measured about 190 mV of smooth ripple at VOUT at 12 V, 210 mV with the edge spikes (ours, read from figure, TIDUDX6 Sec. 6.1). §9.1 explains the factor of two.
C19 and C20 are bulk and damping parts, not ripple parts. The BOM lists them as EEE-FK 47 µF 80 V with “0.7 Ω” (TI, TIDRTY2). Their ESR damps the L2–C20 resonance and the input filter. Their capacitance holds the output during a load step (§4.4).
Why the boost needs a second stage that the buck did not. In the buck the inductor sits in series with the output, so the output bank sees only a triangle, and the inductor itself is the filter. In the boost the inductor sits at the input. Nothing smooths the Q1 pulse before it reaches the output bank. L2 and C20 give the output the series inductor that the topology lacks. The same argument puts the extra filter at the input of a buck (Lesson 1 §5).

title: 4. The output capacitor
section: 4.4 The load step, the RHP zero and the ESR: No!

title: 5. The input capacitor
text:
The input current is the inductor current: continuous, a mean with a triangle on top (§2.3). If the source supplies only the mean, the input bank takes the triangle. The ripple voltage follows from the charge of half the triangle, as for the buck’s output capacitor (Lesson 1 §4.2):
\Delta V_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{\Delta I_L}{8\,f_s\,C_{\mathrm{in}}}\quad\Rightarrow\quad C_{\mathrm{in}}\geq\frac{\Delta I_L}{8\,f_s\,\Delta V_{\mathrm{in}}}\tag{5.1a}
C_{\mathrm{in}}\geq\frac{4.06\ \mathrm{A}}{8\cdot230\ \mathrm{kHz}\cdot0.1\ \mathrm{V}}=22.1\ \mu\mathrm{F}\tag{5.1b}
Our 100 mV target at 12 V asks for 22.1 µF (ours). TI places three 4.7 µF 80 V X7R ceramics, C2–C4, and the 47 µF aluminium C19 (TI). At 12 V a ceramic keeps about 4.2 µF (ours, DC-bias assumption), so the ceramics give 12.6 µF. By (5.1a) the ripple is 175 mV, and 174 mV with C19 in the harmonic model (ours). No! It exceeds our 100 mV target by 75 %. TI did not capture the input ripple, so this failure is against our target only.
The RMS stress is small:
I_{C\mathrm{in,rms}}=\frac{\Delta I_L}{\sqrt{12}}\tag{5.2a}
I_{C\mathrm{in,rms}}=\frac{4.06\ \mathrm{A}}{\sqrt{12}}=1.17\ \mathrm{A}\tag{5.2b}
Only 1.17 A RMS reach the input bank, against 4.68 A at the output (ours).

The worst case is not at 12 V. The input ripple grows with \Delta I_L, which peaks at 27 V (§3.1). The ceramics also lose capacitance as the input rises. The fitted model of §9.1 gives 174 mV at 12 V, 312 mV at 24 V, 337 mV at 36 V and 188 mV at 48 V (ours, ripple-checks.json). Our target covers only 12 V. If the 100 mV applied over the range, the bank would need even more capacitance at 36 V.
What the model leaves out. The model leaves the source path open: all AC current flows into the bank. On the bench the source and its leads take part of it. The PLECS model of §9.2 includes a 5 mΩ, 2 µH bench source (ours) to show this effect.
Decision. The benefit of TI’s small bank is cost and area: 1.17 A RMS do not need more ceramics for heating. The cost is a ripple of 175 mV against our 100 mV, and more at mid-range. If 100 mV is mandatory, add effective ceramic capacitance first: (5.1b) asks for 22.1 µF at 12 V, at least six 4.7 µF parts at 4.2 µF each. A credible alternative is a small LC filter ahead of the bank, which a solar or automotive input often needs anyway for EMC. A measurement of the input ripple at 24 and 36 V would decide which.

title: 6. The power stage: silicon MOSFETs, body diodes and a snubber
crumbs: 139  6. The power stage: silicon MOSFETs, body diodes and a snubber

title: 6. The power stage: silicon MOSFETs, body diodes and a snubber
section: 6.2 Which device switches at zero, and at which edge
text:
6.2 Which device switches at zero, and at which edge
Name the device and the edge before calling a transition soft (Lesson 1 §6.2). In the boost the roles swap compared with the buck.








Edge
Valley positive (I_o above the boundary)
Valley negative (forced PWM, light load)




Low side off → high side on (55 ns)
the positive inductor current charges the switch node up to V_o. Q1’s body diode conducts, and Q1 turns on at zero voltage
the same: the current at this edge is the peak, which is positive


High side off → low side on (75 ns)
the current keeps flowing through Q1’s body diode. Q2 ∥ Q3 turn on hard at V_o: they discharge the node, overlap V_o with the valley current and recover Q1’s diode
the reversed current swings the node down toward ground during the dead time. Q2 ∥ Q3 turn on at reduced voltage (partial ZVS), and Q1’s diode does not recover



So the hard edge of the boost is the low-side turn-on, at the output voltage. In the buck it was the high-side turn-on, at the input voltage. TI’s board runs forced PWM: Q1 stays on through the valley even when the current reverses. The valley goes negative when the load is below
I_o<\frac{(1-D)\,\Delta I_L}{2}\tag{6.3a}
I_o<\frac{0.222\cdot4.06\ \mathrm{A}}{2}=0.45\ \mathrm{A}\qquad(12\ \mathrm{V})\tag{6.3b}
The boundary is 0.45 A at 12 V, 1.29 A at 24 V, 1.74 A at 36 V and 1.03 A at 48 V (ours). The factor (1-D) appears because the load current is the inductor current times 1-D.
Charge and time must both suffice. To swing the node from V_o to zero, the reversed current must move the output charge of all three MOSFETs and the snubber capacitor within the 75 ns dead time:
|I_v|\geq\frac{3\,Q_{\mathrm{oss}}(V_o)+C_1\,V_o}{t_{dHL}}\tag{6.4a}
|I_v|\geq\frac{3\cdot32.6\ \mathrm{nC}+470\ \mathrm{pF}\cdot54\ \mathrm{V}}{75\ \mathrm{ns}}=\frac{123\ \mathrm{nC}}{75\ \mathrm{ns}}=1.64\ \mathrm{A}\tag{6.4b}
Q_{\mathrm{oss}} = 32.6 nC per device at 54 V comes from the datasheet C_{\mathrm{oss}} curve, scaled to 29 nC at 40 V (ours, design-checks.json). At 0.25 A the valley reaches −0.86 A at 12 V and −0.87 A at 48 V, so the swing stays partial there. At 24 and 36 V it reaches −2.30 A and −2.22 A, past the 1.64 A of (6.4b) (ours, variation-checks.json). Forced PWM buys full ZVS of the low side only at light load in the middle of the range. Never call a transition ZVS before checking current direction, charge and time.
Your choice. You may shorten the 75 ns dead time or remove the 470 pF snubber. Which one helps the partial ZVS of (6.4a) more, and what does each cost at the hard edge?
The snubber across Q1. Q1’s turn-off and the low side’s hard turn-on ring in the loop of the switch node, the MOSFET capacitances and the board inductance. TI places C1 = 470 pF and R1 = 7.5 Ω in series across Q1 (TI, TIDRTY1). The capacitor charges to V_o and discharges every period. Its full energy, twice C_1V_o^2/2, ends in R1 and the channels:
P_{\mathrm{snub}}=C_1\,V_o^2\,f_s\tag{6.5a}
P_{\mathrm{snub}}=470\ \mathrm{pF}\cdot(54\ \mathrm{V})^2\cdot230\ \mathrm{kHz}=0.32\ \mathrm{W}\tag{6.5b}
The snubber costs 0.32 W at every input and every load (ours). It also adds 25 nC to the node charge of (6.4b) and makes the partial ZVS harder. At light load this fixed loss dominates (§8.4).
Bypass. At V_{\mathrm{in}} \geq V_o the LM5122 stops switching and keeps Q1 on, if V_o \geq 9 V and the controller runs forced PWM (SNVS954H Sec. 7.3.9). The input then passes to the output through L1, R2 and Q1. §10.4 shows why the board stops at 50 V.
TI chose, TI measured. TI chose one MOSFET type for all three positions, two in parallel at the low side, an RC snubber and forced PWM. TI did not publish the dead time or the switch-node ringing. The benefit of silicon: an 80 V part with 7.2 mΩ maximum at 10 V, a standard driver and no GaN layout constraints. The cost: the body-diode drop in both dead times and 0.46 W of reverse recovery at 12 V (ours, high estimate). A GaN half-bridge removes the recovery term and shortens the dead time. It becomes preferable when the switching loss at V_o dominates, at high V_o or high f_s. §8 shows that this is already the case at 12 V. The diode of the slides (§10.3) is the other alternative, with the opposite trade-off.

With TI’s compensation the model crosses 1.2 to 1.8 times higher than TI’s four markers, with more phase at 12 V: the BOM’s 0.7 Ω ESR of C20 puts a zero at crossover.


Why TI crosses lowest at 12 V. At 12 V the RHP zero sits at 17.0 kHz. The rule f_{RHP}/4 gives 4.24 kHz, and TI crossed at 2.86 kHz. The phase margin is only 41°, and the gain margin is 12.2 dB at 8.69 kHz (TI). There the RHP zero’s phase lag has already pulled the phase through −180°. At high input the RHP zero moves out to 68 kHz at 24 V and 272 kHz at 48 V (ours). Then the modulator gain A_M, which grows with 1-D = V_{\mathrm{in}}/V_o, sets the crossover, and f_c rises with the input. The crossover of a boost must fall as the input falls. TI’s 2.86 kHz at 12 V against 7.15 kHz at 48 V is exactly that.
The gap: the model crosses 1.2 to 1.8 times higher. The model’s crossover grows faster with the input than TI’s. The cause is an input, not the Table 2 model. Above C20’s ESR zero, 4.84 kHz, the output impedance is about the ESR, so f_c scales with it. The BOM’s 0.7 Ω is likely the part’s maximum. With 0.2 Ω the four margins become 52°, 47°, 42° and 36° against TI’s 41°, 45°, 43° and 42° (ours vs TI). The ripple check of §9.1 points the same way: 0.35 Ω fits TI’s output-ripple captures best.
Now check the competing explanations. Modelling L2 as a full network instead of a short moves the crossover at 12 V from 3.53 to 3.54 kHz. A constant-current load instead of a resistor moves it to 3.62 kHz (ours, esr_sensitivity.other). Neither explains a factor of 1.8.

title: 7. Closing the loop
section: 7.3 The load step, and the price of the RHP zero
text:
7.3 The load step, and the price of the RHP zero



On the 1.25 → 2.5 A step the averaged model drops 1.09 V at 12 V and 0.82 V at 24 V, against about 1.0 V and 0.6 V that TI measured. Our limit is 1.0 V.


The averaged model runs the same loop around 2.5 A with a constant-current load and a 10 µs edge (ours, TI states no slew rate). On the 1.25 → 2.5 A step it drops 1.09 V at 12 V and recovers within 0.69 ms. At 24 V it drops 0.82 V and recovers within 0.49 ms (ours, loop-checks.json). TI measured about −1.0 V at 12 V and about −0.6 V at 24 V, with recovery within about 1 ms (ours, read from figure, TIDUDX6 Sec. 6.3). The overshoot on the step back is about +1.0 V and +0.6 V (ours, read from figure).
At 12 V the model fails our 1.0 V limit by 0.09 V. No!, marginally, and TI’s capture sits right on the limit. At 24 V the model is pessimistic. Two inputs pull in opposite directions there: the 0.7 Ω ESR raises the model’s drop, and its higher crossover lowers it. TI’s trace also includes the switching ripple. The estimate (4.3a) gave 0.85 V for TI’s 55 µF at 4.24 kHz.
The RHP zero is the price. A buck of this power could cross at f_s/10 and hold the same step with a fraction of the capacitance. The boost cannot cross above a quarter of its RHP zero at the lowest input. It pays with a larger bank, here an aluminium part, and a step that uses the whole 1.0 V. A smaller L raises f_{RHP} in proportion and allows a faster loop. It costs more ripple at the input (§3.4) and a higher peak current. A larger C20 or a lower-ESR part keeps the crossover and lowers the drop. If 1.0 V is mandatory at 12 V, add bulk capacitance first, then recheck the ESR condition (4.4a) and the loop.
TI chose, TI measured. TI set R17, C18 and C17 for about 3 kHz at 12 V and measured 41–45° of phase margin at all four inputs (TI). We keep TI’s compensation and its bank. The start-up confirms the slow loop: the output starts at the input level through L1 and Q1’s body diode and reaches 54 V about 15 ms after the input (ours, read from figure, TIDUDX6 Sec. 6.2). C16 = 0.1 µF with 10 µA gives a 12 ms soft start (ours, derived).
Your choice. Suppose the customer asks for a 0.5 V limit on the same step at 12 V. Would you add capacitance, lower L, or both? Say which check of §3–4 you must repeat for each, and which measurement on TI’s board would tell you how much margin the loop really has.

(ours vs calibrated to TI, reverse-engineering-checks.json). The fit moves the budget at 12 V and 2.5 A from 5.19 W to 7.26 W.
The 14.9 mΩ is the story. The fit adds a series resistance in the inductor-current path. At 12 V it carries I_{L,\mathrm{rms}}^2 and costs 2.10 W, more than the low-side conduction, the DCR and the shunt together (0.54 + 0.33 + 0.55 W). Where can 14.9 mΩ hide? In the PCB copper and the vias between R2, L1 and the MOSFETs, in the AC resistance of L1’s winding at 230 kHz and its harmonics, and in the solder joints of a 4 mΩ shunt. All of them carry the input current. A buck hides the same milliohms at the output current. In a boost every milliohm in the input path costs I_{\mathrm{in}}^2, and at 12 V the input current is 4.5 times the output current.
What the fit cannot tell apart. k_{\mathrm{oss}} and k_{rr} multiply nearly the same basis, a charge times V_o f_s, constant with load wherever the low side turns on hard. The fit can split their sum almost freely. Only the light-load points, where partial ZVS removes the two terms in different ways, tell them apart. The same holds for the extra resistance against the conduction terms. As in Lesson 1, a dead-time term at zero does not prove that the board has no dead-time loss. Read the fitted budget as one consistent explanation of TI’s 52 rows, not as a measurement of each term.



Fitted to TI’s 52 rows, the seven-term loss model tracks the measured efficiency to 0.39 pp rms over the 48 loaded points: calibration, not prediction.





Calibrated breakdown at 12 V (ours, calibrated to TI): at full load the fitted extra resistance, the turn-on overlap and the output charge dominate. Below about 0.45 A the low side gains partial ZVS and the overlap and recovery terms vanish.


The fitted model gives 94.90 % and 7.26 W at 12.0 V and 2.5 A (ours, calibrated to TI). TI measured 95.34 % at 12.039 V and 2.522 A. The fit is a compromise over 52 rows, and its largest single loss error is 0.84 W. Never present the fitted curve as a prediction: it agrees with TI because we fitted it to TI.

8.5 Junction temperature: No!
Each low-side device carries half the pair’s conduction, overlap, output-charge and recovery loss: 1.52 W at 12 V (ours). With the datasheet’s thermal resistance:
T_j=T_a+P_{LS}\,R_{\theta JA}\tag{8.5a}
T_j=25\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}+1.52\ \mathrm{W}\cdot50\ \mathrm{K/W}=101\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\qquad(12\ \mathrm{V},\ 2.5\ \mathrm{A})\tag{8.5b}
R_{\theta JA} = 50 K/W is Infineon’s value for one device alone on a 40 × 40 mm FR4 board with 6 cm² of one-layer copper (TI’s part, BSC072N08NS5 Table 3). TI measured a 107 °C hot spot at 12 V full load, with no airflow and a 22–24 °C background (TI, TIDUDX6 Sec. 5). The hot area is the low-side pair and inductor region.
