107 °C is a thermal-camera reading, the scale maximum of the image. It is a surface temperature, not T_j. The surface cannot be hotter than the junction under it. If the hot spot is a low-side MOSFET, its junction is at least 107 °C, and our 101 °C is low. No! Our estimate is optimistic. The datasheet losses are low by 1.45 W at this point (§8.1). The 25 °C ambient is ours.
The comparison is also unfair the other way. On the board three MOSFETs, the inductor, the shunt and the snubber resistor heat the same copper. R_{\theta JA} assumes one device alone on 6 cm². Always compare like with like: a thermal-camera reading is a surface temperature, and a datasheet R_{\theta JA} is not this board. At 24 and 48 V the estimate also sits just below the surface reading. That the other three inputs agree within about a kelvin is a coincidence of two errors, not a validation.
What would we improve first? At 12 V, find the 14.9 mΩ: measure the drop from the input connector to the switch node at full load. A lower-resistance layout attacks the largest fitted term. Then the overlap: a stronger low-side gate drive shortens the 12.6 ns, but it raises the ringing that the snubber must damp. At 48 V the fixed terms dominate: snubber, output charge and gate drive. There a smaller snubber capacitor or a GaN stage helps more. Let the intended operating range decide which comes first.
Your choice. The product will run 90 % of its life at 24 V and half load. Which three loss terms of the table would you attack first, and which of them does the fit of §8.4 tell you to distrust?

title: 9. Proof by simulation
text:
9.1 Python waveform checks against TI’s scope captures
ti-pmp21274/scripts/ripple_checks.py solves the four operating points TI captured: full load at 12, 24, 36 and 48 V, at the measured 228 kHz (period 4.39 µs). It uses TI’s parts and the losses calibrated on TI’s measurement (§8.4). It then sums the harmonics of the pulsed Q1 current through the two output stages of §4.3, and of the inductor triangle through the input bank of §5 (ripple-checks.json):
(ours, model, and ours, read from figure, TIDUDX6 Sec. 6.1). TI probed VOUT, after L2. TI did not probe node A.
The single-capacitor estimate misses by a factor of almost six. At 12 V the first-order formula on C5–C8 gives 1.10 V. TI measured 190 mV at VOUT, less than a fifth of it. The second stage explains the factor. The model’s second stage divides by only 2.9 at 12 V, because C20’s ESR, not its capacitance, sets its impedance at f_s. The model therefore stays high by a factor of 2.1, 2.3, 1.8 and 1.6 at the four inputs.
The gap points to the same input as the loop. We sweep only C20’s ESR and keep the rest (ours, esr_sweep):
The sweep’s best is 0.35 Ω, with 21 mV rms error. The loop gap of §7.2 points the same way. Two independent measurements, the loop gain and the ripple, agree that C20’s ESR on the board is about half the BOM’s 0.7 Ω. The C5–C8 derating, 2.0 µF each at 54 V, is ours and moves the result as well. TI’s trace adds the switching spikes from the probe loop and the ESL, which the model leaves out. We keep 0.7 Ω in the base model and report the gap. Tuning it to 0.35 Ω would hide the one question an impedance measurement can answer.
What these checks prove. They show that the two-stage ripple model, with one plausible input changed, reproduces four captures in shape and size. They do not prove that C20’s ESR is 0.35 Ω: the ceramic derating and the probe also move the result. The loop gap and the ripple gap point to the same part. That makes C20 the first part to measure, not a solved question.
Input ripple. The model gives 174 mV at 12 V, 312 mV at 24 V, 337 mV at 36 V and 188 mV at 48 V, with the source path open (ours). TI did not capture it. §5’s No! stands until a measurement replaces the model.
The other two proofs are already on the page: the efficiency curve against TI’s measured points (§8.3) and the averaged load step against TI’s capture (§7.3).

title: 10. What if? Four variations of the finished design
text:
10.1 Critical (boundary) conduction: No!
The base design runs in continuous conduction at full load over the whole range. Appendix D.1 gives the condition: with K = 2Lf_s/R, CCM holds while K > K_{\mathrm{crit}} = D(1-D)^2. That boundary has its maximum, 4/27 = 0.148, at D = 1/3 (Appendix D.1). At full load K = 0.213 (ours), above the maximum, so full load is CCM at every input. Each variation below changes one thing and states what changes in the numbers, the waveforms and the parts (variation-checks.json).
Hold the current triangle so that it just touches zero each cycle. Its ripple is then twice the input current, and the frequency or the inductance follows:
I_{\mathrm{pk}}=2\,I_{\mathrm{in}},\qquad f_s=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}\,D}{2\,L\,I_{\mathrm{in}}},\qquad L=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}\,D}{2\,f_s\,I_{\mathrm{in}}}\tag{10.1a}
I_{\mathrm{pk}}=22.5\ \mathrm{A},\qquad f_s=\frac{12\cdot0.778}{2\cdot10\ \mu\mathrm{H}\cdot11.25}=41.5\ \mathrm{kHz},\qquad L=\frac{12\cdot0.778}{2\cdot230\ \mathrm{kHz}\cdot11.25}=1.80\ \mu\mathrm{H}\tag{10.1b}
Keeping TI’s 10 µH means running at 41.5 kHz (ours). Keeping 230 kHz needs a 1.80 µH inductor rated for 22.5 A. Either way the peak is 22.5 A at 12 V. That is far above the 18.0 A at which TI’s ferrite core has lost 10 %, and above the 21.5 A of the 20 % drop (TI’s part). No! A hard-saturating core cannot run there. The RMS current rises to 2I_{\mathrm{in}}/\sqrt{3} = 13.0 A (ours).
What critical conduction buys. The low side turns on at zero current. The turn-on overlap, 1.51 W at 12 V, and the reverse recovery, 0.46 W, disappear (§8.1). Those are the two largest switching terms of the boost. The output charge is still lost unless the current goes slightly negative (§6.2). The frequency then moves with load and input: at half the load, twice the frequency.
When would we choose the boundary? Not on this board. Its inductor, its 18.75 A current limit and its fixed-frequency controller all exclude it. Boundary control is a redesign option for a lower power or a higher V_o, where the switching loss at V_o dominates. It needs a core rated for twice the input current, a controller with a zero-current detector, and an input filter for a 100 % triangle.

section: 10.2 Discontinuous conduction with diode emulation
text:
10.2 Discontinuous conduction with diode emulation
With MODE tied low, the LM5122 runs diode emulation: it turns Q1 off when the current reaches zero instead of letting it reverse (SNVS954H). Below the boundary the current then rests at zero until the next pulse. The cycle has three intervals: low side on (D), Q1 on (D_2), and both off. Appendix D.2 derives the gain. The boundary load at each input follows from (D.1a):
K=\frac{2\,L\,f_s\,I_o}{V_o},\qquad I_{o,\mathrm{crit}}=\frac{V_o\,K_{\mathrm{crit}}(D)}{2\,L\,f_s}=\frac{(1-D)\,\Delta I_L}{2}\tag{10.2a}
I_{o,\mathrm{crit}}=0.45\ \mathrm{A}\ (12\ \mathrm{V}),\qquad 1.29\ \mathrm{A}\ (24\ \mathrm{V}),\qquad 1.74\ \mathrm{A}\ (36\ \mathrm{V}),\qquad 1.03\ \mathrm{A}\ (48\ \mathrm{V})\tag{10.2b}
(ours). The boundary is highest, 1.74 A, at 36 V, where D = 1/3 and K_{\mathrm{crit}} is at its 4/27 maximum. These are the same loads as the ZVS boundary of (6.3a). Below them forced PWM gives a negative valley, and diode emulation gives DCM.
Example at 12 V and 0.25 A. K = 0.0213, below K_{\mathrm{crit}} = 0.0384, so the converter is in DCM (ours). With (D.10a) the duty falls from the CCM 0.778 to 0.579. The current falls back to zero after D_2 = 0.165, so it flows for D + D_2 = 0.745 of the period, and the peak is 3.02 A (ours). The gain M = (1+\sqrt{1+4D^2/K})/2 of (D.9a) now depends on the load. The controller must reduce D as the load falls.

What the real controller adds. The LM5122 detects the zero crossing with a 6–7 mV threshold across the 4 mΩ shunt, that is at 1.5–1.75 A (ours, from SNVS954H). 10.3 The diode rectifier of the slides instead of Q1

section: 10.4 Bypass at V_in ≥ V_o, and why the board stops at 50 V
text:
10.4 Bypass at V_in ≥ V_o, and why the board stops at 50 V
As the input rises toward 54 V, the duty falls toward zero. The minimum low-side on-time, 158 ns with R14 = 30 kΩ (ours, from SNVS954H), sets the lowest duty, 0.036 at 230 kHz. Regulation therefore ends below V_o:
V_{\mathrm{in,end}}=V_o\,\left(1-t_{\mathrm{on,min}}\,f_s\right)\tag{10.5a}
V_{\mathrm{in,end}}=54\ \mathrm{V}\cdot\left(1-158\ \mathrm{ns}\cdot230\ \mathrm{kHz}\right)=52.0\ \mathrm{V}\tag{10.5b}
Between 52.0 V and 54 V the controller skips pulses (ours). At V_{\mathrm{in}} \geq V_o the LM5122 keeps Q1 on through its charge pump, if V_o \geq 9 V (SNVS954H Sec. 7.3.9, TI’s board note). The output then follows the input minus the drop of the path:
\Delta V=I_o\,\left(R_{HS}+r_L+r_s\right)\tag{10.6a}
\Delta V=2.5\ \mathrm{A}\cdot16.4\ \mathrm{m\Omega}=41\ \mathrm{mV},\qquad P=0.10\ \mathrm{W}\tag{10.6b}
(ours). Bypass is efficient. It is not safe without limits:

No regulation. Above 54 V the output is the input. The 80 V MOSFETs and capacitors see whatever the source delivers.
No current limit. The cycle-by-cycle limit ends the low-side pulse. In bypass there is no low-side pulse, so nothing limits the current. A boost has no series switch to open: a short at the output draws the source current through L1 and Q1’s channel or body diode.
A saturated loop. The error amplifier sees the output too high and drives COMP low. When the input falls back below 52 V, the loop must recover from saturation, with an overshoot or a dip.

These are reasons to stop the tested range at 50 V, 4 V below V_o (TI). Decision. Use bypass only where the source cannot exceed the parts’ rating and an upstream fuse or eFuse limits the fault current. Otherwise a buck-boost, or a boost with an input disconnect switch, is the credible alternative.

title: 11. What to retain
text:
The boost works at the input current. At 12 V the inductor, the shunt and the low side carry 11.25 A for a 2.5 A load. Every milliohm in that path costs I_{\mathrm{in}}^2: the fit’s 14.9 mΩ costs 2.10 W.
The duality with the buck breaks at the worst cases. The inductor ripple peaks at V_o/2, in the middle of the range. The lowest valley sits at 38.4 V. The largest current sits at the lowest input. Find each worst case from its equation.
The output current is pulsed, the input current continuous. The output bank takes a rectangle and needs a second stage or much more capacitance. The input bank takes only a triangle.
The right-half-plane zero sets the loop. The crossover must stay below a quarter of f_{RHP} at the lowest input, so the bank, not the loop, holds the load step. Check the ESR against |Z_C| at crossover.
Check real parts under real conditions. A ferrite core saturates hard: check it at the current limit, not only at full load. Ceramics lose most of their capacitance at 54 V.
Every hard turn-on happens at V_o, on the low side. The body diode of a silicon MOSFET adds dead-time and recovery loss. Name the device and the edge before calling anything soft.
A model gap points to an input first. C20’s ESR explains the loop gap and the ripple gap together. The fit’s series resistance explains the loss gap. The fit says what we missed, never what we predicted.

title: 12. Training: problem-driven exercises
text:
T1 — How far can a real boost step up?
Start each exercise by making a prediction. Sketch the current path or waveform before calculating. Then choose a model and solve the problem. Compare the alternatives and explain which one you would use.
Try the problem before reading its solution. For every exercise, state your choice, one benefit and one cost. Compare a credible alternative and name the condition or measurement that would change your choice. Keep the operating point and requirements clear.
Operating points. T1 works the boost of the lecture deck with its parasitic elements. T2 is the 2025 course exercise U2, a teaching boost from 10–16 V to 24 V. E1–E3 use their own authored values. E4 is the 2025 course exercise U3, the PLECS boost the lecturer assigned in the lecture of 2026-10-30. None of them uses PMP21274’s numbers. Every Problem states its own operating point; never carry a number from one operating point to another.
The exercises go beyond the live route. Session 3 works one or two of them in class; the rest are assigned as reading.

title: 12. Training: problem-driven exercises
text:
Problem
The ideal boost promises any ratio: M = 1/(1-D) grows without limit as D \to 1. The real boost of the deck (slide 8) does not. At which duty does M peak, what are M and the efficiency \eta there, and at which M would you stop using CCM? Derive the answer from the model of Appendix C, then decide.
Operating point. The numerical example of slide 8: V_{\mathrm{in}} = 10 V, resistive load R = 10 Ω, constant diode drop V_D = 0.7 V, inductor winding resistance R_L = 40 mΩ, MOSFET on-resistance R_{\mathrm{DSon}} = 60 mΩ. CCM and small ripple are assumed. The slide gives no L and no f_s. Solution A checks what CCM needs. This is a teaching model, not PMP21274. Never carry its numbers to Part I, or the reverse.
Predict before calculating. Sketch M(D) for this boost. Guess the duty of the peak and the efficiency there. Then name the efficiency you would accept and read the highest M it permits.


Why we do it
In the ideal model the duty sets the ratio. In a real boost the duty also sets the input current, and the input current sets the losses. A designer who reads M = 1/(1-D) and sets D = 0.95 for a ratio of 20 gets a ratio of about 4 and a hot board. The lecture of 2026-10-30 called the unlimited ideal gain a promise from Santa Claus. This exercise puts a number on that remark.
The peak also matters for control. On the far side of the peak, a larger duty gives a lower output. A voltage loop that raises D to raise V_o then drives the duty to its limit.


What matters

For a fixed load, the input current is I_{\mathrm{in}} = I_o/(1-D), and I_o itself rises with M. The losses in R_L and R_{\mathrm{DSon}} grow with I_{\mathrm{in}}^2.
The ideal boost presents the load to the source as (1-D)^2R. The series resistances compete with this reflected resistance, which falls quickly as D \to 1.
In this model the output power is V_oI_o and the input power is V_{\mathrm{in}}I_{\mathrm{in}}, so \eta = M(1-D) (Appendix C).
Model limits: CCM, constant diode drop, no switching loss, no ripple in the I^2 terms. A real board adds switching loss at V_o, so its peak is lower.



Where it appears in practice

PMP21274 at 12 V input (Part I, §2): D = 0.7778 for M = 4.5. The low-side switch and the inductor carry the input current, and §8 shows what it costs.
Photovoltaic and fuel-cell front ends. A low source voltage is boosted to a DC bus. The ratio and the source current set the efficiency.
High-ratio supplies at light load, such as LED strings, piezo drivers or detector bias supplies. They reach large ratios because their load current is small.



Possible solutions
Solution A — the closed form and its derivative. Write x = 1-D and three dimensionless ratios, a = V_D/V_{\mathrm{in}}, b = R_{\mathrm{DSon}}/R and c = (R_L+R_{\mathrm{DSon}})/R. The gain (C.5a) becomes a ratio of two polynomials in x:
M=\frac{x-ax^2}{x^2+c-bx}\tag{T1.1a}
a=\frac{0.7}{10}=0.07,\qquad b=\frac{0.06}{10}=0.006,\qquad c=\frac{0.04+0.06}{10}=0.01\tag{T1.1b}
Set dM/dx = 0. The cubic terms cancel, and a quadratic remains:
(1-ab)\,x^2+2ac\,x-c=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad x=\frac{-ac+\sqrt{a^2c^2+c\,(1-ab)}}{1-ab}\tag{T1.2a}
x=0.09932,\qquad D=1-x=0.9007\tag{T1.2b}
Put x back into (T1.1a). The efficiency follows from \eta = M(1-D):
M_{\max}=M(x),\qquad \eta=M_{\max}\,x\tag{T1.3a}
M_{\max}=5.119\ (V_o=51.19\ \mathrm{V}),\qquad \eta=5.119\cdot0.09932=0.5084\tag{T1.3b}
At the peak the ideal model promises 10.07. The real boost gives 5.119, and it wastes about half of its input power.
Why one half? Set a = 0 (no diode drop). Then (T1.2a) gives x^2 = c, that is (1-D)^2R = R_L + R_{\mathrm{DSon}}: the reflected load equals the series resistance. This is the maximum-power-transfer condition, so the efficiency is close to one half:
M_{\max}\approx\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{R}{R_L+R_{\mathrm{DSon}}}}\tag{T1.4a}
M_{\max}\approx\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{10}{0.1}}=5.0;\qquad \mathrm{exact\ with\ }a=0:\ M_{\max}=5.155,\ \eta=0.5155\tag{T1.4b}
Is it CCM? At the peak I_{\mathrm{in}} = 51.54 A, and the inductor sees v_{L1} = V_{\mathrm{in}} - I_{\mathrm{in}}(R_L+R_{\mathrm{DSon}}) = 4.846 V while the switch conducts. The valley stays positive if \Delta I_L/2 < I_{\mathrm{in}}:
Lf_s>\frac{v_{L1}D}{2I_{\mathrm{in}}}\tag{T1.5a}
Lf_s>\frac{4.846\cdot0.9007}{2\cdot51.54}=0.04235\ \mathrm{H/s},\quad\mathrm{e.g.}\ L>0.4235\ \mu\mathrm{H}\ \mathrm{at}\ 100\ \mathrm{kHz}\tag{T1.5b}
Any practical inductor meets this. The CCM assumption holds near the peak.
Solution B — a numerical sweep with the I^2 losses. Sweep D and solve the power balance (C.6a) for V_o at each step. teaching_examples.py finds the same M as the closed form at 100 duties, and the same peak by a bounded numerical search.

Solution C — leave CCM (Appendix D). In the lecture of 2026-10-30 the lecturer put the practical CCM limit at a factor of ten or twenty: above that it becomes really difficult. Higher ratios need DCM, soft switching and low-loss parts. Test what DCM changes and what it does not.

What DCM changes. The gain no longer depends on 1/(1-D) (D.9a). It depends on D and the load parameter K. The switch turns on at zero current, and the diode has already stopped. There is no reverse recovery and less turn-on loss at V_o. This is where the soft switching comes from.
What DCM does not change. The mean input current is P_o/V_{\mathrm{in}} in every mode, and R_L carries the input current at all times. Because an RMS value is never below the mean, R_LI_{\mathrm{in}}^2 is a lower bound on the winding loss in any mode:

P_{R_L}\geq R_L\left(\frac{P_o}{V_{\mathrm{in}}}\right)^2,\qquad \eta\leq\frac{P_o}{P_o+P_{R_L}}\tag{T1.6a}
M=10:\ P_o=\frac{(100\ \mathrm{V})^2}{10\ \Omega}=1000\ \mathrm{W},\quad I_{\mathrm{in}}\geq100\ \mathrm{A},\quad P_{R_L}\geq400\ \mathrm{W},\quad \eta\leq71.4\ \%\tag{T1.6b}
A DCM triangle makes this worse, not better: at the boundary its RMS squared is 1.333 times its mean squared, and deeper in DCM the ratio grows. At this 10 Ω load, no mode gives a ratio of ten with good efficiency.

What sets the limit. (T1.4a) says the load relative to the series resistance sets it. Keep the same parts and raise the load to R = 1 kΩ: the peak moves to M_{\max} = 50.12 at D = 0.9900, and \eta \geq 90 % holds up to M = 29.95. High ratios belong to light loads. That is where DCM, soft switching and low-loss parts pay.



Pros and cons








Solution
Pros
Cons




A. Closed form and derivative
Exact for the model; gives the peak in one line; (T1.4a) shows what sets the limit
Needs the algebra; hides the loss split; CCM only


B. Numerical sweep
Shows the loss split and the efficiency at every duty; reads the decision off a table; extends to any loss term
One operating point per sweep; the general rule (T1.4a) is not visible


C. Leave CCM
Removes reverse recovery and turn-on loss; reaches high ratios at light load
Does not remove the I_{\mathrm{in}}^2 loss; higher RMS current; the gain depends on the load (Appendix D.2)





Conclusion
For the slide-8 boost, M peaks at 5.119 at D = 0.9007, with \eta = 50.8 %. Never operate near this peak. Half of the input power heats the resistances, and the loop gain changes sign at the peak. Limit the maximum duty well below 0.9007.
Recommendation. If the application needs \eta \geq 90 %, stop CCM at M \approx 2.9 (D = 0.6942) with these parts. If 80 % is acceptable, CCM reaches M = 4.109. To go higher, lower R_L + R_{\mathrm{DSon}} first: the limit scales with \sqrt{R/(R_L+R_{\mathrm{DSon}})} (T1.4a). Choose DCM only when the load is light enough that R_LI_{\mathrm{in}}^2 stays small. If the load is heavy and the ratio high, a single boost stage is the wrong topology: use two stages, a coupled inductor or a transformer.
Slide 11 limits CCM near M = 6, and the lecture puts it at a factor of ten or twenty. Read both as rules of thumb for typical parts and loads. The calculation shows what sets them. Compute \sqrt{R/(R_L+R_{\mathrm{DSon}})} for your own load before you choose a mode.

title: 12. Training: problem-driven exercises
section: T2 — The course boost: which input voltage sizes the inductor?
text:
T2 — The course boost: which input voltage sizes the inductor?

Problem
A boost converter must supply 24 V at a nominal 120 W from a 10–16 V source at 50 kHz. (a) What is the smallest inductance that keeps the peak-to-peak inductor ripple at or below 20 % of the mean inductor current, at nominal load, over the whole input range? (b) Down to which load power does no input voltage in the range enter discontinuous conduction? Predict first: does the 10 V end or the 16 V end set the inductor, and does the same end set the DCM limit?
Operating point. Ideal lossless boost: V_{\mathrm{in}} = 10–16 V, V_o = 24 V, P = 120 W, f_s = 50 kHz. The mean inductor current is the input current, P/V_{\mathrm{in}}. (2025 course exercise U2.)


Why we do it
Lesson 1 sized the buck inductor at its maximum input, where the ripple is largest. The boost does not obey that rule. Its ripple V_{\mathrm{in}}D/(Lf_s) peaks in the middle of the range (§3.1), and its mean current falls as the input rises. A ripple ratio therefore has its own worst case, and it is not the one the absolute ripple has. The DCM boundary follows the same logic, with a different answer. Students who carry the buck’s rule to the boost size the wrong end of the range.


What matters
At input V_{\mathrm{in}} with D = 1 - V_{\mathrm{in}}/V_o, the ratio of the ripple to the mean inductor current is
r=\frac{\Delta I_L}{\langle i_L\rangle}=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}D}{Lf_s}\cdot\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}}{P}=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}^2\,(1-V_{\mathrm{in}}/V_o)}{L\,f_s\,P}.\tag{12.1}

The numerator V_{\mathrm{in}}^2(1 - V_{\mathrm{in}}/V_o) grows with V_{\mathrm{in}} until V_{\mathrm{in}} = 2V_o/3 = 16 V. Over 10–16 V the ratio therefore grows monotonically. Check this before you trust the end point.
The DCM boundary is \langle i_L\rangle = \Delta I_L/2. The boundary power P_b = V_{\mathrm{in}}\Delta I_L/2 = V_{\mathrm{in}}^2D/(2Lf_s) has the same numerator, so the same end of the range sets it.
Both results are ideal: no losses, no inductance drop with current, no tolerance.



Where it appears in practice

PMP21274 (§3). Its ripple ratio, stated against the input current, is 0.36 at 12 V input and far larger at 48 V, where the input current is small. The same design can be “low ripple” and “high ripple” depending on which input you quote.
Battery-input boosts (12 V automotive to 24–48 V) see exactly this range ratio. The inductor is sized at the high-voltage end, the switch at the low-voltage end.
MPPT boosts sweep the input on purpose. Their ripple ratio and their DCM entry move with the sweep.



Possible solutions
A — Closed form at the ends of the range. Solve (12.1) for L with r = 0.20:
L=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}^2\,(1-V_{\mathrm{in}}/V_o)}{r\,f_s\,P}\tag{12.2a}
L(10\ \mathrm{V})=\frac{100\cdot0.5833}{0.20\cdot50\ \mathrm{kHz}\cdot120\ \mathrm{W}}=48.6\ \mu\mathrm{H},\qquad L(16\ \mathrm{V})=\frac{256\cdot0.3333}{1.2\cdot10^6}=71.1\ \mu\mathrm{H}\tag{12.2b}
The 16 V end sets L = 71.1 µH. With it, the ripple at 10 V is 1.64 A, or 0.137 of the 12 A mean. For (b), P_b at 16 V is 12.0 W, and at 10 V with the same inductor it is 8.2 W. Above 12 W every input stays in CCM.
B — A sweep over the range. scripts/course_exercises.py evaluates (12.1) at 601 inputs and takes the maximum. It returns the same 71.1 µH at 16 V and 12.0 W at 16 V, and it checks the ramp of (12.2b) by integrating V_{\mathrm{in}}/L over the on-time. The sweep costs nothing and protects against a range whose worst case lies inside, as it would if the input went up to 20 V (the maximum of (12.1) sits at 16 V).
C — The K criterion of Appendix D. With K = 2Lf_s/R and K_{\mathrm{crit}} = D(1-D)^2, the converter is in CCM when K > K_{\mathrm{crit}}. At 16 V, D = 1/3 and K_{\mathrm{crit}} takes its largest value 4/27. With R = V_o^2/P, K > K_{\mathrm{crit}} gives P > V_o^2 K_{\mathrm{crit}}/(2Lf_s) = 12.0 W, the same answer through the slides’ route.


Pros and cons








Route
Benefit
Cost




A, end points
two evaluations, shows the mechanism
wrong if the worst case lies inside the range


B, sweep
finds any interior maximum, checks the ramp independently
needs the script; hides the mechanism unless you plot it


C, K criterion
reuses the slide’s constant, generalises to any load
needs K_{\mathrm{crit}}(D) and its maximum first





Conclusion
Choose 71.1 µH or the next standard value above it, sized at 16 V, the high end of this range, and expect 20 % ripple there and 13.7 % at 10 V. Keep the load above 12 W if the design must stay in CCM at every input. Repeat the sweep if the range changes: with an upper end above 16 V the worst case moves inside the range, and the end-point shortcut fails. If the inductor loses inductance with current, size at the low end of its tolerance and recheck the 10 V peak current, 12.8 A with this value.

title: 12. Training: problem-driven exercises
section: E1 — The capacitor charger works at its target voltage. Will it survive startup?
text:
E1 — The capacitor charger works at its target voltage. Will it survive startup?

Problem
A conventional diode boost converter charges a capacitor from a DC source. A designer calculates the duty cycle at the final voltage and applies it immediately. The output voltage rises, but the successive inductor-current valleys also rise. Is this normal CCM, an intended charging transient, or evidence that the controller is losing control of current?
Use the following ideal teaching model. The inductor is linear only below the stated saturation knee. Neglect winding resistance, diode drop, switching loss and capacitor ESR for the calculations. Stop a linear calculation when it reaches the knee; no post-saturation inductance curve is supplied.







Quantity
Teaching assumption




Input voltage
12 V, stiff source


Target capacitor voltage
24 V


Capacitance
2200 µF


Inductance below its knee
100 µH


Illustrative saturation knee
1.8 A


Cycle-by-cycle peak-current limit, when enabled
1.5 A, ideal zero delay


Fixed switching frequency for the CCM candidate
100 kHz


Maximum permitted duty cycle
0.95


Initial state for the controlled-charging study
Capacitor at 14 V; inductor current zero


External output load during charging
None


Charging-time requirement
Reach 24 V from 14 V within 60 ms



The 14 V initial condition represents an externally established precharge, not a prediction of natural input connection. In the first few pulses, freeze the capacitor voltage at 14 V to isolate the current mechanism. Later, allow the voltage to change. End charging at the target using an ideal supervisory stop; practical stop delay and tolerance are outside the numerical model.
Predict before calculating. Sketch the first four current pulses if the controller immediately applies the final-voltage CCM duty cycle. Choose a first diagnostic measurement and explain what would make you change your explanation. Does limiting duty to 0.95 solve the problem?

Derive the on-state and off-state inductor-current slopes, and a cycle-to-cycle expression for the change in valley current. Identify the condition for a constant valley at a locally fixed capacitor voltage. Distinguish that condition from a zero valley.
Disable the peak-current limit in the mathematical model. Apply the final-voltage duty cycle at the 14 V initial condition. Calculate the first three peaks and valleys. Determine whether the saturation knee is reached during the fourth pulse. Stop there; do not infer device failure from a linear model.
Enable the 1.5 A peak limit. Assume a trip terminates the on interval, holds the switch off until the next clock and has no blanking, minimum on-time or delay. Find the first trip and its following valley. Explain why protected CCM can charge the capacitor without requiring zero current each cycle. Find the locally balanced duty cycle and valley at 14 V once every cycle reaches the peak limit.
Replace the clocked control with ideal CrCM: start at zero current, switch off at 1.5 A, then wait for the current to reach zero before starting again. Calculate the on-time, off-time and frequency at 14 V and 24 V. Explain what zero-current detection prevents and what protection is still needed.
For the CrCM candidate, derive the average input current, average output charging current and ideal charging time. Is the capacitor charged by constant current or constant power under this particular control law? Check the 60 ms requirement. Compare with the protected CCM candidate without assuming that equal peak current means equal power.
Near the target, suppose the 100 kHz controller reduces its peak-current command. At a locally fixed 24 V, find the boundary peak current at which the valley just reaches zero. Sketch what must change when the command is reduced further and reverse current is blocked. Explain why the fixed-frequency CCM conversion ratio cannot simply be carried into DCM.
Return to an initially uncharged capacitor at input connection. Identify the current path with switching disabled. Explain why the controlled-charging calculations above do not bound this inrush, and what additional model or measurement is needed.

Finish by choosing protected CCM or CrCM for the stated charging task. Give one benefit, one cost and one condition that would change your choice. Separate a timing concept from a checked controller and magnetic-component selection.


Why we do it
A periodic steady state has no net change of inductor current over a switching period. Charging a capacitor changes the operating point continuously. A duty cycle that balances the inductor at the target can produce a large positive current increment earlier in the charge.
The diagnostic task is to distinguish useful charging from uncontrolled current accumulation. CCM itself is not a fault, and a zero-current start alone does not bound the peak of the next pulse.


What matters

Label capacitor voltage, inductor current and switch state on the same time axis. Compare successive valleys as well as peaks.
Keep the input-connection transient separate from controlled charging after precharge.
State whether duty, peak current, frequency or average power is held fixed before comparing modes.
Distinguish current limiting from saturation. A protection trip is an event in the controller; saturation changes the magnetic component’s current slope.
Treat the frozen-voltage calculation as a local model. Estimate its voltage-change error before extending it to the whole charge.



Where it appears in practice
Capacitor energy-storage supplies, instrument power rails and supplies with substantial output capacitance must reach their operating point without exceeding current limits. Restart after a disturbance can revisit the same problem. A useful trace includes input connection, precharge, the first switching pulses and the approach to regulation.


Solution
Released after the deadline in the Enrolled companion.

title: 12. Training: problem-driven exercises
section: E2 — A boost converter supplies the DC bus of an electrosurgical RF stage
text:
E2 — A boost converter supplies the DC bus of an electrosurgical RF stage

Problem
A boost converter supplies a DC bus. A downstream RF stage draws energy from that bus during activation. The bus must remain within its allowed voltage range when the RF stage starts and stops. Does sizing the boost for average power establish that requirement?
Use this scaled, abstract bus model. It represents only the power envelope at the RF stage’s DC input. It does not model RF generation, electrodes, tissue interaction, isolation or clinical performance. The 12 W quantity below is power drawn from the bus, not power delivered to tissue.
12 V source → boost converter → DC bus capacitor → RF-stage input-power model
                                      ↑
                              bus-voltage feedback







Quantity
Teaching assumption




Regulated DC bus voltage before either event
24 V


Allowed bus voltage range
22–25 V


RF-stage bus demand while active
Constant 12 W over the event interval


RF-stage bus demand while idle
0 W


Activation duration / repetition period
20 ms / 100 ms


Bus power supplied by boost during first 2 ms after activation
0 W


Bus power available for subsequent recovery
Up to 15 W, tapered to 12 W at 24 V


Bus power supplied during 2 ms after RF deactivation
15 W


Additional energy delivered after that deactivation delay
2 mJ


Initial capacitor candidates
470 µF and 1000 µF


Capacitance tolerance for the final recommendation
−20% worst case



Study activation and deactivation as separate events, each starting at 24 V. The 2 mJ is a specified upper bound on further energy actually delivered to the bus after the 2 ms interval. It already includes residual conversion energy; do not add the inductor’s energy again. The boost cannot sink bus energy. Neglect ESR, ESL, leakage and RF-cycle ripple; capacitance means effective capacitance at the operating condition before applying the stated tolerance.
Predict before calculating. Choose which event you expect to set the larger capacitance requirement. Would a 48 Ω resistor represent the active RF stage adequately during bus droop? State a measurement that could make you change that choice.

Draw the power flow during activation, recovery and deactivation. Explain why the current in the boost inductor is not identical to either RF-stage input current or capacitor current.
Derive the bus-energy equation using power delivered by the boost and power drawn by the RF stage. Calculate the bus voltage after the activation delay for both capacitor candidates. Compare the constant-power model with the current and power of a 48 Ω resistor at 22 V.
Find the minimum capacitance for the activation requirement. For the 1000 µF candidate, estimate the recovery time after the 2 ms delay if the boost delivers 15 W until the bus returns to 24 V. Is recovery possible within the stated activation interval?
Starting again at 24 V, calculate the deactivation overshoot for both candidates, including the additional 2 mJ. Find the minimum capacitance for the 25 V ceiling. Explain why reducing duty to zero does not imply that all bus charging stops immediately.
Compare three remedies against the same 22–25 V limits: more capacitance, a shorter deactivation delay, or a circuit able to absorb surplus energy. For 1000 µF, calculate the largest permitted deactivation delay if the additional delivered energy remains 2 mJ. Account for −20% capacitance tolerance in your final recommendation. Do not silently relax the load demand or bus limits.
Calculate the RF-stage mean bus power over the 100 ms repetition period. Explain why this number alone cannot select the converter or capacitor. Identify what bus-voltage and power-envelope measurements are needed before replacing the abstract load with a real RF stage.

Recommend a bus-level solution conditionally. State what the calculation establishes and what must still be checked about control response, current stress, capacitor ripple and the downstream stage.


Why we do it
The boost controls the DC bus; the RF stage controls a different process downstream. The bus capacitor supplies a temporary energy deficit and accepts surplus energy when the load stops. These two events can impose different limits even when mean power is modest.
Choosing the load model is part of the engineering decision. A regulated downstream stage may draw more current as the bus falls, while a resistor draws less. A constant-power approximation must therefore be tied to a measured operating range and time scale.


What matters

Define the system boundary at the RF stage’s DC input. Do not equate bus power with delivered RF power.
Use energy balance for finite voltage excursions. Check a small-ripple approximation against it.
Keep power, current and stored energy separate. The specified power envelope is an assumption, not a derived converter-control response.
A larger capacitor changes startup energy and charging time as well as bus droop. Recheck startup rather than treating capacitance as a free improvement.
A bus model does not establish whole-system stability. The downstream controller’s bandwidth and the boost’s closed-loop output impedance remain relevant.



Where it appears in practice
An electrosurgical generator provides the application context: a DC supply feeds a downstream RF power stage. The same bus-energy reasoning applies to a boost feeding an RF amplifier or another intermittent regulated load. The exercise establishes a power-supply requirement; it is not a design for an electrosurgical output stage.


Solution
Released after the deadline in the Enrolled companion.

title: 12. Training: problem-driven exercises
section: E3 — Boosting only the difference: is this a partial-power converter?
text:
E3 — Boosting only the difference: is this a partial-power converter?

Problem
The schematic shows a synchronous boost with one change: the output capacitor returns to the input-positive node, not to ground. The capacitor therefore holds only V_C=V_\mathrm{out}-V_\mathrm{in}. A colleague calls the circuit a partial-power boost. The input already supplies part of the output voltage, and S_1 conducts for only 25% of the period at 10 V input. Does the circuit process less power than a conventional boost, or does it give the same converter a different name?



Synchronous boost with the output capacitor C connected from the output rail to the input-positive node. The inductor L runs from the input-positive node to the switching node x. S1 connects x to the output rail, S2 connects x to ground, and the load R is connected from the output rail to ground.


Figure E3.1 — Ideal complementary switches: S_1 conducts for dT_s, S_2 for (1-d)T_s. V_C and V_\mathrm{out} are positive at the output rail.







Quantity
Teaching assumption




Input voltage
10–20 V, ideal stiff source


Regulated output voltage
40 V


Load
4 Ω, from the output rail to ground


Switching frequency
100 kHz


Inductor current ripple
At most 10 A peak-to-peak over the input range


Duty-cycle definition
d is the conducting fraction of S_1


Switches
Ideal and complementary, no dead time


Capacitor
Large enough for negligible voltage ripple


Conduction mode
CCM


Inductor winding resistance, task 9 only
10 mΩ


Reference converter for comparison
Conventional synchronous boost, capacitor from output to ground, same L, f_s and operating point



Predict before calculating. At 10 V input, S_1 conducts for 25% of the period. The low-side switch of a conventional boost conducts for 75%. Which converter has the lower semiconductor RMS current? Choose the first quantity that you would measure to support your answer.

Apply volt-second balance to the inductor. Derive V_\mathrm{out}/V_\mathrm{in} as a function of d.
Find the duty-cycle range for the given input range.
Find the minimum inductance for the ripple limit. At which input voltage is the ripple largest?
Find the blocking voltage of S_1 and of S_2.
At 10 V input, find the average current of S_1.
At 10 V input, find the average inductor current. Find its peak with the inductance of task 3.
Draw the switching intervals of both converters at 10 V input on one time axis. Compare inductor voltage and current, switch RMS currents, blocking voltages, capacitor DC voltage and capacitor RMS current. Which quantities differ?
Find the current drawn from the input source in each interval and its RMS ripple. Compare it with the conventional boost. What does a real source with internal impedance need in front of this circuit?
Add the 10 mΩ winding resistance. Compare the winding loss of both converters at 10 V and 20 V input. Does boosting less reduce loss, and does it reduce loss differently in the two converters?
Split the output power into the part that the source delivers directly to the load and the part that passes through the energy stored in the inductor. Compare this split with the partial-power ratio k=(V_\mathrm{out}-V_\mathrm{in})/V_\mathrm{out}.
Sketch an architecture whose converter stage processes only (V_\mathrm{out}-V_\mathrm{in})I_\mathrm{out}, with components rated for the difference voltage. What power does that stage process at 10 V and at 20 V input? Which property of the stage makes this possible?

Finish by classifying the circuit. Support the classification with one waveform or one number, not with the value of the duty cycle.


Why we do it
A duty-cycle number depends on which switch it refers to. Losses depend on currents, voltages and switched energy. A circuit can look different and still apply the same waveforms to every component.
Partial-power processing is attractive when the input already supplies most of the output voltage. This exercise separates a real reduction in processed power from a change of reference or of name.


What matters

Define d before you use it, and state which switch it refers to.
Compare converters at the same operating point: same input, output, load, L and f_s.
Conduction and switching losses follow RMS current, blocking voltage and switched energy. A smaller duty-cycle number alone changes none of them.
Follow the AC current loop of each capacitor back to its source. A different capacitor reference can move ripple current to another component.
Keep the voltage contribution of the source separate from the power that a converter stage processes.



Where it appears in practice
Series partial-power converters appear in photovoltaic strings, battery chargers and electric-vehicle fast-charging stations. In these applications the input voltage already supplies most of the output voltage. Wind and fuel-cell sources with a large DC offset raise the same question. A converter stacked on its own input is a real partial-power stage only if a stress analysis shows lower component loading.


Solution
Released after the deadline in the Enrolled companion.

title: 12. Training: problem-driven exercises
section: E4 — The PLECS boost: predict, then simulate
text:
E4 — The PLECS boost: predict, then simulate

Problem
Build the boost of the 2025 exercise U3 in PLECS: an ideal switch and diode, V_{\mathrm{in}} = 10 V, L = 24 µH, C = 150 µF, R = 5 Ω, f_s = 100 kHz, a fixed duty of 60 %. Before you simulate, predict the output voltage, the mean inductor current, the inductor ripple and the output ripple. Then simulate to 10 ms with a maximum step of 1 ns and compare. Does the output voltage agree with V_{\mathrm{in}}/(1-D)? Is the circuit in CCM? What would you change to make it enter DCM?
Operating point. As stated. Ideal parts, no losses, fixed duty, no feedback. (2025 course exercise U3; assigned in the lecture of 2026-10-30.)


Why we do it
A simulation that you cannot predict cannot be checked. This circuit is the simplest boost that still shows the start-up, the steady state and the CCM/DCM question. Lesson 1 §9 made the same point for the buck: compare the overlapping predictions of the averaged model and the switching model before trusting either.


What matters

With fixed duty and an ideal circuit, V_o = V_{\mathrm{in}}/(1-D) holds only in CCM. Check the valley current, or K against K_{\mathrm{crit}} (Appendix D), before you use it.
The output ripple of a boost comes from a pulsed capacitor current: the capacitor supplies the load alone for the whole on-time (§4.1).
The start-up is open loop: the inductor current overshoots before the capacitor charges. Record the peak and compare it with the steady-state peak.
Use the deck’s K = 2Lf_s/R. The 2025 notebook defines its inverse.



Where it appears in practice

PMP21274 §9.2. The lecturer’s PLECS model of the real board starts from this circuit, with the parasitic elements and the LM5122 loop added.
Any fixed-duty test. Bring-up of a board often starts in open loop at a safe duty. The predicted output tells you whether the stage is healthy before the loop is closed.
Model choice. The averaged relation gives the operating point in one line. The switching model gives the ripple and the start-up. Each answers a different question.



Solution
Released after the deadline in the Enrolled companion.

title: Appendix A — The boost of the slides
text:
A.1 Two switch positions
The slides of lecture 2 describe the classical boost with a transistor and a diode. Part I designs a synchronous boost, PMP21274, in which a second MOSFET replaces the diode. The diode boost remains the clearest place to see the two switch positions, the constant-voltage loss and the third interval of DCM. Appendices A–D carry the slide theory. §10.3 compares the diode boost with the synchronous one.
The slides use the German symbols. This lesson uses the symbols of Part I:
The boost places the inductor L at the input. A changeover switch connects the right end of L either to the return or to the output. The switch toggles periodically between the two positions. As in the buck, a transistor Q and a diode D build this switch.
In interval 1 the inductor current rises. The diode blocks, so the capacitor alone feeds the load. When Q turns off, the inductor current can only continue through the diode. It flows into the capacitor and the load.
Small-ripple approximation. The output capacitor is large, so the slides treat its voltage as constant, v_o(t) \approx V_o, over one period. The inductor voltage is then constant in each interval, and i_L(t) is made of straight lines. Appendix B.3 computes the ripple that this approximation neglects.
Why V_o must exceed V_{\mathrm{in}}. In interval 2 the current must fall, or it would rise in both intervals and never settle. A falling current needs V_{\mathrm{in}} - V_o < 0. The boost can therefore only step up. At power-up the diode conducts at once and charges the output to about V_{\mathrm{in}}. Below that value the boost cannot regulate.

M(0.5)=2\cdot\frac{1-0.5\cdot0.07}{1+(0.04+0.5\cdot0.06)/(0.25\cdot10)}=2\cdot\frac{0.965}{1.028}=1.877\tag{C.5b}

Limit cases. At D = 0 the switch never conducts: M = 0.9263, set by the diode drop and R_L. As D \to 1 the real gain falls to zero. At D = 0.99 it is 0.9953. Between the two limits the gain rises, peaks and collapses.

The efficiency. The model reaches its highest efficiency, 94.1 %, at D = 0.3961, where M = 1.559. At D = 0.8 the gain is 4.041 instead of 5 and the efficiency is 80.8 %. The highest efficiency at a ratio a little above 1 agrees with the remark of slide 11 (Appendix D.3).

I_{\mathrm{pk}}=\Delta I_L=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}D}{Lf_s}\tag{D.5a}
The volt-second balance now has only two nonzero terms. It gives the diode interval D_2:
V_{\mathrm{in}}D+(V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_o)D_2=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad D_2=D\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}}{V_o-V_{\mathrm{in}}}=\frac{D}{M-1}\tag{D.6a}
The load current is the mean diode current, a triangle of height I_{\mathrm{pk}} and width D_2T_s:
\frac{V_o}{R}=I_o=\frac{I_{\mathrm{pk}}}{2}D_2\tag{D.7a}
Insert (D.5a) and (D.6a):
\frac{V_o}{R}=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}^2D^2}{2Lf_s(V_o-V_{\mathrm{in}})}\quad\Rightarrow\quad M(M-1)=\frac{D^2}{K}\tag{D.8a}
Solve the quadratic for the positive root:
M=\frac{1+\sqrt{1+4D^2/K}}{2}=\frac{1}{2}+\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}+\frac{D^2}{K}}\tag{D.9a}
The second form is the one on slide 10. For a regulated output, solve (D.8a) for the duty instead:
D=\sqrt{K\,M(M-1)}\tag{D.10a}
Check at the boundary. Insert K = D(1-D)^2 into (D.9a). The root becomes (1+D)/(1-D), and M = 1/(1-D): the DCM gain meets the CCM gain.
Numbers. teaching_examples.py checks each sample against a second route: it integrates the diode-current triangle numerically and solves “mean diode current = V_o/R” for V_o.
K=0.05,\ D=0.3:\quad M=\frac{1+\sqrt{1+4\cdot0.09/0.05}}{2}=1.932\ (\mathrm{CCM}:\ 1.429),\qquad D_2=0.3220\tag{D.9b}

section: D.3 Remarks on the boost converter
text:
D.3 Remarks on the boost converter
The opening of the lesson compresses the remarks slide. Here it is in full.







Remark of slide 11
How to read it




Efficiency similar to the buck, up to more than 98 %
A property of a design, not of the topology. The slide-8 model reaches 94.1 % at best (Appendix C.2). §8 shows why a boost at a high ratio stays below a buck with the same parts.


Best efficiency for ratios a little above 1
The slide-8 model peaks in efficiency at M = 1.559 (Appendix C.2).


In CCM the ratio is limited near M = 6 by losses
The slide-8 boost peaks at M = 5.119. The limit scales with \sqrt{R/(R_L+R_{\mathrm{DSon}})}, so it is not a fixed number (T1).


DCM reaches somewhat higher output voltages
The DCM gain lies above the CCM curve at the same duty (D.2). It does not remove the I_{\mathrm{in}}^2 losses (T1, Solution C).


Switching frequency depends on the application: at least 20 kHz to stay above the audible range; up to about 1 MHz where small size matters; most applications at about 70 kHz to 300 kHz
Indicative ranges. PMP21274 switches at 230 kHz (Part I).


Used over a very wide power range
From small bias supplies to multi-phase stages.


Only for an output voltage above the input voltage and without galvanic isolation
Appendix A.1 explains the step-up limit. Other cases need the buck-boost or an isolated topology of the following lessons.



These are historical ranges, not design limits. As for the remarks slide of Lesson 1 (l01-s36), use them to check a design for plausibility, not to set its specification.

title: Lesson 3 — Design an inverting buck–boost
text:
Power Electronic Systems · HTWG · 2026
A positive source must supply a negative rail. How do the required polarity, pulsed port currents and summed switch-voltage stress change the design?
We follow the method of Lessons 1 and 2. State the requirements, estimate each component, compare with TI’s fitted part, and test the model against published evidence. Theory enters when a design step needs it. The diode circuit of the original deck remains in the appendices.
Our example. TI PMP30916 is a synchronous inverting converter with discrete power MOSFETs. The four-switch non-inverting converter has its own lesson. The capacitor lesson develops component technologies and thermal limits.
Evidence labels. TI identifies a published value. Ours, calculated identifies a derived result. Ours, assumed identifies a teaching target or model parameter. A fitted loss curve would be calibration, not an independent prediction. All current ripples are peak to peak unless labelled RMS.

title: 2. Duty, summed voltage stress and the worst current
text:

D=\frac{V}{V_g+V},\qquad I_L=\frac{I_o}{1-D}=I_g+I_o,\qquad \Delta I_L=\frac{V_gD}{Lf_s}.

The switch must withstand the sum. When Q1 opens, the switch node falls toward −8 V. Q1 spans the positive source and that negative node:
V_{DS,off}\simeq V_g-V_o=V_g+|V_o|.
At maximum input, 56+8=64 V. Q5 also has about 64 V blocking stress during Q1 conduction. TI’s 80 V devices leave 16 V between the ideal plateau and their rating. That is available headroom, not a measured overshoot margin. Check the real drain-source waveform, input transients and tolerances before accepting it. A diode version needs the same summed reverse-voltage check.



Calculated voltage and current stresses across the PMP30916 input range


Use TIDT280 Figures 3-1, 3-2, 3-5 and 3-6 to test the voltage prediction. Observe that the Q1 capture is source-to-drain and referenced to VIN. Its sign differs from a drain-to-source plot. Measuring the switch node against system ground is a different measurement.
crumbs: 155  2. Duty, summed voltage stress and the worst current

title: 3. Choose the inductor, then the capacitors
text:
Our 30% ripple target at low input gives
L_{min}=\frac{V_gD}{0.30 I_Lf_s}=\frac{9\cdot0.4706}{0.30\cdot3.778\cdot400000}=9.34\ \mathrm{\mu H}.
TI uses 22 µH. At 9 V it gives 12.7% ripple instead of 30%. This reduces peak current and ripple but increases stored energy and can lower the right-half-plane zero. We retain 22 µH to compare with the board. A smaller inductance becomes attractive if size or response dominates and the extra peak current passes.
The 4.018 A ideal peak is a screening value. Saturation qualification also needs tolerances, current-limit excursions, DC-bias inductance and temperature. The BOM’s 33 mΩ gives P_{Cu}=I_{L,rms}^2R_L=0.472 W at 9 V. Core loss and hot winding resistance add to this.
The inverting converter interrupts both port currents. Use the complete triangular pulse for RMS stress:
I_{Cout,rms}^2=I_o^2\frac{D}{1-D}+(1-D)\frac{\Delta I_L^2}{12}.
At 9 V this is 1.888 A RMS. The corresponding source-port ripple current is also about 1.888 A RMS. They happen to be close here. Do not replace either by the 0.481 A inductor ripple.
For a first output-capacitance estimate, allocate the full 80 mV target to charge ripple:
C_{min}\simeq\frac{I_oD}{f_s\Delta V}=\frac{2\cdot0.4706}{400000\cdot0.080}=29.4\ \mathrm{\mu F}.
This leaves no ESR or ESL budget and cannot qualify a real bank. TI’s four effective 16 µF values give 64 µF and 36.8 mV capacitive ripple at 9 V. That leaves 43.2 mV of this assumed target for other effects, subject to the actual waveform.
The source-to-ground bank totals 6.6 µF nominal. With an ideal constant source current, the simple two-interval charge estimate is I_LD(1-D)/(C_{in}f_s): 0.356 V at 9 V. This is a screening model, not TI’s measured input ripple. The physical circuit also has 6.6 µF nominal from input to negative output. These capacitors see the summed DC voltage and couple the port ripple. Their bias-dependent values and source impedance require a coupled network calculation. Do not add all six input capacitors as if they shared the same two nodes.
For our 1 A load increase, a constant current deficit would use 0.4 V across 64 µF in C\Delta V/\Delta I=25.6 µs. ESR and ESL reduce the available charge margin. This bound tells us to examine the loop and inductor-current response before declaring the transient target met.
crumbs: 156  3. Choose the inductor, then the capacitors

title: 4. Check MOSFETs, the reference potential and the loop
text:
The BSC117N08NS5 datasheet gives maximum on-resistance of 11.7 mΩ at 10 V gate drive and 16.3 mΩ at 6 V, at its stated conditions. TI’s schematic annotates a 7.5 V gate supply. Do not use the 10 V resistance without qualification.
Using 16.3 mΩ for both switches gives a room-temperature screening sum
P_{Q,cond}\simeq\left(I_L^2+\frac{\Delta I_L^2}{12}\right)R_{DS(on)}=0.233\ \mathrm W
at 9 V. Q1 carries 2.593 A RMS and Q5 carries 2.751 A RMS in our ideal model. Add hot resistance, switching overlap, output-capacitance energy, gate-drive power and dead-time diode loss for a full estimate. The resistance above is not a guaranteed hot-device value.
The controller’s local ground is −8 V. Its VIN pin therefore sees about 17–64 V relative to that local ground. Enable and measurement references need the same check. This explains the level-shifter circuit. It also explains why a controller’s positive input rating cannot be checked against system input alone. See the LM5146-Q1 datasheet.
The feedback and compensation network crosses these reference potentials. Trace R17, R18 and the injection network on the schematic before applying a textbook divider formula. Treat the −8 V requirement and annotated −8.07 V setting as distinct values. A divider copied from a ground-referenced buck can give the wrong answer.
For an ideal voltage-mode inverting stage with load resistance R=V/I_o, the right-half-plane zero is
f_{RHP}=\frac{R(1-D)^2}{2\pi LD}.
At 9 V and 2 A, R=4 Ω gives f_{RHP}=17.23 kHz. This is not the boost formula: the additional D matters. With 64 µF, the lossless power-stage resonance estimate is (1-D)/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})=2.25 kHz. Both use ideal duty and our declared capacitance model.
The schematic annotates 15.22 kHz for the RHP zero using its design estimates. Our ideal result differs because duty, current and parasitics differ. Use TI’s measured loop as a check rather than claiming these estimates reproduce it. TIDT280 Table 2-1 reports 5.7 kHz bandwidth and 66° phase margin at 9 V. At 24 V it reports 9.56 kHz and 43.7°. These values identify the harder measured phase-margin condition among those two points.
Keep crossover comfortably below the RHP zero, then verify gain and phase over input and load. A fixed fraction is an initial design rule. It is not a replacement for the measured loop.
crumbs: 157  4. Check MOSFETs, the reference potential and the loop

title: 5. Explain losses and temperature with the report
text:
At 24 V, our winding and MOSFET conduction estimates sum to only 0.352 W. At 48 V they fall to 0.271 W. Yet high input increases switching voltage. A conduction-only explanation is therefore incomplete.
The schematic’s C18/R19 damping branch illustrates the missing mechanism. If a capacitor fully charges and discharges each period, its dissipation scale is CV_{swing}^2f_s. For 1 nF and 400 kHz, this is 0.410 W at 32 V swing and 1.254 W at 56 V swing. This scale is not an exact snubber-loss prediction. R19 and the ringing network determine the waveform.
TIDT280 §2.5 supports the diagnosis: at 48 V input and 2 A load, R19 reads 106.6 °C and Q1 reads 86.1 °C. These are published surface temperatures. They are not junction temperatures or a new thermal measurement. The report does not establish our assumed laboratory ambient.
Predict which part gets hotter before reading the thermal image. If high-line heat dominates, investigate switching and damping loss before reducing winding resistance. Removing damping may reduce dissipation while increasing overshoot. Accept that trade only after voltage and EMI measurements pass.
For efficiency, compare \eta=P_o/(P_o+P_{loss}) with TIDT280 Figures 2-1, 2-2 and 2-5 at the same input and load. The report gives plots, not a numerical efficiency table. No digitized efficiency dataset or fitted coefficient is claimed here.

title: Appendix A — Predict the current path
text:

title: Appendix B — Derive the ratio and stresses
text:
Volt-second balance gives DV_g-(1-D)V=0. Thus
\frac{V_o}{V_g}=-\frac{D}{1-D},\qquad D=\frac{V}{V_g+V}.
Capacitor charge balance gives I_o=(1-D)I_L. The mean source current is I_g=DI_L. Therefore I_L=I_g+I_o. This identity uses positive current magnitudes. It explains the current penalty compared with a buck or boost at the same port conditions.
\Delta I_L=\frac{V_gD}{Lf_s},\qquad I_{L,pk}=I_L+\frac{\Delta I_L}{2}.
Include triangular ripple when calculating heating:
I_{L,rms}^2=I_L^2+\frac{\Delta I_L^2}{12}.
I_{Q,rms}^2=D I_{L,rms}^2,\qquad I_{D,rms}^2=(1-D)I_{L,rms}^2.
The mean switch current is DI_L. The mean diode current is I_o. Both blocking voltages approach V_g+V, before switching overshoot.
I_{C,rms}^2=I_o^2\frac{D}{1-D}+(1-D)\frac{\Delta I_L^2}{12}.
For the capacitive part of output ripple, \Delta V_C\simeq I_oD/(Cf_s). The ESR contribution follows the capacitor-current steps. It cannot be replaced by the buck formula using only triangular inductor ripple.
Calculated example. Choose 10 V to −15 V at 1 A, 100 kHz, 100 µH and 100 µF. These are teaching assumptions. Then D=0.6, I_L=2.5 A, \Delta I_L=0.6 A and I_{L,pk}=2.8 A. The switch blocks 25 V ideally. The capacitor carries 1.230 A RMS and has about 60 mV capacitive ripple. A 1 A load therefore does not justify a 1 A inductor or capacitor.
Choose this topology if the negative rail is required and its current and voltage stresses remain acceptable. If a positive common-ground output is required, change the topology rather than just changing the sign in the equation.
crumbs: 162  Appendix B — Derive the ratio and stresses

title: Appendix C — Add conduction losses before increasing duty
text:
Retain CCM and small ripple. Include winding resistance r_L, switch resistance r_Q and constant diode drop V_D. Use I_L\simeq V/[R(1-D)] for a resistive load of magnitude R.
V\simeq\frac{DV_g-(1-D)V_D}{(1-D)+\frac{r_L+Dr_Q}{R(1-D)}}.
The output remains V_o=-V. This estimate omits switching loss, core loss and thermal feedback. It is not an efficiency model.
For the deck’s 10 V input, 10 Ω load, 0.7 V diode, 40 mΩ winding and 60 mΩ switch, D=0.6 gives V=13.65 V instead of 15 V. Raising duty increases current and conduction loss. An ideal infinite ratio is not available in hardware.
The deck’s approximate ratio, power and frequency limits describe its teaching context. They are not universal topology ratings. Check devices, magnetics, cooling and control for the actual requirement.
crumbs: 163  Appendix C — Add conduction losses before increasing duty

title: Appendix D — Boundary conduction and DCM
text:
At the boundary, I_L=\Delta I_L/2. Define K=2Lf_s/R. Substitution gives K_{crit}=(1-D)^2. CCM requires K>K_{crit} under these ideal assumptions.
In discontinuous conduction (DCM), the diode stops before the next cycle. A third interval has zero inductor current. Let D_2 be the discharge fraction. Then D_2=V_gD/V and
\frac{V}{V_g}=\frac{D}{\sqrt{K}},\qquad D+D_2<1.
The output now depends on load resistance. The CCM ratio alone cannot predict it. At D = 0.6, R = 10 Ω and 100 kHz, the boundary inductance is 8 µH. A 100 µH inductor is in CCM there. At light load, check this boundary again.

title: Four-switch non-inverting buck–boost — design the LM5176EVM-HP
text:
Power Electronic Systems · HTWG · 2026
A source crosses the required positive output voltage. How can one converter keep the output regulated with common ground? Follow this lesson from requirements through the three operating modes, component sizing and TI’s published waveforms.

These are total ideal bank currents at 7 A load. They are not currents assigned to each parallel capacitor. The 660 µF estimate uses only the nominal polymer bank and omits the ceramics’ contribution and all impedance effects.
At 6 V, a 120 mV charge-only target needs C\geq7\cdot0.5/(250000\cdot0.12)=116.7 µF. TI fits substantially more bulk capacitance. The 3 A load step gives another reason: a constant deficit uses 0.6 V across 660 µF in 132 µs. ESR, current ramp and the loop determine the real deviation.

The input bank has 32.9 µF nominal ceramic plus 100 µF polymer. It must handle the pulsed buck current and the source impedance. Do not size it from the small boost input ripple alone.
The left devices ideally block the input rail, at most 36 V. The right devices block the 12 V output rail. TI uses 60 V and 30 V parts respectively. Unlike the inverting circuit, a device does not normally block the 48 V sum at the 36 V input point. Include ringing and abnormal conditions separately.
Q1 and Q2 share the left-upper current. At 6 V in boost, that pair conducts almost continuously. Q5 and Q7 alternate at the right. In buck, Q1/Q2 and Q3 alternate while Q5 conducts continuously. Use each interval’s RMS current to calculate I^2R loss. Equal sharing is an assumption to check with gate layout and thermal symmetry.

title: 5. Current limit, compensation and losses
text:
R7 is the 4 mΩ cycle-current shunt in the common low-side return. It carries current during the boost charging interval or the buck freewheel interval. It does not carry the full inductor current throughout the cycle. R1 is a separate 4 mΩ output-current shunt between the ceramic and bulk output banks.
At 6 V and 7 A load, our ideal R7 loss is D(I_L^2+\Delta I_L^2/12)R_7=0.393 W. R1’s DC loss floor is I_o^2R_1=0.196 W. Its ripple loss depends on current division between the output banks. The 3.35 mΩ winding estimate adds 0.658 W. Their 1.247 W subtotal excludes R1 ripple, MOSFETs, switching, gate drive and core loss. It cannot predict total efficiency.
In boost, increasing the current command initially extends the interval during which the output capacitor supplies the load alone. The output therefore initially moves the wrong way. The approximate boost RHP zero is
f_{RHP}\simeq\frac{R(1-D_{boost})^2}{2\pi L}.
At 6 V and 7 A, R=12/7 Ω gives 14.51 kHz. A first crossover ceiling of one third is 4.84 kHz. At 10 A it falls to 10.16 kHz, with a 3.39 kHz ceiling. Our 15.24 µH alternative lowers the 7 A zero to about 4.48 kHz. A larger inductor is therefore not automatically better.
TI uses R23 = 6.19 kΩ, C22 = 33 nF and C29 = 270 pF. Their simple RC zero is 1/(2\pi R_{23}C_{22})=779 Hz. The approximate high-frequency pole is 1/(2\pi R_{23}C_{29})=95.2 kHz. These component frequencies do not establish the complete loop crossover or phase margin. Current-sense gain, slope compensation and the selected mode also enter. Unlike PMP30916, this guide does not supply a measured loop-gain plot.
The divider gives V_o=0.8(1+280/20)=12 V. The 33.2 kΩ timing resistor and datasheet frequency relation give about 247.4 kHz, consistent with a 250 kHz default. Use the actual measured period when comparing ripple.
The current-limit threshold is a peak criterion in boost and a valley criterion in buck. Apply the appropriate threshold tolerance before subtracting or adding half the ripple. R1’s nominal average-current threshold is separately 50\ \mathrm{mV}/4\ \mathrm{m\Omega}=12.5 A. Neither number alone guarantees output capability at every input.
Use the datasheet’s current-mode compensation model for a new design. Retain TI’s compensation for the published waveform comparison. A changed L, shunt, capacitor bank or output current requires a new loop and current-limit check.

title: 7. Deeper comparison: define what stays equal
text:
7.1 Same input, power and duty
Can the same four-switch bridge behave like a classical buck–boost, a buck, or a boost? Predict the inductor voltage and port-current paths before comparing component sizes. The switching sequence, not the name, determines the answer.
“Non-inverting buck–boost” correctly describes the conversion function. The classical inverting topology stores energy in one interval and delivers it in the other. A four-switch stage can also transfer power while both ports connect to the inductor. These are different physical operating conditions.
All new comparisons use 24 V input, 120 W output-power magnitude and 100 kHz. The polarity remains negative for the inverting buck–boost (IBB) and positive for NIBB. These are authored teaching cases. They are not measurements of PMP30916 or LM5176EVM-HP.
A numerical duty of 0.5 does not mean the same conversion ratio in every mode:
M_{IBB}=\frac{D}{1-D}.
M_{buck}=D_{AH},\qquad M_{boost}=\frac{1}{1-D_{BL}}.
Here M=|V_o|/V_g.
At 24 V input and 0.5 duty, those output voltages are −24 V, +12 V and +48 V. Equal power then requires different output currents. The requested same-duty experiment is valid, but it changes the output-voltage requirement. It cannot by itself rank components for one common load voltage.
We therefore show two experiments. Experiment A holds the numerical active-switch duty at 0.5. Experiment B also matches output-voltage magnitude. In Experiment B the classical duty remains D_*=M/(1+M) for each matched pair. We report the NIBB leg duties explicitly. D* is a conversion-ratio coordinate, not a claim that all gate pulses have the same width.
Use synchronous rectification in both circuits. Comparing a diode IBB against synchronous NIBB would add a rectifier-technology change to the topology comparison.

title: 8. Experiment B: match the output-voltage magnitude
text:
8.1 State intervals reveal the mechanism
Now hold the output magnitude equal within each pair. Keep 24 V input, 120 W, 100 kHz and the same initial magnetic and capacitor models. The output currents are 10 A at 12 V magnitude, 5 A at 24 V, and 2.5 A at 48 V.
Only the Paired case has the classical charging duty as its actual charging-state fraction. In the buck and boost rows, matching both the output magnitude and the classical numerical gate duty would violate their different gain equations. The table makes this change explicit.
Write 1 when a leg connects its inductor terminal to the positive rail. Write 0 when it connects to ground. With ideal complementary gates, the lower switch has the opposite state.
At unity ratio, Paired spends 0.5T in 10 and 0.5T in 01. It reproduces the classical two energy intervals. Transition90 spends 0.8T in 11 and 0.1T in each of 10 and 01. Most of its power passes during direct transfer. The assumed timing is illustrative and does not reproduce the proprietary LM5176 control law.
Overlap50, from Experiment A, uses 0.1T in 10, 0.4T in 11, 0.1T in 01 and 0.4T in 00. Its recirculation interval consumes time without supplying the load. This explains why its current remains much higher than Transition90 even though both have a small ripple.
The exact port-current averages give a useful identity:
I_g+I_o=I_L+\langle s_{11}i_L\rangle-\langle s_{00}i_L\rangle.
Thus the classical result I_L=I_g+I_o also holds for Paired. Direct transfer reduces the required mean inductor current. Recirculation can increase it. In general, integrate the gated current. Replacing \langle b(t)i_L(t)\rangle with d_B\langle i_L\rangle can lose the current/timing correlation.
Predict first. At M = 1, choose Paired or Transition90 for the same +24 V, 120 W requirement. Name one current-stress benefit and one control or switching cost. Identify the waveform measurement that would change your choice.

title: 9. Switch utilization: count voltage, current and switching separately

A utilization number needs a definition. We use two explicit ideal stress burdens:

title: 10. Flux, energy and area product
text:
10.1 Compare the same magnetic first
In the declared linear, gap-dominated inductor model,
\Phi(t)=\frac{Li_L(t)}{N}.
B(t)=\frac{Li_L(t)}{NA_e}.
\Delta B=\frac{1}{NA_e}\int_{rise}v_Ldt.
The last equation determines flux swing. The DC current and magnetic reluctance determine the bias. Zero average inductor voltage means periodic flux. It does not mean zero average flux.
For the initial 20 µH, 20-turn, 100 mm² model, each ampere corresponds to 10 mT and 1 µWb. At M = 1, IBB has 70–130 mT flux density. Transition90 has 49.56–61.56 mT. Paired has exactly the IBB waveform.
The gap-energy screen is E_{max}=LI_{pk}^2/2. At unity ratio it is 1.690 mJ for IBB/Paired and 0.379 mJ for Transition90. This is magnetic stored energy, not all energy delivered to the load in one cycle. A DC-biased inductor does not empty on each period.
Use the same current density, fill and flux limit for an area-product screen:
A_p=A_eW_a\ \geq\ \frac{L I_{pk} I_{rms}}{K_u J B_{allow}}.
This follows from the peak flux-linkage constraint and the RMS copper-window constraint. Convert m⁴ to cm⁴ with a factor of 10^8. It is a lower-bound sizing screen. It does not select a catalog core or prove core/winding temperature.
At M = 0.5 the NIBB buck carries the output current rather than the sum of both port currents. At M = 2 the NIBB boost carries the input current. Those changes reduce both peak energy and window demand under the matched conditions. At M = 1, a benefit appears only when the modulation supplies useful direct-transfer intervals.
See the magnetics area-product appendix for the distinction between saturation and core-loss limits. A_p alone omits mean turn length, AC winding resistance, gap fringing and material loss. Lower A_p is not a validated volume or efficiency result.

title: 12. Loss comparisons: state the semiconductor and core assumptions
text:
12.1 Two conduction comparisons
With 10 mΩ per conducting device, the IBB current passes through one device at a time. NIBB current passes through two. The second comparison fixes the total conducting-path resistance at 20 mΩ: 20 mΩ for each IBB device, and 10 mΩ for each NIBB device. Both columns use the same ideal current waveforms.
Neither normalization guarantees equal silicon area or equal purchase cost. Higher-voltage devices do not automatically have the same resistance, capacitance or gate charge. These controlled comparisons expose path-count and current effects. A component-level efficiency claim needs an actual technology, drive voltage and thermal design.

title: 12. Loss comparisons: state the semiconductor and core assumptions
section: 12.2 Authored dynamic and core-loss scenario
text:
12.2 Authored dynamic and core-loss scenario
For a numerical scenario, assume 10 ns per gate edge, constant 200 pF output capacitance per position, and 20 nC gate charge at 10 V. Count each gate’s transitions from the actual sequence:
P_{edge}=f_s\sum_{edges}\frac{1}{2}V_{block}|i_{edge}|t_{edge}.
P_{Coss}=f_s\sum_{turn-ons}\frac{1}{2}C_{oss}V_{block}^2.
P_{gate}=f_s\sum_{turn-ons}Q_gV_{drive}.
This deliberately assumes that every commanded edge is a hard edge. It is a scenario, not a measured switching loss or a rigorous loss bound. Actual commutation can share or recover energy. Reverse recovery, nonlinear Eoss, dead time, ringing, driver overhead and temperature require a separate device model. The Coss term is the stated turn-on dissipation assumption; the edge term represents load-current overlap only.
Use a waveform-sensitive core-loss teaching law with exponents 1.5 and 2.5. Assume 0.20 W for the same core under symmetric triangular 50 mT peak-to-peak flux at 100 kHz. This is an authored reference, not a ferrite datasheet value:
P_{core}=0.20\left(\frac{\Delta B}{0.050}\right)^{1.0}\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T\left|\frac{dB/dt}{10000}\right|^{1.5}dt.
The denominators are 0.050 T and 10000 T/s. This normalized form follows the waveform dependence of an improved generalized Steinmetz model. It has no fitted DC-bias correction or relaxation model. Its absolute watts cannot validate a core or establish a thermal limit. Use measured material data for a hardware design.
Add winding loss I_{L,rms}^2\cdot20 mΩ and capacitor loss (I_{Cin,rms}^2+I_{Cout,rms}^2)\cdot10 mΩ. The total scenario uses the 20 mΩ conducting-path column, not both semiconductor columns.

title: 13. Maximum and minimum values over the declared range
text:
13.1 A hardware rating envelope is another calculation
For a range comparison, keep 24 V input, 120 W and 100 kHz. Sample M=0.25,0.5,0.75,1,1.5,2,3,4. The output magnitude spans 6–96 V. The classical duty D* is the same conversion-ratio coordinate for both families at each sample, while NIBB uses buck below unity, Transition90 at unity and boost above unity.
These are sampled extrema, not proven continuous global extrema. The assumed transition region has only its unity point. No interpolation is claimed for a real controller’s transition band.
There is no finite universal maximum over all duties. At fixed input voltage and output power, the classical mean current is I_L=P_o/(V_gD) and diverges as D approaches zero. Its blocking voltage is V_g/(1-D) and diverges as D approaches one. The positive-current CCM assumption can fail before those limits for a fixed L. Specify the usable range and control policy before treating an extremum as a hardware design limit.
Each row states its unit. IL valley and IL peak are the minimum and maximum within a switching cycle. For example, the minimum of the IL peak row is the smallest cycle peak among the sampled operating points.
A fixed set of devices must survive every required operating point. Find each position’s maximum blocking voltage and maximum current separately. They need not occur at the same M.
The 6–96 V output sweep is an abstract comparison range. It does not describe either kit’s configured output or establish that its fitted components support this range.
For example, the IBB maximum blocking voltage is 120 V at M = 4, but its 26.2 A peak occurs at M = 0.25. NIBB’s right upper position also combines a high-output voltage rating with its high current at low output. Do not select the hardware from one row or from the minimum of an operating-point utilization metric. Add transient, tolerance and thermal margin after this ideal envelope.

title: 14. What the comparison establishes
text:
The statement “NIBB is not a real buck–boost” is too broad. Its conversion function is buck–boost. In pure buck and boost operation, its current paths differ from the classical inverting energy-transfer cycle. Paired modulation can reproduce that cycle’s inductor, capacitor and flux stresses exactly, with positive output polarity.
Use clamped-leg buck/boost operation when the voltage ratio permits it and its pulse constraints pass. Near unity, compare the actual direct-transfer, charging, discharge and recirculation intervals. Transition90 is preferable to Paired in this declared ideal case because it reduces current, flux swing, capacitor stress and the sizing screen. Its practical cost is more involved timing, minimum-pulse and commutation behavior that requires controller-specific evidence.
The calculation supports a conditional selection. It does not establish that every NIBB implementation beats every IBB design. Match the electrical requirements, identify the actual switching sequence, and qualify the component and loss model before choosing hardware.
