title: Capacitors — choose by impedance, current and temperature
text:
A converter meets its nominal capacitance target but fails ripple or temperature limits. Which model reveals the cause? Hold voltage, current spectrum, ambient and mounting conditions fixed before comparing parts.
This lesson rewrites slides 13–26 of the 2025 Lesson 3 deck. It follows the converter lesson. Nominal capacitance alone is not a selection criterion.
crumbs: 184  Capacitors — choose by impedance, current and temperature

title: 1. The electrical equivalent
text:
Use C with a leakage resistance in parallel, plus series ESR and ESL. ESR is equivalent series resistance. It represents real power loss at a specified frequency, temperature and bias. It is not a separate resistor hidden inside the package.
When leakage is negligible at the frequency of interest,
Z(j\omega)=ESR(\omega)+j\left(\omega ESL-\frac{1}{\omega C}\right).
Below self resonance the reactive term is capacitive. Above it the component is inductive. Near resonance the reactances cancel, leaving ESR in this simple model. The rise of impedance above resonance does not by itself prove a rise of ESR.
f_0=\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{ESL\,C}}.
For a narrow frequency band, a fixed RLC model can be useful. A broad-band prediction needs frequency-dependent loss and possibly several relaxation branches.

title: 2. Why ESR changes with frequency
text:
An electric field polarizes the dielectric. Some polarization mechanisms follow the field with delay. This lag dissipates energy. Electrode, termination and electrolyte resistance add other loss mechanisms.
For a low-loss capacitive model with loss tangent \tan\delta,
ESR_{diel}\simeq\frac{\tan\delta}{2\pi f C}.
If C and loss tangent are approximately constant, this dielectric contribution falls as 1/f. Neither parameter is constant over all frequencies. Dipole relaxation, temperature and bias change the response. At high frequency, conductor current distribution and skin effect can increase the resistive contribution. Ferrites also have a complex material response, but their magnetic loss is not a universal inverse law for capacitor ESR.



Calculated impedance and loss contributions


This plot uses a declared illustrative model: 10 µF, 5 nH, loss tangent 0.02 and a 5 mΩ conductor term. It demonstrates a mechanism, not a measured capacitor.
Predict first: if frequency doubles while C and loss tangent remain fixed, what happens to dielectric ESR? What happens to loss if RMS current stays fixed? Would your answer change if RMS voltage stayed fixed instead?
For a switching-current spectrum, use the RMS current of each harmonic:
P_{cap}\simeq\sum_n I_{n,rms}^2 ESR(f_n,T),\qquad \Delta T\simeq P_{cap}R_\theta.
This thermal relation assumes a suitable steady-state thermal resistance for the actual mounting. A single ESR value at 100 kHz can miss loss at other harmonics. Leakage adds DC loss when relevant.
Sources: Murata on impedance and ESR, and TDK film technical information, §§2.3–2.6. The equations and illustrative plot are our model.

title: 4. Film: dielectric, construction and terminals
text:
Polyester (PET, often MKT when metallized) and polypropylene (PP, often MKP when metallized) are distinct dielectrics. Construction also matters: separate foil, metallized film, winding and stacking change the available current paths. Self-healing in a suitable metallized design can isolate small defects. It does not make sustained overstress harmless.
Use the TDK technical handbook, especially §1, §3.2.2 and §6.2. It distinguishes voltage, thermal and contact-current limits. These limits answer different questions.
Terminal current. Treat “2 A maximum per pin” as an unverified part-specific rule. The retrieved handbook does not establish it as a universal limit. Find the exact series, lead arrangement, frequency and thermal conditions before using that number. Internal end contacts and PCB connections can limit current even when dielectric loss is small. Multiple pins do not guarantee equal sharing.
Corona and partial discharge. Gas in small internal gaps can ionize under electrical stress. Repeated discharge can damage metallization and reduce capacitance. Check the AC voltage-versus-frequency envelope as well as peak voltage and pulse stress. A DC rating alone does not qualify repetitive AC operation.
Voltage rating. Keep DC working voltage, AC RMS voltage, repetitive peak voltage, transient withstand and permitted dv/dt separate. Apply temperature derating and the manufacturer’s waveform conditions. Use i=C\,dv/dt to estimate pulse current, then check both pulse and RMS ratings.
Choose PP film where its loss and pulse capability justify its volume. A ceramic bank may be preferable for compact local filtering. That alternative still needs a bias, thermal and mechanical check.

title: 6. The small-package dilemma
text:
Low ESR reduces heating at a fixed current. A small package can still have a high thermal resistance. Compare the product I_{rms}^2 ESR R_\theta, not ESR alone.
Consider two hypothetical parts under the same 3 A RMS current and 20 K permitted rise. Part A has 5 mΩ ESR and 500 K/W thermal resistance. Part B has 10 mΩ and 100 K/W. A dissipates 45 mW but rises 22.5 K. B dissipates 90 mW but rises 9 K. The lower-loss part fails this assumed temperature-rise target.
The corresponding thermal current limits are \sqrt{\Delta T_{max}/(ESR R_\theta)}: 2.83 A and 4.47 A. These are estimates, not package ratings. Real thermal impedance depends on solder joints, copper area, nearby heat sources and airflow. MLCC mechanical cracking and DC-bias loss remain separate checks.
Choose B under these assumptions if its effective capacitance and other ratings also pass. Choose A if improved mounting reduces its thermal resistance enough. The measurement that can change this choice is temperature rise under the actual ripple spectrum and PCB conditions.

title: 8. Parallel capacitors and life
text:
A small film or ceramic part can reduce high-frequency impedance alongside a bulk electrolytic. Its effect at the switching frequency depends on both impedances and layout. Unlike the deck’s categorical wording, “no effect at switching frequency” is not a general rule. Check current division and possible anti-resonance between branches.
For wet electrolytics, temperature strongly affects life. The familiar doubling per 10 K reduction is an approximation for applicable series and conditions. Use the manufacturer’s life model and ripple corrections. Case temperature is not automatically the internal hot-spot temperature.

text:
Choose a capacitor bank for the classical converter’s pulsed output current. Identify the harmonic data and thermal evidence still needed.
Explain why doubling frequency can reduce dielectric ESR while increasing loss at fixed AC voltage.
Compare two real film candidates against the same DC, AC, pulse and terminal-current requirements. Locate the exact source of any per-pin limit.
Compare X5R, X7R and C0G against the same effective capacitance and temperature target. Name a condition that changes your choice.
Decide whether the 470 µF archive example meets a 50 mV ripple target. State the next calculation or measurement required.

title: Control — Who is telling the truth? Pole placement versus small-signal models
text:
Power Electronic Systems · HTWG · 2026 · Draft for teaching review
Prerequisites: Lesson 1 §7 and Exercise E4, the boost exercises of Lesson 2, and the control part of the circuit-foundations recap.
Two engineers get the same task: design the voltage controller of a DC/DC converter. The control engineer draws the LC filter, writes its state equations and places the closed-loop poles. The power-electronics engineer starts from the two switch positions, averages them over a switching period, finds the operating point and linearizes. They get two different transfer functions for the same circuit. Both say that their model is the plant.
Who is telling the truth? This lesson does not pick a winner. It shows when the two models are the same model, when they differ, and which omitted physics makes them differ. All numbers come from the Example script scripts/model_comparison.py, and its checks are in model-checks.json.
How this lesson is built. This lesson does not follow the design-led structure of Lessons 1 and 2. It compares models, and no single reference design shows every effect. It follows one live session of 90 minutes, in seven parts. The circuit values are teaching assumptions, not checked component selections. Each one is stated where it is used.
crumbs: 195  Control — Who is telling the truth? Pole placement versus small-signal models

title: Learning outcomes and teaching route
text:
By the end, students should be able to:

separate four activities that both engineers do: physical modeling, linearization, controller synthesis and implementation
derive the state-space model of an LC plant and place its poles by state feedback
derive the averaged and linearized model of a buck, a boost and a buck-boost from their two switch positions
say for each topology whether the duty cycle moves the poles, the zeros or only the gain
explain the right-half-plane zero of the boost and buck-boost physically, and say what it costs the controller
explain why a stiff-link inverter can often use the simple LC model, and when it cannot
check a linear model against a switching model and name the source of each error: the operating point, the size of the perturbation, averaging or delay.

title: 1. Two engineers, one converter
text:
The control engineer. “The converter is an LC filter with a load. I write \dot x = Ax + Bu, check controllability and place the poles. The switching is fast. I can ignore it.”
The power-electronics engineer. “The converter changes its topology twice per period. I average the two states, find the operating point and linearize. My transfer function changes with the duty cycle. A model with fixed LC poles is wrong.”
Predict before reading on. Answer each question in one sentence. Keep your answers. §7 returns to them.

If two models have the same poles, are their transfer functions the same?
Can a controller move the poles of a converter without changing L or C?
Does a converter that switches at 20 kHz have a pole at 20 kHz?

The disagreement is smaller than it sounds. Pole placement and small-signal modeling are not competing theories. Pole placement is a method to design a controller. Small-signal modeling is a method to get a linear plant. Each engineer does four separate things, and the disagreement is in the first two:

Physical modeling. Which states, switch positions and energy stores does the model contain?
Linearization. About which operating point is the model valid?
Controller synthesis. How are the closed-loop poles, the bandwidth and the damping chosen?
Implementation. What changes when the controller drives a real switched converter through a modulator with sampling and delay?

Draw the plant as two boxes in series:
controller ──► duty d ──► [ switch network ] ──► u ──► [ LC + load ] ──► v_o
                                  ▲
                         V_in, operating point
The control engineer models only the right-hand box and takes u as the input. The power-electronics engineer models both boxes. The switch network turns d into u, and the input voltage and the operating point enter there. The rest of this lesson asks one question: when does the left-hand box change the answer?








Question
Passive-network model
Averaged converter model




What is modeled?

Switch network, LC and load


Duty cycle

Part of the averaged dynamics

Not needed for a linear passive plant
Needed for the linearization

Not represented

Controller design
Pole placement, LQR, PID
Pole placement, PI, PID, loop shaping


Main limit
Can omit the converter’s own dynamics
Valid locally, and only as far as averaging holds



Note the third row. Neither model represents the switching frequency. The basic averaged model is just as blind to PWM delay, sampling and ripple as the LC model. Both need extra modeling for those effects (§6.4).

title: 2. The control engineer’s model: an LC plant and pole placement
text:
2.1 The LC plant
Drive an LC filter with load R from a controllable voltage u. The states are the inductor current and the capacitor voltage, x = (i_L,\ v_o):
L\dot{i}_L = u - v_o,\qquad C\dot{v}_o = i_L - \frac{v_o}{R}\tag{2.1}
The state matrix A has the rows (0,\ -1/L) and (1/C,\ -1/(RC)). The input vector is B = (1/L,\ 0)^T.
The open-loop poles solve \det(sI - A) = 0:
s^2 + \frac{1}{RC}s + \frac{1}{LC} = 0\tag{2.2}
These are the natural frequencies of the passive plant. Nothing here knows how u is made.
crumbs: 198  2. The control engineer's model: an LC plant and pole placement

title: 2. The control engineer’s model: an LC plant and pole placement
section: 2.2 State feedback places the poles
text:
2.2 State feedback places the poles
Feed back both states, u = -k_i i_L - k_v v_o + N r. The closed loop is \dot x = (A - BK)x + BNr, and its characteristic polynomial is
s^2 + \left(\frac{k_i}{L} + \frac{1}{RC}\right)s + \frac{1 + k_v}{LC} + \frac{k_i}{LRC} = 0\tag{2.3}
Match it to s^2 + 2\zeta\omega_n s + \omega_n^2. Two gains set two coefficients, so any pair of poles is possible. The plant must be controllable, and the duty cycle must not saturate. Lesson 1, Exercise E4 places the poles of a buck this way.
Pole placement changes the closed-loop dynamics. It does not repair a wrong plant model. The gains are only as good as A and B.

title: 2. The control engineer’s model: an LC plant and pole placement
section: 2.3 What if the input is a duty cycle?
text:
2.3 What if the input is a duty cycle?
A real controller does not command a volt. It commands a duty cycle. For an ideal buck the switch-node voltage averages to u = dV_{\mathrm{in}}, so the input vector in duty units is B_d = (V_{\mathrm{in}}/L,\ 0)^T.
The open-loop poles do not change. The duty-unit gains do depend on V_{\mathrm{in}}. Take the Lesson 1 teaching buck: 48 V, 60 µH, 100 µF, 2.4 Ω, and design for 2 kHz and \zeta = 0.7 at 48 V. Keep the gains fixed and let the input move:

title: 3. The power-electronics model: averaging and linearization

title: 3. The power-electronics model: averaging and linearization
section: 3.2 Linearize about the operating point
text:
3.2 Linearize about the operating point
Write each quantity as its operating-point value plus a small deviation: x = X + \hat x, d = D + \hat d, u = U + \hat u. The operating point solves 0 = A(D)X + B(D)U. Keep the first-order terms only:
\dot{\hat x} = A(D)\,\hat x + B(D)\,\hat u + E_d\,\hat d,\qquad E_d = (A_1 - A_2)X + (B_1 - B_2)U\tag{3.3}

A(D) holds the dynamics of the averaged plant at this duty cycle.
B(D) is the sensitivity to the input voltage.
E_d is the sensitivity to the duty cycle. It contains the operating point X. The same circuit responds differently to \hat d at different loads and voltages.

The duty-to-output transfer function follows directly. With the output y = Cx:
G_{vd}(s) = C\,(sI - A(D))^{-1}E_d\tag{3.4}
crumbs: 199  3. The power-electronics model: averaging and linearization

title: 3. The power-electronics model: averaging and linearization
section: 3.3 What the model assumes
text:
3.3 What the model assumes
Name the approximations before using the model:

Averaging. The dynamics of interest are slow compared with the switching frequency. The ripple is small.
Linearization. Products of two deviations are neglected. The perturbation must be small.
One operating point, one conduction mode. The model holds for one D, one load and CCM.
No switching detail. The model has no ripple, no sampling and no modulator delay.

A large change of operating point does not invalidate the nonlinear averaged model (3.2). It invalidates the idea that one linearization (3.3) is good everywhere. §6 measures each error separately.
\mathrm{switching\ model} \rightarrow \mathrm{average} \rightarrow \mathrm{operating\ point} \rightarrow \mathrm{linearize}

title: 4. Buck, boost and buck-boost: does the duty cycle move the poles?
text:
4.1 The buck: duty only scales the input
Apply §3 to the three basic topologies. Write the averaged equations, then look at one thing: does d multiply a state?
Each converter is checked in CCM at D = 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8. At 20 kHz the buck-boost leaves CCM at D = 0.2: its inductor current is 0.31 A, and half the ripple is 0.50 A. It therefore switches at 50 kHz. The boost at D = 0.8 delivers 500 V and 2.5 kW into the fixed 100 Ω. This is a fixed-load comparison, not a fixed-power one.
L\dot{i}_L = dV_{\mathrm{in}} - v_o,\qquad C\dot{v}_o = i_L - \frac{v_o}{R}\tag{4.1}
The duty cycle multiplies V_{\mathrm{in}}, which is not a state. With a constant input the averaged buck is already linear, and
G_{vd}(s) = \frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}}{LCs^2 + (L/R)s + 1}\tag{4.2}
At all three duty cycles the poles sit at f_0 = 2055 Hz with Q = 3.10, and the gain is 48 V. For the ideal buck, the control engineer’s LC model and the averaged model are the same model. The passive LC model is not always wrong.

The resonance moves. From D = 0.2 to 0.8 it falls by a factor of four, from 403 Hz to 101 Hz.

title: 4. Buck, boost and buck-boost: does the duty cycle move the poles?
section: 4.5 Why the output first goes the wrong way
text:
4.5 Why the output first goes the wrong way
Predict. Increase the duty cycle of a boost in one step. Does the output voltage rise immediately?
It does not. A higher duty cycle keeps the switch on for longer. The inductor stores more energy, but the diode conducts for a shorter part of each period. In the first periods, the inductor current has not risen yet, and less charge reaches the output capacitor. The output falls. Only when the inductor current has grown does the output rise to its new value.



Boost at D = 0.8, duty step to 0.805. The cycle-averaged output of the exact switching model falls by 156 mV in the first 0.28 ms and crosses zero after 0.53 ms. The linearized averaged model predicts the same dip.


This inverse response is the time-domain picture of the RHP zero. The zero adds phase lag, as a pole does, while it raises the gain, as a zero does. No stable controller can remove it. A controller that cancelled it would need an unstable pole. In practice, the RHP zero limits the loop crossover. A common rule of thumb keeps the crossover below about one fifth of the lowest RHP-zero frequency in the operating range. Lesson 2 meets the same mechanism in the charging boost.

title: 5. Inverters and motor drives: why the simple model often works
text:
5.1 The inverter with a stiff DC link
A full-bridge inverter drives an LC output filter. Its averaged bridge voltage is mV_{\mathrm{dc}}, with the modulation index m \in [-1, 1]:
L\dot{i}_L = mV_{\mathrm{dc}} - v_o,\qquad C\dot{v}_o = i_L - \frac{v_o}{R}\tag{5.1}
This is the buck equation (4.1) again, with m in place of d. If V_{\mathrm{dc}} is stiff, the modulation changes only the excitation. It does not change the filter poles. With 1 mH, 20 µF and 50 Ω the filter resonates at 1125 Hz with \zeta = 0.071, at every modulation index.
This is why inverter and motor-drive engineers can use LC models and state feedback with good results. Their converter is, to first order, a buck with a stiff source. The duty-dependent reflection of §4.2 never appears.

section: 5.2 When the DC link is not stiff
text:
5.2 When the DC link is not stiff
Feed the DC link from a 400 V source through a source resistance R_s = 2 Ω into a link capacitor C_{\mathrm{dc}} = 50 µF. The link voltage is now a state:
C_{\mathrm{dc}}\dot{v}_{\mathrm{dc}} = \frac{V_s - v_{\mathrm{dc}}}{R_s} - m\,i_L\tag{5.2}
Linearize the bridge voltage:
\hat v_{\mathrm{bridge}} = V_{\mathrm{dc}}\hat m + M\hat v_{\mathrm{dc}}\tag{5.3}
The operating point M now enters the dynamics, in (5.2) and in (5.3). This is the same mechanism as the boost: the modulation multiplies a state. The three-state model at a DC operating point gives:

title: 5. Inverters and motor drives: why the simple model often works
section: 5.3 The motor-drive model
text:
5.3 The motor-drive model
A permanent-magnet synchronous machine in the rotor frame has
L_d\dot{i}_d = v_d - R_{\mathrm{st}} i_d + \omega_e L_q i_q,\qquad L_q\dot{i}_q = v_q - R_{\mathrm{st}} i_q - \omega_e\left(L_d i_d + \psi_f\right)\tag{5.4}
with the stator resistance R_{\mathrm{st}}, the electrical speed \omega_e and the magnet flux linkage \psi_f. The model assumes sinusoidal quantities, known parameters and the dq transformation. The speed-dependent cross-coupling terms are usually compensated by feedforward. Each current axis is then a first-order RL plant, driven by an inverter that the model treats as an ideal voltage source.
Motor-control engineering does not use an incomplete model. It uses the model that fits the dynamics it controls. The complete drive also has DC-link dynamics, dead time, modulator saturation, sampling delay and parameter changes with speed and current.
Ask. At which current-loop bandwidth does the “ideal controllable voltage source” stop being good enough? No single number answers this. The answer depends on the switching frequency, the PWM update method, the sampling and the robustness the drive needs. §6.4 gives the first estimate.
crumbs: 201  5. Inverters and motor drives: why the simple model often works

title: 6. Which model predicts the switching converter?
text:
6.1 The experiment
A model is a claim about a physical system. Test the claim against something closer to the system than the model itself.
Take the boost of §4. Compare three models with a fourth reference:
All four use the same input and output: duty step \hat d = 0.005, output voltage. A voltage-to-output transfer function cannot be compared with a duty-to-output one. The gain from duty to voltage must be inside the model. The live session uses a PLECS switching model in place of the Python reference.

title: 6. Which model predicts the switching converter?
text:
Model A: passive LC. Fixed 1 mH, 100 µF and 100 Ω, poles at 503 Hz with Q = 31.6. Its gain is matched at D = 0.5. It has no RHP zero.
Model B: averaged, linearized at D = 0.5. One model for all operating points.
Model B′: averaged, linearized at the actual D. One model per operating point.
Reference: the exact switching converter. The Example script solves the two linear switch-position equations exactly, period by period, from the periodic steady state. It plots the average over each switching period, so ripple does not hide the comparison.

title: 6. Which model predicts the switching converter?
section: 6.4 Toward the switching frequency
text:
6.4 Toward the switching frequency
Ask. What happens when the crossover moves toward the switching frequency?
The averaged model starts to fail, and several effects appear that no model above contains: the modulator delay, the sampling of a digital controller, aliasing and the ripple in the measured signal. A first estimate treats the total effect as a pure delay T_d:
G_{\mathrm{delay}}(s) = e^{-sT_d},\qquad \varphi_{\mathrm{delay}} = -\omega T_d\tag{6.1}

At 20 kHz, 75 µs is 1.5 switching periods. This value is common for a digital controller that computes for one period and updates the PWM once per period. It is an estimate, not a rule. Take T_d from the actual sampling and PWM implementation.
An averaged model can describe the low-frequency behaviour well and still miss the effects that limit the achievable bandwidth. When the crossover reaches a significant fraction of f_s, a sampled-data model is the next step. Corradini, Maksimović, Mattavelli and Zane develop it for digital control of converters.

title: 7. Quick check and conclusion
text:
Answer true or false, and give one sentence of reason.

Pole placement requires an LC-only model.
In an ideal CCM buck with constant input voltage, the duty cycle changes the open-loop LC poles.
In an ideal CCM boost, the duty cycle changes the plant dynamics.
A basic averaged model captures PWM delay and sampling effects.
A linearized model can be accurate at one operating point and inaccurate at another.

Now return to the three predictions of §1. Change any answer that this lesson contradicts, and name the section that changed it.
Who was telling the truth? Both engineers can be right. Each must know what the model includes, what it excludes, and over which range it stays valid. Three principles summarize the lesson:

A model is not the system. Its validity follows from the assumptions used to derive it.
The design method does not decide the model’s accuracy. Pole placement on a correctly linearized converter model is good power-electronics practice.
Match the model to the question. An LC model is enough for a buck or an inverter with a stiff link. A boost or buck-boost needs the duty-dependent averaged model. A loop near the switching frequency needs a sampled-data model.

A correct controller cannot compensate for a fundamentally wrong model. Robust feedback tolerates model error, but only within its stability and performance margins.
crumbs: 203  7. Quick check and conclusion

title: 8. What to retain
text:
Pole placement designs controllers. Small-signal modeling builds plants. The disagreement is about the plant, never about the method.
Ask whether d multiplies a state. In the ideal buck it does not, so the LC model is exact. In the boost and buck-boost it does, so the reflected inductance L/D'^2 and the RHP zero move with the operating point.
The RHP zero is physical. The output first moves the wrong way. It limits the crossover, and no stable controller can remove it.
Gains designed at one duty cycle are a different controller at another. Check the worst operating point, not only the design point.
Separate the errors. Operating-point error comes from a fixed linearization. Linearization error grows with the perturbation. Averaging error and delay grow as the bandwidth approaches f_s.
Neither basic model sees the switching frequency. Add the delay, then a sampled-data model, before trusting a fast loop.

title: 9. Training: problem-driven exercises
text:
T1 — Is the bare LC model of the boost good enough?
As in Lessons 1 and 2, start each exercise with a prediction. Choose a model, solve, compare the alternatives and defend a decision. For every exercise, state your choice, one benefit and one cost. Name the condition or measurement that would change your choice.
Every Problem states its own operating point. Never carry a number from one operating point to another.

title: 9. Training: problem-driven exercises
text:
Problem
A control engineer must design the voltage loop of the §4 boost at D = 0.5: 100 V in, 1 mH, 100 µF, 100 Ω. The engineer models the plant as the bare LC filter with L = 1 mH and matches its DC gain to the boost. The planned crossover is 50 Hz, to be raised later to 1 kHz. Is the bare LC model good enough? If not, what is the smallest change that makes it good enough?
Predict. Will the bare LC model put the resonance too high or too low? By how much?


Why we do it
Most control engineers meet power electronics through the inverter, where the LC model works (§5.1). This exercise finds the exact point at which their habit fails in a DC/DC converter. It also shows that the fix can be small.


What matters

Compare the resonance and the phase of the two models. The DC gain is matched by construction.
The averaged model has a zero that the LC model cannot have.
The planned crossover decides which errors matter. An error far above crossover changes little.



Where it appears in practice
PFC boost stages, battery boost converters and photovoltaic MPPT boosts are often controlled by engineers trained on drives or inverters. The same check applies to every interleaved and multiphase boost.


Possible solutions
(a) Keep the bare LC model. Its poles are at 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC}) = 503 Hz with Q = 31.6. The averaged model has them at D'/(2\pi\sqrt{LC}) = 252 Hz with Q = 15.8 (§4.4). The resonance is a factor of 2 = 1/D′ too high. In the step test of §6.2 this model is 34 % wrong even at D = 0.5.
(b) Reflect the inductor. Use L_e = L/D'^2 = 4 mH in the LC model. Then the poles and Q are exact, because the denominator of (4.6) is the LC polynomial with L_e. Only the RHP zero at 3.98 kHz is missing.
(c) Use the full averaged model (4.6). It adds the RHP zero. It is exact at D = 0.5 to the accuracy of §6.2: 2.7 % RMS error.
(d) Use a switching simulation. It needs no derivation, but it gives no transfer function to design with.


Pros and cons








Model
Benefit
Cost




(a) bare LC
Familiar; no operating point needed
Resonance wrong by 1/D′; no RHP zero


(b) reflected LC
One line of change; exact poles
Valid only at one D; still no RHP zero


(c) averaged
Exact at its operating point; shows the RHP zero
Must be re-linearized when D changes


(d) switching
Includes ripple, and delay if modelled
No transfer function; slow to iterate





Conclusion
At 50 Hz, (b) is sufficient. The RHP zero at 3.98 kHz is 80 times above crossover, and its phase lag at 50 Hz is \arctan(50/3979) = 0.7°. At 1 kHz the same zero costs \arctan(1000/3979) = 14° of phase. That is too much to ignore, and the crossover is above the one-fifth rule of §4.5, so use (c). If the boost must also run at D = 0.8, the zero falls to 637 Hz, and a 1 kHz crossover is not possible at all. Then the decision is not about the model. The requirement must change, or the control structure must change, for example to an inner current loop. Use (d) to confirm the final design, not to create it.

title: 9. Training: problem-driven exercises
section: E1 — One state-feedback controller for the whole duty range?
text:
E1 — One state-feedback controller for the whole duty range?

Problem
The §4 buck-boost (100 V in, 1 mH, 100 µF, 100 Ω, 50 kHz) must regulate its output from 25 V to 400 V, so D runs from 0.2 to 0.8. A designer places the closed-loop poles at 500 Hz, \zeta = 0.7, at D = 0.5, using duty-unit state feedback \hat d = -k_i\hat i_L - k_v\hat v_o + N\hat r on the averaged model.

Derive the linearized buck-boost model (4.8) and compute the gains and N at D = 0.5.
Keep the gains fixed. Find the closed-loop poles, the step overshoot or undershoot and the DC gain at D = 0.2 and D = 0.8.
Compare two remedies: (a) schedule the gains with D, so the poles are at 500 Hz, \zeta = 0.7 at every D; (b) keep fixed gains, but choose a slower target of 150 Hz, \zeta = 0.7, at D = 0.5. Test both at D = 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8.
Locate the RHP zero at each D. Say which remedy it limits and why.

Predict. Which remedy is safer: faster scheduled gains, or slower fixed gains?


Why we do it
§4.6 shows the boost result. This exercise asks for a decision. A slower controller usually feels safer, but this plant can show otherwise. The task is to find out before the hardware does.


What matters

Use the linearized model at each D. Do not reuse a matrix from another operating point.
Report real closed-loop poles as two frequencies, not as one f_n and \zeta.
Check stability first. Overshoot and DC gain mean nothing for an unstable loop.
Gain scheduling needs a measured or estimated D. Name what you would measure.



Where it appears in practice
Wide-range converters: battery chargers, LED drivers, photovoltaic and fuel-cell converters, and the inverting buck-boost stages of portable equipment. Commercial controllers solve the same problem with current-mode control and input-voltage feedforward.


Solution
Released after the deadline in the Enrolled companion.

title: 9. Training: problem-driven exercises
section: E2 — How stiff must the DC link be?
text:
E2 — How stiff must the DC link be?

Problem
The §5 inverter (1 mH, 20 µF, 50 Ω output filter) runs at a DC operating point M = 0.8. Its DC link is fed from 400 V through a source resistance R_s into a link capacitor C_{\mathrm{dc}}. Consider R_s = 0.5, 2 and 10 Ω, and C_{\mathrm{dc}} = 50 µF and 500 µF.

Write the three-state averaged model with the states v_{\mathrm{dc}}, i_L and v_o. Find the operating point.
Linearize and find the filter resonance, its damping and the DC-link pole for each of the six combinations.
Compare each result with the stiff-link LC model (1125 Hz, \zeta = 0.071). For a voltage loop that crosses at 300 Hz, decide which combinations allow the stiff-link model.
Explain why a larger C_{\mathrm{dc}} brings the filter back to the stiff-link values, and what it costs.

Predict. Which matters more for the filter resonance: R_s or C_{\mathrm{dc}}?


Why we do it
The stiff-link assumption is the reason why the simple inverter model works (§5.1). This exercise turns that assumption into a check with numbers, so you can defend it or reject it.


What matters

The link voltage at the operating point falls with R_s. Use it in the linearization.
Two different questions: does the filter move, and how slow is the new DC-link pole?
A pole far from crossover can still matter for a slow outer loop or for the upstream converter.



Where it appears in practice
Inverters fed from long DC cables, from batteries with high internal resistance, or from an upstream PFC stage with its own voltage loop. The same coupling explains interactions between cascaded converters.


Solution
Released after the deadline in the Enrolled companion.

title: 10. Extension: who owns the current? CCM, DCM and the fourth leg
text:
10.1 The question
This extension is not part of the 90-minute route. It answers a question from the lecture: why does the switching not set the output current of a buck in CCM? It then applies the answer to a converter where this question decides the design, the fourth leg that balances a split DC link. All numbers come from the Example script scripts/current_ownership.py, and its checks are in current-checks.json.
Two intuitive answers are common. First, in CCM the inductor and the capacitor exchange only a ripple of energy in each period, so they act as a filter and not as an energy store. Second, the impedance of the inductor at DC is zero, so the inductor cannot limit the DC current. Both answers point in the right direction. Neither shows why the load, and not the inductor, sets the current. The averaged equations show it.
Predict. A buck runs in CCM at D = 0.5. Double the inductance. Does the output current change?
crumbs: 206  10. Extension: who owns the current? CCM, DCM and the fourth leg

title: 10. Extension: who owns the current? CCM, DCM and the fourth leg
section: 10.2 In CCM the inductor drops out of the operating point
crumbs: 206  10. Extension: who owns the current? CCM, DCM and the fourth leg

title: 10. Extension: who owns the current? CCM, DCM and the fourth leg
section: 10.3 In DCM the current resets in every period
text:
10.3 In DCM the current resets in every period
In DCM the inductor current returns to zero before the next period starts. The peak current, the falling interval D_2T_s and the average current are
I_{pk} = \frac{(V_{\mathrm{in}} - V_o)D}{Lf_s},\qquad D_2 = D\,\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}} - V_o}{V_o},\qquad I_o = \frac{I_{pk}}{2}(D + D_2)\tag{10.5}
Substitute:
I_o = \frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}(V_{\mathrm{in}} - V_o)}{2Lf_sV_o}D^2\tag{10.6}
Now L and f_s appear in the operating point. Each period moves one charge packet, and the duty cycle sets its size. DCM does not make the converter an ideal current source, because the current still depends on V_o. Critical conduction mode (CrCM) is the boundary where D + D_2 = 1.
Apply it to the Lesson 1 buck. At D = 0.5 the ripple is 2.0 A peak-to-peak, so the buck leaves CCM above 24 Ω. At 48 Ω it needs D = 0.354, not 0.5, to hold 24 V. The peak current is 1.41 A, and D_2 = 0.354. A time-stepped switching simulation with an ideal diode settles at 24.06 V.
Linearize (10.6) about the operating point: \hat i_o = g_d\hat d + g_v\hat v_o, with
g_d = \frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}(V_{\mathrm{in}} - V_o)D}{Lf_sV_o},\qquad g_v = -\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}^2D^2}{2Lf_sV_o^2}\tag{10.7}
Add the output capacitor and the load:
G_{vd}(s) = \frac{g_d}{Cs + 1/R - g_v}\tag{10.8}
This plant has one pole. In the example it is at 99.5 Hz. The same L and C in CCM resonate at 2055 Hz (§4.4). The pole agrees with the reduced-order DCM model of Erickson and Maksimović, \omega_p = (2 - M)/((1 - M)RC) with M = V_o/V_{\mathrm{in}}. In DCM the inductor current is no longer a state of the low-frequency model. The duty cycle sets the average current directly.

title: 10. Extension: who owns the current? CCM, DCM and the fourth leg
section: 10.4 The fourth leg: a split DC link that must stay balanced
text:
10.4 The fourth leg: a split DC link that must stay balanced
A three-phase four-wire inverter in a UPS or a vehicle-to-load system connects the load neutral to the midpoint of a split DC link. An unbalanced load draws a neutral current i_N from the midpoint and charges one half of the link more than the other. A fourth half-bridge drives an inductor into the midpoint and moves charge back. It must react within one tenth of a grid cycle, 2 ms at 50 Hz. The energy it moves is small, so the converter and its inductor should also be small. In practice, CCM control of such a balancer was slow and difficult, and DCM solved the problem. Why?



Parameter
Value




Total DC link V_{\mathrm{dc}}
800 V


Capacitance per half C
10 mF


Fourth-leg inductance L
100 µH


Switching frequency f_s
20 kHz


Balancing current
2 A


Required response
2 ms



These are teaching values. Define the imbalance e = v_+ - v_-, with v_+ across the upper and v_- across the lower capacitor. The inductor current i_L flows from the switch node into the midpoint, and i_N flows from the midpoint to the load neutral. The switch node is at +v_+ or -v_- relative to the midpoint. With a stiff total link, v_- = (V_{\mathrm{dc}} - e)/2, and the averaged model is
C\dot e = i_N - i_L,\qquad L\dot i_L = dV_{\mathrm{dc}} - v_-\tag{10.9}
Linearize at balance, D = 1/2 and e = 0. The term v_- adds \hat e/2 to the inductor voltage:
\frac{\hat e(s)}{\hat d(s)} = -\frac{V_{\mathrm{dc}}}{LCs^2 + 1/2},\qquad \omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2LC}}\tag{10.10}
The denominator has no first-order term. The ideal balancing plant has a pair of poles on the imaginary axis. All damping must come from losses, from the load or from the controller. With the teaching values the resonance is at 112.5 Hz. The neutral current of a nonlinear load contains the triplen harmonics, and its 150 Hz component is close. Zhao et al. report the 180° phase change at this resonance as a source of instability. They stabilize the loop with inductor-current feedback and a feedforward of the neutral current.
Predict. Is the undamped resonance the reason why CCM is difficult here?
crumbs: 206  10. Extension: who owns the current? CCM, DCM and the fourth leg

title: 10. Extension: who owns the current? CCM, DCM and the fourth leg
section: 10.5 In CCM the ripple dwarfs the useful current
text:
10.5 In CCM the ripple dwarfs the useful current
CCM is not slow. The largest current slope is (V_{\mathrm{dc}}/2)/L = 4 A/µs. A properly designed current loop is much faster than 2 ms. With an inner current loop, the outer plant is
\frac{\hat e(s)}{\hat i_L(s)} = -\frac{1}{Cs}\tag{10.11}
and this plant is simple to control. The difficulty is elsewhere. With complementary PWM at D = 0.5, the inductor sees V_{\mathrm{dc}}/2 for half a period:
\Delta i_{L,pp} = \frac{V_{\mathrm{dc}}}{4Lf_s}\tag{10.12}
This is 100 A peak-to-peak around a useful average of 2 A. The peak current is 52 A, and the RMS current is 28.9 A. The current loop must measure a 2 A average inside a 100 A triangle.
The memory of the CCM current makes small errors grow. Around balance, \dot{\bar i}_L = (V_{\mathrm{dc}}/L)(d - 1/2). A duty error of 0.1 percentage points, from dead time, PWM resolution or sampling, gives a slope of 8000 A/s: 8 A after 1 ms, four times the useful current. In CCM the duty cycle sets the rate of change of the current, so every duty error integrates.
crumbs: 206  10. Extension: who owns the current? CCM, DCM and the fourth leg

title: 10. Extension: who owns the current? CCM, DCM and the fourth leg
section: 10.6 In DCM the controller commands a charge packet
text:
10.6 In DCM the controller commands a charge packet
For a positive packet, turn the upper switch on for t_+ = DT_s. Then turn both switches off. The lower body diode carries the falling current, and the current stops at zero. The packet charge and the average current are
Q_+ = \frac{v_+V_{\mathrm{dc}}}{2Lv_-}t_+^2,\qquad \bar I_L = f_sQ_+\tag{10.13}
At balance, v_+ = v_- = V_{\mathrm{dc}}/2:
\bar I_L = \frac{V_{\mathrm{dc}}}{2Lf_s}D^2\tag{10.14}
For a negative packet, pulse the lower switch. The inverse law gives the pulse for a requested current I^*:
D^* = \mathrm{sgn}(I^*)\sqrt{\frac{2Lf_s|I^*|}{V_{\mathrm{dc}}}}\tag{10.15}
The sign selects the switch, so D^* is not the upper-switch duty ratio of §10.5. The rise and the fall take 2|D^*|T_s together, so DCM needs 2|D^*| \leq 1. At balance this limits the average current to V_{\mathrm{dc}}/(8Lf_s) = 50 A. At this limit the balancer runs in CrCM.
For 2 A the pulse is D = 0.1, or 5 µs. The peak current is 20 A, the packet is 100 µC, and the RMS current is 5.2 A. A time-stepped simulation of one packet gives the same charge. The same duty error of 0.1 percentage points now changes the average current by 0.04 A, and this error does not grow. In DCM the duty cycle sets the current itself. This is the answer to the question of §10.1.
An outer charge controller closes the loop on the imbalance:
\bar i_L^* = \hat i_N + \frac{C}{\tau}e\tag{10.16}
with the estimated neutral current \hat i_N and the balancing time constant \tau. For \tau = 2 ms the gain C/\tau is 5 A/V. Limit the command to the 50 A that DCM can deliver.

title: 10. Extension: who owns the current? CCM, DCM and the fourth leg
section: 10.7 The charge to move is the same in both modes
text:
10.7 The charge to move is the same in both modes
The capacitors fix the charge. A correction of \Delta e within \Delta t needs the average current
I = \frac{C\,\Delta e}{\Delta t}\tag{10.17}
in CCM and in DCM. With 10 mF per half, 10 V within 2 ms needs 50 A, which is exactly the CrCM limit at these values. At 2 A the same 10 V take 50 ms. A faster or larger correction needs a lower switching frequency or a smaller inductance, both with a higher peak current, or a return to CCM. DCM changes how the current is made and controlled. It does not reduce the charge that must move.
Ask. Must the fourth leg carry the full neutral current of an unbalanced load, or only correct the imbalance of the two capacitors? These are different converters. The first carries tens of amperes continuously, and CCM with an inner current loop suits it. The second moves small charges at intervals, and DCM charge packets suit it.

title: DC converters under changing load
text:
Square-wave harmonics and attenuation
Predict. A 24 V buck supplies 12 V at 100 kHz through 60 µH. At what load does the diode stop conducting before the next cycle?
During the on interval the inductor sees 12 V for 5 µs. Its current rises by 1 A. In steady continuous conduction it falls by the same amount during the off interval. At 0.5 A average current, the valley just reaches zero. Below that load a diode prevents reverse current. A controller that holds the output at 12 V must then change the duty ratio or the pulse pattern. An ideal synchronous stage that permits negative current can retain the original duty ratio.
For the ideal boost and inverting buck–boost in continuous conduction, the voltage ratios are 1/(1-D) and -D/(1-D). At fixed output voltage, a drop in input voltage requires a larger duty ratio. A sudden duty increase initially shortens the time that the boost diode feeds the load. The inductor current rises later. This inverse response explains the right-half-plane zero. A root locus shows how the closed-loop poles move as gain changes. Raising the gain cannot cancel that zero with a stable controller.
For loss and temperature, apply the current waveform to each device separately. A MOSFET with 20 mΩ on-resistance carrying 4 A for half of each period dissipates 0.16 W through conduction. Switching energy of 5 µJ per complete cycle adds 0.5 W at 100 kHz. At 30 K/W to ambient, these two terms raise the steady junction temperature by about 20 K. Gate resistance changes the transition duration. Check switching energy and peak voltage again after changing it. For a diode with v_F=V_0+r_di, use P=V_0 I_{avg}+r_d I_{rms}^2 over the full period.
A square wave drives a filter at its fundamental and harmonics. Multiply each Fourier component by the filter response at that frequency. For a lossless, unforced LC interval, energy gives a second check. Plot capacitor voltage against Zi_L, with Z=\sqrt{L/C}. The trajectory is circular because v_C^2+(Zi_L)^2 is constant. A DC forcing voltage moves the center. Resistance shrinks the trajectory toward equilibrium.
Continue with the existing buck design, boost design and control lesson for component selection, measured losses and loop response.

title: Choosing an energy-transfer path
text:
Ćuk energy transfer
A 12 V source must supply either +18 V or −18 V with continuous input current. Predict which topology preserves polarity. In ideal continuous conduction, a SEPIC produces +D/(1-D) times the input voltage. A Ćuk stage produces the negative of that ratio. Both need D=0.60 here. Both use a series capacitor to transfer energy. The Ćuk output inductor smooths load current. The SEPIC output diode feeds the output in pulses, so check output-capacitor RMS current.
For isolation, first ask when the secondary receives energy. A flyback stores energy while the primary switch conducts. The secondary receives that energy after turn-off. Refer all quantities to the primary when comparing equivalent circuits. A current measured on the secondary changes scale with the turns ratio. In discontinuous operation, the winding currents reach zero before the next on interval. At 100 kHz, 40 µH and 3 A peak, a fully discharged flyback transfers Lf_s I_{pk}^2/2=18 W ideally. Check that the reflected secondary voltage resets the current within the available time before using that estimate.
Ampere-turns Ni drive flux \Phi=Ni/\mathcal R in a linear magnetic circuit. Flux density is B=\Phi/A_e and magnetizing inductance is N^2/\mathcal R. A gap increases reluctance and permits more current before saturation for the same winding. Applying voltage sets the flux change by \Delta B=\int v\,dt/(NA_e). The turns ratio sets the induced voltage ratio. Load ampere-turns largely cancel across the windings while the primary still supplies magnetizing current. See the transformer characterization lesson for measurements.
A full bridge can transfer power through the transformer during both voltage polarities. With 48 V, 12 primary turns and 80 mm² of core area, a 4 µs pulse changes flux density by 0.20 T. Equal opposite volt-seconds reset this change. A 0.1 µs mismatch at 48 V adds 5 mT per cycle in the ideal model. Check pulse symmetry before increasing load. A current-doubler rectifier alternately energizes two output inductors. Their average currents add at the load. Size each winding for its own peak current and check ripple cancellation at the actual duty ratio.

title: Diode rectifiers and the power grid
text:
Diode conduction intervals
Why can a larger reservoir capacitor reduce DC ripple and increase input current peaks? Trace a bridge through a mains half-cycle. A resistive load draws current with the rectified voltage. Series inductance sustains current as voltage falls. Between charging pulses the load discharges the capacitor. With negligible source inductance, the bridge conducts again when the rectified source exceeds the capacitor voltage plus two diode drops. A stiff DC bus creates a similar conduction threshold. During blocking, the capacitor alone supplies the load.
At 50 Hz, a single-phase full-wave bridge recharges approximately every 10 ms. A 1 A load on 1000 µF therefore loses about 10 V between short recharge intervals. A half-wave circuit doubles the interval and the estimated droop. Two opposite transformer half-windings can feed a common output through two diodes. A voltage doubler instead charges two capacitors on alternate half-cycles and adds their voltages. With ideal light-load peaks, a 110 V RMS doubler and a 220 V RMS bridge both produce about 311 V. The doubler setting on 220 V predicts 622 V. Use these as circuit-analysis cases.
For sinusoidal mains voltage, power factor is \cos\phi_1/\sqrt{1+\mathrm{THD}_I^2}, where current THD is harmonic RMS divided by fundamental RMS. A bridge can have zero fundamental phase shift and 75% current THD. Its power factor is then 0.80. Harmonic currents cause voltage drops across the grid impedance. Record voltage and current together to distinguish a distorted supply from distortion caused by the load.
Three identical single-phase loads on a four-wire supply can cancel fundamental neutral current while their third harmonics add. Three 1 A RMS third harmonics give 3 A RMS neutral current. An open neutral prevents this return current and permits a floating load star point to shift. Unbalanced phase voltages change conduction intervals and capacitor recharge peaks. Compare all phase currents before sizing a neutral or diagnosing one overloaded phase.
In a three-phase bridge with continuous DC current, the highest phase feeds the positive terminal and the lowest phase receives the return current. The conducting pair normally changes every 60 electrical degrees. During an ordinary commutation, the incoming diode and the outgoing diode on the same DC rail briefly conduct together. The diode on the opposite rail continues to carry the DC current. DC-side inductance smooths load current. AC-side inductance limits the rate of current transfer. If both are present, solve the line-current transfer during overlap and the DC-current slope between transfers. A capacitor at the DC terminals introduces a separate recharge condition. Count the actual output pulses per line period for each winding and diode connection. A six-pulse bridge on 50 Hz has 300 Hz ripple.

title: Active rectification and energy storage
text:
Boost PFC with a zero-current interval
A single-phase rectifier supplies 1 kW from 230 V RMS, 50 Hz. If input current is sinusoidal and in phase, its RMS value is 4.35 A. Instantaneous input power still varies from zero to 2 kW. The load draws constant power, so the DC-link capacitor must exchange energy at 100 Hz.
The amplitude of the energy swing is P/(2\omega)=1.59 J, with \omega=2\pi f. For 470 µF at 400 V, the small-ripple estimate gives \Delta V_{pp}=P/(\omega C V)=16.9 V. A fast current loop shapes the line current. A slower voltage loop sets the requested conductance from the DC voltage error. If that outer loop follows the 100 Hz ripple closely, its varying command distorts the line current.
In a boost power-factor corrector, inspect the inductor valley each switching period. Discontinuous conduction leaves a zero-current interval. Critical conduction starts the next pulse at zero. Continuous conduction retains positive valley current. At a fixed point on the line cycle, a boundary-mode triangular pulse from 0 to 8 A and back has 4 A mean and 4.62 A RMS. If the same triangle occupies half the period, mean current falls to 2 A and RMS current to 3.27 A. To size a switch or diode, integrate only its conduction interval, then average the squared current across the line cycle.
For three-phase service, a single-switch discontinuous boost rectifier uses one command to shape three phase currents. Check its peak current and line distortion. The Vienna rectifier uses three controlled switches and a split DC bus. Each phase can connect to the midpoint or, through a diode, to a rail selected by current direction. Check midpoint balance as well as total bus voltage. A three-switch buck rectifier selects line-to-line voltage intervals for a continuous DC load current. It can reduce the output voltage. When the available rectified voltage falls below the required bus, a downstream boost stage can supply the missing gain. At 300 V intermediate voltage and 400 V output, the ideal boost duty is 0.25. At high line, check whether the buck stage can regulate with the boost idle.

title: Inverter voltage, modulation and current ripple
text:
Carrier comparison
Can a 48 V full bridge produce a 30 V RMS sinusoidal fundamental? For linear sinusoidal pulse-width modulation (PWM), fundamental peak voltage is mV_{dc}. The required modulation index is 30\sqrt{2}/48=0.884. A bipolar bridge switches the load between +48 V and −48 V. Unipolar modulation adds zero-voltage intervals. With complementary sinusoidal references and one triangular carrier, the differential output has two switching events per carrier half-cycle in typical operation. Compare the ripple with equal carrier frequency and equal fundamental voltage.
Square-wave operation maximizes the fundamental but creates low-order harmonics. A symmetric full-bridge square wave has fundamental RMS 4V_{dc}/(\pi\sqrt{2})=43.2 V here. Clipping a sinusoidal reference above the carrier range enters overmodulation. Fundamental voltage then grows nonlinearly and the low-order spectrum changes. In a three-phase bridge, six-step operation advances the active switching vector once per 60 electrical degrees.
For a filter inductor, apply \Delta i=(v_{inv}-e-Ri)\Delta t/L during each switching state. With 12 V net across 400 µH for 5 µs, current rises 0.15 A. A hysteresis controller selects the state when the current error crosses a band edge. For locally constant rising and falling slopes of +3 and −1 A/ms, a ±0.1 A band gives a period of 0.267 ms and about 3.75 kHz. Delays cause overshoot. With an isolated neutral, the sum of phase currents must stay zero. A state change in one leg then alters other phase voltages relative to the floating neutral.
For grid connection, draw the fundamental phasors using V_{inv}=E+(R+j\omega L)I, with current directed toward the grid. If the required voltage exceeds the modulation limit, the requested current cannot track at that operating point. For balanced sinusoidal operation, total active power is \sqrt{3}V_{LL} I_L\cos\phi using RMS magnitudes. An unbalanced grid introduces a negative-sequence component, which rotates in the opposite direction. Harmonic grid voltage introduces additional current error unless the controller provides the corresponding compensating voltage.

title: Switching vectors and device current
text:
Ripple against a sinusoidal source
A two-level three-phase bridge has eight switch states. Six give active line-voltage vectors and two give zero line voltage. Over one switching period, weight the adjacent vectors by their dwell times and assign the remaining interval to zero voltage. For dwell fractions 0.3 and 0.4 at 20 kHz, the active times are 15 and 20 µs. The zero states share the remaining 15 µs. If the requested active times sum to more than one period, the reference lies outside that sector’s linear operating range.
Construct the current-ripple trajectory by integrating the voltage-error vector over each dwell. For a sinusoidal opposing source, hold its vector approximately fixed for one short switching interval. A rectangular source changes sector abruptly. Split the interval at that transition. For a PWM source on the opposite side of the inductor, split at every edge of either converter. Two converters with equal average voltage can still create substantial ripple when their switching edges differ.
Adding the same voltage to all three pole commands leaves line-to-line voltages unchanged. This zero-sequence freedom permits redistribution of zero-state time in a three-wire system. A neutral or parasitic return path permits common-mode current. Swapping two phases reverses the phase sequence and the direction of the fundamental rotating vector.
For an ideal transistor with an antiparallel diode, route current using both its sign and the commanded state. For positive current out of a leg, the upper transistor feeds the phase from the positive rail in the high state. In the low state, the lower diode feeds the same positive phase current from the negative rail. Reverse current exchanges the roles. A gated MOSFET can also carry reverse channel current. For a 6 A rectangular transistor pulse at 25% duty, full-period average and RMS currents are 1.5 A and 3 A. Use RMS for resistive loss and mean for a constant forward drop. To find DC-link capacitor stress, subtract the inverter input current from the source current sample by sample. A source delivering a constant 3 A over one switching period into an inverter drawing alternating equal intervals of 0 and 6 A gives 3 A RMS capacitor current despite zero mean.

title: Thyristor bridges and controlled power flow
text:
Thyristor triggering and turn-off
Can a line-commutated bridge return mechanical energy to the grid? A gate pulse can start conduction in a forward-biased thyristor. The external circuit must then bring current below the holding current and provide recovery time. With continuous positive DC current and negligible overlap, a single-phase fully controlled bridge gives V_d=(2\sqrt{2}/\pi)V_{ac}\cos\alpha. A three-phase six-pulse bridge gives V_d=(3\sqrt{2}/\pi)V_{LL}\cos\alpha. Voltages on the right are RMS. With 400 V line-to-line and a 120° firing angle, the latter gives approximately −270 V. A DC source must maintain the positive current for sustained inversion.
Trace the conducting windings before applying a bridge formula. A single-phase midpoint circuit uses alternate halves of a center-tapped secondary. A three-phase midpoint circuit selects one phase at a time and returns current through the transformer neutral. Their winding utilization, pulse count and blocking stresses differ from full bridges. An interphase transformer allows two rectifier groups to supply current in parallel despite their instantaneous voltage difference. Check volt-seconds across its winding and current sharing between groups.
Source inductance prevents instantaneous current transfer. During overlap, integrating the commutating line voltage supplies the inductive volt-seconds needed to move the load current to the next valve. Higher current or a voltage sag can extend overlap. In inverter operation, the extinction angle is \gamma=180^\circ-\alpha-\mu, where \mu is overlap. At 145° firing delay and 20° overlap, 15° remain. At 50 Hz that is 0.833 ms. Compare this interval with the device recovery requirement including margin. Incomplete recovery can cause commutation failure.
A freewheeling diode gives an inductive load a local path when its applied voltage would reverse. The resulting voltage clamp changes the average output and limits inversion. A DC drive needs both voltage polarities and both current directions for four-quadrant operation. Two antiparallel controlled bridges can supply opposite armature currents. In a noncirculating arrangement, confirm zero current and allow recovery before enabling the opposite bridge.

title: Motor torque and direct AC conversion
text:
Rotating stator field
A four-pole permanent-magnet synchronous motor (PMSM) rotates at 1500 rpm. Predict the required electrical frequency. With two pole pairs, each mechanical revolution spans two electrical cycles, so the balanced stator currents must produce a 50 Hz rotating field. Reversing the phase sequence reverses the field.
A separately excited DC machine with fixed flux develops torque proportional to armature current. Its commutator maintains the current orientation. A PMSM drive measures or estimates rotor angle and resolves stator current into direct and quadrature components. For a surface PMSM with equal axis inductances and peak-current convention, T=(3/2)p\psi_m i_q. With two pole pairs, 0.10 Wb magnet flux linkage and 5 A quadrature current, torque is 1.5 N·m. The inner loop regulates current. The speed loop requests torque from speed error. Use J\dot\omega=T-T_{load} to predict acceleration. At a voltage limit, check field weakening and the current rating before promising the same torque at higher speed.
A direct matrix converter connects each output phase to one input phase through bidirectional switches. During transfer it must preserve inductive load current and avoid shorting two input phases. With known positive load-current direction, first disable the nonconducting direction of the outgoing switch. Enable the current-carrying direction of the incoming switch, disable the outgoing current path, then enable the remaining incoming direction. Reverse the directional choices for negative current. Current-sign uncertainty near zero requires a separate commutation strategy.
An indirect matrix converter coordinates an input rectifier and an output inverter without a large energy-storage capacitor between them. Schedule an inverter freewheeling state so the intermediate current reaches zero before the rectifier changes its input connection. On a timing diagram, check the intermediate current at each rectifier edge. Load current can remain nonzero throughout that interval because the inverter provides its path.

title: Finding the source of conducted noise
text:
Commutation-loop interference
A switching converter shows a 3 V spike during a current transition of 0.5 A/ns. If loop inductance alone causes the spike, L=V/(di/dt)=6 nH. Reduce the commutation-loop area and repeat the measurement at the same operating point. A longer probe ground lead can generate an apparent spike by the same mechanism. Change the probe connection first if the measured amplitude depends strongly on lead orientation.
Pulse repetition sets the spacing of spectral lines. Pulse width sets the envelope zeros of a rectangular pulse, and finite edge duration reduces high-frequency content. A 2 µs ideal rectangular pulse has its first envelope zero at 500 kHz. Slowing the edge can reduce noise while increasing switching loss. Stray capacitance conducts displacement current proportional to voltage slew. Stray inductance converts current slew into voltage. Together they can ring at 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC}). Change one known capacitance and observe the frequency shift to test that explanation.
A filter can pick up noise through mutual inductance. A 2 nH coupling path exposed to 0.5 A/ns induces 1 V beyond the intended filter path. Rotate or separate the inductors and compare the result at the same source current. For a three-phase drive, include motor-winding and cable capacitance to the frame. A common-mode step of 2 kV/µs across 1 nF produces a 2 A displacement-current pulse. Measure the sum of the phase currents with one current probe around all three phase conductors to observe the net return current through other paths.
Damping a filter limits its resonant peak. A capacitor from line to chassis also carries line-frequency current. At 230 V RMS and 50 Hz, 4.7 nF carries about 0.34 mA RMS for one sinusoidal branch. Evaluate each return path and its voltage before adding capacitance. If the peak changes with damping but the broadband floor changes with probe routing, pursue the two mechanisms separately.

title: Spectrum / Filtering of Square Wave
text:
Square-wave harmonics and attenuation
An ideal buck switch node alternates between 0 and 24 V at 50% duty and 100 kHz. Assume continuous inductor current or forced synchronous switching.



When Q closes, the source feeds L. When Q opens, positive inductor current continues through D.


Its AC fundamental and third harmonic have peak amplitudes 48/π and 48/(3π) V. A series 100 µH and shunt 1 µF have a 15.9 kHz resonance. With a light resistive load and negligible losses, well above resonance the gain is approximately 1/|1 − (f/f₀)²|. The two output peaks are about 0.40 V and 0.014 V. The filter passes the 12 V DC component. Check damping near resonance before applying this approximation to a load step.



At 100 kHz, the fundamental falls from 15.3 V to 0.40 V peak. The panels use different vertical scales.




Practice exercise
For a 0–24 V square wave at 50% duty, the filter gain at the third harmonic is 0.010. Find the frequency and peak amplitude of that harmonic at the output for 100 kHz switching.


Check your reasoning

The third harmonic is at 300 kHz. Its input peak is 48/(3π) = 5.09 V. The filter reduces this to 50.9 mV peak.

Square-wave harmonics and attenuation (ECPE)

title: Efficiency and Losses
text:
Converter efficiency
A converter delivers 48 W and dissipates 2 W. What input current should a 12 V supply show?
Conservation of power gives 50 W input, 4.17 A and 96% efficiency. If the meter reads 4.0 A, it implies zero loss at this load. Check meter bandwidth and where the auxiliary supply draws power. The boost design, section 8 compares calculated and measured loss. To locate peak efficiency at fixed output voltage, model loss in watts as 1 + 0.2I + 0.04I² with I in amperes. Loss per output ampere is smallest when 1/I = 0.04I, or 5 A. Fixed loss dominates at light load and copper loss at high load.



Loss per output ampere reaches its minimum at 5 A, where fixed loss equals resistive loss.




Practice exercise
A 12 V converter supplies 45 W at 90% efficiency. What input current and heat dissipation must the design support?


Check your reasoning

Input power is 45/0.90 = 50 W. The source supplies 4.17 A and the converter dissipates 5 W.

Converter efficiency (ECPE)

title: Control of Switching Behavior (MOSFET)
text:
MOSFET gate drive and edge speed
A MOSFET has 12 nC of Miller charge.
During the Miller plateau, 4 V appears across 8 Ω of total gate-path resistance. Estimate the drain transition time before doubling that total resistance. Gate current is 0.5 A, so charge divided by current gives 24 ns. At 16 Ω the estimate is 48 ns. For a 48 V, 5 A hard transition, the linear-overlap estimate rises from 2.88 to 5.76 µJ per edge. Verify the plateau and drain overshoot together before choosing the resistor.



At constant 5 A drain current, the slower Miller transition doubles the voltage–current overlap area.




Practice exercise
A driver supplies 0.30 A during a 12 nC Miller plateau. Estimate the transition time and turn-on energy for a linear 40 V drain-voltage fall at 5 A.


Check your reasoning

The plateau lasts 12 nC/0.30 A = 40 ns. Integration of the triangular power pulse gives ½ × 40 V × 5 A × 40 ns = 4 µJ.

MOSFET gate drive and edge speed (ECPE)

title: Passive Components / Filter Circuits
text:
Passive filter response
A continuous-current buck has 1 A peak-to-peak triangular inductor ripple at 100 kHz.



When Q closes, the source feeds L. When Q opens, positive inductor current continues through D.


A 10 µF output capacitor with negligible ESR gives about 1/(8 × 100 kHz × 10 µF) = 125 mV peak-to-peak. Doubling inductance halves ripple current at fixed duty, input voltage and frequency. Doubling capacitance instead keeps current ripple and halves capacitive voltage ripple. With 50 mΩ ESR the original current adds a 50 mV peak-to-peak resistive component. Inspect the waveform before trading capacitor volume for inductance.



The capacitor integrates ripple current. Its voltage extrema occur at current zero crossings. The ESR voltage follows the current directly.




Practice exercise
A buck output capacitor carries zero-mean triangular ripple of 0.8 A peak-to-peak at 100 kHz. Find the ideal capacitive ripple with 20 µF and the ESR ripple with 30 mΩ.


Check your reasoning

The positive triangle transfers 0.8/(8 × 100,000) = 1 µC. This gives 50 mV peak-to-peak across the ideal capacitor. ESR contributes 0.8 × 0.030 = 24 mV peak-to-peak. The two components reach their peaks at different times.

Passive filter response (ECPE)

title: Thermal Design
text:
Loss and junction temperature
At 55 °C ambient, can a 3 W device stay below a 125 °C design target?
The total junction-to-ambient budget is (125 − 55)/3 = 23.3 K/W. Junction-to-case and interface resistances of 2 and 1 K/W leave 20.3 K/W for the sink. An 18 K/W sink predicts 118 °C under its rated airflow. Recheck loss at that temperature.



Follow the heat flow from the 118 °C junction to 55 °C ambient. The sink accounts for 54 K of the rise.




Practice exercise
At 50 °C ambient a device dissipates 4 W. Its junction-to-case and case-to-sink thermal resistances total 3 K/W. Size the heat sink for a 110 °C junction limit.


Check your reasoning

The total allowance is (110 − 50)/4 = 15 K/W. The sink-to-ambient path may use at most 12 K/W at the specified airflow.

Loss and junction temperature (ECPE)

title: LC Resonant Circuit State-Plane Trajectory (uZi-Diagram)
text:
LC trajectories in the state plane
Start a lossless 100 µH, 1 µF tank with 10 V on the capacitor and zero current. Where does the trajectory cross zero capacitor voltage?



The charged capacitor drives circulating current through the ideal inductor. The marked terminal defines positive capacitor voltage.


The impedance scale is 10 Ω. The initial 50 µJ becomes magnetic energy at a current magnitude of 1 A. The first crossing occurs after a quarter period, π√(LC)/2 = 15.7 µs. The current sign follows the chosen reference direction. A shrinking radius on successive cycles measures energy loss.



Positive current leaves the capacitor’s positive plate. After a quarter turn, all 50 µJ is in the inductor.




Practice exercise
Start the illustrated tank at 5 V with zero current. Find the first current peak and the time it takes to reach it.


Check your reasoning

The characteristic impedance is √(100 µH/1 µF) = 10 Ω, so the peak magnitude is 0.50 A. One quarter-cycle takes (π/2)√(LC) = 15.7 µs.

LC trajectories in the state plane (ECPE)
