title: u1 Constant / Load Variable
text:
Buck operation as load changes
A 24 V buck supplies 12 V through 60 µH at 100 kHz. At 50% duty its peak-to-peak inductor ripple is 1 A.



When Q closes, the source feeds L. When Q opens, positive inductor current continues through D.


A 12 Ω load draws 1 A and gives a 0.5 A valley. At 24 Ω the valley reaches zero. At 48 Ω a diode cannot support the negative valley predicted by the continuous model. Choose a discontinuous-current model for the light-load case.



At the 24 Ω boundary, the valley just reaches zero at the end of the period.




Practice exercise
The buck has 1 A peak-to-peak ripple. Sketch its current for a 0.75 A mean load. At which mean load does the valley first reach zero?


Check your reasoning

Center the triangle on 0.75 A to get 0.25 A and 1.25 A. The critical mean load is half the ripple, 0.50 A.

Buck operation as load changes (ECPE)

title: u1 Variable / u2 Controlled
text:
Buck line regulation
A buck in continuous conduction regulates 9 V as the input falls from 18 to 12 V.



When Q closes, the source feeds L. When Q opens, positive inductor current continues through D.


Volt-second balance requires duty to rise from 0.50 to 0.75. In continuous conduction, a 0.70 duty limit gives 8.4 V at low line. At light load a diode buck can exceed that value. For example, at 9 V output and 0.70 duty, the on-state inductor voltage is +3 V and the conducting off-state voltage is −9 V. Volt-second balance gives a diode interval of 0.70 × 3/9 = 0.233 of a period. The current is zero for the remaining 0.067. Check the current valley and maximum on-time before diagnosing a regulation error.



At 12 V input and 9 V output, diode current stops after 93.3% of the period. The remaining idle interval permits the DCM operating point.




Practice exercise
Regulate 9 V from 15 V in ideal buck CCM at 100 kHz. Label the switch and diode intervals and check volt-second balance.


Check your reasoning

Duty is 9/15 = 0.60. Q conducts for 6 µs and D for 4 µs. The inductor receives +6 × 6 and −9 × 4 V·µs, which sum to zero.

Buck line regulation (ECPE)

title: Dynamic Behavior
text:
Buck transient response
A buck load steps up by 2 A. The controller holds the old duty for 10 µs.



When Q closes, the source feeds L. When Q opens, positive inductor current continues through D.


With 100 µF and 20 mΩ capacitor ESR, the initial voltage step is 40 mV. If inductor current stays approximately constant, charge depletion adds 2 × 10 µs / 100 µF = 0.20 V. Expect about 0.24 V total droop at the end of the delay. Separate the abrupt step from the later slope on the trace.



The load step causes an immediate 40 mV ESR drop, followed by 200 mV of charge depletion during the 10 µs delay.




Practice exercise
A 1.5 A load step leaves a constant current deficit for 8 µs. Estimate the drop across a 120 µF capacitor with 20 mΩ ESR just before the regulator responds.


Check your reasoning

The capacitor loses 12 µC, giving 0.10 V of droop. ESR adds an immediate 0.030 V step, for a total drop of about 0.13 V.

Buck transient response (ECPE)

title: Boost Converter - u1 Variable / u2 Controlled
text:
Boost line regulation
A boost operating in continuous conduction supplies 48 V at 1 A as the input falls from 24 to 12 V.



Q stores energy in L during its on-time. When Q opens, positive inductor current flows through D into the output. Vin is the instantaneous stage input.


Ideal duty rises from 0.50 to 0.75. Input current doubles from 2 to 4 A because output power remains 48 W. A 3 A input limit prevents regulation at low line. Compare required input power with that limit before tuning the voltage loop.



The 3 A limit intersects the ideal 48 W demand at 16 V input.




Practice exercise
An ideal boost regulates 48 V from 16 V at 96 W. Find the duty and the average input and output currents.


Check your reasoning

Duty is 1 − 16/48 = 2/3. The input supplies 96/16 = 6 A and the load draws 96/48 = 2 A. The diode carries the inductor current during the remaining third of the period.

Boost line regulation (ECPE)
crumbs: 228  Boost Converter - u1 Variable / u2 Controlled

title: Boost Converter - Root Locus Diagram, RHP-Zero
text:
Boost root locus and inverse response
A normalized boost plant has denominator s² + 2s + 1 and numerator 1 − s/4. Where do its poles go under unity negative feedback with proportional gain K?



Q stores energy in L during its on-time. When Q opens, positive inductor current flows through D into the output. Vin is the instantaneous stage input.


The characteristic polynomial is s² + (2 − K/4)s + 1 + K. At K = 4 its poles are −0.5 ± j2.18. At K = 8 they reach ±j3. Higher gain gives positive real parts. The numerator zero at +4 also gives an initial inverse step response. These numbers illustrate a root locus in normalized time. Use the actual operating-point plant to set the hardware gain.



The poles reach the imaginary axis at gain 8. The curves trace both poles as gain rises from 0 to 10.




Practice exercise
For the normalized plant above, increase the proportional gain to K = 8. Find the closed-loop poles and classify the ideal response.


Check your reasoning

The characteristic polynomial is s² + (2 − K/4)s + 1 + K. At K = 8 this becomes s² + 9, with poles at ±j3. The ideal linear system is at the sustained-oscillation boundary.

Boost root locus and inverse response (ECPE)
crumbs: 229  Boost Converter - Root Locus Diagram, RHP-Zero

title: Buck-Boost Converter - u1 Variable / u2 Controlled
text:
Inverting buck–boost regulation
An inverting converter must hold −12 V from 8 to 16 V.



Q charges L from Vin. When Q opens, D conducts and the output is negative relative to the return.


Ideal continuous operation requires D = 12/(12 + input voltage), giving 0.60 and 0.429. At 1 A output the mean inductor current is 1/(1 − D), or 2.50 and 1.75 A. Check peak current at low line and blocking voltage at high line, where the ideal switch sees 28 V.



Holding −12 V at 1 A requires higher duty and higher average inductor current at low line.




Practice exercise
An ideal inverting buck-boost in CCM takes 18 V and delivers −6 V into 3 Ω. Find the duty, load current magnitude and mean inductor current.


Check your reasoning

Duty is 6/(18 + 6) = 0.25. The load draws 2 A. The diode delivers current for 75% of the cycle, so the mean inductor current is 2/0.75 = 2.67 A.

Inverting buck–boost regulation (ECPE)
crumbs: 230  Buck-Boost Converter - u1 Variable / u2 Controlled

title: Cuk Converter
text:
Ćuk energy transfer
At 12 V input and −18 V output, the ideal continuous Ćuk stage needs 60% duty. What DC voltage does its transfer capacitor carry?



The transfer capacitor connects the two inductor branches. Q and D conduct in alternate intervals in continuous operation.


The input inductor sees +12 V during on-time and 12 V minus capacitor voltage during off-time. Zero volt-seconds gives 12 − 0.4Vcap = 0, hence 30 V. A 25 V capacitor fails the DC requirement before ripple is considered.



The input winding gains and loses equal volt-seconds. The transfer capacitor holds 30 V.




Practice exercise
For an ideal CCM Ćuk converter at 24 V input and −12 V output, find duty and average transfer-capacitor voltage magnitude.


Check your reasoning

The conversion ratio gives D = 12/(24 + 12) = 1/3. The transfer capacitor supports 24/(1 − D) = 36 V on average.

Ćuk energy transfer (ECPE)

title: SEPIC Converter
text:
SEPIC energy transfer
For a 12 V to +18 V SEPIC supplying 1 A, ideal input current is 1.5 A.



The two inductor currents add in Q during its on-time and in D during energy delivery.


With negligible inductor ripple the diode carries the sum, 2.5 A, during the 40% off interval. Its mean is 1 A. The output capacitor carries +1.5 A then and −1 A during on-time. Its RMS current is √(0.4 × 1.5² + 0.6 × 1²) = 1.22 A. Select its ripple rating for the actual temperature.



Both inductor currents feed the diode during off-time. Subtracting the 1 A load current gives the capacitor current.




Practice exercise
An ideal CCM SEPIC converts 9 V to 18 V at 0.5 A output. Neglect ripple. Estimate switch current during the on-state and check average diode current.


Check your reasoning

Input current is 9 W/9 V = 1 A. The switch carries 1 + 0.5 = 1.5 A. With duty 2/3, the diode carries 1.5 A for one third of the period, averaging 0.5 A.

SEPIC energy transfer (ECPE)

title: MMF, Magn. Ind., Magn. Flux
text:
Ampere-turns, flux density and flux
A 20-turn winding carries 0.5 A on a linear core of reluctance 100 000 A/Wb and cross-section 400 mm².
The drive is 10 ampere-turns, flux is 100 µWb and flux density is 0.25 T. Halving cross-section at the same specified flux doubles flux density. Recalculate reluctance if you actually change the core. For a separate air-core wiring example, the external loop inductance per length of two widely separated round conductors is approximately (μ₀/π)ln(d/r). With 0.5 mm radius and 10 mm center spacing it is 1.20 µH/m. Doubling spacing gives 1.48 µH/m. A wider return loop links more flux at the same current.



With fixed linear reluctance and core area, 10 ampere-turns produce 0.25 T.




Practice exercise
Drive the 20-turn winding with 0.25 A. For the same linear reluctance and core area, calculate MMF, flux and flux density.


Check your reasoning

MMF is 5 A-turn. Flux is 5/100,000 = 50 µWb. Dividing by 400 mm² gives 0.125 T.

Ampere-turns, flux density and flux (ECPE)
crumbs: 233  MMF, Magn. Ind., Magn. Flux

title: Magnetizing Current
text:
Current required to establish flux
An unloaded winding has 2 mH magnetizing inductance.
Apply 24 V for 5 µs from zero current. The magnetizing current reaches 60 mA, storing 3.6 µJ. Adding a secondary load adds reflected load current to the primary trace. Use the no-load trace to estimate magnetizing inductance before comparing loaded currents.



A 24 V pulse across 2 mH raises magnetizing current by 12 mA per microsecond.




Practice exercise
Apply +8 V to a 2 mH winding for 30 µs, then −4 V. How long must the second pulse last to restore the starting current?


Check your reasoning

The rise is 8 × 30 µs/2 mH = 0.12 A. Reset needs equal and opposite volt-seconds, so the −4 V pulse lasts 60 µs.

Current required to establish flux (ECPE)

title: Reluctance Model
text:
Magnetic reluctance networks
A core and its air gap have series reluctances of 0.2 and 1.8 million A/Wb.
With 20 ampere-turns, the common flux is 10 µWb. The core accounts for 2 ampere-turns and the gap accounts for 18. At the same flux, energy is proportional to reluctance, so the gap holds 90%. Use this split to decide whether a more accurate gap model matters.



The core and gap carry the same flux. The gap consumes 18 of the 20 applied ampere-turns.




Practice exercise
A magnetic circuit has core and gap reluctances of 0.2 and 1.8 million A/Wb. With 30 A-turn applied, find flux and the MMF consumed in the gap.


Check your reasoning

Series reluctance is 2 million A/Wb. Flux is 15 µWb. The gap consumes 1.8 million × 15 µWb = 27 A-turn.

Magnetic reluctance networks (ECPE)

title: Dep. of Ind. on Magn. Circ. Param.
text:
Inductance and core geometry
A gap dominates the reluctance of a 20-turn inductor with 100 mm² cross-section and a 0.5 mm gap.
Neglect fringing. Using L = μ₀N²A/g gives about 101 µH. Doubling the gap gives about 50 µH. Restoring 101 µH requires about 28 turns. Check winding space and copper loss before choosing that change.



Increasing gap length reduces inductance. Increasing turns can recover the original inductance.




Practice exercise
Increase the gap from 0.5 to 1.0 mm and turns from 20 to 30. Estimate the ratio of new to old inductance under the gap-dominated model.


Check your reasoning

At fixed area, L is proportional to turns squared divided by gap length. The ratio is (30/20)² × 0.5/1.0 = 1.125.

Inductance and core geometry (ECPE)
crumbs: 236  Dep. of Ind. on Magn. Circ. Param.

title: Transfomer Vol. / Curr. Transform.
text:
Transformer voltage and current ratios
A 40:10 ideal transformer has 80 V RMS across the primary and 5 A RMS load current on the secondary.
The secondary voltage is 20 V and the primary load-current component is 1.25 A. Both sides carry 100 VA. A measured excess in primary RMS current can include magnetizing current. For sinusoidal currents, add the reflected load and excitation currents as phasors. Determine transformer loss from measured real input power minus real output power.



The 4:1 turns ratio reduces voltage and increases load current by the same factor. Both ports carry 100 VA.




Practice exercise
Connect an 8 Ω resistive load to the secondary of the ideal 40:10 transformer and apply 80 V RMS to the primary. Find the impedance and current seen by the source.


Check your reasoning

The turns ratio is 4. The reflected load is 4² × 8 = 128 Ω. Primary current is 80/128 = 0.625 A RMS.

Transformer voltage and current ratios (ECPE)

title: Magnetic Components
text:
Energy storage in a flyback
A flyback with 40 µH primary inductance ramps from zero to 3 A.



The dots mark equal instantaneous winding polarities. Q stores energy in the coupled windings. D delivers it to the output after Q opens.


Stored energy is 180 µJ. At 100 kHz, transferring the whole packet each cycle gives 18 W before losses. If the valley becomes 1 A at the same peak, the transferable increment falls to 160 µJ. Use the difference of squared currents for a continuous-current cycle.



At a 1 A valley, 20 µJ remains in the magnetic field. The next transfer uses the difference between the two energy levels.




Practice exercise
A 40 µH flyback ramps from 2 A to 4 A at 80 kHz. Find the power delivered if it returns to 2 A every cycle and all released energy reaches the load.


Check your reasoning

Energy released is ½ × 40 µH × (4² − 2²) = 240 µJ per cycle. At 80 kHz this delivers 19.2 W.

Energy storage in a flyback (ECPE)

title: DCM: Principle
text:
Flyback demagnetization
A 24 V primary drives 40 µH for 5 µs, giving 3 A peak.



The dots mark equal instantaneous winding polarities. Q stores energy in the coupled windings. D delivers it to the output after Q opens.


A 30 V reflected output removes current at 0.75 A/µs. Reset takes 4 µs, leaving 1 µs idle at 100 kHz. If the reflected voltage falls to 20 V, reset takes 6 µs. The assumed zero-current start cannot repeat at that operating point.



Primary-referred magnetizing current reaches zero at 9 µs. Both winding currents are zero during the final microsecond.




Practice exercise
In the illustrated flyback, keep the 24 V, 5 µs primary pulse but increase the reflected reset voltage to 40 V. Mark the end of demagnetization and the idle time in a 10 µs period.


Check your reasoning

The primary pulse applies 120 V·µs. Reset takes 120/40 = 3 µs, so demagnetization ends at 8 µs and the last 2 µs are idle.

Flyback demagnetization (ECPE)

title: Equivalent Circuits
text:
Flyback-equivalent switching circuits
Replace a flyback secondary by its primary-referred circuit.



The dots mark equal instantaneous winding polarities. Q stores energy in the coupled windings. D delivers it to the output after Q opens.


With a 2:1 primary-to-secondary turns ratio and a 15 V output, the off-state clamp magnitude is 30 V. A 3 A primary-referred current becomes 6 A secondary current at turn-off. Both descriptions give 90 W instantaneous transfer. Reversing the current scaling would violate ideal power balance. As a waveform check, a unity-ratio flyback and an inverting buck–boost with the same inductance both see +12 V on-time and −18 V off-time. At D = 0.60 their average winding voltage is zero. The ideal magnetizing-current ramp is identical even though the flyback isolates the ports.



At turn-off, both winding references give the same instantaneous power. Voltage and current scale in opposite directions.




Practice exercise
A flyback has 30 primary turns and 10 secondary turns. During demagnetization, the secondary winding sees 8 V in magnitude and carries 6 A. Refer both quantities to the primary.


Check your reasoning

The primary-referred voltage magnitude is 3 × 8 = 24 V. Referred current is 6/3 = 2 A. The instantaneous power magnitude is 48 W on either side.

Flyback-equivalent switching circuits (ECPE)

title: Bidirectional Magnetization
text:
Transformer flux balance
A 48 V full bridge drives 12 primary turns on an 80 mm² core. A 0.1 µs difference between opposite pulse widths adds 48 × 0.1 µs / (12 × 80 mm²) = 5 mT per cycle.



Terminals A and B connect across the load. Selecting opposite rails gives a positive or negative line voltage. Selecting the same rail gives zero.


A persistent 5 mT flux drift per cycle consumes a 0.10 T margin in 20 cycles, or 0.20 ms at 100 kHz. Integrate the measured primary voltage over complete cycles to test for imbalance. The linear estimate ends when saturation changes the current waveform.



Compare flux at the same switching instant each cycle. A 0.1 µs timing mismatch consumes the 0.10 T margin in 20 cycles.




Practice exercise
The 48 V bridge has a persistent 0.05 µs pulse-width mismatch. How many cycles consume a 0.10 T flux margin with 12 turns and 80 mm² core area?


Check your reasoning

Each cycle adds 48 × 0.05 µs/(12 × 80 mm²) = 2.5 mT. At constant mismatch the margin lasts 0.10/0.0025 = 40 cycles.

Transformer flux balance (ECPE)

title: Full-Bridge / Current Doubler Output
text:
Current-doubler rectification
Two matched output inductors deliver 12 A total.



The transformer secondary drives the two inductor branches. Follow each branch to the common output and back through the conducting rectifier.


Each carries 6 A average with 2 A peak-to-peak triangular ripple. At equal half-cycle dwell, one rises as the other falls, so their ideal sum is 12 A. A 20% smaller ripple in the second leaves 0.4 A peak-to-peak residual. Rate each inductor for its individual peak of up to 7 A even if the measured output ripple is small. At 12 A load a diode bridge with two conducting 0.7 V diodes loses about 16.8 W. A center-tapped two-diode secondary has one conducting diode and loses about 8.4 W under the same drop assumption. Check winding utilization and reverse voltage before choosing the secondary.



Matched branch ripple cancels at the load while each inductor reaches 7 A.




Practice exercise
One branch rises from 5 to 7 A while the other falls linearly from 6.8 to 5.2 A over the same interval. Find the output current at both ends and its residual swing.


Check your reasoning

The two sums are 11.8 and 12.2 A. Unequal branch ripple leaves a 0.4 A peak-to-peak swing even with opposite slopes.

Current-doubler rectification (ECPE)

title: Isolated Full-Bridge Converter
text:
Phase-shift power transfer in a dual-active bridge
Two active bridges apply 50% duty square waves to a transformer with a 1:1 ratio, 48 V on each bus and 10 µH total referred leakage inductance.



Bridge 1 and Bridge 2 are represented by their square-wave terminal voltages. Their referred voltage difference drives current through the leakage inductance.


At 100 kHz, delay the secondary by one eighth of a period. During the 1.25 µs disagreement interval the inductor sees 96 V and its current changes by 12 A. In symmetric steady operation the ramp goes from −6 to +6 A. The bridges then agree for 3.75 µs of the half-cycle and current stays at +6 A. Mean primary power over that half-cycle is 48 × 6 × 3.75/5 = 216 W. Reversing the phase shift reverses ideal power flow. At zero phase shift with equal bus voltages the model gives zero transferred power.



The leakage current ramps when the bridge voltages differ and holds when they agree. The secondary transitions lag by 1.25 µs.




Practice exercise
Keep both bridges at 48 V and reduce the secondary delay to 0.625 µs at 100 kHz. Sketch the leakage current and estimate mean transferred power for 10 µH.


Check your reasoning

The 96 V disagreement changes current by 6 A. Symmetry gives a ramp from −3 to +3 A, then a 4.375 µs plateau. Mean primary power is 48 × 3 × 4.375/5 = 126 W.

Phase-shift power transfer in a dual-active bridge (ECPE)

title: Conduction / Switching Losses
text:
Device loss over a switching cycle
A device carries 8 A for one quarter of each period through 25 mΩ.
Its full-period RMS current is 4 A and conduction loss is 0.40 W. Measured turn-on and turn-off energies sum to 6 µJ. At 100 kHz they add 0.60 W. Doubling frequency raises the total from 1.0 to 1.6 W if the waveform and energies stay fixed. Use this split when selecting cooling.



At fixed current and edge energy, conduction loss stays at 0.40 W while total loss grows with switching frequency.




Practice exercise
A switch carries 6 A through 40 mΩ for 40% of each period. Its combined turn-on and turn-off energy is 8 µJ per cycle at 50 kHz. Find total mean loss.


Check your reasoning

Conduction contributes 6² × 0.040 × 0.40 = 0.576 W. Switching contributes 8 µJ × 50 kHz = 0.400 W. Total is 0.976 W.

Device loss over a switching cycle (ECPE)

title: Power Semiconductor: Transistor
text:
Transistor output characteristics
A MOSFET output curve at fixed gate voltage passes through 4 A at 0.20 V.
The ratio of voltage to current at that point gives 50 mΩ of static on-resistance. At a higher drain bias the same curve rises from 5.0 to 5.1 A between 3 and 4 V. Its local incremental resistance there is 10 Ω. Extrapolating 50 mΩ to 4 V would predict 80 A. Choose the portion of the curve traversed by the load line.



The two regions of the same curve have different slopes. Each panel covers only the voltage interval used in the example.




Practice exercise
A MOSFET in its ohmic region drops 0.15 V at 3 A. Estimate its on-state loss at 6 A at the same temperature and gate voltage.


Check your reasoning

The inferred resistance is 0.15/3 = 0.050 Ω. If that resistance holds, 6 A produces 6² × 0.050 = 1.8 W while on.

Transistor output characteristics (ECPE)

title: Power Semiconductor: Diode
text:
Piecewise-linear diode model
Fit a diode model to 0.70 V at 2 A and 0.85 V at 5 A.
The slope is 0.05 Ω and the intercept is 0.60 V. For 5 A pulses at 40% duty, the average drop-times-current loss is 0.4 × 5 × 0.85 = 1.70 W. The equivalent full-period calculation gives 0.60 × 2 + 0.05 × 10 = 1.70 W. Refit if the junction temperature changes.



The fitted forward model passes through 0.70 V at 2 A and 0.85 V at 5 A. The intercept is an extrapolation.




Practice exercise
Use the diode model fitted from 0.70 V at 2 A and 0.85 V at 5 A. Estimate average loss when a 4 A rectangular pulse flows for 30% duty.


Check your reasoning

Slope resistance is 0.05 Ω and the intercept is 0.60 V. At 4 A the drop is 0.80 V, so average loss is 0.30 × 4 × 0.80 = 0.96 W.

Piecewise-linear diode model (ECPE)

title: Current Ripple
text:
Buck inductor ripple
Hold a buck input at 24 V, L at 60 µH and frequency at 100 kHz.



When Q closes, the source feeds L. When Q opens, positive inductor current continues through D.


In continuous operation the peak-to-peak ripple is 24D(1 − D)/(Lf). It is 0.75 A at duty 0.25 and 1 A at duty 0.50. Duty 0.75 gives 0.75 A again. Check the midpoint of the duty range when choosing the inductor.



At fixed input, inductance and frequency, the ripple peaks at 50% duty.




Practice exercise
The 24 V buck runs at 100 kHz with 60 µH. Compare ripple at 25% and 75% duty in ideal CCM.


Check your reasoning

Ripple is Vin × D(1 − D)/(L × f). Both duties give 24 × 0.1875/6 = 0.75 A peak-to-peak. The two traces have different slopes and dwell times.

Buck inductor ripple (ECPE)

title: Basic Diode Function
text:
Diode conduction intervals
A 20 V peak sine drives 10 Ω through one ideal diode.



In the resistive case, the forward-biased diode completes the path from the AC source through R.


During the positive half-cycle the peak current is 2 A. Integrating the positive half-sine over the full period gives 2/π = 0.637 A average. On the negative peak the diode blocks 20 V. Add the actual forward drop when the supply amplitude is comparable to it.



Current follows the positive half-sine. During the negative half-cycle the diode blocks.




Practice exercise
A 30 V peak sine drives 15 Ω through one ideal diode. Sketch one cycle and calculate the RMS load current.


Check your reasoning

The positive half-sine peaks at 2 A. Current is zero over the negative half-cycle. Averaging the squared half-wave over a full cycle gives 2²/4, hence 1 A RMS.

Diode conduction intervals (ECPE)

title: R, RL, C, UDC=const. Load
text:
Rectifiers with four load models
At one instant a half-wave source is +8 V. Which loads can still draw current?



In the resistive case, the forward-biased diode completes the path from the AC source through R.


A 4 Ω resistor draws 2 A. With 10 mH in series and 3 A already flowing, the inductor sees 8 − 12 = −4 V, so current falls at 400 A/s while the diode remains on. A capacitor previously charged to 10 V blocks the diode. A stiff 6 V bus behind 1 Ω accepts 2 A. The stored state determines which circuit equation applies.



At the same +8 V source instant, the charged capacitor blocks. The RL branch still carries 3 A from its previous state.




Practice exercise
At one instant the source is +9 V. Compare ideal-diode current into a 3 Ω resistor, a stiff 12 V bus through 2 Ω, and a stiff 5 V bus through 2 Ω.


Check your reasoning

The resistor draws 3 A. The 12 V bus reverse-biases its diode, giving zero current. The 5 V bus draws (9 − 5)/2 = 2 A.

Rectifiers with four load models (ECPE)
crumbs: 250  R, RL, C, UDC=const. Load

title: Single Diode Rectifier Combination
text:
Two-diode rectifier arrangements
Two 12 V RMS half-windings in antiphase feed a center-tapped rectifier.



The two source symbols represent opposite half-windings. Current returns to their center tap through the load connected across the output.


Each half charges the common capacitor to about 17 V at light load. The idle diode can see 34 V reverse when its winding is at −17 V. A two-capacitor doubler on a single 12 V RMS winding instead charges each capacitor to 17 V and supplies about 34 V in series. Trace which capacitor each diode charges before assigning voltage ratings.



The two half-windings alternate in supplying the common reservoir. The ideal light-load voltage approaches one half-winding peak.




Practice exercise
Each half of a center-tapped transformer supplies 15 V RMS. With an ideal reservoir charged to the peak, find the reverse voltage across the idle diode at the opposite winding peak.


Check your reasoning

The charged cathode is at +21.2 V and the idle anode at −21.2 V relative to the tap. The reverse voltage is approximately 42.4 V.

Two-diode rectifier arrangements (ECPE)

title: Purely Capacitive Smoothing on a Bridge Rectifier
text:
Capacitor-input bridge ripple
A 50 Hz full-wave bridge must keep reservoir droop below 2 V at 0.4 A.



Connect the line across A and B and the DC load across the marked rails. A diagonal diode pair conducts when the rectified line voltage can drive load current.


Approximate the recharge time as short. Charge balance gives 2 mF for exactly 2 V of droop. The effective capacitance must exceed 2 mF to keep droop below 2 V in this model. A 2200 µF capacitor predicts 1.82 V droop. Check its minimum capacitance and ripple-current rating because a short recharge interval concentrates current.



Between recharge pulses the constant 0.4 A load removes charge. The instantaneous recharge is the short-pulse approximation.




Practice exercise
A full-wave bridge on 60 Hz mains feeds a 0.60 A constant load. Estimate the minimum reservoir capacitance for 1.0 V peak-to-peak droop.


Check your reasoning

Recharge occurs every 1/120 s. Using the short-recharge approximation, C = 0.60/(120 × 1.0) = 5 mF.

Capacitor-input bridge ripple (ECPE)
crumbs: 252  Purely Capacitive Smoothing on a Bridge Rectifier

title: AC-side Inductance, Input Current Formation, UDC=const
text:
Line inductance and charging current
A bridge feeds a stiff 300 V bus through 2 mH total line inductance.



Connect the line across A and B and the DC load across the marked rails. A diagonal diode pair conducts when the rectified line voltage can drive load current.


Near a rectified line voltage of 320 V the charging-current slope is +10 A/ms. Later, at 290 V, it is −5 A/ms while current remains positive. Starting at 1 A, that slope reaches zero in about 0.20 ms if the line voltage changes little. Stop the conducting-state integration at zero.



From the same 1 A initial current, the two local voltage samples produce opposite slopes. The diode prevents negative current.




Practice exercise
A conducting bridge has 2 A line current in 2 mH. For a short interval the rectified source is 280 V and the bus is 300 V. When does current reach zero?


Check your reasoning

The slope is −20/0.002 = −10,000 A/s. The current reaches zero after 200 µs. For the same voltage ordering the diodes then block.

Line inductance and charging current (ECPE)
crumbs: 253  AC-side Inductance, Input Current Formation, UDC=const

title: 110V/220V Input
text:
Dual-voltage bridge and doubler
An ideal 110 V RMS doubler gives two capacitor voltages of 156 V.



In doubler mode the two diodes charge opposite capacitors on alternate half-cycles. The load sees their series voltage.


Their sum nearly matches the 311 V peak of a 220 V bridge. If the low-line setting remains selected at 220 V, each capacitor tends toward 311 V. Compare this with a 200 V per-capacitor rating. The series total alone hides which component exceeds its rating.



The low-line doubler approximates the high-line bridge voltage. The wrong doubler setting charges each capacitor to 311 V.




Practice exercise
Compare the ideal no-load bus voltage of a 115 V RMS doubler with a 230 V RMS bridge. What voltage does each capacitor in the balanced doubler carry?


Check your reasoning

The doubler gives 2√2 × 115 ≈ 325 V. The bridge gives √2 × 230 ≈ 325 V. Each doubler capacitor charges to about 163 V.

Dual-voltage bridge and doubler (ECPE)

title: Power Factor, THD
text:
Distortion and true power factor
A rectifier draws 4 A RMS fundamental and 3 A RMS harmonics.
The total is 5 A and THD is 75%. With fundamental displacement factor 0.9, true power factor on a sinusoidal supply is 0.9 × 4/5 = 0.72. At 230 V it consumes 828 W and loads the supply at 1150 VA. Use the total 5 A RMS for the conductor-heating calculation.



Orthogonal current components add in quadrature. Conductor heating follows the total RMS current.




Practice exercise
A rectifier on sinusoidal mains draws 6 A RMS fundamental and 2 A RMS harmonic current. The displacement factor is 0.95. Find THD and true power factor.


Check your reasoning

THD is 2/6 = 33.3%. Total current is √40 = 6.32 A. True PF is 0.95 × 6/6.32 ≈ 0.901.

Distortion and true power factor (ECPE)

title: Mains Current Distortion
text:
Harmonics in line current
Approximate a rectifier input as alternating ±10 A rectangular pulses, each 60° wide and centered on a voltage peak.
Current flows for one third of the cycle, giving 5.77 A RMS. The fundamental peak is (4 × 10/π)sin(30°) = 6.37 A, or 4.50 A RMS. The remaining harmonic RMS is √(5.77² − 4.50²) ≈ 3.6 A. A fundamental-only meter misses the resulting heating.



Each current pulse spans 60°. The sinusoid shows the fundamental component of the pulse train.




Practice exercise
Narrow the alternating ±10 A rectangular line pulses to 36° each. Find line RMS current and compare it with the original 60° case.


Check your reasoning

There are two pulses per cycle. The new RMS is 10√(72/360) = 4.47 A. The original was 10√(120/360) = 5.77 A. Both figures assume the same pulse height.

Harmonics in line current (ECPE)

title: Mains Voltage Distortion
text:
Harmonic voltage at the supply
A fifth-harmonic current of 2 A RMS passes through a 0.20 Ω grid resistance and 0.50 mH inductance.
At 250 Hz their impedance magnitude is √(0.20² + 0.785²) = 0.81 Ω. The harmonic voltage drop is 1.62 V RMS. Compare upstream and load-terminal phasors at 250 Hz before assigning all measured distortion to the supply.



The fifth-harmonic drop contains a resistive component in phase with current and an inductive component in quadrature.




Practice exercise
A 1.5 A RMS seventh harmonic flows through a grid impedance of 0.20 Ω in series with 0.50 mH at 50 Hz fundamental. Estimate its RMS voltage drop.


Check your reasoning

At 350 Hz the inductive reactance is 2π × 350 × 0.00050 = 1.10 Ω. The drop is 1.5√(0.20² + 1.10²) ≈ 1.68 V RMS.

Harmonic voltage at the supply (ECPE)

title: Three-Phase Combination / Neutral Current
text:
Neutral current from single-phase loads
Three identical single-phase rectifiers draw 4 A RMS fundamental and 1 A RMS third harmonic each.
The fundamentals cancel in the neutral. A 120° fundamental phase displacement becomes 360° at the third harmonic, so the three third harmonics add to 3 A RMS. Under this spectrum the phase conductor carries √17 = 4.12 A RMS. Check both conductors when the load spectrum changes.



With neutral current directed back to the supply, the three fundamentals cancel and the third harmonics add.




Practice exercise
Balanced phase currents each contain 3 A RMS fundamental and 0.6 A RMS third harmonic. Find phase and neutral RMS currents for a four-wire supply.


Check your reasoning

Each phase carries √(3² + 0.6²) = 3.06 A. The fundamentals cancel at neutral. The in-phase third harmonics add to 1.8 A RMS.

Neutral current from single-phase loads (ECPE)

title: Discontinuous Conduction Mode
text:
Boost PFC with a zero-current interval
At one point on a rectified line cycle, input is 100 V, bus is 400 V and inductance is 100 µH.



Q stores energy in L during its on-time. When Q opens, positive inductor current flows through D into the output. Vin is the instantaneous stage input.


A 2 µs on-time raises current from zero to 2 A. The off slope is −3 A/µs, so current returns to zero in 0.667 µs. At a 10 µs period the average input current is 0.5 × 2 × 2.667/10 = 0.267 A. Confirm the remaining idle interval before using the triangular model.



The switch establishes the rising ramp. The diode then carries the falling current, followed by an idle interval.




Practice exercise
A boost PFC stage sees 80 V rectified input and 320 V bus. From zero current, turn Q on for 3 µs with 120 µH. Mark peak, diode interval and idle time in a 10 µs cycle.


Check your reasoning

Peak is 80 × 3 µs/120 µH = 2 A. The diode interval lasts 120 µH × 2/240 V = 1 µs. The stage idles for 6 µs.

Boost PFC with a zero-current interval (ECPE)

title: Critical Conduction Mode
text:
Boost PFC at the conduction boundary
A boost rectifier operates at 100 V instantaneous input with a 400 V bus and 100 µH inductance.



Q stores energy in L during its on-time. When Q opens, positive inductor current flows through D into the output. Vin is the instantaneous stage input.


To average 2 A at the conduction boundary, choose a 4 A peak. The on ramp takes 4 µs and the off ramp takes 1.33 µs. Starting at the next zero crossing gives about 188 kHz. Delay that start and the converter enters discontinuous operation. Check peak frequency over the line cycle.



At the boundary the next pulse starts as soon as the diode current reaches zero.




Practice exercise
At the same 80 V input and 320 V bus, turn on for 3 µs and restart as soon as current returns to zero. Find the boundary-mode frequency.


Check your reasoning

Reset uses 80 × 3/240 = 1 µs. The period is 4 µs and the frequency is 250 kHz, neglecting transition delays.

Boost PFC at the conduction boundary (ECPE)

title: Continuous Conduction Mode
text:
Boost PFC with continuous current
At 200 V input and 400 V output, an ideal boost uses 50% duty.



Q stores energy in L during its on-time. When Q opens, positive inductor current flows through D into the output. Vin is the instantaneous stage input.


With 1 mH and 50 kHz, the ripple is 2 A peak-to-peak. A 4 A mean gives a 3 A valley. Fixed-frequency PWM holds the period at 20 µs. A hysteresis band of ±1 A also gives 20 µs here, but changing the line voltage changes both slopes and the hysteresis frequency.



At this line instant the inductor swings between 3 and 5 A. The diode turns off with positive current at the next switch transition.




Practice exercise
A CCM boost has 150 V input, 300 V output, 300 µH and 100 kHz switching. Sketch the current around a 4 A mean.


Check your reasoning

Duty is 0.5 and the rising interval lasts 5 µs. Ripple is 150 × 5 µs/300 µH = 2.5 A peak-to-peak. The limits are 2.75 and 5.25 A, so the valley stays positive.

Boost PFC with continuous current (ECPE)

title: Calculation of Component Stresses
text:
Peak and RMS device stress
At one point on the line cycle, approximate inductor current as 4 A with small ripple and duty as 0.75.



Q stores energy in L during its on-time. When Q opens, positive inductor current flows through D into the output. Vin is the instantaneous stage input.


The switch carries 3 A mean and 3.46 A RMS over each switching period. The boost diode carries 1 A mean and 2 A RMS. Their means add to 4 A and their squared RMS values add to 16 A². Average the squared results over the entire mains cycle for a thermal rating.



The switch and diode partition the same continuous 4 A inductor current.




Practice exercise
At one line instant the boost inductor carries nearly constant 5 A at 64% duty. Find the switch and diode RMS currents over that switching period.


Check your reasoning

The switch carries 5 A for 64% of the period, giving 5√0.64 = 4 A RMS. The diode carries it for 36%, giving 3 A RMS.

Peak and RMS device stress (ECPE)

title: Single-Phase System Power Flow
text:
Twice-line-frequency energy storage
A unity-power-factor rectifier supplies 1 kW from single-phase 50 Hz mains. With a 400 V bus and a 470 µF capacitor, the energy swing amplitude is P/(4πf) = 1.59 J. The estimated voltage ripple is 16.9 V peak-to-peak. Increase the constant load to 2 kW.
The energy swing amplitude doubles to 3.18 J. The same small-ripple estimate gives 33.9 V peak-to-peak. Maintaining the old ripple requires about 940 µF. Check the line-frequency RMS capacitor current as well as capacitance.



At 2 kW the capacitor supplies the deficit near each voltage zero. Its stored energy swings twice per line cycle.




Practice exercise
A unity-PF single-phase rectifier supplies 1.5 kW at 50 Hz. Size a 400 V bus capacitor for 10 V peak-to-peak ripple using the small-ripple model.


Check your reasoning

The peak-to-peak energy swing is P/(2πf). Since ΔE ≈ C × V × ΔV, C ≈ 1500/(2π × 50 × 400 × 10) = 1.19 mF.

Twice-line-frequency energy storage (ECPE)

title: Control Concept & Loop Dynamics
text:
Rectifier current and voltage loops
A 230 V RMS PFC stage draws 1 kW.
Its current-loop conductance command is 1000/230² = 18.9 mS. At 200 V instantaneous input, the current reference is 3.78 A. If the voltage loop adds a 100 Hz sinusoidal modulation to this command, multiplication by the 50 Hz voltage creates a 150 Hz current term. Look for that harmonic before increasing outer-loop bandwidth.



A constant 18.9 mS conductance command makes the line-current reference proportional to line voltage.




Practice exercise
A PFC controller draws sinusoidal current proportional to voltage. At 200 V RMS, what conductance and peak current command deliver 800 W?


Check your reasoning

Conductance is P/V² = 800/200² = 20 mS. RMS current is 4 A and peak current is 5.66 A.

Rectifier current and voltage loops (ECPE)

title: DC-side Inductance, Cout
text:
DC choke and bus capacitor
A six-pulse bridge feeds a bus through a 4 mH DC choke.



The upper diode connects the highest available phase to +DC and the lower diode returns current to the lowest phase outside commutation overlap. External chokes and the DC load connect at the terminals.


During a 0.2 ms interval the bridge provides 310 V and the bus stays near 300 V. Choke current rises from 2 to 2.5 A. If the load draws 2 A, average capacitor current is 0.25 A. A 500 µF capacitor gains 0.10 V. The small voltage change checks the assumed constant bus voltage over this interval.



Capacitor current starts at zero and rises with choke current. Integrating it gives 0.10 V of bus rise.




Practice exercise
A 4 mH DC choke initially carries the full load current. A constant 8 V excess drives it for 0.25 ms. Estimate the rise on a 500 µF output capacitor.


Check your reasoning

Choke current increases by 0.50 A. The excess current triangle transfers ½ × 0.50 × 0.25 ms = 62.5 µC. Bus rise is 0.125 V.

DC choke and bus capacitor (ECPE)

title: AC-side Inductance, Cout
text:
Line choke and bus capacitor
Consider a three-phase bridge with a choke in each AC line and a capacitor across the DC bus.



The upper diode connects the highest available phase to +DC and the lower diode returns current to the lowest phase outside commutation overlap. External chokes and the DC load connect at the terminals.


When two phases conduct, two 1 mH chokes lie in series. With 12 V excess line-to-line voltage, input current rises 0.6 A in 100 µs. With only 0.1 mH per phase it would rise 6 A. Larger chokes limit peak charging current, but their fundamental voltage drop also grows. Check displacement and distortion together when comparing power factor.



Two phase chokes are in series during a two-diode conduction interval. Ten times the inductance gives one tenth of the current rise.




Practice exercise
Two conducting line chokes are each 0.8 mH. A line pair exceeds the bus by 16 V for 80 µs outside overlap. Estimate the current rise.


Check your reasoning

The conducting loop contains 1.6 mH. The rise is 16 × 80 µs/1.6 mH = 0.80 A.

Line choke and bus capacitor (ECPE)

title: Commutation
text:
Diode current transfer
A six-pulse bridge transfers 10 A between two phases with 100 µH per phase.



The upper diode connects the highest available phase to +DC and the lower diode returns current to the lowest phase outside commutation overlap. External chokes and the DC load connect at the terminals.


Assume constant DC current and a mean incoming-minus-outgoing source voltage of 20 V over the transfer. At the natural crossing itself, that voltage is zero. Both chokes participate, so transfer takes 2 × 100 µH × 10 A / 20 V = 100 µs. During overlap both diodes conduct and the shared rail voltage lies between the two phase voltages. Look for a terminal-voltage notch coincident with the current transfer.



Using the stated mean commutating voltage as a constant-voltage approximation, two same-rail diodes share 10 A during transfer.




Practice exercise
Two phase inductors are each 150 µH. A constant 30 V line difference transfers 6 A. Find the overlap duration and both valve currents halfway through.


Check your reasoning

The transfer loop has 300 µH, giving a slope of 0.10 A/µs. Transfer takes 60 µs. After 30 µs both valves carry 3 A.

Diode current transfer (ECPE)

title: DC+AC-side Inductance, Cout
text:
Chokes on both sides of a bridge
Compare two designs outside overlap.



The upper diode connects the highest available phase to +DC and the lower diode returns current to the lowest phase outside commutation overlap. External chokes and the DC load connect at the terminals.


Two conducting 0.5 mH line chokes and one 2 mH DC choke give 3 mH in the active loop. A 30 V excess produces 1 A rise in 100 µs. A 3 mH DC choke alone predicts the same rise. During phase commutation the common DC choke carries the sum, while the individual line chokes oppose redistribution. Check both overlap and bus ripple before treating the designs as equivalent.



Outside overlap, both designs present 3 mH to a charging-current change. Only the AC chokes act directly in the phase-transfer loop.




Practice exercise
Outside overlap a bridge has 0.5 mH per conducting AC phase and 1 mH on the DC side. For 20 V excess over 50 µs, compare the rise with the DC choke bypassed.


Check your reasoning

With both line chokes and the DC choke the path has 2 mH, giving 0.50 A rise. With only the two line chokes the rise doubles to 1.0 A.

Chokes on both sides of a bridge (ECPE)

title: Mains Neutral Connection
text:
Rectification with a mains neutral
A split DC link has a measured open-circuit third-harmonic midpoint voltage of 6 V RMS relative to mains neutral.
Model the midpoint circuit at 150 Hz by a 2 Ω Thévenin impedance. Bonding the midpoint to neutral now gives 3 A RMS at that harmonic. An open connection carries zero current even though the voltage exists. Verify the midpoint spectrum and return impedance before choosing the connection.



The open midpoint shows a voltage but carries no current. Closing the neutral path gives 6 V / 2 Ω at 150 Hz.




Practice exercise
A midpoint has a 4 V RMS third-harmonic Thevenin voltage relative to neutral. Its source resistance is 1 Ω. Find the neutral current when connected through another 3 Ω.


Check your reasoning

The effective series resistance is 4 Ω, so 1 A RMS flows at the third harmonic. The remaining midpoint-to-neutral voltage across the connection is 3 V RMS.

Rectification with a mains neutral (ECPE)

title: Unbalanced Mains
text:
Unequal phase voltages
At a recharge instant the three phase potentials are +160, −60 and −100 V.



The upper diode connects the highest available phase to +DC and the lower diode returns current to the lowest phase outside commutation overlap. External chokes and the DC load connect at the terminals.


An ideal bridge selects the largest difference, 260 V. If the positive phase sags to +128 V, only 228 V is available. With negligible line inductance and small positive source resistance, the bridge charges a 240 V capacitor in the first case and its diodes block in the second. Repeat this voltage test to locate possible charging intervals. Calculate current peaks from the source impedance and the evolving capacitor voltage.



Positive voltage margin permits charging. The sag makes the line-pair voltage too low to recharge the 240 V capacitor.




Practice exercise
At a recharge instant A, B and C are +130, −20 and −110 V. Identify the diode pair and test whether it can charge a 250 V bus from zero line current.


Check your reasoning

The candidate pair is upper A and lower C. Their line voltage is 240 V. With ideal diodes it cannot start charging a 250 V bus.

Unequal phase voltages (ECPE)

title: 2/3/4-pulse System
text:
Pulse count and output ripple
For equally spaced sinusoidal phases feeding a full-wave diode bridge, draw the highest phase minus the lowest.
Two opposite phases give two peaks per cycle. Three phases change the active pair six times. Four phases at 90° intervals form two opposite pairs, giving four peaks. On 50 Hz the lowest ripple frequencies are therefore 100, 300 and 200 Hz. Count the envelope peaks before sizing a DC filter.



The bridge selects the highest phase minus the lowest. Count two, six and four peaks respectively over one full cycle.




Practice exercise
For 60 Hz mains, find the lowest ripple frequency for the two-, three- and four-phase full-wave bridges illustrated, with equally spaced phases.


Check your reasoning

Count maxima of highest minus lowest phase. There are 2, 6 and 4 per cycle respectively, giving 120, 360 and 240 Hz.

Pulse count and output ripple (ECPE)

title: Single-Switch DCM Boost
text:
Single-switch three-phase boost
For three equal 200 µH line inductors, take instantaneous phase voltages of +100, −60 and −40 V.
The switch shorts the bridge DC terminals for 4 µs from zero current. The three current ramps end at +2, −1.2 and −0.8 A. They sum to zero. The positive phase supplies the switch current, which peaks at 2 A here. Check that all currents reset during off-time before applying this result at the next pulse.



During the 4 µs shorting interval the three input currents sum to zero. The positive phase supplies the switch current.




Practice exercise
During the three-phase boost shorting interval the phase voltages are +80, −50 and −30 V across three equal 100 µH inductors. Starting at zero, find all currents after 2 µs.


Check your reasoning

Using Δi = vΔt/L gives +1.6, −1.0 and −0.6 A. Their sum is zero. The positive phase supplies 1.6 A through the rectified shorting path.

Single-switch three-phase boost (ECPE)

title: Three-Switch CCM Boost (VIENNA)
text:
Vienna rectifier switching states
A Vienna phase leg carries positive current into a 600 V split bus.



One Vienna phase leg. For positive input current, closing Q selects midpoint M. Opening Q sends current through the upper diode.


With balanced capacitors it selects the midpoint at 0 V or the upper rail at +300 V. A +120 V average terminal command needs 40% rail dwell and 60% midpoint dwell. At 5 A constant current, the latter delivers 3 A switching-period average into the midpoint from this phase. Sum all three midpoint contributions before predicting capacitor imbalance.



For positive phase current the diode selects the upper rail during 40% of the period. The active midpoint path carries current during the remainder.




Practice exercise
A Vienna phase carries +4 A with a balanced 800 V bus. Synthesize +100 V average at the phase terminal. Find both dwells and mean midpoint current from this phase.


Check your reasoning

The upper rail is +400 V. Use upper-diode dwell 100/400 = 25% and midpoint-switch dwell 75%. The phase contributes 4 × 0.75 = 3 A mean into the midpoint.

Vienna rectifier switching states (ECPE)

title: Three-Switch Buck
text:
Three-switch step-down rectifier
During one sector a three-switch buck rectifier can select line-pair voltages of 300 V and 200 V, plus a freewheeling state.
Use dwell fractions 0.4, 0.3 and 0.3. The average bridge voltage is 180 V. At 10 A continuous DC current the selected pairs carry 10 A during their active dwells. Check that the freewheel path carries the same current during the zero dwell.



Two active line pairs deliver power. The zero state carries load current without applying line voltage.




Practice exercise
A buck rectifier selects 320 V for 25% of a period and 200 V for 50%. The remaining interval freewheels. Find mean bridge voltage and the energy delivered to a constant 4 A load in 20 µs.


Check your reasoning

The active dwells contribute 80 V and 100 V to the mean. At 180 V average the energy is 180 × 4 × 20 µs = 14.4 mJ.

Three-switch step-down rectifier (ECPE)

title: Three-Switch Buck & Boost: System Dimensioning
text:
Combined buck and boost sizing
A downstream stage must supply 400 V at 2 A.
At low line the buck front end can supply only 300 V, so boost duty is 0.25 and ideal intermediate current is 800/300 = 2.67 A. At high line, with 500 V available, regulate the front end to 400 V at 0.80 effective duty and idle the boost. Check the low-line current limit, the handover between stages and high-line blocking voltage.



Below 400 V the boost stage regulates. Above 400 V the buck stage reduces its effective duty.




Practice exercise
A cascaded ideal buck and boost stage must supply 400 V at 3 A from an available 320 V. Run the buck at unity duty. Find boost duty and mean intermediate current.


Check your reasoning

Boost duty is 1 − 320/400 = 0.20. The load needs 1.20 kW, so mean intermediate current is 1200/320 = 3.75 A.

Combined buck and boost sizing (ECPE)
