title: Basis of Pulse Width Modulation
text:
Carrier comparison
Compare a normalized triangular carrier spanning −1 to +1 with a nearly constant reference of +0.4.



The upper and lower devices select the pole voltage. Follow the antiparallel diode that can carry the inductor current when its transistor blocks.


The reference exceeds the carrier for (1 + 0.4)/2 = 70% of the period. With pole levels ±24 V, the mean is 0.7 × 24 − 0.3 × 24 = 9.6 V. Repeat with reference zero to check that equal dwell gives zero mean.



The switch selects +24 V whenever the reference exceeds the carrier. The high state occupies 70% of the period.




Practice exercise
A triangular carrier spans −1 to +1. Set the constant reference to −0.25 and the pole levels to ±40 V. Calculate high dwell and mean pole voltage.


Check your reasoning

The high fraction is (1 − 0.25)/2 = 0.375. The mean is 40 × (0.375 − 0.625) = −10 V.

Carrier comparison (ECPE)
crumbs: 277  Basis of Pulse Width Modulation

title: Square Wave Operation / Relation of DC- and AC-Quantities
text:
Full-bridge square-wave gain
A 48 V full bridge applies a symmetric square wave to 12 Ω.



Terminals A and B connect across the load. Selecting opposite rails gives a positive or negative line voltage. Selecting the same rail gives zero.


The total RMS voltage is 48 V and load power is 192 W. Its fundamental is 43.2 V RMS and accounts for about 156 W. The difference is harmonic heating. Use the total RMS value when rating a resistive test load.



The square-wave fundamental can exceed 48 V peak. Its RMS value still falls below the RMS value of the full waveform.




Practice exercise
A full bridge supplies a resistor of 18 Ω from a 36 V bus with a symmetric bipolar square wave. Find load RMS current, mean load current and mean DC input current.


Check your reasoning

The current alternates between ±2 A, so its RMS is 2 A and its mean is zero. The resistor consumes 72 W, requiring 2 A mean from the ideal DC source.

Full-bridge square-wave gain (ECPE)
crumbs: 278  Square Wave Operation / Relation of DC- and AC-Quantities

title: Bi- and Unipolar PWM
text:
Bipolar and unipolar bridge switching
At one carrier interval a 48 V bridge must average +12 V.



Terminals A and B connect across the load. Selecting opposite rails gives a positive or negative line voltage. Selecting the same rail gives zero.


Bipolar drive needs 62.5% at +48 V and 37.5% at −48 V. A unipolar sequence can use 25% at +48 V and 75% at zero. Both averages are 12 V. Across a 1 mH inductor facing a 12 V opposing source, their steepest falling current slopes are −60 and −12 A/ms. Use the actual dwell sequence to predict ripple.



These ideal dwell sequences both average +12 V. The zero state reduces the magnitude of the falling current slope.




Practice exercise
Produce +18 V average from a 60 V bridge. Find the dwell fractions for bipolar PWM and for a positive active state alternating with zero.


Check your reasoning

For bipolar PWM, 60(2D − 1) = 18 gives 65% positive and 35% negative. Using +60 V and zero requires 30% active and 70% zero.

Bipolar and unipolar bridge switching (ECPE)

title: AC-Side Current Ripple
text:
Inductor ripple on the AC side
An inverter applies +36 V to a 400 µH inductor facing +24 V for 5 µs.



The upper and lower devices select the pole voltage. Follow the antiparallel diode that can carry the inductor current when its transistor blocks.


Current rises 0.15 A. To close the triangular ripple with a zero-voltage state, the −24 V inductor voltage needs 2.5 µs. A longer zero dwell gives a negative net current change over the two intervals. Each repeated cycle starts at a lower current while the assumed voltages and conduction states hold. Verify volt-second balance when a simulated ripple fails to repeat.



The +36 V command raises current for 5 µs. A zero command needs 2.5 µs to undo that rise against the 24 V source.




Practice exercise
An inductance of 500 µH faces +20 V back EMF. Apply +40 V for 4 µs, then zero. Find the current rise and the zero dwell that restores the starting current.


Check your reasoning

The active-state rise is (40 − 20) × 4 µs/500 µH = 0.16 A. During zero dwell the inductor sees −20 V and needs another 4 µs to lose 0.16 A.

Inductor ripple on the AC side (ECPE)

title: Hysteresis Control / Switching Frequency Variation
text:
Hysteresis band and switching period
A ±0.1 A hysteresis band has 0.2 A between thresholds.



The upper and lower devices select the pole voltage. Follow the antiparallel diode that can carry the inductor current when its transistor blocks.


With slopes +3 and −1 A/ms, the two crossings take 0.0667 and 0.200 ms. If back EMF changes the slopes to +2 and −2 A/ms, the same band gives 0.200 ms per cycle, or 5 kHz. Rate switching loss for the highest frequency in the operating range.



The same ±0.1 A band produces different periods when the two voltage states give different error slopes.




Practice exercise
The error band is ±0.15 A. The rising and falling slopes have magnitudes 3 and 1.5 A/ms. Find the switching frequency for one complete excursion.


Check your reasoning

Each leg traverses 0.30 A. Rise takes 0.10 ms and fall takes 0.20 ms, so the period is 0.30 ms and frequency is 3.33 kHz.

Hysteresis band and switching period (ECPE)
crumbs: 281  Hysteresis Control / Switching Frequency Variation

title: Phasor Diagram / Operating Range
text:
Voltage phasors and current limits
A grid phase is 230 V RMS. Inject 10 A RMS in phase through 0.5 Ω and 10 mH at 50 Hz.
The inverter must produce 235 + j31.4 V RMS, a magnitude of 237.1 V at +7.6°. A 235 V RMS fundamental limit cannot sustain the command. Reduce current or increase available phase voltage, then check the phasor again.



With current in phase with the grid, resistance adds an in-phase voltage and inductance adds a quadrature voltage.




Practice exercise
Inject 5 A RMS in phase into a 120 V RMS grid through 1 Ω and 5 mH at 60 Hz. Find the inverter phase-voltage magnitude and lead angle.


Check your reasoning

The in-phase component is 120 + 5 = 125 V. The quadrature component is 2π × 60 × 0.005 × 5 = 9.42 V. The inverter needs 125.4 V RMS at about +4.31°.

Voltage phasors and current limits (ECPE)

title: Square Wave Operation
text:
Three-phase six-step switching
A 60 V two-level bridge uses states 100, 110, 010, 011, 001 and 101 for equal intervals.



Each pole A, B or C selects one DC rail. In a switching word ABC, 1 selects the upper rail and 0 selects the lower rail. The switches represent ideal legs with reverse-current paths.


Subtract pole B from pole A. The six line-voltage samples are +60, 0, −60, −60, 0 and +60 V. Their RMS is 60√(4/6) = 49.0 V. At 50 Hz each state lasts 3.33 ms. Distinguish line voltage from phase-to-neutral voltage when checking the waveform.



Bits give the A, B and C upper-switch commands. Read AB voltage by subtracting the B pole voltage from A.




Practice exercise
For a 90 V two-level bridge, write the AB line voltage during each state of 100, 110, 010, 011, 001, 101. Find its RMS over equal dwells.


Check your reasoning

Subtract pole B from pole A to obtain +90, 0, −90, −90, 0 and +90 V. Four of six slots have full magnitude, giving 90√(4/6) = 73.5 V RMS.

Three-phase six-step switching (ECPE)

title: Sinusoidal PWM, Single Carrier
text:
Single-carrier sinusoidal modulation
Three sinusoidal references have modulation index 0.8 and share one carrier.



Each pole A, B or C selects one DC rail. In a switching word ABC, 1 selects the upper rail and 0 selects the lower rail. The switches represent ideal legs with reverse-current paths.


With a 300 V DC bus the phase fundamental peak is 0.8 × 150 = 120 V. Balanced line-to-line fundamental RMS is 120√(3/2) = 147 V. At a phase-reference crest its upper-switch duty is 0.90. Verify both duty and line voltage to catch normalization errors. In a carrier-based current loop, a normalized feedforward command of 0.60 plus a current-error correction of 0.10 requests 0.70. Duty becomes 0.85. In a 300 V leg the average pole voltage measured from the midpoint rises from 90 to 105 V, increasing current slope.



All three references use one carrier. The lower trace shows pole A for an illustrative nine carrier cycles per electrical cycle.




Practice exercise
At one carrier interval the normalized phase references are +0.6, −0.3 and −0.3. Find the upper-switch duties and mean AB voltage for a 100 V bus.


Check your reasoning

The duties are (1 + reference)/2, giving 0.80, 0.35 and 0.35. The common reference rail cancels in AB, giving (0.80 − 0.35) × 100 = 45 V.

Single-carrier sinusoidal modulation (ECPE)

title: Overmodulation
text:
Reference clipping
Set the sinusoidal reference amplitude to 1.2 times the carrier peak.



Each pole A, B or C selects one DC rail. In a switching word ABC, 1 selects the upper rail and 0 selects the lower rail. The switches represent ideal legs with reverse-current paths.


Duty saturates at one when sin θ exceeds 1/1.2. The flat region extends from 56.4° to 123.6° in the positive half-cycle. Increasing the reference during that interval cannot increase pole voltage. Expect a nonlinear fundamental gain and inspect the low-order spectrum.



The requested reference exceeds the positive rail from 56.4° to 123.6°. The negative half-cycle clips symmetrically.




Practice exercise
A normalized reference is 1.25 sin θ and the carrier peaks at +1. Find the interval around the positive crest where the upper switch stays on.


Check your reasoning

Clipping starts when sin θ = 0.8, at 53.13°. It ends at 126.87°. High dwell saturates for about 73.74 electrical degrees.

Reference clipping (ECPE)

title: Hysteresis Current Control: Current error details
text:
Current error at band crossings
A hysteresis comparator detects +0.20 A current error, but the bridge changes state 2 µs later.



The upper and lower devices select the pole voltage. Follow the antiparallel diode that can carry the inductor current when its transistor blocks.


If error is still rising at 0.04 A/µs, actual peak error is 0.28 A. A specified ±0.25 A limit is exceeded. To retain a 0.20 A threshold, total delay must stay within 1.25 µs at that slope.



The error keeps rising during the 2 µs delay. It crosses the allowed limit before the bridge changes state.




Practice exercise
A bridge changes state 1.5 µs after detecting a +0.18 A error. The error continues rising at 0.04 A/µs. Can the design meet a +0.22 A ceiling?


Check your reasoning

The peak is 0.18 + 1.5 × 0.04 = 0.24 A. The available margin is 0.04 A, so the delay must be at most 1 µs at this slope.

Current error at band crossings (ECPE)
crumbs: 286  Hysteresis Current Control: Current error details

title: Hysteresis Current Control, open / Connected Neutral
text:
Hysteresis with a floating or connected neutral
Apply pole voltages (60, 0, 0) V to equal star-connected inductors with negligible back EMF.



Each pole A, B or C selects one DC rail. In a switching word ABC, 1 selects the upper rail and 0 selects the lower rail. The switches represent ideal legs with reverse-current paths.


With the star floating its potential is 20 V, giving phase voltages (40, −20, −20) V. With the star tied to the 30 V DC midpoint they become (+30, −30, −30) V. For 1 mH over 10 µs the first phase rises 0.4 or 0.3 A respectively. Only the connected case permits nonzero sum current.



For state 100, opening the neutral raises the star to 20 V. Tying it to the DC midpoint fixes it at 30 V.




Practice exercise
Apply pole voltages (90, 0, 0) V to equal star-connected inductors. Find the winding voltages for a floating star and for a star tied to the 45 V midpoint.


Check your reasoning

The floating star sits at (90 + 0 + 0)/3 = 30 V. Winding voltages are (60, −30, −30) V. With the midpoint tie they are (45, −45, −45) V.

Hysteresis with a floating or connected neutral (ECPE)
crumbs: 287  Hysteresis Current Control, open / Connected Neutral

title: Output Current Ripple Space Vector (Sinusoidal-Source)
text:
Ripple against a sinusoidal source
Two sinusoidal voltage vectors are momentarily (100, 0) V and (98, 4) V in stationary αβ axes.
Across 2 mH their difference gives current slopes (1000, −2000) A/s. Over 20 µs the vector moves about (+0.020, −0.040) A. Shorten the step if either source rotates appreciably during it.



The instantaneous voltage difference (2, −4) V moves the current vector into the fourth quadrant in 20 µs.




Practice exercise
In αβ coordinates the converter voltage is (60, 10) V and the opposing source is (50, 15) V. For 1 mH per axis, find the current increment over 20 µs.


Check your reasoning

The difference is (10, −5) V. Multiplying by 20 µs/1 mH gives (+0.20, −0.10) A.

Ripple against a sinusoidal source (ECPE)
crumbs: 288  Output Current Ripple Space Vector (Sinusoidal-Source)

title: Output Current Ripple Space Vector (Rectangular-Source)
text:
Ripple against a rectangular source
A six-step source holds (40, 0) V, then jumps to (20, 34.64) V at a sector boundary.



Each pole A, B or C selects one DC rail. In a switching word ABC, 1 selects the upper rail and 0 selects the lower rail. The switches represent ideal legs with reverse-current paths.


Treat the opposing sinusoidal source as (20, 0) V for two 10 µs intervals. Through 1 mH the first increment is (+0.20, 0) A and the second is (0, +0.346) A. The trajectory changes direction at the edge. A single endpoint slope misses the corner.



Two 10 µs dwells give two current increments. The six-step sector change creates the corner.




Practice exercise
A six-step source changes from (30, 0) to (15, 26) V against (15, 0) V back EMF. With 1 mH per axis and two 10 µs dwells, sketch the path from zero incremental current.


Check your reasoning

The first increment is (0.15, 0) A. The second is (0, 0.26) A. The tip turns at (0.15, 0) and ends at (0.15, 0.26) A.

Ripple against a rectangular source (ECPE)
crumbs: 289  Output Current Ripple Space Vector (Rectangular-Source)

title: Output Current Ripple Space Vector (PWM-Source)
text:
Ripple between a PWM inverter and a sinusoidal source
A PWM source alternates (40, 0) V and zero against a sinusoidal source locally at (10, 0) V.



Each pole A, B or C selects one DC rail. In a switching word ABC, 1 selects the upper rail and 0 selects the lower rail. The switches represent ideal legs with reverse-current paths.


In 40 µs, choose 10 µs active and 30 µs zero. With 1 mH the current first rises 0.30 A then falls 0.30 A on the α axis. The matched average voltages leave zero net change but 0.30 A peak-to-peak ripple.



The 10 µs active state and 30 µs zero state retrace the same α-axis segment. Net change is zero.




Practice exercise
A 40 V active vector along α acts against a 16 V source on the same axis. Apply it for 8 µs, then apply the zero vector. Find zero dwell for zero net ripple over the cycle.


Check your reasoning

Active dwell adds 24 × 8 = 192 V·µs. Zero dwell applies −16 V and needs 12 µs to cancel that area. The complete cycle has 40% active dwell.

Ripple between a PWM inverter and a sinusoidal source (ECPE)
crumbs: 290  Output Current Ripple Space Vector (PWM-Source)

title: Mains Unbalanced
text:
Negative-sequence grid voltage
Represent an unbalanced grid by a forward voltage vector of magnitude 100 V and a reverse vector of 10 V.
When aligned their resultant is 110 V. Half a relative revolution later it is 90 V. Use amplitude-invariant Clarke coordinates and assume a three-wire connection. To maintain 1.5 kW with current parallel to voltage, use p = (3/2)(vαiα + vβiβ). Current magnitudes are 9.09 and 11.11 A. The peak current requirement grows even at constant real power.



Adding counter-rotating 100 V and 10 V vectors produces an ellipse with semiaxes of 110 V and 90 V.




Practice exercise
A forward sequence vector has magnitude 80 V and a reverse sequence vector has magnitude 8 V. Find the largest and smallest resultant magnitudes over a line cycle.


Check your reasoning

When aligned the vectors add to 88 V. Half a relative revolution later they oppose, giving 72 V. Their relative angle advances at twice line frequency.

Negative-sequence grid voltage (ECPE)

title: Mains Distortion
text:
Distorted grid voltage
A balanced grid has 5% fifth and 3% seventh voltage harmonics relative to a 230 V RMS fundamental.
Their RMS values are 11.5 and 6.9 V. If the inverter commands only the fundamental across a 5 mH coupling inductor, the residual fifth harmonic at 250 Hz drives about 1.46 A RMS. The seventh at 350 Hz drives about 0.63 A. Compare harmonic current limits before selecting compensation bandwidth.



These are the separate harmonic-current components for zero inverter harmonic voltage. The assumed grid harmonics start at a positive voltage crest; current is directed from grid to inverter.




Practice exercise
A grid phase voltage has 4% fifth and 2% seventh harmonic relative to a 200 V RMS fundamental, with no other harmonics. Find harmonic RMS and voltage THD.


Check your reasoning

The components are 8 V and 4 V RMS. Combined harmonic RMS is √80 = 8.94 V, giving 8.94/200 = 4.47% THD.

Distorted grid voltage (ECPE)

title: Space Vector Modulation
text:
Space-vector dwell times
Use adjacent vectors (40, 0) and (20, 34.64) V to produce (20, 13.86) V on average.



Each pole A, B or C selects one DC rail. In a switching word ABC, 1 selects the upper rail and 0 selects the lower rail. The switches represent ideal legs with reverse-current paths.


The vertical coordinate requires 0.40 dwell on the second vector. The horizontal coordinate then gives 0.30 on the first. The remaining 0.30 is zero dwell. At 20 kHz the times are 15, 20 and 15 µs. For this sector, use 100 for the first vector and 110 for the second. A symmetric sequence is 000 → 100 → 110 → 111 → 110 → 100 → 000. Assign successive dwells of 3.75, 7.5, 10, 7.5, 10, 7.5 and 3.75 µs. Each transition changes one leg and the total dwell is 50 µs.



Each raised gate trace commands its upper switch. Only one leg changes at each boundary, and the seven dwells total 50 µs.




Practice exercise
Use the illustrated adjacent vectors with total dwells of 12 and 8 µs in a 40 µs period. Give the seven durations for 000–100–110–111–110–100–000, sharing zero time equally between zero states.


Check your reasoning

Zero time is 40 − 12 − 8 = 20 µs. Split active dwells symmetrically and divide the 000 dwell between the ends. Durations are 5, 6, 4, 10, 4, 6 and 5 µs. Only one bit changes per transition.

Space-vector dwell times (ECPE)

title: Decoupling of Zero Sequ. Quantity
text:
Zero-sequence injection
At one instant three phase commands are (80, −20, −60) V with pole limits ±75 V.



Each pole A, B or C selects one DC rail. In a switching word ABC, 1 selects the upper rail and 0 selects the lower rail. The switches represent ideal legs with reverse-current paths.


Add a common −10 V to obtain (70, −30, −70) V. Line differences remain 100, 40 and −140 V in cyclic order. The common component is now −10 V, while the αβ vector stays fixed. Use the extra headroom only after checking common-mode return paths.



A −10 V common shift moves all three poles inside the ±75 V rails and preserves their differences.




Practice exercise
Pole limits are ±60 V and requested phase commands are (70, −10, −50) V. Find a common offset that makes the commands feasible. Verify line AB.


Check your reasoning

Subtract 10 V from every phase to get (60, −20, −60) V. The original and shifted AB commands both differ by 80 V.

Zero-sequence injection (ECPE)
crumbs: 294  Decoupling of Zero Sequ. Quantity

title: Phase-Order
text:
Phase sequence and rotation
With phase currents (6, −3, −3) A the amplitude-invariant Clarke vector lies at (6, 0) A.
One quarter cycle later a positive sequence gives (0, +5.20, −5.20) A, mapping to (0, +6) A. Interchanging B and C produces (0, −6) A instead. Magnitude alone cannot identify reversed phase order. Check rotation over time.



Both current vectors start at (6, 0) A. Swapping B and C reverses the quarter-turn.




Practice exercise
Use the amplitude-invariant Clarke transform on currents (0, 3, −3) A. What happens to the vector when the B and C sensor inputs are swapped?


Check your reasoning

For this balanced set α = 0 and β = (B − C)/√3 = 3.46 A. Swapping B and C reverses β to −3.46 A while α stays zero.

Phase sequence and rotation (ECPE)

title: Transistor / Diode Current
text:
Transistor and diode current paths
At a positive voltage crest, suppose the upper transistor is commanded on for 90% of the interval.



The upper and lower devices select the pole voltage. Follow the antiparallel diode that can carry the inductor current when its transistor blocks.


Assume unidirectional transistors with antiparallel diodes, negligible dead time and nearly constant phase current. At +5 A flowing out of the leg, the upper transistor carries 4.5 A local-period average and the lower diode 0.5 A. With −5 A regeneration the upper diode and lower transistor carry those respective magnitudes. The leg voltage can look the same while the hottest device changes.



The +5 A phase current uses the upper transistor in high state and the lower diode in low state. For −5 A these paths become upper diode and lower transistor.




Practice exercise
A leg carries −4 A phase current, with positive current defined out of the pole. Identify the conducting devices for 75% upper and 25% lower dwell in the transistor–diode model.


Check your reasoning

Negative current flows from phase to +DC through the upper diode in high state, and from phase to −DC through the lower transistor in low state. Their period-average current magnitudes are 3 A and 1 A.

Transistor and diode current paths (ECPE)

title: Transistor / Diode Current Calculator
text:
Device RMS and average currents
A conducting transistor carries 6 A for half a PWM period in one operating interval and for one quarter in a second interval of equal duration.



The upper and lower devices select the pole voltage. Follow the antiparallel diode that can carry the inductor current when its transistor blocks.


Across both intervals its conduction fraction is 0.375. Its average current is 2.25 A and RMS is √(36 × 0.375) = 3.67 A. Average the squared samples before taking the root. Repeat with the diode conduction mask for its rating.



Full-record RMS uses both periods, including all zero-current intervals. The total on-time is 37.5%.




Practice exercise
A transistor carries rectangular 8 A pulses in two equally long intervals, at duties 0.2 and 0.6. Find average and RMS transistor current over the combined interval.


Check your reasoning

Overall conduction fraction is (0.2 + 0.6)/2 = 0.4. Mean current is 8 × 0.4 = 3.2 A and RMS current is 8√0.4 = 5.06 A.

Device RMS and average currents (ECPE)

title: Power Flow in Three-Phase Systems
text:
Three-phase real power
A balanced sinusoidal system supplies 10 A RMS at 400 V line-to-line RMS and 0.8 lagging displacement power factor.
Apparent power is √3 × 400 × 10 = 6.93 kVA. Real power is 5.54 kW and reactive power is 4.16 kvar. Reversing all three current references reverses signed real and reactive power. State the current direction before deciding whether the converter regenerates.



The phase powers pulsate at twice line frequency. Their sum stays at 5.54 kW for the balanced sinusoidal load.




Practice exercise
A balanced three-phase load draws 8 A RMS from 400 V line-to-line at 0.6 lagging displacement factor with sinusoidal waveforms. Calculate apparent, active and reactive power.


Check your reasoning

S = √3 × 400 × 8 = 5.54 kVA. P = 0.6S = 3.33 kW. Positive inductive Q is 0.8S = 4.43 kvar.

Three-phase real power (ECPE)
crumbs: 298  Power Flow in Three-Phase Systems

title: DC Capacitor Current Stress
text:
RMS current in the DC-link capacitor
A DC source supplies steady 3 A while the inverter draws 0 A for 25%, 3 A for 50% and 6 A for 25% of a period.
Capacitor current is +3, 0 and −3 A. Its mean is zero and its RMS is √4.5 = 2.12 A. With 40 mΩ ESR this produces 0.18 W. A DC ammeter in the capacitor lead will miss the heating.



The difference between source and inverter current charges and discharges the DC capacitor. Its mean is zero.




Practice exercise
A DC source supplies 4 A steadily. The inverter draws 0 A for 25%, 4 A for 50% and 8 A for 25%. Find capacitor RMS current and check charge balance.


Check your reasoning

Take capacitor charging current as source minus inverter current. Its levels are +4, 0 and −4 A. Mean is zero and RMS is √(0.25 × 16 + 0.25 × 16) = 2.83 A.

RMS current in the DC-link capacitor (ECPE)

title: Basic Thyristor Converter
text:
Thyristor triggering and turn-off
A single thyristor feeds 20 Ω from a 100 V peak sine.



The gate pulse starts conduction through T and R when T is forward biased. Load current reaches zero at the end of the positive half-cycle.


Fire at 60° during the positive half-cycle. The initial current is 100 sin(60°)/20 = 4.33 A. For an ideal resistive load it turns off at 180°. Integrating from 60° to 180° over a full cycle gives 100(1 + cos 60°)/(2π) = 23.9 V average. A gate pulse during reverse bias cannot start the next half-cycle.



With a resistive load, the valve starts current at the 60° gate pulse and extinguishes at the line zero crossing.




Practice exercise
Fire a single ideal thyristor at 90° on an 80 V peak sine feeding 10 Ω. Find current immediately after firing and the mean load voltage over a full cycle.


Check your reasoning

Initial current is 8 A. Conduction ends at 180°. The mean is 80(1 + cos 90°)/(2π) = 12.7 V.

Thyristor triggering and turn-off (ECPE)

title: Single-Phase Full-Bridge
text:
Single-phase controlled bridge
A fully controlled single-phase bridge supplies continuous current from 120 V RMS.



One upper and one diagonally opposite lower thyristor carry continuous load current between firings.


To obtain 54 V average, solve cos α = 54/(0.9003 × 120) = 0.500. Fire at about 60° after the natural commutation point. Two valves carry current at once. At 10 A, a 1 V drop in each subtracts about 2 V from the ideal result.



Continuous DC current keeps the old diagonal conducting past each source zero. The bridge changes diagonal at 60° and 240°.




Practice exercise
A fully controlled single-phase bridge has continuous DC current, 100 V RMS AC and negligible overlap. Choose a firing angle for +45 V mean output.


Check your reasoning

The ideal maximum is 2√2 × 100/π ≈ 90.0 V. Set cos α = 45/90, giving α ≈ 60°.

Single-phase controlled bridge (ECPE)

title: Three-Phase Full-Bridge
text:
Six-pulse controlled bridge
A 400 V line-to-line six-pulse bridge operates at 60° firing delay with 8 A continuous DC current.



Each conducting pair connects two phases to the DC terminals. At a firing, the incoming and outgoing devices can share current during overlap.


Its ideal mean DC voltage is 1.35 × 400 × 0.5 = 270 V and output power is 2.16 kW. At 120° the voltage becomes −270 V and power becomes −2.16 kW if a DC source sustains current. Check that the load can supply that energy before predicting inversion.



Each conducting pair changes after 60 electrical degrees. With positive DC current, delaying firing past 90° reverses average power.




Practice exercise
A six-pulse controlled bridge operates from 230 V line-to-line RMS with continuous current at 120° firing delay. Find mean DC voltage and interpret the sign for +5 A DC current.


Check your reasoning

Mean voltage is 1.35 × 230 × cos 120° ≈ −155 V. DC terminal power is about −776 W using positive rectifier output current, so power returns from the DC side to the AC supply.

Six-pulse controlled bridge (ECPE)

title: Single-Phase Half-Bridge with Transformer
text:
Single-phase midpoint connection
A center-tapped transformer has 60 V RMS per half-winding.



Alternate firings select opposite transformer half-windings. Load current returns to the center tap.


In continuous conduction at 30° delay, the two-pulse midpoint converter gives 0.9003 × 60 × cos 30° = 46.8 V average. Each thyristor carries the full load current for half a period. At a steady 8 A DC load current, each half-winding carries 5.66 A RMS. Use the half-winding voltage in the gain formula.



Each half-winding supplies the full DC current for 180°. The natural reference is the secondary-voltage crossing.




Practice exercise
A center-tapped two-pulse controlled rectifier has 50 V RMS per half-winding, continuous current and negligible overlap. Find mean voltage at 45° firing delay.


Check your reasoning

The mean is (2√2/π) × 50 × cos 45° = 31.8 V. Use the RMS of one half-winding since a single half supplies each conduction interval.

Single-phase midpoint connection (ECPE)

title: Three-Phase Half-Bridge with Transformer
text:
Three-phase midpoint connection
Three star-connected transformer phases provide 100 V RMS phase-to-neutral.



The fired thyristor connects its phase to the load. Current returns through the transformer neutral.


A three-pulse midpoint rectifier with continuous current selects one phase for 120° at a time. At zero delay, averaging the segment from 30° to 150° gives 3√6/(2π) × 100 = 117 V. At 60° delay this falls to 58.5 V. A 9 A DC load gives each valve 3 A mean and 5.20 A RMS.



One phase winding supplies the midpoint load for 120°. Delayed selection lowers the average output.




Practice exercise
Three star-connected phase windings each supply 80 V RMS. For an ideal three-pulse midpoint converter at zero delay and continuous current, find mean output voltage and individual valve dwell.


Check your reasoning

The average of the highest phase is 3√6/(2π) × 80 = 93.6 V. Each valve conducts for 120°.

Three-phase midpoint connection (ECPE)

title: Parallel Connection with Interphase Transformer
text:
Parallel groups and interphase coupling
Two three-pulse groups feed the ends of an ideal center-tapped interphase winding.
At one instant their voltages are 110 and 90 V. The midpoint delivers 100 V while the winding absorbs the 20 V difference. Take the 20 V difference as constant for 100 µs. Define circulating current as half the difference between branch currents. The 2 mH inductance measured end to end then gives a circulating-current change of 20 V × 100 µs / 2 mH = 1 A. With 10 A initially in each branch the currents become 11 and 9 A. Total load current remains 20 A.



A sustained 20 V mismatch changes circulating current by 1 A. The two branches change in opposite directions while their sum stays at 20 A.




Practice exercise
The two ends of an ideal center-tapped interphase winding are at 110 and 90 V. The load draws 12 A shared equally. Find tap voltage, half-winding voltage magnitudes and branch currents.


Check your reasoning

The tap is at the mean, 100 V. Each half supports 10 V in magnitude. Each rectifier branch supplies 6 A.

Parallel groups and interphase coupling (ECPE)
crumbs: 305  Parallel Connection with Interphase Transformer

title: Commutation / Converter Equivalent Circuit
text:
Overlap and average DC voltage
A continuous-current six-pulse bridge has 0.5 mH source inductance per phase, 50 Hz supply and 20 A DC current.



Each conducting pair connects two phases to the DC terminals. At a firing, the incoming and outgoing devices can share current during overlap.


The mean commutation drop is 3ωL I/π = 3.0 V. At 100 V line-to-line and zero delay, ideal mean voltage falls from 135 to 132 V. Doubling load doubles this drop in the overlap model. Check measured DC regulation against the slope. For a three-pulse midpoint converter there are three transfers per cycle instead of six. Each transfer loses area L times load current, so the corresponding drop with these same values is 3fLI = 1.5 V.



Each transfer loses volt-seconds in proportion to load current. The six-pulse bridge has twice as many transfers per line period.




Practice exercise
Find the mean commutation drop in a six-pulse bridge with 0.30 mH per phase, 60 Hz mains and 15 A continuous load current.


Check your reasoning

There are six transfers per line cycle. The drop is 6fLI = 6 × 60 × 0.00030 × 15 = 1.62 V.

Overlap and average DC voltage (ECPE)

title: Loss of Commutation
text:
Inverter commutation failure
An inverter operates at 145° delay on 50 Hz mains.



Each conducting pair connects two phases to the DC terminals. At a firing, the incoming and outgoing devices can share current during overlap.


With 20° overlap, recovery time is 15°/360° × 20 ms = 833 µs. A voltage sag extending overlap to 30° leaves only 278 µs. If the specified recovery allowance is 400 µs, the second operating point falls 122 µs short of the recovery allowance. Commutation failure is possible. Reduce firing delay or current to recover margin.



Both cases fire at 145°. A 400 µs allowance needs 7.2° at 50 Hz. The second case provides only 5°.




Practice exercise
At 50 Hz a line-commutated inverter fires at 150° with 20° overlap. Find the recovery time and margin over a 450 µs requirement.


Check your reasoning

Extinction angle is 180 − 150 − 20 = 10°. At 50 Hz this gives 10/360 × 20 ms = 556 µs. The margin is about 106 µs.

Inverter commutation failure (ECPE)

title: Basic Thyristor Converter / Free-Wheeling Diode
text:
Freewheel path on a thyristor load
A single-thyristor half-wave rectifier feeds a series resistance and a large smoothing inductor. A freewheel diode spans the complete load.



T connects the source to the RL load. When the source reverses, Df carries positive load current around the local loop.


Take 100 V source peak, 60° firing delay and continuous load current. The source feeds the load from 60° to 180°. The diode carries current during the rest of the cycle and clamps ideal load voltage to zero. Mean voltage is 23.9 V. With 4.775 Ω load resistance, average current is about 5 A. Treat ripple as negligible. The mean resistor voltage is 23.9 V. The inductor has zero net volt-seconds over a cycle. The diode conducts for 240° and averages 3.33 A. Check the diode rating even while source current is zero.



Continuous load current transfers to the freewheel diode at 180°. The load voltage then stays near zero.




Practice exercise
For the freewheel circuit, current is continuous and the SCR fires at 90° on a 120 V peak sine. Identify the source and freewheel intervals and find mean load voltage with ideal devices.


Check your reasoning

The SCR applies source voltage from 90° to 180°. The freewheel diode carries load current for the other 270°. The mean is 120(1 + cos 90°)/(2π) = 19.1 V.

Freewheel path on a thyristor load (ECPE)
crumbs: 308  Basic Thyristor Converter / Free-Wheeling Diode

title: Parameters of Current Commutation (Theory)
text:
Commutating voltage and transfer time
During a transfer, incoming and outgoing phases each have 100 µH.
To transfer 8 A the line voltage must supply 2L × 8 = 1.6 mV·s. If commutating voltage rises linearly from zero at 0.020 V/µs, the area is one half times slope times time squared. Solving gives 400 µs, or 7.2° at 50 Hz. Using the final voltage for the entire interval would halve the calculated time.



A linearly increasing commutating voltage transfers current quadratically. At 400 µs the incoming valve carries the full 8 A.




Practice exercise
Two 100 µH line inductors share a transfer. The commutating voltage rises linearly from zero to 20 V in 100 µs. How much current transfers in this time?


Check your reasoning

The voltage triangle has area ½ × 20 V × 100 µs = 1000 V·µs. Divide by the 200 µH loop inductance to obtain 5 A.

Commutating voltage and transfer time (ECPE)

title: Four-Quadrant Converter for DC-Drive
text:
Reversible DC drives
A fixed-field DC drive has ±100 V armature voltage and ±5 A current available. (+100, +5) and (−100, −5) each absorb 500 W.
Opposite signs return 500 W. For two antiparallel controlled groups in circulating-current operation, choose complementary firing angles, for example 60° and 120°, to match average terminal voltage after polarity reversal. A remaining 12 V instantaneous mismatch across a 3 mH reactor changes circulating current by 0.4 A in 100 µs. Include it in both valve ratings.



At the armature terminals, equal voltage and current signs give positive absorbed power. Opposite signs return power.




Practice exercise
A fixed-field drive holds +80 V armature voltage and −4 A current at positive speed. Determine electrical power and torque direction, and identify the energy destination for an ideal regenerative converter.


Check your reasoning

With current positive into the motor, power is 80 × (−4) = −320 W. Negative armature current gives negative torque. The motor brakes and returns 320 W through the converter to the supply.

Reversible DC drives (ECPE)

text:
Rotating Field

title: Rotating Field
text:
Rotating stator field
Three equal windings have axes at 0°, 120° and 240°.
At one instant their currents are (4, −2, −2) A. Adding their axis vectors gives 6 normalized ampere-turn units along the first axis for one turn per winding. A quarter electrical cycle later currents are (0, +3.46, −3.46) A and the sum points 90° ahead with the same magnitude. This rotating field turns at 1500 mechanical rpm for 50 Hz and two pole pairs.



One quarter of an electrical cycle moves the resultant winding field from the α axis to the β axis.




Practice exercise
A four-pole-pair machine is supplied with balanced currents at 80 Hz electrical frequency. Find the mechanical speed of the rotating stator field and describe the effect of swapping any two phases.


Check your reasoning

The field speed is 60 × 80/4 = 1200 rpm. Swapping two phases reverses the rotation while preserving its speed magnitude.

Rotating stator field (ECPE)

title: DC Machine vs. PMSM
text:
DC and synchronous machine torque
A fixed-field DC machine has torque constant 0.30 N·m/A.
It needs 5 A armature current for 1.5 N·m. A surface PMSM with two pole pairs and 0.10 Wb magnet flux needs 5 A peak quadrature current for the same torque. If its current vector is misaligned by 30°, useful quadrature current falls to 4.33 A and torque to 1.30 N·m. Check rotor angle and current conventions when comparing the two drives.



At fixed 5 A current magnitude, the PMSM loses useful quadrature current as the electrical angle error grows.




Practice exercise
A fixed-field DC motor and a surface PMSM both produce 0.4 N·m per productive ampere. At 6 A, compare DC torque with PMSM torque for a 30° current-vector error from the q axis.


Check your reasoning

DC torque is 0.4 × 6 = 2.4 N·m. The PMSM has 6 cos 30° = 5.20 A on the q axis, giving 2.08 N·m with negligible reluctance torque.

DC and synchronous machine torque (ECPE)

title: Torque-Control of PMSM
text:
Rotor-oriented torque control
A surface PMSM with two pole pairs and 0.10 Wb magnet flux must produce 2.4 N·m.
The quadrature current command is 2.4/(1.5 × 2 × 0.10) = 8 A peak. With a 7 A current limit the available torque is 2.1 N·m at zero direct-axis current. Limit the torque command before tuning the speed controller.



The requested 8 A would produce 2.4 N·m. The current limiter caps torque at 2.1 N·m.




Practice exercise
A surface PMSM has three pole pairs and 0.08 Wb permanent-magnet flux linkage. Find peak q-axis current for −1.8 N·m using the amplitude-invariant dq convention and zero d-axis current.


Check your reasoning

The torque constant is (3/2) × 3 × 0.08 = 0.36 N·m/A. The command is −1.8/0.36 = −5 A.

Rotor-oriented torque control (ECPE)

title: Speed-Control of PMSM
text:
Cascaded speed control
A shaft with inertia 0.020 kg·m² must increase speed by 20 rad/s in 0.20 s against 1 N·m constant load.
Required torque is 0.020 × 100 + 1 = 3 N·m. A current loop limited to 2 N·m leaves 1 N·m for acceleration, or 50 rad/s². The shortest ideal ramp is then 0.40 s. Extend the speed ramp and prevent the speed integrator from accumulating error during current limiting.



With 1 N·m of net accelerating torque the shaft needs 0.40 s to gain 20 rad/s.




Practice exercise
A shaft has inertia 0.030 kg·m² and a constant opposing torque of 0.8 N·m. The motor can produce 2.0 N·m. Find the shortest ideal time for a 12 rad/s speed increase.


Check your reasoning

Net torque is 1.2 N·m, so acceleration is 1.2/0.030 = 40 rad/s². The speed change requires 12/40 = 0.30 s.

Cascaded speed control (ECPE)

title: Multi-Step Commutation
text:
Directional switch commutation
Transfer a +3 A inductive output current from input A to B.



F conducts from input to load and R from load to input. The branch labels match the four gate commands in the sequence.


Denote the forward and reverse directional paths in each bidirectional switch by F and R. Start with AF and AR enabled. Disable AR, enable BF, disable AF, then enable BR. During the overlap both AF and BF are enabled toward the output. The input voltages determine which carries the current. Neither enabled path can carry current back into the other input. For −3 A, disable AF, enable BR, disable AR, then enable BF. Separate gate commands by intervals that allow the preceding device transition to finish. Both sequences require a known current sign throughout the transfer.



Read each panel from left to right. Both forward paths can be enabled together for positive current. For negative current the reverse paths overlap.




Practice exercise
Reverse the illustrated transfer: move a known positive 3 A output current from input B to input A. Write the four commands, then identify which paths can carry current during overlap.


Check your reasoning

Start with BF and BR enabled. Disable BR, enable AF, disable BF, then enable AR. During overlap BF and AF both point toward the output, so the phase voltages decide which carries current without enabling a return path to the other phase.

Directional switch commutation (ECPE)

title: Zero DC Link Curr. Commutation
text:
Zero intermediate-current switching
A sparse matrix converter needs 0.9 µs for rectifier transfer plus 0.2 µs guard time at each end.



Each pole A, B or C selects one DC rail. In a switching word ABC, 1 selects the upper rail and 0 selects the lower rail. The switches represent ideal legs with reverse-current paths.


An inverter zero state lasts 1.5 µs. The required 1.3 µs fits with 0.2 µs spare. In state 000, balanced load currents (+6, −2, −4) A return to the same rail and sum to zero, so intermediate current vanishes ideally. Confirm the zero-current window on the timing trace before moving the rectifier edge.



One valid schedule uses 0.30 µs guards on each side of the 0.90 µs rectifier transfer. Both guards exceed the required 0.20 µs.




Practice exercise
The input rectifier needs 1.1 µs for transfer and 0.25 µs guard time on each side. Can it commute inside a 1.5 µs inverter zero dwell? State the minimum dwell.


Check your reasoning

The transfer and guards require 1.1 + 2 × 0.25 = 1.60 µs. The proposed dwell is short by 0.10 µs. Allocate at least 1.60 µs with zero link current.

Zero intermediate-current switching (ECPE)
crumbs: 317  Zero DC Link Curr. Commutation

title: Voltage and Current Time Behavior
text:
Sparse matrix converter timing
During a 10 µs interval the inverter first applies state 100 for 6 µs with 200 V on the intermediate link.



Each pole A, B or C selects one DC rail. In a switching word ABC, 1 selects the upper rail and 0 selects the lower rail. The switches represent ideal legs with reverse-current paths.


Line AB sees +200 V and link current equals phase A current, here +4 A. It then applies 000 for 4 µs while the rectifier changes line pair. Line AB voltage and link current both fall to zero. Average AB voltage is 120 V and transferred energy is 200 × 4 × 6 µs = 4.8 mJ. The motor current still has a path during the zero interval.



State 100 transfers energy for 6 µs. In 000 the load freewheels, leaving a zero-current interval for the input-stage transfer.




Practice exercise
The sparse converter uses state 100 for 4 µs at 250 V link voltage and +3 A phase A current, then 000 for 6 µs. Find mean AB voltage and energy transferred over the period.


Check your reasoning

The active dwell gives +250 V across AB and 3 A link current. State 000 gives zero AB voltage and zero link current. Mean voltage is 100 V and energy is 250 × 3 × 4 µs = 3 mJ.

Sparse matrix converter timing (ECPE)

title: DC-DC Converter: noise generation by commutation
text:
Commutation-loop interference
A buck commutates 5 A in 10 ns through a 6 nH loop.



When Q closes, the source feeds L. When Q opens, positive inductor current continues through D.


Expected inductive overshoot is 3 V. Halving the loop inductance reduces it to 1.5 V at the same slew rate. Doubling the transition time gives the same voltage reduction but increases switching overlap. Compare drain loss and measured loop geometry before choosing which parameter to change.



The 6 nH loop develops voltage only during the current ramp in this idealized model.




Practice exercise
A 4 nH commutation loop transfers 8 A in a linear ramp. What minimum transition time keeps the inductive voltage magnitude at or below 2 V?


Check your reasoning

From v = L × Δi/Δt, the minimum time is 4 nH × 8 A/2 V = 16 ns. Doubling the time halves the predicted voltage.

Commutation-loop interference (ECPE)
crumbs: 320  DC-DC Converter: noise generation by commutation

title: Spectral influence of pulse parameter
text:
Pulse shape and spectral envelope
A 100 kHz pulse train has 2 µs on-time.
Spectral lines are 100 kHz apart, and the ideal rectangular envelope first vanishes at 500 kHz, the fifth line. Halving on-time moves the first zero to 1 MHz. Slowing the edges with pulse width unchanged mainly reduces the high-frequency tail. Check the spacing, first null and edge spectrum separately.



Line magnitudes are normalized to the DC coefficient of each pulse train. The first envelope zero moves from 500 kHz to 1 MHz.




Practice exercise
At 100 kHz repetition rate, shorten the rectangular on-pulse to 1.25 µs. Locate the first nonzero-frequency envelope null and identify its harmonic order.


Check your reasoning

The first null occurs at 1/1.25 µs = 800 kHz. This coincides with the eighth harmonic of 100 kHz.

Pulse shape and spectral envelope (ECPE)
crumbs: 321  Spectral influence of pulse parameter

title: DC-DC Converter:Influence of measurement methods to noise
text:
Probe-dependent noise readings
A long ground lead and a short spring probe read 7 V and 3 V spikes on the same node.
At 0.5 A/ns, the 4 V difference is consistent with 8 nH of effective pickup. Repeat with the probe tip shorted to its local ground and the same loop orientation. A remaining pulse implicates pickup. Compare both measurement bandwidths before treating 3 V as the actual device stress.



The 4 V difference corresponds to 8 nH of effective pickup at the stated slew rate. These are peak readings, not reconstructed waveforms.




Practice exercise
Two probe connections on the same node differ in peak reading by 3 V during a 0.75 A/ns edge. Estimate the extra effective pickup inductance and propose a control measurement.


Check your reasoning

The difference corresponds to 3/(0.75 A/ns) = 4 nH. Repeat on the same switching edge with the same probe, bandwidth and tip point while shortening only the return connection.

Probe-dependent noise readings (ECPE)
crumbs: 322  DC-DC Converter:Influence of measurement methods to noise

title: DC-DC Converter:Influence of parasitic components (1)
text:
DC-link parasitics and supply noise current
Can the local DC-link capacitor keep a 10 MHz commutation current out of the supply cable?



The noise current divides between the local capacitor branch with loop inductance and the supply cable.


Model its branch as 1 µF in series with 5 nH, and the supply branch as 50 nH. Neglect resistance. At 10 MHz the capacitor branch is inductive, with reactance 0.314 − 0.0159 = 0.298 Ω. The supply branch has 3.14 Ω. Current division sends 0.298/(3.14 + 0.298) = 8.7% of the noise current into the cable. Raising capacitor-loop inductance to 20 nH increases that share to 28%. Shorten the local return path and compare cable current at the same frequency.



At 10 MHz a longer local capacitor loop diverts more of the commutation noise current into the cable.




Practice exercise
A 1 µF local capacitor has 4 nH total series loop inductance. Estimate its self-resonant frequency and decide whether the branch is inductive or capacitive at 10 MHz.


Check your reasoning

Resonance is 1/(2π√(LC)) ≈ 2.52 MHz. Above this frequency the series branch is inductive. At 10 MHz its net reactance is approximately 0.251 − 0.016 = +0.235 Ω.

DC-link parasitics and supply noise current (ECPE)
crumbs: 323  DC-DC Converter:Influence of parasitic components (1)

title: DC-DC Converter:Influence of parasitic components (2)
text:
Choke capacitance and filter attenuation
A nominal 100 µH filter choke has 20 pF winding capacitance in parallel.



Winding capacitance bypasses the series choke at high frequency. Vo is the voltage across the termination.


Its ideal self-resonance is 1/(2π√(LC)) = 3.56 MHz. At 20 MHz the winding alone would have 12.6 kΩ reactance. The parallel combination has about 411 Ω capacitive reactance in magnitude. Into a 50 Ω receiver from a low-impedance source, voltage transmission is about 50/√(50² + 411²) = 0.121, or −18.4 dB. The ideal winding predicts about −48 dB. Check the component impedance curve before increasing nominal inductance.



Above self-resonance the winding capacitance bypasses the choke. The ideal lossless model exaggerates the depth of the notch.




Practice exercise
A 100 µH choke has 10 pF parallel winding capacitance. Find its ideal self-resonance and compare it with the same choke at 20 pF.


Check your reasoning

Resonance is 1/(2π√(LC)) = 5.03 MHz. Halving capacitance raises the resonant frequency by √2 from about 3.56 MHz.

Choke capacitance and filter attenuation (ECPE)
crumbs: 324  DC-DC Converter:Influence of parasitic components (2)

title: DC-DC Converter:Influence of inductive coupling to filter
text:
Magnetic pickup across a filter
An output-side filter trace couples to a switch loop through 2 nH mutual inductance.
A 5 A transition in 10 ns induces 1 V. Doubling ideal filter attenuation does little if that voltage appears downstream. Rotating the loop reduces the observed pulse to 0.25 V at the same slew rate, consistent with 0.5 nH effective coupling. Test geometry before increasing filter order.



At identical current slew, reducing mutual inductance from 2 nH to 0.5 nH cuts induced voltage by four.




Practice exercise
A switch loop slews at 0.8 A/ns. Rerouting reduces its mutual inductance to the filter trace from 1.5 nH to 0.5 nH. Find induced voltage magnitudes before and after.


Check your reasoning

Using the same orientation, the magnitudes are M × di/dt = 1.2 V and 0.4 V. The reroute cuts this coupling contribution by a factor of three.

Magnetic pickup across a filter (ECPE)
crumbs: 325  DC-DC Converter:Influence of inductive coupling to filter

title: 3ph Converter - Influence of the load capacities to the
text:
Three-phase load capacitance
Three motor phases each present 0.5 nF to the frame.
If all three undergo the same 100 V common-mode step in 50 ns, their currents add to 3 A. If only one phase switches with the same slew rate, the predicted sum is 1 A. Clamp all three phase conductors together, leaving protective earth outside the probe. The probe measures their net current. To identify the return path, compare that trace with separate measurements on protective earth and the cable shield.



Each 0.5 nF branch carries 1 A while its voltage rises by 100 V in 50 ns. The probe sees the sum.




Practice exercise
Each phase has 0.4 nF to the motor frame. Find the frame-current magnitude if one phase slews at 4 kV/µs while the other two hold still. Repeat for three simultaneous edges of the same sign.


Check your reasoning

One edge drives C × dv/dt = 1.6 A. Three simultaneous equal edges add to 4.8 A. The return path must carry this displacement current.

Three-phase load capacitance (ECPE)

title: 3ph Converter - Filter damping and influence to leakage
text:
Filter damping and leakage current
Model a common-mode path as a series 1 mH, 10 nF and effective 50 Ω resistance, with output across the capacitor.



The source drives the series common-mode path. Observe Vo across the capacitor as the effective resistance changes.


Its undamped natural frequency is 50.3 kHz and Q = √(L/C)/R = 6.32. Raising the effective series resistance to 200 Ω gives Q = 1.58. For this capacitor-voltage transfer function, the gain peak occurs at the natural frequency times √(1 − 1/(2Q²)). It moves from about 50.0 to 45.0 kHz as damping increases. Increasing line-to-chassis capacitance instead also increases line-frequency leakage. At 230 V, 50 Hz, changing 4.7 to 10 nF raises a single branch from 0.34 to 0.72 mA RMS. Use measured resonance and the permissible leakage to choose a damping network.



Increasing series resistance lowers the voltage peak and moves it from about 50 to 45 kHz.




Practice exercise
For the illustrated series 1 mH and 10 nF path, find the total series resistance for critical damping. Compare it with 50 Ω.


Check your reasoning

For the capacitor-voltage step response, critical damping requires R = 2√(L/C) ≈ 632 Ω. A 50 Ω path has damping ratio 50/632 ≈ 0.079 and is underdamped.

title: Magnetics · Appendix A — Area product by magnetic kind (draft)
text:
Draft appendix to the magnetics lesson, which the 2025 lectures V8 (inductor design) and V9 (transformer design) cover until the 2026 lesson is written. Numbers come from scripts/area_product_bias.py and are recorded in area-product-checks.json.
V8 sizes an inductor from the stored energy and the window. V9 sizes a transformer by iteration, from the balance of copper loss and core loss. Both methods give an area product A_p = W_aA_e. This appendix shows why one flux density cannot serve both.
A size proxy that uses one flux density for every magnetic gives a biased result. It sizes DC-dominated chokes well, but it makes AC-flux magnetics far too small. An audit of six built components showed this pattern. The DC chokes landed within −30 % to +42 % of the real area product. The AC-flux magnetics (an ICT, an ICMCI and a DAB transformer) came out 64 % to 74 % too small.
This appendix explains the cause and gives the fix. Saturation limits the flux in a choke. Core loss limits the flux in an AC-flux magnetic. The two kinds therefore need two sizing methods: the core-geometry constant K_g for chokes, and K_{gfe} for AC-flux parts.
crumbs: 328  Magnetics · Appendix A — Area product by magnetic kind (draft)

title: A.1 What the area product says
text:
A magnetic must satisfy two conditions at the same time. The core must carry the flux without exceeding a flux density limit \hat B. The window must hold the copper at a current density J.
The peak flux linkage per turn \hat\lambda sets the core area. The sum of winding ampere-turns, divided by the turns of one reference winding, sets the copper area:
A_e \ge \frac{\hat\lambda}{N\hat B},\qquad K_uW_aJ \ge N I_{\mathrm{tot}}.
Here A_e is the effective core area, W_a the window area, K_u the fraction of the window that holds copper, and I_{\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_j (N_j/N)I_{j,\mathrm{rms}}. Multiply the two conditions and the turns count N cancels:
A_p = W_aA_e \ge \frac{\hat\lambda\, I_{\mathrm{tot}}}{K_u\,J\,\hat B}.
This one equation covers both kinds. For a choke, \hat\lambda = L\hat I and I_{\mathrm{tot}}=I_{\mathrm{rms}}, so A_p = L\hat I I_{\mathrm{rms}}/(K_uJ\hat B). For a transformer with a square-wave voltage V at frequency f, \hat\lambda = V/(4f). The result is the familiar A_p = P_t/(4K_uJ\hat Bf), with the apparent power P_t=\sum V_jI_j.
The equation is exact for a full window. If a design fills its window, the equality holds with the real K_u, J and \hat B of that design. A proxy that inserts fixed values K_{u0}, J_0 and B_0 is therefore wrong by exactly
\frac{A_{p,\mathrm{proxy}}}{A_{p,\mathrm{real}}} = \frac{\hat B}{B_0}\cdot\frac{J}{J_0}\cdot\frac{K_u}{K_{u0}}.
The bias has no other source. To explain it, find which of the three factors moves, and why.
crumbs: 329  A.1 What the area product says

title: A.2 Which limit sets the flux density
text:
In a DC choke, the DC current sets most of the flux. The ripple adds only a small AC swing. In the buck choke of section A.5, the peak flux density is 300 mT but the AC amplitude is only 27 mT. Core loss is small, so saturation sets \hat B. The design value is about 0.8B_{\mathrm{sat}}.
In an AC-flux magnetic, all of the flux alternates. The core loss per volume follows the Steinmetz equation:
P_v = k\,f^{\alpha}\hat B^{\beta}.
The Ferroxcube 3C90 datasheet gives three loss points at 100 °C:

Two pairs of points give the exponents directly, without a curve fit:
\beta = \frac{\ln(450/80)}{\ln 2} = 2.49,\qquad \alpha = \frac{\ln(450/80)}{\ln 4} = 1.25.
At saturation flux, the core cannot get rid of its heat. At 100 kHz and \hat B = 300 mT, 3C90 loses 1.24 MW/m³. An ETD54 core (35.5 cm³) would dissipate 44 W. The same core can lose only about 8 W at a 40 K temperature rise. Core loss, and not saturation, sets \hat B in this part. The usable value is near 100 mT, a third of the saturation value.
This is the main term of the bias. A proxy that uses B_0 = 300 mT for an AC-flux part overstates \hat B by about three times. It understates A_p by the same factor.
The window fill adds a second term. A DC choke uses solid round wire, and K_u = 0.4 is a normal value (McLyman, ch. 4). An AC-flux part at 100 kHz needs litz wire or foil to control skin and proximity loss. Litz strands, serving and air between bundles reduce K_u to about 0.25 to 0.30. A transformer with reinforced isolation also needs tape, margins or triple-insulated wire, and K_u falls to about 0.2.

title: A.3 DC-dominated chokes: Kg at saturation flux
text:
The core-geometry method (Erickson and Maksimović, ch. 14) replaces the fixed current density with a copper-loss budget P_{cu}. The winding resistance is R = \rho N^2\,\mathrm{MLT}/(K_uW_a), where MLT is the mean length of a turn. Combine this with N = L\hat I/(\hat BA_e):
K_g = \frac{A_e^2W_a}{\mathrm{MLT}} \ge \frac{\rho\,L^2\hat I^2 I_{\mathrm{rms}}^2}{\hat B^2P_{cu}K_u}.
K_g depends only on the core. The right side depends only on the specification. A core is large enough if its K_g is above the requirement. For a choke, \hat B is the saturation design limit.
Worked example: buck choke 48 V to 12 V, 30 A, 100 kHz. The specification is L = 15 µH, \Delta I = 6 A, \hat I = 33 A and I_{\mathrm{rms}} = 30.05 A. Use \hat B = 0.30 T, K_u = 0.40, and copper at 100 °C with \rho = 2.26 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. The loss budget is the loss that gives a 40 K rise on the core in question (section A.5).

ETD39 has A_e = 125 mm². The turns count is N = L\hat I/(\hat BA_e) = (15 µH × 33 A)/(0.30 T × 125 mm²) = 13.2, so wind 14 turns. The core loss is 0.04 W, which confirms that the choke is DC-dominated.
Mueller (2025) uses the same logic for powder-core DC filter inductors. He prefers K_g to A_p, because K_g sets a loss and not an assumed current density. A powder core has no gap to adjust, so a material “saturation constant” \Gamma = B_{\max}^2 replaces \hat B^2. The method ignores AC core loss by assumption. That assumption is the boundary of this appendix: K_g at saturation is valid only while the AC flux is small.

title: A.4 AC-flux magnetics: Kgfe
text:
For an AC-flux part, the flux density is a free design variable. More turns lower \hat B and the core loss, but they raise the copper loss:
P_{fe} = K_{fe}\hat B^{\beta}A_el_e,\qquad P_{cu} = \frac{\rho\,\lambda_1^2I_{\mathrm{tot}}^2\,\mathrm{MLT}}{4K_uW_aA_e^2}\cdot\frac{1}{\hat B^2}.
Here K_{fe} = kf^{\alpha} is the Steinmetz coefficient at the operating frequency. The quantity \lambda_1 is the peak-to-peak flux linkage per turn, so \hat B = \lambda_1/(2NA_e). Set dP_{\mathrm{tot}}/d\hat B = 0. The total loss is a minimum when
\beta P_{fe} = 2P_{cu}.
For 3C90, \beta = 2.49, so core loss is 0.80 of copper loss at the optimum. Insert the optimum into P_{\mathrm{tot}} \le P_{\max}. This gives the condition of Erickson and Maksimović (ch. 15):
K_{gfe} = \frac{W_aA_e^{2(\beta-1)/\beta}}{\mathrm{MLT}\;l_e^{2/\beta}}\left[\left(\frac{\beta}{2}\right)^{-\frac{\beta}{\beta+2}}+\left(\frac{\beta}{2}\right)^{\frac{2}{\beta+2}}\right]^{-\frac{\beta+2}{\beta}} \ge \frac{\rho\,\lambda_1^2I_{\mathrm{tot}}^2K_{fe}^{2/\beta}}{4K_u\,P_{\max}^{(\beta+2)/\beta}}.
No flux density appears in this condition. The method picks \hat B from the loss balance at the operating frequency. It does not assume \hat B. The script checks the closed form against a numerical loss minimum on all seven ETD cores, with agreement to 10⁻⁴.
Worked example: DAB transformer, 400 V, 1.5 kW, 100 kHz. The winding voltage is a ±400 V square wave, so \lambda_1 = V/(2f) = 2.0 mV s. The turns ratio is 1:1 and each winding carries 4.5 A rms, so I_{\mathrm{tot}} = 9.0 A. Use K_u = 0.20 for litz wire with reinforced isolation. In SI units, K_{fe} = 2.48 × 10⁷ W m⁻³ T⁻β.

Kazimierczuk and Sekiya (2009) give area-product equations for resonant inductors in terms of the loaded quality factor, the output power and the frequency. Their equations have the correct form, but \hat B and K_u are still inputs. Their examples compare a single-wire and a multiple-strand winding, with skin, proximity and fringing effects. K_{gfe} removes the guess of \hat B, which is the larger of the two errors.

title: A.6 For KPI owners: the acceptance rule
text:
An area-product KPI that uses one flux density for all magnetics compares parts of different kinds on a biased scale. The fix has three rules:

Report the area product separately for each magnetic kind.
For DC-dominated chokes, keep A_p or K_g at the saturation flux density.
For AC-flux magnetics (ICT, coupled inductors, transformers), use K_{gfe}. It sets the flux swing from core loss at the operating frequency.

K_g alone does not remove the bias, because it still sizes the flux at saturation.
Acceptance test. Replay the six components of the earlier proxy audit with the new method. Fit nothing to those six parts. Calculate the bias between kinds as in section A.5. If the bias is below 1.5×, the KPI is qualified. If it is 1.5× or more, report the KPI as unqualified.
The audit gave a bias of 3× to 4× with the old proxy. This appendix predicts that most of the bias comes from \hat B, with a smaller part from K_u. If the replay still fails, check K_u first. Litz construction and isolation build-up differ more from part to part than the core loss does.
crumbs: 334  A.6 For KPI owners: the acceptance rule

title: A.7 What if
text:
What if the core size steps? The reference rejects ETD49 for the DAB transformer by 0.3 % of loss (6.47 W against 6.45 W). With a small fan, or with 3 % less current, ETD49 is sufficient and the proxy error becomes −74 %. Catalog steps of 1.5× to 1.8× in A_p limit the resolution of any single-part comparison.
What if the voltage is a square wave? Steinmetz data come from sine-wave tests. Square-wave flux with short transitions has more loss. The improved generalized Steinmetz equation (iGSE) corrects this by using only the same three parameters (Venkatachalam et al., 2002).
What if a choke has a large ripple? A boundary-mode choke has \Delta I = 2I, so its AC flux is as large as its DC flux. Its core loss is not small. Size it with both K_g and K_{gfe}, and use the larger core.
What if the DC flux is not zero? A DC bias raises ferrite core loss at the same AC amplitude. An ICT with unequal phase currents has a DC flux, so check its saturation margin as well.
What if a powder core is used? Powder cores have a soft saturation and higher core loss than ferrite. Use Mueller’s \Gamma method for a DC-dominated powder choke. For AC flux, use K_{gfe} with the Steinmetz data of the powder material.

title: Transformer characterization: the low-frequency magnetizing-inductance trap
text: Working teaching note for the future transformer and Bode 100 laboratory section. This material is separate from the introductory recap. It concerns a transformer with one or a few primary turns, not a device with only one winding. The numerical example is authored; no hardware measurement has been performed.
crumbs: 338  Transformer characterization: the low-frequency magnetizing-inductance trap

title: 1. The riddle: is the measured voltage ratio the turns ratio?
text:
A high-current DC/DC transformer can have a very small number of primary turns and a small magnetizing inductance. Apply a sine wave to the primary with the secondary unloaded. At low frequency the secondary voltage can be much smaller than the ideal turns ratio predicts. This is a real circuit effect: the magnetizing reactance becomes small compared with series resistance, leaving little voltage across the magnetic branch.
The consequence is not that low-frequency characterization is universally impossible. A raw transfer ratio can be a poor estimate of turns ratio, and parameter extraction becomes sensitive to small measured voltages and phase errors. The useful measurement method and frequency depend on the parameter being identified.
crumbs: 339  1. The riddle: is the measured voltage ratio the turns ratio?

title: 2. Start with the smallest useful circuit
text:
Let n = Ns/Np. Initially neglect leakage inductance, core loss, capacitance and receiver loading. Rp is the primary winding resistance; Rs is the generator’s Thévenin resistance. Vg is the generator’s open-circuit Thévenin voltage, Vp is the voltage at the primary terminals, and Vm is the voltage across Lm and the ideal transformer’s primary.
 Vg ---- Rs ----+---- Rp ----+---- ideal transformer, ratio 1:n ---- Vsecondary
               |            |
             Vprimary       Lm
               |            |
 primary return+------------+

 Secondary is unloaded; its return is a separate winding terminal.
 Vprimary is measured across the entire primary winding, including Rp.
The magnetizing branch forms a divider with the winding resistance:

\frac{V_m}{V_p}=\frac{sL_m}{R_p+sL_m},\qquad \frac{V_{sec}}{V_p}=n\frac{sL_m}{R_p+sL_m}.

Its corner is fp = Rp/(2πLm). At frequencies far below fp the secondary/primary-terminal voltage ratio rises at +20 dB/decade, rather than equalling n. Far above fp it approaches n within this simplified model. The terminal voltage includes the copper drop; measuring Vp does not directly measure Vm.
Referencing the output to the generator instead gives a different ratio:

\frac{V_{sec}}{V_g}=n\frac{sL_m}{R_s+R_p+sL_m},\qquad f_g=\frac{R_s+R_p}{2\pi L_m}.

Measuring Vsec/Vp removes the generator divider from the ratio algebraically. It does not restore signal amplitude or eliminate the winding divider. These are different issues.
For a fixed core and linear magnetic circuit, Lm scales approximately with Np². Reducing primary turns therefore tends to reduce Lm strongly. Rp also changes with conductor length, section and construction; the corner cannot be inferred from turn count alone. With a given external Rs, reducing Lm raises the generator-related corner directly.

At 1 Hz, the predicted secondary signal is only about 1.005 µV RMS for a 1 V RMS open-circuit generator. The model still has a well-defined transfer ratio, but measuring it accurately requires an adequate noise and systematic-error budget. At 1 kHz the terminal-referenced ratio is already close to four, while the generator-referenced ratio is still only about 0.001. Confusing these ratios would imply a wildly incorrect turns ratio.
For less than 1% magnitude error relative to n in the terminal-referenced ratio, this idealized example requires f > 1.117 kHz. This is a magnitude-only condition, not a phase-accuracy or complete measurement-uncertainty requirement. Leakage, loading and capacitance impose additional constraints on the upper usable frequency.



Simplified low-frequency transformer model: terminal-referenced versus generator-referenced gain, and the impedance phase that controls inductance-extraction sensitivity.


The curves extending toward 100 MHz show the mathematical model only. They do not claim that this low-frequency equivalent circuit remains accurate there; real capacitances and resonances may intervene before a clean generator-referenced plateau appears.

title: 4. Which parameter becomes difficult to identify?
text:
With an open secondary, negligible core loss and negligible leakage, input impedance is

Z_{oc}=R_p+j\omega L_m,\qquad L_m=\frac{\operatorname{Im}(Z_{oc})}{\omega}=\frac{|Z_{oc}|\sin\phi}{\omega}.

At very low frequency the impedance is mainly resistive. Lm is then recovered from a small imaginary component, so a small phase error can produce a large relative inductance error. Holding magnitude exact, a small phase error δφ in radians gives

\frac{\delta L_m}{L_m}\approx\cot\phi\,\delta\phi.

Here the impedance phase at 1 Hz is only 0.360°. An illustrative +0.1° phase error would cause approximately +27.8% inferred-inductance error. At 10 Hz it causes about +2.78%. The 0.1° is a sensitivity example, not a Bode 100 accuracy specification; magnitude error, calibration residuals, fixture resistance and noise must also be considered.
Low frequency can be useful for winding-resistance extraction because inductive reactance is small, while being poorly conditioned for inductance extraction. Conversely, an open-secondary inductance measurement includes primary leakage as well as magnetizing inductance. An open-circuit sweep alone does not separate them. A short-circuit measurement estimates the referred leakage/resistive network, subject to short-fixture impedance and the chosen equivalent-circuit convention.
crumbs: 342  4. Which parameter becomes difficult to identify?

title: 5. Bode 100 measurement plan for the future laboratory
text:
OMICRON’s Transformer modelling application note, V2.0 is the primary practical reference for combining winding-resistance, open/short-circuit, transfer and capacitance measurements into an equivalent circuit. Its worked transformer differs from the few-turn scenario here; neither its test frequencies nor its excitation levels should be copied as universal settings.
The Bode 100 Revision 2 technical data specifies a 50 Ω source and selectable receiver impedances of 1 MΩ or 50 Ω. The high-impedance input also has 40–55 pF capacitance. Its stated typical receiver sensitivity is 1 µV RMS at 10 Hz RBW with zero input attenuation; that is not a guarantee of accurate ratios at a 1 µV DUT signal. Confirm the revision and settings of the instrument actually used.

Define the parameter and reference plane. Record the winding under test, open/short/loaded secondary, frequency, excitation and temperature. Label Vg, Vp and Vsec explicitly. A gain measurement and a 50 Ω S21 measurement are different configurations.
Measure winding resistance separately. For milliohm windings use a suitable four-wire resistance measurement and inspect connections. A fixture contact resistance comparable with Rp changes the divider substantially.
Choose an impedance method for the actual range. Use a calibrated mode and fixture suited to low impedances. The manufacturer’s measurement-mode overview identifies shunt-through as a low-impedance method. A one-port reflection measurement near a short can be poorly conditioned because Γ is close to −1; use the method’s uncertainty information rather than assuming equal accuracy throughout the range.
Measure gain at the DUT terminals. Put the reference channel at the primary terminal plane and the other channel at the secondary plane, with terminations included in the model. Follow the instrument manual for grounding and connections: the two measurement channels must not be assumed to provide independent isolated differential inputs. The bench fixture is a defined unpowered transformer test, not the previous common-mode isolation test.
Calibrate at the intended fixture plane. Use the procedure appropriate to the selected measurement mode. Calibration can correct specified fixture/system errors; it cannot remove real winding loss, recover unlimited SNR or make an unsuitable equivalent model valid.
Sweep excitation as well as frequency. Repeat at several levels and look for invariance of extracted parameters. For sinusoidal core voltage, Bpk = Vm,RMS/(4.44 f Np Ae). Use the induced core voltage, not blindly the generator setting. In the resistance-dominated limit Vm falls with frequency, so constant generator amplitude does not automatically imply unlimited flux as f tends to zero. If terminal voltage is actively held up, flux and magnetizing current still require explicit checks.
Fit a useful frequency window. Seek adequate phase and signal amplitude below the region dominated by parasitic capacitance and resonance. Add leakage, core loss and receiver loading when needed, and compare predicted impedance and gain against independent sweeps. Report residuals and sensitivity, not just a fitted Lm value.

Receiver loading deserves an explicit check. With n = Ns/Np, a secondary load ZL refers to ZL/n² at the primary and appears in parallel with the magnetizing branch. Selecting 50 Ω instead of high impedance can therefore change the DUT response. High impedance is also not an ideal open at every frequency because of receiver and cable capacitance.
Low-impedance fixtures also require attention to return currents. OMICRON’s Impedance Measurements application note, V1.1, §2.2.3 explains that internal source/receiver ground connections can produce a shunt-through ground-loop error, especially at low impedance and low frequency. A Kelvin-like connection alone does not guarantee that this systematic error is negligible.
crumbs: 343  5. Bode 100 measurement plan for the future laboratory

title: 6. Recall exercise and reproducibility
text:
Ask students to predict the two corners, explain why CH2/CH1 can differ from output/generator, and identify whether a failed low-frequency extraction is caused by an incorrect circuit model, poor signal amplitude, phase sensitivity or nonlinear excitation. Then change only Lm, Rp or Rs. Replacing the generator with a lower-impedance source changes the excitation and available SNR; it does not eliminate the internal Rp–Lm divider.
scripts/transformer_low_frequency.py exports figure 73 and transformer-low-frequency-checks.json. It verifies both transfer ratios against an independent two-node solution at 41 frequencies and checks winding active-power balance. The phase-error examples are calculated sensitivity tests. No instrument automation, actual Bode 100 measurement or full nonlinear magnetic simulation is claimed.
This note can later be joined to the existing transformer equivalent-circuit discussion and the common-mode injection example. Recap §11.7 develops the sum/difference basis, power normalization and symmetry that distinguish the modes. Keep differential parameter extraction and common-mode interwinding-capacitance characterization as distinct fixtures with explicit connections.

title: Matching objectives: maximum voltage, maximum power or maximum efficiency?
text: Working teaching note for the two-port and resonant-converter sessions. It joins three ideas that courses often teach apart: the maximum-power-transfer theorem, the reflection coefficient of a 50 Ω measurement, and the load design of a resonant converter. All numbers are authored teaching values, not a measured converter. Part B uses the LISN three-port exercise of the recap as its measurement example.
crumbs: 345  Matching objectives: maximum voltage, maximum power or maximum efficiency?

title: 1. The problem
text:
A Thévenin source has an RMS open-circuit voltage Vth and a series resistance Rs. A load RL takes power from it. Three questions have three different answers:

Which RL gives the largest load voltage?
Which RL gives the largest load power?
Which RL gives the largest efficiency, defined as load power divided by the power the ideal internal source delivers?

Then the same source becomes a 50 Ω generator, and finally a series resonant tank driven by a full bridge. The closing question is the design question of the course: a 30 kW converter must reach 98 % efficiency. Why must its load not sit at the maximum-power point of its Thévenin equivalent?
Predict before calculating. Sketch VL, PL and efficiency against RL/Rs on one log axis. Mark where each curve is largest. Then guess the ratio RL/Rs that gives 98 % efficiency, and the fraction of the available power that remains at that ratio.

title: 2. Why we do it
text: Students meet “impedance matching” in RF and measurement courses as a goal in itself. In a power converter the same words describe a design failure. The exercise shows that matching serves an objective, and that the objective decides the optimum. The same algebra gives all three results, so the confusion is not mathematical. It is a confusion about what is being optimized.
crumbs: 347  2. Why we do it

title: 3. What matters
text:
The three objectives have three different optima. Maximum power sits at RL = Rs. Voltage and efficiency have no finite optimum: both rise with RL.
At the maximum-power point the source resistance dissipates as much as the load. Efficiency is 50 %.
Matching to a reference resistance Z0 and matching to a source resistance Rs are the same algebra only when the generator itself has Rs = Z0.
A converter is designed for the power it must deliver, with the losses it can afford. Available power is not a target.

title: 4. Where it appears in practice
text:
Objective
Typical condition
Where

Voltage probes, buffers, sense dividers


Maximum available power
ZL = Zs* (conjugate match)

Maximum efficiency

The conjugate-match row describes the simple Thévenin equivalent with a dissipative source resistance. A full resonant network can be matched for its own objective without the 50 % limit of that equivalent. Part C shows this.
crumbs: 349  4. Where it appears in practice

title: 5. Part A: resistive Thévenin source
text:
Use Vth = 10 V RMS and Rs = 1 Ω. Let r = RL/Rs. The load voltage, load power and efficiency are:

\frac{V_L}{V_{th}}=\frac{r}{1+r},\qquad P_L=\frac{V_{th}^2R_L}{(R_s+R_L)^2},\qquad \eta=\frac{P_L}{V_{th}I}=\frac{r}{1+r}.

The derivative of PL with respect to RL is:

\frac{dP_L}{dR_L}=V_{th}^2\frac{R_s-R_L}{(R_s+R_L)^3}.

It is positive below RL = Rs and negative above, so the load power has one maximum, Pmax = Vth²/(4Rs) = 25 W. The normalized power is 4r/(1+r)². At that point VL = Vth/2 and η = 50 %.
