The power curve is symmetric on the log axis: r = 0.25 and r = 4 give the same 64 % of Pmax. The efficiency curve is not symmetric. To reach 98 % the load must be 49 times the source resistance, and the load then takes only 7.84 % of the available power. Figure 89, panel A, plots the three curves.



Figure 89. A: Thévenin voltage, power and efficiency versus RL/Rs. B: 1 − |Γ|² is the same power curve. C: series resonant converter output power versus switching frequency for three loads. D: load sweep at resonance with the maximum-power point and the 98 % design point.
crumbs: 350  5. Part A: resistive Thévenin source

title: 6. Part B: the same curve as a reflection coefficient
text:
Give the source a real reference resistance Z0 = 50 Ω, as in the LISN exercise and in every 50 Ω measurement. For a real load ZL = r Z0 the reflection coefficient and the absorbed fraction of the incident power are:

\Gamma_L=\frac{Z_L-Z_0}{Z_L+Z_0}=\frac{r-1}{r+1},\qquad \frac{P_{abs}}{P_{inc}}=1-|\Gamma_L|^2=\frac{4r}{(1+r)^2}.

The absorbed fraction is the Part A power curve. Γ = 0 at r = 1 is the maximum-power condition again, and the 98 % load of Part A shows Γ = 0.96, a return loss of only 0.35 dB. Panel B overlays the two expressions. They coincide at every r.
Three precisions keep the two parts consistent:

Γ is a wave ratio, not a power ratio. In a one-port measurement with the matching reference, Γ equals S₁₁. The reflected power fraction is |S₁₁|², not S₁₁.
The identity above holds when the generator itself has Rs = Z0. A source with Rs ≠ Z0 re-reflects the returning wave, and the delivered power needs the full S matrix with its terminations. In a two-port, |S₂₁|² is the transmitted power only for matched source and load, as §11.4 of the recap states.
A complex load with the right real part is not matched. ZL = 50 + j50 Ω against Z0 = 50 Ω gives |Γ| = 0.447, and 20 % of the incident power returns. Against a complex source, the maximum-power condition is the conjugate match ZL = Zs*.

The LISN exercise applies this to a three-port: the 50 Ω termination at the receiver port fixes S₂₂ and S₃₂, and the 150 kHz to 30 MHz impedance presented to the DUT is a design target of the network, not a matching goal for the DUT.
crumbs: 351  6. Part B: the same curve as a reflection coefficient

title: 7. Part C: series resonant converter at the fundamental
text:
Replace the generator by a full bridge from Vin = 800 V and the load by a full-bridge rectifier with a capacitive filter. Use the fundamental harmonic approximation (FHA): the bridge is a sinusoidal source of RMS value V₁ = 4Vin/(π√2) = 720.3 V, the rectifier and DC load are a resistance Req = (8/π²) Rdc, and the output voltage is Vout = (π/(2√2)) V₂, where V₂ is the RMS fundamental at the rectifier input. The tank is Lr = 27 µH and Cr = 93.8 nF, so f₀ = 100 kHz and the characteristic impedance √(Lr/Cr) is 16.96 Ω. A series resistance Rloss collects the conduction loss of the tank, switches and rectifier:

Z_{tank}=R_{eq}+R_{loss}+j\left(\omega L_r-\frac{1}{\omega C_r}\right),\qquad P_{out}=\frac{V_1^2R_{eq}}{|Z_{tank}|^2},\qquad \eta=\frac{R_{eq}}{R_{eq}+R_{loss}},\qquad V_{out}=\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt2}\,\frac{V_1R_{eq}}{|Z_{tank}|}.

At resonance the reactance vanishes and the tank is the Part A circuit with Rs = Rloss and RL = Req. The 30 kW, 98 % requirement fixes both resistances:

The ratio Req/Rloss is 49, the 98 % ratio of Part A. The maximum-power point of the same tank sits at Req = Rloss = 0.339 Ω. There the tank would deliver 383 kW at 50 % efficiency with a tank current of 1063 A RMS, and 383 kW would also be dissipated inside the converter. The 30 kW design uses 7.84 % of that available power on purpose. The design question is answered: the converter must deliver 30 kW, not the maximum the equivalent can deliver, and every watt of the available power that stays unused is a watt that Rloss does not dissipate.
Panel C shows Pout against the switching frequency for three loads, light (49.8 Ω), nominal (16.6 Ω) and heavy (5.5 Ω). All three peak at f₀. The heavy load reaches 83 kW at resonance with a 122.6 A tank current and 94.2 % efficiency. The light load gives 10.3 kW at 99.3 %. Above f₀ the series reactance reduces the current, which is how a frequency-controlled series resonant converter regulates power. In this model η does not depend on fs, because Rloss is fixed and in series with Req. A real converter adds switching loss that grows with fs, so its efficiency optimum is a point in (fs, Req), not a line.
Panel D sweeps Req at resonance. Power peaks at Req = Rloss, while efficiency and Vout keep rising with Req. The design point sits far to the right of the peak, where the power curve is almost flat in log scale and the efficiency curve has reached its target.

title: 8. Pros and cons of the three objectives
text:
Objective
Pros
Cons




Maximum voltage, RL ≫ Rs
Smallest loading error, simplest measurement
Delivers almost no power; sensitive to source noise and capacitance


Maximum power, RL = Rs or ZL = Zs*
Uses all available power, standard for 50 Ω instruments, no reflections on lines
50 % efficiency in the dissipative equivalent; current and loss at their maximum


Maximum efficiency, loss-driven
Smallest heat, smallest semiconductors and cooling for a given output
Requires a controlled source, not a fixed Rs; needs the loss model, not only the tank
crumbs: 353  8. Pros and cons of the three objectives

title: 9. Conclusion
text:
The optimum load depends on the objective function. The maximum-power theorem gives the largest power a fixed source can deliver, at 50 % efficiency. A measurement system adopts that condition because the instrument’s reference is fixed and reflections must vanish. A power converter is not a fixed source. Its bridge is controlled, its tank is designed, and its objective is the required power at the smallest loss. The series resonant tank at resonance reproduces the Thévenin algebra exactly, so the 98 % target forces Req ≈ 49 Rloss and a tank that could deliver 383 kW delivers 30 kW.
Change one thing. Keep 30 kW and demand 99 %. Req stays near 17 Ω, because the tank current is fixed by V₁ and the power. Rloss must halve to 0.171 Ω, the ratio Req/Rloss rises to 99, and the usable fraction of the available power halves to 3.96 %. The efficiency target is a loss budget, not a load choice. Alternatively keep Rloss and double the output power to 60 kW at the same V₁: Req falls to 7.95 Ω, the tank current doubles to 86.9 A, the loss grows four times to 2.56 kW, and the efficiency falls to 95.9 %.

title: 10. Literature
text:
These references were supplied with the exercise brief. The titles are as given there.

Zhu and Gao, Optimal load impedance in LCC-compensated inductive power transfer, 2022. Derives the optimum load with conduction and switching losses, so it separates maximum power from maximum efficiency.
Maximizing efficiency through impedance matching, IEEE ISCAS 2013. Connects resonant circuit theory, source and load impedances and efficiency in wireless power transfer.
Theoretical analysis and optimal design of LLC resonant converter, IEEE EPE 2007. Uses the FHA for gain, load, efficiency and tank design.
Comparison among different analysis methodologies for LLC resonant converter, IET Power Electronics 2019. Shows where the FHA fails, which bounds Part C before S parameters of a passive tank are applied to a switching converter.

University extension. Measure or compute the S parameters of the passive tank at 50 Ω references and check how far they predict the converter’s gain and loss before switching, harmonics and the rectifier’s non-linearity make the linear model insufficient.

title: 11. Reproducibility
text: scripts/matching_objectives.py exports figure 89 and matching-objectives-checks.json. It checks the sign change of dPL/dRL, the three closed forms against the swept circuit, the identity 1 − |Γ|² = 4r/(1+r)², the SRC design point, the complex-power balance of the tank at every frequency, the power peak at f₀ for each load and at Req = Rloss for the load sweep, and the 7.84 % ratio between the design power and the maximum-power point. The FHA model has no switching loss, dead time, rectifier drop, magnetizing branch or control loop. No time-domain simulation is claimed.

title: Converter tolerances: analytical sensitivity and Monte Carlo
text: Student exercise · Averaged continuous-conduction models
crumbs: 357  Converter tolerances: analytical sensitivity and Monte Carlo

title: Engineering question
text:
Do identical parasitic components cause identical gain errors in buck, boost, and inverting buck-boost converters? Predict which converter is most sensitive before you calculate the results. Then test your prediction with symbolic differentiation and random sampling.
The comparison holds input voltage, load resistance, and duty cycle fixed within each case. Output voltage, output power, and inductor current differ between converters. This is a comparison of gain degradation, not an equal-power hardware selection.

title: Given values and model boundary
text:
The nominal values come from the two lecture slides supplied for this exercise. The tolerance ranges, distributions, and operating points below are authored teaching assumptions. They are not component specifications or measurements.

Use independent parameter distributions. Use 200,000 samples and random seed 20261106. Reuse the same parameter samples for both mathematical models and all converters. This pairing reduces sampling noise in comparisons.
Assume steady state, continuous conduction mode (CCM), and small inductor-current ripple. Use a constant diode drop and constant resistances at a fixed temperature. Ignore switching losses, capacitor ESR, core losses, reverse recovery, and self-heating. The duty cycle does not change to regulate output voltage.
For a CCM plausibility check, use L=2 mH and switching frequency f_s=100 kHz. Assume a sufficiently large output capacitor for negligible voltage ripple. These values establish a teaching operating regime, not a checked magnetic-component design.
crumbs: 359  Given values and model boundary

title: Conversion-gain models
text:
Use positive gain magnitude g=|U_a/U_e| for the comparison. For the inverting buck-boost, the signed gain is M=-g. Write R_S=R_{\mathrm{DS(on)}}.
Define the denominators:
Q_b=R+R_L+D R_S,
Q_x=R(1-D)^2+R_L+D R_S.
The three gains are:
g_b=\frac{R[D U_e-(1-D)U_D]}{U_e Q_b},
g_{boost}=\frac{R(1-D)[U_e-(1-D)U_D]}{U_e Q_x},
g_{inv}=\frac{R(1-D)[D U_e-(1-D)U_D]}{U_e Q_x}.
The last two expressions are algebraically equivalent to the supplied slide formulas. Use only the positive-current region of these models.

title: Part A — Predict and establish the nominal point
text:
Set all parasitic values to zero and recover the three ideal conversion ratios.
Calculate the nine nominal gains using the specified nonzero parasitic values.
Calculate the gain shortfall relative to each converter’s ideal gain.
Predict which parasitic parameter dominates at each duty cycle.
Explain why equal duty cycle and equal load resistance do not give equal output power.

Use this common comparison metric:
e=100\left(1-\frac{g}{g_{ideal}}\right).
Here, e is a percentage. A change in e is measured in percentage points.
crumbs: 361  Part A — Predict and establish the nominal point

title: Part B — Derive the sensitivity weights in Maxima
text:
Use the parameter vector p=[R_L,R_S,U_D] and nominal vector p_0=[0.04,0.06,0.70].

Enter each gain expression in Maxima using exact rational nominal values.
Differentiate each expression with respect to each parasitic parameter.
Evaluate the derivatives at every nominal operating point.
Derive a first-order multivariable Taylor approximation around the nonzero nominal parasitic set.
Compare dimensional weights, normalized sensitivities, and tolerance-weighted effects.

The required form is:
g_{lin}=g_0+\sum_i w_i\Delta p_i,\qquad w_i=\left.\frac{\partial g}{\partial p_i}\right|_{p_0}.
For a total-degree expansion, substitute p=p_0+\epsilon\Delta p and expand in \epsilon through order one. This avoids retaining unwanted mixed higher-order terms from separate single-variable expansions.
Useful Maxima commands are diff(expression, variable) and taylor(expression, eps, 0, 1). Keep the other circuit parameters constant during differentiation.
The normalized sensitivity is:
S_i=\frac{p_{0,i}}{g_0}w_i.
For independent uniform variations with half-width a_i, the parameter variance is a_i^2/3.

Predict the mean and standard deviation of the linearized gain.
Calculate each parameter’s fraction of the predicted gain variance.

E[g_{lin}]=g_0,\qquad \sigma_g^2=\sum_i w_i^2\frac{a_i^2}{3}.
crumbs: 362  Part B — Derive the sensitivity weights in Maxima

title: Part C — Run paired Monte Carlo calculations
text:
Monte Carlo analysis repeatedly evaluates a model with randomly sampled inputs. Here, each sample represents one possible component set within the assumed tolerances. It does not represent a switching cycle or a time trace.

Generate the three independent uniform parameter arrays.
Evaluate the original nonlinear gain and the Taylor approximation for each sample.
Compare the analytical standard deviation with both sampled standard deviations.
Compare the sample means, medians, and fifth and ninety-fifth percentiles.
Repeat with half and quarter tolerance widths, keeping the same normalized random samples.
Calculate the root-mean-square difference between paired nonlinear and linearized gains.

Require the sampled linear standard deviation to agree with the analytical value within 1%. Require its mean to lie within five analytical standard errors of the nominal gain. Use the tolerance-scaling experiment to assess Taylor error separately from Monte Carlo sampling error.
Do not require exact equality between nonlinear and linearized results. Explain any systematic mean shift and any asymmetric distribution.
crumbs: 363  Part C — Run paired Monte Carlo calculations

title: Part D — Make box plots and tornado diagrams
text:
Make paired box plots of gain shortfall for the two models.
Use separate panels for the three duty cycles and a common vertical scale.
Show the median and interquartile range, with fifth-to-ninety-fifth-percentile whiskers.
State that the outer tails are omitted from these whiskers.
Make a tornado diagram for each converter and operating point.
Rank parameters by their tolerance-weighted effect on gain shortfall.

For the tornado bars, vary one parameter between its limits while keeping the others nominal. Overlay exact nonlinear endpoints on the Taylor prediction. These are deterministic sensitivity ranges, not confidence intervals or a joint worst-case calculation.

title: Part E — Defend an engineering conclusion
text:
Identify where the resistance-amplification hypothesis agrees with your calculations.
Identify where diode-drop sensitivity changes the ranking.
Explain why numerical agreement does not validate the physical model against hardware.
Choose one parameter whose tolerance you would tighten at D=0.8.
State one benefit, one cost, and one new operating condition that could change your choice.

Discuss when feedback regulation, temperature dependence, or switching losses would require a different model. Submit the Maxima derivation, numerical summary, plots, and a short conditional recommendation.

title: Part F — Compare the same ideal conversion ratio
text:
Equal duty cycle gives boost and inverting buck-boost different ideal conversion ratios. Now compare the same ideal gain magnitude G with the same input, load resistance, and parasitic samples. Use G=1.25, G=2, and G=5. The corresponding ideal output magnitudes are 12.5 V, 20 V, and 50 V.

Derive each converter’s ideal duty cycle for the target gain.
Use the following duties, fixed during each tolerance calculation.

D_{boost}=1-\frac{1}{G},\qquad D_{inv}=\frac{G}{1+G}.

Substitute these duties into the gain models before deriving the sensitivities in Maxima.
Repeat the paired Monte Carlo calculations with the original tolerance distributions and seed.
Make matched-gain box plots and tornado diagrams with numerical values.
Plot the paired additional buck-boost shortfall for each target gain.

\Delta e=e_{inv}-e_{boost}=100\frac{g_{boost}-g_{inv}}{G}.

Explain why the buck-boost needs a higher duty cycle and how this affects the resistance penalty.
Identify which comparison better answers a requirement for a specified output-voltage magnitude.

The two converters now have equal ideal output magnitude and ideal load power. Parasitics reduce their actual outputs by different amounts. This is an open-loop comparison at equal ideal target, not a regulated comparison at equal actual output. The metric remains voltage-gain shortfall, not efficiency loss.

title: Part G — Adjust duty to deliver the same load power
text:
Use the same 10 V input, 10 ohm load, and paired component samples. Set output-voltage magnitudes to 12.5, 20, 40, and 50 V. Boost supplies positive voltage. Inverting buck-boost supplies negative voltage.

For each sample, solve the nonideal gain equation for the duty that reaches the target.
If two duties are feasible, choose the lower duty and explain its current advantage.
Count the feasible samples for each converter and the pairs that reach the target together.
Calculate inductor current, winding loss, MOSFET conduction loss, diode loss, and efficiency.
Plot the efficiency distributions for feasible pairs and the nominal component losses in watts.
Check input power against load power plus losses. Explain the efficiency difference at 40 V.

Find the stationary point and verify that it gives the maximum in the physical duty range.
Mark the peak and its duty on each nominal voltage curve.
Plot the peak voltage against its duty for each of the 200,000 paired component sets.
Add a 50 V reference line and compare the resulting counts with Part G.
